docs.title: Logbook
docs.text: A diary that writes itself: your life, in a folder you hold, read back to you as days. The README is the landing page; this is every page, one line each.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
• Questions: six first questions, each answer a few sentences with the file or test that backs each one.
  • Install: one line on each platform, for someone who has never opened a terminal, with what each step prints.
  • Try it: five minutes with a demo record, every reader on a month that never happened.
  • The first hour: logbook setup screen by screen, for someone who has never used a terminal.
  • The commands: the 32 commands by what you are doing, and the older names each still answers to.
  • The tour: every command on your own record, from the first import to handing a day to a friend.
  • A life in a record: logbook demo --years N, a synthetic life in phases from a childhood of scanned photos to the boat.
  • Your life in a folder: the launch post, with everything in it synthetic.

docs.title: Why
docs.text:
• Vision: the record, the recount, the circle, and the list of things the product refuses to have.
  • Lore: where the logbook comes from, ships, pilots, diaries, and the log in computing.
  • Roadmap: what is done, what is next, what 1.0 means.
  • Open problems: what the format cannot do yet, stated so a collaborator can pick one.
  • Letters: the captain to the builders; the first one is about the freeze.
  • Letter 0: why it was built, why it is given away, and why under a pen name.
  • Release notes: what each version changed for you, five bullets each.
  • Changelog: every change, in full.

docs.title: The format
docs.text:
• Specification: the folder, the line, the chain, the tiers, the profiles, conformance. One page, CC0.
  • Architecture: the five layers and what each may depend on.
  • How a line becomes a Day: one line followed from the adapter through the index to the page.
  • Conformance: the sample record and the head every implementation must reproduce.
  • Decisions: the architecture decision records, numbered, never edited after acceptance.
  • RFCs: the payload profiles and spec changes, each with a schema and one synthetic example.
  • RFC 0025, the shared bundle: the signed page one logbook hands another.
  • RFC 0027, reflection: the digest's closing question comes from the record.
  • RFC 0034, the signed day: agents draft, the owner signs, only signed days cross.
  • RFC 0037, entities: orgs, ideas, places and assets reviewed like people, one no for every kind, and a status the owner disposes (draft, its questions decided).
  • RFC 0038, speakers: who spoke in a recording, and who they are; a model proposes, the owner names, and no voiceprint leaves the machine (draft).
  • Benchmark, per-line sealing: what encryption at rest would cost on a three-million-line record.

docs.title: Reading the record
docs.text:
• The Day: one calendar day read back, and show days for a window of them.
  • The signed day: day sign, the readiness row, and the gate on the crossing.
  • The Year: one year composed from every reader, and one trip read back on its own.
  • The rollups: countries, flights, nights, places, people, health, listening, attention, summed over a range.
  • The digest: the day in 25 lines at most, ending in one question you may ignore.
  • The ledger: the record's money read back in context, by month or by trip.
  • People: everyone the record knows, what it knows of each, merging the duplicates, reviewing who the sources saw, and a priority you can argue with.
  • Review: one sitting for what the sources saw — people, orgs, ideas, assets and places — and the three profiles it writes, status among them.
  • Promises: the sentences in your own words that read as commitments, and whether they were kept.
  • Tasks: every task line, open or done, and the evidence that one was finished.
  • Search: full text across notes, transcripts, messages, mail and events, within a tier.
  • In a browser: logbook serve, the record read on this machine only.
  • The shelves: promises, goals and agents in logbook serve; each one only reads.
  • On paper: the year and the trip laid out for A4 and Letter.
  • The vault: the record as a folder of Markdown with wikilinks for Obsidian or Logseq.
  • Describing keepers: a local vision model's note per photo you marked a keeper.
  • The MCP server: the record served to an agent on this machine, behind a tier gate.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
• Adapters: what an adapter is, the three names it exports, the rules it keeps.
  • Adapter bounties: the adapters not yet written, each with its export, profile and tier.
  • Google Takeout: one archive, many witnesses; the sub-adapters for Tasks, Maps, Home and YouTube.
  • Mail: one line per message from a Takeout mailbox, at 20 GB scale, and the same mailbox live over IMAP, read-only.
  • Health: Apple Health, Withings and MyFitnessPal as health-sample/v1.
  • Apple Photos: the library, its albums, favourites and the names you gave the faces.
  • Apple Wallet: boarding passes and tickets as flights and events.
  • Listening: Spotify, Apple Music and Apple Podcasts as listen/v1.
  • Screen Time: which app, from when to when.
  • Voice memos: the recordings, and their transcripts from a local model.
  • Videos: the family's digitised tapes in a Drive folder; each scene's place and time proposed on this machine, confirmed by you.
  • Weather: the weather of the places your days were spent at, one line per day.
  • Passages: a ship's deck log transcribed to CSV as the vessel's own movement.

docs.title: Keeping it
docs.text:
• Backup: copy the record to another disk, verify it there, restore it; the monthly restore test.
  • The schedule: sync --all and doctor four times a day, the 06:00 run closing the day, the outcome in state/last-run.json, one message when something is wrong.
  • On a home server: the record on an always-on machine at home, as a runbook for one hour: two users, the pages and the schedule as system daemons, the env file, one writer and read-only checkouts, backups, the local model, the phone over a private network.
  • The record's settings: your timezone, where your day begins (day_start), your places and assets.
  • When verify fails: what each failure means and the one command that answers it; repair fork for two chains forked at one head.
  • The attachment store: the content-addressed bytes a line points at.
  • Shared trips: two people on one trip exchange their records of it.
  • The crossing: one window of the record for one member of your circle, under the tier policy; the output folder replaced whole.

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
• Contributing: one way to do everything, from the first clone to the merged pull request.
  • Governance: one captain, public decisions, RFCs for profiles.
  • Releasing: the checklist the captain follows.
  • Security: the threat model on one page, and how to report.

docs.title: Architecture — one package, three tiers
docs.text:
logbook/
  core/      the format and what is frozen with it: canonicalisation, the hash chain, the record and its
             index, the attachment store, the privacy tiers and the crossing policy, the day package, and
             the readers whose JSON a second implementation is held to (SPEC §3.2, §6.1): derive stays,
             day, days, trips, year, people, person, the pages, places, the rollups
  contrib/   what reads the world into the record and the record out into the world: the adapters (one
             registry, one module per source), import-backup, sync, setup's stores, the exports (vault,
             Volumes, trip bundles), serve, the MCP server, the derived readers whose output is
             a reader's own (digest, promises, tasks, gaps, people merge, the trip page), the demo record
  labs/      everything that runs a model, or is still an experiment: transcribe, describe, promises
             --judge, demo --years
  commands/  the CLI, one module per command family; cli.py is the entry point

The arrow points down. Core imports core and nothing above it. Contrib imports core and contrib, never labs. Labs and the commands import anything, and a command imports an adapter or a labs module only inside the function that runs it, so logbook --help loads no adapter and no model code and import logbook.cli imports nothing but the entry point. logbook/layout.py declares which module is in which tier; tests/test_layout.py holds the tree to it, the arrow included. Every 0.5 import path (logbook.store, logbook.adapters.immich) still imports, the same module object, with a DeprecationWarning, until 0.7 (docs/migration-0.6.md).

docs.title: The layers, as the tiers carry them
docs.text:
5  Agents      any agent with MCP: add, ask, confirm, verify. the UI.          contrib/mcp_server
4  Surfaces    day page · timeline · person · year · paper · vault · shared    core readers, contrib exports
3  Engines     logbook → days, trips, people, places. versioned. recomputable. core
2  Adapters    one per source. export in → observations out. pure.            contrib/adapters
1  Logbook     the folder, the chain, the CLI. the standard.                   core, commands

An adapter never knows an engine exists. A surface reads derived rows and notes, never the raw log. Agents are operators, not authors: they may run adapters and draft, they may never write a note, a confirmation or a visibility decision — that stays with the human, enforced in layer 1.

Layer Contract Where 1 the format (SPEC.md); logbook add/show/verify/export logbook/core/, logbook/commands/ 2 run(input_path, since) -> iterator[Observation]; fixture-tested; no network by default logbook/contrib/adapters/, one module per source (ADR 0012); a third-party adapter is a package that registers the logbook.adapters entry point 3 a reader: read(logbook, window) -> derived rows, idempotent, stable derived IDs, never a line (ADR 0013, ADR 0019) logbook/core/ (frozen by SPEC §3.2), logbook/contrib/ (a reader's own) 4 reads derived rows + notes; writes only notes and confirmations (as tier-2 lines) logbook serve, year --html, --print, export vault, export world, the shared page and trip bundle 5 MCP server exposing the record's readers over stdio logbook mcp (logbook/contrib/mcp_server.py)

Every layer ships in this one package. The second implementation, logbook-ts, is a separate repository built from SPEC.md alone (CONTRIBUTING, the clean-room rule).

docs.title: Derived is disposable
docs.text: Days, trips, people and places are computed from the log and can be thrown away. Their IDs are derived from (owner, kind, rounded start, place) so a recompute yields the same ID and human notes stay attached. Human input — notes, confirmations, visibility choices — is written to the log as tier-2 lines, so it survives any recompute and any export.

docs.title: The circle (layer 4/5, transport to be defined)
docs.text: A shared page is a signed bundle: one day's lines the owner's policy lets cross, the attachments they point at, the day-package summary, and the owner's Ed25519 signature over the manifest — shared-page/v1, RFC 0025 (docs/rfcs/rfc-0025-shared-page-bundle.md), written by logbook share day and verified by logbook receive, which keeps the page beside the record and never in its chain. Transport is undecided (peer-to-peer over a relay vs. a small server); the bundle format came first, so that two implementations can exchange pages by any means, including a USB stick.

docs.title: Reference stack
docs.text: Python 3.12 and the standard library: the format, the chain, the record, the index (SQLite) and every frozen reader need nothing installed beyond tzdata on Windows. What else a feature needs is an extra, named where the feature is: openlogbook[stream] (ijson, streaming JSON for the five adapters that read a multi-gigabyte export), [crypto] (cryptography, for an encrypted iOS backup and the signed page), [ais], [transcribe], [speakers] (the diarizer, apart from [transcribe] so that hearing a memo needs no torch), [judge], [describe], [mcp]. PostGIS is a plugin, never a requirement. Web layer: server-rendered HTML. Everything runs on one machine that is always on, or on a laptop that sometimes is: the record's home (ADR 0022), which holds the only writable copy, runs the sync schedule, the MCP server and the local models, and serves the Day page over the owner's own network. Every other device is a reader, and an orchestrator elsewhere reaches the record only through the crossing.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• The MCP write tools add_note and promise_done are refused unless the mcp entry of policy/crossing.json names them under write and has not expired, as sign_day and note_day are, and the lines they write have source mcp, never manual: an agent never writes as the owner.
  • A signature never confirms pencil: the dream's draft, a note a model derived (a photo's description, a meeting's summary) and a line an agent wrote through the door are left out of confirmed by day sign, day reflect --sign, the Library's Sign and the door's sign_day, and a disposition a standing signature gave one is no longer carried forward.
  • export share day holds a draft to the entry it was written under, as every other crossing and the MCP door do: a draft whose dream entry is missing, lowered under its tier or expired stays home, counted in the manifest's held_back and the crossing line's held_back_by_entry.
  • sync heard fetches only from the public internet: an address that is not global (the tailnet's 100.64.0.0/10, Tailscale's 100.100.100.100 and a MagicDNS name that resolves into it among them) is refused, the connection goes to the address that was checked and never to a second answer of the resolver, on every redirect, never through a proxy the environment names, and an https page's redirect to http and a port other than 80 and 443 are refused.
  • sync heard fetches a feed's transcript only under a heard entry in policy/crossing.json, {"heard": {"max_tier": 2, "fetch": true}}: LOGBOOK_HEARD=feed alone fetches nothing, the entry is checked before any request, and doctor names it.
  • export world and the Library's /world fail closed: a record whose policy names no world entry shows tier 1 alone, and {"world": {"max_tier": 2}} adds the chapters; doctor names it on a world line.
  • doctor --packet sends its probe of the dream endpoint, with the bearer key, only while the policy's dream entry allows the dream; with no entry, or one expired, it says the probe was not sent and why. SECURITY.md lists every command that may open a socket.
  • logbook serve reads for this machine and for your phone through Tailscale Serve once logbook setup phone names it, and nobody else: a page asked under any other Host (a website pointing its name at 127.0.0.1, DNS rebinding) is a 421, and a request through any other proxy, another login, two Host headers or Tailscale Funnel is a 403, both before anything is read. Without setup phone, the phone no longer reads the pages through Tailscale Serve: run it once. Through an SSH tunnel, use the same port on both ends (ssh -L 8765:127.0.0.1:8765).
  • No Library page can be framed by another (frame-ancestors 'none', X-Frame-Options: DENY), and a form posted from a frame or from another site (Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-Site) writes nothing.
  • logbook day and the Day page, its ribbon's tooltips and its spoken label included, print a calendar entry's title and then its time after a word (Dinner with Ola Nordmann, from 19:30 to 21:00, Ola Nordmann's birthday, from 19:30), so a clock touches no name at either end of a title; the ribbon's label says then between its entries; an entry several calendars carry says from 2 sources (…) after its title, in logbook day, the Day page, digest and tasks, never ×2 beside a name.
  • A digit stuck to a name with no space between (Ola Nordmann2, 3Ola) counts as a number beside that name, and so does one through a separator that is a letter (3xOla), with no boundary asked of the name: the dream holds the sentence, every reader holds a stored draft's, a name the dream entry withholds is still found there (and held out of a confirmed event's title), and doctor --packet scrubs the owner's name with a digit stuck to it. Guillemets, an ellipsis, +, ~, _ and the zero-width spaces count as separators too.
  • A week's threads print their kind and count in words after the title (“Dinner with Ola Nordmann” calendar 1 time), so a count stands beside no title that holds a name.
  • The Day page holds the reflection to its tier, as every other line of it: through a gate below the reflection's tier (a note, tier 2) a page or a built Library page neither shows, quotes, offers nor numbers it, nor its Wispr Flow dictation (tier 3); Sign still signs with it, its form naming no line.
  • A sentence kept from a draft as a note above the page's tiers no longer reads "kept as #N" on that page; keeping it again there is refused in one sentence that names no line.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Keep and sign on the Day page: in the evening, and when a signed day is signed again, the Sign form keeps the pencil's sentences and links (numbered as --keep takes them), a kept decision's revisit day, the day in a word and each task of the day answered (done, tomorrow, let go; a task shown by its title alone, no number beside it), then signs, in one click and one hold of the writer lock; the page writes what logbook day sign DAY --keep … writes, byte for byte, and any refusal writes nothing and says why in one sentence. A page that reads fewer tiers than the record shows and keeps only the draft its gate shows, as the rest of the Day does, and neither shows nor quotes a day's word above its gate.
  • Today's evening offers Dream the day so far (logbook dream day TODAY --evening) while your dream entry stands, its draft in pencil above the form; without the entry, or on a page whose tier gate is below the entry's, the page says why in one sentence, and nothing is sent.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The dream sends a name only at its entry's tiers: a person the record names only in a tier-3 resolution never reaches the model under a dream entry of max_tier 2, in the day, the week, the month, the journey or the chapter, and a draft's tier rises to the tier of a name it was given. day sign --accept refuses a person the dream entry's tiers do not name, and writes a name learned at tier 3 at tier 3.
  • No number beside a name in a dream's draft: the journey and the person dreams hold such a sentence as the day does, and day, the Day page, show trip, the journey's page, the week, month and chapter readers and export letter hold one in a day, journey, week, month or chapter draft already stored, whatever wrote it. A gated Day names a proposal's people only at its tiers.
  • The Library on a phone: every target the pages name is 44 px or more (a Day's line as written, every fold's summary, the Places review's name, skip and reject, the week's keep box and day links, the life's years and zooms, the Days' links, window and show button, the pagers, the world's map buttons); a Day's eyebrows, its ribbon, a row's kind, ids, evidence and the footer are at least 13, 12 or 14 px; and a row's kind and a promise's or an asset's badge keep 4.5:1 on the page in the light face and the dark.
  • /world on a phone: its play button and scrubber sit above the doors' bar instead of under it, and a navigation of its own wraps inside the screen.
  • Names, dates and sources in exports are held to the tier of the lines that give them. An output names a person only from resolutions at its own tiers: a name only a tier-2 or tier-3 resolution gives is no longer in a tier-1 export vault, export site or export trip-bundle, a name only a tier-3 resolution gives is in none below tier 3, and neither is counted in a bundle's held_back.people. export site's Today, its span and its years and export world's window come from the lines that cross, so a tier-3 health line no longer moves them; a vault's day page counts only the sources and flights that cross, and a day with none has no page; a trip bundle's trip.json carries only the flights, stays and moves whose lines cross.
  • No date or clock time sits beside a person's name with only separators between: people not-with writes "from DAY to DAY", a proposed event "from 19:30 to 22:10" after its title, a site's people index names only, and a vault's year row puts its people last; the dream holds a sentence that sets a date or a clock beside a name, as it holds a count, and a confirmed event's title holds a surname and a genitive too.
  • The readers print people by name only, the most days together first, never with a count beside a name: rollup people reads Per Hansen last 2026-06-30 · Office (was 10 days · 0 nights · … · 11 confirmed), and show year's people section and its page the same; show asset and show place read with Anders Vik, Ola Nordmann, Sigrid Moen (was Anders Vik (2 days), …); the Library's People page names each person with their last real contact, the evidence uncounted (was 10 days together, evidence · 11 lines). rollup places --with lists each place's people, with Per Hansen, Liv Berg, and rollup people --drifting each person's last real contact (last 2026-06-12), the quiet channels and the last shared place, without the counts, the fall or the days ago. The year's page sets with before a place's people, a trip's paper edition names a day's people last, and an org proposal on the Manifest the names it was seen under without their count. The counts stay in --json, unchanged; a person's own page (show person, /people/ID) still counts the days together.
  • No date, clock time or other number sits beside a person's name with only separators between: the digest's promise reads Kari Nordmann, due 2026-06-05 (by Friday) (was Kari Nordmann, 2026-06-05) and rollup listen's top artists Kari Nordmann played 0.2 h · 4 listens.
  • An event the owner accepts from the dream (day sign --accept, day reflect --sign --accept) is a tier-1 line, and names a person only from the resolutions at tier 1: someone the record knows only by tier-2 or tier-3 lines is no attendee, and their name in the title reads someone.
  • A fast test checks the site's people pages at tier 1 and at tier 1,2 on a small synthetic record: a tier-1 site has a page for the person a tier-1 resolution names and none for one named only at tier 2 or 3, and a tier-1,2 site has pages for both the tier-1 and the tier-2 people. Before, only the slow forty-year export, which pull requests skip, checked these pages.
  • export --day and --days with no folder entry record what is true in their crossing line: no entry exists and the default applied ("entry": null, "default_tier": 1), never a max_tier no policy set; an entry is recorded by name with its ceiling. The refusal of a tier above the default says the file names no folder entry, and doctor's new export-day line says the same.
  • In a clone run with uv, doctor's install hint is the short uv sync --extra <name> again, the clone named before it; since uv sync keeps only the extras it is given, the line names every extra the clone has beside the new one, so following it removes none. The pipx and uv-tool lines are unchanged.
  • A night the record does not place reads not recorded on Today (Last night: not recorded), the Day page and logbook day; in transit only when the Day holds a move or a flight across that night. The Day's JSON is unchanged.
  • logbook doctor before any record exists says No record yet: runlogbook demo --out ~/Demo/Logbookto try one, orlogbook setupto start yours. (it still exits 1). Its install line for an extra is the short one for how this Logbook was installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[ais]==…" (with PIPX_HOME only when the venv is not in pipx's own home), uv tool install --force "openlogbook[ais]==…" (with the --python the receipt asked for, if any), and in a clone uv sync --inexact --extra ais, the clone named before it.
  • doctor's home row is now schedule and says what it is: which machine runs the scheduled syncs. Its restore-test warn says to run logbook backup DEST once first when no backup is recorded.
  • The Day page and Today, on a machine with no transcription engine, give the command that adds one for how this Logbook was installed (doctor's line), never install openlogbook[transcribe].
  • The Day page: the with row's words and its field are apart (proposed below · add); its footer says what is true, Reflect and Sign, the with field and the stars write to your record; nothing else here does, in place of read-only; a past day is headed by its weekday alone, the shape's name (morning, live, evening) being today's.
  • logbook show stats names the record's format as such, record format logbook/0.3, beside a program whose version is another number.
  • An asset is printed by its registered name, once: rollup places, rollup nights, rollup people, rollup places --with, show year, show person, show place, people and places propose read aboard Nordlys and Nordlys (yacht) (were aboard nordlys and Nordlys (nordlys) (yacht)). The JSON SPEC §6.1 compares keeps the id.
  • show trip, the trip's page and its paper say the day you came home in words, back on 21 June, for the morning after the last night (SPEC §3.2.6's until, unchanged in the JSON); they said until 2026-06-21, which read as one night too many.
  • show person counts a person's days together as rollup people does, by the confirmed evidence (a face on the morning after a confirmed evening is no day together; the demo's Ola reads 3 days in both, was 4), and says so: first confirmed … · last confirmed …, 3 days together, by the confirmed evidence, last 6 shared stays, confirmed or proposed. show asset reads the runs aboard as rollup places does, so its stays, hours and people agree with it.
  • logbook export --day DAY --out DIR (and --days) reads its ceiling from a folder entry of policy/crossing.json, as the vault and the site do, tier 1 without one; --tier may lower it, never raise it, and a tier above it is refused naming the entry. Each run that writes a folder appends a crossing/v1 line like every other export: destination folder, the folder's last part, the tiers, the kinds, the line count and the folder's digest (ADR 0026). It wrote every tier and left no line, though the README promises that your record keeps a line that says it left. docs/export.md.

docs.title: Adapters
docs.text:
• add beeper and sync beeper mark your own bots as machine text, as the Telegram adapters do: a line a named sender wrote carries extra.machine, every line of a one-on-one chat with one extra.counterpart of kind agent, so no reader takes the bot for a person. The senders are yours to name, never in the code: logbook setup agents list|add SENDER [--name NAME]|remove SENDER keeps them in policy/agents.json (your own agents).
  • logbook doctor has an agents line: the lines marked machine, per source, and the senders named.
  • Mail lines keep Gmail's inbox tab and the list headers, never their links (RFC 0015, amendment of 20 October 2026): every new line from add mail (a Takeout or any mbox), sync mail and sync gmail may carry extra.gmail_category (primary, social, promotions, updates, forums; from Takeout's Category … labels and the API's CATEGORY_*, never over IMAP, which does not say the tab) and extra.list (unsubscribe, one_click, id from List-Unsubscribe, List-Unsubscribe-Post and List-Id, of which only the list-id itself is kept). The unsubscribe URLs and mailto addresses, and a List-Id's phrase, links and addresses, are never kept. labels, raw_id and every dedupe key are unchanged; lines already in the record are not rewritten, so older lines lack both keys. A list header that does not parse is kept by its name and counted.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Close the week, on the week page and at the command line (RFC 0043 §8, slice D part 2): each goal open on the Sunday with the five verdicts of review goal as one choice, your words on it and the command beside it, and the two honest moves when it stalls (goal add --supersedes written out for the goal); the week's one proposal, or your own sentence, kept as next week's intention, one note/v1 labelled intention on the Sunday. One press, one writer lock, every item checked before the first line: a refusal writes nothing. logbook day reflect SUNDAY --intention "…" keeps the same line, byte for byte; kept again in other words, it supersedes the first, never a second. Next week's mornings show the intention under For, in ink, with its Sunday, in place of the pencil (the week).
  • The Day page shows everything a day held, folded: under each stay or move, its messages by conversation (who, the network, how many; each message's time, sent or received and its text, the whole a click away on its line), and at the foot Everything this day held, every line of the day by source, each linked to its line. Every fold is closed until opened, or ?open=1.
  • Today is the Library's front door (/, RFC 0047 §4.1): the date and where you spent the night; what's open, the promises both ways in pencil, the day's tasks from the task tool and the replies owed, seven at most, the oldest first, each a link to its moment; one memory, this day a year ago, else the same date in the nearest earlier year with a signed reflection, a starred photo or a trip; and the Day's Reflect and sign. It works on a phone first, renders live, and export site writes it as today.html.
  • The doors share one header: the wordmark, Today, Life, People and Places (a bar at the foot on a phone), the Ask field, which searches the record, and the gear. Its stylesheet carries the owner's colours, and its typefaces (Instrument Serif, Inter, JetBrains Mono, under the SIL Open Font License) ship with the package and are served by the Library itself; nothing is fetched.
  • people ask and dream person send the days you spent together in the window (RFC 0036 amendment 2): each its date, the places.json name of the place you shared (a place with no name when it has none, never coordinates) and the references of the lines it rests on, under the same gate as the lines, so a sentence about time together cites them; people ask --json counts them (days_together) (the relationship reader).
  • logbook dream month [YYYY-MM] drafts a month once it is over, told from the days you signed (their drafts and your reflections, never a raw line's text), with where it went computed by the code (places, nights by class, people in order and never with a count), what the month shows for each goal, one proposal for next month and one question; logbook dream chapter [ID] drafts a chapter from the month and week drafts it spans: its arc, its rules, what it held and what it closed. Both are pencil, every sentence cited, --json prints the draft, and dream --catch-up dreams the month before on the first close of a month and a chapter on the first close after it closes, again only when what it read changed.
  • logbook export letter FROM TO: a range of your signed days read back as one HTML file to print or hand to someone, and the same as Markdown: a page per day, week, month or journey with the dream's story in pencil, your reflections, your stars and starred photos, your goal reviews, who was there and where; --unit month --card makes the month card. A crossing under the policy's letter entry, recorded as one crossing/v1 line (the letter).
  • logbook add gift DAY NAME WHAT [--received] writes what you gave someone, or were given: one note in your words labelled gift, the person under extra.recipient or extra.giver; a name that is nobody, several people or you is refused in one sentence. logbook people gifts [NAME] [--json] reads them back both ways (gifts).
  • logbook lab companies DAY [--json]: the orgs the Manifest names that a day touched (an update mailed from one of their domains, a meeting with someone of theirs, a document in one of their repositories), each with its lines and the people of theirs on them, never a bare address; grouped by portfolio; status and portfolio only where tier 3 is read (companies).
  • The money slot's reader, money.money_in: a window's transactions with merchant and amount (tier 3), and, when no payment source covers it, No payment source covers this day — the last ends <date>, never an empty sum.
  • day sign DAY --keep N,N and day reflect DAY --sign --keep N,N keep what you choose of the dream's draft before they sign: a sentence learned, decided or about an idea as a note, a proposed link as the entity line review writes, the photo of the day as a star with its note. logbook day DAY numbers them after the proposed events. --mend N="…" keeps a sentence in your own words, --revisit N=YYYY-MM-DD gives a kept decision the day it comes back, and --word WORD keeps the day in a word, one a day. Every item is checked before the first line is written; one refusal writes nothing.
  • The plan answered at the close: day sign DAY --done T,T --tomorrow T --let-go T writes one note per task, labelled task, with the Notion row, its line and the answer, for the agent that runs your task tool; it crosses with the signed day. show plan numbers today's tasks and marks the ones you answered, and a task's day is its Planned date, else its Due date, unless the mapping names one.
  • Search in the Library: /search?q=… in logbook serve, under search in the navigation, finds the record's words through the function logbook search calls and holds every hit to the page's tier gate. Each hit shows its day (a link to the Day), its kind, an excerpt with the match marked and its line's id (a link to /line/ID); a hit a later line supersedes is marked as the command marks it, superseded by #N, with the last correction the gate lets through. The filters by kind and year and the pages of fifty are links, never state in the browser. An empty query is the form alone; a query with no hit says so in one sentence. A GET form only: nothing written, no script, nothing fetched, phone width first (search).
  • RFC 0044 (draft), local days: proposes that, behind a local_days setting off by default, a day is the local calendar day where the owner was when it began (a flight west makes a long day, east a short one), and that a signed day keeps the zone and the span it was signed in and is never moved. Nothing changes in the readers yet.
  • logbook lab hold census senders counts, per sender, its mails with List-Unsubscribe and in Promotions, Social or Updates, in the report and its JSON (list_unsubscribe, tabs, lists_and_tabs); the terminal summary gives the totals and still prints no address.
  • export share day shares a day of a sealed record whose lines name an attachment: each sealed file is opened with this machine's identity, checked against its name and zipped opened, as the lines are; a store file that does not hash to its name, sealed or not, still stops the share (#320).
  • export site leaves a model's drafts (pencil) out: no Day page or Year pick carries a day's draft, its week's or a call's synthesis unless --with-drafts, which puts them in headed with their model, as the Day page heads them; the owner's reflection follows its own tier as before (the site).
  • A voice's name keeps its tier (RFC 0038): the name a reader shows for a voice bound to a person takes the highest tier of the lines that give it, and a reading below that tier (a site, a vault, a trip bundle, a gated Day) shows a named voice in its place and names nobody in its company from that voice.
  • People's mail, one rule (RFC 0045, draft): a mail is a person's when someone the record names as a person sent it to you or you sent it to one; no-reply addresses, agents and companies are not people. logbook people mail [--since DAY] [--until DAY] [--json] counts people's mail and the rest, never an address or a name in the terminal (people's mail).
  • export crossing sends people's mail only and counts the rest as mail_held_back; --all-mail sends every mail as before, and the manifest says so (the crossing).
  • The owner's own phone may write through the Library behind Tailscale Serve, off by default: logbook setup phone --origin https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net --login LOGIN names it in logbook.json after a yes typed at a terminal, and the Day's Reflect, With, Star and Sign and the shelves' forms are then answered from that origin, that Host and that Tailscale-User-Login as from this machine; a form from any other origin, Host or login is still a 403 with nothing written. --off removes it, and doctor says on its phone line whether the phone may write and from where (from your phone, ADR 0024).
  • A form posted through Tailscale Serve, or any proxy (a Host that is not 127.0.0.1 or [::1], or a Tailscale-* or X-Forwarded-* header), is answered only as the phone's: a program on another tailnet device that sends no Origin is refused, the setting on or off, where before it was answered as this machine. Requests to http://127.0.0.1:8765 or http://[::1]:8765 from this machine are answered as before; one naming any other host, localhost included, is treated as coming through a proxy.
  • logbook import pickup FOLDER [--write] [--source NAME] [--tier N] [--keep] moves a folder of call transcripts collected from the receiving side (the Purser's) into the record: one transcript line per file through the transcript adapter, each with its own source, its text stored, where it came from under extra.picked_up. A file already taken is skipped by its hash; a dry run unless --write, which removes each file taken from the folder unless --keep (the pickup).
  • review receipts [--since D] [--json] proposes the receipt mails the record holds as payments, the money bridge until a payment source covers the day (RFC 0043 §12): a received mail from an order or no-reply address, or a domain an org of the Manifest binds, never a person the record names, whose subject or kept body carries an order or receipt marker and an amount with a currency, read by rules (CHF 1'234.50, € 12,90, $12.90, NOK 1 840), the total over the line items, a refund as money in. --accept N,N writes one tier-3 transaction/v1 line each (source: receipts, extra.from the mail's line), a second mail of one payment in the same batch refused and counted; --reject N one tier-3 not-a-payment line (receipt-review/v1), never proposed again; the queue never shows a sender's address, it names a merchant by its domain; a receipt another source already holds is shown and never written, and one a payment source delivers later is listed as covered, with the retraction that lets the source's line win (receipts).
  • logbook search marks a hit that a later line of its kind supersedes: the row ends · superseded by #N, and --json gives every hit standing and superseded_by; --standing shows standing hits only, still filling --limit (search).
  • The dream learns (dream-day/4, RFC 0043 slice B): a day's draft holds the goodnight story, with its last line about tomorrow computed by the reader and never written by the model; one answer per lens, a question of policy/questions.json marked "ask": "day" (RFC 0027 amendment, at most five, never drawn by the digest, and — the day doesn't answer this printed by the reader); what was learned and decided; the ideas the day moved; one question where there were two; the photo of the day; and proposed links of a line to an idea or an org (draft/v1 amendment 2). The material adds the chapter and its rule, the open goals and the named ideas and orgs with their ids, under the entry's ceiling; a figure the cited lines do not give marks the sentence unsupported, no number ever stands beside a person, and the draft's tier is the highest of every line it drew on, the goals and chapter included. logbook day DAY --json carries the new parts.
  • logbook dream day TODAY --evening dreams today so far (extra.evening, extra.read_until); the catch-up still never dreams today. Kept lines (an accepted event, a kept sentence, the reflection) never make a day be dreamed again; after a signature only a line that arrived later does, and the reader shows what is new since you signed, a proposal already kept matched by its fields and never accepted twice.
  • CI moves the tag stable to each commit of main whose every check passed; a machine that updates itself installs @stable (docs/install.md, "Following stable").
  • The map: one offline OpenStreetMap file (a PMTiles v3 vector extract, a Protomaps build you put on the home machine) drawn by the server as inline SVG, light and dark, no script and nothing fetched, the OpenStreetMap attribution on every map. logbook setup map PATH names the file after reading its header (--off removes it); logbook lab map render --bbox … [--track DAY] draws one to check by eye; for an unnamed stay the map proposes the named thing within 50 m. No page draws it yet (the map, RFC 0043 §11).
  • show plan [DAY] [--json] [--coverage] reads the plan you keep in Notion back from the lines sync notion wrote, for one day: today's open tasks (dated today, or overdue in the current sprint; five, the rest counted; between sprints, one line says no overdue task is shown), the current sprint and its dates and the next trip as a countdown, each row with its Notion link and never its text. It reads tier-1 sync notion lines and nothing else. Which databases are which is a plan entry in policy/notion.json; without it, one sentence. --coverage says how much of each database the record knows. Nothing is written, to the record or to Notion (RFC 0043 §9; the plan).
  • The week page, /week/YYYY-Www in logbook serve, read-only: seven ribbons, one a day, each a link to its Day; where the week went (the week draft's numbers, each with its lines; sleep and training only where tier 3 is read); each goal with what the week shows for it, the five verdicts and the command that gives one; the one proposal for next week, in pencil; the stale question, once; the people who moved, names only; the sprint and the next trip; Hold's census, counts only. Every Day and the Sunday's week draft link to it (the week, RFC 0043 §8, slice D part 1).
  • The timeline: /timeline in the Library and logbook show timeline [--day | --week | --month | --year | --life] [--json], the record's moments beside the map at five zooms. A moment is a stay of note with its place, time, the people confirmed apart from the proposed (each with its reason), its photos, what passed during it and, at tier 3 only, what was paid; the month and the year count the nights by class, and all years lists each place and vessel with who was there, by name only (the timeline, RFC 0043 §11-12).
  • A place's class (home, family, aboard, away), the colour of its nights on the timeline, read from what places.json already says: a place of kind home, a place tagged family, a night aboard an asset, else away.
  • logbook doctor --attachments lists the lines whose attachment the store lacks, by source.
  • What you heard (RFC 0046, draft): sync heard stores the words of the podcasts and videos you played, one heard/v1 line beside each listen or watch, the text kept as it came in the attachment store: a feed's own transcript fetched once (WebVTT, SRT, JSON or plain text; at most LOGBOOK_HEARD_MAX_FETCHES a run, two seconds apart, a failed fetch counted and not retried for a week), the transcripts Apple Podcasts cached on this Mac, and a video's captions from your own folder (YouTube documents no keyless way to fetch them). Opt in with LOGBOOK_HEARD.
  • logbook show heard [--day D | --since D --until D] [--json] lists the texts with a one-line excerpt and their length; logbook search finds words inside them. A crossing or a shared page leaves every text at home unless the destination's entry in policy/crossing.json says "heard": true.
  • Who was there, as commands and readers (RFC 0043 §11, §12): logbook with --from D1 --to D2 NAME states a person on every day of a stretch, at each day's longest stay; people not-with, people lives-with and people lives-in are your word as one note each; review with --journey ID|--week YYYY-Www|--from D1 --to D2 asks once who was with you over the stretch, the evidence in words, faces from your own camera only, answered with --accept N[,N] [--days D,D] and --not NAME; people city CITY [--trip ID] lists your people in a city, seen or not yet on a journey (who was there).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• export crossing ships the resolution lines that name a mail's addresses (from, to, cc, bcc) and a transcript's participants (email, phone, provider id) in resolution.jsonl, as it did for a message's sender and a calendar guest; before, a mail or a transcript crossed with nobody on it named (the crossing, RFC 0005).
  • The Day's ribbon says the time before the entry (19:30 — Dinner with Per Hansen), so a clock time never follows a name in its tooltips or its screen-reader sentence.
  • A draft is held to the entry it was written under: a person's draft (dream person) to the relationship entry, every other unit to the dream entry. Once the relationship entry's until has passed, or its max_tier is below a person draft's tier, the MCP door holds the draft back and counts it, export crossing leaves it home (held_back_by_entry), and doctor names it, whatever the dream entry allows; a day's draft reads as before (the dream, When the entry changes).
  • Through the MCP door, sign_day with confirm: "all" confirms only the page's lines at or under the door's ceiling, the ones the agent could be shown, and says how many above it were left unconfirmed (unconfirmed, above_ceiling: a count, never the lines). day sign --confirm all and the Library's Sign still confirm the whole page (RFC 0034 amendment 4; the MCP server).
  • A dream's sentence that puts a number beside a person's name is dropped, not only marked: the draft keeps its slot as held: a number beside a name, unsupported, with the evidence it cited under extra.held (a day's), so day, the Day page and export site --with-drafts never print its words. A sentence the number rule had already marked is held too. A day's, a month's and a chapter's dream (RFC 0043; the dream).
  • dream day drops a proposed event whose title, or a proposed link whose text or note, puts a number beside a person's name, counted as a number beside a person.
  • export crossing holds every draft to the entry it was written under: a day's, a journey's, a week's draft and a call's synthesis cross only while the dream entry allows their tier, whatever the member's ceiling, and one that stays home is counted in held_back_by_entry, as a person's draft already was under the relationship entry; a record with drafts and no dream entry crosses none of them, and a video scene's draft, written on this machine under no entry, still crosses by its tier. The export crossing line that counts them now names the entry (the crossing).
  • Through the MCP door, sign_day without confirm on a day not yet signed confirms only the page's lines at or under the door's ceiling, as confirm: "all" does, and says how many above it were left unconfirmed (unconfirmed, above_ceiling: a count, never the lines). day sign and the Library's Sign still confirm the whole page (RFC 0034 amendment 4; the MCP server).
  • people ask and dream person send a day together only when the location lines behind the stay it names are at or under the relationship entry's max_tier too: the place's name takes the highest tier of the owner's location lines behind the stay and of the line that names the company, so at max_tier 1 a day at a stay found by tier-2 locations is held back and counted, never its name alone (the relationship reader).
  • The Library's Day page no longer crashes when the day, or a day it looks back to, has a flight line with no arrival: such a flight counts as ending at its departure, and one with no departure is skipped. export vault writes it at its departure time.
  • The shelves listed (/shelves, the Library's front page until Today took /) answer in a second on a record of millions of lines. The page counted the lines and found the first and last stamp in one pass over the whole index; it now reads the count from the record's head, as logbook doctor prints it, and the first and last day two steps down the day index. The page reads as before; a record with a torn tail past its head (a crash before logbook repair tail) is counted to its head, as doctor counts it. Today, at /, makes no pass over the lines on the request either.
  • A journey's name is held to the tier of the line that gave it: the Journeys shelf and a journey's page, read through a tier gate that stops at 1, no longer show a name given in a tier-2 note; the journey reads as it would unnamed, by its dates and places, with nothing that says a name exists. At tiers 1,2, and in serve, which reads every tier, the name shows as before.
  • Two Library pages asked for at once no longer fail on Windows when both save the same reading kept beside the index: each thread writes a temporary file of its own, and a save that cannot finish leaves the reading for the next one to make.
  • A Library page read while a sync was between logbook.json and the index no longer keeps that earlier reading as the record's: what the server shares between pages, the Day's readings and the morning's replies owed and revisits are kept under the head the index held, and the review pages' tables of observed people, orgs, ideas, assets and places are stamped with it, so the next page after the sync reads the new line. The tables live in the index, so a restart no longer kept the earlier one either. The page's footer and the built pages' record name that head too.
  • The Library (logbook serve) on a record of millions of lines: a page asked again at the same head is answered from what the server kept (warm, under a second on every page), and the pages that read the whole record read it once per head for all of them. A night is found by bisection over the owner's stays instead of every stay once a day (the People pages, the World, Trips and Journeys); the people review compares only the pairs that share an address, a number or a name word; the Promises and Agents shelves stream the messages instead of holding them all. The pages are the same, byte for byte. scripts/bench_library.py measures every route on a synthetic record of millions of lines.
  • index.sqlite gains an index on a line's id and one on the lines that supersede another; an index built before them is given them when it is next opened.
  • serve: every form of the Library (Name this place, Sign, Reflect, Star, With, the review queues, the status forms) is answered in a real browser again. The pages were sent with Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, under which Chrome, Firefox and Safari post a form with Origin: null, and the write gate refused it (403, nothing written); they are now sent with same-origin, so a form names its own page's origin and no other site is sent a referrer. The gate is as strict as it was.
  • A payment with its mailed receipt is counted once. When you accepted a receipt in review receipts and your payment source then delivered the same payment, the Day's spend, rollup ledger, rollup money, a trip's spend and an org's money counted it twice until you retracted the receipt. They now count the source's line alone, on its own day, and name the receipt as its evidence (1 with its receipt). One card line covers one receipt, the nearest in time, in the queue's covered rows too.
  • A trip's spend reads a corrected transaction in the place of the line it supersedes, as the ledger does, instead of counting both.
  • A receipt's merchant is never a raw email address: a sender with no name and no registered domain (x@localhost, an address with no domain) is a sender, and two such senders are two merchants.
  • A week draft's people are printed by name only, the most time together first, never with a count beside a name (with Kari Nordmann · Ola Nordmann, was contacts Kari Nordmann 12): in dream week, logbook day and day --json on its Sunday, the Day page, export site --with-drafts, and for a week dreamed before as well. A chat among the week's threads is named without its count, and a title is quoted beside its count. The line keeps each person's name, id, lines and contacts (the week page compares the contacts to name who moved, and prints none), no longer the counts by channel or the days together; and the week's own sentences are held as the day's, month's and chapter's are: one that names a person and writes a figure is dropped, held: a number beside a name (dream-week/2; RFC 0043 §2.5).
  • The readers of a day, a week, an org and an idea set no number beside a person's name either: a call on the Day (logbook day, the Day page) reads 19 min ← Ola Nordmann (was ← Ola Nordmann, 19 min); a recording's voices are named in the order of who spoke most, without their minutes, you · Kari Nordmann and 1 unnamed; the digest's with reads Kari Nordmann and 1 proposed; an org's and an idea's people (show org, show idea, the Library) read Kari Nordmann, last 2026-06-12; the week's paper, the vault's People lists and the lab's chapters name the people, the most days first, without the days.
  • export notion counts a person's days together over their whole history in the record, not the export's window: days_together with first_together and last_together in the facts, and on the page "Tage zusammen: N (zuerst …, zuletzt …)", or no line at all when there are none. Before, every page said "seit" the window's first day, and most said 0 (export for Notion).
  • export notion lists only the open promises said in the 365 days before the export, from a conversation the person is a direct party to (a one-to-one chat, a mail you are both on and no list sent, a call they spoke in), newest first, at most ten a side, then "und N weitere" (promises_more in the facts). Before, a page listed every promise of the window, group chats included.
  • export notion leaves out a promise that talks of money without a figure (a payment, an invoice, a transfer, a price, in German or English) and counts it under sentences_with_money, as one with a sum.
  • export notion lists only promises: your own and the person's own. A request is no longer listed, on either side; before, one the person made of you appeared under "Offene Versprechen von mir" (export for Notion).
  • export notion lists only whole sentences: never a line quoted in a reply, a chat line pasted with its time stamp, or a run of more than 40 words without a full stop (a whole chat message).
  • export notion --dry-run says how wide the pages' two long sections are, in totals and never a name: pages: days together: N lines on N pages; promises: N lines (N listed, N more not listed).
  • The World's time slider ends on today, not on the latest line the record holds: one calendar entry in 2055 no longer stretches it thirty years into the future. --from and --to still reach any day, the future included.
  • /gaps in the Library counts each silence to the server's own clock, so the same page read twice is the same page (the slow test that turned main red on 1dd86c2).
  • A sealed record keeps no reading of its tier 2–3 lines in plain text on this disk: the readings kept beside the index, the review pages' tables of observed people, orgs, ideas, assets and places, and the Library's built pages stay in the process's memory instead, and what an earlier version left there is removed. logbook serve --built renders every page live on a sealed record, to its end, and says why; serve --build refuses in one sentence, and the 06:00 close says the build is off. "plaintext_cache": true in logbook.json keeps them on disk as before, 0600 in the cache folder; off by default. The index's own columns stay as RFC 0029 §8 has them (sealing; RFC 0047 §15).
  • doctor's extra:* hints add the missing extra to this Logbook exactly as it is installed, or print no line (#334): this venv's pip (uv's pip in a venv uv made) at the installed version; pipx runpip in the venv pipx made, which keeps its Python, its options and its suffix; uv tool install --force on the Python running now, at the installed version or git commit, with every extra already there, the index options and each companion at its installed version; in a checkout, uv sync --inexact --no-default-groups on the Python running now, which removes nothing and brings back no group. It prints no line and says in one sentence why and where in docs/install.md to read under Homebrew, beside a receipt it cannot read or one naming a password or token, where uv's receipt names another Python, where the source may have changed since (a folder, a URL, a wheel), outside a venv, and under uvx or uv run --with, whose environment is uv's cache.
  • setup never adopts the demo record: it says it is the demo, how to make your own (unset LOGBOOK_HOME, then logbook setup) and exits 2 without writing. logbook demo marks the record it writes ("demo" in logbook.json); a demo 0.7.0 wrote is known by its owner (#334).
  • init on a folder that holds a record says so in one sentence and exits 2, never a traceback; with no path it makes the record where LOGBOOK_HOME points, as every other command finds it (#334).
  • doctor's hints name the current commands (logbook repair index, logbook setup places add …) (#334).
  • logbook --help says where a newcomer starts; dream names person; init --help describes path and --timezone (#334).
  • show person counts the open promises with the person (logbook promises lists them), or says none open, in place of a note about RFC 0007; the MCP person tool gives the same counts and command, under its ceiling, never a promise's words (#334).
  • demo --out on a record says which --out to pick, and that an earlier demo may be removed (#334).
  • setup's timezone question says in words which zone Enter takes and that the other is an example; setup places propose --top N prints the total and how many it shows (#334).
  • What the Library says to someone reading the record for the first time (#334): the front page links Promises, Goals, Agents and the World, as the navigation does; a Day the record holds nothing for (/today on the demo, read months later) says so and names the record's first and last day, each a link; /gaps and /assets on a record that went quiet before yesterday say when, while every silence and age still runs to today; the Day's with row says "nobody confirmed; proposed below" when a row below proposes who was there; the headers of the Manifest, Ideas, Promises, Goals and Agents say "nothing read above tier N" or "no lines" for "tier N" and "tier -", the tiers explained on hover; the Manifest and Ideas say why what was seen and not placed has nothing to review, so the counts and the sentence under them agree.
  • The text of a trip's route names its places (show trips, show year, show trip, /trips, the Journeys and a Journey's page): an unnamed stay is near <place>, x km or the nearest airport's city (Zurich), the coordinates only where nothing names it or where two stays side by side would read the same. The JSON keeps the label SPEC §3.2.6 gives. show year names an asset as it is registered ("aboard Nordlys", not "aboard nordlys"), and show year --json gives each trip's asset_name.
  • logbook serve never hangs: a page reads for at most --limit seconds (15 by default) and is then built in the background, said in one sentence; at most two pages are read at once; a browser that leaves stops its reading, and a broken pipe is no longer a traceback; an idle connection is closed.
  • A page read while a sync writes reads the record up to the last indexed line instead of rebuilding the whole index from under the sync.
  • serve --status says "not answering" for a server that takes the connection and says nothing for 5 s, with the command that restarts it; the server's own watchdog leaves for its service manager to start it again, and the scheduled run restarts a service that does not answer. kill -USR1 writes every thread's stack to the server's log.
  • add transcript stores the file a transcript/v1 JSON's content reference names when the export holds it (at the reference's own path, attachments/<sha256> or <sha256> beside the JSON; a spans file too), so Granola's and Fireflies' exports no longer leave a missing attachment behind. Bytes that do not hash to the reference are refused and counted; adding an export again fills the store for lines already in the record and writes no line (the attachment store).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The Day page's morning looks ahead with what the record already holds: today's tasks from the task tool (five at most, each linked to its line and to Notion) and the next trip as a countdown in words; who you'll see, by name; one person to reconnect with, from the drift rule, in words and never the same person two mornings running; the week's one proposal, in pencil. Loose ends adds the replies owed for more than a week and the decisions to revisit on the day, which Looking back brings back too.
  • The Day page takes one of four shapes from the hour: morning, live, evening (from LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_EVENING_HOUR, and every past day not signed) and signed. ?shape= shows another shape for reading. New parts, all read from the record: what the day was for (the chapter and the goals it touched), Yesterday, the ribbon of the planned beside the lived, Today, Loose ends both ways, People by time together, a birthday this week, Looking back 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 years, and one line naming the parts with nothing. The record is folded with counts on each fold, the dream's draft is in pencil on ruled paper, and the page has a new look in light and dark. No model call and no new write.
  • The list of the Library's shelves, which was the front page, is at /shelves, behind the gear.
  • Every page of the Library carries the doors' header (the wordmark, Today, Life, People and Places, Ask and the gear) in place of the list of fifteen links, with the door the page belongs to marked; the page's own look is unchanged. Every page's policy allows fonts from the Library itself and nowhere else.
  • Today's What's open lists the promises said in the fortnight before today, as the Day's morning does, so a promise years old never fills it; every promise stays on the Promises shelf.
  • A draft's proposals of a kind this reader does not know are counted, not malformed: the Day shows the proposals of the kinds it knows, counts the others as proposals_unknown in its JSON, and says malformed only for a known kind of the wrong shape or a proposal with no kind; every writer still writes only the kinds it knows and refuses any other (draft/v1, forward compatibility, 19 Oct 2026).
  • A signature never confirms the dream's draft line (RFC 0043 §6 rule 3): day sign, --confirm all, day reflect --sign, the Day page's Sign and the door's sign_day leave it out of confirmed, and naming it in --confirm or a disposition is refused. The page digest still covers it.
  • logbook serve answers every door and shelf from pages built ahead of time, at the 06:00 close and after every act on a page, instead of reading the record while you wait; a built page says when it was built in its footer. Today's Day is always current. serve --build builds them now, serve --live renders every page as it is asked for. The pages are kept beside the index, never in the record's folder, readable by you alone.
  • A new record names no one it may send what was said to: init and demo write a policy file with the MCP door at tier 1 and nothing else. You add an entry for each destination yourself. A record whose file already names one keeps it.
  • logbook serve renders every page as it is asked for by default again, with no limit on how long a page reads unless --limit SECONDS gives one, so the heavy pages (People, a person, the Manifest, the World, Promises) answer on a large record instead of Still reading. Pages built ahead are a lab, logbook serve --built (15 s limit, --limit 0 none); --live is still accepted. The 06:00 close builds the Library only on a machine where serve --built or serve --build turned it on, and otherwise says library: not built in one line. docs/serve.md lists what the built pages do not do yet.
  • export share day refuses a day that holds sealed lines (a tier-2 or tier-3 line of a record with recipients, at a tier the page would send), in one sentence and before anything is written: the page carried them opened, and the receiver's import page refused it because their hashes cover the sealed reference. A sealed day shares after v1, when a page can carry sealed lines to the receiver (RFC 0029); a day whose only sealed thing is an attachment still shares, its file opened as before (#364).
  • The Library's build renders what the lines since the last build touched: every door, a Day only when a line landed on it, a journey only when it holds such a day. serve --build --full renders every page, and is never needed in normal use.
  • The people of the whole record, the promises and each person's last real contact are kept beside the index between readings and brought forward by the lines appended since, instead of read again from every line: on two million lines a person's page reads in seconds rather than minutes. A resolution, a retraction, a corrected line, a backfill or a changed setting reads the whole record again, as before.
  • The world keeps each year before the current one beside the index and reads only the current year again, unless a line comes for an earlier year's days.
  • The Manifest and each org's page read the org sightings and touches kept beside the index and the lines appended since, instead of every mail, meeting and chat.
  • serve --build names the five pages that took longest to build.
  • The agents' shelf keeps which lines are a session's beside the index and streams only the messages appended since, instead of every message of the record.
  • A year's trips and journeys are built again only when a line lands on the days they were read from (a journey that ran on past the year included), or a draft is written.
  • The People page's year so far is brought forward with the record, and a closed year's ranking is kept until a line lands on its days.
  • The world reads its tracks and stays from the index rather than from every line of the year, and counts the lines it holds back in one query: the same page, in a third of the time.
  • Gaps keeps every source's activity beside the index and adds the lines since; of two equally long silences it names the first.
  • A year's trips and journeys read only the lines a trip is made of (flights, weather, events, transcripts, notes and photos) and the stays from the index: the same pages, read faster.
  • A build of a large record renders its pages on several processes, the doors first, side by side (LOGBOOK_BUILD_WORKERS sets how many).
  • Places keeps the owner's stays and what the lines name beside the index: a day reads the owner's track from a month before it, and the names of the lines appended, rather than the whole record.
  • The People page's review queue keeps each kind's observed people beside the index and reads only the lines appended since.
  • The ideas keep which lines name an idea beside the index, and read those and the lines appended since rather than every event, page, task and call.
  • Who was there, the owner's answers: people city CITY --trip ID takes the journey (--journey there still works until the release after 1.0, saying once that it is now --trip; --journey is people nearby's alone); review with --accept N[,N] takes the queue's numbers like the rest of review, each printed on a line of its own under the person, and a name there is refused; the longest stay a stretch's day is stated at counts its waking hours only, from day_start to midnight; review with refuses every option it does not take, --since included (who was there).

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• The pages a newcomer reads first agree with 0.7.0 (#334): install.md prints 0.7.0 and names the sealed and stream extras and what speakers costs; the tour uses the current command names, names its stores with --only and has its Docker and Nix lines; first-hour.md's check-up is the eighteen checks; serve.md lists the Promises, Goals and Agents shelves; try-it.md's samples are what 0.7.0 prints; index.md's RFC link works; and the release notes have 0.7.0.
  • The README is shorter and opens on a day; a new FAQ answers six first questions, each with the files that back it; Try it ends in the browser; RULES.md and SECURITY.md say what the code does about other people's words and the default tiers.
  • RFC 0043 amended after the task tool's agent read it: a task's day is its Planned date, else its Due date; let go closes the row with a status of its own, never the task tool's archive or trash, and tomorrow moves the planned day, never the due date; the week page's 90 days count only the owner's own edits, from the row's first line; the agent carries out a verb only on the row as the line saw it; an agent's meeting proposal shows under with as a proposal; a crossing that carries a signature carries the lines it gives a disposition to.
  • The show trips sample in the five-minute tour and the Year's trip rows print the route as show trips prints it, route Zurich, and aboard Nordlys; the Year's JSON names each trip's asset_name; RFC 0043 marks as proposed what main does not do (the folded draft, promises to you among loose ends, transcript consent, --keep) and says that Sign already writes delegations as notes.
  • The launch post says encryption at rest for tiers 2 and 3 is built and off until logbook key init turns it on, with the envelope plain and older backups still plain, as SECURITY.md does; the adapter bounties no longer list Mac Screen Time, which screentime reads.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• A stop becomes a stay only through an event that happened somewhere: one that carries a location or attendees, or comes from a calendar (ios-calendar, ics) or Google Home's history. A Notion page edited or a Drive file changed (by you or by someone else on your file) inside a ten-minute stop no longer makes it a stay; the Day still shows the edit under the stop. derive stays, day, days, trips and places propose agree (the Day, What makes a stop a stay).
  • sync gtasks writes task/v1 (RFC 0016), not event/v1: the Takeout Tasks adapter's own mapping, source google-takeout, so logbook tasks reads a task seen live and a Takeout export of the same tasks writes nothing, whichever comes first. A changed task is a new snapshot superseding the last; a done one carries how long it was open (extra.open_for_s); the notes stay a digest. A record that ran sync gtasks before this fix keeps the event/v1 lines it wrote (they promote no stay); logbook sync gtasks --since 2000-01-01T00:00:00Z once writes every task as it stands. sync reads a live source's own lines by the source it writes (gtasks → google-takeout, gmail → mail), so a first sync gtasks after a Takeout backfill carries on from its newest task.
  • doctor's last-run warns when the schedule is installed both for you (the agents or user timers) and for the system (--install-schedule --system's daemons or units): every run would happen twice. The last run is read the same whichever install wrote it (the schedule).
  • dream --catch-up, which the 06:00 close runs, synthesizes only the calls of the last 7 days (by the call's own start on the record's day_start), never a record's whole backlog of transcripts at once: an older call without a synthesis is counted and named in one line (N calls before DAY not synthesized; run …) and sent only when you ask, with dream --catch-up --since DAY or transcript synthesize --day DAY. The close never passes --since; the days it dreams are unchanged (the last 14). doctor has a synthesis line counting the calls without a synthesis inside the week, before it and above the dream entry's ceiling (the synthesis of a call).
  • promises never reads a line you pasted back into your own turn under an agent's own name (Claude: …, Claude Code: …) as your promise: it is the agent's, as a line under assistant: already was.
  • claude-sessions: an older copy of a session (a backup, an earlier export) added after a newer one is never written back over it; it writes nothing, as an unchanged session does.
  • export crossing builds every bundle in a fresh folder beside --out DIR, checks it against its own manifest and renames it into place, replacing DIR whole. A second export into the same folder used to overwrite only the files it wrote, so a tier-1 crossing into the folder of an earlier --tier 1,2 one left the earlier resolution.jsonl and tier-2 attachments beside a manifest that said there were none. The manifest now lists every file of the package under files (path, sha256, bytes). A DIR that exists and is not an earlier bundle is refused before anything is written, unless --force; the record, a folder that holds it and any path in it outside export/ are refused even then. A failed export leaves DIR as it was. export trip-bundle writes the same way and takes --force too (the crossing).
  • A portfolio typed in an org's status form comes back typed, in its field, when the form is sent again after a busy 409; it came back hidden.
  • The dream, transcript synthesize and the doctor --packet probe can now use a model that refuses any temperature: LOGBOOK_DREAM_TEMPERATURE=none sends the request with no temperature field, a number from 0 to 2 is sent as given, and unset keeps 0.2, so an existing setup sends what it sent before. Anything else is refused, naming the variable. An HTTP 400 that names the temperature now says set LOGBOOK_DREAM_TEMPERATURE=none for a model that takes no temperature; the request is never retried without one on its own. The packet's dream endpoint section names the temperature that will be sent.
  • A draft follows the dream entry of policy/crossing.json, not only the head: a draft above the entry's max_tier today (the ceiling lowered, the until passed, the entry removed) is no longer shown on the Day, on serve's Day page or through the MCP door, though no line was appended. The Day says superseded by policy and why in one row, and nothing of the draft's text (draft_withheld under --json); the door holds it back from every tool and counts it with the lines above its ceiling; doctor warns, naming the days. Every draft now records the version of the entry it was dreamed under (extra.policy_version, the SHA-256 of the entry's max_tier, until and model), and dream --catch-up dreams a day again when its draft is above the entry or was dreamed under another version of it, superseding the old draft; an expired entry still dreams nothing. The old draft stays in the record (the dream, When the entry changes; ADR 0016).
  • A source's first scheduled run reads its last 14 days, not its whole history. A live source added to the schedule started from nothing, so the first sync --scheduled walked everything it held (a Drive activity walk of 1.25 million entries spent the account's API quota for the day). Now a source with no watermark yet reads the record's last 14 local days on its first scheduled run, keeps its watermark, and says so in one line with the logbook sync <source> --since <date> that reads the rest. The next scheduled runs carry on from the watermark, or from the same instant while there is none, so nothing is skipped or written twice. sync <source> and sync --all by hand start where they always did, and --since always wins. doctor notes first run bounded to 14 days; history not read on the source's sync: line until a run reads back past it (--since, --restart) (the schedule). ais, adsb, telegram and weather read no history and are never bounded.
  • A dry run stops on one line at the source's quota or rate limit instead of waiting it out: sync: drive: dry run stopped at the source's limit after 0 lines: HTTP 429: …, exit 1, nothing written. The Google sources, notion, github, granola and adsb say so; a run that writes waits the limit out as before.
  • sync mail --since on a folder with no mark yet and no message from that day on marks the folder at its last message, so the next run no longer reads the whole folder; sync github --since marks a repo with nothing from then on at that time, so the next run no longer reads it from its beginning; a first sync gmail --since that finds nothing keeps its time as the newest date, so a later list by date (after Gmail drops the history id) starts there, not at the first message.
  • The health export reader (the CSV reader the Withings, MyFitnessPal and Google Takeout Fit adapters share) no longer emits an empty row for a degenerate file. A row with no text under any column the header names — its only text past the header, or under a blank name — is skipped as a blank row is, so such a file reads as an empty export does: no lines and nothing counted, where each such row was counted as a bad date or a bad start. A column name the header repeats keeps the last cell with text under it; a blank or missing cell under the repeat no longer covers the text. Found by the reader's property test.
  • review idea no longer counts a Notion row's relations line (sync notion --relations-backfill) as one more line of its idea: a relations line links a row to others and touches nothing. The observed table is rebuilt once.
  • One email is one line, whichever road brought it: add mail (a Takeout mbox), sync mail (IMAP) and sync gmail each skip, before they write, a message the record already holds by its Message-ID from any of the three, and say so per mailbox (3,412 already in the record from mail (an import without --account)), dry runs included. A Takeout added without --account was keyed <Message-ID> and the live roads <account>:<Message-ID>, so a sync over a period the export covered wrote every message a second time. payload.message_id is now the id normalised (brackets and surrounding whitespace off, the domain part lower-cased, the part before the @ as written) and a message the record holds under another spelling is found among the lines of its days; a copy in another of your mailboxes is still a line of its own (RFC 0015 rule 1, amended). Nothing written is touched; a message without a Message-ID is keyed by its bytes and dedupes on its own road, as before, and so is one whose id has no @ (unknown), never a key across roads. Message-ID: <> now counts as none instead of folding every such message into one line: a Takeout holding such messages, imported before, writes each of them once more on a re-import, one of them a second copy of the line the old key kept (Mail).
  • The health row lost the record's day_start for every line read after the first sleep stage.
  • Under a day_start, the Day showed no weather: a weather line starts at midnight, on the page of the day before. The Day now takes it by its own day.
  • The Day shows a Notion row once when sync notion --relations-backfill saw it again: the backfill's relations line folds into the page's own line on the day, which stands for both (--json lists both ids under lines, notion its one source). It showed as two rows in day and on the Day page of logbook serve, and counted twice in a stay's attachments under days. show lists both lines, as it lists every line (the Day).
