  • logbook sync notion no longer stops at a page that holds a block Notion's API withholds from integrations, such as an AI block: reading its blocks answered 400 validation_error ("Block type ai_block is not supported via the API for your bot type") and the whole run aborted, on a real workspace a thousand pages in. The page's line is written with extra.body {"unavailable": "withheld"} in place of the digest and word count, never a digest of part of the text; the summary, the dry run's too, says also N pages with blocks the API withholds; the block type is named once a run on stderr, never the page. A block deleted while a page is read (404) marks the body {"unavailable": "not_found"} and is counted as pages with a block deleted while they were read, where before the body was left off without a word. Any other 400 still stops the run on one line with the watermark kept. words_delta counts against the page's latest line that has a word count.
  • scripts/check_pii.py reads a commit range: run by pre-commit run --from-ref A --to-ref B, as a merge desk runs it over a pull request, it checks the lines git diff A..B adds instead of the staged diff, which is empty then, and no longer reports Passed having checked nothing. --tree REF checks every line of every file tracked at REF, for a sweep of a whole branch. Every run ends with one line of counts, check-pii: 18 patterns, 9879 lines, 0 matches in …, shown on a pass too; no patterns file, a file of comments only, or nothing to read is that line as a warning. A match names the file, the line and the pattern (its first named group, or its line in the patterns file), never the text.
  • seal and migrate now refuse a record whose original hashes do not verify: key seal --all and repair migrate check every hash, under the rule the record was written with, and every link across the whole record before a line is rehashed, verify the new files before they replace the old, and on a failure name the first failing line and its id and change nothing.
  • A day signed again keeps your confirmations: day sign DAY and the MCP tool sign_day, without --confirm, keep what the standing signature confirmed, its dispositions and its note, as the Day page's Sign again and day reflect --sign already did; a line added since stays unconfirmed. --confirm all confirms the whole page (RFC 0034 amendment 4).
  • A line superseded twice reads alike everywhere (#321): a superseder that is retracted supersedes nothing, and a line stays superseded while any superseder not retracted stands, in the index and so in show, review speakers, the voiceprint registry and every reader that asks it; the MCP door marks a transcript heard again as show does.
  • logbook serve: when a sync moved the head and left the index stale while the server ran, requests that arrived together each started their own rebuild of the index and all but one failed with database is locked. The index is now brought to the new head once, under a lock, by the first request after the head moves, and the others wait for it.
  • day sign --at (and sign_day and day reflect --sign, which sign through the same code) checks the moment against the day's start under day_start, by the rule the index puts every line on its day by, rather than against midnight: with the day beginning at 06:00, a moment at 01:30 signs the day before and is refused for the date it falls on, which has not begun, so a signature never covers a page that starts after it. A signature already in the record is never checked again.
  • status KIND ENTITY DISPOSITION --reason "…" for an idea, a place or an asset writes the reason's note/v1 first and then the status/v1 line, whose note names it, as RFC 0037 §10.5 says; it wrote them the other way round, the note naming the status under extra.status and carrying the disposition. The note now carries the words and the entity only. A pair written the old way is read the same, and status list --json names each status's note (note). An org's status is unchanged: one tier-3 line, the reason on it, no note (the profiles).
  • A crash between the fsync of an appended line and the replacement of logbook.json (SPEC §3, write order) left the files one line ahead, which verify reported; the recovery this documented, repair index then append, then wrote a second line of the same seq, the index refused it with UNIQUE constraint failed: lines.seq, and the record held a fork. append and append_many now refuse under the writer lock while the files end past logbook.json, or at its seq under another head, in one sentence naming logbook repair tail, and write nothing. repair tail checks every line past the head as verify does (envelope, seq, prev, hash, timestamps, a sealed line opened when the identity is here) and only then sets logbook.json to the last of them and extends the index, in that order; --dry-run lists the tail and what would be done; a line that does not verify, the files behind logbook.json, or the same seq under another head makes it refuse with the first failing line and change nothing. The gate of key seal --all and repair migrate checks timestamps too now, as verify reports them.
  • A writer waiting for state/writer.lock no longer dies with FileNotFoundError when the holder's release removes state/ between the waiter's making the folder and creating the lock: it makes the folder again and tries again under the same rules, so a lock another writer took in the meantime is still waited for, or refused under --no-wait. Seen once on Windows CI.
  • day and serve show one calendar entry once when two calendars carry it (ios-calendar and ics, or two calendars gcal writes as ics): starts less than a minute apart, the same duration or one side all-day, the same title or flight. The richest line stands and names the others, ×2 sources (ics, ios-calendar); the fold is at read time, every line stays (docs/day.md).
  • A move names an airport pair (OSL → ZRH) only when it is a flight: its speed and distance are a flight's, or a flight line covers it. A car move between two points near an airport no longer prints ZRH → ZRH.
  • verify walks the attachments the lines name (SPEC §1.1), as it always said it would and never did: a file the store does not hold is listed under attachments: with the first line that names it and is not an error; a present plain file whose bytes do not hash to its name is an error naming the line, hashed by default (--no-attachment-digests leaves present plain files unhashed on a large store); with the identity, a sealed file is opened and a plaintext that does not hash to its name, or a file that does not open, is an error, which no flag skips. A missing file, a corrupted plain one and a sealed one swapped for valid ciphertext of other bytes all passed before. doctor looks for the same files and counts the missing ones in its record line, without hashing them.
  • Timestamps must be RFC 3339 instants. append took any at, end or recorded_at ending in Z, so not-a-dateZ was written, verify said nothing, and the index rebuild then failed; it refuses one now, and verify reports one a line already carries as an error naming the line. A valid stamp is still written exactly as given (it is hashed as written), and one with a numeric offset is still converted.

docs.title: Adapters
docs.text:
• telegram: logbook add telegram-export <folder> reads Telegram Desktop's JSON export of your bot chats (and nothing else: a chat with a person, a group or a channel is counted and never read) → one message/v1 line per message, your words as yours and the bot's marked extra.machine, the bot as every line's counterpart (extra.counterpart, an observed entity of kind agent), media referenced by its path and digest and never copied, a forward marked as one. logbook sync telegram reads your own bots over the Bot API (LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKENS, LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_OWNER_ID), read-only: getMe, getWebhookInfo, and getUpdates only when something is pending, never an offset (no update is confirmed, so your bot still gets every one), never a method that sends or changes; a message from anyone but you is counted and never written; a bot on a webhook is one line and is left alone. Both write the same line under one key, since Telegram gives one message two ids, yours and the bot's.
  • claude-code: logbook add claude-sessions ~/.claude/projects → one transcript/v1 line per Claude Code session, your turns as owner and the assistant's as a participant marked machine, the text stored once under its digest; tool calls counted by name and their output never kept, nor a subagent's conversation, a compaction summary or thinking; words counted per side; the session, project and working directory under extra. A session that grew is a :v2 line that supersedes the one before.
  • immich.place asks the server for one asset's place by id, and apple_photos.places reads the places Photos named for given assets from a library, its schema confirmed first.
  • takeout-location reads the Semantic Location History of a Takeout archive (placeVisit, which carries the place's name and address, and activitySegment), and the iPhone's own Timeline export (location-history.json, a top-level array); the docs give the steps to export Timeline from the phone.
  • immich keeps the city, state and country Immich gave a photo under extra.place; apple-photos keeps the address, city and area names Photos gave it (ZREVERSELOCATIONDATA) under extra.place.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• An agent is never a person (docs/adapters/agents.md): people, person, drift, the company of a stay and people review pass over a conversation with one of your agents and a transcript participant marked machine, whatever its name; promises reads only your own words in it (a bot's message and a forwarded one are counted under skipped); the dream marks an agent's words for the model and its prompt says agents are not people (dream-day/3).
  • The MCP tool note_day writes through the same note path as day reflect (logbook/core/notes.py); what it writes is unchanged.
  • doctor checks five extras: extra:speakers joins ais, crypto, sealed and transcribe, a pass when pyannote.audio is installed and a warn with pip install "openlogbook[speakers]" when not. It is asked by the installed distribution, so neither pyannote nor torch is imported to find out. A machine with [transcribe] and without [speakers] now has that one warn (the doctor).
  • The notion entry's example in export for Notion has no write key, as the refusal that names the entry has none: left out, write is the empty list it must stay, and an entry that spells out "write": [] is read the same.
  • people review --reject writes an entity-review/v1 line of type person; a people-review/v1 line is read as the same no, forever.
  • setup places review --reject, and the Places page of serve, write the pair as an entity-review/v1 line of type place, and state/places-review.json is a cache rebuilt from the lines. --migrate-rejects writes the pairs the file held before as lines, once; until then review says how many are not lines yet.
  • What the sources saw is one table in the index, observed_entities; observed_people and observed_places are views over it for one release. The index is rebuilt once, on the first command after the upgrade.
  • sync github and add github-export: a line from a private repository is tier 2, with the reason on the line (extra.tier_reason: private repository), so an issue's text, a review and other people's comments in a private repository no longer go wherever tier 1 crosses by default; a public repository's lines stay tier 1. The live sync reads each repository's own private and visibility from the answer it already asks for (GET /repos/{repo}, or GET /user/repos with --all): public only when the API says so, so an internal repository is private too. The account export's mark per repository is used where it exists; a clone says nothing of its visibility, so its lines, and those of a repository the export does not mark, are tier 2 (repository visibility not known) unless you pass add github-export DIR --public for that run, which never overrides a repository the export marks private. A visibility that changes applies to the lines written from then on; a line already in the record is never rewritten, and the same commit or issue read again at the other tier is the line already there, never a second one. In a record that seals (RFC 0029) both need the identity to write, a tier 1 line too, since only the identity sees an act the record holds sealed; without it they refuse on one sentence before asking anything (--dry-run needs none).
  • One Google sign-in for every Google source (service_account): the key file and the user from the two existing variables, a read-only scope per call, an hour's token held in memory and never written to disk; no refresh token anywhere. The tour's new Google, on one key names the five scopes, gives the one setup and says which sources it covers; the mail page says when to use IMAP (any mailbox) and when sync gmail (Gmail on your own Workspace).
  • doctor's sync:<name> line names the variables a source reads, and a source with two ways in (gcal) says what to set in words.
  • sync --all runs meet and gaudit after gtasks whenever the Google key is set. A key delegated before this release lacks their two scopes: add them in the Workspace admin console (the tour, Google, on one key, step 4) or switch the two sources off in policy/import.json, or each scheduled run reports them failed.
  • review idea sees a repository in two more places: an act sync github wrote (its own link, else its repository on github.com: a commit, a README's version), and a task's own url beside its links.
  • A bot's line is nobody's (the owner's decision of 14 October 2026): a line whose actor is a bot (sync notion's bot, sync github's Bot) or whose words an agent wrote (extra.machine) is never a touch of an idea in review idea, never a person seen on one, and adds no words to one; an agent among a call's participants is nobody, whatever address it joined under.
  • RFC 0037 §4.3, amended 2026-10-16: a database row is its own root. A row of a Notion database (its lines carry the row's database) is an idea of its own in review idea, never folded into the page above the database; a page under a row is the row's.
  • review idea proposes a Notion database row as an idea only when its Type select says Idea (the owner's decision of 14 October 2026), as the row's latest line with extra.properties has it; a page under a row of another type is not proposed either, and a page that is no row is proposed as before. idea_rows in policy/entities.json names another select and option ({"property": "Kind", "value": "Spark"}, case aside). sync notion already writes the select's name and option on the row's line, and nothing else of it.
  • serve answers a busy record one way: while another command holds the writer lock, every act of the Library (the Places, Journeys and People forms, the Manifest's review and status, the Day's Reflect, Sign, star and with…) is a 409 with one sentence, Another command is writing to the record; nothing was written. Try again in a moment., the command that holds the lock, and the form you sent kept to send again (a recording is chosen again). Nothing is written.
  • Every page serve serves fits a phone's 400 px column: on the Day, the days, trips, places, assets and gaps a wide table scrolls inside its own box, and the Places queue's maps and the World page's canvases keep to the column. One test walks every page from / and holds each to it, the Day among them.
  • serve's navigation wraps on a narrow screen and names journeys and people (/trips stays, from the front page). A draft of a journey (RFC 0036, unit journey) is read by its id: a subject that is the trip's id, or an array naming it. It follows the dream entry as a day's draft does: one above the entry's max_tier today is not shown, and the journey's row and page say superseded by policy and why, nothing of its text.
  • logbook serve's navigation wraps on a narrow screen instead of pushing the page wider than a phone's 400 px column; the Day page, its new forms included, holds that column without scrolling sideways.
  • logbook day sign reads the page and appends under one hold of the writer lock and re-reads the head before it appends, refusing when another writer moved it.
  • logbook sync weather asks nothing unless LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1 is set, by name as in sync --all: it is the source's one setting. Unset, the command says so and exits 2 without a request. The first run asks about yesterday alone, no longer the record's whole history (--since backfills), and the week's lookback never reaches before the first day a run covered (docs/adapters/weather.md).
  • logbook sync notion records a database row's database and its relations. Every line of a row carries extra.database ({id}), so a reader can tell "a row of Notes" from the record alone; the line that holds the row as it is (the one with the body's digest) carries extra.relations, each relation property as {name: [page id, …]} — the ids of the rows it links to exactly as Notion gives them, in its order, never their titles, bodies or rollups, and no related page is ever looked up. RFC 0009 has no field for links between entries, so they go under extra. A relation is a change like any other: an edit that only links or unlinks writes its one line, with extra.relations_changed ([{name, added, removed}]) saying which relation gained and lost which ids since the row's latest line with relations; a reorder is no change, and a re-sync of an untouched row writes nothing. A relation of more than 25 links, which Notion serves cut short, is read whole from the page property endpoint; when that fails the field is left off the line and the row counted (rows whose relations could not be read whole), never the first 25 alone. Lines written before keep no relations; a row gets them with its next edit.
  • logbook sync notion --relations-backfill [--since DAY] [--dry-run] writes them now: one line per database row whose relations the record does not hold yet (or whose links changed from the other side of a relation with its edit time left alone), extra.action relations, dated at the row's last edit, raw_id <page id>/<day>/relations, with the row's reference, path, parent, database and its relations as the backfill reads them, and no body, property or actor. --since takes a local day; --dry-run counts the rows. A row the record holds no line of is left to the next sync; the watermark is never moved. The same pacing as the sync, three requests a second; a rate limit that does not lift stops it on one line, exit 1, the lines already written kept, so running it again finishes the job. A backfilled row shows once more in its Day, at its last edit.
  • review org sees an org in two more places: a transcript participant's address, and an act sync github wrote (its own link's code-host org, else its repository's on github.com). A calendar's rooms and a code host's relay (resource.calendar.google.com, users.noreply.github.com) name no company, and your own code-host account (a github: handle in policy/owner.json) is yours, never an org. A person's own account is hinted personal, and a family's domain is one whose names are each a given name the address itself spells (kari@ "Kari Nordmann"), so a newsletter in its own name ("Nordmann Nytt", news@) is a company. The observed table is rebuilt once.
  • The diarizer is its own extra, openlogbook[speakers] (RFC 0038, open question 13): openlogbook[transcribe] brings the Whisper engine and nothing of pyannote.audio, torch's diarization stack or CUDA; voices need openlogbook[transcribe,speakers]. Without it derive transcripts transcribes as before and says speakers: not separated (install openlogbook[speakers], then logbook setup speakers --fetch-model); setup speakers and derive speakers exit 2 with that sentence. A machine that installed [transcribe] from main for its voices adds speakers.
  • SPEC 0.4: §3.2.3 rule 5 says what #263 made the reference do. An event makes a stop a stay only when it happened somewhere: it comes from a calendar (ios-calendar, ics) or Google Home's history, or it carries a location or attendees. A page edited or a file changed promotes nothing and is not counted in attached; transcripts, notes, calls, messages and photos promote as before (ADR 0023). A reader's rule, not the format: a record still names logbook/0.3, and no conformance fixture or head changes. SPEC gains a version history.
  • logbook --help lists 31 commands on 48 lines: star, unstar and with join the write group.
  • export crossing carries a star only beside its line, as export share day and the trip bundle do; and every crossing carries a photo's memory keeper (your star on it, or the library's favourite) only beside its photo, so a favourite whose photo stays home stays home too.
  • A keeper that names an earlier one in supersedes replaces it, as SPEC §3.2 defines a standing line.
  • A live source's pull may take recorded (its own lines from the day before since on, for a source that folds several items into one line or writes snapshots), and a live adapter that writes under a file adapter's source names it as SOURCE, which sync then reads its own lines by.
  • A live source's pull may take existing (which of a batch of keys the record holds), owner_emails and notice, and may keep a lasting resume state through the checkpoint keeper (RESUMES), described per folder after the summary.
  • The test suite drops every LOGBOOK_* variable the shell exported before a test runs (the live sources' hosts and keys, the dial prefix, the notifier's token, a backup password), so a developer's shell can no longer change doctor's output under a test.
  • A live source's pull may take previous: the payloads the record holds under a raw_id prefix, in chain order, for a source that keeps no history of its own.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• claude-export: logbook add claude-export <zip> reads the Claude apps' data export (Settings → Privacy → Export data; the zip as it came, the folder it unpacks to, or its conversations.json) → one transcript/v1 line per conversation in the shape and tier of a Claude Code session: your turns as owner and the assistant's as a participant marked machine, the text stored once under its digest, words counted per side; the conversation's id, its name as the title, its project's name and its created and updated times under extra. Files you gave or uploaded are named and counted, never copied (the text the apps extracted from them never read); tool calls counted by name, their input and output never kept; thinking never kept; users.json never opened; only the branch a conversation stands on when the export links its messages; the thinking and the artifacts an older export writes inline are dropped, never kept. A conversation that grew is a :v2 line that supersedes the one before; an unchanged one writes nothing, nor does an export older than one already imported; a malformed one is skipped and counted; --dry-run says how many conversations, new, grown, unchanged and older. people, promises and the dream read these lines as they read Claude Code's: your words count, the assistant's never (docs/adapters/agents.md).
  • The Day page of logbook serve shows a row's photos as a strip under it, starred first: a thumbnail for each photo whose pixels the record's own attachment store holds (/photo/ID), the rest counted, never a broken image, and nothing fetched from a photo library (In a browser).
  • A photo review at the foot of the Day page: the day's photos with no star, each with Star (its memory keeper) and Not a keeper, which stops the review asking and writes no line (state/photo-review.json); both answer 409 while another command writes, as every act does.
  • The Day page draws the day's track from the stays' own coordinates, an inline drawing with no map tile; links every row that is a line to /line/ID, the line as written, read-only and through the page's tier gate; shows the week's draft on its Sunday and links to it from the other six days; and says in one sentence under the header what crosses where.
  • Many edits of one Drive file read as one row on the Day page, the file's name and what was done to it counted (Budget 2027 · 5 edits, 2 comments); logbook day lists each line as before.
  • logbook with DAY NAME… and the Day page's with… field say who was there on a day no device saw, the night the phones were off: the same line from either, and the page says why it saw nobody.
  • logbook day reflect YYYY-MM-DD: close the day in your words. The reflection is typed (--text), heard on this machine (--audio FILE, the openlogbook[transcribe] extra, refused with the install hint without it), recorded from the microphone on macOS (--mic SECONDS, with ffmpeg), or the day's Wispr Flow dictation that begins with the word "reflect" (offered as a draft and written only when you confirm it, or with --from-wispr [SEQ]). It is one note/v1 line on the day, tier 2, source reflect, reflection in its labels, printed back a sentence a line. Rules only, no model, read it with the cue tables of promises: your commitments, delegations to a named counterpart ("ask Ola to ...", "Ola should ...", "Ola soll ..."), and what became of the commitments on the day's page (kept, missed, dropped, carried; matched by token overlap at 0.5), all printed as numbered proposals and none written until you accept it. --sign with --accept N,N (or one y/n each on a terminal) writes the accepted delegations as note/v1 lines labelled delegation and signs the day through signing.sign, the reflection among the lines confirmed, the accepted dispositions in the signature and --at the moment you spoke; a day signed before is signed again, keeping what its signature said. --dry-run writes nothing.
  • day and the Day page of serve show the latest reflection in a section of its own, below the header and above the timeline; day --json carries it under reflection, a key present only on a day that has one.
  • day_start (RFC 0036): logbook setup day_start 06:00 writes "day_start": "06:00" to logbook.json, and from then on a line whose local clock is before 06:00 belongs to the day before. Every reader that puts a line on a day goes by it, from one rule: the index, show, day and days, the nights before and after a day, trips, doctor sources --gaps, the digest, the signed day's page and the crossing of signed days, promises, the rollups, the Year, people, the vault, the printed pages, the shared page, the MCP tools' days and serve's pages, /today included. The comparison is on the wall clock, so the night the clocks change moves no line; no line, hash or month file changes. The Day's header says 06:00 to 06:00 the next day and its JSON carries day_start when the day does not begin at midnight, and only then. Setting it rebuilds an index that exists and counts the signed days whose page moved; a value that is not a clock HH:MM is refused by every reader that groups by day, naming it (docs/settings.md).
  • logbook doctor has a day-start line when the day does not begin at midnight, warns when the index was built under another boundary, and fails a value that is not a clock.
  • The schedule runs four times a day: sync --scheduled at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00 local, and sync --scheduled --close at 06:00, which runs dream --catch-up after the sync when this version has the dream and policy/crossing.json a dream entry (else one line saying why not), then the rest of the run and one summary line. Two launchd agents or two systemd user timers; sync --install-schedule --system writes daemons or system units for a machine nobody logs in to and prints the two sudo commands that install them, as serve --install-service --system does. Installing again moves a schedule of two runs to the four; --uninstall-schedule removes them all. The Sunday message comes from the 18:00 run.
  • logbook export site writes a Day page for each of the Year's twelve picks, days/<day>.html: serve's Day page written down with every toggle open, nothing to submit, the site's navigation above it. The pick's row in the Days index links its page; any other day stays a row, which a Day page's neighbours link. About twelve pages a year, never one per day. The site's pages in serve's stylesheet, the Day page among them, need no sideways scroll on a phone: a table wider than the column scrolls inside itself.
  • logbook doctor --packet [--out FILE]: a plain-text diagnostic to hand a collaborator when something fails, with no line's content, no name, no path under the home directory and no value of a variable in it (docs/doctor.md, "Sending a diagnostic"). It holds the OS and its version, the architecture, the RAM, Python, openlogbook and the extras installed; the record's line count and head; each source's last-run result and watermark date; the schedule, the last scheduled run and the serve service; the dream endpoint's host and port and model with one probe, the fixed prompt Reply with the single word ready. sent once, and the reply's HTTP status and body as they came; the names of the variables set; and the last 40 lines of the sync and service logs. What it quotes is scrubbed: the home directory becomes ~, the record's folder [record], the owner's names, handles, addresses and numbers from policy/owner.json (a number however it is spaced) and the login name [owner], the machine's name [host], places and assets [place] and [asset], a variable's value its name in brackets. The probe is the packet's one network call, made only when LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT is set and a model is named.
  • dream day YYYY-MM-DD [--dry-run] [--show-prompt]: a model reads one day under the dream entry of policy/crossing.json (max_tier, until, optional model; no entry or an expired one refuses in one sentence) and writes one draft/v1 line (RFC 0036): the day in a paragraph, the threads it moved, two questions, the people and promises it proposes, every segment with the ids of the lines it rests on or marked unsupported. The model is any OpenAI-compatible chat completions endpoint, LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT, LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL and, when it needs one, LOGBOOK_DREAM_KEY, through one small client with a timeout and one retry and no SDK. The material is the Day under the ceiling, messages by counterpart with their count and text, notes, commitments and the signing note, never a raw line above the ceiling; the prompt is logbook/contrib/dream-prompt.md (docs/dream-prompt.md) and says which language to write in, the language most of the day's lines are in. An evidence id the day does not have makes the segment unsupported; more than 30 % unsupported refuses the answer and nothing is written. The draft's tier is the highest tier it read; read_head and read_count say what it read; dreaming a day again supersedes the standing draft; the whole run holds the writer lock and a head that moved is HeadMoved, nothing written. dream --catch-up [--days N] dreams each of the last N days that has no draft or whose lines changed, one line per day (docs/dream.md).
  • The Day shows the standing draft between the header and the timeline, above every note, headed with the model, the head and count it read and dreamed N×, last on DATE; an unsupported segment set apart with ~ and the word; day --no-dream leaves it out and --json carries it as draft; serve shows the same. show lists a draft line on the day it was written. doctor lists the dream entry on its crossing line with the model it names.
  • dream journey ID drafts a journey once it has come home, and the first 06:00 close after it does dreams it: the trip as a whole, its days, places with their hours, who was on it, what was decided and promised, the photos it would star and one name it proposes. show trips and show trip carry the draft (draft or draft_withheld under --json, when it has one).
  • dream week [DAY|YYYY-Www] drafts an ISO week from its seven days and their drafts once its Sunday is over, and the close of each Sunday dreams it: the time by place, person and thread, sleep and training when the health lines cross (else no data), who moved against the week before, the promises open both ways, a review proposed for each open goal, one proposal for next week and a personal part. Every figure is computed from the lines, with their ids; a sentence that writes another is marked unsupported. day of a Sunday carries it (week, week_draft, week_draft_withheld under --json).
  • Both follow the dream entry as a day's draft does: read under its ceiling, the version recorded, withheld by the readers when the entry no longer allows them, dreamed again by --catch-up when their lines or the entry change.
  • The dream proposes events: beside its segments, dream day asks the model for the events the day held ({title, start, end, place, people, evidence}; the prompt is now dream-day/2) and keeps them inside the draft/v1 line under proposals, kind event, never as event lines. A stay at a restaurant with two photos and a recording is a dinner with the people in it. The material gives each stay its place (a named place's name, or place:<lat>,<lon>) and the day's canonical people by id; a proposal with a time, a place, a person or evidence not of the day is dropped and counted under extra.dropped, an unresolved person among them (docs/dream.md, Proposed events).
  • day sign and day reflect list the proposed events, numbered; --accept N writes one as an event/v1 line, the calendar adapter's own mapping of its fields, source owner, tier 1, extra.from the draft's id, under the writer lock the signature takes and confirmed in it. Nothing is written without --accept.
  • The Day shows a proposed event greyed (? and proposed in text) and a confirmed one as an event of the day; day --json carries them under draft.proposals, each with confirmed.
  • Proposed events follow the policy with their draft: a draft the dream entry no longer allows is withheld with its proposals, so the Day shows none of them and day sign/day reflect list none and refuse --accept for them with the reason; the draft the entry still allows, shown in its place, brings its own. An event confirmed before the entry changed stays in the record.
  • logbook review KIND (RFC 0037): one sitting for the five kinds of thing the record names — person (= people review), org, idea, asset, place (= setup places review), the two old commands printing the same as before, byte for byte (review). The org queue is the registered domains of your mail and calendar (a public provider and your own domains name nobody's org), the code-host orgs of the pages and tasks, the group chats and the recurring merchants; the idea queue the Notion roots, the repositories and the recurring titles; the asset queue the track subjects and aircraft registrations the registry does not name; each proposed against what you named with the evidence, or as a new one. --accept, --name N "…", --reject, --all-above; nothing written unless told, nothing looked up. review alone lists every queue.
  • logbook status KIND ENTITY DISPOSITION [--reason "…"] [--at DATE]: what you decided about an org (hold, add, sell, let-go, exited, passed), an idea (spark, exploring, build, built, killed), a place (let-go) or an asset (sold, let-go), one status/v1 line, no money on it, tier 3 for an org (its dispositions describe a position in money) and 2 for the rest; --reason puts your words on the line, and for an idea, a place or an asset also as a note/v1 at tier 2; an org's reason stays on its tier-3 line, never a note. A place let go and an asset sold close their registry entry with until and keep it. status list KIND says the current status of each, the stale ones and the proposals muted for a year by a status you gave a reason.
  • Three profiles in draft with RFC 0037 (the profiles): entity/v1 (an org, an idea, an asset or a place, and the refs that are it; tier 2, never citing a tier-3 line), entity-review/v1 (every no, for every kind) and status/v1. A resolution/v1 of type company is read as an org. policy/entities.json holds the public mail providers and the review's thresholds.
  • export notion FOLDER [--since DAY] [--include-unsigned] [--dry-run]: the record's facts for the program that keeps your Notion, as a crossing. Persons you had contact with in the window, by their emails, phones and handles: the last contact and its kind, the days together, the promises open both ways (the sentence, its day, its line), and the page in German, emitted whole; ideas with a Notion page: the status, your reason note quoted as written, a dated German entry per status; orgs by domain: the days they were touched, and nothing else. Anything without a key is left out and counted, and so is a sentence that names money. Nothing leaves without the notion entry of policy/crossing.json; signed days only unless the entry says "include_unsigned": true and you type --include-unsigned; tier 3, an org's status and money never. The folder is written fresh each run and one crossing/v1 line says what left; nothing is asked of or created in Notion (export for Notion).
  • logbook export world [--out DIR] [--from DATE --to DATE] [--tier 1|1,2|1,2,3]: the record as one self-contained HTML page, a globe you can scrub (the world). On a canvas, with no WebGL and nothing fetched: the world's outline from Natural Earth's 1:110m land (public domain, bundled under 48 KiB as logbook/tables/land.json, written by scripts/make_land.py), the places of places.json as anchors, the assets of assets.json as dots moving along their own tracks, your stays as dots (aboard, you ride with the boat), the journey/v1 lines as tracks, and a time scrubber at the bottom that moves everything, the standing chapter/v1 lines as bands on it. Clicking an anchor or an asset opens its summary: nights, journeys, photos, the first and last day. The record's part of the page is one JSON block under 1,000,000 bytes, the tracks thinned to fit (never the counts); every id it refers to is checked before the page is written, and no coordinate is more precise than the record's own (a stay's centre to the fewest decimals of the fixes inside it, four at most). Tier-gated like an export: tiers 1 and 2 by default, under a new world entry of policy/crossing.json (2 when the file does not name it); every export appends one crossing/v1 line, and a re-run over an unchanged record rewrites nothing.
  • logbook serve: the same page at /world (?from=&to= narrows it), its one script named by its hash in the page's Content-Security-Policy, and world in the Library's navigation.
  • goal add TEXT --horizon life|year|quarter [--from DAY] [--until DAY] [--supersedes GOAL] writes one goal/v1 line (RFC 0036) in your words, tier 2 and source manual; a goal reworded is a new goal that supersedes the old, and the chain is one goal. goal review GOAL advancing|stalled|done|let-go|superseded [--note TEXT] [--at DAY|RFC3339] [--period day|week|month|quarter|year] writes your verdict as one review/v1 line on the day it is about, recorded_at saying when you wrote it; one verdict per goal, period and day, never in the future or before the goal's first day. goal list [--open] [--json] lists every standing goal with its latest review. goal import FILE is the first backfill: one goal per line of a text file (text | horizon | from), and --review let-go --at 2026-08-31 applies one verdict to all of them, every line checked before any is written (docs/goals.md).
  • chapter open NAME [--from DAY] [--to DAY] [--rules TEXT], chapter close [--to DAY] and chapter list [--json]: a named stretch of your life as one chapter/v1 line, tier 2; chapters do not overlap, the same name from the same day is written once, and closing writes the chapter again with its last day.
  • Every one of these writers holds the writer lock for its whole run and reads the head again before it appends: a head that moved under it writes nothing, exit 2; --no-wait refuses while another command writes.
  • The Day names the chapter a day is in, in its header after the signed state, lists a row per goal review on the day the verdict is about with the goal's current text and written <when> when it was written later, and lists the goal and chapter lines written on the day, marked when superseded; under --json as chapter, reviews, goals and chapters, each only on a day that has one. show and the serve Day page show the same; under a ceiling of 1 none of it is there.
  • logbook sync gmail: a Gmail mailbox over the Gmail API v1, read-only (gmail.readonly), on the one Google service-account key → mail/v1, tier 2, source mail: the line logbook sync mail (IMAP) writes for the same message, through the same parser and with the same dedupe key (<account>:<Message-ID>), so a mailbox synced by IMAP yesterday and by the API today is written once, and a Takeout imported with --account dedupes against both. Labels in the profile's slot as IMAP spells them (Inbox, Sent, Important, Starred, your own by name; UNREAD and the category tabs dropped), the thread id in decimal; the body as the mail source stores it; attachments named, sized and digested, never stored. Drafts, Spam and Trash are counted, not written. Headers first: no body the record already holds is fetched. The state is Gmail's history id, else the newest internal date less a day when Gmail no longer keeps the history; --since, --dry-run, --restart, paging and backoff. sync --all runs it after mail.
  • logbook sync gcal on the service account: with LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY and LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER set it reads the calendars you own over the Calendar API v3 (calendar.readonly), each event turned into the VEVENT its iCal feed carries and read by the same ics reader, so the line, its raw_id and its source are the ones the feed and an export give. An existing gcal watermark carries over and nothing is written twice (the tour, Google Calendar, has the migration note). Without the two variables the iCal feeds are read as before.
  • Drive lines carry the folder path of their file, root first (["My Drive", "Boat"]), with the drive.metadata.readonly scope: each folder's name asked once and kept in state/drive-cache.json for a week, never in the record. Without the scope the lines carry none and the run says so; lines already written are never rewritten.
  • doctor shows one google line: the key present, the user set, and which of gmail, gcal, drive and gtasks are on it and enabled; it asks Google nothing.
  • logbook people review --from-google: your Google contacts and other contacts (People API, contacts.readonly and contacts.other.readonly, on the one Google key) as a name source for the review. A contact that holds an observed address or number and a canonical person's own is evidence for that pair; one that touches no one the record names proposes to name the observed person as a new person (same email, same phone, same name); contacts that share an address or a number are proposed as one, to merge in Google Contacts. Nothing is merged unless you say so, and no contact becomes a line: accepting writes the name and the identifiers the record already saw, rejecting writes no line. The contacts are cached in state/google-contacts.json for 24 hours and never printed.
  • logbook sync meet: your Google Meet calls from the Meet REST API (meetings.space.readonly), one event/v1 line per call that has ended (tier 1, the participants as Meet names them, the conference record as the reference), and when Meet transcribed it one transcript/v1 line built as Granola's is (tier 3, the words in attachments/). A Granola transcript of the same call stays its own line.
  • logbook sync gaudit: your own sign-ins from the Workspace's login audit log (Admin SDK Reports API, admin.reports.audit.readonly), one event/v1 line per sign-in event, tier 1, with how and the place Google derived; the IP address is never in a line, not even as a digest.
  • doctor's google line names meet, gaudit and what people review --from-google reads.
  • logbook show ideas and logbook show idea NAME (RFC 0037 §7, §11): the ideas you named by stage (build, exploring, spark, built, killed, no status), the most recent touch first, each with its reason (a killed idea that sparked again keeps its old one, said with its day), the words written this year (--year), its repositories, how many people it was discussed with and never their names, the days since its spark, its latest titles and the stale ones said (an exploring over two years with nothing since); one idea's page with every touch newest first, the people by name, its Notion pages and repositories as references (a README's versions), its title thread, the words by month and every status line (ideas read back). A touch is a line that resolves to the idea as review idea finds it; a bot's, an agent's and a relations line are none.
  • The Ideas shelf under logbook serve (Ideas): /ideas, the ideas you named by stage, the most recent touch first, the stale flagged, each with its reason and its evidence folded, the people it was discussed with counted and named only on its own page, and below it the review queue of review idea; /idea/ID, one idea with its status form, first said, every touch, the people by name, its documents, its title thread and its words by month. Accept, Name and No write what review idea --accept, --name and --reject write, the status form what status idea writes (with a reason, the note first), through the same functions, byte for byte; from this machine only, and while another command writes the record an act is a 409 and nothing is written. One column, phone first; an exported site has no Ideas.
  • logbook lab hold census files PATH…, senders and drive: Hold v0, read-only censuses of what you hold (Hold, RFC 0042 draft). files walks the folders you name, never through a link and never into a system or Claude folder: counts and sizes by type and year, duplicates by SHA-256, the 50 largest, folders untouched for two years. senders reads the record's mail lines: senders by count and last seen, the ones never answered, newsletters when a line holds the List-Unsubscribe header. drive reads the record's Drive lines. Each writes a report under state/hold/; the names stay in it, the terminal gets counts, and nothing is moved, renamed, deleted or appended.
  • logbook serve has two new shelves, phone first (a 400 px column), every derived row with its evidence folded (what it rests on, the day, the line ids). Journeys (/journeys?year=): the trips that began in a year, the latest first, each with its name or dates, nights away, return day, route, photos, places, the people the record names (the unplaced counted, a link to the review) and the journey's draft folded; one journey (/journeys/FIRST/LAST) with its stays as dots on a plain canvas drawn by the server (no tile host), its days one row each linking the Day, and the promises made on it (serve). People (/people?year=): the people the record names, by days together this year, then the last real contact; one person (/people/ID) with days together by year, the last real contact and what it was, drift and why, promises both ways, the coming month's anniversaries and the places shared (serve).
  • logbook add --trip ID-OR-DAY "NAME" names a journey (ADR 0019): one note/v1 line in your words, label name, the id under extra.trip, dated inside the journey. The Journeys page's Name this journey writes it through the same function, byte for byte.
  • The People page carries the review queue of people review, the one place an observed person appears: Merge writes what --accept N writes and Not the same person what --reject N writes, through the same functions. Like the Places page's form, both acts and the naming are answered from this machine only (a loopback client, an Origin of 127.0.0.1), one at a time, under the record's writer lock without waiting for it: another command writing is a 409, nothing written.
  • logbook serve's Places page asks you to name the places you return to: the named places first (nights, last visit), then the review queue of setup places review in its order, twenty a page, each cluster with a dot on a plain canvas drawn by the server (the spot, its radius, the nearest named place and distance; no tile host), its facts, its evidence folded, a field prefilled with the best proposal, and Name, Skip and Not a place (Enter, Space, n). Name and Not a place go through the review engine's own accept and reject, so places.json, the naming note and state/places-review.json are byte for byte what --name, --accept and --reject write; the page is read again after each write. The Library's first write act: the form is answered only from this machine (a loopback client, and a browser Origin of 127.0.0.1 when one is sent), else 403 and nothing written (serve). A Day's stay printed as coordinates links to its cluster there (name this place).
  • setup places review folds its evidence: the addresses one source wrote along one street are one line (dawarich: "Plattformveien" (38 addresses, 217 stays)), three lines are shown and … and N more counts the rest; --verbose prints every name as before. The Places page shows the same folding, from the same code.
  • logbook serve's Day page closes the day: Reflect and sign at its foot. Configured by the environment alone: LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN (a fine-grained token, read-only), LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS (owner/name or links, or --all for every repo the token sees but the forks), LOGBOOK_GITHUB_URL (a GitHub Enterprise Server). A watermark per repo, read back a week; a repo with no mark is read whole; --since, --dry-run; every list paged by its Link header, never to another host; GitHub's secondary limit waited out as Retry-After says, its hourly limit until its reset, a 5xx backed off doubling, and a wait too long stops the run on one line with the watermark kept. How many files a commit changed, who closed and who merged are asked only for lines the record does not hold. doctor lists sync:github by name only; sync --all runs it.
  • logbook add github-export DIR: an old project's clone (a working copy or a bare repository, from GitHub or anywhere) or GitHub's account export, read once. A line per commit from the git log with its message in full, and a line per version of a README or a doc with its blob, digest, length and word count, never its text, so an old project's ideas have a first-said date. The account export's issues, pull requests, reviews and comments are the lines sync github writes, so the same commit (by sha) and the same issue (by number) read both ways are one line. Git runs read-only and never fetches; a clone is never called deletable.
  • policy/owner.json lists handles: your logins (ines-example, @ines-example, github:ines-example), by which sync github and the export mark your own acts. Optional, as the other keys are; init writes it empty.
  • people review: a GitHub handle is an observed person, keyed by github:<login> after an email and a phone, named by the name a commit gives, and proposed to the person of that name; your own handles are never listed.
  • logbook sync mail: the mailbox live over IMAP, read-only — folders opened with EXAMINE, bodies fetched with BODY.PEEK[], never a STORE, COPY, MOVE, EXPUNGE, APPEND or flag change, which the tests assert on a fake server's command log. Configured by the environment alone: LOGBOOK_IMAP_HOST, LOGBOOK_IMAP_USER (the mailbox address, the account on every line), LOGBOOK_IMAP_PASSWORD (an app password, never logged, never written), optional LOGBOOK_IMAP_PORT (993, TLS always) and LOGBOOK_IMAP_FOLDERS (default: the folder flagged \All, Gmail's All Mail, else INBOX and the \Sent folder). Every message goes through the mbox adapter's own parse_message, so a Takeout import with --account and the live pull of the same mailbox never write a message twice; headers are fetched first and the record asked which Message-IDs it holds, so no body the record would refuse is fetched. Per folder a mark of UIDVALIDITY and the highest UID, written only once the lines up to it are in the record (state/mail.json): a lost connection resumes from the last batch written, a UIDVALIDITY change reads the folder again and writes nothing new, --since searches from that day, --restart drops the marks, --dry-run counts and writes nothing. With Gmail's extension the labels and the thread id are taken once at ingest, as the import takes them. doctor shows sync:mail; sync --all runs it among the quick sources.
  • logbook sync notion: what happened in Notion on each day, never what the pages say. One event/v1 line (RFC 0009) per page, local day and action — created, edited, moved, archived — with the page's title, the titles above it, its id and url, and who acted (id, name, person or bot, and owner or other); raw_id <page id>/<day>/<action>, so a page edited twice on one day is one line. The body is never stored: the line holds its SHA-256, its length, its word count and the words since the page's previous line, so the Day can say "+340 words" without the text. A database row also carries its status, select, multi-select, date and checkbox values and, for each that changed since the page's previous line, the old and new value; never text, a number, a person, a phone, an email, a url, a file or a relation. A move carries where the page was. Tier 1, as SPEC §4 and RFC 0009 give event/v1, whoever acted. Configured by the environment alone: LOGBOOK_NOTION_TOKEN (an internal integration's secret; share the top-level pages with it), LOGBOOK_NOTION_ROOTS (page or database ids or links to limit to; default everything the integration can see), LOGBOOK_NOTION_OWNER_ID (used only to mark the owner's own actions; else the integration's owning user when Notion names one). Read-only — GET, and POST only to Notion's search — at most three requests a second; a 429 or 503 waits what Retry-After says, another 5xx backs off doubling, and a limit that does not lift stops the run on one line with the watermark kept. The watermark is the newest last_edited_time seen, read back two hours; --since and --dry-run as for every live source. doctor lists sync:notion by name only and asks Notion nothing; sync --all runs it among the quick sources; setup says where the token comes from.
  • review goal: each open goal is asked once a week in the review sitting and answered with --say N advancing|stalled|done|let-go|superseded [--note N TEXT], the line goal review … --period week writes, byte for byte (RFC 0036 amendment 1).
  • dream week asks one stale question a week about the stalest holding or idea (RFC 0037 §10.6), kept in the week's draft as extra.question: never a line of its own, never a status, never above the draft's tier.
  • The call synthesis proposes up to three ideas the call put forward, new or refining one you named; they wait in review idea, marked [call], and reach the Ideas shelf only when you accept one.
  • With the Telegram notifier set, the schedule sends "Your Day page for is ready" after the 06:00 close (LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_LINK_HOST adds the link) and the evening question at LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_EVENING_HOUR: one message each a day, nothing of the day beyond the date, the count and the question.
  • doctor warns on lines dated outside their source's plausible range (calendars 1970 to now plus 5 years, mail 1990 to now plus 1 day, the rest 1970 to now plus 1 day), per source with the earliest and the latest; doctor --implausible lists the line ids; policy/plausible.json overrides a range per source. Nothing is deleted or hidden (docs/doctor.md).
  • transcript synthesize ID|--day DAY [--dry-run] [--show-prompt] [--again]: a model reads one call through the dream's engine, under the same dream entry of policy/crossing.json, and writes one draft/v1 line (unit event, subject the transcript line's id): the actions proposed on top with assignee and due hint, the topics consolidated across the whole call, the decisions (settled, not discussed), the open threads and a short personal part. The schema and the work-only rule are the prompt's (logbook/contrib/synthesis-prompt.md, docs/synthesis-prompt.md), never a filter in the code. Utterances are not lines, so every segment's evidence is the transcript line and the utterances it rests on, with their time into the call, are kept under extra.segments; a reference the material did not give makes the item unsupported and more than 30 % unsupported refuses the answer. A call above the entry's max_tier stays home (the granola and transcript adapters write tier 3); one the same model synthesized is unchanged and nothing is sent; another model or --again supersedes (docs/transcript-synthesis.md).
  • dream --catch-up, and so the 06:00 close, synthesizes each call of the days it covers that has no synthesis yet, and counts the calls the ceiling held back.
  • The Day shows a call's synthesis as one collapsed row under the call's own row, beside the day's draft and never in its place (one draft per unit, RFC 0036 amendment 1); serve opens it behind a toggle, actions on top; day --json carries the items under syntheses; --no-dream leaves them out.
  • A call's synthesis follows the policy like any draft: it records the dream entry it was made under (extra.policy_version); one above the entry's max_tier today is withheld, the Day saying superseded by policy under the call (syntheses_withheld in JSON) and nothing of it; one made under another version of the entry is synthesized again by transcript synthesize and dream --catch-up.
  • The family's home videos as a source (Videos, RFC 0040). logbook sync drive --videos writes one tier-2 video/v1 line per video file in the Drive folder LOGBOOK_DRIVE_VIDEOS_FOLDER names and its subfolders, from Drive's metadata alone (id and path, size, length, frame size, the md5 Drive reports, Drive's created and modified times kept as the upload's under extra, never as when anything was filmed); the line's at is when it was imported; no byte is downloaded, the photos beside the videos are never listed, a quota answer stops with one line and the watermark kept, and each Drive id is written once.
  • logbook videos fetch [--limit N] [--again] [--cache-gb N], the only command of the videos that uses the network: the next files nobody has inferred, one at a time, into a bounded cache under state/videos/ (8 GB unless you say, kept for the next run), each verified against Drive's md5 and resumed from its byte when a download drops; a file bigger than the cap is refused and said so; --again fetches the inferred files too, to infer them under other models or settings. --models fetches the speech and vision models once. Needs drive.readonly delegated to the Google key.
  • logbook videos infer [--since DAY] [--limit N] [--keep] [--dry-run], on this machine with no socket opened: each cached file cut into scenes (one continuous recording each: a cut in the picture, a weak cut with a break in the soundtrack, or a gap of silence; breaks closer than 3 s merged), each scene's speech heard by the transcribe extra and three of its frames looked at by the describe extra; one transcript/v1 line per file (WebVTT, the cues' times the file's; no call, so the 06:00 close and promises leave it out, and transcript synthesize refuses it by day or by id) and one draft/v1 per scene proposing a place from your places.json and assets.json (a sign, a boat's name, what was said) and a date no more precise than a burned-in camcorder stamp or a year written or said, every sentence citing the frames or the speech it rests on, a scene with nothing to go on saying so. Needs ffmpeg on the PATH. The file leaves the cache once inferred; a file inferred again supersedes its earlier draft of each scene cut the same way.
  • logbook review video, one more queue of RFC 0037's one review sitting, listed with the others by review alone: one scene at a time, the surest first, with the frames and speech the proposal cites and, for a proposed day the rules trust, where the record had you and your assets; --accept writes one attribution/v1 line binding the scene to the place and/or date or range (the video's own line is never touched), its own options --place and --date (refused for every other kind) confirm with your own, --reject writes the scene's no, one scene-review/v1 line of its own (RFC 0040 §5, never RFC 0037's entity-review/v1, so no place's or asset's queue reads it), and the proposal does not return while the no stands, --ask keeps the scene in an open task for a later page for the family. doctor gains a videos line: files, fetched, inferred, scenes proposed and confirmed, the cache against its cap.
  • logbook export world --style chart: the record on a period chart, beside the globe in the same folder (world-chart.html; the chart). Mercator's sea chart drawn on the canvas with no image in it: sepia paper, the coasts of the same Natural Earth land hachured, a compass rose and its thirty-two rhumb lines, the graticule engraved with a graduated border, names and dates in the system's serif; stays as pricked positions, journeys as dashed tracks with day marks, assets named along their tracks; the globe's scrubber, line for line; the paper stays light in dark mode. The track is evidence: the page's record JSON is the globe's byte for byte, a track is the straight segments between its own fixes, an asset is at its last fix (never between two), and a day mark is at a recorded position, dated by the record's own days.
  • export world --chart FILE --control-points FILE --chart-credit "…": your own scanned chart (PNG or JPEG) as the paper. Three or more control points (pixel → lat, lon) fit an affine transform (a scan), or with six or more a projective one (a chart photographed at an angle); each point's leave-one-out residual is shown in a corner, and a fit worse than 1 % of the image's diagonal is refused, as are points in a line or a mirror image. The image is carried in the page (at most 4 MiB; a PNG over it downscaled, a JPEG refused), with its EXIF, XMP, text, profile and anything after its end left out, and nothing is fetched: the page's policy stays default-src 'none'. The legend credits the chart in your words.
  • export world --journey ID: one page per journey, in either style — a trip as show trips names it (trip:FIRST:LAST, its days to the return day) or one journey/v1 line (its days, it alone) — each its own file and its own crossing/v1 line.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
• The demo site, bighydro.github.io/logbook/ines/, is exported at tier 2: Ines Nordmann does not exist, so her notes and messages are shown. The docs workflow writes the site entry into the demo record's policy/crossing.json and runs export site --tier 1,2; her health and money, tier 3, never go to a site. One of her days is the way in, at the same path on every build: days/2025-06-14.html, a night at the cabin with Ola. docs/site.md and docs/demo.md say so.
  • docs/home-server.md: running Logbook on a home server, a runbook to follow in an hour. Two users (records holds the record and runs every writer, owner runs the sudo lines Logbook prints), where the record lives and why no synced folder may hold it, serve --install-service --system and sync --install-schedule --system with what each prints, the env file written with read -s, day_start, one writer with an ssh alias and read-only checkouts on the laptop, backups and the monthly restore test, the local model as a daemon of its own and the dream entry, the pages on a phone over a private network, what doctor shows when all is well, and a troubleshooting table. Linked from docs/index.md and the site's navigation.
  • docs: the manifesto, the ten rules, and Letter 0 — why I built it.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
• tests/test_no_network.py runs every reader logbook --help names under the guard that refuses every connection, 147 forms where there were 46: promises and promises tasks, goal list, chapter list, review and each of its kinds, status list, people with merge, review, drift and nearby, show person, asset and place, lab introductions and lab chapters, setup places propose and review, setup assets list, setup questions list, setup day_start, doctor (with --implausible and --packet), doctor sources, import inbox list, import attachments status and verify, key show, backup list, and the dry runs of derive flights, keepers and descriptions, day reflect, repair, export crossing and export trip-bundle; and show orgs and show org NAME on the orgs of tests/orgs_record.py, since the demo names none. Every page serve answers is read under it too: /journeys and one journey, /people and one person, and /world join the eight there were, the Manifest, its people and one org's page read the orgs record, /today is held to its redirect and /favicon.ico to its empty answer. And day reflect DAY --audio FILE, with the Day page's recording form, is heard under it (tests/test_day_reflect.py). No reader or page asked for a connection; no code changed.
  • SECURITY.md, Nothing leaves: dream and transcript synthesize join the commands behind which a socket opens, for the model endpoint the dream entry allows.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: • star/v1 (RFC 0041, draft): the owner's star on a line, line, kind, note, supersedes, at the starred line's at and tier. keeper/v1 gains the MAY field note by a dated amendment of RFC 0024; RFC 0030's trip bundle carries the stars on its lines by another. No envelope change.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• doctor, verify and every reader of the chain hold at most a handful of month files open at once, however many the record has: the chain-order merge (Logbook.lines), the sorted fallback, the index's reads, migrate, seal and append_many each keep a bounded set of handles and reopen a file where they left off. A record of a few decades (hundreds of month files) failed doctor and verify on macOS with [Errno 24] Too many open files under the default limit of 256.
  • logbook sync immich says what it is walking before it starts and never a number that reads as the total unless it is one: the first line is immich: N assets on the server, M already in the record (N from GET /api/assets/statistics, the key's own count, else the server's GET /api/server/statistics; total unknown when neither answers; M through the index), then one page line as x of N assets (x assets since <watermark> on an incremental pull, x assets so far (total unknown) otherwise). A first walk of a 426,121-asset library printed an opening line that was read as a total of about 85,000 and then counted past 467,000, and was stopped as a suspected loop.
  • Each asset is fetched once: pages are ordered by fileCreatedAt, which is not unique (a burst, a live-photo pair, a batch of scans or received files stamped by the importing device share a second), and the cursor names a stamp, not an asset, so the page after a boundary inside a run of equal stamps began at that stamp again and served the run's earlier members a second time — about 41,000 more fetches than assets over that library. The adapter keeps the ids of the previous page's last-stamp run and drops them when they come again; the summary says also N served again by the server at a page boundary, counted once. A run longer than a page grows the page (up to Immich's 1,000) and one longer than that stops the walk with one clear error naming the stamp, never a loop. The record's dedupe by (source, raw_id) stays the safety net.
  • An interrupted walk resumes: after every page the adapter tells sync where the walk could continue, and sync writes that checkpoint (cursor, assets so far, the boundary ids, the watermark so far) under walk in state/immich.json at every checkpoint of the record, never ahead of the lines on disk; the next run says resuming where the last run stopped, at x of N assets and asks for nothing before the saved cursor. The walk's watermark is written only once the walk completes and is never later than the moment the walk began, so what the server changed meanwhile is pulled next time. --restart walks the whole library again; --since begins a new walk; a dry run resumes too and saves nothing.
  • logbook sync --all runs the quick sources first and immich last, and its first line says the order (running dawarich, imessage, …, then immich last), so a photo walk of hours never holds up the messages, the calendar, the positions or the weather. --all refuses --restart as it refuses --since.
  • logbook add <mbox> --dry-run counts a message that appears twice in the same mbox (Takeout writes one under every label it carries) as the real run does — written once, the repeat refused — and says 1 repeated in the input beside what is already in the record, instead of counting both as lines it would add. The counts of sync's summary line carry thousands separators.
  • One writer at a time (#234): append and append_many, and add, sync and import backup for the whole of their run, hold state/writer.lock in the record folder, so a sync's walk is inside it. A second writer prints another logbook command is writing to this record (<command>, since <time>); waiting and waits, or with the global --no-wait refuses with exit 2; a lock whose process is gone is taken over with one line saying so; a reader never takes it. The guard behind the courtesy: before every batch is written, append_many reads logbook.json again and refuses (HeadMoved, one sentence, exit 2, nothing written) when the head moved since the batch was computed, so a batch chained from a stale head can never reach the files. A long sync whose head another command had moved past used to lose its batch with sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: lines.seq from the index, after the month files had taken it.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• logbook serve mcp gains three read tools behind the same mcp ceiling of policy/crossing.json as the nine before (docs/mcp.md): day_lines(day?, kinds?) is logbook show DAY as one object per standing line, in time order, with the line's id, kind, profile, local time, counterpart and the text part of the row show prints, kinds keeping only the profile families asked for (mail, message, transcript, note, location, photo, calendar); line(id) is one line in full, the row, the payload and the text, a transcript's turns read from the attachment store as promises reads them; digest(period?, date?) is the text logbook digest DATE prints, or the seven digests of the ISO week that holds the date. Lines above the ceiling are left out of day_lines and counted in above_ceiling with nothing of them crossing, not even an id; line refuses one naming its tier and nothing else; the digest is read through the gate, so at a ceiling of 1 it is the digest of a record that holds only tier 1. An agent on this machine could search a day's lines but not read them without a word to search for, read a transcript's summary but not its text, and not get the digest; now it can, under the ceiling. The server logs one line per call on the logbook.mcp logger (stderr): the tool, the day or id, and counts — never content. The row show prints for a line moved from logbook/commands/rows.py to logbook/contrib/rows.py so a contrib reader can print it (the commands import the same names); nothing any command prints changed.
  • logbook people review (logbook/contrib/people_review.py, docs/people.md): the record's people in two layers. An observed person is what one source saw, keyed by its strongest identifier — the email address, else the phone number in E.164 (a WhatsApp JID read as the number it spells), else the folded name — never by a per-observation id, so an address seen under three display names is one person; they are a derived table in the index, observed_people, built from the standing mail, message, transcript and event lines, stamped with the head and rebuilt when the record grows, nothing stored in the record. A canonical person is one the resolution lines name, as people lists them. The command proposes each observed person not yet placed against the canonical people, ranked by the evidence (same email 60, same phone 50, same name 20 and +5 per further source, together on the same days 2 per day) and numbered; --accept N[,N] writes the alias line people merge writes, one per identifier as the lines wrote it; --reject N[,N] writes one people-review/v1 line (RFC 0035, draft) saying the two are not the same person, so the pair never comes back; --all-above SCORE accepts at or above. Nothing is promoted on its own; every number is checked before the first line is written; --json carries the queue, the unplaced and a stable id per pair.
  • logbook people --priority [--year YYYY] ranks the canonical people heard in the last year by a plain sum printed beside each name: 3 per day together, 1 per message exchanged (the smaller direction, up to 50), 2 per meeting, 10 when the last real contact is within 30 days and 5 within 90. No model.
  • logbook promises reads mail and messages (docs/promises.md): every mail/v1 and message/v1 line beside the transcripts and the notes, by rules alone, in two sections. I promised is every commitment cue in a line you wrote (a mail from one of your addresses, a message with from_me, your turn of a transcript, a note); I was asked is every request cue in a line you received. Who wrote the line decides, from owner_emails, policy/owner.json and the resolution lines, never the words: a request in your own mail is you asking and is not proposed, a commitment in someone else's is theirs and --all lists it apart. Each row carries the day, the counterpart (to Ola Nordmann, by Kari Nordmann: the person the record resolves behind the address, the number or the chat), the sentence, the due hint, the proposal's id for promises done and the origin line's id, which logbook day sign DAY --confirm takes (RFC 0034). New flags --mine, --theirs and --source mail|message|transcript|note; --since as before. The cue list, documented in full, gains the terse forms of both languages (will do, on it, mach ich, schick ich dir, erledige ich, versprochen, a short by Friday or bis Freitag on its own) and the requests (can you, could you send, would you mind, please confirm, let me know, don't forget to, kannst du, könnten Sie, schick mir, sag mir Bescheid, vergiss nicht). A mail body is read up to its first reply header or signature delimiter with the quoted lines left out, so a reply that quotes a promise never proposes it again. The rules show by default; the judge stays opt-in (--judge), reads your commitments only (never a request), and a verdict of no, or below 0.6, sets a candidate aside, which --all still lists. Under --json every proposal carries role, counterpart and line; the report carries sources, mine_only, theirs_only and all where it carried judged_only. Recall test on a synthetic fortnight of the Oslo persona (24 planted commitments, 12 planted requests, 60 distractor lines across mail, iMessage, WhatsApp and one transcript; tests/test_promises_wider_net.py): the rules read 22 of 24 and 11 of 12 at precision 0.97; the test holds them to 20, 10 and 0.8.
  • logbook repair fork [--apply] (logbook/core/fork.py, #234): a record whose month files hold two chains forked at one head — a long sync wrote its batch chained from a head another command had moved past, and the index refused it after the files took it — is diagnosed (the fork, each orphan chain's count, seq range, sources and files, logbook.json against the record's chain; counts and hashes only, nothing written) and with --apply repaired: every orphan line is copied in order to repair/<stamp>-removed.jsonl in the record folder with a repair/<stamp>-report.json, each touched month file is written again without them with every kept line byte for byte, logbook.json is set to the record's head, the index rebuilt and verify run. The record's chain is the one the index agrees with, else the longer one, else the command refuses; --keep-head <hash> (a full head as the dry run prints every chain's, or a unique prefix) names it and overrides both rules, and without an index the dry run says it is the safer choice; it also refuses a break that is not a fork, a torn month file, a sealed orphan line it cannot open, and a folder under a sync client. doctor's record check names it beside logbook verify; docs/recovery.md is the page.
  • logbook day sign YYYY-MM-DD takes --confirm none and --at RFC3339, RFC 0034 amendment 2 (docs/rfcs/0034-the-signed-day.md, docs/signed-day.md). --confirm none signs a day with nothing confirmed: the signed-day/v1 line carries an empty confirmed, the page digest is still over the page as shown, the header says signed and the day's lines cross as those of any signed day; the word goes alone, and none beside an id or with --kept, --missed, --dropped or --carried is refused in one sentence. --at is the moment the owner clicked rather than the moment the command ran, an RFC 3339 moment with an offset or Z, stored in UTC and shown in the header in local time; a malformed moment (refused with an example), one more than five minutes ahead of this clock, or one before the day signed starts in the record's zone is refused and nothing is written. Without either flag nothing changes.
  • Dispositions on the signed day, RFC 0034 amendment 1 (docs/rfcs/0034-the-signed-day.md, docs/signed-day.md): logbook day sign YYYY-MM-DD gains --kept ID,ID, --missed ID,ID, --dropped ID,ID and --carried ID,ID, and the signed-day/v1 line an optional dispositions object, a confirmed line's id → one of the four words; a line given one is confirmed by that, and an unknown id, a retracted line, a line given twice or a flag that names no line is refused in a sentence. day DAY prints ✓, ✗, – or → before each line the signature disposed of and carries the map under signed.dispositions; show counts them on the signature's row; promises treats kept and dropped as closed, missed as closed and flagged (missed on <day>), carried as still open, and carries disposition in its JSON; export crossing carries the field with the line. The field is optional: every signature written before, the conformance samples' 32nd line included, is valid and its hash unchanged.
  • The signed day, RFC 0034 (docs/rfcs/0034-the-signed-day.md, docs/signed-day.md, logbook/core/signing.py): logbook day sign YYYY-MM-DD [--note TEXT] [--confirm ID,ID] appends one signed-day/v1 line, tier 1, source manual, saying the owner read the day's page and these are its facts — the day, the owner as subject, the ids confirmed (every line on the page by default, else the seqs or ids named), the digest of the page as shown (the SHA-256 over the hashes of the lines the page listed, in order, so any implementation recomputes it) and an optional one-line note. Nothing is rewritten; a day signed again is superseded by the later line, and a retracted signature leaves the earlier one standing. Only the owner signs: the MCP server has no such tool. show DAY says signed <when> or unsigned in its header and lists a signature as a row on the day it was written; day DAY says the same after the weekday, , the page has changed since when the day grew after signing, and carries it under signed in --json. The conformance sample gains a 32nd line, the first day signed on the last evening (new heads in conformance/README.md).
  • logbook export crossing crosses the lines of signed days only, by default (RFC 0034 rule 5): a line's day is the local day of its at, a signature crosses with the day it signs, the console says how many lines were held back on unsigned days, and --unsigned crosses them too.
