A fixture is ten rows for the Oslo persona, every merchant invented, every amount round; a real statement never enters the tree, scrubbed or not.

docs.title: Claiming one
docs.text: Open an issue titled adapter: <source> saying which export you hold and which profile you will write; the captain answers within the week. One adapter per PR, named the same. The expected output file is generated on the first test run and checked in, so the review reads the fixture, the mapping and the expected lines side by side. A profile that does not exist yet goes through rfcs/ first, two weeks of comment, then the adapter.

docs.title: The attachment store
docs.text:
<root>/attachments/<sha256> is where the record keeps the bytes a line points at: a photo, a voice message, a transcript (SPEC §1.1, ADR 0015). One file per distinct content, named by the lowercase hex SHA-256 of its exact bytes, no extension, no subdirectories. The store is write-once and never pruned; a line that points at a file is the reason the file stays. The chain covers lines, not bytes: the digest is in the line, so a changed file is detectable, and verify of the chain never fails because a file is missing. It lists the missing ones and hashes the present ones against their names, a sealed one with the identity (When verify fails).

Three commands tend it. None of them appends a line.

logbook attach import-backup <backup> --only whatsapp,imessage,photos            # fill it from the phone
logbook attach import-backup <backup> --only photos --since 2026-01-01 --dry-run  # what it would store
logbook attach status                                                           # referenced, present, missing
logbook attach verify                                                           # every file against its name

docs.title: Where the references come from
docs.text:
A phone adapter writes the line first and leaves the bytes on the phone. The line names the file by digest and by where the phone keeps it, under extra.media, the same shape for every source:

Source extra.media.local_path The file in the backup whatsapp Media/<jid>/a/b/photo.jpg, below the app's Message/ folder the WhatsApp app group, Message/<local_path> imessage ~/Library/SMS/Attachments/ab/12/<guid>/<name>, or the same under /var/mobile/ MediaDomain, Library/SMS/Attachments/<the part after Attachments>; a message with several files keeps the rest under extra.more_media apple-photos DCIM/100APPLE/IMG_0001.HEIC, below the library's Media/ folder (ZDIRECTORY/ZFILENAME) CameraRollDomain, Media/<local_path>; the digest is also RFC 0002 content_hash

import-backup hashes each file as it writes the line — WhatsApp's and Messages' from the copies it made beside the store, the Photos library's straight from the backup, decrypted on the way when the backup is and never copied — so the line carries {local_path, sha256, bytes}. A file that was not there is extra.media_missing and counted; the line then names no digest, and no pass can fetch what the backup does not hold. LOGBOOK_WHATSAPP_HASH_MEDIA=0, LOGBOOK_IMESSAGE_HASH_MEDIA=0 and LOGBOOK_APPLE_PHOTOS_HASH_MEDIA=0 skip the hashing on a large store; such a line carries the path alone and is counted as without a digest by the pass.

A synthetic line, the Oslo persona's:

{"at":"2026-03-02T17:44:10Z","end":null,"tz":null,"source":"whatsapp","kind":"message","tier":2,
 "payload":{"schema":"message/v1","raw_id":"4790000001@s.whatsapp.net:3EB0A1F5C2D4E6B9","from_me":false,
  "media_kind":"image","extra":{"media":{"local_path":"Media/4790000001@s.whatsapp.net/a/b/photo.jpg",
  "sha256":"5f0c…a41e","bytes":21}}}}

docs.title: Transcripts: what the export holds
docs.text:
A transcript exported as transcript/v1 JSON (Granola's, Fireflies', or a crossing package's) names its text by a reference, content: {sha256, path, bytes, media_type}, and the bytes sit beside it in the export. logbook add transcript <folder> looks for them there, in this order, and nowhere else: the reference's own path (read by its parts, never one that leaves the folder) below the JSON's folder and below the folder you named, then attachments/<sha256> below each, then a file named <sha256> beside the JSON. A spans file (diarization.spans, RFC 0038) is looked for the same way.

  • A file whose bytes hash to the reference is stored under its digest, before the line is written.
  • A file there under one of those names whose bytes hash to something else is refused: never stored, and counted.
  • None found is missing: the line is written all the same, and names a file the store does not hold until an export that holds it is added.
added 0 lines from transcript
  60 already in the record (same source and raw_id), nothing written twice
  also 60 attachments stored

The same export added again finds its lines in the record (by raw_id) and writes none, but stores every file it holds that the store lacks: that is how a transcript imported before its file was there gets it.

docs.title: The lines whose file is missing
docs.text:
logbook doctor --attachments lists every standing line whose attachment (the one import attachments status counts) is not in the store, per source, the most first, then the count by source. Read from the index when it is current, else from the month files; nothing is changed, and it exits 0, since SPEC §1.1 allows a missing file.

granola: 41 lines whose file the store lacks
  019a3c2e-…  transcript  2026-03-02T08:00:00Z  7ed527057371…
fireflies: 30 lines whose file the store lacks
  019a3c2f-…  transcript  2026-03-04T14:00:00Z  2b81fe0c4d19…
71 lines name a file the store lacks: granola 41, fireflies 30. Adding the export that holds them again stores them (…); nothing was changed

docs.title: attach import-backup
docs.text:
logbook attach import-backup <backup> --only <sources> [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--dry-run] reads, through the index, every standing line of the sources named — whatsapp, imessage, photos (or apple-photos); not a retracted line; from the local day --since on when given — and for every digest they name:

  • a file already under that name in the store is present: skipped without being read, which is what makes a run resumable — stop it anywhere, run it again, and it carries on with what is left;
  • a file the backup's Manifest.db lists at the line's path, with its bytes there, is stored: streamed from the backup a chunk at a time — decrypted on the way when the backup is, with the password from LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD exactly as import-backup takes it, never a flag — into a temporary file beside the store, hashed as it goes, and renamed into place under the digest only when the bytes hash to it. A file is never held whole, and a crash leaves no half file under a digest;
  • a stream whose bytes hash to another digest is refused: nothing lands under the name, one line on stderr names the file and both digests, the rest of the run goes on, and the command exits 1 at the end. A blob the backup damaged, or one that does not decrypt, is treated the same;
  • a path the backup does not list, or lists with no bytes, is not in the backup: an iCloud-optimised library keeps a thumbnail on the phone and the pixels elsewhere, and a message's file may have been deleted since.

The same bytes referenced by several lines, or by two sources (a photo forwarded from WhatsApp to Messages), are one file: the second reference finds it present. --only is required, as every run against a real backup should name what it reads (a source disabled in policy/import.json is skipped and said so). --dry-run counts what would be stored and how many bytes, and writes nothing; on an encrypted backup it decrypts Manifest.db into the inbox folder and nothing else. One line per source closes the run, then the store's size:

whatsapp: 1 file referenced by 1 line: 1 stored, 0 present, 0 not in the backup, 0 refused; 1 line without a digest
imessage: 2 files referenced by 2 lines: 1 stored, 1 present, 0 not in the backup, 0 refused

docs.title: attach status
docs.text:
Per source whose standing lines point at an attachment — the one a line points at, as stats counts it: payload.media, else payload.content, else extra.media — the distinct digests referenced, the lines naming one, how many are present and how many missing; then the store: files and bytes, the files no standing line references (left by a line since retracted, or by a run that stopped after the file and before anything pointed at it), and entries under a name that is not a digest. Read from the index and one listing of the folder, nothing else; --json gives the same as one object.

  source        referenced  present  missing  lines
  imessage               2        2        0      2
  whatsapp               1        1        0      1
  apple-photos           1        0        1      1
attachments/: 3 files, 56 bytes (56 B)

docs.title: attach verify
docs.text:
Every file under attachments/ whose name is a digest is streamed through SHA-256 and compared with its name. A file whose bytes hash to something else is listed and the command exits 1 (SPEC §1.1: a present file whose bytes do not match its name is an error); an entry under another name — a temporary file a run left behind — is counted and ignored. A progress line every 500 files. It walks the store, every file whether a line names it or not; logbook verify walks the lines, every file one names, and lists the ones the store does not hold.

attachments/: 3 files checked, 56 bytes, every file matches its name

docs.title: What it never does
docs.text: No thumbnails, no derived files, no cache beside the store (ADR 0015: the store holds the bytes a line names and nothing else). No line is appended, rewritten or removed: the pass writes files the lines already point at. Until it runs, and after a run that stopped, such a line names a file the store does not hold — a missing attachment, which SPEC §1.1 allows: the chain's verify reports it separately and exits 0, status counts it, and the next run fills it in. Nothing is fetched from anywhere but the backup folder on this machine, and add transcript reads nothing but the export folder it is given.

docs.title: Audit — October 2026
docs.text: Measured on 3 October 2026 against commit 4d70394 (main after #200, version 0.5.0). Every number below comes from a command in the appendix; re-run them on a later commit before quoting them.

docs.title: 1. Summary
docs.text:
1. The package is logbook/ (there is no src/ layout): 131 Python files, 57,227 lines, 20,331 of them in logbook/adapters/.
  2. logbook/cli.py is 5,709 lines, imports 61 package modules at module level, and import logbook.cli loads 77 of the package's 131 modules before any command runs.
  3. logbook --help lists 46 top-level commands in 119 lines.
  4. 66 modules sit under logbook/adapters/; the BUILT_IN tuple names 58; pyproject.toml registers 25 entry points, every one a duplicate of a BUILT_IN name.
  5. 31 profile strings appear in the package: 27 line profiles and 4 package manifests. 21 line profiles are read by a reader, rollup, derive or page; 6 are written and read by nothing but show or search; commitment/v1 and commitment-close/v1 are neither written nor read.
  6. RFC number 0025 names two different documents; RFC 0028 is one file under two names; 22 of the 27 RFCs in rfcs/ are not on the docs site, and the site build has 48 broken links.
  7. The README names 17 commands and 14 profiles; all exist. 28 of the 46 top-level commands are not named in the README.
  8. The suite collects 2,853 tests in 141 files (50,594 lines); 7 are stress, 7 slow; 21 Hypothesis properties; 587 readouterr() calls; 8 whole-output equality assertions; 22 monkeypatches of underscore-prefixed names.
  9. No test loads a model: judge, describe, transcribe and promises --judge are tested through an injected importer and a FakeEngine.
  10. The runtime dependency is ijson (5 adapter modules) plus tzdata on Windows; encrypted and share are the same extra; judge and describe install nothing off Apple silicon.

docs.title: 3. What is unused or dead
docs.text:
• commitment/v1 and commitment-close/v1 (RFC 0007): specified, listed in SPEC.md §4 and docs/promises.md, never written, never read. promises writes task/v1 instead.
  • migration/v1: written once per migrate, read by no module.
  • crossing/v1: written by every export and share, read back by nothing but show.
  • browse/v1, watch/v1, trip/v1, highlight/v1: written by 4, 1, 3 and 2 adapters respectively, read by show and search only. No Day, rollup, page or derive consumes them.
  • The 25 entry points in pyproject.toml: each names a module BUILT_IN already loads; all_adapters() imports them a second time and discards the duplicates.
  • logbook/adapters/takeout/calendar.py: a complete adapter (NAME, sniff, run) in no registry; add Takeout/Calendar reaches the same files through ics.
  • logbook demo and logbook demo --years: demo.py and demo_life.py are 2,696 lines (4.7% of the package), imported by cli.py at module level for every command.
  • 22 RFCs under rfcs/ are not in mkdocs.yml; the site links to them and the links are broken.

docs.title: 4. What disagrees with itself
docs.text:
• Two adapter registries. BUILT_IN (58) and the entry points (25) register the same modules by different names (apple-books vs apple_books); 33 adapters are in one and not the other; docs/adapters/README.md describes third-party adapters registering the entry point, which is the only purpose the group serves.
  • screentime writes kind app-use with schema event/v1; every other writer of event/v1 writes kind event. rollup attention selects by screentime.KIND, so the lines are read; day.py's event selection does not see them.
  • RFC 0025 is two documents: rfcs/0025-trip-bundle-v1.md (trip-bundle/v1, trip-share/v1, received/v1; 119 lines, dated 2026-10-03) and docs/rfcs/rfc-0025-shared-page-bundle.md (shared-page/v1; 217 lines, dated 2026-10-02). rfcs/README.md links both under the same number.
  • RFC 0028 is one file with two names: rfcs/0028-story-v1.md and the symlink docs/rfcs/0028-story.md; mkdocs.yml names it "0028 story/v1 (draft, unfinished)".
  • RFC 0027 exists only under docs/rfcs/; the sequence in rfcs/ skips it.
  • rfcs/README.md calls commitment/v1 a seed profile and links its RFC; the code has no writer and no reader.
  • SPEC.md §4 places commitment/v1 and commitment-close/v1 in the tier table beside profiles the code writes.
  • README vs code. Every command the README names exists: 17 top-level names in backticks, 50 two-word forms (export vault, backup restore, infer keepers, add story, rollup money, …), all dispatched in cli.py. Every profile the README names (14) is written by the code. The README does not name 28 of the 46 top-level commands: assets circle days describe digest import import-backup index infer keepers ledger migrate people person questions receive repair retract rollup search share show stats tasks transcribe trip trips verify year (several appear in two-word forms or without the logbook prefix). The README's live-source table names 5 of the 9 live adapters; adsb, ais and weather appear in command examples, apple-podcasts nowhere.
  • The docs site builds with 48 warnings, every one a link to a file outside docs/: 26 from rfcs/README.md, 15 from index.md, 6 from CHANGELOG.md, 1 from CONTRIBUTING.md. mkdocs build --strict fails; .github/workflows/docs.yml deploys without --strict.
  • Pre-commit excludes docs/rfcs/*.md from the whitespace hooks because the files are symlinks; three of them are regular files.

docs.title: 5. Tests: what the suite guards and what it only pins
docs.text:
What it guards:

  • The envelope and the chain: conformance/sample-logbook with conformance/expected.json is verified in CI by logbook verify --expect, and tests/test_jcs.py pins RFC 8785 hashing.
  • Adapters against drift: 21 Hypothesis properties in 16 files generate exports and assert every yielded line validates; test_fuzz_readers.py carries 3 of the 7 slow marks.
  • No network on the default path: tests/test_no_network.py and the socket guards in conftest.py, test_describe.py, test_promise_judge.py, test_transcribe.py, test_ais.py, test_gcal.py, test_serve.py, test_mcp.py.
  • The CLI end to end: 26 files run logbook through subprocess.run.

What it only pins:

  • Console text. 587 readouterr() calls and 862 substring assertions on captured output check wording, column layout and phrases from cli.SKIP_PHRASES. A rename of a command or a rewording of a line fails tests without any line of the record changing. Whole-output equality is rare (8 assertions), so the pinning is by phrase, not by screen.
  • Private names. 22 monkeypatch.setattr calls target underscore-prefixed attributes (_together, _finite, …); those tests bind the suite to the current factoring of the module.
  • The model commands. test_promise_judge.py (16 tests), test_describe.py (19) and test_transcribe.py (20) pass a fake importer or a FakeEngine into judge.py, describe.py and transcribe.py; no test imports mlx_lm, mlx_vlm, mlx_whisper or faster_whisper, and tests/test_mcp.py is the only importorskip. The suite proves the plumbing around a model, never a model's answer.
  • Markers. slow tests run only with LOGBOOK_SLOW=1 (CI: push to main and nightly, not pull requests); stress never runs in CI. A pull request therefore runs 2,839 of the 2,853 collected tests and skips 7; the one test that takes 56% of the wall clock, test_demo_years.py::test_the_long_trips, has no mark and runs on every pull request.

docs.title: 6. Dependencies
docs.text:
• One runtime dependency, ijson, carried by 5 of 66 adapter modules; the other 126 modules of the package need the standard library only. A core without adapters has no third-party dependency.
  • Two extras are one: encrypted and share both declare cryptography>=42 and resolve identically.
  • Three extras are Apple-silicon-only in effect: judge and describe install nothing on any other platform and the commands exit 2 with an install line; transcribe falls back to faster-whisper, which pulls torch (45 packages).
  • mcp pulls 32 packages (pydantic, starlette, uvicorn, jsonschema, …) for one command, logbook mcp.
  • The dev group installs pytest, pytest-xdist, pytest-cov, hypothesis, ruff, mypy, pre-commit; mkdocs-material and pymdown-extensions are not in the lockfile and the docs workflow fetches them with uvx.

docs.title: 7. The three decisions
docs.text:
Recorded as the owner gave them on 3 October 2026.

Decision 1 — Commands: 46 top-level commands become 22. Every old name stays as a hidden alias that prints one line naming the new command. Help fits on one screen.

Decision 2 — Profiles: the profiles read by readers are frozen for v1.0 (expected 18); profiles written but never read are parked (expected 10): their adapters keep writing them, their schemas are marked "parked, may change", nothing is frozen about them. commitment/v1 and commitment-close/v1, neither written nor read, are deleted. trip/v1 is renamed journey/v1 with a reader-side alias for existing records. The freeze is specified in its own RFC.

Decision 3 — Packaging: one package, openlogbook, with three tiers inside it — core (format, record, verify, the frozen profiles' readers), contrib (adapters, exports, derived readers), labs (model-touching and experimental commands). Old import paths keep working through shims for one minor version. No split into two distributions before v1.0.

docs.title: Measured against the expected counts
docs.text:
Set Expected Measured (§2.5) Difference Read by readers (to freeze) 18 21 3 more: voice-memo/v1 (read only by transcribe, a labs command), received/v1 and trip-share/v1 (read only by the shared section of trip <id>). Without those three the set is the expected 18. Written, never read (to park) 10 6 line profiles; 10 with the 4 package manifests The 6: browse/v1, watch/v1, trip/v1, highlight/v1, crossing/v1, migration/v1. The manifests crossing-package/v1, day-package/v1, trip-bundle/v1, shared-page/v1 are formats of a folder, not of a line; the freeze RFC has to say whether they are in scope. Neither written nor read (to delete) 2 2 none

The counts differ from the expectation on the first two rows. The 21 and the 6 are what the commands in the appendix return; the freeze RFC must name its 18 and its 10 explicitly and decide the fate of the five profiles that fall between the two definitions (voice-memo/v1, received/v1, trip-share/v1, crossing/v1, migration/v1).

Two facts the decisions rest on, checked: the distribution is already named openlogbook (pyproject.toml line 2; the import package is logbook); trip/v1 is written by easypark, sbb, passages and demo and read by no reader, so the rename to journey/v1 touches 4 writers, the show renderer, search.KINDS, RFC 0020 and the README.

docs.title: 8. Order of work
docs.text:
1. Hygiene first, because every later step is measured against a baseline without duplicates: delete the 25 entry points or BUILT_IN (one registry); move the three regular files out of docs/rfcs/ or the 22 missing RFCs into mkdocs.yml; renumber one of the two 0025s; make mkdocs build --strict pass and run it in CI; remove commitment/v1 and commitment-close/v1 from SPEC.md §4, rfcs/README.md and docs/promises.md and mark RFC 0007 withdrawn. No behaviour changes; no changelog line a user needs.
  2. One package, three tiers (Decision 3), because the command and profile work must land in the tier it belongs to: logbook/core, logbook/contrib, logbook/labs, with shims at the old paths. The import graph in §2.2 is the checklist: cli.py must stop importing 61 modules at module level or every tier loads for every command.
  3. Commands (Decision 1), because it depends on the tiers: 46 become 22, old names become hidden aliases, and the 862 substring assertions on console output in §2.7 tell which tests pin the old wording.
  4. Property tests for the frozen readers, because the freeze needs a guard that does not depend on console phrases: one Hypothesis property per frozen profile asserting that any valid line is read without error and that Day is a function of the lines alone, alongside the 21 properties that already cover adapters.
  5. The freeze RFC (Decision 2) last, because it names the 18 and the 10 from the tiers and the readers as they stand after steps 2–4, renames trip/v1 to journey/v1, and is the one document the v1.0 tag points at.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
logbook backup DEST copies the record to another disk, verifies the copy there, and prints its head, which is the head of the live record or the command fails. Every snapshot is a complete record of its own that logbook verify accepts and logbook backup restore brings back; a file that did not change since the last snapshot is a hard link to it, so the second snapshot and every one after costs only the bytes that changed.

logbook backup /Volumes/Backup/Logbook                 # one snapshot, verified
logbook backup /Volumes/Backup/Logbook --keep 14       # then prune to the newest fourteen
logbook backup /Volumes/Backup/Logbook --verify        # also hash every attachment against its name
logbook backup list /Volumes/Backup/Logbook            # what is there, with lines, head and size
logbook backup restore /Volumes/Backup/Logbook/<owner_id>/2026-06-02T071500Z ~/Records/Logbook

backup: 2026-06-03T071500Z → /Volumes/Backup/Logbook/019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-000000000010/2026-06-03T071500Z
  214 files, 1.2 GiB: 3 copied (4.1 MiB), 211 linked to 2026-06-02T071500Z
  valid — 12,772 lines, head 53d39fda0b2c9e1f…
  kept 14 snapshots; pruned 2026-05-20T071500Z

docs.title: What a snapshot holds
docs.text:
DEST/<owner_id>/<timestamp>/, the record's files at their own paths and nothing else:

In the snapshot Left out logbook.json index.sqlite — a derived locator; the next reader rebuilds it (ADR 0007) logbook/<YYYY>/<MM>.jsonl, the record inbox/ — copies of exports, not the record policy/ — crossing ceilings, disabled sources, the owner's aliases state/ — sync watermarks, bookkeeping; a restored record syncs again from the start and appends nothing twice places.json, assets.json export/, logbook-0.1/, anything else attachments/ — content-addressed, write-once a file whose name begins with . (an attachment still being written) notes/ voiceprints.age — the voiceprint registry, a cache rebuilt from the audio the snapshot carries (setup speakers --rebuild); one copy of a biometric is the most there should be (Speakers)

The timestamp is UTC, 2026-06-02T071500Z, so snapshots sort by name on any filesystem (no colon; Windows refuses one). Two snapshots in the same second get -2, -3. <owner_id> is the record's, from logbook.json, so one backup disk can hold several records without the snapshots mixing, and --keep only ever counts one owner's.

docs.title: Hard links
docs.text:
The second snapshot links against the first: a file whose size and modification time are those of the same path in the previous snapshot becomes a hard link to it, the way rsync --link-dest does it, and only a file that changed is copied. A month file grows as the month goes on and is copied until the month closes; logbook.json changes with every line; an attachment never changes, so the store, which is where the gigabytes are, is copied once. Every snapshot is still a whole record: a hard link is the same bytes under two names, each name as good as the other, so pruning one snapshot never touches another, and restore copies, never links, so the restored record is independent of the backup disk.

A filesystem that refuses the link (exFAT, a network share, a snapshot on another volume) gets a copy, and the command says how many files were linked and how many copied. The copy is pure Python and streams: a file is read a chunk at a time, never whole, and nothing is shelled out to.

docs.title: Verified, every time
docs.text:
The copy is written under .<timestamp>.partial, then logbook verify runs on it, by the files alone, and its head must be the head logbook.json named when the copy began. Only then is the directory renamed to <timestamp>. A copy that does not verify, or whose head is not the live head, is removed and the command exits 1 saying why; backup list never shows a dotted directory. So a crash leaves at most a .partial directory you can delete, and a directory that looks like a snapshot is one that verified.

A line appended while the copy ran makes the month files run ahead of the copied logbook.json (SPEC §3, write order); that copy does not verify and the command says the record changed while it was copied; run the backup again. A scheduled backup at a quiet hour never meets this.

--verify also hashes every file in the copy's attachments/ against its name (SPEC §1.1: a file whose bytes do not match its name is an error). It reads every attachment, so it costs what the store weighs; without it the chain is verified and the attachments are copied as they are. The chain covers lines, not bytes, so a corrupt attachment on the live disk is caught only by --verify, and then before the snapshot is kept: run it now and then, and always before trusting a disk you are about to retire.

docs.title: Where a backup may go
docs.text: The destination is refused, before anything is written, when it is inside the record (a backup goes to another disk) or under a folder a sync client owns, by the same detection logbook doctor uses for the record itself: iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive, by any part of the path, its resolved path, or the OneDrive variable Windows sets. A sync client keeps the backup on someone else's server and may evict it; back up to a plain local disk or a drive you plug in. A folder that is a file is refused too.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text:
logbook backup restore SNAPSHOT TARGET copies the snapshot — never links — to a folder that does not exist yet or is empty, verifies the result and prints its head. It never writes over anything, the record included: to replace a damaged record, move it aside first. A target under a sync client's folder is refused as above, and a code checkout is never empty, so that rule covers it. The restored record has no index.sqlite; the next reader builds it, or run logbook index. Point LOGBOOK_HOME at it.

A snapshot is an ordinary record: logbook verify --root SNAPSHOT checks it where it lies, and LOGBOOK_HOME=SNAPSHOT logbook day 2026-06-02 reads one day from the backup disk without restoring anything (the reader builds its locator in your cache directory, keyed by the record's owner_id; nothing is written into the snapshot). Never append to a snapshot; the next backup links against its files.

docs.title: backup list
docs.text:
019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-000000000010
  2026-06-01T071500Z  12,760 lines  head 9a0e4c31d2b7…  1.2 GiB (1.2 GiB new)
  2026-06-02T071500Z  12,768 lines  head 7c15e0aa94d3…  1.2 GiB (3.9 MiB new)
  2026-06-03T071500Z  12,772 lines  head 53d39fda0b2c…  1.2 GiB (4.1 MiB new)

One owner per block, snapshots oldest first, each with the lines and head its logbook.json claims (what was verified when it was written; list reads the file, it does not verify again), the size of the whole snapshot, and in parentheses how many of those bytes are its own — not shared, by a hard link, with an earlier snapshot in the list. The last number is what deleting the snapshot would free. A directory whose logbook.json cannot be read is listed as not readable, with the reason, and the listing goes on. list needs no record and can run on the backup disk from any machine.

docs.title: The monthly restore test
docs.text:
A backup that was never restored is a hope. logbook backup --restore-test takes the latest snapshot of the last backup, restores it into a temporary folder, verifies it there, compares it with what the record said when the backup was taken, deletes the restore, and writes state/last-restore-test.json, which logbook doctor reads. The schedule runs it on the first Sunday of every month, after the sync, once that day; by hand it runs any time.

logbook backup --restore-test                          # the last backup's latest snapshot
logbook backup --restore-test /Volumes/Backup/Logbook  # a destination by name
logbook backup --restore-test --to ~/Restored          # restore into DIR and keep it there

restore test: 2026-10-04T030000Z
  valid — 12,772 lines, head 53d39fda0b2c9e1f…; line 12,772 of the live chain
  passed; state/last-restore-test.json

What is tested, in order:

  1. The copy restores: backup restore into the temporary folder, so the same code path a real restore takes is the one tested, refusals included.
  2. The copy verifies, by the files alone: every hash recomputes and its logbook.json names the last line. A snapshot whose month file was changed by a byte fails here. A record that seals tiers 2 and 3 is verified with the identity (--identity-file, LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE, or the default path), so every sealed line is opened and checked against its digest: a backup you could not read is a backup you do not have.
  3. It is the backup the record made: logbook backup DEST writes state/last-backup.json (where the snapshot went, and the live record's line count and head at that moment); the restored copy must have that count and that head, and that head must be the hash of that line in the live chain. A snapshot of another record, or one whose files were replaced, fails here.

The outcome is passed, failed with the reason, or skipped: no backup recorded yet (run logbook backup DEST once), or a sealed record whose identity the run cannot see. The scheduled run never prompts, so the identity has to be in the agent's environment: LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE=<path> in ~/.config/logbook/sync.env, or the restore test is skipped and doctor warns with that line until it is. The exit status is 0, 1 and 2 for the three outcomes. --to DIR keeps the restore (DIR must be new or empty, and never under a sync client's folder) for you to look at with logbook verify --root DIR or LOGBOOK_HOME=DIR logbook day …; delete it when done.

doctor has a restore-test line: a pass when a test passed within 35 days, a warn when there has been none, the last is older, or it was skipped, saying what to do, and a fail when the last test failed, with its reason. state/last-restore-test.json is bookkeeping: a snapshot leaves state/ out, so a backup never carries it or last-backup.json.

docs.title: A schedule
docs.text:
logbook backup is a one-shot command, so the machine's own scheduler runs it the way logbook sync --install-schedule runs sync --scheduled (the schedule). Once a day at 03:00, after the evening sync, keeping two weeks:

macOS, launchd. ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.logbook.backup.plist, with the Python that has logbook installed (which logbook tells you the path to put in place of /usr/local/bin/logbook):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
  <key>Label</key><string>org.logbook.backup</string>
  <key>ProgramArguments</key>
  <array>
    <string>/usr/local/bin/logbook</string>
    <string>backup</string>
    <string>/Volumes/Backup/Logbook</string>
    <string>--keep</string><string>14</string>
  </array>
  <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
  <dict><key>LOGBOOK_HOME</key><string>/Users/ines/Records/Logbook</string></dict>
  <key>StartCalendarInterval</key>
  <dict><key>Hour</key><integer>3</integer><key>Minute</key><integer>0</integer></dict>
  <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>/Users/ines/Library/Logs/logbook-backup.log</string>
  <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>/Users/ines/Library/Logs/logbook-backup.log</string>
</dict>
</plist>

launchctl bootstrap gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.logbook.backup.plist
launchctl bootout gui/$(id -u) ~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.logbook.backup.plist   # to remove it

A drive that is not mounted at 03:00 makes /Volumes/Backup a plain folder on the system disk, and the backup lands there: give the agent a path only the mounted drive provides, or a .plist whose ProgramArguments runs /bin/sh -c 'test -d /Volumes/Backup/Logbook && exec logbook backup …'.

Linux, a systemd user timer. ~/.config/systemd/user/logbook-backup.service and .timer:

# logbook-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=logbook backup: one verified snapshot, keep fourteen
# the backup disk is a mount: nothing runs when it is not there
ConditionPathIsMountPoint=/mnt/backup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
Environment=LOGBOOK_HOME=%h/Records/Logbook
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/logbook backup /mnt/backup/Logbook --keep 14

# logbook-backup.timer
[Unit]
Description=logbook backup at 03:00 local

[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 03:00:00
Persistent=true
Unit=logbook-backup.service

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

systemctl --user daemon-reload
systemctl --user enable --now logbook-backup.timer
systemctl --user list-timers logbook-backup.timer      # the next run
journalctl --user -u logbook-backup.service -n 20      # the last run's output
systemctl --user disable --now logbook-backup.timer    # to remove it

Persistent=true runs a missed night the next time the machine is up; ConditionPathIsMountPoint skips a night the disk is not plugged in rather than writing to the mount point's empty folder. Either scheduler prints the same four lines the command prints by hand, to the log file or the journal, and a backup that did not verify is an exit status 1 there and no new directory under DEST.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It does not encrypt: a snapshot is the record as it is, plain, and the disk it is on needs the protection the record's own disk has (FileVault, LUKS, a drive in a drawer). It does not go to a server, a bucket or a sync folder, and refuses the last. It does not keep state/, so a restored record's next sync by hand reads each live source from its start, and its first scheduled run each source's last 14 days (the schedule); append_many skips what is already in the log, so nothing doubles. And it does not replace logbook verify on the live record: a backup of a broken record is refused, not repaired, and the command says to run logbook verify (When verify fails says what each failure means).

docs.title: The commands
docs.text:
logbook has 32 commands, grouped here by what you are doing. logbook --help is this list on one screen; logbook <command> --help has a command's arguments. Everything that was a command of its own before 0.6 still answers to its old name: it prints one line saying the new one and runs it (the table at the end, generated from the code by scripts/command_aliases.py).

One writer at a time: a command that appends (add, sync, import backup, and every other through append) holds state/writer.lock in the record folder for its whole run, a sync's walk included. A second writer says another logbook command is writing to this record (sync immich, since 2026-09-10T06:00:00Z); waiting and waits; with the global --no-wait it refuses and exits 2. A lock whose process is gone is taken over with one line saying so. Readers (show, day, verify, every reader) never take it. The lock is the courtesy between writers; what keeps the chain whole is that a writer reads logbook.json again before every batch and writes nothing when the head has moved.

docs.title: Start
docs.text: Command What it does init create a logbook (default ~/Logbook) setup the guided first run, one question at a time, resumable; and the record's settings: setup places, setup assets, setup questions, setup day_start (where your day begins), setup phone (whether your own phone writes through the Library behind Tailscale Serve, off by default, from your phone), setup agents list|add SENDER [--name NAME]|remove SENDER (your own bots by the sender id Beeper gives them, whose lines add beeper and sync beeper mark machine text, your own agents), setup speakers (what separates voices on this machine and the voiceprints it keeps; --fetch-model downloads its models, the one network event; --rebuild makes the voiceprint registry again from the record, speakers); setup map PATH names the offline OpenStreetMap file maps are drawn from, its header read first, --off to remove it (the map); setup places review names the places you return to from what the record already knows, offline, and with --ask-photos from what your photo libraries say about the photos already in it (places) doctor the check-up, one line per check, exit 1 on a fail, the crossing ceilings, the record's home (ADR 0022), the last scheduled run, the last restore test and the serve service among them, and lines dated outside their source's plausible range (--implausible lists them, The doctor); --attachments lists the lines whose attachment the store lacks, by source (the attachment store); --packet [--out FILE] is a diagnostic to send a collaborator, with no line's content, no name, no home path and no value in it, and one probe of the dream endpoint when it is set (Sending a diagnostic); doctor sources lists every adapter and, with --gaps, where each went quiet

docs.title: Write
docs.text: Command What it does add a sentence in your words, an export file, a folder of them, or flight "LX 561 NCE ZRH …"; --trip ID "NAME" names a journey; add gift DAY NAME "WHAT" [--received] what you gave someone, or were given: one note/v1 line labelled gift, the person under extra.recipient or extra.giver; a name that is nobody, several people or you is refused in one sentence (gifts) import import backup DIR reads every phone source of an iOS backup; import trip-bundle FOLDER a trip another record exported; import page FILE a day someone shared; import inbox what is in inbox/; import attachments the attachment store; import pickup FOLDER [--write] a folder of call transcripts collected from the receiving side, moved into the record (the pickup) sync pull new items from a live source (immich, dawarich, imessage, beeper, gcal, drive, gtasks, meet, gaudit, granola, mail, gmail, notion, telegram, github, ais, adsb, weather, heard); --all for every configured one, immich last; beeper: --networks chooses the bridged networks; an interrupted immich walk resumes, --restart walks the library again; sync mail reads a mailbox over IMAP, read-only, resumed per folder from the last batch written (LOGBOOK_IMAP_HOST, _USER, _PASSWORD; --since searches from that day, --restart drops the marks); sync notion writes what happened to each Notion page on each day, one event/v1 line per page, day and action, never the page's text, a database row with its database and the ids of the rows its relations link to (LOGBOOK_NOTION_TOKEN; LOGBOOK_NOTION_ROOTS, LOGBOOK_NOTION_OWNER_ID), and --relations-backfill [--since DAY] one line per row whose relations the record does not hold yet (--dry-run counts them); sync telegram writes what you sent your own bots from what the Bot API still holds, read-only, never confirming an update (LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKENS, LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_OWNER_ID; Your own agents); sync github writes a line per commit, issue or pull request created, closed or merged, review and comment, read-only, a watermark per repo (LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN, LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS; your handles in policy/owner.json), and add github-export DIR an old project's commits and doc versions (a private repository's lines are tier 2, a clone's too unless --public); sync gmail, sync gcal, sync drive, sync gtasks, sync meet and sync gaudit read Gmail (the line sync mail writes), the calendars you own, Google Drive's activity with each file's folder path, Google Tasks, your Meet calls (and their transcripts, as Granola's are) and your own sign-ins from the Workspace's login audit log (never the address), read-only, with one Workspace service account, a scope per source (LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY, LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER; gcal reads its iCal feeds, LOGBOOK_GCAL_URLS, only without them; the tour's Google, on one key); sync drive --videos lists the family's video folder (LOGBOOK_DRIVE_VIDEOS_FOLDER) instead, one video/v1 line per file from Drive's metadata, nothing downloaded (Videos); sync heard stores the words of the podcasts and videos you played, a feed's transcript fetched once (at most LOGBOOK_HEARD_MAX_FETCHES a run, two seconds apart), Apple Podcasts' cached transcripts and your own caption files, one heard/v1 line each, after every other source but the photo walk (LOGBOOK_HEARD=feed,apple,captions; What you heard); --install-schedule runs sync --scheduled (sync --all, then doctor, the outcome to state/last-run.json, one message when something is wrong; a source's first scheduled run reads its last 14 days, never its whole history, the schedule) at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00, and at 06:00 sync --scheduled --close, which closes the day (the dream's catch-up after the sync); --system for a machine nobody logs in to goal your goals, one goal/v1 line each in your own words, tier 2 (goals): goal add TEXT --horizon life\|year\|quarter [--from DAY] [--until DAY] [--supersedes GOAL] writes one (a goal reworded is a new goal that supersedes the old); goal review GOAL advancing\|stalled\|done\|let-go\|superseded [--note TEXT] [--at DAY\|RFC3339] [--period day\|week\|month\|quarter\|year] your verdict on it, on the day it is about (written in October about August, it is on the August Day); The orgs you named in the Manifest (entities) show up in a day's lines: a mail from one of their addresses, a meeting with someone of theirs, a link into one of their repositories. logbook lab companies DAY reads them back for one day, each with what touched it and the lines (RFC 0043, §11 and §12). docs.title: What touches an org
docs.text:
Through the refs the record binds to the org, the way show orgs finds its touches, on a line of the day that stands (not retracted, not superseded):

What The line update a mail from an address at one of the org's domains mail a mail to someone there, or copied to them meeting a calendar entry with an attendee (who did not decline) or the organizer at one of its domains; a transcript with a participant there; a call whose counterparty is an address there document a link into one of its repositories: a page browsed, a task, an act sync github wrote

Each touch names the people of theirs on the line, by the record's name for the address, else the name the mail, the transcript or the calendar entry shows, else someone at the org (someone at Nordmann Verft AS): never a bare address. Your own addresses and domain are never an org's, and a calendar's rooms are the service's. A group chat and a merchant bind an org too; neither is an update, a meeting or a document, and what was paid is the money slot's (below).

docs.title: Status and portfolio: tier 3
docs.text:
An org's status (hold, add, sell, exited, passed, let-go) is tier 3 (RFC 0037 §8), and so is its portfolio, the field of its latest status line that carries one (logbook status org NAME hold --portfolio "Fund I"; RFC 0037 §10.2 as amended on 15 October 2026; the Manifest's entity/v1 line never carries one). A row says them only where tier 3 is read, and the rows group by portfolio, in its words, the orgs in none last under no portfolio. Your terminal reads every tier. Through a gate without 3 (a page served at a lower entry) no row carries a status or a portfolio, every row is in one group, and the reading says status not shown: an org's status is tier 3, and this reads no tier 3.

--json gives day, statuses (whether tier 3 was read), hidden (the sentence, when it was not) and groups, each a portfolio and its companies: org, name, status, portfolio and the touches, each what, kind, line, seq, title and people.

The reader is logbook.contrib.companies.companies_of(lb, day, tiers=None). It reads one day's lines through the index and the naming lines by kind, as show orgs does; never a sweep of the record's mail.

docs.title: The money slot
docs.text:
What a day paid is logbook.core.money.money_in(lb, start, end, tiers=None): the transaction/v1 lines of the local days start to end, each with its merchant, amount and currency, and the totals per currency, read as the ledger reads them (a correction stands in place of the line it corrects; a retracted line is out; a line the source marks deleted is listed, marked, and never summed). Every one of them is tier 3, and so is where they end: through a gate without 3 nothing of it is shown, not a line, a total or a date.

It never shows an empty sum. A payment source covers the days from its first transaction line to its last; when none covers the day, it says so from the record's own lines:

  • No payment source covers this day — the last ends 2026-10-06, for a day after the last line;
  • … — the first begins 2026-10-01, for a day before the first;
  • … — the record holds no payment lines, for a record with none;
  • No card lines for this day, for a day inside the span with nothing paid.

A window that runs past the last line lists what it holds and names the days past it. There is no command of its own: the Day page will show it. Receipt mails proposed as payments are not read here.

docs.title: The crossing
docs.text:
logbook export crossing --to <member> --since <RFC3339|last> [--until RFC3339] [--tier 1|1,2|1,2,3] [--kinds a,b] [--unsigned] [--open] [--out DIR] [--force] [--dry-run] hands one member of your circle the lines of a window that the tier policy lets cross: a crossing-package/v1 folder (RFC 0005) under the member's ceiling in policy/crossing.json (ADR 0016), the lines of signed days only unless --unsigned (the signed day), and one crossing/v1 line in the chain that says what left. --dry-run counts and writes nothing.

logbook export crossing --to kari --since 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z --until 2026-03-02T00:00:00Z --dry-run
logbook export crossing --to kari --since last --out ~/Handover/kari

A member is a person, never a name the policy keeps for its own reader or door: mcp, hermes, dream, site, vault, world, folder, heard, chat, phone, notion, letter and relationship, in any case, are refused in one sentence before anything is written, by export crossing and export share day alike, so a package never lands under a reader's entry, watermark or folder.

docs.title: Drafts follow the entry they were written under
docs.text: A model's draft (draft/v1, the dream) crosses only while the entry it was written under allows its tier, whatever the member's ceiling: a person's draft (dream person) the relationship entry, every other draft (a day's, a journey's, a week's, a call's synthesis) the dream entry. Once that entry's until has passed, it is removed, or its max_tier is below the draft's tier (and, for the relationship entry, when it has no until), the draft stays home and counts says how many did, held_back_by_entry (written only when one did); a record with drafts and no dream entry ships none of them. A shared page (export share day) holds its drafts the same way: one its entry no longer allows stays home, counted in the manifest's held_back and in the crossing line's held_back_by_entry. A video scene's draft (video review) is written on this machine under no entry and crosses by its tier like any line. With the entry in force the package is what it was.

docs.title: A shared page holds what a package holds
docs.text: export share day sends one day to one person, as a package sends a window, and holds it to the same rules through the crossing's own functions: only a day you have signed leaves (an unsigned one is refused in one sentence that names logbook day sign), and a mail crosses only when a person is on it. The page's manifest counts each: held_back_unsigned always, mail_held_back whenever the day held a mail; both are part of held_back, and the crossing line's counts say the same. A shared page has no --unsigned and no --all-mail.

docs.title: People's mail
docs.text: Since 21 October 2026 (RFC 0045), mail crosses only when it is a person's: a mail you received from someone the record names as a person, or one you sent to one, its sender not let go in Hold (people's mail). Whenever mail is among the kinds (no --kinds, or --kinds naming mail), the rest stays home, its resolutions and attachments with it, and counts says how many as mail_held_back, written whenever the window held a mail the tiers and signed days let through (0 when every one was a person's); a package with no mail is what it was, byte for byte. --all-mail crosses every mail the tiers and signed days let through, as before, and the manifest's policy says "mail": "all".

docs.title: The package
docs.text:
<DIR>/
  manifest.json          what crossed and why, and the list of every other file in the folder
  entries.jsonl          the lines that crossed, verbatim
  resolution.jsonl       the resolution lines their refs resolve through, when any cross
  attachments/<sha256>   the files those lines point at that the store holds

A line's refs are the {kind, value} refs in its payload (a message's sender, a calendar guest), a mail's from, to, cc and bcc addresses, and a transcript's participants' email, phone and provider id, so the resolution that names someone on a mail or in a transcript crosses with it.

manifest.json lists every other file of the package under files, in path order:

"files": [
  {"path": "attachments/<sha256>", "sha256": "<hex sha256>", "bytes": 48213},
  {"path": "entries.jsonl", "sha256": "<hex sha256>", "bytes": 1840}
]

path is relative to the package, with / on every platform. sha256 and bytes are those of the file as it is in the package: for an attachment resealed to the member, of the sealed file, while its name and its entry in blobs give the plaintext's. The digest of manifest.json itself is the package_sha256 the crossing line records. A reader checks that the folder holds these files and manifest.json and nothing else, and hashes each one.

docs.title: The output directory
docs.text:
Without --out, every run writes a folder of its own, <root>/export/crossing/<member>/<time>. With --out DIR, the bundle replaces DIR whole, so DIR never holds anything the new selection left out.

The bundle is built from nothing in a hidden folder beside DIR, .DIR.<random>.staging, on the same disk. It is checked against its own manifest, every file in it listed in files and every listed file there at its length, and only then renamed to DIR. Whatever was at DIR is first renamed aside, to .DIR.<random>.old, and removed once the new bundle is in place. At every moment DIR is the earlier bundle whole, nothing, or the new one whole, never a mix: a tier-1 crossing into the folder of an earlier --tier 1,2 one leaves none of its tier-2 lines, resolutions or attachments behind.

What DIR may be:

  • Missing. It is made, and its parents with it.
  • An empty folder. It is used.
  • An earlier bundle. A folder whose manifest.json is a crossing-package/v1 manifest, from a crossing or a trip bundle, of this version or an older one. It is replaced, and so is anything you put in it since.
  • Anything else. A file, or a folder that holds anything and no such manifest, is refused (exit 2) before anything is written: no crossing line, no watermark, no policy file. --force replaces it and removes everything in it.
  • The record, or a part of it. The record's own folder, a folder that holds it, and any path inside it that is not under <root>/export/ (where the default --out is) are refused whatever the flags, --force included, and a path inside it is refused even before it exists, so a second run is never the first refused. Folders are told apart by the disk, not by the name, so ~/logbook on a disk that ignores case is the record at ~/Logbook.

A symbolic link at DIR is followed: the folder it names is replaced, and the link names the new bundle.

An export that fails, for example on a store file that no longer hashes to its name or a full disk, removes its staging folder and leaves DIR as it was, and appends no line. A crash part of the way can leave .DIR.<random>.staging (a bundle not yet in place) or .DIR.<random>.old (the earlier one) beside DIR, and, between the two renames, DIR itself missing. Nothing reads either folder: delete them, and run the export again.

Before this, a second export into the same DIR overwrote the files it wrote and left the rest. A folder that more than one export was written into may hold files its manifest does not name: an attachments/<sha256> that is not in blobs, or a resolution.jsonl when the manifest has no resolution_file. Look before you hand such a folder over, or export into it once more.

logbook export trip-bundle (shared trips) writes its package the same way, its trip.json among the listed files, and takes --force too. logbook export notion (export for Notion) writes its folder the same way, its own manifest listing its files, and replaces only an earlier folder of its own.

docs.title: The pickup
docs.text:
What crosses can come back. The receiving side keeps the calls it was handed or recorded itself (Granola's, Fireflies'), and the Purser, a separate program on your Mac, collects them into a folder of its own. Until they are moved in, they wait outside the record. logbook import pickup moves them:

logbook import pickup ~/Purser/pickup                       # what it would take; nothing written
logbook import pickup ~/Purser/pickup --write               # take them: store, append, move out
logbook import pickup ~/Purser/pickup --write --source granola   # the provider of the files that name none
logbook import pickup ~/Purser/pickup --write --keep        # take them, leave the files where they are

pickup ~/Purser/pickup: 61 files
  58 to take: granola 31, fireflies 27
  skipped: 2 already taken (by hash), 1 without a source (name it with --source)
took 58 files: 58 lines appended (granola 31, fireflies 27); 58 files removed from the folder

Every file below the folder, in path order, subfolders included, is read by the transcript adapter, the one mapping every transcript source shares, and so takes what logbook add transcript takes: a transcript/v1 JSON, a WebVTT, an SRT or a Markdown file. Hidden files, and an attachments/ folder where an export keeps the files its JSON references, are passed over. Each call becomes one transcript/v1 line:

  • Its source is its own. A transcript/v1 JSON names its source (its source, else its payload's provider), and the line keeps it, --source or not. A WebVTT, SRT or Markdown file names none: --source names its provider, and without it the file is left in the folder, counted without a source. Nothing is taken as manual by default.
  • Its tier is the file's, else 3, as for any transcript (it carries other people's words in full); --tier sets one for every line.
  • Its text is stored in the attachment store before the line that points at it (SPEC §1.1, ADR 0015).
  • It says where it came from: payload.extra.picked_up is {"sha256", "file"}, the SHA-256 of the file's bytes and its path below the folder.

A file already taken is skipped by its hash: the same bytes again, under any name, in any later run, are already taken, never a second line. A file whose call the record already holds by the same source and raw_id (the same Granola note pulled by sync granola, say) is already in the record: no line is written, its text is stored if the store lacks it, and the file is left for you to look at. A file the adapter does not read, or one with no start, is counted and left.

A dry run unless --write. Without it nothing is written, stored or removed. With it, the files taken are removed from the folder once their lines are in the record, and so is a file found already taken (a move an earlier run left half done, say by a crash between the append and the removal); --keep leaves every file where it is. A file that cannot be removed is named on stderr and the command exits 1; its line is in the record, and the next run finds it taken. The folder is never the record or a part of it, told apart by the disk and not by the name (exit 2), and nothing is fetched from anywhere: the files are on this machine.

docs.title: The Day
docs.text:
logbook day YYYY-MM-DD [--json] reads one calendar day back from the record: where you slept either side of it, which country it counts for, how you moved and where you stayed, what attached to each stay and who was there, the flights, when you slept and the day's steps, the weather, and which sources spoke. It is a reader (ADR 0013): a function of the record at its head, derived every time and never written. Nothing is appended, and not even policy/stays.json is created by it.

logbook day 2026-06-13          # a Saturday, as text
logbook day 2026-06-13 --json   # the same Day as one JSON object, every row with its line ids
logbook day 2026-06-13 --no-anniversaries   # without the days together years ago
logbook day                     # today
logbook day sign 2026-06-13     # sign it: you read the page and these are the day's facts (RFC 0034)
logbook day sign 2026-06-13 --kept 4181 --carried 4183   # and what became of the commitments on it
logbook day sign 2026-06-13 --confirm none --at 2026-06-13T22:10:00+02:00   # nothing confirmed, signed when you clicked
logbook day reflect 2026-06-13 --audio evening.m4a --sign   # close it in your words, then sign it

The header says whether you have signed the day (· unsigned, or · signed 2026-06-14 08:15), and the last row, readiness, says for each class of source — mail, message, meeting, location, photo, calendar — whether the day has lines of it and which usual sources have not delivered. Both are the signed day; day sign and day reflect are the things under day that write: day sign one line, day reflect the reflection as one note and, with --sign, the delegations you accept and the signature. On a signed day a symbol stands before each line the signature disposed of (✓ kept, ✗ missed, – dropped, → carried); an unsigned day prints none. A day with a reflection shows it in a section of its own, reflection, below the header and above the timeline: your words, as you said them (closing the day by voice).

docs.title: What a Day is
docs.text:
The record's atom is the line. The reader's atom is the stay: a span at one place, as derive stays finds it. A Day is the ordered list of stays and moves between 00:00 and 24:00 in the record's zone (between your day_start and the same clock the next morning when you set one, below), with everything else — calendar entries, transcripts, notes, mail, calls, messages, photos, keepers — attached to the stay or move it falls inside. The night of a day is the longest stay in the night window (22:00 to 08:00 by default), and it decides home or away; a night with no such stay is in transit.

Aboard an asset (a boat, an aircraft, a car registered in assets.json) the grammar nests: when your position matches the asset's own track, the run of stays and moves aboard it is one stay aboard <asset>, and inside it the same grammar runs on the asset's position — a berth, a passage, an anchorage. The asset's movement never fragments the stay. The rule is below, under Aboard an asset.

docs.title: The day begins at…
docs.text:
…midnight, unless you say otherwise. logbook setup day_start 06:00 writes "day_start": "06:00" to logbook.json (the record's settings), and from then on a line whose local clock is before 06:00 belongs to the day before: the concert that ended at 01:30 on the 13th is on the Day of the 12th, the coffee at 07:00 on the 13th's. The Day of the 12th then runs from 06:00 on the 12th to 06:00 on the 13th, and its header says so:

2026-10-12  Monday · unsigned · 06:00 to 06:00 the next day

Everything on the page follows: the timeline is clipped to that span (a stay that began the evening before shows from 06:00), the lines attached and unplaced are the ones on the day so defined, the sources and the health line count them, and the signed day's page is that page. The nights keep their window (22:00 to 08:00, policy/stays.json); the night after is the one that holds the day's end, the stay you were at at 06:00 the next morning, and the night before the one that holds its start. With 06:00 those are the nights they are at midnight; a boundary at or after the night's start, 23:00 say, ends the day inside the next date's night, and that night is the night after. The comparison is on your wall clock, so the night the clocks change moves no line. A day_start that is not a clock HH:MM ("6am") is refused, naming it, and nothing is guessed. At midnight the header and the JSON are as they always were.

docs.title: What it shows, in order
docs.text:
1. Header — the date and weekday; the night before and the night after (a named place, aboard <asset> with the asset's position that night, or the coordinates; home when the stay lies in a place of kind home or within 400 m of one — the night then names that place — else away; in transit when no stay reaches the minimum); the country, from the night's position by the same rule rollup countries uses (a place's own country, else the nearest large airport's zone), from the longest stay of the day when the night is in transit; the day's all-day calendar entries; and, on a day you said who was there (logbook with, the acts), with: everyone a row confirms and everyone you stated, your word marked (you said). Beside the night after's place, the day's weather in short, 4° · rain, when the day has a weather line of that place.

Under the night before, the Night line, when a night ends on the day:

  night before  Home · home
  night         slept 23:10–06:40 · 7 h 20 min · training 45 min
  night after   Home · home · 4° · rain

When you slept — the first and the last minute asleep, on the record's clock — how long asleep (never in bed or awake), and the day's training when it has some. It is derived when the Day is read, from the health-sample/v1 lines already in the record (Apple Health's sleep stages and workouts), and nothing is written. A night is one device's asleep stages with no gap over two hours between them; it belongs to the day its last stage ends in, under your day_start, so with 06:00 a night from 23:10 to 06:40 is one night of the 13th, never split between the 12th and the 13th. Of the nights that end on a day (a nap is one) the longest is its night, and of two devices the longer, never their sum. Training is the union of the day's workout spans (on the day they start), so a run the watch and a phone app both recorded counts once. A day no night ends on has no row; under --json it is night (start, end, start_local, end_local, asleep_s, device, lines — the stages — and training: minutes and lines, or null), a key present only on such a day, so the Day's object is otherwise the one SPEC §3.2.7 gives. 2. Timeline — one row per stay, stop, move and flight that touches the day, in time order. A stay that began the evening before shows from 00:00 and one that runs on shows to 24:00 (from and to the day's start under day_start); the duration printed is the part on the day, and --json keeps the real span beside it. An unnamed stay at an airport is the airport's code and city (ZRH, Zurich: within 3.5 km of the reference point of an airport with scheduled traffic, 2 km of any other); else its coordinates, with near <place>, x km for the nearest named place within 5 km (59.9200,10.7400 near Home, 1.0 km), else the city of the nearest large airport within 30 km in parentheses (53.5998,10.0130 (Hamburg)), the trips route's rule. A stop with nothing attached says so. A move prints its distance, duration and mode (walk, car, train, boat, flight), with the airports (OSL → ZRH) only when it is a flight: its speed and distance are a flight's (mode flight), or a flight/v1 line lies inside it or over at least half of it, whose departure and arrival it then names. A car or train move whose ends lie near an airport — a 1.6 km drive from the car park to the terminal — names none. A move with no points that lasts a silence or more (merge_gap_s) and is not a flight is a gap: the tracker did not see it, so it places nothing. Flights come from the flight/v1 lines standing — the merged set infer flights maintains, one line per flight — with their evidence: tracked, inferred or declared; the move a flight covers names it under --json. Under each row: its attachments, named for events (with their time; an entry several calendars carry is one event, see below), transcripts (with their voices when the line has them, who spoke most first and never a time beside a voice, Middag · you · Kari Nordmann and 1 unnamed · recorded with consent: unknown, a voice not yet named by its label, who they are; a transcript another of the day supersedes is not listed beside it), notes (the first line), mail threads (with the message count), calls (the length first, 19 min ← Ola Nordmann, never beside the name) and keepers, and counted for messages and photos; then with, the people there, split into confirmed — declared in a note (with <name>, only a name the record's resolution lines make a person: with US names nobody), speaking in a transcript (a voice you named, or a participant; the far end of a call is never there, and a person you would not name is counted, with.unnamed), attending a timed calendar entry that overlaps the stay — and proposed — a face the photo library tagged, by id or by the name it gave it (extra.faces; a person only when the name is exactly a resolution line's label, else as written), an attendee of an all-day entry. The owner is never their own company. A move carries attachments but no company. A line you starred (logbook star) is marked ★ where it is listed, your goal, review and chapter rows among them. 3. Unplaced — the day's events, transcripts, notes, mail and calls that fall inside no stay or move: what the calendar planned where the track has nothing, or what happened while the tracker was silent. Then Stories about this day (RFC 0028, a draft): the story/v1 lines standing whose refers_to covers the date — a told year, month, day or decade — each as show prints it (📖 refers to 1961 — told by Ola Nordmann to Kari Nordmann) with the teller's confidence and the day it was told, and its first line under it. A story is a line on the day it was told; it is never in the timeline of the day it is about, because the timeline is what was observed and a story is what someone said. A story whose time is a phrase (before the war) is about no day. The section is absent when no story is about the day. Then anniversaries: the days together exactly 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 years before, with the same canonical person — a stay together, and so a day of a journey together, by the rule people counts a day together with (the with module's confirmed set) — one row each, the nearest years first, then by name, five at most: 1 year ago, 2024-11-03: Kari Nordmann · Office. A person only the sources saw, never named by a resolution line, is never one. Under --json it is anniversaries (years, day, id, name, where, lines), a key present only on a day that has one, so the Day's object is otherwise the one SPEC §3.2.7 gives. --no-anniversaries leaves them out. See people. 4. Health — the night's sleep in hours (the asleep stages of the night that ends on the day, per device the union of their spans, the longest device), the day's steps (the larger device per quarter hour, summed), the resting heart rate (the day's mean), from the health-sample/v1 lines standing. A correction that supersedes a line wins over it. The text says the sleep once, on the Night line, so the health row prints the steps and the resting heart rate, and a day whose health lines were only sleep has no health row; the JSON keeps sleep_h as SPEC §3.2.7 gives it. 5. Weather — when the day has weather/v1 lines (RFC 0026, logbook sync weather, adapters/weather.md), one row: the lowest and highest temperature, the precipitation, the strongest wind, the weather in a word, sunrise and sunset, for the place of the night when the day has one, else the first, and · 2 places when the day was spent in more than one. A day without them has no row. 6. Sources — every source with a line on the day, how many, and its newest line's time, so a tracker that fell silent in the afternoon is seen to have. 6. From the circle — one from <name> section per page someone shared for this day and logbook receive verified (RFC 0025, <root>/circle/<name>/<date>/): how many lines by kind, the tier it was shared at and the day it was shared, then the titles of its events, transcripts, notes, mail and calls, one per row. The page is read from the folder it was kept in, never from the chain; under --json it is received, each named line with its id. A day nobody shared has no such section. 7. The draft — printed between the header and the timeline, above every note of the day: the standing draft/v1 line a model wrote about the day (the dream, RFC 0036), headed draft with the model's name, the head and how many lines it read, how many times the day was dreamed and when last, and how many segments are unsupported; then one row per segment with the part it belongs to (day, thread, question, people, promise), its text and its evidence ids shortened. An unsupported segment starts with ~ and ends with unsupported (and why, when the reader found an id that is not on the day), never run into the prose around it and never as a fact. Then the events it proposes (the dream), one row each, event N with the span, the title, the place and the people: a proposal waiting for you starts with ? and ends with proposed and its evidence (greyed on the serve page); one you accepted (day sign --accept N) says confirmed as #seq, and its event line sits among the day's events in the timeline, where it places its people as a calendar entry does. What you can keep is numbered after the proposals: a sentence learned, decided, about an idea and the photo of the day end their row with it (keep 3; at the end, so no number stands beside a name the sentence opens with), a proposed link keeps its own (link 2), and day sign --keep N keeps one before it signs; a sentence or link you kept says kept as #seq (Keep and sign). The draft is a proposal; your signature and your notes are the facts. --no-dream leaves it out. An earlier draft of the day stays in the record, listed by id under --json, and show lists every draft line on the day it was written. A draft follows the dream entry of policy/crossing.json, not the head: one above the entry's max_tier today (lowered, expired or removed since) is not shown, and when the day's standing draft is one, the row says superseded by policy and why, and nothing of the draft, its proposed events included (the dream, When the entry changes). 8. Goals, reviews and chapters (RFC 0036, goals) — the chapter the day is in, in the header after the signed state (· chapter The Lofoten summer, with , clashes with <name> should two standing chapters hold the day); after the draft, a reviews row per review standing on the day the verdict is about, let go · month · <the goal's current text> · <note>, ending written 2026-10-11 20:30 when it was written on a later day; then the goal and chapter lines written on the day, each · superseded when a later line replaced it. 9. A call's synthesis — one row under a transcript's own row, whether the call is attached to a stay or unplaced, collapsed: synthesis · 1 action, 2 topics, 1 decision, 1 open thread, 1 personal · model:…, with how many items are unsupported when any is. It is the standing draft/v1 line of unit event a model wrote about that transcript (the synthesis of a call, transcript synthesize); its items, actions on top, are behind a toggle in serve and under syntheses in --json. --no-dream leaves it out with the draft. A synthesis follows the dream entry as the draft does: one above the entry's max_tier today is not shown, and the row under the call says superseded by policy and why, and nothing of the synthesis (the synthesis of a call, When the entry changes).

docs.title: What makes a stop a stay
docs.text:
A short cluster of points — the ten minutes at the cafe — is a stop unless something of the owner's falls inside it: an event, a transcript, a note, a call, a message or a photo (SPEC §3.2.3 rule 5). Then it is a stay, marked promoted: the evidence says the owner was there, and duration is only the fallback.

An event counts only when it happened somewhere:

  • it carries a location (any source: a Wallet pass with its venue, a ticket with its address), or
  • it carries attendees (someone was invited to it), or
  • its source is one whose entries are places and times whatever they carry: a calendar (ios-calendar; ics, which sync gcal and Takeout's Calendar/ write too) or Google Home's history (Takeout's Home App, an arrival or the alarm at the door; source google-takeout, calendar google-home).

A Notion page edited, a Drive file changed — by the owner or by someone else on the owner's file — happen nowhere: they carry no location and no attendees, and their sources are not physical. Inside a stop they do not make it a stay, and attached does not count them (stays.somewhere). SPEC 0.4 §3.2.3 rule 5 says the same, test for test, and ADR 0023 says why. The Day still shows them under the row their time falls in (Boat jobs, Edited Crew list ×3), as it does any event; they are simply not evidence of where the owner was. A task (task/v1, sync gtasks) is not an event and was never evidence.

docs.title: One event from several calendars
docs.text:
The same entry often reaches the record twice: from the phone's calendar (ios-calendar) and from a Google calendar or a subscribed .ics (ics; sync gcal writes its lines under that source, so two calendars of one source are told apart by the calendar they name). Two event lines are one event when they come from different calendars, start less than a minute apart, last as long as each other or one of them is all-day, and carry the same title (case, accents and whitespace aside) or name the same flight (XY561, XY 561). The Day shows it once: the richest line of the set — a timed entry before an all-day one, then the one that fills the most fields (location, attendees, notes) — with the others named, Check-in XY 561, from 07:40 to 08:00 · from 2 sources (ics, ios-calendar), and under --json its sources (its own first) and the ids of every line it stands for. The fold is at read time only: every line stays in the log as written, and the sources row counts each.

A Notion row seen by sync notion and again by sync notion --relations-backfill is one event too. The backfill's relations line adds the row's relations to an edit the record holds already, so the Day shows the page's own line on the day, with notion its one source and the backfill's line among the ids it stands for; the Day page of logbook serve shows it once as well. A page with no other line on the day keeps the backfill's line as its row. show still lists both lines, as it lists every line of the day.

sync drive writes one line per Drive file, hour and activity, so a morning spent on one document is several lines. The Day page of logbook serve reads them as one row, the file's name and what was done to it counted, Budget 2027 · 5 edits, 2 comments, standing for every line it folds; the fold is the page's alone, and logbook day and --json list each line, as before (In a browser).

docs.title: In a browser
docs.text:
The Day page of logbook serve is this Day with what a page can add: a sentence under the header on what crosses where (the tiers in plain words), the week's draft on its Sunday and a link to it from the six days before, the day's track drawn from the stays' own coordinates, each row's photos as a strip under it (starred first, a thumbnail only from the record's own attachment store, the rest counted), a link from every row that is a line to the line as written (/line/ID), a photo review at its foot, and the acts: a star, with…, Reflect and Sign (In a browser, the acts). A day no device saw, the phones off, still takes with…: "I was with Ola" is one line, the line logbook with writes.

The page also shows everything the day held, folded so it stays readable (In a browser). Under each stay or move, where this page counts the messages, the page lists them by conversation: who it was with (the person the record names, else the handle as the line has it, a group by its name), the network (whatsapp, telegram, instagram, …) and how many, then each message's time, sent or received and its text, the first 280 characters of it, the whole a click away on its line. A conversation of more than 30 shows its first 10 and folds the rest under show all N. At the foot, Everything this day held: every line of the day, by source and in time order, each with its time, its kind, one line of what it was and a link to it, the count per source on its summary as the sources row has it. Every fold is closed until you open it, or until ?open=1 opens them all. Both come from the one reading the page makes of the day; logbook day and --json are as they were, and so is a static site's Day (logbook export site), which counts the messages.

docs.title: The page's four shapes
docs.text:
The Day page has one look and four shapes, and it takes the one that fits the hour each time it is asked for. Nothing about the shape is stored; it is worked out from the clock, the evening hour and the day's signature on every request.

  • morning: today, from the day's start until 11:00, or until the first stay of note after the night (somewhere that is not where you slept), whichever comes first.
  • live: the rest of today.
