  • evening: today from the evening hour, the one the daily messages use (LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_EVENING_HOUR, in the environment or in ~/.config/logbook/sync.env), and every earlier day not signed. With no evening hour set, today stays live until midnight.
  • signed: a day with a standing signature.

A day ahead of today is live: nothing lived yet, the plan so far. A static site (logbook export site) has no clock, so its Day is the evening's, or the signed day's. It also skips the two parts that read beyond the day for every page it writes, the promises of Loose ends and Looking back.

The demo record (logbook demo --out ~/Demo/Logbook), Tuesday 23 June, in the evening, before it was signed; the same day signed leads the README. The demo carries no real drafts, so the pencil here is a stand-in model's (stub-model), written for the picture from the day's own lines. Nothing in it is real.

docs.title: ?shape=
docs.text: /day/2026-06-17?shape=morning (or live, evening, signed) shows the same day in another shape, for reading. It says that it is shown for reading and links to the day's own shape. The forms on it are the page's own and do what they always do. A word that is not one of the four gets the shape the clock gives.

docs.title: The ribbon
docs.text: The day in two lanes, from its start to its end (midnight to midnight unless day_start says otherwise), with the hours every three. PLANNED shows the calendar's timed entries: filled when something lived is beside one (the Day placed it at a stay or a move), hollow and dashed when nothing is (an entry the Day leaves unplaced). An all-day entry is not drawn. LIVED shows the stays, moves and time aboard in their colours, with calls as thin ticks. The task tool's tasks of the day that carry a time are ticks on the PLANNED lane in the morning (of the five the plan shows). On today a line marks now. When the calendar has nothing timed the lane says so, and a day with no stay says why. A sentence for a screen reader says the same, and a legend names the colours. Every block's tooltip and the sentence say the time first, then the entry (19:30 — Dinner with Per Hansen), so a clock time never follows a name. Nothing on it weighs the plan against the day.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
• The header: the weekday, the shape and the time; the date; where the night was spent, the weather when the record has it, and who was there. Under it, as before, the nights, the country, the signature and the with… row.
  • For: the chapter the day is in (its rules in quotes) and the goals the day touched, each linked. A goal is touched when a line of it, a review of it, or a review naming one of the day's lines as what it rests on was written on the day. With no chapter and no goal written at all, the page says it can't tell what the day was for; with some written but none for this day, it says that instead. In the morning, under them, This week: the intention you kept on the Sunday before (closing the week), in ink, with that Sunday, linked to its Day.
  • Yesterday (morning): signed or open, how many it kept, what arrived after its signature (with a link to sign again), what it carried, and the nearest earlier day still open, within 60 days.
  • Today (morning): the ribbon so far, then the day's timed entries and the promises due today, a row each; then, each in its fold, open, with its summary: Today's tasks from the task tool and the next trip, and Who you'll see; then the week's one proposal, in pencil (The morning, below).
  • One person (morning): a birthday in the coming week, from a resolution line's extra.birthday; on a morning with none, one person to reconnect with (The morning, below). Nothing when there is neither.
  • Loose ends: the promises made on the day and the ones due on it, both ways (yours, asked of you, owed to you), the replies owed, the decisions the day's call syntheses wrote, and the decisions to revisit (these two in the morning). Read-only: the verbs (keep, carry, let go) come later. A promise is due on a day when it was said in the 14 days before it.
  • People: who showed up, the most time together first, from the people confirmed at a row, the ones you said were there and the people on the day's calls. Birthdays in the coming week are listed too. A name never has a count, an age or a score beside it: a birthday is only its day.
  • Looking back: in the morning the decisions whose revisit day is the day, first; then this day 1, 2, 3, 5 and 10 years ago, the ones the record has: where the night was spent, who was there, how many photos were starred, and the first sentence of that day's reflection.
  • Photos: how many, how many starred, the starred ones this machine holds, then the photo review. In the morning they are folded into the record, so Add to today comes straight after it.
  • The record: the folds, each with its summary in counts: the timeline under the day's track, everything the day held, the sources and the rest. Nothing from names, in one line, every part that has nothing for the day. The timeline and the sources are always there: a day with no line says nothing logged and none.
  • The pencil: the dream's draft, as the page has always shown it, on ruled paper. Each sentence has its evidence marks, and a sentence nothing supports is in italics, marked unsupported. A signed day folds it at the foot, with how many of its proposals you confirmed.
  • Close the day (Add to today in the morning and live): Reflect and Sign, the same forms as before.

Every row is computed from the record. What a model wrote is in pencil, with the lines it rests on.

docs.title: The morning
docs.text:
What the morning looks ahead with, each read from a reader the record already has, through the page's gate, and each named in Nothing from when it has nothing. Through a gate, the reconnect and the replies owed name a person only when it reads every tier from 1 up to theirs (through tiers 1 and 3, nobody whose evidence reaches tier 3). None of it writes a line, and none of it is on a site (logbook export site): a site's Day is never the morning.

  • Today's tasks, from the task tool's rows sync notion wrote (logbook show plan, docs/plan.md), tier 1 alone, so only on a page whose gate reads tier 1. A task's day is the plan's: its Planned date, else its Due date, unless policy/notion.json names others (docs/plan.md). Five at most, each linked to its line (/line/ID) and to its page in Notion (a link you follow; nothing is fetched), the rest one line: and 4 more in Sprint 24 — open in Notion. Then the next trip as one countdown in words: Per's wedding in Bergen — in five weeks. A mapping the page cannot read is one sentence saying why, never an error page.
  • Who you'll see: the attendees of the day's timed calendar entries who did not decline, by name, each once, never the owner, with no count. A person the record resolves is named as it names them when the page's gate reads their resolution; otherwise by the name the entry gives, or not at all.
  • One reconnect, on the morning only, the day itself: one person the drift rule names (logbook people drift, its defaults: twenty days together in their best year and no real contact in over a year), with the reason in words and no digit: Per Hansen: you saw each other often the year before last; the last real contact was a day together in the summer that year. Never the same person two mornings running: the pick is the day's ordinal among the people the drift rule names, in the order of their ids, skipping the one the day before would pick (with one person, every other morning). A birthday in the coming week comes first, and that morning has no reconnect. The drift rule reads the whole record (minutes on a record of millions of lines), so the page reads it once a day and keeps it for the day, whatever syncs in meanwhile.
  • Replies owed, in Loose ends, in the morning: a person the record names whose last word to you (a direct message, a mail of theirs, a call you did not answer) is more than a week old (replies_owed, RFC 0045 §5), said with a name and weekday words only: Ola Nordmann wrote on a Thursday in May, Kari Nordmann wrote on Tuesday last week.
  • Decisions to revisit: a note/v1 line labelled decision whose extra.revisit is a local day, YYYY-MM-DD, comes back on that day's morning, in Looking back and in Loose ends: A year ago you decided: “Keep the berth in Vollen.” How did it turn out? This is the format the close writes when you keep a decision with a date to revisit:
{"schema": "note/v1", "text": "Keep the berth in Vollen.", "labels": ["decision"],
 "extra": {"revisit": "2027-06-09"}}
  • The week's one proposal: when the standing draft of the week before (written on its Sunday, so it proposes for this week) made one (its next_week part), one line under Today, in pencil, headed with the model's name and linked to the draft. Through the gate and the dream entry as every draft on the page; never on a page built without drafts. Once you keep an intention for the week (on the week page, or logbook day reflect SUNDAY --intention "…"), the intention is under For, in ink, and the pencil is not drawn: kept, it is yours. An intention that would set a number beside a person's name is withheld, the row saying so.

The task tool's plan, the reconnect, the replies owed and the decisions to revisit read more than the day: the plan every sync notion line, the drift rule the whole record (minutes on a record of millions of lines), the replies owed the ninety days before the day, the revisits every note (seconds each). logbook serve reads them beside the page, on one thread it starts once the page is rendered, so no page waits for them: until a reading has arrived its part is not drawn and not named as empty, and the page is read again when it has (its tag names what arrived). The plan, the replies owed and the revisits are read again after a sync, and the page shows the earlier reading meanwhile; the drift is read once a day. On a record of five million lines the morning answers in the Day's usual time, and the reconnect arrives some minutes later (Performance, below).

docs.title: A synthetic example
docs.text:
The Oslo persona of the test suite, who does not exist, spends a June Saturday aboard the yacht Solvind. The owner's position matches the boat's AIS track from the marina out to the anchorage, so the day is one stay aboard, with the berth, the passage and the anchorage inside it, a note that declares who was there, and the night aboard:

2026-06-13  Saturday
  night before  Home · home
  night after   aboard Solvind · 59.8500,10.6000 · away
  country       NO (nearest airport OSL)

  00:00–09:00  stay   Home · 9 h
  09:00–09:15  move   1.4 km · 15 min · walk
  09:15–24:00  aboard Solvind (yacht) · 14 h 45 min · 1 note, 1 photo, 1 keeper
      09:15–10:00  stay   Marina · 45 min
      10:00–12:00  move   9.7 km · 2 h · boat
      12:00–24:00  stay   59.8500,10.6000 · 12 h
      note         Anchored in the bay with Ola Nordmann. Grilled.
      keeper       IMG_131730.HEIC (memory)
      with         Ola Nordmann (note)

  health        no lines
  sources       dawarich 888 lines, last 23:58 · immich 1 line, last 19:30 · keeper-inference 1 line, last 19:30 · manual 1 line, last 19:00

A Thursday whose tracker was silent from nine to five, with a lunch in the calendar during the silence and an all-day entry, and the night's sleep, the steps and a resting reading (corrected once) in the record:

2026-07-02  Thursday
  night before  Home · home
  night after   Home · home
  country       NO (nearest airport OSL)
  all day       Kari in town

  00:00–09:00  stay   Home · 9 h
      with         proposed Kari Nordmann (calendar)
  09:00–17:00  gap    8 h · no points · 6.3 km
  17:00–19:00  stay   59.9600,10.8199 · 2 h
      with         proposed Kari Nordmann (calendar)
  19:00–19:30  move   6.4 km · 30 min · car
  19:30–24:00  stay   Home · 4 h 30 min
      with         proposed Kari Nordmann (calendar)

  unplaced      12:00–13:00  event  Lunch

  health        sleep 7.0 h · 3,250 steps · resting 56 bpm
  sources       dawarich 191 lines, last 23:55 · apple-health 6 lines, last 17:00 · ios-calendar 2 lines, last 12:00

The gap is a row, said so; the lunch is unplaced rather than attached to it, because the track says nothing about where the owner was; the all-day entry proposes its attendee at every stay and confirms Kari at none.

docs.title: Aboard an asset
docs.text:
A stay aboard an asset is a container. derive stays finds it and day shows it; the rule is the stays engine's (logbook/core/stays.py), and trips, days and the rollups read what it finds.

  • Boarding is twenty minutes. You are aboard an asset when its own location lines (subject = the asset's id, from sync ais, sync adsb or a saved stream) lie within the stay radius (radius_m, 150 m) of your points for aboard_min_s — 20 minutes by default, a setting in policy/stays.json — or longer. At anchor that is the asset's fixes inside the radius of your stay's centre, first to last; under way it is your points within the radius of the asset's position at that instant, read between the asset's two fixes around it when they are at most twice aboard_window_s apart (an AIS fix every ten minutes places a boat under way well enough), else from the nearest fix within the window. A boat that passes the quay once while you sit at the cafe does not board you; your own boat alongside for the afternoon does.
  • The run is one stay. Consecutive stays and moves aboard one asset fold into one stay aboard <asset>, from the first's start to the last's end; the run is inside it, and the asset's movement never fragments it. Its centre is the inner stay you spent longest at (the anchorage of the night, not the berth of the morning), and that is the coordinate in its id. A single move aboard with no stay either side (a ferry walked on and off) stays a move.
  • The night names the asset. The overnight rule counts the stay aboard whole, so a passage through the night is a night aboard, never a night in transit, and the night carries the asset's position: the inner stay that held the longest part of the night window. The header reads night after aboard REDUCE · 59.3400,10.5500 · away; the country is that position's.
  • Downstream. days prints the night as aboard <asset>; trips makes a night aboard a route element aboard <asset> and counts the trip's nights aboard per asset; rollup places has an aboard section, one stay per run aboard with the run's whole hours, while the berths and anchorages inside it are still unnamed places of their own, each marked aboard, and a night aboard counts at the anchorage the asset lay at; rollup nights counts nights aboard per asset.

The test fixture is the yacht REDUCE (MMSI 970123456, which does not exist), which weighs anchor at 22:30 and motors 40 km south through the night with the persona aboard, at anchor again by 03:00: the Friday is one stay aboard with the first anchorage, the passage and the second anchorage inside it, and the night is aboard REDUCE at the second anchorage. In the control case the persona spends the same night at a cabin 3 km from the first anchorage while the boat moves without them: the night is at the cabin's coordinates, the boat's passage is the boat's own, and nothing says aboard.

docs.title: The JSON
docs.text: --json prints one object: day, weekday, tz; day_start (HH:MM) only when the record's day does not begin at midnight; nights.before and nights.after (day, the date the night's window starts on, where, home, aboard, in_transit, position — the night's lat and lon, the asset's for a night aboard — the stay's id and its first and last location line); country (code, method, by, from); all_day; timeline, one entry per row — a stay, stop or move as derive stays --json gives it plus within_day (the part on the day), gap, attached (events, transcripts, notes, mail, calls, keepers with their line ids, a transcript with voices adding speakers, {label, person, name, seconds, basis, consent, owner} each; messages and photos as counts with their line ids) and with (confirmed, proposed, each person with their sources, reasons and lines); an aboard entry adds asset and inside; a flight entry carries the flight line's fields and line; a move lists the flights that cover it — then flights, unplaced, stories (the stories about the day: line, told_at, title, text, refers_to, teller, listener, confidence, source), health (with the ids of the lines each number came from), sources, and received, one object per page the circle shared for the day (from, owner_id, created, max_tier, lines, held_back, by_kind, named with each line's id, attachments); and, only on a day a model has dreamed, draft, the standing draft (line, seq, source, model, tier, at, read_head, read_count, language, segments each with text, evidence, supported, why and part, and on a sentence you can keep keep (its number) and kept (line, seq, or null), unsupported as a count, proposals each with number, kind, title, start, end, start_local, end_local, place, where, people (id, name), evidence, supported, why and confirmed (line, seq, or null), proposals_unknown, how many proposals are of a kind this reader does not know (counted, never shown, never malformed: draft/v1, Forward compatibility), supersedes, earlier newest first, dreamed, last, malformed), left out under --no-dream; and, only on a day whose standing draft the dream entry no longer allows, draft_withheld (line, seq, tier, max_tier, why, and nothing of the draft's text or proposals), left out under --no-dream too; and, only on a day with a synthesized call the dream entry allows, syntheses, one per transcript of the day that has one, in the day's order (transcript, the transcript line's id, then line, seq, source, model, tier, at, read_head, language, utterances, segments each with text, evidence, supported, why, part, utterances as {n, offset}, assignee and due as {phrase, date}, counts per part, unsupported, supersedes, earlier, synthesized, last, malformed); and, only on a day with a call whose standing synthesis the entry no longer allows, syntheses_withheld (transcript, line, seq, tier, max_tier, why); both left out under --no-dream too, and neither changes draft or draft_withheld, which are the day's alone. On a day with a reflection (day reflect, or a note labelled reflection through the MCP door) the object carries reflection, the latest standing one: line, seq, at, at_local, source and text; the key is absent on every other day. Likewise chapter (name, line, from, to, and clash when another standing chapter holds the day), reviews (line, goal, goal_text, disposition, period, note, recorded_at), goals and chapters (the lines written on the day, each with superseded) are there only on a day that has them (goals). On a day with a star standing (logbook star, RFC 0041) it carries stars, each {line, star, kind, note}: the starred line, the star line, the starred line's kind and your note; a photo's star is its keeper, under keepers as before. On a day you said who was there (logbook with) it carries stated, each {person, name, at, line}. Both keys are absent on every other day (the acts).

docs.title: A window of days
docs.text:
logbook days --from YYYY-MM-DD --to YYYY-MM-DD [--json] reads a window back one line per day, composed from the Day of each: the date and weekday; where the night was spent (the night after, as the Day's header has it: a named place, aboard <asset>, the home place a night within 400 m of it lies by — the night rule, whatever the place's radius — or the coordinates with near <place>, x km for a named place within 5 km or the city of the nearest large airport, and the country when the night is away; in transit when no stay reaches the minimum; no location when the day has no location line at all, since nothing then says the owner moved); the kilometres moved (every move that started on the day, the flights' included, and aboard an asset its passages); the flights (XY 561 OSL→ZRH); the stays — a stay or a run aboard an asset; a stop is not one — with how many lines are attached across the day's rows; the people confirmed present (with 2; a proposed face is not counted); the health triple when the day has one; and a gap marker. Both bounds default to the days the owner's track covers.

logbook days --from 2026-06-08 --to 2026-06-21          # the persona's fortnight, as text
logbook days --from 2026-01-01 --to 2026-12-31 --json   # a year, one JSON object per line
logbook days                                            # the whole record

The fortnight of the test persona, who does not exist:

2026-06-08  Mon  Home                             1.2 km  3 stays
2026-06-09  Tue  Home                             1.2 km  3 stays
2026-06-10  Wed  Home                             4.4 km  5 stays (2 attached) · with 1
2026-06-11  Thu  Home                             1.3 km  3 stays (2 attached) · with 1
2026-06-12  Fri  Home                             1.2 km  3 stays
2026-06-13  Sat  aboard Solvind NO               11.1 km  2 stays (2 attached) · with 1
2026-06-14  Sun  Home                            11.1 km  2 stays
2026-06-15  Mon  47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich) CH     1,471 km  XY 561 OSL→ZRH · 4 stays (1 attached)
2026-06-16  Tue  47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich) CH       0.0 km  1 stay (2 attached) · with 1
2026-06-17  Wed  47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich) CH       0.0 km  1 stay
2026-06-18  Thu  Home                           1,471 km  XY 562 ZRH→OSL · 4 stays
2026-06-19  Fri  Home                             1.2 km  3 stays
2026-06-20  Sat  Home                             1.2 km  3 stays
2026-06-21  Sun  Home                             0.0 km  1 stay

The gap marker names every usual source with no standing line on the day — gap dawarich when the tracker said nothing all day, gap apple-health, dawarich on a day with nothing logged (the line then reads no location and nothing logged). A source is usual when it has a line on at least four in five of the window's days that have any line: the tracker, the watch, the boat's AIS, the messages; not the photos or the notes, which come every other day, and not a calendar that spoke once. The share is counted on the index in one aggregate (Index.source_days), nothing read from the files, before the first line is printed.

Every number is the Day's: the night is nights.after, the country is the Day's, the flights are the Day's flight rows, the stays and their attachments are its timeline rows, the people are the union of its rows' confirmed company, the health row is its health line. What the window clips is a stay's start, and the night's stay id carries it: a hotel stay of three nights starts, in a reading that opens on its second day, at that day's midnight, as it does for day of that day.

Under --json the output is JSON Lines — one object per day per line, so a year streams as text does: day, weekday, night (where, home, aboard, in_transit, stay), country (the code), moved_m, flights (carrier, number, from, to, evidence, line), stays (count, attached, with_attachments), people (confirmed, names), health (as the Day's, with its line ids), sources (as the Day's) and gaps.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text:
A Day is located through index.sqlite: one reading of the day and the day before (the night before is that day's night), the retraction and resolution lines, and the health lines of the two days, each by an indexed column. A record of millions of lines reads a day in the time that day's lines take; the files are never swept.

days reads the window in chunks of a month through one reading each — the chunk's days and the day before, so the first day has its night before, and the chunk's health lines in one indexed query — and asks that reading for each day in turn: a year is a dozen readings, never one per day, and the lines stream out as each chunk is read. A year of the demo record (logbook demo --days 365, 155,000 lines) prints in seconds, the first line within one.

On the synthetic records of scripts/bench_library.py (ten years, docs/serve.md, Performance), the busiest Day of the last year answers in the Library in 0.14 seconds at a million lines and 0.67 at five million, the first time it is asked after the server starts; asked again at the same head it is the page the server kept, and answers in a millisecond. Fourteen /days take 0.49 and 2.3 seconds.

The morning's readings beyond the day, on the same five-million-line record (a 4-CPU container, the plan mapped): the task tool's plan about three seconds (60,000 sync notion lines), the replies owed about five (129,000 lines of the ninety days), the decisions to revisit about one (25,000 notes), the drift about six minutes. Read in the request the morning would answer in 339 seconds; read beside it, as logbook serve does, it answers in 4.5 seconds cold and a millisecond warm, and its other shapes read none of them. While those readings run, a page the server renders beside them shares the one interpreter with them and takes up to twice its time.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
Not a narrative: no title, no summary, no score. The reader never writes a note, a confirmation or a naming; those are yours, and when you make one it is a line in the record that the next Day reads.

Nor is it finished. RFC 0043, the Day page and its rhythm (a draft) is the design the page grows toward: what the day was meant for (the chapter, the goals, the plan) beside what it held, with no verdict drawn; the loose ends in one place, promises both ways, replies owed and decisions, each kept, carried or let go when you sign; a page whose shape follows the hour, morning, live, evening and signed; and one form that keeps what you choose of the model's draft and signs the day. Every part of it is marked built or proposed there, and nothing in this page changes until a slice of it is built. The rule above holds: a model's story of the day is the draft's, set apart as a draft, never the reader's, and a summary line is a count.

docs.title: A life in a record
docs.text:
logbook demo writes a month (--days, try-it.md). logbook demo --years N writes a life instead: Ines Nordmann, who does not exist, from her birth to 30 June 2026, in phases that change the shape of the data. The record is invented in code (logbook/labs/demo_life.py, on the month's logbook/contrib/demo.py), reads nothing, and is a function of --years and --seed: the same two numbers give the same chain head on any machine.

logbook demo --years 40 --out ~/Demo/Life     # born 1 July 1986; forty years to 30 June 2026
export LOGBOOK_HOME=~/Demo/Life

demo record: 40 years, 1986-07-01 to 2026-06-30, seed 1; nothing in it is real
wrote 114,786 lines to ~/Demo/Life, head 1d0a9bb43049…

She is born the day after the record ends, N years earlier, so the record closes on the eve of a birthday and every year of her life is whole. --days and --years are one or the other.

You can browse these forty years without installing anything: bighydro.github.io/logbook/ines/ is this record, seed 1, rendered by logbook export site at tier 2 (site.md) — a Year page per year, a Day page for each of its picks, every trip, a Days index per year, the places and the people — and published with the docs on every push to main.

docs.title: The phases
docs.text:
The phases are by age, so a short life is a child's and a long one reaches the boat. Each changes which sources write, how often, and how dense the phone's track is.

Age Phase Where What the record holds 0 to 5 childhood Bergen, the family home Scanned photos (provenance other, faces tagged), the birthday and Christmas Eve as entries the owner typed in later (source manual), a summer at the family cabin, and stories told about her: a note a year in the voice of her sister Kari or of Ola, the boy from across the street (Kari Nordmann: …), as promises reads a speaker. No track, no phone: twenty lines a year. 6 to 13 school Bergen The calendar fills: football practice every Wednesday with Mia and Jens, the class trip, the first day of school; more photos; a diary from 10. Still no track. 14 to 18 school, with a phone Bergen A thin track (a point per stay: where she slept, where she spent the day), texts over iMessage with Mia, Jens and Ola, calls. The family's weeks at the cabin (Easter, July) become trips; a package holiday every other summer, Mallorca, London, Barcelona, brings the first flights, declared from memory (evidence declared). 19 to 23 university Copenhagen, the student flat Lectures three mornings a week with Hanna and Freja, exams, mail, pages, music, the first transactions. A term in Barcelona at 21, the first long trip (131 nights); a week in London with Hanna at 22; Christmas flights home to Bergen, where the family home is still a home region, so Christmas is not a trip. 24 to 31 work Copenhagen, the office Meetings twice a week with Bjørn, the first boss, and Freja; a transcript the first Thursday of each month; mail three times a week; Zürich for a client twice a year from 26 (Marta and Jonas); a month in Lisbon at 28. Ola comes back at 29, and from then there is a chat with him every other day. The flight tracker from 30: flights are tracked from here. 32 on work, after the move Oslo: Home, Office, the cabin The move on 1 October of her thirty-second year, one flight and a note. Per and Liv at the office, Nils at the cabin, six cabin weekends a year with Ola, a Copenhagen visit to Freja each autumn, Zürich twice a year with the tracked flight out and the flight home the record infers from its own points, as in the month. The watch at 34: health starts there, and a run in the park with Tore every other Sunday. The boat at 35: Nordlys at the marina, a summer cruise every July with the boat's own AIS track, day sails on Saturdays. Three weeks in Rome at 37. the last month June 2026 Oslo The month logbook demo writes on its own, at the phone's full resolution (a point every five minutes, the watch's quarter hours, every profile), when the life is 36 years or longer. A shorter life ends thin.

People drift in and out, as the people reader shows: Jens stops after school (last contact 2005), Mia calls once at 21 and writes once at 24 and is not heard from again, the grandmother Solveig is in the photos until Ines is 27, Hanna writes once more at 33, Ola is in the childhood photos from 3, absent through the university years, and back for good at 29.

docs.title: The knobs
docs.text:
• --years N: the length of the life, 1 or more. A one-year record is a baby's: photos and family entries, no track. Fourteen years and more have a phone; thirty-six and more end with the full month and have the boat.
  • --seed S: the same seed gives the same record; another seed is the same life with other noise, other step counts, other days for the photos and the cabin weekends. The dates of the phases, the journeys and the moves do not depend on the seed.
  • The ages are constants at the top of logbook/labs/demo_life.py (PHONE_AGE, STUDENT_AGE, WORK_AGE, OLA_BACK_AGE, TRACKER_AGE, MOVE_AGE, WATCH_AGE, BOAT_AGE), and the journeys of each year are planned in one place (_journeys), so a different life is a small edit.

docs.title: Size
docs.text:
Old years are thin, so forty years stay a record a laptop reads at once: about 115,000 lines, of which 72,000 are location points, most of them in the last six years. Lines per calendar year, seed 1:

1988 1995 2002 2008 2015 2019 2021 2025 2026 (to June) 18 63 1,671 3,162 2,831 3,149 7,890 9,781 17,134

The month alone is 12,800 lines; a year of the month's story (--days 365) 155,000.

docs.title: What to try
docs.text:
logbook trips --year 2001          # Easter and July at the family cabin, the first year with a phone
logbook trips --year 2008          # the Barcelona term, 131 nights, and the summer flights home
logbook trips --year 2025          # cabin weekends, Zürich twice, the cruise aboard Nordlys, Copenhagen
logbook rollup flights             # declared until 2016, tracked and inferred after
logbook rollup countries --year 2007   # a Copenhagen year: DK 353 days, NO 12
logbook day 1989-07-01             # a third birthday: one entry, one scanned photo, no track
logbook day 2022-07-23             # a day of the first cruise, aboard, with the night at anchor
logbook stats --health             # from 1 July 2020, the day the watch appears
logbook people --year 1998         # Mia and Jens, every Wednesday

trips 2001-01-01 – 2001-12-31: 2 trips
  2001-03-28 – 2001-03-31  4 nights · route the family cabin · places the family cabin · trip:2001-03-28:2001-03-31
  2001-07-10 – 2001-07-16  7 nights · route the family cabin · places the family cabin · with Solveig Nordmann, Kari Nordmann, Eva Nordmann · trip:2001-07-10:2001-07-16

people over the whole life lists everyone with their first and last contact, and shows who is a decade gone, but the reader asks for the overnight stay of every one of the 14,600 days against every stay of the window, so on a forty-year record it takes minutes today; people --year is quick. The tests read the same report from the channels alone.

Nothing of the life is real: the people, the boat, the airline XY, the aircraft ZZ-ABC, the addresses, the numbers (UK 07700 900xxx, example.org), the cities she lived in. The record pretends the phone always had a track from the day she got one and that the texts of 2000 were iMessages; the shape of a life is the point, not the era.

docs.title: Describing keepers
docs.text:
logbook describe keepers [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--limit N] [--photos DIR ...] [--model NAME] [--fetch-model] [--dry-run] [--json] has a local vision model look at each photo you marked a keeper (RFC 0024) and write down what is in it: one factual sentence and a short list of the visible things. The words go into the record as a derived note (RFC 0010), on the photo's day, beside the keeper. A photo is described once, however many lanes it is in and however often the command runs. No model runs unless you ask, never a cloud one, and nothing leaves the machine: the engine is mlx-vlm on Apple silicon, an optional extra, with the Hugging Face hub told it is offline while it runs. The model is never told who is in the picture or where it was taken, is told not to guess either, and an answer that names a face your library knows is refused.

logbook describe keepers                                      # every keeper whose photo file is reachable, oldest first
logbook describe keepers --since 2026-06-01 --limit 20        # twenty this run; the next run carries on
logbook describe keepers --photos ~/Pictures/Photos\ Library.photoslibrary   # where the originals are
logbook describe keepers --photos ~/Pictures/Photos\ Library.photoslibrary --photos /Volumes/Archive/2026
logbook describe keepers --dry-run                            # what would be described; no engine needed, nothing written
logbook describe keepers --fetch-model                        # download the model first; the only time the command uses the network
logbook describe keepers --model mlx-community/Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct-4bit   # a larger model
logbook show 2026-06-10                                       # the description under its keeper

Without the engine, or with a model not yet on this machine, the command prints the two lines that put them there and exits 2:

describe: no vision engine is installed; install openlogbook[describe] (mlx-vlm, Apple silicon only)
  install:  pip install "openlogbook[describe]"      # or: uv tool install "openlogbook[describe]"; Apple silicon only
  fetch:    logbook describe keepers --fetch-model   # downloads mlx-community/Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct-4bit once; the only network use

docs.title: What is written
docs.text:
One note/v1 line per photo, source description, tier 2 (a note is tier 2, RFC 0010), at and tz the photo line's, so the note sits on the photo's day at the photo's time:

{"at":"2026-06-10T17:00:00Z","end":null,"tz":"Europe/Oslo","source":"description","kind":"note","tier":2,
 "payload":{"schema":"note/v1","raw_id":"01a0f6a2-068b-7572-94ea-f492e749c3d6",
  "text":"A wooden sailing boat moored at a stone quay under a grey sky.\nVisible: boat, quay, ropes, sky",
  "extra":{"derived":true,"engine":"mlx-vlm","model":"mlx-community/Qwen2-VL-2B-Instruct-4bit",
   "photo":{"line":"01a0f6a2-068b-7572-94ea-f492e749c3d6","asset_id":"9B4E2C10-5F3A-4D21-8A7B-000000000001","library":"apple-photos","file_name":"IMG_1700.HEIC"},
   "keeper":"01a0f6a2-1b2c-7d3e-9f40-5a6b7c8d9e0f","things":["boat","quay","ropes","sky"]}}}
  • raw_id is the photo line's id: the (source, raw_id) dedupe of the store means a photo is described once, whatever model is set later and however many keepers point at it (a photo in both lanes has one description). A description you retract is never written again, as a retracted keeper is not.
  • text is the sentence, then Visible: … on a second line, so logbook search boat finds the photo.
  • extra.derived says the words are a model's, never yours; extra.engine and extra.model say which; extra.photo is the photo as the keeper names it ({line, asset_id, library, file_name?}); extra.keeper the keeper line the run read; extra.things the list, cleaned.
  • The chain is appended to, one line per photo as soon as it is described, so an interrupted run keeps what it did. Nothing is ever rewritten.

show <day> prints the description under the first keeper row for its photo, indented to the text column and without a clock of its own; when no keeper for the photo is standing on the day (you retracted it), the note is a row of its own, note description IMG_1700.HEIC: A wooden sailing boat ….

2026-06-10
  hero  IMG_1700.HEIC, IMG_1030.HEIC
  10:30  photo      immich         camera=SimPhone 3, file_name=IMG_1030.HEIC, …
  10:30  keeper     keeper-inference hero photo (memory): IMG_1030.HEIC
                                   A table set for two with bread and coffee by a window. · table, bread, coffee, window
  17:00  keeper     keeper-inference hero photo (memory): IMG_1700.HEIC
                                   A wooden sailing boat moored at a stone quay under a grey sky. · boat, quay, ropes, sky
  17:00  keeper     keeper-inference hero photo (art): IMG_1700.HEIC

docs.title: What the model is asked, and what it may not say
docs.text:
The prompt is fixed (describe.PROMPT) and the model sees nothing but the pixels and that prompt: no file name, no date, no location, no face, no caption. It is asked for one JSON object, {"description": one factual sentence, "things": [short lowercase noun phrases]}, and told two things it must never do:

  • Never name or identify a person. Faces are the photo library's job: the names it gave them are on the photo line (extra.faces) and keepers --people reads them, proposed and never confirmed. The model writes "a person", "two people", "a child". An answer that carries any word of a face's name the library put on that photo is refused: counted (N answers could not be read), never written, tried again on the next run.
  • Never guess where the picture was taken. No place, city, country, landmark, shop or brand. Where you were is what the location lines say; a model's guess from a skyline is not an observation and has no place in the record.

The answer is read as the first JSON object in it, fences and prose aside. The sentence has its whitespace collapsed; the things are lowercased, trimmed, deduplicated, anything over four words dropped, at most twelve kept; a things that came back as one comma-separated string is split. An answer with no sentence is no description.

docs.title: Where the file is
docs.text:
A photo line points at pixels it does not hold (RFC 0002). The command looks in two places, in this order:

  1. The record's own store. A media, attachments, file or content reference of the §1.1 shape whose path is attachments/<sha256> and whose file is there.
  2. The folders --photos names, any number of them. An Apple Photos library (a folder ending in .photoslibrary) is read by the asset's UUID, which is the name of its original under originals/<first character of the UUID>/, so nothing is walked; any other folder is walked once per run into a map of file names (case aside, since both macOS and Windows ignore it) and the photo found by its file_name.

A keeper whose photo file is in neither is a counted skip (skipped 3 without its photo file …), never an error; so is a keeper whose photo line is not in the record. Immich keeps its originals on the server; the record has no path to them, so Immich keepers are described when a --photos folder holds a copy by file name.

docs.title: The engine
docs.text: openlogbook[describe] is mlx-vlm and pillow-heif (for the HEIC originals a phone takes), both on Apple silicon only; elsewhere the extra installs nothing and the command says so. The model is any vision model the hub serves in MLX format, by repository name (--model); the default is a 4-bit Qwen2-VL-2B, about 1.5 GB, which reads a photo in a second or two on a laptop. The model is sampled at temperature 0 for at most 200 tokens. --fetch-model downloads it once; every run after that sets HF_HUB_OFFLINE for its duration, so the engine cannot reach out whatever it would do. A faked engine in the tests asserts that no socket is opened while a run is under way.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not pick keepers (RFC 0024 rule 1: a keeper is your act). It describes the ones you marked.
  • It does not describe every photo. The library has thousands; the keepers are the ones worth words.
  • It does not caption with people or places, as above.
  • It does not read the description back into the Day, the trip or the year pages yet; show and search do.

docs.title: The digest
docs.text:
logbook digest [YYYY-MM-DD] [--json | --markdown] is the day in at most 25 lines: what the owner reads of it in the evening, not the Day itself. Its shape in three lines, the flights, the open promises due within the week, the usual sources that had nothing to say, what the calendar holds for tomorrow, and one closing question the owner can answer in a word, drawn from the record's own question bank. It is composed from the readers that already exist — the Day, the promises, sources --gaps — and derives nothing of its own; it writes nothing to the record (the question bank's defaults and a note of what it asked are files beside it, never lines) and it sends nothing. The command only says what the message would be; the schedule delivers two lines of it.

logbook digest                       # today, as text
logbook digest 2026-06-10            # a Wednesday
logbook digest 2026-06-10 --markdown # the same lines as Markdown, for a message that renders it
logbook digest 2026-06-10 --json     # the whole sets behind the lines, every row with its line ids

docs.title: What it says, in order
docs.text:
1. where — the stays of the Day's timeline in order (a run aboard an asset as aboard <asset>, an unnamed stay as its coordinates with the nearest large airport's city), the first six and …, then where the night after was spent: night at Home, night away, aboard Solvind, night in transit. A day with no line at all is nothing logged.
  2. with — the people the Day confirms present (declared in a note, speaking in a transcript, attending a timed calendar entry at the stay); never the owner, never a face in a photo or an attendee of an all-day entry, who are only proposed — and 1 proposed after the names says how many are (nobody confirmed (1 proposed) without a name), never a count beside a name. A person proposed at one stay and confirmed at another is confirmed.
  3. attached — how many of each kind attached across the day's rows (1 event, 1 note, 3 photos), and how many lines fell inside no row (2 unplaced).
  4. flight — the flights of the day from the flight/v1 lines standing, as the Day lists them: XY 561 OSL→ZRH 07:05–09:15, with the evidence when it is not tracked; three at most, then +N more flights.
  5. due — the open promises due on the day or within seven days after it, from the promises reader: the sentence as written, who said it (you for the owner), the due day and the phrase it was read from; three at most, then +N more due this week. A promise closed with promises done is out. A promises reader that judges its proposals (a model that reads them after the rules) puts the ids it holds to be promises on its report as judged; when that set is there, only those count. The rules do not judge, so today every open proposal counts.
  6. gaps — the usual sources with no line on the day, one line: dawarich: usual, no line. A source is usual when it has a line on four in five of the logged days of the fortnight ending on the day (the days rule, days.usual_sources); it is missing when sources --gaps, asked from the day with those sources expected, counts the day among its missing days or holds no line of it at all. A note written once in the fortnight is not usual, so it is never missed.
  7. tomorrow — the timed calendar entries of the next local day, from the event/v1 lines standing (retracted lines out; an entry several calendars carry is one, ×N sources, as the Day folds them), with the attendees the record names: 12:00–13:00 Lunch · with Kari Nordmann. An all-day entry is not timed and is not here. Three at most, then +N more entries.
  8. The question, last, after a blank line. One, from the record's own bank — policy/questions.json, written with its defaults the first time and yours to edit — so that the owner can answer in a word and the day closes itself (ADR 0005: one nudge, one channel). Each question in the bank says which facts of the day it asks on (when: travelled, aboard, night_away, reunion, !photos, long_sleep, ... — the table is in RFC 0027) and how much of the draw it takes (weight); the digest draws one of the questions whose conditions hold, never the same one two days running, and remembers what it asked in state/questions.json. The defaults are the nudges the digest used to choose in code, each as a question with the condition that chose it:
when the question nothing logged Where were you? a usual source is missing Was dawarich switched off? the night after is in transit Where did you sleep? a person is proposed and confirmed nowhere Was Kari Nordmann with you? a calendar entry fell inside no row Did “Lunch” happen? a promise is due on the day or before Is “I'll send the photos by Friday.” done? someone seen again after ninety days How was it, seeing Per Hansen again? travelled What did you see today that you had not seen before? a long night's sleep Did the long sleep help? any logged day What were you glad of today?, Anything to add?

The content of the bank — which questions, with what research behind them (source) — is left to a future author (RFC 0027, The question bank — to be written); these defaults cite nothing. logbook questions list|add|disable manages the file:

logbook questions list                                   # id, kind, weight, when, text
logbook questions add sea-air --text "What did the sea smell of?" --kind savouring \
    --when aboard --when '!night_in_transit' --weight 2 --source "a placeholder citation"
logbook questions disable sea-air                        # kept in the file, never asked

The answer is the owner's to write — a note, a promises done, a confirmation — and the digest never writes it for them.

docs.title: The limit
docs.text: Twenty-five lines is a hard limit, not a target. The parts are capped as above, so a day with six flights, eight promises and nine meetings tomorrow still fits with room over; should a day ever not, digest.fit cuts lines from the middle for one … row and keeps the header and the question. The JSON is never cut: it holds the whole sets, and lines says how many lines the text has. The digest is never a list of everything — that is what logbook day is for.

docs.title: A synthetic example
docs.text:
The Oslo persona of the test suite, who does not exist, on a Wednesday with a lunch at an unnamed cafe, a promise made the evening before, and two entries in tomorrow's calendar:

2026-06-10  Wednesday
  where      Home → Office → 59.9200,10.7400 → Office → Home · night at Home
  with       Kari Nordmann
  attached   1 event, 1 photo
  due        “I'll send Ola the mooring photos by Friday.”  you, 2026-06-12 (by Friday)
  tomorrow   09:00–09:30  Standup
  tomorrow   12:00–13:00  Lunch · with Kari Nordmann

Anything to add?

The Monday they fly to Zürich:

2026-06-15  Monday
  where      Home → OSL, Oslo → ZRH, Zurich → 47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich) · night away, 47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich)
  with       nobody confirmed
  attached   1 event
  flight     XY 561 OSL→ZRH  07:05–09:15
  tomorrow   19:00–21:00  Dinner · with Ola Nordmann

Anything to add?

A day the record holds nothing for:

2026-06-10  Wednesday
  where      nothing logged
  with       nobody confirmed
  attached   nothing

Where were you?

--markdown prints the same lines as a heading, a bulleted list with the labels in bold, and the question in bold on its own:

## Saturday 13 June 2026
- **where** Home → aboard Solvind · night away, aboard Solvind
- **with** Ola Nordmann
- **attached** 1 note, 1 photo

**Anything to add?**

docs.title: The JSON
docs.text:
--json prints one object: day, weekday, tz; shape (where, the stays in order; night with where, home, aboard, in_transit; with with confirmed and proposed as names; attached as count and noun pairs; unplaced); flights, the Day's own with their line ids; promises (within_days, judged, and open, every proposal as promises --json prints it); gaps (usual and missing); tomorrow (day and entries, each with title, start, end, their local forms, with, sources and lines); unplaced, the Day's list; sources, the names with a line on the day; question (id and kind of the question in the bank, text with its placeholders filled, and facts, the names of the day's facts that held, so a when can be written against what the chooser saw; id is null when nothing in the bank could be asked); and lines.

The week, rather than the day, is logbook digest --paper [--week YYYY-Www]: four pages of A4 with the days one line each, who was there and the keepers, the promises due and what was read, in On paper.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It does not send anything or schedule anything: a delivery layer that takes the text, picks the channel and keeps to one message a day is the next decision, not this command. It remembers only which question it asked on which day (state/questions.json, the last seven), so as never to ask the same one two days running; it does not remember the text, nor any answer. It does not read a day that has not come: a day after today in the record's zone is refused. It does not derive anything the Day, the promises reader and sources --gaps do not already derive, so a change in their rules is a change here; the one setting of its own is the question bank, which is the owner's file and not the code's.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
The digest is not sent whole. The schedule's notifier, when it is set (the schedule), sends two short messages a day through Telegram, and nothing else of the day:

  • after the 06:00 close, Your Day page for 2026-10-16 is ready · 42 lines, with the link to the Day when LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_LINK_HOST is set;
  • at LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_EVENING_HOUR, Your question for 2026-10-16: What were you glad of today?, the question this command closes with, drawn the same way and remembered in state/questions.json, so logbook digest that evening asks the same one. A question of the bank with a placeholder, filled from the day (a name, a promise's sentence), is not sent: Your question for 2026-10-16 waits in `logbook digest`.

One message each, at most once a day; the token is never printed.

docs.title: The doctor
docs.text: logbook doctor is the check-up: one line per check, pass, warn or fail, and exit 1 when anything fails. It reads and never writes, but for the file --packet --out names. The checks and their rules are listed in the module's own documentation (logbook/contrib/doctor.py); the schedule runs it four times a day (The schedule). logbook doctor sources --gaps says where each source went quiet; logbook doctor --packet is the diagnostic to send a collaborator (Sending a diagnostic).

docs.title: The files the lines name
docs.text:
The record line is verify on the files, and looks for every attachment a line names as verify does (When verify fails). The missing ones are counted in the pass and are not a warn, since SPEC §1.1 allows them:

pass  record  1,204 lines, head 4dc18fde900d…, verified; 3 attachments missing (SPEC §1.1 allows it; `logbook attach status`); /Users/ines/Logbook

Their bytes are not hashed here, nor a sealed one opened: the doctor runs four times a day, and a store of photos is read by logbook verify by hand, or by logbook backup --verify.

logbook doctor --attachments names them: per source, the most first, each standing line whose file the store lacks, with its kind, its time and the first twelve characters of the digest, then the count by source (the attachment store). It exits 0 and changes nothing.

docs.title: Agents
docs.text:
A record with a line marked machine text, or a policy/agents.json that names a sender, gets an agents line after owner (your own agents): the standing lines marked machine per source (a message an agent wrote, a transcript with an agent among its participants), the most first, and how many senders the file names, the owner's own bots the Beeper adapters mark.

pass  agents  lines marked machine: telegram 412, beeper-telegram 96, claude-code 31; 1 sender named in policy/agents.json

It reads the transcripts and the messages of the sources that write the mark (telegram, beeper, beeper-<network>), from the index when it is current. A file that is not the shape is a fail naming it.

docs.title: Voiceprints
docs.text:
A record whose transcripts carry voices, or that keeps a voiceprint registry, gets a voiceprints line after assets (Voiceprints, RFC 0038 §5). It says that the file is there, when it was written and, opened with this machine's identity, with which embedding model and for how many people; never what is in it:

pass  voiceprints  voiceprints.age written 2026-10-11 10:12 with pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM, for 3 people, you among them; 2 voices not yet named

A warn when the file was written with a model that is not the configured one, whose vectors it cannot compare (logbook setup speakers --rebuild makes it again), or when it will not open with this machine's identity. On a machine without the identity it says only that the file is there and when. A record that names no recipients keeps no registry, and the line says so: the review hears the voices it compares for each run and keeps nothing. A record with voices and no file yet: none yet: logbook setup speakers --rebuild makes voiceprints.age; on a machine without the identity, which writes no registry, what a write there answers: none, and none is written here: no identity on this machine, and voiceprints.age is sealed to the record's recipients and needs one. (Such a machine sees the voices only of transcripts written before the record had recipients; of sealed ones it sees none, and says nothing.) The line opens the file and writes nothing.

docs.title: Where the day begins
docs.text: A record whose day does not begin at midnight (day_start) gets a day-start line after index: a pass naming the boundary (pass day-start the day begins at 06:00: a line before 06:00 belongs to the day before); a warn when index.sqlite was built under another boundary, naming both (the next reader rebuilds it, or logbook repair index does now); a fail when the value is not a clock HH:MM, which every reader that groups by day refuses. A record whose day begins at midnight, with an index that agrees, has no such line.

docs.title: What leaves, and what may be fetched
docs.text: The crossing line lists each entry of policy/crossing.json as it counts today (mcp 1, hermes 2 until 2026-12-31, heard 2 fetch). When LOGBOOK_HEARD names feed and no heard entry lets a transcript be fetched, it says which entry to write, {"heard": {"max_tier": 2, "fetch": true}}. The world line says what export world and the Library's /world show: tier 1 alone when the file names no world entry, and the entry that adds the chapters, {"world": {"max_tier": 2}}. The export-day line says what a folder that export --day or --days writes may hold: up to the folder entry's ceiling, or, when the file names none, that no entry exists and the default tier 1 applies, as the crossing line the export keeps records it ("entry": null, "default_tier": 1); --tier may lower it, never raise it (a day to a folder).

docs.title: Drafts the policy no longer allows
docs.text: A draft follows the dream entry of policy/crossing.json, not the head (the dream, When the entry changes). When a day's standing draft is above what the entry allows today (the ceiling lowered, the until passed, the entry removed), no reader shows it, and a drafts line after crossing names the days: warn drafts 1 day(s) with a draft above what the dream entry allows, which no reader shows: 2026-06-10 (#5440, tier 3); the 'dream' entry allows max_tier 2 now; `logbook dream --catch-up` dreams them again under it. A record with no such day has no line.

docs.title: Calls without a synthesis
docs.text:
When policy/crossing.json has a dream entry, a synthesis line after drafts counts the calls (transcript/v1 lines) that have no synthesis (the synthesis of a call), in three parts, each only when it counts any: those of the last 7 days and today, which the 06:00 close synthesizes; those before, which the close leaves, with the --since that reaches the oldest; and those above the entry's max_tier, which never leave the machine:

pass  synthesis  4 calls without a synthesis: 1 since 2026-10-07, which the 06:00 close synthesizes (`dream --catch-up`); 2 before 2026-10-07, which the close leaves: `logbook dream --catch-up --since 2026-08-21`; 1 above the dream entry's max_tier 2, which stays on this machine

It is a pass: the close leaves older calls by design, so a record with years of transcripts does not send them all to the model one morning. A record without a dream entry, or whose every call has a synthesis, has no such line. A retracted or superseded call is not counted, nor a call whose synthesis was made under another version of the entry: it has one.

docs.title: The family's videos
docs.text:
When the record names the family's videos (sync drive --videos) or the cache under state/videos/ exists, one videos line says how many video files the record holds and their size, how many videos fetch has fetched and videos infer has inferred, how many wait in the cache, how many scenes the latest inference of each file found, how many it proposed a place or a date for and how many you confirmed with review video, and the cache against its cap:

pass  videos  25 video files in the record (78.4 GB); 6 fetched, 5 inferred, 1 waiting in the cache; 212 scenes, 61 proposed, 14 confirmed; cache 3.1 GB of 8.0 GB

A cache over its cap (a cap lowered with --cache-gb below what it holds) or a state/videos.json that is not the shape is a warn. Nothing is asked of Drive (Videos).

docs.title: The Google key
docs.text: When either variable of the Google service-account key is set (LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY, LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER), one google line comes before the sync: lines of the sources it covers: the key file present and a service-account key, the user an address, which of gmail, gcal, drive, gtasks, meet and gaudit are on it, a source switched off in policy/import.json named as disabled, and what people review --from-google reads on it — pass google key present, user set; sources on the key: gmail, gcal, drive, gtasks, meet, gaudit; people review --from-google: contacts, other contacts. A key not set, not readable or not a service-account key, or a user that is not an address, is a warn naming the variable. The line reads the key on this machine and asks Google nothing, and never prints the path or the address (the tour, Google, on one key).

docs.title: A source whose history was never read
docs.text: A source's first scheduled run reads its last 14 days, not its whole history (the schedule). Until a run reads the rest (--since before that window, or --restart), the source's sync: line says so after what it says of the variables: pass sync:drive configured (LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY, LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER); first run bounded to 14 days; history not read (before 2026-09-25: `logbook sync drive --since <date>`). The note never changes the line's status: nothing is broken, and the history may be one you never want read.

docs.title: Implausible dates
docs.text: A calendar entry a parser placed in 1948, or a mail a sender's broken clock dated 2612, is not a day of the owner's life. The dates line counts the lines whose timestamp lies outside their source's plausible range, per source with the earliest and the latest, and warns: warn dates 2 line(s) dated outside their source's plausible range: ics 1 (1948-03-01 to 1948-03-01); mail 1 (2612-03-01 to 2612-03-01); …. The ranges are: calendar entries (kind event) from 1970-01-01 to now plus 5 years; mail from 1990-01-01 to now plus 1 day; every other line from 1970-01-01 to now plus 1 day. A record overrides them per source in policy/plausible.json, either field optional — {"sources": {"ios-calendar": {"earliest": "1960-01-01", "ahead": "10y"}}}, ahead a count of years or days (5y, 1d); a file that is not this shape is a fail naming it. Nothing is deleted, hidden or rewritten: the lines stay in the log and in every reader as they were written. logbook doctor --implausible lists them, one row each: the line id, the source, the kind, the timestamp and the range it missed, then the count.

docs.title: The extras
docs.text:
One extra: line per optional extra the doctor knows, ais, crypto, sealed, speakers and transcribe, in that order after dates: a pass naming the package that makes it, or a warn with its install line (optional extras). They are this machine's, so a doctor that finds no record prints them too, after its failed record line.

pass  extra:ais         websockets is installed
pass  extra:crypto      cryptography is installed
pass  extra:sealed      pyrage is installed
warn  extra:speakers    pyannote.audio not installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[speakers]==0.7.0"
pass  extra:transcribe  faster-whisper is installed

transcribe passes on either Whisper engine, mlx-whisper or faster-whisper. speakers is its own extra, apart from transcribe since it brings torch, so a machine that transcribes voice memos without telling the voices apart has that one warn. Nothing is imported to find out, since an engine loads its model on import: a module is looked for on the path, and pyannote.audio by its installed distribution, as derive speakers asks for it. A pass says the package is here, not that its models are: logbook setup speakers --fetch-model fetches those.

docs.title: Sending a diagnostic
docs.text:
When something fails — the dream's model endpoint answers 500, a sync adapter stops, the service will not stay up — a collaborator needs to see this machine without seeing the record. logbook doctor --packet prints a plain-text packet to send instead of a description put together by hand; --out FILE writes it to a file. It holds:

  • machine: the OS and its version, the platform string, the architecture, the RAM, the Python and openlogbook versions, and which extras are installed, with the version of each package that makes one.
  • record: the line count and the head as logbook.json names them (the head is a hash, not a line), the format, where the day begins and whether index.sqlite is current. No line is read.
  • sources: one line per live source the record uses or the last scheduled run listed — configured, or the variables it still needs by name; the last run's result and lines; and the date of its watermark in state/<name>.json, the date alone (immich: configured; last run ok, 12 lines; watermark 2026-10-12).
  • schedule and service: which installs of the schedule this machine has, the last scheduled run (when, the lines per source, the sources that failed, the doctor's counts and the names of the checks that warned or failed), and the serve services with their ports.
  • dream endpoint: the host and port of LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT (never its path), the model, the policy's dream entry, the temperature the request carries (temperature: 0.2 (the default), the value of LOGBOOK_DREAM_TEMPERATURE, or none, when no temperature field is sent), and one probe: the dream's own request, the key as its bearer token when LOGBOOK_DREAM_KEY is set, with the fixed prompt Reply with the single word ready. where a day would be, sent once. The reply's HTTP status and body follow as they came (up to 64 KiB): a model's error is not the record's content. A 400 whose body names the temperature adds hint: set LOGBOOK_DREAM_TEMPERATURE=none for a model that takes no temperature.
  • environment: the names of the variables set that logbook reads — every LOGBOOK_*, the proxies, the config and cache folders — never a value.
  • sync log and service log: the last 40 lines of each, from ~/Library/Logs/logbook-sync.log and ~/Library/Logs/logbook-serve.log on macOS, from the journal on Linux (journalctl for the timers and the service installed here); none elsewhere.

The probe is the packet's one network call, and it is made only when LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT is set and a model is named (LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL, or the model of the policy's dream entry), and only while the policy's dream entry allows the dream: the probe carries your key to the endpoint, so with no dream entry, or one past its until, it is not sent and the packet says why (probe: not sent, …). Without them nothing is fetched. Unlike doctor's serve line, the packet does not ask the service's port whether a server answers: that would be a second request.

Whatever the packet quotes rather than writes — a log line, the reply, an error, a source's result — is scrubbed first, the longest match first:

replaced by what ~ the home directory, as given and resolved, with either separator [record] the record's folder [owner] the owner's names and each word of them, handles (with and without @), addresses and numbers from policy/owner.json and owner_emails, and the login name unless it is a generic account (root, admin, runner, …); a number is found by its last eight digits however it is spaced, so +44 7700 900461, 07700900461 and (+44) 7700-900-461 are one [host] this machine's name, in full and before its first dot [place], [asset] the names of the places in places.json and of the assets in assets.json, as written [NAME] the value of the variable NAME: every LOGBOOK_* but LOGBOOK_HOME, LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL and LOGBOOK_DREAM_TEMPERATURE, every proxy, and any variable named like a key, a token or a password

A policy/owner.json that cannot be read is said at the top: the owner's names are then not replaced. What the packet does not know it cannot replace — another person's name a sync printed, a calendar's title — so read it before you send it.

docs.title: The dream's prompt
docs.text: logbook dream sends a model two messages: the prompt, which is the file logbook/contrib/dream-prompt.md in the package with the day and the language filled in, and the day's material as JSON. This page explains the prompt; logbook dream day DAY --show-prompt prints both as they go. The prompt's name, dream-day/4, is kept in every draft's extra.prompt, so a draft says which wording wrote it; a change to the prompt that changes what a draft holds bumps the number (dream-day/2 added the proposed events, so a dream-day/1 draft has none; dream-day/3 added rule 5, agents; dream-day/4 the goodnight story in the day paragraph's place, the lenses, learned, decided, the ideas, the photo of the day, the links, one question where there were two, rules 6 and 7, and RFC 0043 §7's voice, the dream).

docs.title: What it asks for
docs.text:
One JSON object, every key but the last two a list of segments, in the order the Day prints them, and the last two the proposed events and links:

Key What How many story the goodnight story: second person, past tense, calm, concrete, in the order it happened, ending where the day ended; never a line about tomorrow, which the reader computes five or six sentences lens:<id> one per lens of the material's lenses: the lens's answer from the day; an empty list when the day gives nothing for it, never a sentence saying so one threads the threads the day moved: a conversation continued, a plan made, a trip under way, a promise given or kept at most four learned what the day shows was learned one sentence each decision what the day shows was decided one sentence each ideas an idea of the material's named the day moved, each segment with entity, the idea's id one sentence each questions a question for the owner's reflection, resting on something the day holds exactly one people the people the model thinks were there, one sentence each, with the items that show it as many as the material names promises the promises it thinks were made or kept that day, in the words the material gives as many as the material shows photo the photo of the day from the material's photos (own camera first, starred first): a one-line reason, its evidence that photo's one reference one, or none events the events it thinks the day held that the calendar does not have: {title, start, end, place, people, evidence}, the place a stay's place, the people ids from the material's people, never a name at most four links lines of the day that belong to an idea or an org of named: {entity, text, evidence, note?}, entity an id the material gave at most four

A segment is {"text": "...", "evidence": ["L1", "L2"]} or {"text": "...", "unsupported": true}. The references are the ones the material carries; the record turns them into line ids before the draft is written and keeps nothing of the prompt (the dream, the evidence rule). A proposed event that names a time, a place, a person or a reference the material does not give is dropped and counted (the dream).

docs.title: The rules it gives the model
docs.text:
1. Evidence or a mark. Every sentence names the items it rests on, or says unsupported. Never an invented reference, never an item cited for a sentence it does not support. The record checks this afterwards and refuses an answer that is mostly unsupported, so the rule is enforced, not only asked.
  2. Only what the material says. No guessed feelings, no weather the day has no line for, nothing where the record is silent; where it is silent the draft is silent or asks.
  3. The names as given. No nicknames, no titles, no guess at who someone is.
  4. Brief and plain. No headings, no bullets inside the text, no greeting and no sign-off.
  5. Agents are not people. A counterpart marked agent is a program the owner runs (a Telegram bot, a coding assistant) and a text marked machine is what it wrote (your own agents): never one of the people, and its words never the owner's or anyone's promise. The owner's own words to it are the owner's.
  6. Ids from the material. An idea, an org or a goal by an id of named or for.goals, a person by one of people, a photo by a reference of photos; never a made-up id, never a name in its place.
  7. Intention is not a verdict. for, the chapter and the goals, is what the day was meant for; one is named only where a line touches it, and the draft never says the day was good, on track or well spent.

Then the voice of RFC 0043 §7, word for word: never moralise and never flatter; every number one the material gave; an inference says so, in the sentence; at most one proposal of change beside the proposals to confirm; one question; the day's language; the story calm, concrete, short.

The prompt also says the day ($day, $weekday, $tz) and the language to write in ($language, a BCP 47 tag, and $language_name): the language most of the day's own text is in, as the dream decided it from the notes, messages, titles and subjects of the day.

docs.title: The material
docs.text: The second message is the material as JSON: day, weekday, tz, max_tier (the ceiling it was read under), night_before and night_after (where, home or away, the references), country, all_day, timeline (one entry per stay, move, stop or flight as the Day shows it, with its events, transcripts, mail threads, calls, photos as a count, keepers and who was there, confirmed and proposed, each with references and, for a canonical person, the person id; a stay or stop also its place, a named place's name or place:<lat>,<lon>), unplaced, messages (by counterpart: the count, the references, the texts and the counterpart's person id when the record resolves one; agent on a counterpart that is one of the owner's agents, machine on a text it wrote), notes (in full), commitments, photos (own camera first, then starred, each ref, at, provenance, starred), people (every canonical person the material names, id and name; never the owner), for (chapter and goals), named (the ideas and orgs the owner named, id, kind, name) and lenses (id, text), health (only when tier 3 is under the ceiling) and signed (when and the note you wrote on signing). Every item carries ref, a reference such as L12; a reference stands for one line id of the day, and only lines of the day get one, so the model cannot cite a line from the night before even though the material describes that night.

docs.title: Why a file in the package
docs.text: So that the words a model is given are versioned with the code that checks its answer, readable without running anything, and the same on every machine: an orchestrator that rebuilds a Day from the record and a second implementation that writes drafts can read the same prompt and know what a dream-day/4 draft was asked for.

docs.title: The journey's and the week's
docs.text: A journey and a week have prompts of their own beside it, dream-journey-prompt.md (dream-journey/1) and dream-week-prompt.md (dream-week/2), with the same first rule, evidence or unsupported, and one more: numbers are given, never made. A figure is written only as an item it cites gives it, never added up, rounded or estimated, and a day's or a call's drafted text, a model's words, never lends one; the code marks a sentence that breaks it. The week's says too that no number stands beside a person (its third rule, since dream-week/2): a sentence that names one and writes a figure is held (Journeys and weeks). The journey's asks for eight lists: journey, days, places, people, decisions, promises, photos (the ones to star, at most six) and name (one). The week's asks for six: time, energy (empty when the material says no data), people, goals ({goal, disposition, text, evidence}, one per goal the week holds anything for), next_week (exactly one) and personal, and says, as a rule of its own, never moralise. --show-prompt prints either as it goes.

docs.title: The dream
docs.text:
Every morning a model reads yesterday and writes one line about it: the goodnight story, an answer to each of your lenses, the threads it moved, what the day shows was learned and decided, the ideas it moved, one question for your reflection, and proposals, the people it thinks were there, the promises it thinks were made, the photo of the day, the events it thinks the day held and the lines it thinks belong to one of your ideas or orgs (The dream learns, below). Every sentence points at the lines it came from. The line is a draft/v1 (RFC 0036, the profile), and the Day shows it above your note, labelled as a draft.

logbook dream day 2026-06-13            # one day, one line
logbook dream day 2026-06-13 --dry-run  # ask the model, check the answer, write nothing
logbook dream day 2026-10-21 --evening  # today so far: the draft says `the day so far`
logbook dream journey trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-17   # a journey that has come home, or any day of it
logbook dream week 2026-W25             # a week whose Sunday is over; no week: the last one over
logbook dream --catch-up --days 14      # every day of the last fortnight that needs it, its weeks, the calls, the journeys
logbook dream --catch-up --since 2026-05-01   # the same, and every call since 1 May that has no synthesis

A journey and a week are dreamed by the same engine under the same entry and the same evidence rule (Journeys and weeks).

docs.title: What the dream is, and is not
docs.text:
The dream is a proposal. Your signature (day sign) and your notes are the facts; a draft is never one, however many times the model agrees with itself. No reader derives anything from a draft: not a stay, not a person, not a promise. You confirm a sentence by confirming the lines it rests on, in a signed day; a sentence that rests on nothing is confirmed by nothing but you writing it down yourself.

The dream never writes a note, a signature or a review. It writes one draft line, source model:<name>, and nothing else. Dreaming a day again writes a new line whose supersedes names the one before; the earlier text stays in the record and the Day lists its id. Nothing is edited and nothing is deleted.

docs.title: The policy entry
docs.text:
Sending a day to a model is a crossing like any other, so it is governed by policy/crossing.json (ADR 0016, ADR 0022). The dream needs a dream entry:

{"hermes": {"max_tier": 2},
 "mcp": {"max_tier": 1},
 "dream": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2026-12-31", "model": "qwen2.5-7b-instruct"}}

You write each entry yourself; a new record names only mcp, at 1.

  • max_tier is the ceiling the day is read under. The model sees only lines at or under it: with 2, the stays, photos, calendar, notes and messages; with 1, no note and no message at all, since those are tier 2; tier 3 (health, money) only when you write 3.
  • until is the last day the entry holds. From the next day it counts as max_tier 0 and the dream refuses, as every expired entry does; logbook doctor names it.
  • model, optional, is the one model the day may go to. When the entry names one, it is the model used, and a LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL that says otherwise is refused: the entry is a ceiling, not a default.

No entry, or an expired one, and dream refuses in one sentence saying what to write. Nothing is read and nothing leaves the machine. doctor lists the entry on its crossing line as it lists every ceiling: dream 2 until 2026-12-31 model qwen2.5-7b-instruct.

The draft's tier is the highest tier among the lines the model actually read, not the ceiling and not the lines it cited (SPEC §4: derived data inherits the highest tier of its evidence, and the evidence of a draft is everything it read). A day of locations and photos dreamed under a ceiling of 2 is a tier-1 draft; the same ceiling over a day with a note is tier 2, and is sealed as tier 2 is in a record that seals.

docs.title: When the entry changes
docs.text:
A draft is derived through the dream entry, so it follows the entry, not the head (ADR 0016, Derived material follows the policy, not the head). Lowering the ceiling, letting until pass or removing the entry appends no line, so nothing in the record moves; what changes is what the readers show.

  • Every draft names the entry it was dreamed under: extra.policy_version, the SHA-256 (lowercase hex) of the RFC 8785 JSON of the entry's three deciding values, {"max_tier": 2, "model": null, "until": "2026-12-31"} (model and until null when the entry does not set them).
