The other exports, each with its own page: the crossing (a circle member's package), the vault, the site, the world, the letter, Notion and a trip's bundle (shared trips). logbook export FILE.jsonl writes the whole log, every line as it is, for re-entry: a copy of your own record, not a page that leaves.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text:
Six questions people asked the first time they saw it. Each answer ends with the files that back it: a page of the docs, a decision record, or a test that fails when the answer stops being true. Where the program does less than you might expect, the answer says so.

A path in code is a file in the repository; a test is named file::test.

docs.title: Is my data sent anywhere?
docs.text:
Not when you read it.

Reading a day, a page of the Library or anything a command prints opens no connection. A test holds the code to that. It replaces every way out of the program with one that refuses and records the attempt, then runs every reader and every page against a demo record. One attempt fails it. It runs on every pull request, on Linux, macOS and Windows. The test guards the code. It does not run inside the program on your machine.

Something crosses only on a command that says so. sync reaches the sources you name. --fetch-model downloads a model this machine does not have. dream and transcript synthesize send a day or a call, and people ask what passed between you and one person, to the model your policy names. serve mcp hands lines to an agent on this machine, up to the tier you allow. Where the agent sends them, the program cannot see. If you set them up, two short messages a day say the page is ready and ask the evening question. They carry the date, a count, the question and, if you set one, a link to the page. Nothing else.

A page you hand someone leaves when you type the command, to the person you name, and your record keeps a line that says it left.

Where this is written. docs.title: Which model reads my days?
docs.text:
None you did not ask for.

The Day is computed from your lines each time you open it. No model writes it, and the page says so at its foot.

Four commands send your lines to a model server, each through its own entry in policy/crossing.json. dream drafts a day, a journey or a week, and transcript synthesize a recorded call, both through the dream entry. people ask and dream person read what passed between you and one person, through the relationship entry. Without its entry a command refuses, and nothing leaves the machine. After the entry's last day it refuses again. With the schedule installed, the 06:00 close dreams the days that ended and the week's calls.

The entry sets the highest tier the model sees. At 1 it sees where you were and your calendar, and no note and no message. At 2 it sees your notes and messages too. Your health and your recorded calls reach it only at 3. If the entry names a model, every other model is refused.

What comes back is a draft. It sits above your day, marked as a draft. Each passage points at the lines it rests on, or is marked as resting on nothing. If more than three passages in ten rest on nothing, the program refuses the whole answer and writes nothing. Nothing else in the program builds on a draft.

What the code does not check. It does not check where the dream's model runs. An entry at tier 3 sends your health and your calls to whatever address you give it, on your machine or on someone else's. Keeping tier 3 at home is your policy. The program does not enforce it. The people reader is stricter for now: its model is a cloud one, so its entry may not go above tier 2.

docs.title: A model on your own machine
docs.text:
Some commands run a model on this machine: they transcribe recordings, describe photos, judge promises, tell voices apart and hear a spoken reflection. They need no entry, since the model runs here. While they run, the program tells the model's libraries not to fetch anything. The library that tells voices apart reports usage by default, and the program switches that off. A model the machine does not have is never fetched by itself. Only --fetch-model downloads one, and videos fetch --models the models for videos.

That is an instruction to the libraries, not a wall. The tests prove that the program's own code opens no connection. They run with a stand-in for the model, so they say nothing about the model itself, and the model files are outside the threat model. The program does not vouch for the models, or for who made them.

dream can also send a day to a model server on this machine, at an address such as http://127.0.0.1:8080, with no key. That server is a separate program, which you run. The same holds for it.

Where this is written. docs.title: Why open source, and why a pen name?
docs.text:
Because a log you cannot take with you is not yours.

The code is Apache-2.0. The specification is public domain, CC0, so anyone may write a program that reads a logbook without asking. One already exists: logbook-ts, written in TypeScript from the specification. On every pull request one program writes a line and the other verifies it. Version 1.0 is frozen only when both agree.

I write as bighydro so the format can be bigger than its author. Nothing personal enters the repository. Before a change merges, a check on my machine reads it for anything of mine.

Where this is written. Letter 0 · LICENSE · SPEC.md · conformance and .github/workflows/ci.yml · RULES.md, rule 8 · ADR 0010 · Security, Housekeeping

docs.title: Can someone else read my record?
docs.text:
Only what you hand them, up to the tier you allow.

You hand someone a page: one day, signed with your key, for one person you name. policy/crossing.json holds the highest tier each person may receive. A page carries tier 1, where you were, unless you ask for more. Ask for more than the file allows and nothing is written. Someone the file does not name receives nothing. Every page you hand over is a line in your record. The person keeps it with their record, never in its chain.

There are three limits. Someone who takes the folder can read tier 1. Once sealing is on, tiers 2 and 3 open only with your key. Lines written before stay plain until you seal them, with one command. Then whoever takes the folder learns where you were and when a message came, and none of the words. The Library shows every tier, so whoever can reach your machine's pages reads all of it. Keep them to your own devices. An agent you connect sees tier 1 unless you raise its ceiling.

Where this is written. docs.title: What if I stop using it?
docs.text:
Your record stays readable without the program.

It is a folder of files. Your lines are JSON, one file a month, and any editor opens them, today or in twenty years. The photos and recordings they point at sit beside them, each as its own file. The index the program builds is a cache, kept outside the folder. Delete it and it is rebuilt from the files. A sealed line carries what it says as an age file. age is an open format, with programs in Go, Rust and TypeScript. Your key opens it, and the key is never in the folder. The format is one page, SPEC.md, which anyone may implement without asking.

You can leave at any time, with everything.

Where this is written. SPEC §1, and §2, Sealed lines · The tour · ADR 0001 · RFC 0029 §3 · Security, Confidentiality at rest and The keys · The manifesto

docs.title: Is this an app?
docs.text:
Not yet. There is no app to download. The record on a phone is on the roadmap, in the passage called Everyone.

What exists is the Library, logbook serve: pages your own machine serves to your browser. It answers that machine and no other. A phone reaches it through a tunnel, or through Tailscale Serve once logbook setup phone names it; nothing else reads it. /today opens today's page, the one to keep on a phone.

At the foot of each day you write a few sentences about it. Once a transcription model is installed, you can say them instead. The page proposes the promises it finds in your words, and you tick the ones you made. Then you sign. On the machine itself, or from a phone through a tunnel, the evening needs no terminal. Through Tailscale Serve, once logbook setup phone names your phone, you can read the pages and sign them too.

Where this is written. ROADMAP.md, 4 · Everyone · In a browser: Three rules, Reaching it from another device, Reflect and Sign · tests/test_serve.py::test_refuses_to_bind_anything_but_loopback · tests/test_serve.py::test_today_is_the_current_day_in_the_records_timezone · The signed day

docs.title: The first hour
docs.text:
You have installed logbook and you have a terminal open. Maybe for the first time. This page walks through the hour that follows: logbook setup asks you six things, one at a time, and this is what each screen looks like, what to type, and what happens to it. Nothing you type is sent anywhere; it stays in a folder on this computer.

Every example here is the Oslo persona, Ines Nordmann, who does not exist; the addresses are at example.org and the numbers are in a reserved range. Put your own in their place.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Open a terminal: on a Mac, Terminal in Applications → Utilities; on Windows, Terminal from the Start menu; on Linux, you know. Type the lines shown after $ and press Enter. Everything else on the page is what the computer prints back.

$ pipx install openlogbook
$ logbook --version

If the second line prints a version, you are ready. If it says the command is not found, close the terminal, open a new one, and try again: pipx tells the shell about new commands on the next start. If you do not have pipx, or you are on a Mac and would rather brew install bighydro/logbook/logbook, install.md takes the install one step at a time, with what each step prints.

docs.title: logbook setup
docs.text:
$ logbook setup
Welcome. This sets up your logbook, one question at a time.
Enter takes the answer in brackets, s skips a step, q stops.
Nothing you type here is sent anywhere; it stays in the record's folder.

Three keys do everything: Enter takes the answer shown in brackets, s skips the step, q stops. Stopping loses nothing: what you answered is kept, and logbook setup again continues at the first question you have not answered. Every question says why it is asked, under Why:.

docs.title: Step 1: where to keep the record
docs.text:
── Step 1 of 6: where to keep the record ────────────────────────────────────
Why: The record is a folder of plain files: that is the whole product. It must be a folder no
     sync service (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive) touches: those evict files
     to the cloud, rewrite them underneath the writer and keep your record on someone else's
     server.
Where should the record live? [~/Logbook]:
Created ~/Logbook: the record, its policy/ and inbox/ folders, no lines yet.

Press Enter. ~/Logbook is a folder called Logbook in your home folder, where every command looks for it without being told. The only wrong answer is a folder a sync service owns, and the wizard refuses it with the reason:

Where should the record live? [~/Logbook]: ~/Dropbox/Logbook
Not there: ~/Dropbox/Logbook is under Dropbox; a sync client evicts files to the cloud and fetches them
back on demand, rewrites month files and logbook.json underneath the writer, and keeps the record on
someone else's server; move it to a plain local folder and point LOGBOOK_HOME at it.
Pick a plain local folder, such as ~/Records/Logbook.
Where should the record live? [~/Logbook]:

If you do pick a folder other than ~/Logbook, the last screen tells you the one line to put in your shell profile so every command finds it. If a record is already in the folder you name, the wizard says Found your record at ~/Logbook; keeping it and carries on with that record's setup.

docs.title: Step 2: your timezone
docs.text:
── Step 2 of 6: your timezone ───────────────────────────────────────────────
Why: Every time in the record is stored in UTC; your zone is how the days are cut and shown
     (SPEC §3.2). A flight landing at 23:30 your time is on that day, not the next.
Your timezone, as the zone database names it [Etc/UTC] (the record's zone now, which Enter keeps; or type another, such as Europe/Oslo): Europe/Oslo
Timezone set to Europe/Oslo (was Etc/UTC).

The answer in brackets is what this computer thinks its zone is; Enter accepts it. A zone is spelled as a continent, a slash, and the nearest big city: Europe/Oslo, America/New_York, Asia/Tokyo. A name this machine does not know is refused and the question asked again, never swapped for a guess:

Your timezone, as the zone database names it [Etc/UTC] (the record's zone now, which Enter keeps; or type another, such as Europe/Oslo): Mars/Olympus
'Mars/Olympus' is not a zone this machine knows; Europe/Oslo, America/New_York and
Asia/Tokyo are: a continent, a slash, the nearest big city.
Your timezone, as the zone database names it [Etc/UTC] (the record's zone now, which Enter keeps; or type another, such as Europe/Oslo): Europe/Oslo
Timezone set to Europe/Oslo (was Etc/UTC).

docs.title: Step 3: who you are
docs.text:
── Step 3 of 6: who you are ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Why: The record meets you under many names: the address a friend writes to, the number a contact
     saved, a nickname. Listing them in policy/owner.json tells every reader which lines are
     you, so you are never your own company when it counts who you spent the day with.
Your names, as contacts and mail know you, separated by commas [skip]: Ines Nordmann, Ines
Your email addresses, separated by commas [skip]: ines.nordmann@example.org
Your phone numbers, separated by commas [skip]: 07700 900123
Wrote ~/Logbook/policy/owner.json: 4 added. Edit it any time; it is yours, never in the chain.
The emails are owner_emails in logbook.json too, so mail and chat imports know your side.

Why this matters: when the record counts who you spent a day with, it must know which messages, calls and photos are you. Without this list, the day you texted yourself a shopping list reads as a day with a very close friend. Three questions, commas between several answers, Enter on a question you have nothing for. The file is policy/owner.json in the record; open it in any text editor later to add more. If the file already lists something, the screen says already listed: and what you type is added.

Nothing here is a password. The wizard never asks for one, anywhere.

docs.title: Step 4: your home place
docs.text:
── Step 4 of 6: your home place ─────────────────────────────────────────────
Why: A night is at home when you slept within this circle; trips, nights away and the countries
     you were in are counted from it. Coordinates only, never an address: the record keeps what
     you paste, so paste the two numbers a maps app shows when you press on your front door.
Your home, as latitude, longitude [skip] (e.g. 59.9139, 10.7522): 59.9139, 10.7522
What to call it [Home]:
named 59.9139,10.7522 as Home (line #1); a circle of 120 m in places.json.

Open Google Maps or Apple Maps on your phone or in a browser, press and hold on your front door, and two numbers appear, something like 59.9139, 10.7522. Copy them, paste them here. That is all the record keeps: a point and a circle of 120 metres, under the name Home, in places.json. It is also the first line in your record: named 59.9139,10.7522 as Home, the day you gave your home its name.

An address is refused. The record keeps what you type, so it never asks for one:

Your home, as latitude, longitude [skip] (e.g. 59.9139, 10.7522): 12 Example Street
'12 Example Street' is not coordinates. In Google or Apple Maps, press and hold on the spot and
copy the two numbers it shows, like 59.9139, 10.7522. Never type an address here.
Your home, as latitude, longitude [skip] (e.g. 59.9139, 10.7522):

Not sure yet? Enter skips it; logbook setup places name 59.9139,10.7522 Home --kind home does it later, or logbook setup --step home asks again.

docs.title: Step 5: what is on this machine
docs.text:
The wizard looks in three places and tells you what it found. Nothing is read beyond what it takes to recognise an export, and nothing is written until you say so, twice: once for a dry run that only counts, once for the import.

── Step 5 of 6: what is on this machine ─────────────────────────────────────
Why: The record grows from exports you already have. Each one found here is offered with a dry
     run first: the adapter reads it and counts, and nothing is written until you say so. An
     export is only ever read; your files stay where they are.

A Google Takeout is a folder called Takeout in your Downloads, once the zip Google sent you is unzipped (double-click it). Each product Google exported that the adapters read is listed, with the ones your policy has switched off:

Google Takeout at ~/Downloads/Takeout:
  google-takeout-chat: ~/Downloads/Takeout/Google Chat
  google-takeout-meet: ~/Downloads/Takeout/Google Meet
  google-takeout-activity: switched off in policy/import.json (every search and app opened; opt in)
Dry run these 2 import(s)? Nothing is written [Y/n]:
google-takeout-chat: 6 lines would be added, 0 already in the record (dry run, nothing written)
  skipped 1 without a timestamp, 0 with unusable coordinates
  skipped 1 without a body
  also 1 with media hashed, 1 without a message id, keyed by time and text
google-takeout-meet: 4 lines would be added, 0 already in the record (dry run, nothing written)
  skipped 1 without a timestamp, 0 with unusable coordinates
  also 1 without a conference id, keyed by start and organizer
Write these lines to the record? [Y/n]:
added 6 lines from google-takeout-chat
  skipped 1 without a timestamp, 0 with unusable coordinates
  skipped 1 without a body
  also 1 with media hashed, 1 without a message id, keyed by time and text
added 4 lines from google-takeout-meet
  skipped 1 without a timestamp, 0 with unusable coordinates
  also 1 without a conference id, keyed by start and organizer

The dry run is the real import with the writing left out: the same reader, the same counts, and already in the record tells you what a second run would skip. Answer n to either question and nothing happens; logbook add ~/Downloads/Takeout/"Google Chat" does the same later. A Takeout still zipped is named and left alone: unzip it first (double-click it), then run logbook setup --step sources again.

An iPhone backup is what Finder (or iTunes, or the Apple Devices app on Windows) makes when you plug the phone in and press Back Up Now. The wizard finds it where those apps keep it, lists the stores in it that the adapters know, and shows the exact command it is about to run, always with --only the stores found and never the whole backup unasked:

iPhone backup 00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60 at ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60:
  stores found: ios-contacts, imessage, ios-notes
  the command: logbook import-backup ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60 --only ios-contacts,imessage,ios-notes
Dry run it? Nothing is written [Y/n]:
ios-contacts: AddressBook.sqlitedb (20,480 bytes) → ~/Logbook/inbox/ios-backup-00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60/ios-contacts
imessage: sms.db (61,440 bytes) + sms.db-wal (0 bytes) + 2 media files (50 bytes) under Attachments/ → ~/Logbook/inbox/ios-backup-00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60/imessage
ios-notes: NoteStore.sqlite (12,288 bytes) → ~/Logbook/inbox/ios-backup-00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60/ios-notes
dry run: 3 of 3 sources found, 94,258 bytes would be copied to ~/Logbook/inbox/ios-backup-00008030-000A1B2C3D4E5F60; nothing written
Copy these stores into inbox/ and import them? [Y/n]:
added 8 lines from ios-contacts
  skipped 1 with a phone or email already seen, 1 without a phone or email
added 13 lines from imessage
  skipped 2 reactions, 1 group system events, 1 with an unusable date, 1 without a chat, 2 without a body
added 4 lines from ios-notes
  skipped 1 password protected, 1 with an unusable date
valid — 25 lines, head cfa62f52b875e25dd949e23cbc4a3006c993660f6a4ca83f448bd7a596f11e0f

The backup itself is only read. Each store is copied into the record's inbox/ folder, checked against the backup, and read from there; the counts say what each adapter added and what it skipped, and the last line is verify: the chain is intact. (The dry run and import above are from a synthetic backup the tests build; yours will list more stores and many more lines.)

An encrypted backup (Encrypt local backup ticked in Finder) holds more: Health, the call log, Safari. It needs its password, and the wizard will not take it. It names the variable to put it in and how, and moves on:

iPhone backup 00008030-00000000000000BB at ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/00008030-00000000000000BB:
  encrypted: it holds more (Health, calls, Safari) and needs its password in LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD, which setup never asks for. In a terminal, type
    read -s LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD && export LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD
  (typed once, never shown), then `logbook import-backup <folder> --only <sources>`.

read -s reads what you type without showing it on the screen; the password is held by your terminal for that session only, never written to a file, never printed, never part of an error.

Messages on a Mac is the Mac's own Messages database. It is read live, new messages each time, by logbook sync imessage; the first time, macOS will ask you to give your terminal app Full Disk Access (System Settings → Privacy & Security), or refuse the read:

Messages on this Mac: ~/Library/Messages/chat.db
  `logbook sync imessage` reads it, new messages each run; the terminal app needs Full Disk
  Access (System Settings → Privacy & Security) or macOS refuses the read.
Dry run it? Nothing is written [Y/n]:
  13 messages in 0s
imessage: 13 lines since 2026-03-01T18:01:10Z (dry run, nothing written)
  first 2026-03-02T17:42:10Z  last 2026-03-02T18:01:10Z  watermark 2026-03-02T18:01:10Z
Write these messages to the record? [Y/n]:

Nothing found is the common first answer, and the wizard says where each kind would be:

Found nothing to import yet. Where each kind would be:
  Google Takeout: the Takeout folder (unzipped) in ~/Downloads
  iPhone backup: Finder → your iPhone → Back Up Now; it lands under
    ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup
    (Windows: %APPDATA%\Apple Computer\MobileSync\Backup)
  Messages on a Mac: ~/Library/Messages/chat.db (`logbook sync imessage`)
Any export: `logbook add <file-or-folder>`; the adapters recognise it.

Live sources come last. These are services that logbook sync <name> pulls from on their own, each needing a key or an address in a variable of your shell. The wizard prints the variable's name and where the key comes from, and never a value, set or not:

Live sources pull on their own with `logbook sync <name>`; each needs a variable set:
  immich: set LOGBOOK_IMMICH_URL and LOGBOOK_IMMICH_KEY — Immich → Account settings → API keys, with only the asset.read permission; the URL is yours
  dawarich: set LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_URL and LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY — Dawarich → Settings → Account → API key; the URL is your Dawarich's address
  granola: set LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_KEY — Granola → Connectors → API keys (Business and Enterprise plans)
  gcal: set LOGBOOK_GCAL_URLS, or LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY and LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER — the Google service account (the tour, Google, on one key), else Google Calendar → Settings → the calendar → Integrate calendar → Secret address in iCal format
  drive: set LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY and LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER — a Workspace service account with domain-wide delegation (the tour, Google, on one key): its JSON key file, kept at mode 600 outside the record, and the address it reads as
  gtasks: set LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY and LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER — the same service account and address as drive, with the Tasks read-only scope delegated too
  ais: set LOGBOOK_AISSTREAM_KEY — a free key from aisstream.io, for the vessels registered in assets.json
  adsb: works without a key; optional LOGBOOK_OPENSKY_USER and LOGBOOK_OPENSKY_PASS — an account at opensky-network.org (optional: anonymous access works, with a lower rate)
  gmail: set LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY and LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER — the same service account and address as drive, with Gmail's read-only scope delegated too
  beeper: set LOGBOOK_BEEPER_TOKEN — Beeper Desktop → Settings → Developers → Approved connections (+); the token reads every chat and can send as you, so it is a password; the app must be running, Remote Access off
  telegram: set LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKENS and LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_OWNER_ID — @BotFather → /mybots → each bot of yours → API Token, comma-separated (each reads and sends as its bot, so it is a password); your numeric user id is personal_information.user_id in Telegram Desktop's export
  notion: set LOGBOOK_NOTION_TOKEN — Notion → Settings → Connections → Develop or manage integrations → New integration (internal, Read content only), then share each top-level page with it (••• → Connections)
  github: set LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN and LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS — GitHub → Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens: read-only Metadata, Contents, Issues and Pull requests on the repos LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS names (owner/name, or --all); your logins go under handles in policy/owner.json
A key goes in the variable in your shell profile, never in a file of the record, never here.

One you have set shows as configured (LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_URL, LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY): the names, so you can see it took; never what they hold. Setting one is a line in your shell profile, such as export LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY=...; the tour has each service's section.

docs.title: Step 6: a check-up
docs.text:
── Step 6 of 6: a check-up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
Why: `logbook doctor` is the check-up: one line per check, pass, warn or fail. Run it any time.
pass  record            11 lines, head b9f126fcd8fc…, verified; /Users/ines/Logbook
pass  index             index.sqlite is current with logbook.json
pass  owner             policy/owner.json names 2 names, 1 emails, 1 phones
pass  places            1 place(s), home: Home
pass  assets            no assets.json; nothing is tracked as a subject
pass  dates             every line is dated inside its source's plausible range (policy/plausible.json)
warn  extra:ais         websockets not installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[ais]==0.7.1"
warn  extra:crypto      cryptography not installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[crypto]==0.7.1"
warn  extra:sealed      pyrage not installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[sealed]==0.7.1"
warn  extra:speakers    pyannote.audio not installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[speakers]==0.7.1"
warn  extra:transcribe  mlx-whisper or faster-whisper not installed: pipx inject openlogbook "openlogbook[transcribe]==0.7.1"
pass  crossing          mcp 1
pass  world             export world shows tier 1 alone: policy/crossing.json names no world entry; {"world": {"max_tier": 2}} would add the chapters
pass  export-day        export --day puts tier 1 alone in a folder: policy/crossing.json names no folder entry, so the default tier 1 applies; {"folder": {"max_tier": 2}} would let tier 2 go
pass  phone             the Library is written from this machine only; `logbook setup phone` lets your phone write too
pass  schedule          no machine runs the scheduled syncs yet: `logbook sync --install-schedule` on the one that keeps the record makes it that machine (ADR 0022)
pass  last-run          no schedule on this machine; `logbook sync --install-schedule` runs `sync --all` and `doctor` four times a day and writes it
warn  restore-test      no restore test yet: run `logbook backup DEST` once, then `logbook backup --restore-test`, which restores the latest snapshot into a temporary folder and verifies it; the schedule runs it on the first Sunday of the month
pass  serve             no serve service on this machine; `logbook serve --install-service` keeps the pages at http://127.0.0.1:8765/ from load (docs/serve.md)
pass  disk              29.8 GiB free on the record's volume
pass  folder            a plain local folder, no sync client
21 checks: 15 pass, 6 warn, 0 fail

Setup is complete. Your record is at ~/Logbook.
Next:
    logbook add "had lunch with a friend by the lake"    # a line in your words
    logbook show today                                   # the day read back
    logbook verify                                       # the chain is intact
docs/first-hour.md walks through the first hour.

warn is advice, not a problem: here, the optional extras for transcribing voice memos and telling the voices of a recording apart are not installed, and no backup has had its restore test yet. fail names what to fix. logbook doctor runs these checks any time, and changes nothing.

docs.title: Stopping, skipping, and coming back
docs.text:
Press q at any question, or close the terminal, and this is the whole screen:

Your names, as contacts and mail know you, separated by commas [skip]: q

Stopped. Run `logbook setup` again any time: it continues where you stopped.

The steps answered are kept in state/setup.json inside the record (bookkeeping, not part of the record itself), and the next logbook setup starts at the first one not yet answered. s skips a step and moves to the next; a skipped step is remembered as skipped, not asked again. To revisit one:

$ logbook setup --step owner      # one step again: folder, timezone, owner, home, sources, doctor
$ logbook setup --again           # every step again; the record is kept

Once every step is answered, logbook setup says so and offers those two.

docs.title: The rest of the hour
docs.text:
The record is a folder. Open ~/Logbook in Finder or Explorer: logbook/ holds the lines, one file a month, plain text; policy/ your settings; inbox/ the copies of what you imported. Nothing in it needs this program to be read.

$ logbook add "coffee with Kari, talked about the summer"
$ logbook show today
$ logbook show stats
$ logbook verify

add with a sentence is a note in your words. show today reads the day back: what was imported, what you wrote. show stats counts what the record holds, by kind, source and year, and never shows a line's text. verify recomputes every hash and says valid; it will say so every time, until a byte changes.

Then, at your pace: Try it runs every command on a demo record of a person who does not exist; the 32 commands are one page, with the older names each still answers to; the tour's Sources lists the exports the adapters read, with the command for each; and logbook doctor is there whenever something feels off.

docs.title: --yes
docs.text: logbook setup --yes takes every default and asks nothing: the record in ~/Logbook (or where LOGBOOK_HOME points), the detected timezone, the steps with no default skipped, every found export dry-run and imported, the check-up at the end. It is for tests and scripts; a person should answer the questions.

docs.title: Gifts
docs.text:
What you gave someone, and what you were given, is something only you can say. The gift act is one line in the record, in your words, appended through Logbook.append like every other line and never an edit (RFC 0043, §11 and §12).

$ logbook add gift 2026-10-10 "Per Hansen" "a book on knots"
#54 given to Per Hansen: a book on knots
$ logbook add gift 2026-10-11 Ola "cloudberry jam" --received
#55 received from Ola Nordmann: cloudberry jam

docs.title: What it writes
docs.text:
One note/v1 line (RFC 0010) through the notes path every note on a day takes (logbook/core/notes.py):

  • the text is the gift in your words, as you typed it, never filtered;
  • the label is gift;
  • the person is under extra.recipient when you gave it and under extra.giver with --received: the person's entity id, as the record's resolution lines name them;
  • tier 2, as every note is; source manual.

No new profile: a reader that does not know gifts reads a note.

When: on the day as every note on a past day is, at its last minute (23:59, or 05:59 the next morning when your day begins at 06:00, where your day begins); now when the day is today. A day that has not begun is refused: a gift is written on the day it changed hands. The same gift said twice on one day, the same person, the same way and the same words, is one line.

docs.title: The name
docs.text:
NAME is the person logbook people NAME would open: a label (case aside), a unique first or last name, an entity id, or an address the record resolves. A name the record cannot place is refused in one sentence, and nothing is written:

$ logbook add gift 2026-10-11 Nordmann "a jar of honey"
add: 'Nordmann' names several people: Ines Nordmann, Kari Nordmann, Ola Nordmann; nothing was written

The same for a name that is nobody the resolution lines name, and for your own name: a gift is given to someone or received from them. logbook people review places the people the sources saw under the names the record holds.

docs.title: Reading them back
docs.text:
$ logbook people gifts
1 given, 1 received
2026-10-10  given to Per Hansen: a book on knots  #54
2026-10-11  received from Ola Nordmann: cloudberry jam  #55
$ logbook people gifts Per
gifts with Per Hansen
1 given, 0 received
2026-10-10  given to Per Hansen: a book on knots  #54

logbook people gifts [NAME] [--json] lists every gift both ways, in the day's order, or one person's; a retracted gift is not listed (logbook repair retract). --json gives person, name, given, received and each gift's day, direction, person, name, what and line.

The reader is logbook.core.gifts.gifts(lb, person=None, window=None): a person's name as above, and a window of local days (first, last). Through a gate without tier 2 it lists nothing, since every note is tier 2. A person's page is to print one row for it, under the person's name and never beside it, gifts 3 given, 1 received: logbook people gifts NAME (gifts.counts), once the person page takes it.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text:
• Not a score. No count of gifts stands beside a person's name, on a page or in the terminal, and nothing is ranked by them.
  • Not a model's. A gift is written only when you say it; a draft may mention one, and never writes it.
  • Not a receipt. What a gift cost is the ledger's, at tier 3 (the ledger); a gift note is tier 2 and says only what you wrote.

docs.title: Goals, reviews and chapters
docs.text:
The record holds what happened. These three hold what you are for, what became of it, and what you call a stretch of your life. Each is one line in your own words, and nothing else in the record is derived from it (RFC 0036): a goal (goal/v1), a review, your verdict on a goal at a date (review/v1), and a chapter, a named stretch (chapter/v1). The profiles each have a page: goal/v1, review/v1, chapter/v1.

logbook goal add "Sail to Lofoten and back between June and August." --horizon year --from 2026-01-01
logbook goal review 12 let-go --period month --at 2026-08-31 --note "Engine gone in Bodø. Next summer."
logbook goal list
logbook goal import goals.txt --horizon year --review let-go --at 2026-08-31
logbook chapter open "The Lofoten summer" --from 2026-06-20 --rules "Every night at anchor counts."
logbook chapter close --to 2026-08-09
logbook chapter list

All three are tier 2, always: they are your words, as private as a note (SPEC §4, note/v1). A tier is where a line may travel, not who wrote it, so no option sets another one, and a reader under a ceiling of 1 (the MCP door at its default, a crossing at tier 1) never sees a goal, a review or a chapter, nor the chapter name in a Day's header. Every line is source manual: you wrote it, not a tool and not a model. A model that proposes a goal writes a draft or a note labelled proposal; the goal is yours to write.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
goal add TEXT --horizon life|year|quarter writes one goal. --from is the first day it holds for (today by default, in your day: under a day_start of 06:00, 05:30 is still yesterday), --until the last, when it has one. The line's at is now, when you wrote it; from is the stretch, which is often earlier (the year's goal, written in its first week).

One line is one goal. Asked for the same words twice, it writes two goals, and you retract one (repair retract SEQ REASON). A goal said better or bounded differently is a new goal that names the old one: --supersedes GOAL, by id or by seq as goal list prints it. The earlier words stay in the record, marked superseded where they are shown; the chain of supersedes is one goal. A goal that is superseded already cannot be superseded again: reword the standing one.

goal list prints every standing goal with its latest review, and how many are open; --open only the open ones, --json the same with line ids. A goal is open until a review says done, let go or superseded, or its until has passed.

2 goals · 1 open
  #2     year     from 2026-01-01 until 2026-12-31   Sail to Lofoten and back between June and August.
         let go 2026-08-31 · month · Engine gone in Bodø on the 9th. Towed home. Next summer.
  #5     quarter  from 2026-10-01                    Learn to splice a rope.
         unreviewed

docs.title: Reviews
docs.text:
goal review GOAL DISPOSITION is your verdict on a goal, one of five: advancing and stalled keep it open, done, let-go and superseded close it. The line stores let go with a space, the profile's word; the command line takes let-go so it needs no quotes. A later review stands over an earlier one: a goal closed and then reviewed advancing is open again, and the record shows the change of mind.

--period day|week|month|quarter|year is the stretch the verdict covers (default: the goal's horizon, a year for a life goal). --note is the verdict in your words.

--at is the day the verdict is about, and a review is often written long after it: let go in August, written down in October, the line's at is in August and its recorded_at in October, and the review is on the August Day. A day, YYYY-MM-DD, is that day's last minute (23:59, or 05:59 the next morning when your day begins at 06:00), or now when it is today; a moment with an offset or Z (2026-08-31T22:00:00+02:00) is itself. A verdict more than five minutes in the future is refused, and so is one before the goal's from.

One verdict per goal, per period, per day: asked to review the same goal (any line of its chain) for the same period on the same day again, the command writes nothing and says which review is there. A second opinion on the same day is a retraction of the first and a new review.

docs.title: The first backfill
docs.text:
goal import FILE reads a plain text file, one goal per line, with two optional columns:

# the year so far
Sail to Lofoten and back. | year | 2026-01-01
Rebuild the engine. | quarter | 2026-07-01
Read one book a month.
Keep the boat. | | 2026-03-01

A line without a horizon takes --horizon, one without a first day takes --from (today by default); blank lines and lines starting with # are skipped. --review DISPOSITION writes one review of every goal imported, with --at, --period (each goal's horizon's by default) and --note as goal review takes them: the year's goals written down in October and let go at the end of August are one command. Every line is checked before any is written, and they are all written in one batch: a line that does not read, or a review before a goal's first day, names the line and writes nothing. --dry-run prints what would be written. A file saved on Windows (a byte order mark, CRLF) reads as any other.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text:
chapter open NAME names a stretch from --from (today by default) with its --rules, what counts in it and what you are for in it, as plain text no reader interprets. A chapter is usually named once you know it is one: --to gives its last day when it is already over. chapter close closes the open chapter on --to (today by default): the chapter written again with its last day and every other field, its rules included, superseding the open line. chapter list prints every standing chapter, its rules under it, and · today beside the one today is in.

Chapters do not overlap: a stretch that shares a day with a standing chapter is refused, naming it (and, when that one is open, saying to close it first). The same name from the same day is the same chapter: asked for it twice, the command writes nothing and says so. This is not lab chapters, which reads a table of contents out of the track and writes nothing.

docs.title: On the Day
docs.text:
day, show and the Day page of serve show these lines on the days they are about (docs/day.md):

2026-07-04  Saturday · signed 2026-07-05 08:15 · chapter The Lofoten summer
  • The chapter, in the header, after the weekday and the signed state: the standing chapter whose stretch holds the day. Should two standing chapters hold one day (two writers, or a retraction that reopened one), the later by from is shown and the header says , clashes with <the other>.
  • The reviews, one row per review on the day the verdict is about, with the goal's current text (a review of the earlier line of a reworded goal shows the reworded words), and written <when> when it was written on a later day, so a backfilled verdict never passes for one made on the day. Of two reviews of one goal for one period on a day, the later is shown; a retracted one is not.
  reviews       let go · month · Sail to Lofoten and back between June and August. · Engine gone in Bodø on the 9th. Towed home. Next summer. · written 2026-10-11 20:30
  • The goal and chapter lines, on the day you wrote them, as every line is: goal <text> (year, from 2026-01-01), chapter The Lofoten summer 2026-06-20 – 2026-08-09, each · superseded when a later line replaced it. show lists a review as let go · month · <goal text>.

Under --json the Day carries chapter (name, line, from, to, and clash when there is one), reviews (line, goal, goal_text, disposition, period, note, recorded_at), goals and chapters (the lines written on the day, each with superseded, the id of the line that replaced it). Each key is there only on a day that has one, as draft and reflection are, so the Day's object is otherwise what it was and the conformance fixtures do not move: a day in no chapter has no chapter key, where RFC 0036 writes null, and a day with no review no reviews key, where it writes an empty list. days, digest, year and the printed pages are unchanged.

A goal, a review and a chapter whose at is on a day are on its page, so writing one on a signed day makes its signature read as the page having changed since, as any line does (RFC 0034); sign again.

docs.title: One writer at a time
docs.text: Every one of these commands is a writer: it holds the record's writer lock for its whole run, from the first read of the record to the append, and with --no-wait it refuses with exit 2 while another command writes. Before it appends it reads the head again; when another writer moved it in between (one that did not take the lock), it writes nothing and says the head moved, exit 2.

docs.title: What you heard
docs.text:
The record knows which podcast episodes you played (Apple Podcasts, listen/v1) and which videos you watched (YouTube's watch history from a Takeout export, watch/v1). sync heard adds what was said in them: the episode's transcript or the video's captions, stored once in the attachment store, and one heard/v1 line beside the listen or watch it belongs to. logbook show heard lists them; logbook search finds words inside them. The design is RFC 0046 (draft).

The words are someone else's, published to anyone. The line is tier 2 all the same, because it says you heard them, as the listen line does. Nothing leaves: a crossing and a shared page leave every text home unless the destination's entry names it (below).

docs.title: Turn it on
docs.text:
export LOGBOOK_HEARD=feed,apple,captions   # the text sources you want; any of the three
logbook sync heard --dry-run               # what it would fetch and read, nothing written
logbook sync heard

feed fetches a transcript from the podcast's host, and each fetch tells that host which episode you played, a tier-2 fact like the listen itself. So the variable alone fetches nothing: feed needs a heard entry in policy/crossing.json that says so, with the tier of the listens (2) and, if you like, an until:

{"heard": {"max_tier": 2, "fetch": true, "until": "2026-12-31"}}

Without it, or once it has expired, every feed transcript is a counted skip (feed transcript not fetched), the entry is checked before any request or lookup, and one line says what to write; logbook doctor names the entry on its crossing line. apple and captions read files on this machine and need no entry.

Until LOGBOOK_HEARD is set, sync --all and the schedule skip the source and say so. Once set, the schedule runs it after every other source but the photo walk, so it sees the listens the podcasts sync wrote. A dry run fetches nothing: it counts what it would fetch. To switch it off without unsetting the variable, list it in policy/import.json as any source: {"disabled": [{"source": "heard", "reason": "not now"}]}.

Variable What it does LOGBOOK_HEARD the text sources: feed, apple, captions (a comma list). Required LOGBOOK_HEARD_MAX_FETCHES network fetches a run at most (default 20); the rest wait for the next run LOGBOOK_HEARD_DELAY_S seconds between two fetches (default 2) LOGBOOK_HEARD_CAPTIONS_DIR the folder of caption files, for captions LOGBOOK_HEARD_LANGUAGES which caption language wins when a video has several, e.g. nb,en LOGBOOK_HEARD_TTML_DIR Apple Podcasts' transcript folder, when it is not the Mac's own LOGBOOK_PODCASTS_DB Apple Podcasts' store, as for sync apple-podcasts

docs.title: Where the words come from
docs.text:
feed — the podcast's own transcript. Many feeds publish an episode's transcript (<podcast:transcript>); sync apple-podcasts keeps its URL on the listen line and never fetches it. sync heard fetches it, once: WebVTT, SRT, podcasting 2.0's JSON and plain text are kept exactly as they came; an HTML transcript is skipped and counted, and so is a URL that points at this machine or your own network or any address that is not on the public internet (localhost, 127.0.0.1, 192.168.…, the tailnet's 100.64.0.0/10 and Tailscale's 100.100.100.100), which is never requested, nor a port other than 80 and 443. A host name (a MagicDNS name among them), or an address not written out in full (127.1), is looked up once and refused if any address it gives is one of those; a host that does not look up is a failed fetch, never a request. The connection goes to the address that was checked and no other, never through a proxy your environment names, while the name is still what the host and its certificate are checked against: a name that answers differently the second time is never asked twice. A redirect is followed only to another public http(s) address, three at most, and each hop is checked and connected the same way; one that points at this machine, your network, another scheme or port, or from an https page to http, is refused before it is requested. At most LOGBOOK_HEARD_MAX_FETCHES a run, two seconds apart. A fetch that fails is one counted skip; the same URL is not tried again for a week, and never after its third failure.

apple — what Apple Podcasts cached on this Mac. The app keeps the transcripts it shows as TTML files under ~/Library/Group Containers/243LU875E5.groups.com.apple.podcasts/Library/Cache/Assets/TTML/. Apple does not document that folder: it is where the files are today, and a macOS update may move it (LOGBOOK_HEARD_TTML_DIR then names the new one). Each file is matched to its episode through the Podcasts store's own columns, read-only. Nothing is fetched.

captions — a video's captions, from your folder. YouTube has no documented way to fetch a video's captions without a key, and the record does not scrape. So the captions come from a folder you fill with a tool of your choice, named by the video's id:

~/Captions/aB3dE5fG7hI.vtt        # one language
~/Captions/aB3dE5fG7hI.nb.vtt     # or one file per language
~/Captions/aB3dE5fG7hI.en.vtt

export LOGBOOK_HEARD_CAPTIONS_DIR=~/Captions, and the next sync heard writes a line for every watched video whose id has a file. The video itself is never downloaded.

local — a transcription on this machine. Reserved, not built: the record holds no audio of a podcast or a video to transcribe.

docs.title: What was heard
docs.text:
logbook show heard                             # the last 14 days
logbook show heard --day 2026-10-14
logbook show heard --since 2026-10-01 --until 2026-10-14
logbook show heard --day 2026-10-14 --json

2026-10-14 Wednesday
  08:40  feed      nb  41,237 chars  7,012 words  Episode 12: the east berth — Havnepodden
         «Velkommen til Havnepodden. I dag snakker vi om østkaia, og om hvorfor…»
  21:05  captions  en   3,912 chars    702 words  Splicing a three-strand rope — Knots by Ola
         «Today we splice a three-strand rope. First, unlay about a hand's width…»

A text is listed on the day of the listen or watch it belongs to: the first time you played the work. Playing an episode again writes no second text. A sealed text needs your identity to show anything; without it the row says [sealed heard/v1].

docs.title: Searching inside
docs.text:
logbook search finds words inside every text, as it finds them in a call's transcript. In a record that seals (after logbook key init), a text's line is sealed and the search index never holds the words of a sealed line, so search finds no heard text there, as it finds no sealed transcript:

logbook search splice                 # every line with the word, the texts among them
logbook search '"east berth"' --kinds heard

docs.title: Nothing leaves
docs.text:
A crossing (export crossing --to D) and a shared page (export share) leave every heard line, and its text, at home unless the destination's entry in policy/crossing.json says so:

{"hermes": {"max_tier": 2, "heard": true}}

The crossing counts what it left home under held_back_by_entry. The trip bundle never carries a text; the vault, the site, the world and the Notion export never copy an attachment; mcp serves the line, never the text.

docs.title: Hold
docs.text:
Hold is the layer that will give everything you own one place: your files, your apps, the senders in your mailbox, your Drive, later your boxes and the objects in them. Each thing gets a fate (keep it, shelve it, archive it, let it go), the attention it costs falls, and one number says how much is left. The whole design is a draft, RFC 0042.

Hold v0 only counts. It is three censuses in the lab, each a report you read. No line is written; nothing is moved, renamed or deleted, ever.

logbook lab hold census files ~/Documents ~/Desktop   # what is in these folders
logbook lab hold census senders                      # who writes to you, from the mail the record holds
logbook lab hold census drive                        # your Drive, from the Drive lines the record holds
logbook lab hold census senders --tier 3 --json      # tier-3 mail too; the summary as JSON

Each census writes its report, Markdown to read and JSON to keep, in the record folder:

<record>/state/hold/files.md      files.json
<record>/state/hold/senders.md    senders.json
<record>/state/hold/drive.md      drive.json

A run replaces the census's last report. The folder is the owner's alone (mode 0700, the reports 0600, where the system has modes). The terminal gets a summary: counts and where the report is, never a file name, a folder inside the ones you named, or an address.

hold census files: 18,204 files, 61.3 GB, in 1,912 folders under 2 given; 412 duplicate sets (3.1 GB held more than once); 37 folders untouched for two years
skipped: links 14, system folders 6, system files 210
report (tier 3; names stay in it): /Users/ines/Logbook/state/hold/files.md
  and /Users/ines/Logbook/state/hold/files.json; nothing was moved, renamed or deleted

--json prints the same summary as one object. The report's JSON is in the lab's terms: its shape may change between releases.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
census files PATH… walks the folders you name and reads them, nothing more.

  • By type, by extension and by year: how many files and how many bytes, the type by the extension (image, video, audio, document, spreadsheet, presentation, archive, code, mail, other, none), the year by the file's modified time in the record's zone.
  • Duplicates: files with the same bytes, found by SHA-256 of the bytes, read a megabyte at a time. Only files whose size another file shares are read at all; an empty file is never a duplicate. Each set says how many copies and how much space is held more than once.
  • The 50 largest, with their modified day.
  • Untouched for two years: the highest folders under which no file was modified in 730 days, by size. A folder inside one listed is not listed again; a folder you named, untouched as a whole, is listed as ..

What the walk never does:

  • It never writes in your folders. A file is opened read-only, and only when its size is shared with another (to hash it). Nothing is moved, renamed, deleted or created there; the report's changed block says 0 for each, and the tests hold the folder byte for byte to what it was. The one exception is the report itself: when the record lies inside a folder you named (census files ~ with the record at ~/Logbook), the report is written in the record's state/hold/, which the walk never enters. A state/hold that is a link, or not a folder, is refused: no report.
  • It never makes your computer fetch a file. A file whose bytes are elsewhere (an iCloud file not downloaded to this Mac, a OneDrive or Google Drive file on demand, an offline file) is counted from its metadata under not_local and never read, so it is never in a duplicate set; such a folder is not entered. A folder on another disk than the folder you named (a share or a disk mounted inside it, /proc) is counted under other_disk and not entered.
  • It never leaves the folders you named. A symbolic link (or a Windows junction) is counted under skipped: links and never followed, wherever it points, so a link to another disk is not walked. A folder you named that is itself a link is followed to its folder once, because you named it. A FIFO, a socket or a device is counted (special) and never opened. A folder inside another you named is walked once.
  • It checks what it reads is what it listed. A folder is entered only if it is still the folder the listing saw (same inode, not a link), and a file is hashed only if it is still the file; one swapped in between is counted under changed_during_census and left alone.
  • It skips the system's folders and Claude's. .git, .hg, .svn, .Trash, .Trashes, $RECYCLE.BIN, System Volume Information, .Spotlight-V100, .fseventsd, .DocumentRevisions-V100, .TemporaryItems, .AppleDouble, .AppleDB and .claude anywhere; Library and AppData only directly inside a folder you named (the home's are the system's; a Library of books further down is yours), and so the top folders of a whole disk given as / or C:\ (Windows, Program Files, Program Files (x86), ProgramData, $WinREAgent, System, Volumes, private, dev, proc, run, sys); Claude's own folder (Claude) under Application Support, .config, Roaming or Local. Names are compared with case folded. .DS_Store, Thumbs.db, desktop.ini, .localized and .claude.json are not counted as your files.
  • It skips the record. A record inside a folder you named is counted under skipped: record and not walked; naming the record itself, or a folder inside it, exits 2. An error names the argument by its place (PATH 2 of 3 is not a folder), never by its path.
  • A file reached by two names (a hard link) is one file, never its own duplicate (hard_links). A folder or a file it cannot read is counted (unreadable_folders, unreadable_files), and one that changed size while it was read is counted (changed_during_census) and left out of the duplicates.

Reading a file may set its access time on a disk that keeps one; the census reports modified times only. A name is written into the Markdown as text: every character a viewer reads as markup (<, [, (, *, …) is escaped, so a name shaped like a link or an image fetches nothing when you open the report in a previewer.

docs.title: Senders
docs.text:
census senders reads the record's own mail/v1 lines (RFC 0015), from any road that wrote them (a Takeout, sync mail, sync gmail). No connection is opened.

  • Every sender of received mail, by its address lower-cased: messages, bytes, first and last seen, threads, the display name it used most.
  • Answered: yes when you ever wrote to the address (a sent line with it under to, cc or bcc) or sent a message in one of its threads (joined on thread, never the subject). The report keeps both: written_to and threads_answered.
  • By count, by last seen, never answered and newsletters are the report's sections.
  • Newsletters by the List-Unsubscribe header, when the line holds it: extra.list.unsubscribe, which every mail road writes since 20 October 2026 (RFC 0015, amendment of that day), or an older producer's key under extra or a headers object. Lines written before that day hold none, and a re-import does not rewrite them, so on a record of older mail the section may say newsletters are unknown, not that there are none.
  • Lists and tabs, per sender: how many of its mails carry extra.list.unsubscribe, and how many sit in Gmail's Promotions, Social or Updates tab (extra.gmail_category, written by a Takeout import and sync gmail; never by sync mail, since IMAP does not say the tab). In the report as a section and in the JSON as list_unsubscribe and tabs on each sender, with the totals under lists_and_tabs; the summary on the terminal says the totals only, never an address.

docs.title: Drive
docs.text:
census drive reads the record's own Drive lines (event/v1 of source drive, written by logbook sync drive). No connection is opened, and nothing is asked of Google.

  • Every file the lines name, by its Drive id: its latest name, type, folder path (when the metadata scope was delegated), activities by kind, first and last activity, whether you acted on it.
  • By type, by folder, by year of the last activity, most active.
  • Untouched: no activity for two years. Shared: a share added and not removed since, by the lines; the report names the kind of each share (user, group, domain, anyone), never the address. Trashed or deleted: the last such activity with no restore after it.

The record holds a Drive file only from the activity Drive reported since sync drive began: a file nobody touched since then is not in the census at all. That is the census's largest blind spot.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text:
A report is derived material and takes the highest tier it read (SPEC §4). The senders and Drive censuses read lines up to --tier N (default 2, as search), leave the lines above it out, count them under left_out: above_tier and put the highest tier they read under tier. A sealed line the identity on this machine cannot open is counted (sealed) and never guessed at. A file has no tier, and a file name can say anything, so the files report is tier 3.

The reports live under state/, which nothing carries anywhere: no line holds them, so no crossing, export or shared page does; backup leaves state/ out; doctor --packet names no file under it. They are plain files on your disk, though, not sealed, even in a record that seals its lines: delete state/hold/ when you no longer need a report, and keep full-disk encryption on.

docs.title: What it cannot see
docs.text:
• Folders you did not name, and links. The census is as wide as the paths you give it.
  • Duplicates under another encoding. The same photo saved twice as JPEG is two files with different bytes: the census finds identical bytes, never similar content.
  • Who you answer by other roads. A sender you call or message instead of mailing back is "never answered" here.
  • Drive files without activity since the source began, as above.
  • Your own mail, unless the record knows your addresses. A mail line is sent only when its sender is one of owner_emails in logbook.json (RFC 0015 direction). A mailbox imported before they were set reads as all received: you are your own top sender and nobody is answered. The report and the terminal say so when the record holds no sent mail.
  • Files whose bytes are elsewhere (not_local) are counted, never compared: a duplicate of one is not found.

docs.title: Running Logbook on a home server
docs.text:
This page sets up the record's home (ADR 0022): one small machine at home, always on, that holds the only writable copy of the record, runs the pages and the schedule as system daemons, runs a local model for the dream, and is reached from a laptop by ssh and from a phone over your own private network. It is a runbook: do the steps in order, check each one where it says so, and the whole takes about an hour. Every logbook command on it is the CLI as it is, and the commands shown as printed are what it prints.

The names are synthetic. The server is server.example, the laptop laptop.example, the record belongs to Ines Nordmann of Oslo, who does not exist, and the two accounts on the server are owner and records.

laptop.example ── ssh as records ──▶ server.example ◀── private network ── phone
  development,                         records: the record, serve, the     the pages, read
  a read-only checkout                 schedule; the local model beside

Nothing cloud-synced holds the record. Not the record folder, not a backup, not a read-only checkout on the laptop. The phone reaches the pages, never the files.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• The server: Linux with systemd, always on, a disk with room for the record and its attachments, and a second disk for backups, mounted at /mnt/backup. A Mac works too; what differs is at the end (On a Mac).
  • An administrator account on it, owner, that can sudo and that you reach by ssh from the laptop.
  • The laptop, with an ssh key (~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub).
  • A Logbook with the dream and the system daemons: the release after 0.6.1. logbook --help lists dream under derive, and logbook sync --help lists --system. Until that release is out, install from main (step 2 says how).

Each block of commands starts with a comment saying who runs it and where; a block without one is what a command printed.

docs.title: 1. Two users, and why (5 minutes)
docs.text:
account what it is what it may do owner you, the administrator sudo; runs the commands Logbook prints for the system; holds nothing of the record records the record's own user holds the record and runs the pages, the schedule and every command that writes; no password, no desktop login, no sudo; reached by ssh with a key

Why two:

  • The daemons run as the user who installed them, and never as root: --system refuses to run as root, since the daemon would run as root with root's home. They need an account, and it should be one that does nothing else.
  • records's home is closed (mode 700), so nothing that runs as owner (a browser, a build, a tool you are trying) can read the record, and nothing that runs as records can become root.
  • The commands that install a daemon need an administrator. Logbook never runs sudo; it writes the file in records's home and prints the commands, and owner runs them after reading what they copy.
  • A collaborator, one day, is a third account on this machine, after sealing at rest (ADR 0022, point 5), never a copy of the folder.
# as owner, on server.example
sudo useradd --create-home --shell /bin/bash records    # no password is set: no console or desktop login
sudo chmod 700 /home/records

Let the laptop's key in as records (the account has no password, so ssh-copy-id cannot do it):

# on laptop.example
scp ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub owner@server.example:laptop.pub

# as owner, on server.example
sudo install -d -m 700 -o records -g records /home/records/.ssh
sudo install -m 600 -o records -g records ~/laptop.pub /home/records/.ssh/authorized_keys
rm ~/laptop.pub

Check: ssh records@server.example whoami on the laptop prints records. From here on, "as records" means that ssh session, or sudo -iu records from owner's.

Set the server's clock to the record's timezone. The schedule's timers fire at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 by the system's clock, and the 06:00 run is the one that closes your day:

# as owner, on server.example
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Europe/Oslo
timedatectl          # Time zone: Europe/Oslo (…)

docs.title: 2. Install Logbook as records (5 minutes)
docs.text:
# as records, on server.example
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
exit                 # then log in as records again, so ~/.local/bin is on the path

# as records, on server.example
uv tool install "openlogbook[ais,crypto,sealed,speakers,transcribe]"
# until the release after 0.6.1:
# uv tool install "openlogbook[ais,crypto,sealed,speakers,transcribe] @ git+https://github.com/bighydro/logbook"
logbook --version

The five extras are the ones doctor checks (extra:ais, extra:crypto, extra:sealed, extra:speakers, extra:transcribe); one missing is a standing warn, which makes no scheduled run clean and, with the message set up (step 4), is a message every run until it is fixed. On Linux, transcribe is faster-whisper and speakers is pyannote.audio on the CPU (it brings torch); describe and judge are Apple silicon only and install nothing here (install).

The server runs a released package, installed for records, not a checkout of the repository. The development checkout lives on the laptop and never points at the record: the tests pin LOGBOOK_HOME and the home directory to a temporary folder, and init refuses a code checkout as a record folder.

docs.title: 3. Where the record lives (5 minutes; a move adds the copy)
docs.text:
The record is /home/records/Logbook, which is records's ~/Logbook: the place logbook init makes by default and logbook finds without LOGBOOK_HOME. A plain folder on a local disk.

Never a synced folder. No file-sync client, peer-to-peer sync tool or network share may hold the record, its backups or a read-only checkout. A sync client rewrites logbook.json and the month files underneath the writer, evicts files and fetches them back, and keeps the record on someone else's server; two machines syncing one record are two writers on one chain, which the format has no merge for. doctor's folder line fails a record under iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive by name, and backup refuses them as a destination; any other sync tool it cannot see, so the rule is yours to keep.

A new record:

# as records, on server.example
logbook setup        # the guided first run (docs/first-hour.md); or: logbook init --timezone Europe/Oslo

Moving the record from the laptop, where it lived until now. Home moves by copying the record once, never by syncing it, and the old copy stops writing. On the laptop, stop its schedule and its pages first, then take a snapshot:

# on laptop.example
logbook sync --uninstall-schedule
logbook serve --uninstall-service
logbook backup ~/Transfer          # a verified snapshot, ~/Transfer/<owner_id>/<timestamp>/
scp -r ~/Transfer/<owner_id>/<timestamp> records@server.example:snapshot

# as records, on server.example
logbook backup restore ~/snapshot ~/Logbook     # copied, verified, its head printed
rm -r ~/snapshot

A snapshot leaves state/ out, so every live source is new to the server. A sync by hand reads each from its start, and the record refuses what it already holds, so nothing doubles. The schedule's first run reads each source's last 14 days (a source's first scheduled run): the record already holds what came before the snapshot, and doctor names each source as first run bounded to 14 days; history not read until a logbook sync <source> --since <date> from before the snapshot's day reads the days between and clears it (when the snapshot is from today, there are none, and the record refuses all it reads). If the record seals tiers 2 and 3 (logbook key show says so, and where the identity is), the identity file goes to the server too, by scp, to the same place under records's ~/.config/logbook/identities/, at mode 600. Write nothing more to the laptop's record folder; once the server's first backup has passed a restore test (step 9), delete it, and the snapshot in ~/Transfer with it. A read-only checkout (step 8) takes its place if you want one there.

Check: logbook verify as records prints valid and the head.

docs.title: 4. The env file for secrets (5 minutes)
docs.text:
The schedule reads every key your sources need from ~/.config/logbook/sync.env, one KEY=value per line, mode 600, records's. Logbook never writes it and never prints a value from it. The system units name it by its path (EnvironmentFile=-/home/records/.config/logbook/sync.env), so nothing else needs to know where it is.

Write each secret with read -s, which takes what you type without showing it; printf is a shell builtin, so the value is never on a command line, in the history or in the process list:

# as records, on server.example
install -d -m 700 ~/.config/logbook
touch ~/.config/logbook/sync.env && chmod 600 ~/.config/logbook/sync.env
read -rs -p 'LOGBOOK_IMMICH_KEY: ' v && printf 'LOGBOOK_IMMICH_KEY=%s\n' "$v" >> ~/.config/logbook/sync.env; unset v; echo
read -rs -p 'LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY: ' v && printf 'LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY=%s\n' "$v" >> ~/.config/logbook/sync.env; unset v; echo

Values that are not secret go in the same way without -s, or with an editor:

# as records, on server.example
printf '%s\n' 'LOGBOOK_IMMICH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:2283' 'LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_URL=http://127.0.0.1:3000' >> ~/.config/logbook/sync.env

What goes in it: each live source's variables (logbook sync --help names them; doctor's sync: lines say which are missing), LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE=<path> for a record that seals (the monthly restore test needs it, or it is skipped), the dream's two variables (step 7), and, if you want one message when something is wrong, LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_TOKEN and LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_CHAT (the schedule).

Check, names only, never values:

# as records, on server.example
cut -d= -f1 ~/.config/logbook/sync.env          # the names
stat -c '%a %U' ~/.config/logbook/sync.env      # 600 records

Never cat the file, never paste a key into a command, never put the file in a repository or a synced folder. The serve daemon does not read it: the pages need no secret.

docs.title: 5. Where your day begins (2 minutes)
docs.text:
If your day does not end at midnight, say so before the schedule runs and before you sign a day (settings). Moving the boundary later moves lines between days, and a signed day whose page changed reads as changed.

# as records, on server.example
logbook setup day_start 06:00

day_start: 00:00 → 06:00 in logbook.json; a line before 06:00 now belongs to the day before. No line changed
index: rebuilt, 48,213 lines in 1.6s, each on its day under 06:00

The schedule's close runs at 06:00 by the server's clock (step 1 set it to the record's timezone). With day_start at 06:00 or earlier, the close finds yesterday ended and the dream catches it up; with a later day_start, the day that has not ended waits for the next morning.

docs.title: 6. The pages and the schedule as system daemons (10 minutes)
docs.text: Both are installed the same way: as records, the command writes the unit files into records's home, prints them, and prints the commands an administrator runs; as owner, you read the files and run those commands. Nothing needs a login session, and no loginctl enable-linger: that is what --system is for.

docs.title: The pages: serve --install-service --system
docs.text:
# as records, on server.example
logbook serve --install-service --system

writing /home/records/logbook-serve.service:
[Unit]
Description=logbook serve: the record's pages at http://127.0.0.1:8765/, from this machine only

[Service]
User=records
Environment=LOGBOOK_HOME=/home/records/Logbook
Environment=PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
ExecStart=/home/records/.local/share/uv/tools/openlogbook/bin/python -m logbook.cli serve --port 8765
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

written: a systemd system service running `logbook serve --port 8765` as records from boot, started again when it fails; nothing runs until you install it, as an administrator:
  sudo cp /home/records/logbook-serve.service /etc/systemd/system/logbook-serve.service
  sudo systemctl enable --now logbook-serve.service
then http://127.0.0.1:8765/ (/today is today's page); its output: journalctl -u logbook-serve.service; `logbook serve --status` says whether it answers
the server binds 127.0.0.1 and nothing else; reaching it from another device: docs/serve.md

# as owner, on server.example: the two lines it printed
sudo cp /home/records/logbook-serve.service /etc/systemd/system/logbook-serve.service
sudo systemctl enable --now logbook-serve.service

The unit carries paths and nothing secret: the Python that installed it, the record, and LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE when it was set in the shell that ran the install. It never carries --host; the server binds 127.0.0.1 and refuses anything else (serve).

docs.title: The schedule: sync --install-schedule --system
docs.text:
# as records, on server.example
logbook sync --install-schedule --system

It writes four files to /home/records and prints each: logbook-sync.service and .timer (sync --scheduled at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00) and logbook-sync-close.service and .timer (sync --scheduled --close at 06:00). Each service is Type=oneshot, User=records, EnvironmentFile=-/home/records/.config/logbook/sync.env and LOGBOOK_HOME=/home/records/Logbook; each timer is Persistent=true, so a run missed while the machine was off happens when it is back. Then:

written: 4 files for the system domain, running as records from boot: `logbook sync --scheduled` (`sync --all`, then `doctor`) runs at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00 local, and at 06:00 as `sync --scheduled --close`, which then runs the dream's catch-up when this version has it and policy/crossing.json has a dream entry; nothing runs until you install them, as an administrator:
  sudo cp /home/records/logbook-sync.service /home/records/logbook-sync.timer /home/records/logbook-sync-close.service /home/records/logbook-sync-close.timer /etc/systemd/system
  sudo systemctl enable --now logbook-sync.timer logbook-sync-close.timer
to be told when something is wrong, put LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_TOKEN and LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_CHAT in the same file: one Telegram message when a source fails or doctor warns, and the week's counts on Sunday evening (docs/schedule.md); with them, the daily loop: the Day page after the close, and the evening question at LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_EVENING_HOUR (docs/digest.md)
the variables your live sources need go in ~/.config/logbook/sync.env, one KEY=value per line, mode 600; a source whose variables are not set is skipped
home: this machine (server) is the record's home since 2026-10-13; state/home.json

# as owner, on server.example: the two lines it printed
sudo cp /home/records/logbook-sync.service /home/records/logbook-sync.timer /home/records/logbook-sync-close.service /home/records/logbook-sync-close.timer /etc/systemd/system
sudo systemctl enable --now logbook-sync.timer logbook-sync-close.timer

The last line it printed matters: installing the schedule names this machine the record's home, and doctor on any other machine says writers belong here.

Run either install again later (a new Python, a moved record, a new release that changes the unit) and it prints the replacing commands instead: the same sudo cp, then sudo systemctl daemon-reload and sudo systemctl restart of the service or the two timers. --uninstall-service --system and --uninstall-schedule --system remove the copies in the home directory and print the commands that stop the daemons and remove the system's copies.

Check:

# as records, on server.example
logbook serve --status                        # installed: a systemd system service (/etc/systemd/system/logbook-serve.service), port 8765
                                              # answering at http://127.0.0.1:8765/
systemctl list-timers 'logbook-sync*'         # the next 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 or 18:00 of each timer
(set -a; . ~/.config/logbook/sync.env; logbook sync --scheduled)    # one run now, as the timer runs it

--status exits 0 when the server answers, 1 when it is installed and silent, 3 when none is installed. The run by hand needs the keys, which the timer reads from the env file and your shell does not; the parentheses read them in a subshell, so they leave with it. The run is sync --all, then doctor, and its last line is scheduled run: clean; state/last-run.json.

docs.title: 7. The local model, and the dream (10 minutes, and the model's download)
docs.text:
The dream sends a day to a model and writes the draft back as one line (the dream). Here the model runs on this machine, as a daemon of its own, beside Logbook and not inside it:

  • it takes minutes to load and gigabytes of memory, so it stays up and answers the 06:00 close at once;
  • it never needs the record's files, so it runs as no user that can read them;
  • it listens on 127.0.0.1 only, so a day never leaves the machine;
  • it is replaced by changing two variables, never code.

Any OpenAI-compatible chat completions server will do; llama-server from llama.cpp is the one the dream's docs use. Put the model file where any user can read it (/srv/models here), then a unit of your own, which Logbook neither writes nor reads; the two paths in it are wherever you put the server and the model:

# /etc/systemd/system/local-model.service, written by owner
[Unit]
Description=local model for the dream, at http://127.0.0.1:8080/ only
After=network.target

[Service]
DynamicUser=yes
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/llama-server --model /srv/models/qwen2.5-7b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf --alias qwen2.5-7b-instruct --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

# as owner, on server.example
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now local-model.service
curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health          # ok once the model has loaded

DynamicUser=yes runs it as a throwaway account made for it, which cannot read /home/records. --alias is the name the server answers to; the policy and the variable below use the same one.

The policy entry. Sending a day to a model is a crossing like any other, so the dream does nothing until policy/crossing.json has a dream entry. Add it by hand beside the entries already there:

{
  "hermes": {"max_tier": 2},
  "mcp": {"max_tier": 1},
  "dream": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2027-03-31", "model": "qwen2.5-7b-instruct"}
}

max_tier 2 lets the model read notes and messages; 3 would add health and money. until is the last day the entry holds; after it the dream refuses and doctor names the entry, so a model you stop thinking about stops by itself. model is the only model the day may go to; a LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL that names another is refused.

The endpoint, in the env file (step 4). A local server needs no key, so there is no LOGBOOK_DREAM_KEY:

# as records, on server.example
printf '%s\n' 'LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:8080' 'LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL=qwen2.5-7b-instruct' >> ~/.config/logbook/sync.env
