It proves the format is specified, not described: a second person, with no access to the Python code, produced the same sixty-four hex characters, which means every byte of the canonical form, the pre-image and the digest is pinned by the text. Getting there is why canonicalisation is RFC 8785 exactly and not Python's json.dumps (ADR 0014; the old rule is logbook/0.1, and a record under it is migrated, never verified). It also proves the chain survives a writer it did not come from, which is the point of a chain. And it found what the spec had left to the implementation: the order of a day, where a retraction is listed, when an alias walk names nothing. Those became SPEC §3.2, Readers, so that two implementations print the same day, not only compute the same head.

docs.title: The performance story
docs.text:
The record is never in memory. Two decisions carry that.

Verify streams. Logbook.lines() parses one line from each month file and keeps those in a heap keyed by seq; the smallest is yielded and its file read on. Memory is one line per month file however long the record, and open files are a handful however many month files there are: each file's byte offset is kept, the least recently read files are closed, and a file is reopened where it left off when its turn comes round (a record of decades has hundreds of month files, and macOS gives a process 256 open files by default). On a synthetic record of three million lines over 120 month files:

before after verify 72 s, 4.7 GB peak RSS 54 s, 23 MB export of the whole log 26 s, 6.5 GB 23 s, 29 MB

The writer keeps every file in seq order and the merge relies on it; a file that is not (which the spec allows, since it orders by seq wherever a line is found) raises UnsortedFile, and verify reads again through the two-pass sorted read that migration uses, sixteen bytes a line.

Readers go through the index. show, day, export --day, retract and the dedupe in add ask index.sqlite where the lines they need are, by local day, by (source, raw_id) or by kind and instant, and read only those lines back from the files. A Day on a record of millions of lines reads in the time that day's lines take; the files are never swept. Dedupe is one SELECT per batch of ten thousand drafts against the (source, raw_id) index, with the index extended at every checkpoint so nothing is ever appended past it: one hundred thousand drafts already present in a three-million-line record are skipped in two to three seconds at 41 MB.

Two slow tests (LOGBOOK_SLOW=1) build the three-million-line record in a temporary folder and assert that verify's peak memory on it is within 48 MB of a one-million-line record's and that the dedupe stays under 256 MB, each measured in a process of its own. A third test fails if show or export --day ever lists or scans a month file. The demo walkthrough ends with logbook demo --days 365, a year of about 150,000 lines, which is enough to feel what the index is for.

docs.title: What this page leaves out
docs.text: The five layers and their contracts are in ARCHITECTURE.md; the format is SPEC.md; each decision above is an ADR under Decisions, and the payload profiles are RFCs. The circle, how two records exchange pages, has a bundle format and no transport yet, and that is deliberate: the bundle is defined first so that the first two implementations can exchange pages by any means, including a USB stick.

docs.title: People's mail
docs.text:
Most of a mailbox is not people: shops, banks, newsletters and the machines that notify. One rule says which mail is a person's, and the Day page and the crossing read the same rule, so what the page opens is what crosses. The design is a draft, RFC 0045.

logbook people mail                                          # the last 30 days, counted
logbook people mail --since 2026-03-01 --until 2026-03-31    # one month
logbook people mail --since 2026-03-01 --json                # each line's class, reason and person ids

docs.title: The rule
docs.text:
A mail is a person's mail when someone the record names as a person is on it:

  • a mail you received: its sender;
  • a mail you sent: any of its recipients, to, cc or bcc;

and its sender has not been let go in Hold. "Names as a person" is what people means by it (people): the address has a resolution to a person, and that person is not you. Every other mail is other mail, and the reader says why:

reason what it means no_person nobody the record names as a person is where the rule looks: a stranger, a company's address, a person only in cc of a mail you received no_reply the sender is a no-reply address (no-reply@, noreply@, do-not-reply@, mailer-daemon@, notifications@ and the like), whatever resolves agent an agent wrote it, or the sender resolves to an agent; no mail source marks one today let_go you let the sender go in Hold; Hold writes no fates yet, so this removes nothing today sealed a sealed mail this machine has no key to open: listed and said, never guessed

A company is never a person: an address you named as an org's or a company's stays other mail. A newsletter's list headers and Gmail's tabs are not the rule either: a mail from Per Hansen through the club's list is still a person's mail. When a mail line carries them (extra.list, extra.gmail_category), --json shows them as evidence, the list as true and the tab as its word, never the headers themselves.

docs.title: What it prints
docs.text:
mail 2026-03-01 – 2026-03-31: 412 lines
  people's mail: 37 (21 received, 16 sent), from or to 9 people
  other mail: 375 (290 no person on it, 85 a no-reply sender, 0 an agent's)
  let go in Hold: nothing yet; Hold writes no fates

Counts only: never an address, never a name, no number beside anyone. --json adds each mail line's id, time, day, direction, class, and the ids of the people that make it a person's (or the reason it is not), and never an address.

docs.title: The crossing
docs.text: logbook export crossing sends people's mail only, whenever mail is among the kinds it crosses, and counts the rest in the manifest as mail_held_back. --all-mail sends every mail the tier and the signed days let through, as before, and the manifest says so (the crossing).

docs.title: Requests
docs.text: logbook promises reads a request ("can you send me…", "please confirm…") in a mail you received only when the mail is a person's mail, so a newsletter, a shop or a notification asks you nothing; the Day page's asked of you, the person page and the Notion export read the same proposals (who wrote it).

docs.title: Replies owed
docs.text: The Day page's loose ends (RFC 0043) will read replies owed from the same rule: for each person the record names, over the last 90 days, your direct messages with them (never a group's, never an agent's), your people's mail and your calls; when the last word is theirs (a message, a mail, a call you did not answer) and is more than a week old, a reply is owed. A call you answered or made is your word. No page shows them yet.

docs.title: The map
docs.text: The Library draws its maps itself: one OpenStreetMap file on the home machine, read by the server and drawn as inline SVG in the page. No script, no tile server, nothing fetched when a page is read; light and dark both; the OpenStreetMap attribution on every map. This is the map of RFC 0043 §11, which the Day page and the timeline will draw once they call it; until then logbook lab map render draws one to a file, to check by eye.

docs.title: Getting the file
docs.text:
The Library never downloads the map. Getting it is your step, once, on the home machine:

  1. Install the pmtiles command-line tool (github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles, a single binary).
  2. Cut the region you live and travel in out of a Protomaps basemap build (maps.protomaps.com/builds lists them; each is the whole planet as one PMTiles v3 file, read over the network by ranges, so only your region is downloaded):
pmtiles extract https://build.protomaps.com/20261001.pmtiles ~/Maps/oslo.pmtiles \
    --bbox=10.4,59.8,11.0,60.1 --maxzoom=15

A city is some hundreds of MB; a region or a small country is a few GB. Keep it outside the record folder: it is not the record, and a backup of the record need not carry it. 3. Name it:

logbook setup map ~/Maps/oslo.pmtiles

setup map reads the file's header first (a PMTiles v3 file, vector tiles, gzip), prints what the file holds and the change it will make to logbook.json, and asks. --yes writes without asking. logbook setup map alone says which file is set; logbook setup map --off removes the setting and leaves the file where it is.

setting where set with the map file logbook.json, map_file logbook setup map PATH, --off to remove

Like day_start, it is a setting, not a line: nothing is appended, no hash changes, and the index is not rebuilt. Without it, everything that would draw a map says one sentence instead:

No map file is set: logbook setup map PATH (docs/map.md)

docs.title: Drawing one by eye
docs.text:
logbook lab map render --track 2026-06-08 --out day.svg             # the day's track, the box round it
logbook lab map render --bbox 10.70,59.90,10.76,59.92 --width 390   # one box, printed as SVG

--width is in pixels (390, a phone, by default); the height follows from the box. --track DAY draws the day's track as the Day page numbers it: each stay or stop with a position, in order, one pin for one place however often you were there (two stops closer than a pin on the map are one pin), a straight move between two of them, dashed across a flight, a gap or a stay with no position. A box west of Greenwich or south of the equator is given with =: --bbox=-0.2,51.4,0.0,51.6. The command reads the map file and, with --track, that day of the record, and writes only the SVG.

docs.title: What a map holds
docs.text:
From the bottom: the land; land use and parks; water; piers; buildings, close in (a display zoom of 14.5 or more); roads by class, the widest on top; place names, the most important first, a name left out where it would cover another, a pin or the attribution; then the track and its numbered pins; and the attribution, © OpenStreetMap contributors and what the file's own metadata names (Protomaps' builds name themselves there), on every map.

The zoom follows the box and the width: the tiles of the whole zoom below the one the box asks for, within the file's zooms (past its last, its last is drawn larger), 36 tiles at most of those inside the file's bounds; a box that needs more even at the file's first zoom is refused in one sentence, never drawn with a part missing. Each shape is clipped to its tile and to the map, simplified to half a pixel and rounded to a tenth, and every shape of one kind is one SVG path. A map stays under 300 KB: when everything would be more, the buildings go first, then the footpaths, the minor roads and the land use, each with a coarser simplification; the track, the pins and the attribution are never left out. A damaged or hostile file cannot make a map slow: what one map draws and how long its simplification may look are both capped.

The colours are CSS custom properties with their defaults in the map's own <style>, one set for light and one for dark (prefers-color-scheme): --map-land, --map-landuse, --map-park, --map-water, --map-building, --map-road, --map-road-major, --map-path, --map-rail, --map-label, --map-halo, --map-track. A page that sets them draws the map in its own colours. Names are in the system's sans-serif.

docs.title: Naming a stay from the map
docs.text: For a stay with no name in places.json, the map can propose one: the named thing nearest the stay's centre within 50 m (logbook.contrib.map.nearest.nearest_named), a restaurant, a pier, a marina, a named building, with its kind and how far it is. It is a proposal, shown in grey by places review and the timeline when they read it: nothing is written until you name the place yourself. Roads, a town's point and stretches of water are never proposed.

docs.title: The file, read
docs.text: The reader is the standard library alone (logbook/contrib/map/): pmtiles.py reads the PMTiles v3 header, its root and leaf directories and a tile by z/x/y, gzip through zlib; mvt.py decodes a Mapbox Vector Tile from the protobuf wire format by hand. A file cut short, damaged or made to mislead (a section past its end, a directory that counts more than it holds, leaves that nest without end, a tile that inflates without end) is one error naming the file, never a traceback or a hang. Brotli or zstd archives are refused by name: Protomaps' builds are gzip.

docs.title: The MCP server
docs.text:
logbook mcp serves your record to an agent on this machine over the Model Context Protocol: the host (an editor, a chat client, an agent runner) starts logbook mcp as a child process and calls its tools over that process's own stdin and stdout. That is the only transport. Nothing listens on a port, no socket opens, and the record stays where it is. The agent asks; the readers answer; what it may write goes through Logbook.append like everything else, and two of those writes only when you allow them by name (below).

pip install "openlogbook[mcp]"      # the official Python MCP SDK, the one optional dependency
logbook mcp --inspect               # the tool table and one sample request; needs no record and no SDK
logbook mcp                         # serve the record `logbook` finds (LOGBOOK_HOME, the folder above, ~/Logbook)
logbook mcp --root ~/Logbook        # or this one
logbook mcp --allow-tier-3          # let tier 3 cross when policy/crossing.json allows it for mcp (below)

docs.title: Pointing a host at it
docs.text:
Every MCP host takes the same three things: a command, its arguments and the environment it runs in. For a generic host that keeps its servers in a JSON file:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "logbook": {
      "command": "logbook",
      "args": ["mcp"],
      "env": { "LOGBOOK_HOME": "/Users/you/Logbook" }
    }
  }
}

LOGBOOK_HOME names the record, as it does for every other command; --root in args does the same. A host that cannot find logbook on its own path gets the full path from which logbook, or runs it through uv: "command": "uv", "args": ["run", "logbook", "mcp"] with "cwd" set to the checkout. Give the host the environment the record needs and nothing more: no adapter key is read here, and none should be in reach.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Twelve read tools, and four write tools that are each refused until your policy names it (Write tools). Each read tool is one command you already know, with the same output as its --json (or, for the three that read the lines themselves, as its text):

Tool Arguments The command day date? (YYYY-MM-DD; default today) logbook day --json (the Day) days from?, to? (both default to the days the record covers) logbook days --json, one object per day trips year? logbook trips --json places logbook places list: places.json, one object per named place people logbook rollup people --json person name logbook show person <name> --json promises open?, since? logbook promises --json (promises) gaps since? logbook sources --gaps --json search text, since?, until?, kinds?, limit? lines whose payload mentions text, through the index day_lines day? (default today), kinds? logbook show DAY, one object per line (below) line id one line in full, a transcript's text included (below) digest period? (day, week), date? logbook digest DATE, the text as printed (below) add_note text, at? logbook add "<sentence>": one note/v1 line, tier 2, source mcp; only when the policy names it promise_done id logbook promises done <id>: one task/v1 line, source mcp; only when the policy names it sign_day day, confirm?, kept?, missed?, dropped?, carried?, note?, at? logbook day sign DAY: one signed-day/v1 line, tier 1; a day signed before keeps its confirmations; never confirms a line above the ceiling of its own accord; only when the policy names it note_day day, text, at?, kind? one note/v1 line on day, tier 2, source mcp; only when the policy names it

search is a scan, not the ranked search logbook search is (search). It cuts the window (since and until are local days, inclusive) and the kinds in the index, reads the standing lines in chain order, and keeps those whose payload contains text anywhere, case aside — a note's words, an event's title, a mail's subject, a URL. Each hit is the line's envelope and payload without prev and hash; at most limit (50 by default, 500 at most), and more says when there were more. A retracted line is never a hit, and neither is a retraction.

docs.title: The lines themselves
docs.text:
search finds a line by a word; the three tools here read the lines without one, so an agent can read a day, open a line, and get the evening's digest, as the owner does at the command line. Each one's description, as the host lists it, says in one sentence what the ceiling does to its answer.

  • day_lines(day?, kinds?) is logbook show DAY, one object per standing line, in time order (the instant, then seq, SPEC §3.2): id, seq, at, end, time (the local clock), kind, profile (payload.schema), source, tier, counterpart and text. The text is the text part of the row show prints: a note's first line, ✉ subject — sender, who: message, title — participants; 12 turns, 25 min. The counterpart is whom the line is with, as the record names them: a mail's sender (its recipients for one you sent), a message's sender or chat, a transcript's participants, an entry's attendees, a call's counterparty; null for a location point or a photo. kinds keeps only these profile families: mail, message, transcript, note, location, photo, calendar (the event/v1 lines). A retracted line is left out and counted in retracted; a retraction is never a row. Lines above the ceiling are left out and counted in above_ceiling, and nothing of them crosses, not even an id: the count comes from a query that reads nothing else of them.
  • line(id) is one line in full: the fields day_lines gives, the row show prints as row, the whole payload, and text, the line's full text where it has one — a note's, a mail's body, a message's, and a transcript's turns read from the attachment store as promises and the search index read them, one Speaker: text per turn (null when the store does not hold the file, and for a home video's soundtrack, which is no call: its words go to no model). A retracted line is the marker show prints, retracted #seq: reason, and nothing of the line. A line above the ceiling is refused naming its tier and the ceiling, and nothing else of it: the index is asked the line's tier first, by a query that reads nothing else, and the refusal is line '…' is tier 3, above the mcp ceiling of 2.
  • digest(period?, date?) is the text logbook digest DATE prints (the digest), line for line, under text, with lines counted; period week is the seven digests of the ISO week that holds date, Monday to Sunday, each as the command prints it, a blank line between, with the week under week and the days digested under days (a day that has not come is left out of a week, and refused for a day, as the command refuses it). The digest is read under the ceiling as every reader is: a line above it is in no part of it, where, with whom, what attached, the promises due or the question, as if it were not in the record — so the digest at a ceiling of 1 is the digest of a record that holds only tier 1, and the test holds it to exactly that. The question bank and the state of what was asked are files beside the record, written as the command writes them; the record itself is untouched.

Every answer is one JSON text:

{"data": …, "gate": {"destination": "mcp", "max_tier": 1, "withheld": 23}}

data is the tool's output. gate is what the next section is about: the ceiling the answer was read under, and how many lines of the record were left out of it because they sit above that ceiling. A client that sees withheld above zero knows the answer is a partial one and can say so.

docs.title: The ceiling (ADR 0016)
docs.text:
Every tool's output passes the crossing gate. policy/crossing.json — the file that already says how much may cross to each member of your circle — names the mcp destination and the highest tier it may receive:

{"hermes": {"max_tier": 2}, "mcp": {"max_tier": 1}}

logbook init writes it at 1 and writes no other entry; you write the others yourself. A record made before this version, whose file does not name mcp, has a ceiling of 1 as well: the one destination with a default, since the client is an agent on your own machine and tier 1 is what crosses on its own. Raise it by editing the file; the server reads it on every call and never writes it, so the change takes effect at the next call and nothing needs restarting.

Who may read, and from where, is ADR 0022: the server runs on the record's home, the one machine that holds the writable copy, and an agent anywhere else (a VPS, a cron, a phone) reaches the record only through this ceiling and the few write tools you allow by name. A cloud model or service that may see record content gets its own entry in the file, and a temporary one an until date: {"cloud-model": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2026-12-31"}} holds through that day and counts as tier 0 from the next, so nothing crosses until you write a new date or remove the line; logbook doctor names an entry that has expired. The dream entry is one of these: logbook dream sends a day to a model only through {"dream": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2026-12-31", "model": "qwen2.5-7b-instruct"}}, the one model named there when it names one (the dream), and logbook transcript synthesize sends a call through the same entry (the synthesis of a call). What they wrote follows that entry as well as this one: a draft line, a day's draft or a call's synthesis, above the dream entry's max_tier today (lowered, expired or removed since it was written) is held back from every tool as a line above the ceiling is, and counted with them; line refuses it naming the entry (ADR 0016, Derived material follows the policy, not the head). A person's draft (dream person) is written under the relationship entry instead, and is held to that one the same way: past its until, or above its max_tier, it is held back and counted, whatever the dream entry allows.

What the ceiling means in practice:

  • At 1 the agent sees locations, calendar entries, photos, calls, flights, trips and crossing lines: the record's shape. It does not see notes, messages, mail, transcripts or the resolution lines that name people, so people and promises are empty, person knows nobody, and a Day names no company. A display name a calendar entry carries is that entry's own content and crosses with it; the overlay that would resolve it stays home, as it does for an export.
  • At 2 notes, messages, mail, transcripts, tasks and the names of your circle cross too. This is the ceiling to set for an agent that is to work with your notes, your people and your promises.
  • At 3 health samples and money cross as well — and only when you also started the server with --allow-tier-3. A policy edit alone never lets tier 3 through, as it never does for logbook export crossing; without the flag, 2 is the most, whatever the file says.

A line above the ceiling is left out before anything is derived from it, not blanked out afterwards: the readers see the record as if the line were not there, so a tier-2 note is not in the Day's attachments, not in the promises, not in the search, and not in the count of lines a stay carries. The only line that passes whatever its tier is a retraction — a mark on another line, needed so that line stays hidden — and no tool ever returns one. The policy file that is not what it should be (an mcp entry with no tier of 1, 2 or 3) is one error naming the file, for every call, until it is fixed. A file that is not JSON is the same error; neither is ever read as a higher ceiling, and a file that is missing, or names other destinations and not mcp, is the ceiling of 1.

Two things the gate does not do. It does not append a crossing/v1 line: an export hands a bundle to someone else and the record keeps the receipt; a tool call answers a question on this machine, and the record is not the place to log an agent's every question. And it does not change what the write tools write: add_note is tier 2 whatever the ceiling, as logbook add is, so at a ceiling of 1 the agent writes notes it cannot read back. The answer says so (readable: false), and logbook show reads them as ever.

docs.title: The log
docs.text: The server writes one line per call on the logbook.mcp logger, on stderr (stdout is the transport): the tool's name, the arguments that are a day, an id, a window or a switch, and the counts of the answer — day_lines day=2026-06-10 kinds=note,transcript lines=3 count=3 above_ceiling=1 retracted=0 withheld=4, line id=019c… withheld=0, or refused: line '019c…' is tier 3, above the mcp ceiling of 2. Never a line's content, never a search's words, never a name: an argument that is text (search's text, person's name, add_note's and note_day's text, sign_day's ids and note) is not logged. A write tool's line is the tool, the day, and counts: note_day day=2026-06-09 kind=proposal seq=812 tier=2 chars=41 withheld=0, sign_day day=2026-06-09 seq=813 tier=1 confirmed=14 on_page=15 withheld=0.

docs.title: The write tools
docs.text:
add_note appends one note/v1 line — source mcp, tier 2, at the instant given (RFC 3339 with a zone, its day inside the write window) or now — as logbook add "<sentence>" does, but never as manual. promise_done appends the task/v1 line that marks one proposal of promises done, as logbook promises done <id> does, source mcp, and writes nothing for a proposal already done. Like sign_day and note_day, each is refused unless the mcp entry names it under write and has not expired (Write tools). Both return the envelope of the line written (seq, id, at, kind, tier), never its payload. Nothing else writes, and nothing is ever rewritten: verify is green after every call, and the index is extended as a line is appended, as it is for every writer.

The ARCHITECTURE's rule is that an agent is an operator, not an author: it may never write a note or a confirmation in your name. So a line an agent writes through the door says so: its source is mcp, never manual, and manual stays the mark of your own words at the command line and on the Day page. A note with source mcp is pencil, as a draft is: a signature never confirms it, whoever signs (signed day). And no write tool is allowed until you name it in the policy (ADR 0022); the host's own prompt before a tool that writes is a second check, not the first.

docs.title: Write tools
docs.text:
ADR 0022 says it in one sentence: orchestrators reach the record only through the crossing: read tools under the ceiling, and the few write tools the owner allows by name. An orchestrator that builds the Day page used to print a day sign command for you to run by hand, and your verdicts on its proposals lived outside the record. With the tools here, the proposals and your verdicts become lines, and the Day page can be rebuilt from the record alone.

None is allowed until the mcp entry of policy/crossing.json names it under write: sign_day, note_day, add_note and promise_done, each by name.

{"mcp": {"max_tier": 1, "write": ["sign_day", "note_day"], "write_window_days": 60}}
  • No write, an empty one, or no mcp entry at all: no write tool is allowed. Each is refused with one sentence, sign_day is not allowed through the door: the mcp entry of policy/crossing.json does not name it under "write", and nothing is written. An empty list is a fine place to stay: your own way to reflect and sign is the Day page of logbook serve (Reflect and Sign), which never reads this file; the door is for an orchestrator elsewhere.
  • An entry past its until day allows none, whatever it names.
  • write names only sign_day, note_day, add_note and promise_done; anything else in it is one error naming the file, for every call, as a broken ceiling is.
  • write_window_days (60 when absent) is how far back the door writes: a day from that many days before today through today, in the record's zone, and no other. A day outside it is refused naming the window.
  • --allow-tier-3 has no effect on any. None writes above the tier its profile fixes: sign_day writes signed-day/v1 at tier 1, note_day and add_note write note/v1 at tier 2 (RFC 0010 makes a note tier 2, whoever writes it), promise_done writes task/v1 at its tier, and nothing else.

logbook doctor shows the tools on its crossing line (mcp 1 write sign_day,note_day), and logbook serve mcp --inspect lists them, marked [writes one line; only when the policy names it].

sign_day(day, confirm?, kept?, missed?, dropped?, carried?, note?, at?) is logbook day sign DAY through the same code, signing.sign, with no second implementation: confirm is a list of ids or seqs on the page, "all" or "none" (each goes alone); the four dispositions are lists of ids or seqs (RFC 0034 amendment 1); note is one line; at is the moment you signed, with the same rules as --at (amendment 2). The ids are checked against the page as the command checks them, and a day already signed is signed again, the new line superseding the old and, without confirm, keeping what the old one confirmed, its dispositions and its note (RFC 0034 amendment 4): a line added to the day since stays unconfirmed, so a re-sign through the door never confirms a line the owner was not shown; "all", and a day's first signature without confirm, confirm the page's lines the door can show, those at or under its ceiling, and leave every line above it unconfirmed (RFC 0034 amendment 4, 18 and 19 October 2026), since the orchestrator was never shown them: the answer says how many in unconfirmed, 2 lines above the door's ceiling left unconfirmed, and above_ceiling, a count and never their content (day sign, with or without --confirm all, and the Library's Sign still confirm the whole page, which the owner sees there). The line is byte for byte what day sign writes with the same flags and --at (for "all" and a first signature without confirm, --confirm with the ids it confirmed), source manual included: the signature is yours, carried by the orchestrator. The page signed is the whole page, as day sign signs it, lines above the ceiling included, which the orchestrator cannot read; the answer is the line's envelope, header (the first line day sign prints, 2026-06-09: signed 2026-06-09T19:30:00Z as #813 signed-day/v1), kept (what was kept from the signature it supersedes, the sentence day sign prints, or null), and counts: confirmed, on_page, dispositions per word, above_ceiling (with unconfirmed, null unless the door left a line above the ceiling unconfirmed), and supersedes. Like every signature, it never confirms the dream's draft line (RFC 0043 §6 rule 3): a draft on the page is neither confirmed nor counted above the ceiling, and confirm or a disposition naming it is refused. sign_day takes nothing of Keep and sign (day sign --keep, --word, --done, --tomorrow, --let-go; the signed day), and no argument is added for it: agents propose, the owner keeps, on the command line or the Day page.

note_day(day, text, at?, kind?) appends one note/v1 line: source mcp, tier 2, the text exactly as given, never filtered or trimmed, at most 4000 characters (NOTE_MAX; a longer one is refused and nothing is written). kind is one of note (the default), proposal and reflection, carried in the profile's own slot for a label, labels: [kind] (RFC 0010), so a proposal an agent made and the note it came with are told apart without a new profile. at, when given, follows --at's rules and must fall on day in the record's zone; without it the note is now for today and 23:59 of the day for an earlier one. It writes through the same note path as logbook day reflect (logbook/core/notes.py), so a reflection carried through the door and one said at the command line are the same kind of line, but for source. The answer is the line's envelope with readable (false at a ceiling of 1: the agent wrote a note it cannot read back), label and chars.

Both hold the writer lock for the whole call, like any command that writes, and neither waits for it: when another writer holds it the call is refused with another logbook command is writing to this record (logbook sync, since …); the door does not wait for another writer, so nothing was written, and the orchestrator tries again later. sign_day reads the head again before it appends, and when it has moved the call is refused with the record's head moved … nothing was signed; neither tool ever retries on its own.

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text: The tests (tests/test_mcp.py) drive the server through the SDK's in-process client over the synthetic Oslo persona: no child process, no socket. They pin the tool list and its schemas, the gate at 1 and 2 (a tier-2 note must not appear at a ceiling of 1), tier 3 behind the flag, a retracted line staying hidden, a broken policy as one error, every reader answering and writing nothing, and the two writers appending one line each. tests/test_mcp_read_tools.py drives day_lines, line and digest over three synthetic days with lines at tiers 1, 2 and 3 across location, calendar, note, mail, message, transcript and health: at each ceiling day_lines returns exactly the allowed lines with the right above_ceiling and no field of an omitted one, line of a tier-3 transcript refuses at 2 naming the tier and returns the text at 3, and digest at each ceiling matches, line for line, what logbook digest prints over a second record holding only the lines at or below that ceiling; a missing policy file is a ceiling of 1, a broken one is refused; the log holds counts and never content. tests/test_mcp_write_tools.py holds the two named write tools to the policy: refused without write, with an expired entry and outside the window; sign_day's line byte for byte the line day sign writes for the same flags and --at; a re-sign superseding; dispositions in the signature; note_day with each kind; another writer's lock and a moved head refused; a log with counts and never the persona's name. logbook mcp --inspect is the hand check: the table, and a request you can paste.

docs.title: Migrating to 0.6: one package, three tiers
docs.text:
0.6 keeps one package, logbook (the distribution is still openlogbook, the command is still logbook), and sorts its modules into three tiers under it: logbook/core/ (the format and the readers a second implementation is held to), logbook/contrib/ (the adapters, the imports, the exports, the derived readers whose output is a reader's own) and logbook/labs/ (everything that runs a model). The commands live under logbook/commands/, one module per family, and cli.py is a thin entry point. ARCHITECTURE.md describes the tree; logbook/layout.py declares it, and tests/test_layout.py holds the tree to the table.

Nothing a user runs changes: every command, flag and help text prints the same bytes, the conformance head is the same, and the record is untouched. What changes is where code imports from.

docs.title: The old import paths work until 0.7
docs.text:
Every module path 0.5 had still imports. import logbook.store imports logbook.core.store and registers that same module object under the old name, so there is one copy of every module, a patch through either name lands on it, and logbook.store is logbook.core.store. The first import of each old path warns once, a DeprecationWarning attributed to the line that imported it. The old names go in 0.7.

To find them in your code, make the warning an error once:

python -W error::DeprecationWarning -c "import your_module"
pytest -W error::DeprecationWarning

The shim is logbook/_shim.py, a finder on sys.meta_path installed when logbook is imported; the table it reads is logbook.layout.MOVED. A type checker does not see the old paths: it resolves logbook.core.store, not logbook.store.

docs.title: The 62 moves
docs.text:
0.5 0.6 logbook.apps logbook.core.apps logbook.assets logbook.core.assets logbook.attachments logbook.core.attachments logbook.chain logbook.core.chain logbook.countries logbook.core.countries logbook.crossing logbook.core.crossing logbook.day logbook.core.day logbook.days logbook.core.days logbook.drifting logbook.core.drifting logbook.events logbook.core.events logbook.export logbook.core.export logbook.flights logbook.core.flights logbook.health logbook.core.health logbook.index logbook.core.index logbook.keepers logbook.core.keepers logbook.ledger logbook.core.ledger logbook.listen_rollup logbook.core.listen_rollup logbook.pages logbook.core.pages logbook.people logbook.core.people logbook.places logbook.core.places logbook.policy logbook.core.policy logbook.present logbook.core.present logbook.reading logbook.core.reading logbook.repair logbook.core.repair logbook.resolve logbook.core.resolve logbook.rollup logbook.core.rollup logbook.sealing logbook.core.sealing tiers 2–3 sealed at rest (RFC 0029), new on main while 0.6 was built logbook.search logbook.core.search logbook.share logbook.core.share logbook.stays logbook.core.stays logbook.store logbook.core.store logbook.story logbook.core.story logbook.trips logbook.core.trips logbook.weather logbook.core.weather logbook.year logbook.core.year logbook.adapters logbook.contrib.adapters and every adapter under it (logbook.adapters.takeout.maps is logbook.contrib.adapters.takeout.maps) logbook.asset_status logbook.contrib.asset_status logbook.attach logbook.contrib.attach logbook.backup logbook.contrib.backup logbook.demo logbook.contrib.demo logbook.digest logbook.contrib.digest logbook.doctor logbook.contrib.doctor logbook.gaps logbook.contrib.gaps logbook.inbox logbook.contrib.inbox logbook.ios_backup logbook.contrib.ios_backup logbook.ios_backup_crypto logbook.contrib.ios_backup_crypto logbook.mcp_server logbook.contrib.mcp_server logbook.people_merge logbook.contrib.people_merge logbook.print_layout logbook.contrib.print_layout logbook.print_page logbook.contrib.print_page logbook.promises logbook.contrib.promises logbook.questions logbook.contrib.questions logbook.schedule logbook.contrib.schedule logbook.serve logbook.contrib.serve logbook.taskdone logbook.contrib.taskdone logbook.trip_bundle logbook.contrib.trip_bundle logbook.trip_page logbook.contrib.trip_page logbook.vault logbook.contrib.vault logbook.demo_life logbook.labs.demo_life logbook.describe logbook.labs.describe logbook.judge logbook.labs.judge logbook.transcribe logbook.labs.transcribe logbook.setup logbook.commands.setup the wizard drives the commands, so it lives with them

logbook.adapters moves whole: the registry (logbook.contrib.adapters) and every adapter module under it, the Google Takeout sub-adapters included. The entry-point group third-party adapters register under is still logbook.adapters; its name did not change, only the package behind it.

docs.title: The names that lived in logbook.cli
docs.text:
logbook/cli.py held every command. The commands now live in logbook/commands/, one module per family (record, add, sync, derive, day, trips, rollup, people, places, keepers, promises, export, serve; common, skips and rows for what they share; parser for the help order). logbook.cli.main stays. Any other name logbook.cli had (cmd_show, record_stats, SKIP_PHRASES, _tz_default, ...) still resolves, found in its family's module with a DeprecationWarning that names where it lives now, and goes in 0.7.

That lookup hands back the family's binding, so a test that patched logbook.cli.<name> must patch the family module instead (monkeypatch.setattr(logbook.commands.record, "_LOCALTIME", ...)): patching the attribute on logbook.cli changes nothing the command sees.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text: openlogbook[encrypted] and openlogbook[share] are one extra under two names (cryptography); either installs the same thing. ijson, which five adapters stream large JSON exports with, is no longer a dependency of the package but the extra openlogbook[stream]; an adapter that needs it and does not find it says so by name, and nothing else is affected.

docs.title: People
docs.text:
logbook people [--year YYYY] [--json] is everyone the record knows and what it knows of each; logbook person <name-or-ref> [--year YYYY] [--json] is one of them on one page, with the timeline of the days you spent together. Both are readers (ADR 0013): derived from the record at its head, every time, and never written. The owner is never listed: the record is yours, and you are not your own company. people merge finds the same person named twice, people review finds the people the sources saw that the record has not placed, and people --priority ranks everyone by a plain score; each writes only when you say so, and only through the record's own lines. people drift answers "who did I use to see and have drifted from?" and people nearby "who is where I am about to go?", from the record, with the evidence, by rules alone; neither writes anything.

logbook people                          # everyone with evidence in the record, most days together first
logbook people --year 2026              # one year
logbook people --json                   # the report as one JSON object
logbook person "Ola Nordmann"           # a label; a unique first or last name does too: `person Ola`
logbook person ola@example.org          # an address the resolution lines know
logbook person +447700900001            # a phone number
logbook person provider_id:immich:f_01  # any ref as kind:value; the entity id works too
logbook people --priority               # everyone heard in the last year, ranked, with the score
logbook people review                   # who the sources saw that the record has not placed
logbook people drift                    # many days together once, no real contact for a year
logbook people nearby Bergen            # who has been seen within 50 km of Bergen
logbook people nearby --days 2026-12-19 2026-12-23   # who is where you have planned to be

docs.title: Who is a person
docs.text:
A person is an entity the record's resolution lines mint (RFC 0006, entity.type person): a contacts import, a logbook add of a name for an address, an alias that reaches one. The label of the first standing line is the name; every ref that resolves to the entity is one of theirs. Nobody the record has not named appears here: an attendee with a display name and no resolution line is in rollup people under unresolved, not in people. A person with no evidence in the window is not listed by people; person still prints their page and says there is no contact.

The owner is owner_id and owner_emails in logbook.json, every resolution that names those, and the names, addresses and numbers of policy/owner.json, as the with module reads them (present.owner_of). A ref of the owner's counts for nobody.

An agent is never a person, whatever it is called (your own agents): a line of a conversation with one of the owner's bots (extra.counterpart of kind agent), whoever wrote it, and a transcript's participant marked machine (the assistant of a Claude Code session) count for nobody in people, person, rollup people, the company of a stay, drift and review, which never observes one and never proposes one, even a bot named after someone the record knows.

docs.title: What is known
docs.text:
11 people · 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-21 · tier 2
  Ola Nordmann  messages 5 · calendar 1 · transcripts 1 · 3 days · 2 nights · last real contact 2026-06-16 (meeting) · birthday 1985-03-12 · Office, aboard Solvind, 47.3769,8.5417 (Zürich)
  Liv Berg      calendar 1 · 1 day · last real contact 2026-06-09 (meeting) · Office
  Eva Nordmann  calls 1 · last real contact 2026-06-17 (call)
  Jonas Weber   calendar 1

One row per person, most days together first, then the latest contact, then the name. The head names the window and the tier of the report: the highest tier of any evidence it rests on (SPEC §4). A person's own tier is the highest tier of the lines that put them there, the resolution lines that name them included, so it is 2 in practice and 3 when a transcript was written at 3.

  • Channels, each with how many lines, the first and last local day, the highest tier among them and, under --json, the id of the last line:
    • messages: a message/v1 (RFC 0008) they sent, by sender; and one you sent in a direct chat with them. Your line in a direct chat goes to the one person who wrote in that chat; in a chat only you wrote in, to the person the chat's id names (a WhatsApp JID 447700900001@s.whatsapp.net is the phone number; iMessage names a direct chat by the address). Your lines in a group name nobody.
    • calls: a call/v1 (RFC 0012) whose counterparty they are, answered or not.
    • mail: a mail/v1 (RFC 0015) from them, or to them (to, cc, bcc), by address.
    • calendar: an event/v1 (RFC 0009) they attend and did not decline, timed or all-day, wherever it was held.
    • transcripts: a transcript/v1 (RFC 0004) they are a participant of, by email, phone or provider id, else by the spoken name when the record labels exactly one person by it; or one in which a voice you named is theirs, the far end of a call included, adding spoke_s, the seconds they spoke (who they are). A person you bound a voice to and would not name is never a row: the head says and 1 unnamed, and how many voices are not yet named, review speakers; --json carries unnamed and not_yet_named.
    • faces: a photo/v1 (RFC 0002) with their face tagged, through the library's person id (provider_id, <library>:<id>).
  • First and last contact: the earliest and latest day over every channel and every day together.
  • Days together: the confirmed set of the with module (present, the rules of trips and rollup people): an attendee of a timed calendar entry held at one of your stays, a speaker of a recording made inside it, a note written there that says "with ". The day is the evidence line's own. A tagged face and an all-day entry's attendee are proposals, not a day together. logbook with DAY NAME [--at HH:MM] writes that note for you when no source saw them: one line per person, with <name>, at the clock you give (noon without one), so the stay it falls in counts the day (the acts).
  • Nights under one roof: the nights whose overnight stay the person was confirmed at on that day — the night at anchor after the note says you grilled with them, the night of the dinner in the hotel.
  • Places: where the days together were, by days there, most first: the stay's named place, aboard <asset>, or the coordinates with near <place>, x km or the city of the nearest large airport, as the rollups label an unnamed place.
  • Birthday: when a standing resolution line of one of their refs carries one under payload.extra.birthday, as YYYY-MM-DD or --MM-DD (a year unknown), printed as stored. A contacts adapter that reads the card's birthday writes it there; none does yet.
  • Last real contact: the latest of a message (either way), an answered call, or a day together, with how (message, call, meeting; on one day a meeting is named first). A mail is a channel and never a real contact: a newsletter is a mail too, and the record cannot tell it from a letter. A missed call, a tagged face and an all-day entry are not one either.

docs.title: The person page
docs.text:
Ola Nordmann  (ola@example.org, +4790000001) · tier 2
  birthday 1985-03-12
  first contact 2026-06-09 · last 2026-06-16 · last real contact 2026-06-16 (meeting)
  channels  messages 5 (2026-06-09 – 2026-06-14) · calendar 1 (2026-06-16) · transcripts 1 (2026-06-11)
  3 days together · 2 nights under one roof
  places  Office (1 day), aboard Solvind (1 day), 47.3769,8.5417 (Zürich) (1 day)
  shared days
    2026-06-16  47.3769,8.5417 (Zürich) · attendee of Dinner · night
    2026-06-13  aboard solvind · note says with Ola Nordmann · night
    2026-06-11  Office · spoke in Boat plans

The same numbers, then every shared day, most recent first: where, what put them there (the with module's reasons), and night when that night was spent under one roof. Under --json each shared day carries the stay's id, its sources and the ids of its evidence lines.

<name-or-ref> is tried as a ref first — kind:value, an address, a + number — then as an entity id, then as a label (case aside), then as a word of a label: Ola finds Ola Nordmann when no one else is an Ola; Nordmann with three Nordmanns names several and is refused, as is a name nobody has, and the owner's own. Exit status 2 with the reason on stderr.

docs.title: The same person twice
docs.text:
A record gets its people by several roads: the phone's address book mints an entity per card (ios-contacts), a Takeout export mints one per card it cannot match (google-takeout-contacts), and you name a calendar attendee, a mail sender or a transcript speaker by hand. The same person can end up as two or three entities, each with its own refs, each a row of people. logbook people merge finds them, shows why, and merges only when you say so.

logbook people merge                          # the proposals, with the evidence; nothing written
logbook people merge --json
logbook people merge --apply 5891928aa5523867 2f79068fab4863c9   # merge these, by the ids printed
logbook people merge --export-review review.csv                  # one row per secondary, to mark
logbook people merge --apply-review review.csv                   # merge the rows marked yes

4 proposals · 9 people named twice or more · tier 2
  5891928aa5523867  Kari Nordmann ← Kari
    phone +447700900101: +447700900101 (ios-contacts, seq 3) · 447700900101@s.whatsapp.net (manual, seq 6)
  2f79068fab4863c9  Per Hansen ← Per Hansen, Per Hansen
    email per.hansen@example.org: per.hansen@example.org (google-takeout-contacts, seq 7) · Per.Hansen@example.org (manual, seq 9)
    phone +447700900102: +447700900102 (google-takeout-contacts, seq 8) · 07700900102 (ios-contacts, seq 10)
  298bc7a7705e8fbc  Liv Berg ← Berg, Liv
    name Liv Berg ~ Berg, Liv · both on mail
nothing merged: `people merge --apply ID...`, or `--export-review FILE`, mark, `--apply-review`

Every person entity the resolution lines name, never you, is a candidate, with every ref that resolves to it through the alias walk. Two candidates are one person when:

  • a phone meets: a ref of each spells the same E.164 number — a phone ref as written, a number entered without a country code read with LOGBOOK_DIAL_PREFIX (as the adapters read it), or a WhatsApp JID handle (447700900001@s.whatsapp.net);
  • an email meets: an email ref of each, or a handle that is an address, is the same address, case aside;
  • the names are one name and they share a channel: the labels have the same words in any order, case, accents and punctuation aside (Nordmann, Kari is Kari Nordmann), or one spells a first name by its initial (K. Nordmann); both with two words at least — a first name alone names anyone — and never a word one letter off (Anna and Anne are two people); and both are heard on one of the channels above (both through mail, both in transcripts). A name alone is never enough.

A ref resolves to one entity only, so a number never meets itself: what meets is two spellings of one identifier, which is what a second import leaves behind. Matches join (a number between A and B and an address between B and C is one proposal of three). The primary is the candidate with the most refs, then the most lines heard, then the one minted first; the others are secondary. A proposal's id is a digest of its entity ids, the same on every run until something changes.

Applying writes alias lines and nothing else (RFC 0006, alias_of): for each ref of a secondary whose own line names it, one resolution/v1 line, source manual, method owner, saying the ref is an alias of the primary's ref (a phone before an address). The ref, and every ref already aliased to it (a WhatsApp linked-device id that whatsapp-contacts pointed at the number), then resolve to the primary through the ordinary walk, which people, person, the with module and every other reader take; a chain that would run past the walk's four hops gets a line of its own. The line supersedes the line it replaces and carries both as evidence, the primary's label, the head the proposal was read against (logbook_head), and under extra the proposal id, the two entities and what matched. Nothing is retracted and no raw line is touched: retract the alias line and the two are two again. --apply checks every id before writing the first line; an id that is no proposal exits 2 and writes nothing. Under --json, --apply prints the lines it wrote.

Reviewing in a spreadsheet: --export-review FILE writes one CSV row per (proposal, secondary) — proposal, apply, primary_id, primary, primary_refs, secondary_id, secondary, secondary_refs, matched — with apply empty. Write yes (or y, x, true, 1) in apply on the rows to merge and run --apply-review FILE: each marked row is the merge of its secondary into its primary. A row whose secondary already resolves to its primary is said and skipped, so the same file applies twice without harm; a row naming an entity the record does not know, or the same entity on both sides, is refused before anything is written. A file without the three columns is not a review file.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
The record has two layers of people, and the rule between them is the one lesson an earlier system taught the hard way.

An observed person is what one source saw: the address a mail came from, the number a message came from, the attendee on a calendar entry, the name a transcript gave a speaker. Nobody chose them; they are in the record because a line names them. A canonical person is one you have confirmed: an entity the resolution lines name (RFC 0006), minted by a contacts import, a logbook add of a name for an address, or a people merge. people lists the canonical people and nobody else; the observed people are the rest, waiting. There is no third store: a confirmation is the alias line people merge writes, and a rejection is one line too.

The strongest-identifier rule. An observed person's identity is derived from the strongest identifier the observation carries, in this order and never any other way:

  1. the email address, case aside;
  2. else the phone number in E.164 — a +44… as written, a WhatsApp JID (447700900101@s.whatsapp.net) read as the number it spells, a number entered without a country code read with LOGBOOK_DIAL_PREFIX as the adapters read it;
  3. else a handle a service names, github:<login>, case aside: the organizer of a GitHub line (GitHub), named by the name the line gives (a commit's author);
  4. else the name as shown, its words folded and sorted (Berg, Liv and Liv Berg are one).

Never from the id a source gives one observation — a speaker id, a chat guid, a message id, a line id. An address seen under three display names is one observed person with three names; a number seen as +447700900101 in one chat and as a JID in another is one. Keyed the other way, one person explodes into a row per observation, and no queue survives that.

The table. Observed people are the person rows of the index's derived table, observed_entities in index.sqlite (RFC 0037: one table for every kind the record names, read here through its view observed_people, the table it replaces, for one release): one row per strongest identifier with the display names and the identifiers as the lines wrote them, counts per source and per kind, the days seen, first and last seen, the tier of the evidence, a few line ids as evidence, and the canonical person the row resolves to when one of its identifiers has a resolution standing as written — the readers look a ref up as the line carries it, so Per.Hansen@example.org on a calendar entry is not placed by a line for per.hansen@example.org — or, for a name alone, when the people reader would place a speaker of that name. The table is built from the standing mail/v1, message/v1, transcript/v1 and event/v1 lines through the index, your own identities left out (owner_id, owner_emails, policy/owner.json and their closure), stamped with the head it was built at, served while the head stands and rebuilt when the record grows. Its shape is checked with PRAGMA table_info; a table of another shape is built again, never read. Nothing is written to the record.

The queue. logbook people review proposes each observed person not yet placed against each canonical person, ranked by the evidence, numbered from 1, one line each:

15 proposals · 17 observed people not yet placed, 36 placed · tier 2
   1  [80]  eva.nordmann@example.org (Eva Nordmann; event 1) → Eva Nordmann: same email eva.nordmann@example.org · same name Eva Nordmann
   3  [22]  +447700900115 (Astrid Bakke; message 3) → Astrid Bakke: same name Astrid Bakke · together on 1 day
  11  [22]  maren.eide@example.org (Maren Eide; mail 3) → Maren Eide: same name Maren Eide · together on 1 day
  15  [20]  M. Eide (transcript 1) → Maren Eide: same name M. Eide ~ Maren Eide
nothing written: `people review --accept N[,N]`, `--reject N[,N]`, or `--all-above SCORE`

The score is a plain sum of what speaks for the pair:

Evidence Points What it means same email 60 an identifier of the observed person is an address a canonical ref spells, case aside same phone 50 the same E.164 number, by the rules above same name 20, +5 per further source up to +10 a display name and the canonical label are one name by people merge's rule: the same words in any order, or an initial for a first name; two words at least, never a word one letter off together on the same days 2 per day, up to 20 both were seen on the day; days alone never propose

A pair you rejected is never proposed again. An observed person with no identifier a resolution line can carry (a spoken name alone, matching nobody exactly) is listed under observed.unplaced in --json and proposed nothing: there is nothing to write for it; name the speaker with logbook add instead. The numbers are the queue's at this head and change when the record does; --json carries a stable id per pair beside them.

Your say. Nothing is promoted on its own; the owner decides, and only Logbook.append writes.

logbook people review --accept 1,3 --reject 11   # accept these, reject that; numbers from the listing
logbook people review --all-above 50            # accept every proposal at or above 50
logbook people review --json                    # the queue, the unplaced and the placed count
  • --accept N[,N] writes, per identifier of the observed person as the lines wrote it, the line people merge writes: one resolution/v1, source manual, method owner, alias_of the canonical person's own ref (a phone before an address), the logbook_head the proposal was read against, the target's line and the observed lines as evidence, and under extra the proposal id, the entity, the score and what matched. The identifier, and every reader that looks it up, then resolves to the canonical person through the ordinary alias walk.
  • --reject N[,N] writes one entity-review/v1 line of type person (RFC 0037, kind entity-review; the profiles) saying the observed person and the canonical person are not the same: the strongest identifier as ref, the identifiers as written under refs, the display names, the entity, the same head and evidence, tier 2 at least. The pair never comes back; retract the line and it does. A people-review/v1 line (RFC 0035), which people review wrote until 0.7, is read as the same no, forever.
  • --all-above SCORE accepts every proposal at or above the score, a whole number.

Every number is checked before the first line is written; a number the queue does not have, a number both accepted and rejected, or a score that is not a whole number exits 2 and writes nothing. A second people review after accepting is shorter by what was accepted, numbered afresh, and the people rows of the people already placed do not change: a review adds refs to a person, never a person to the list. logbook review person is this sitting under the name every kind shares (review); the two print the same, byte for byte.

docs.title: Names from Google contacts
docs.text:
A review can only propose what the record already says. Your address book knows more: who jakob.holm@example.org is, that the number a message came from belongs to someone whose address you already have. logbook people review --from-google reads your Google contacts and your other contacts (the ones Google saved for you from mail exchanged) as a name source for the review: names, addresses, phone numbers and the photo as a reference. A name source gives names to the review, never lines to the record.

logbook people review --from-google                     # the queue, with what your contacts say
logbook people review --from-google --accept 4 --reject 9
logbook people review --from-google --json

It reads them with the one Google key (the tour, Google, on one key), read-only, through the People API: contacts.readonly for your contacts and contacts.other.readonly for the other ones. A book whose scope the delegation does not grant is left out and said on stderr; neither granted is one line and exit 1. Without the key's two variables the command says what to set and exits 2.

What a contact does in the queue:

  • It links a pair. A contact that holds an observed person's address or number and one of a canonical person's own adds 50 points to that pair, in words: Google contact Maren Eide has maren.eide@example.org and +447700900119. Its name alone, when it is the canonical person's, adds 20: Google contact Maren Eide has maren.eide@example.org. The pair keeps its id, so accepting it writes what an accept always writes.
  • It names a new person. A contact that touches no one the record names (none of its addresses or numbers is a canonical person's, its name is none of theirs) proposes to name the observed people it holds an address or a number of, or whose shown name is its own, scored as a pair is: same email 60, same phone 50, same name 20 (and 5 per further source). The line reads → Jakob Holm, new (Google contacts). Accepting it mints one person: one resolution/v1 line per identifier the record saw, entity a new id, label the contact's name, method owner, source manual, tier 2 at least (the name is your address book's), extra.named_from google contacts. Two proposals of one contact accepted in one run are one person. Nothing else of the contact is written: not its other addresses or numbers, not its photo, not its id in Google.
  • It is proposed with its duplicates. Contacts that share an address or a number are listed as one group with what they share, J. Holm ↔ Jakob Holm: same email jakob.holm@example.org, to merge in Google Contacts (Merge & fix): the key only reads, and a contact is not the record's to merge.

Nothing is merged on its own: every proposal waits for --accept, --all-above or --reject, as any other does. Rejecting a contact's proposal writes no line, since the contact is not in the record: its id, a digest that names no one, is kept in state/google-contacts-review.json and it is not proposed again; delete the file and it comes back.

The cache. The contacts read are kept in state/google-contacts.json, the record's bookkeeping like the sync watermarks, never the record, readable by you alone (mode 600), for 24 hours and for the user they were read as. Within that time --from-google asks Google nothing, so the numbers a listing shows are the numbers an --accept that follows acts on; give --from-google to both. After it, the next run reads the books again; delete the file to read them sooner. The cache is never printed: the review shows a contact's name, the one identifier a proposal matched, the book and whether it has a photo, and a count of what was read:

google contacts: 412 contacts, 1,038 other contacts, read 2026-10-13T18:02:00Z, kept 24 h in state/google-contacts.json
2 groups of duplicate contacts, to merge in Google Contacts (Merge & fix; the key only reads):
  J. Holm ↔ Jakob Holm: same email jakob.holm@example.org
  Nora Aas ↔ Nora Aas: same phone +447700900125

Under --json the report gains contacts (read_at, cached, ttl_hours, books, refused, duplicates), and a proposal from a contact has canonical null and contact (name, book, photo). Without --from-google the review is what it was, and Google is not asked.

docs.title: Priority
docs.text:
logbook people --priority [--year YYYY] [--json] ranks the canonical people heard in the last year of the record (the 365 days ending on its last day, clipped to it; --year is that year) by a score you can argue with, printed beside each name. The score is a sum, nothing more:

  1. 3 per day together in the window (the confirmed days of the with module, as people counts them).
  2. 1 per message exchanged, the smaller of the two directions (their lines to you, your lines to them in a direct chat), up to 50: a conversation, not a broadcast.
  3. 2 per meeting: a timed calendar entry they attended, a transcript they spoke in.
  4. 10 when the last real contact (a message either way, an answered call, a day together) is within 30 days of the window's end, 5 within 90, else 0.
  5. Nothing else: no mail (a newsletter is a mail too), no faces, no model.
priority · 2025-06-22 – 2026-06-21 · 11 people
  47  Ola Nordmann  3 days together · messages 2 from them, 3 from you · meetings 2 · last real contact 2026-06-16
  10  Eva Nordmann  last real contact 2026-06-17

Under --json: window and people, each id, name, score, days, messages (them, me), meetings, last_real_contact and recency. Nothing is written.

docs.title: Drift
docs.text:
logbook people drift [--min-days N] [--quiet-days M] [--year YYYY] [--show] [--json] lists the people you used to see and have drifted from: the canonical people with at least N days together in one calendar year (default 20) whose last real contact is more than M days before the record's last day (default 365; today, when the record runs past it, since a planned entry has not happened). Their best year counts, the year with most days together; --year counts that year instead. Most days together first, then the longest silence, then the name.

A real contact is one of four things, and nothing else:

  • together: a day together, as above: the with module confirmed them at one of your stays;
  • meeting: a timed calendar entry they attended and did not decline, wherever it was held (a video call too), or a recording they spoke in;
  • call: a call with them that was answered, whichever way it went;
  • message: a message in a direct chat with them, theirs or yours.

A mail is never one, sent or received: a newsletter is a mail, and so is your note to forty people about moving house, and the record cannot tell either from a letter. A line in a group chat is the group's, not a contact with whoever wrote it, so a "happy new year" to the crew keeps nobody close. A missed call, a tagged face and an all-day entry are not one either. On one day, a day together is named before a meeting, a meeting before a call, a call before a message. This is stricter than the last real contact of people and --priority, which count any message of theirs, in a group too.

drift · 4 people · 20+ days together in a year · no real contact in over 365 days · to 2025-12-31
  Elin Moe      2022: 25 days · last real contact 2022-06-12 (together, 1298 days ago)
  Astrid Bakke  2022: 24 days · last real contact 2022-03-13 (together, 1389 days ago)
  Dag Solberg   2023: 22 days · last real contact 2023-07-04 (together, 911 days ago)
  Bjørn Lie     2023: 22 days · last real contact 2024-03-10 (message, 661 days ago) · promises open: you owe 1, they owe 1

Each row: the name, the best year and its days together, the last real contact with what it was and how long ago, and the open promises with them both ways, from logbook promises: what you promised them and what they asked of you is you owe, what they promised you is they owe. A promise is theirs when its speaker resolves to them, else when its counterpart is their name and nobody else in the list has it. --show adds, under each row, the days together by year and the id of the line of the last real contact: days, never a word of a message. Under --json: window, until, min_days, quiet_days, year and people, each id, name, best_year (year, days), days (in all), last_real_contact (day, via, line), silent_days and promises (you_owe, they_owe); --show adds days_together, each day, where and the evidence lines.

Only canonical people are listed; an observed person, however many entries they attended, is waiting in people review, not here.

docs.title: Nearby
docs.text:
logbook people nearby PLACE | --journey ID | --days FROM TO [--radius KM] [--json] is a list for a trip: in this city, these people, last seen then. A person is seen at a place on a day together at one of your stays whose centre lies within the radius of it (--radius, default 50 km). Per place they are ranked by days together there, then days together anywhere, then the latest real contact (as drift defines it), then the name.

Bergen · 60.2934,5.2181 · within 50 km · 3 people
  Astrid Bakke  24 days there, last seen 2022-03-13 · 24 days in all · last real contact 2022-03-13 (together)
  Dag Solberg   22 days there, last seen 2023-07-04 · 22 days in all · last real contact 2023-07-04 (together)
  Ingrid Aas    20 days there, last seen 2022-03-01 · 20 days in all · last real contact 2025-09-01 (meeting)

The place is one of three:

  • PLACE, tried in this order: lat,lon; a place of places.json by its name, case aside; a city of the airports table (logbook/tables/airports.csv, the record's own gazetteer), by the city a row's municipality names, case and accents aside, at the airport's reference point (Bergen is Flesland, 12 km out, which the radius covers); an IATA or ICAO code of it. A name none of them knows is refused, exit 2.
  • --journey ID: a journey/v1 (or trip/v1) line, where its to is (its from for a parking), by coordinates when it has them, else by name as above; or a flight/v1 line, its destination airport.
  • --days FROM TO: the places you have planned on those days — every standing calendar entry with a location (its coordinates, else the location text, whole or any comma-separated part: Solsiden, Trondheim is Trondheim), every standing flight dated in them (its destination; a cancelled one left out), every standing journey line. A planned place within the radius of a home place of places.json is home, not a trip, and is left out. Two that share a name or lie within 5 km are one place, listed with every line that planned it; the places come in the order planned. A location no rule places is listed as unplaced.

Under --json: radius_km, days (since, until, or null), places, each label, lat, lon, by (coordinates, places, airports), radius_km, from (the planning lines: kind, day, line, what) and people, each id, name, days_there, last_there, days and last_real_contact; and unplaced.

What it cannot see: a day together is a stay of yours with evidence the person was there, so a friend you met in Bergen with no calendar entry, no recording and no note saying "with" them was never there as far as the record knows.

docs.title: The window
docs.text: The whole record by default: the first to the last local day with a line of any kind, so a message written before the tracker's first point is in. --year is that year, clipped to the record's days; a year with none is no people (and window: null under --json).

docs.title: How it reads
docs.text: Everything comes through index.sqlite and nothing sweeps the files. The resolution and retraction lines are read whole (Index.resolutions, Index.retractions); your stays and nights come from the index's own columns, no line read (reading.owner_track, the reader places propose uses); and the lines of the six kinds above stream one kind at a time over the window (Index.of_kind with its day bounds), each read once and kept only when it names someone — a year of messages is counted as it streams and never held. A retracted line, and one another line of its kind supersedes (a calendar entry edited since), counts for nothing.

docs.title: JSON
docs.text:
{"window": {"since": "2026-06-01", "until": "2026-06-21"}, "tier": 2,
 "people": [{"id": "019c…", "name": "Ola Nordmann", "refs": [{"kind": "email", "value": "ola@example.org"}],
   "tier": 2, "birthday": "1985-03-12", "first_contact": "2026-06-09", "last_contact": "2026-06-16",
   "last_real_contact": {"day": "2026-06-16", "via": "meeting", "line": "019c…"},
   "channels": {"messages": {"lines": 5, "first": "2026-06-09", "last": "2026-06-14", "tier": 2, "last_line": "019c…"}},
   "days": 3, "nights": 2, "places": [{"where": "Office", "days": 1}], "lines": ["019c…"]}]}

lines are the ids of the shared days' evidence; a channel names its last line only, since a year of messages is thousands. The page adds page, window and shared_days, each with day, stay, where, night, sources, reasons and lines.

docs.title: Places
docs.text:
A place is a name for a spot you return to: home, the office, a cabin, a berth. The record keeps them in places.json in the record folder, a setting beside the chain like assets.json: a place is never a line, and renaming one changes no line. What the chain holds is the naming itself, one note/v1 line per place you name ("named 55.6000,4.4000 as Hytta på banken"), so the record says when you gave it.

{"Home": {"lat": 59.9139, "lon": 10.7522, "radius_m": 120, "kind": "home", "tags": ["family"]}}

kind is home, asset-berth or other; a night is at home when its stay lies in a place of kind home. radius_m is how far from the centre a point still counts as there (150 m when left out). Every reader reads the file each time it runs: the Day, day, serve, show days, the trips, the rollups. A stay inside a named place prints its name; one outside prints its coordinates, 55.6100,4.4000 near Hytta på banken, 1.1 km. Name a place and the next page you open says it.

Command What it does logbook setup places list one line per place logbook setup places add NAME --lat --lon [--radius M] [--kind] [--tags] add one, by hand; appends nothing logbook setup places name LAT,LON NAME add one and put the naming in the record logbook setup places propose your unnamed stays grouped and ranked by hours, with what is near; --write asks for a name for each logbook setup places review the places you return to, each with the name the record already holds for it, to accept, name or reject (below); --ask-photos asks your photo libraries too (below); logbook serve's Places page asks the same, in a browser logbook setup places import-takeout PATH Google Maps' saved and starred places as entries, written only with --write

logbook places … still works for each of these, with one line saying the new name.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
You have years of points and a dozen named places, so most of your days print coordinates. review lets you name the places you return to in one sitting, from what the record already knows about each.

$ logbook setup places review
12 places observed · 0 named · 12 to review, by nights then hours
   1  55.6000,4.4000 · 6 visits · 6 nights · 91.5 h · 2026-02-02 – 2026-02-14 → Hytta på banken
          google-takeout timeline: "Hytta på banken" (3 visits) · google-takeout timeline: "Home" (3 visits, type) · immich: "Nordsjøen" (1 photo, city)
   2  55.6000,4.4180 · 3 visits · 3 nights · 48.0 h · 2026-02-04 – 2026-02-13 → Verkstedet
          google-takeout timeline: "Verkstedet" (2 visits)
   3  55.6000,4.4360 · 2 visits · 2 nights · 30.5 h · 2026-02-07 – 2026-02-12 → ____
          no source names it
   …
nothing written: `setup places review --accept N[,N]`, `--name N "…"`, or `--reject N[,N]`

(A synthetic record at sea; nobody lives at those coordinates.)

The evidence is folded: a reverse geocoder names every house number a track passes, so the addresses one source wrote along one street are one line (dawarich: "Plattformveien" (38 addresses, 217 stays)), three lines are shown, and … and N more counts the rest. --verbose prints every name on its own, as before.

docs.title: Observed places
docs.text:
An observed place is a cluster of your stays: the same spot within 75 m (--radius M to change it). Your stays are taken from the longest down; each joins the nearest cluster whose first, longest stay lies within the radius, or starts a cluster of its own. Each observed place has its visits (the stays), its nights (the nights whose overnight stay, as the Day picks it, was there), its first and last visit, its total hours, its centre (the stays' centres weighted by hours), and the names the record holds for the spot. The queue ranks them by nights, then hours: where you sleep comes first.

The observed places are derived, never stored in the record: the place rows of a table in the index (observed_entities in index.sqlite, in your cache directory, read through its view observed_places, the table it replaces, for one release; RFC 0037), built from the lines and kept until the record, places.json, assets.json or policy/stays.json changes, then built again. Building it reads your track from the index alone, as propose does, and opens only the lines that can carry a name: the Timeline visits, the photos, the calendar entries, and the first and last point of each stay.

docs.title: Where the names come from
docs.text:
Only from lines already in the record. Each name is shown under the source that said it, with how often:

Source What names a spot Weight a line Google Timeline a place visit of the archive's Semantic Location History names the place and its address (placeVisit.location.name, else address), by its coordinates 3 any Timeline visit whose type is home or work (TYPE_HOME, INFERRED_WORK, Home) says Home or Work 1 Calendar the location of a timed entry held during one of the cluster's stays (overlapping it for half its length or more), its first line as you typed it; not an online meeting (a link, Zoom, Teams, Meet, Webex, Skype, FaceTime), not one whose own coordinates are more than 1 km away, not an all-day entry, not a cancelled one 3 Photos the place the photo's library named: Photos' area name or address (extra.place, written by apple-photos), by the photo's coordinates or, without them, its time 2 Immich's city (exifInfo.city, written by immich as extra.place.city) 1 Dawarich the place Dawarich's own reverse geocoder wrote on the first and last point of a stay (name, else street and number), once per stay 2

A name with coordinates names the observed place nearest them within 150 m, one you were at that hour first. The proposal's name is the one with the most weight; a name already in places.json, or one you rejected for that spot, is passed over for the next. Where no source names a spot, the proposal is a blank (____) for you to fill.

The phones' own Timeline exports (Android's Timeline.json, the iPhone's location-history.json) carry Google's place id and a type for each visit, never a name: they give Home and Work at most. The names are in the Semantic Location History of a Takeout archive downloaded before Google moved Timeline onto the phone (the export steps). A location shared in iMessage or WhatsApp would name a spot too, but neither adapter keeps a shared location's coordinates yet, so none is read.

docs.title: Nothing is looked up
docs.text: No coordinate leaves your machine, and no geocoder is ever asked — not an online one, not an offline one. review reads the record and writes places.json; it opens no connection, and the tests hold it to that with the network guard on.
