A spot has a name here only when a source already wrote one into a line: Google's when you exported your Timeline, your calendar's when you typed it, your photo library's when it named the picture on your phone or your Immich server, Dawarich's when your own server geocoded the point. Everything else is a blank, and the name is yours to give. The one exception is yours to make, each time you want it: --ask-photos asks your own Immich server about your own photos, by asset id (Ask the photos).

docs.title: Ask the photos
docs.text:
A record that has synced a photo library for years holds hundreds of thousands of photo lines, and most carry no place name: they were imported before the Immich and Photos adapters kept the place their library named, and the record never rewrites a line, so syncing again adds nothing to them. Your libraries still know where each photo was taken. --ask-photos asks them about the photos already in the record, and offers what they say as evidence like any other source.

Your photos' asset ids go to your own Immich server, and nothing else leaves your machine: no coordinate, no name, no photo, and never a geocoder. Immich answers with the city it named on your server when the photo was uploaded; Photos is read from the library on this machine.

$ logbook setup places review --ask-photos
asking the photos about 7 places: up to 50 photos at each from each library, the nearest its centre first
  immich: 13 photos; sending 13 asset ids to immich.example.org, nothing else, at most 10 a second (about 2 s)
  photos: 4 photos; reading their places from the library at ~/Pictures/Photos Library.photoslibrary/database/Photos.sqlite, on this machine
  immich: 12 named a place, 1 not on the server
  photos: 3 named a place, 1 not in the library
12 places observed · 0 named · 12 to review, by nights then hours
   …
   3  55.6000,4.4360 · 2 visits · 2 nights · 30.5 h · 2026-02-07 – 2026-02-12 → Havbyen
          immich ×12: Havbyen
   …
   7  55.6100,4.4360 · 4 visits · 0 nights · 12.0 h · 2026-02-03 – 2026-02-12 → Plattformen
          photos ×3: Plattformen
   8  55.6100,4.4540 · 5 visits · 0 nights · 10.0 h · 2026-02-04 – 2026-02-13 → ____
          no source names it
   …

(The same synthetic record at sea; the server and every name are invented.)

  • Which places. The blanks among the proposals shown — after --near and --top — or the ones you --accept or --reject. --all asks about the proposals that already have a name too. The queue and its numbers are the same with the flag and without it.
  • Which photos. Your immich and apple-photos photo lines that have coordinates and no place name of their own, at the observed place nearest them within 150 m. Of each place, the 50 photos nearest its centre from each library (--limit N to ask about more or fewer).
  • Immich is asked through the same client sync immich uses: your LOGBOOK_IMMICH_URL, your key (the asset.read permission it already has), one GET /api/assets/{id} per photo, one at a time and at most 10 a second. Its answer is the city, state and country your server named.
  • Photos is the library a Mac keeps at ~/Pictures/Photos Library.photoslibrary, or the one --photos-library PATH names, read only: the address and the area names Photos gave each picture.
  • The cost first. Before anything is sent, one line per library says how many photos it will be asked about, how many the cache answers, and where the rest go. The lines go to stderr, so --json stays one object; with --json the object also carries asked_photos, the same counts.
  • The cache. Every answer — a place, no place, a photo the library no longer has — is kept in state/places-photos.json beside the record, by asset id, for 30 days. A second review within them asks nothing again; after them, it asks again. Deleting the file only means the next review asks.
  • When a library cannot answer. An Immich without its two variables, a library that is not there, and a source you disabled in policy/import.json are said and passed over. A server that fails is said once, with how many photos were not asked, and the review goes on with the other sources; a failure is never cached, so the next review asks again.

What a photo's library says weighs as a photo line's place does: Photos' area name or address 2 a photo, a city (all Immich gives) 1. With --all, a dozen photos' city can outweigh a few Timeline visits' name; the evidence line shows both, and the choice is yours.

Nothing is written: the photo names are evidence, and accepting one is --accept as before. Give --ask-photos with it, so the review sees the name it proposed (the cache answers, so nothing is asked twice):

logbook setup places review --ask-photos --accept 3     # Havbyen, from the photos, into places.json
logbook setup places review --ask-photos --reject 7     # never propose Plattformen for that spot again

docs.title: Your say
docs.text:
Nothing is accepted on its own.

logbook setup places review --accept 1,2           # the names proposed, as they are
logbook setup places review --name 3 "Base"         # your own name for proposal 3
logbook setup places review --reject 4              # never propose that name for that spot again
logbook setup places review --near Home --top 10    # the ten first within 5 km of Home (or of lat,lon)
logbook setup places review --json                  # the queue, with the evidence and its line ids
  • Accept writes the place into places.json: the observed place's centre, a fitted radius (below), kind other — change it with an editor or setup places add if it is a home or a berth — and puts the naming in the record as setup places name does, one note/v1 line.
  • Name is accept with your own words.
  • Reject puts the pair — the spot and the name proposed, or the blank — in the record as one entity-review/v1 line of type place (RFC 0037; the profiles): its ref the spot's centre, its label the name, its evidence the stays' lines, its tier the highest of theirs and never under 2. That name is not proposed for that spot again; reject a blank and the spot stays out of the queue until a source names it; retract the line and the pair returns. The Places page of logbook serve rejects through the same code. state/places-review.json is a cache of those lines, rebuilt from them when the record has moved, never the truth: delete it and nothing you see changes.
  • Migrate (--migrate-rejects): until 0.7 a reject was kept in state/places-review.json only, never as a line, and a backup left it out. Those pairs still count; --migrate-rejects writes each of them once as an entity-review/v1 line, at the moment you said it, and says how many on stderr; a second run writes nothing. Until you run it, review says how many are not lines yet.

The numbers are the queue's as review prints it, also with --near and --top; every number in one command is checked before anything is written, and after a write the queue is numbered again. On a terminal, review asks for each proposal shown: y accepts the name, n rejects it, anything else is the name to give it, Enter skips, q stops. Each answer is written at once. logbook review place is this sitting under the name every kind shares (review); the two print the same, byte for byte.

docs.title: In the browser
docs.text: logbook serve's Places page (serve) asks the same questions without a terminal: the queue in this order, twenty a page, each cluster with a dot on a plain canvas, its facts, its evidence folded, a field prefilled with the proposal, and Name, Skip and Not a place (Enter, Space and n). Name and Not a place go through the same accept and reject as --name, --accept and --reject, so what lands in places.json, the record and state/places-review.json is what the CLI writes. The form is answered from this machine only. A Day's stay printed as coordinates links to its cluster there.

docs.title: The fitted radius
docs.text: The radius an accepted place gets is the distance from its centre within which 95% of its hours were spent, plus 75 m for the scatter of one stay's own fixes, rounded up to 5 m, between 75 and 300 m. When that circle would reach into a place you have named already, it is drawn back to that place's edge, never below 50 m; a spot whose centre lies inside a named place is that place already, and is not proposed. --json shows the radius each proposal would get.

docs.title: The plan
docs.text:
You keep your tasks, your sprints and your trips in Notion, and logbook sync notion already writes what happens there into the record: one line per page, day and action, with a database row's status, select, date and checkbox values and the ids of the rows it links to, never its text (sync notion). logbook show plan reads the plan back from those lines, for one day:

logbook show plan                 # today
logbook show plan 2026-10-21
logbook show plan 2026-10-21 --json
logbook show plan --coverage      # how much of each database the record knows

plan  2026-10-21 · Sprint 24, 2026-10-12 to 2026-10-25  https://www.notion.so/…
  today       1  2026-10-19  Fix the bilge pump · To do · overdue  https://www.notion.so/…
                 2026-10-21  Ask about winter storage · To do · done today  https://www.notion.so/…
              3  2026-10-21  Book the ferry · In progress  https://www.notion.so/…
              4  2026-10-21  Check the life jackets · To do  https://www.notion.so/…
              5  2026-10-21  Clean the cabin · To do  https://www.notion.so/…
             and 3 more in Sprint 24
  next trip  Lofoten · 2026-11-27 to 2026-12-03 · in 37 days  https://www.notion.so/…

The plan is read and never run (RFC 0043, §9). show plan fetches nothing: it reads the lines sync notion wrote and nothing else, of Notion or of the record. It is tier 1 alone: every sync notion line is tier 1, and the plan reads no other line (never the day's stays, its browsing or its messages) and names none, not even by its id; the one exception is your own answers at the day's close (What the record answers, below), read only to mark the tasks you answered. It writes nothing, to the record or to Notion, and it never ranks, reschedules or creates a task. Every row carries its Notion link, https://www.notion.so/ and the row's id, so the place to change a task is Notion. No row's text is ever printed: the record never held it.

docs.title: The mapping
docs.text:
Which of your databases is which is yours to say, in policy/notion.json, under plan, each by its id or by the link Notion copies (Copy link to view):

{
  "plan": {
    "tasks": "https://www.notion.so/ines/Tasks-0123456789abcdef0123456789abcdef?pvs=4",
    "sprints": "…",
    "trips": "…",
    "status": "Status",
    "done": ["Done"],
    "date": "Due"
  }
}

Every key is optional, and a part whose database is not named is left out. A line keeps a property's value and not its type, so three keys say how to read a row: status is the property that says a task is done (default Status): a status or select whose option is one of done (default Done, case aside), or a checkbox, ticked; and date the date property of every database, or a list of them tried in order (default: a task's day is its Planned date, else its Due date, and a task with neither is not dated; a sprint's or a trip's is its first date property, by name).

Without a plan entry, show plan says so in one sentence and prints nothing else; a plan entry that is not this shape is one error naming the file and the key, exit 2. So is a mapping that names cities, people, places or queue: those are for where you are and from the queue (What it is not, at the end), which this version does not have. It is a separate file from policy/crossing.json, whose notion entry says what may leave for Notion (logbook export notion): the mapping says how to read what came from it, and nothing here writes either.

docs.title: The three parts
docs.text:
Each is read for one local day, in your timezone and under your day_start (where your day begins). A row is its latest standing line: a retracted line is not there, and only tier-1 lines are read (every sync notion line is tier 1).

  • The sprint: the sprints row whose date holds the day, with its dates.
  • Today's tasks: the open tasks (not done, not archived) whose date holds today (the day, or a range from Monday to Friday on its Wednesday), and the overdue ones (past their last day) in the current sprint, marked so. Between sprints no task is overdue, and the plan says so in one line under today's tasks, No sprint holds this day, so no overdue tasks are shown.; with no sprints database mapped, every overdue open task is, and nothing is said. In Notion's own date order, then by title; five at most, the rest as a count, and 3 more in Sprint 24 (or and 5 more, 3 of them in Sprint 24 when some are in no sprint). A task in the sprint is one that links to the sprint, or that the sprint links to.
  • The next trip: the trips row whose date starts soonest, today or after, as a countdown: today, tomorrow, in 37 days.

Today's tasks are numbered, 1 to 5 as listed: the numbers day sign --done, --tomorrow and --let-go take (What the record answers, below). A task you answered at the day's close is marked instead (done today, tomorrow, let go) and has no number, so it cannot be answered twice.

--json prints the same as one object: day, mapped (and said, the sentence, when nothing is mapped), tasks (rows, more, more_in_sprint, sprint, and said: that sentence between sprints, else null), sprint and trip (with days). Every row has its id, title, url, line (the sync notion line that holds its state) and, when it has one, date; a task its status, overdue, number (null once answered) and answered (outcome, line, seq of the answer, or null).

docs.title: Coverage
docs.text:
The record knows a row only from a line sync notion wrote of it. A first sync notion by hand reads every page; a source's first scheduled run reads only its last 14 days (the schedule), and LOGBOOK_NOTION_ROOTS reads only the pages under its roots. A task last edited before then, or outside the roots, is not in the record, and the plan cannot show it. show plan --coverage says, for each database you mapped, how many rows and lines the record holds and the day of its first line:

plan coverage: the record knows a row from a line `sync notion` wrote of it
  tasks    13 task rows · 15 lines · first line 2026-09-28
  sprints  2 sprint rows · 2 lines · first line 2026-09-27
  trips    no line yet
  …

If that is less than your plan holds, one logbook sync notion --since <an earlier RFC 3339 instant> reads every page edited since then, each as it is now. show plan never runs it; the decision, and how far back, are yours.

docs.title: What the record answers
docs.text:
At the close of a day you answer its tasks, by the numbers show plan DAY prints, when you sign:

logbook day sign 2026-10-21 --done 1,3 --tomorrow 4 --let-go 5
logbook day reflect 2026-10-21 --text "..." --sign --done 1

Each answer is one note/v1 line on the day, labelled task, written under the same hold of the writer lock as the signature and before it, and confirmed by it. Its text is the task's title, and its extra has three keys, for the agent that runs your task tool:

  • task: the Notion row's id (the page id, dashed, as sync notion writes it);
  • line: the id of the row's line show plan reported, the line that held the row as you saw it;
  • outcome: done (close the row as done), tomorrow (move its Planned date to the next day, set on a row that had none; its Due date is never touched) or let-go (close the row with a status of its own, Let go, beside Done; never the task tool's archive or trash).

The agent applies an answer only while the row is as that line saw it: its status, its Planned and its Due as the line holds them (RFC 0043 §9); a later change you made in the task tool wins. The record itself writes nothing to Notion, and nothing here runs the agent: the notes are lines of your day, so they cross with the signed day under the destination's entry in policy/crossing.json (hermes, notion) at their tier, tier 2, like every note (logbook export crossing --dry-run counts them under note). An unsigned day holds them back with the rest of the day.

A task given two answers, a number show plan does not list, and a task answered on the day already are refused in one sentence, and nothing is written. Signing the day again keeps the answers, as it keeps every line it confirmed, and never writes them twice. They are not the signature's dispositions: those name lines on the day's page, and a task's line is usually an earlier day's (the signed day).

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: Not a task manager: nothing is ticked, moved or written back. Not where you are (the city of the day's stays and the plan's rows for it) or from the queue (a queued note the day's browsing opened): RFC 0043 §9 has both, but they rest on the day's location and browsing lines, which are tier 2, so they wait for a later slice that holds them to the entry they are shown under. Not the Day page: the plan's place there, with done / tomorrow / let go beside each task, is the next part of this slice of RFC 0043 (§9), and the week page's time by project and the crossing preview before you sign are later ones.

docs.title: On paper
docs.text:
logbook year YYYY --html PATH --print and logbook trip ID --html PATH --print write a Year or a Trip as a Volume: one HTML document designed for A4 and US Letter, laid out with CSS paged media, that a browser turns into a PDF or sends to a printer. It is a reader (ADR 0013): a function of the record at its head, derived every time, never written back.

logbook year 2026 --html ~/2026.html --print                        # the year: a cover, contents, a spread a month
logbook trip trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-20 --html ~/week.html --print  # one trip: a spread a day; the id as `trips --json` gives it
logbook trip 2026-06-17 --html ~/week.html --print                  # the same trip, named by a day inside it

Without --print, --html writes the screen page the Year and the Trip already had: every table, the twelve picks, the route with its map. --print is the book: fewer facts, set for paper, with the keepers as hero photos. --print needs --html PATH; alone it exits 2 and says so.

docs.title: What is on the pages
docs.text:
1. The cover: the owner's name, the year or the trip's dates, the dates the record covers. The name is the first entry of names in policy/owner.json; without one, the label a resolution line gives one of the owner's addresses; without that, the first owner email of logbook.json. Nothing is guessed from an address.
  2. Contents: the months of the year with their days, nights away, flights and keepers, and the year's trips; or the days of the trip with the night each ended at, its flights, who was there and its keepers. A trip then has its route on a page of its own: the trip page's map (one path per leg, one mark per stay) and the stays under it.
  3. One spread per month of the year, or per day of the trip. The first page of a spread is the facts: the nights (home, away, in transit, aboard each asset), the places by nights numbered to the map, who was there — the people confirmed present by the with module, never a proposal from a face or an all-day entry — the flights, the sleep and the steps when the record has health lines, the keepers by lane. Beside them the map: the track of the span drawn as an inline SVG from the location lines themselves, the owner's and, while aboard, the asset's, with the places marked and numbered and a scale bar; an equirectangular projection, no tiles, nothing fetched. The second page is the keepers (RFC 0024) as hero photos sized to the page, memory first then art: one photo takes the page, two are stacked, three or four are two by two, more are two by three and run on to another page. A month or a day with no keepers has its facts page and no photo page, and lays out the same.
  4. The colophon: the head the record was read at.

Page numbers come from the page counter and sit in the bottom margin; the cover has none.

docs.title: The photos are the ones you starred
docs.text: A Volume picks no picture of its own. A span's photo page is its keepers (RFC 0024): the photos your library marked favourites (logbook derive keepers reads them in) and the photos you starred, logbook star PHOTO-LINE [--note TEXT] or the star beside a photo on the Day page of serve (the acts). A photo star is a keeper of lane memory; its note is printed under the photo as its caption. To choose the pictures of a year's book or a trip's, star them; to take one out, logbook unstar it. The Art album's keepers (lane art) are laid out too.

docs.title: Photos are referenced, never copied
docs.text:
A keeper points at a photo/v1 line, and the document points at that photo's pixels where they are: at the attachment under the record's attachments/ folder when the record stores them (a SPEC §1.1 reference under content or attachment in the photo line), else at the original path the library wrote in the line (path or original_path, at the payload's top or under extra, as the Immich adapter keeps it), as a file URL when that path is absolute. A photo the record only names gets a frame with its name in the same place, so the page lays out whether or not the file is there — the synthetic demo record names its photos and stores none, so its fixtures are all frames.

Two consequences. The document is one file, but the photos are not in it: move it to another machine and the frames are empty until the record comes too. And a browser shows what it can decode: Safari renders HEIC, Chromium and Firefox do not, so a library of HEIC originals prints with its frames empty in Chromium. An adapter that stores a JPEG rendition as the attachment prints everywhere.

docs.title: Making a PDF
docs.text:
The document is plain HTML with one inline stylesheet, no script and nothing loaded from anywhere, so any browser prints it. The stylesheet sets the page's own margins, so leave the browser's at their default (or none) and keep background graphics on, else the photo frames and the map's border are dropped.

In a browser. Open the file, print, choose Save as PDF, the paper (A4 or Letter — the layout fits both), and turn headers and footers off: the page numbers are the document's own. Chromium and Safari lay out @page margin boxes; Firefox does not yet, so a PDF from Firefox has no page numbers.

Headless Chromium, for a script or a cron job:

chromium --headless --no-pdf-header-footer --print-to-pdf=2026.pdf file:///Users/ines/2026.html

On a Mac the binary is /Applications/Google\ Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google\ Chrome; with Playwright installed, playwright ships one too. The paper is the browser's default (Letter in the US locale, A4 elsewhere); --print-to-pdf has no paper flag, so to pin one set PAGE_SIZE below, or print from the browser and choose it there.

docs.title: The paper, and retheming
docs.text:
The layout fits both papers: the text block is set for the narrower width (A4's 210 mm) and the shorter height (Letter's 279.4 mm), so one document prints on either without a cut or a reflow, and the sheets differ only in their outer margins. @page { size: auto } leaves the paper to the printer.

Every typographic constant — the margins, the text block, the six-column grid, the type scale (a major third from 10 pt), the faces (the system's: a document that fetches nothing carries no webfont), the ink, the map's box, the photo heights per layout — is in one module, logbook/contrib/print_layout.py, whose stylesheet() builds the one stylesheet from them. A designer retheming Volumes changes that file and touches no logic: the renderer (logbook/contrib/print_page.py) names classes and never a length.

docs.title: The poster
docs.text:
logbook year YYYY --poster [--sheet A2|A3] [--html PATH] writes the year on one sheet: twelve columns of thirty-one squares, a month a column and a day a row, each square in the ink of where the night was. Four inks, the four night tokens of print_layout.py — home (the quiet one: most nights), away, aboard an asset, in transit (no stay reached the minimum) — and a day the record has no night for shows the paper. Under the grid, one line: the countries of the year with their days, as rollup countries counts them. Nothing else is on the sheet: no name of a person, a place or an asset, no photo, no map, nothing fetched.

logbook year 2026 --poster --html ~/2026-poster.html              # A2, the default
logbook year 2026 --poster --sheet A3 > ~/2026-poster.html        # A3; without --html the document goes to stdout

The sheet is one inline SVG drawn in millimetres of A2 and scaled by the stylesheet to the sheet chosen: A3 is A2 at 1/√2, the A series keeps its proportions, so the two sheets are the same drawing and a print shop can make either. The page has no margin of its own, the drawing fills it; print with the browser's margins off. --poster and --print are two different documents; the command takes one. The reading is the Year's (year.window, one reading.read), each night classified from the reading's nights: in transit when no stay reached the minimum, aboard before away, home by the home region of places.json, else away. A year the record has no day in is an empty grid that says so in its kicker.

docs.title: The week on paper
docs.text:
logbook digest --paper [--week YYYY-Www | YYYY-MM-DD] [--html PATH | --json] writes the week as four pages of A4, set from the same typographic constants as the Year — the text block, the grid, the type scale, the ink — with the sheet pinned:

  1. The week: the seven days, Monday to Sunday, each with its one line — the line logbook days prints: the night after and the kilometres, then the flights, the stays with what attached, the people confirmed, the health triple and the usual sources with no line.
  2. With: the people confirmed present (never a proposed face, never an all-day attendee), the most days first, by name only, never a count beside a name; then the week's keepers (RFC 0024) by day, lane and name.
  3. Promises due: the open promises due within the week, as the promises reader proposes them (promises.extract, narrowed the way the digest narrows them): when, who, the sentence, where it was said.
  4. Read: what was read — the browse lines of the week, titles only, a title once a day, never the address and never the source.
logbook digest --paper --week 2026-W40 --html ~/w40.html   # an ISO week, Monday to Sunday
logbook digest --paper 2026-10-01 > ~/w40.html             # the week of a day; stdout without --html
logbook digest --paper                                      # this week, by the record's clock
logbook digest --paper --week 2026-W40 --json               # the paper's object, with the lines' ids

A week is an ISO week (2026-W01 begins on Monday 29 December 2025; 2026 has 53). The paper is composed from the readers and derives nothing of its own; nothing is written, not even the digest's question state, since the paper asks no question. The head the record was read at is in the note at the foot of the last page.

docs.title: The fixtures
docs.text: tests/fixtures/demo/print_year_2026.html and print_trip_2026-06-15.html are the documents the demo record of thirty days with seed 7 gives for 2026 and for its yacht week, pinned byte for byte by tests/test_print_page.py, which also checks every document structurally — every tag closed in order, one stylesheet, no script, no link, every src an img's, every img with alt, nothing from the network — and that a day with no photos still lays out. Beside them, poster_year_2026_A2.html and poster_year_2026_A3.html are the same record's poster on both sheets and paper_week_2026-W25.html its yacht week on paper, checked structurally by tests/test_year_poster.py and tests/test_week_paper.py (a square a day in one of the five classes, the four tokens in the legend, no name on the sheet; four pages, seven days, titles and never an address). After a change to a renderer or the layout that is meant, uv run python scripts/make_print_fixtures.py writes them all again. Open any fixture in a browser to see the page; nothing in them is real.

docs.title: Promises
docs.text:
logbook promises [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--mine | --theirs] [--source KIND] [--open] [--all] [--judge] [--json] reads the record's own words for two things: what you said you would do, and what other people asked you to do. "I'll send you the photos by Friday", "ich melde mich bis Montag", "mach ich" in a mail or a message you sent, in your turn of a meeting, in a note; "can you send me the berth number", "kannst du mir die Liste schicken", "let me know by Thursday" in a mail or a message you received, in someone else's turn. It looks in every mail/v1 line (RFC 0015), every message/v1 line (RFC 0008: iMessage, WhatsApp, whatever the adapters import), every transcript/v1 line (RFC 0004) whose text is in the attachment store and every note/v1 line (RFC 0010). The rules find every sentence that carries a cue, by regular expressions alone, and the direction comes from who wrote the line, never from the words. That is the whole reader by default: no model runs, nothing leaves the machine. The judge, a local instruct model, is an opt-in second reading of your own commitments (--judge), as before. What the command prints are proposals, never facts. A sentence that reads like a promise is one until you say so; the command's job is to make sure you see it.

logbook promises                        # I promised / I was asked, by rules, oldest first
logbook promises --mine                 # only what you promised
logbook promises --theirs               # only what you were asked
logbook promises --source mail          # only the mail; `message`, `transcript`, `note`; comma-separate or repeat
logbook promises --since 2026-06-08     # from that local day on
logbook promises --open                 # without the ones you have marked done
logbook promises --all                  # every candidate: others' commitments, unresolved speakers, what the judge set aside
logbook promises --json                 # the report as one JSON object, every proposal with its line id
logbook promises done 7c1d2e3f4a5b6c7d  # it was kept: one task/v1 line, status done; --open hides it
logbook promises done 7c1d… --note "photos came Thursday"
logbook day sign 2026-06-11 --confirm 019e…   # the line a row names: the day's signature confirms it (RFC 0034)
logbook promises --judge                # read your commitments with a local model first, then list

docs.title: The two sections
docs.text:
3 promises proposed: 2 you made, 1 asked of you; read by rules, not facts; confirm one with `logbook promises done <id>` or `logbook day sign DAY --confirm <line>`
I promised
  2026-06-08  09:10  to Ola Nordmann   “I'll send the mooring photos by Friday.”  due 2026-06-12? (by Friday)  3b9e5d0f2a71c846  line 019e…-…
  2026-06-11  14:00  to Ola Nordmann   “I will book the crane for next week.”  due 2026-06-15? (next week)  a1f0…  line 019e…-…
I was asked
  2026-06-10  09:20  by Kari Nordmann  “Kannst du mir die Flugnummer schicken?”  08c4…  line 019e…-…

I promised is every commitment cue in a line you wrote: a mail whose sender is one of your addresses, a message with from_me, your turn of a transcript, a note. I was asked is every request cue in a line a person wrote you: a person's mail, a message from a person, another's turn (who wrote it). A request cue in your own words ("can you send me the invoice?" in a mail you sent) is you asking, and is not proposed; a commitment cue in someone else's words ("I'll send you the photos" from Ola) is theirs, and --all lists it in a third section with the candidates nobody resolves and the ones the judge set aside. The order inside a section is the day's.

Each row is:

  • The day and time of the line: a mail's Date, a message's own stamp, a transcript's start, a note's writing time, in the record's zone. A transcript's turns carry no time of their own, so every promise in a meeting is on the meeting's hour.
  • The counterpart, to whom you promised or by whom you were asked: the person the record resolves (RFC 0006) behind the address, the number or the name, else the name the source wrote, else the address or number itself. In a mail you sent it is the first recipient who is not you; in a message you sent in a direct chat it is the one person the chat's id names (a WhatsApp JID is a phone number, iMessage names a chat by the address) or the chat's name; in a group chat the group's name; in your turn of a transcript the other participant; a note has none and says (note).
  • The sentence as written, whitespace collapsed, never paraphrased.
  • The due hint when the sentence carries a date phrase, with a ? because it is a reading of the words, not a deadline anyone agreed. It is resolved against the day the sentence was said: a weekday is the next one strictly after that day (by Friday on a Thursday is tomorrow; on a Friday it is next week's); next week is its Monday; this week and by the end of the week the Friday on or after the day; tomorrow, morgen, übermorgen, tonight, heute Abend, in two weeks, in drei Tagen, next month; a month and a day (by June 20, 20 June, `bis
  • Juni,bis zum 20.6.) the next such date;the 5thandam 5.` the next fifth.
  • The judgement, when the judge has read it (below).
  • done when you closed it; --open leaves those out.
  • kept, missed on 2026-06-14, dropped, carried is what the signed day of the line the promise was read in says became of it (the signed day, RFC 0034 amendment 1): kept and dropped close the promise, missed closes and flags it, carried leaves it open; --open leaves the first three out. A request is a line's too: a kept request is one you did.
  • The proposal's id: a digest of the origin line's id and the quoted sentence, case and whitespace aside, sixteen hex characters. The same sentence in the same line has the same id however often the command runs, and whichever extractor found it. promises done takes it.
  • The line it was read in, by its id. logbook day sign DAY --confirm <id> takes it (RFC 0034, signed-day): a signed day confirms the lines you name, so the mail or the message that carries the promise can be among the day's confirmed facts while the promise itself stays a proposal.

docs.title: Who wrote it
docs.text:
Direction is never read from the words. A mail is yours when its from is one of your addresses: owner_emails in logbook.json, the emails of policy/owner.json, or any address a resolution line gives your owner_id; when none of those match but the import marked it sent (it knew the mailbox), that counts too. A message is yours when the adapter stored from_me. A transcript's turn is yours when its speaker resolves to you: the source's label (Ola Nordmann: in Markdown, <v Ola Nordmann> in WebVTT, Granola's speaker.name) matched to the line's participants and their email, phone or provider id to a person, me and your own names from policy/owner.json as you. A transcript whose voices were separated is read voice by voice first, through its spans file: a sentence is the voice's that spoke it, yours when the voice is yours (your microphone, or a voice you named as you), a guest's (owed to you) when you named it someone else, as spoken (S2) while it is not yet named (who they are). A note is yours, except for text that carries its own labels (Speaker 2:, or a name the record knows), which belongs to that speaker. A request from a diarizer's Speaker A, who is not you, is counted as asked of you; a commitment from one is nobody's and shows under --all.

A request counts only when a person wrote it. A mail asks something of you when it is a person's mail (people's mail, RFC 0045): its sender resolves to a person, is no no-reply address, no agent's, and not let go. A message asks something of you when its sender resolves to a person and it is no conversation with an agent. A newsletter's "please let us know", a shop's "please confirm", a notification, a company's mail and a message from a number nobody is named by ask you nothing and are not proposed. To have a sender's requests counted, resolve the address or the number to a person (people); the next reading counts them. Read through tiers (a page's, a crossing's), only the resolutions at those tiers name a person, so a request whose sender only a higher resolution names is not proposed there. A commitment cue in the same lines is read as before.

An agent's words are nobody's (your own agents). A message one of your bots wrote (extra.machine), a turn of a transcript's participant marked machine (the assistant of a Claude Code session or of a conversation in the Claude apps) and a message you forwarded (extra.forwarded, someone else's words) are never read, and are counted under skipped (messages_by_an_agent, forwarded_messages). A bot's "I'll have it ready by Friday" is not a promise, and its "can you send me the tide table?" is not a request of you; your own reply to it is yours, as any message you sent. A line of an agent's turn inside your own turn (assistant: …, or under the agent's own name, Claude: …, pasted back) is the agent's and is dropped too, with the lines after it in that turn up to the next speaker's label. A home video's soundtrack (Videos) is nobody's word to you now, and is counted under video_soundtracks.

A mail body is read up to the first reply header (On … wrote:, Am … schrieb …:, -----Original Message-----, From:) or signature delimiter (--), and lines that begin with > are left out, so a reply that quotes your promise never proposes it again. A message is read whole; a transcript is read by its media type as before (WebVTT and SRT cues, Granola's JSON segments, Speaker: text prose). A transcript whose text is not in the store, and a mail or a message with no text, is counted and skipped, never a traceback. A retracted line, and one a later line supersedes, is not read.

docs.title: The cues
docs.text:
A sentence is proposed when it carries one of these. Only the first cue in a sentence counts, and it decides the class. A commitment cue is ignored when it is negated right after (I will not, I'll never, ich werde nicht, mach ich nicht) or the sentence ends in a question mark; a request cue is read in a question or not, since most requests are questions.

Class English German future I'll, I will, I shall, I'm going to, we'll, we will, we're going to, I promise; at the head of a sentence or after ok, sure, yes: will do, on it, consider it done, leave it with me, count on me ich werde, ich schicke, ich sende, ich melde mich, ich kümmere mich, ich rufe, ich bringe, ich liefere, ich erledige, ich besorge, ich übernehme, ich buche, ich bestelle, ich bezahle, ich prüfe, ich organisiere, ich hole, ich mache, ich verspreche, ich sage Bescheid, the same with wir, and the verb first: mach ich, schick ich dir, melde ich mich, erledige ich, kümmere ich mich; versprochen, wird gemacht, wird erledigt, geht klar obligation I need to, I have to, I must, I've got to, I ought to, and with we ich muss, wir müssen offer let me (not let me know), I can send, I can bring, I can check, I can call, I can book, I can pay, I can fix, I can sort, I can look, I can do that deadline a sentence of at most eight words that is a date phrase beginning by, before, until: By Friday., Photos by Friday. the same with bis, spätestens: Bis Freitag, versprochen. request can you, could you, would you, will you (not can you believe, imagine, will you be, would you like), would you mind, any chance you could, are you able to; please with a verb of doing (please send, please confirm, please let me know, please have a look); at the head of a sentence: send me, bring me, call me, forward me, remind me, tell me, show me, give me, get back to me; let me know, don't forget to, make sure you, remember to, I need you to, I'd appreciate it if you, it would be great if you, can I have, could we get, you need to, you have to, you must kannst du, könntest du, würdest du, können Sie, könnten Sie, würden Sie, magst du (not kannst du dir vorstellen, glauben, erinnern), wärst du so nett, bist du so lieb; bitte with a verb (bitte schick, bitte bestätige, bitte überweise); at the head of a sentence: schick mir, bring mir, ruf mich, zeig mir, schreib mir, hol mir, leih mir; schicken Sie mir, rufen Sie mich; sag mir Bescheid, gib Bescheid, melde dich, vergiss nicht, denk dran, ich brauche von dir, wir bitten um, um Rückmeldung, schau mal, mach mal, du musst, Sie müssen

Only the first person counts for a commitment: he will send, they'll get back and will you propose nothing of that class. The rules are plain regular expressions over sentences (cut at a full stop, ! or ? that does not follow a digit, and at every line break); they will miss a promise phrased another way ("expect the draft tomorrow morning") and propose a sentence that is none ("bis Freitag dann!" as a farewell), which is why nothing here is a fact until you close it. The list above is the whole list (promises._CUES, promises._ASKS); a cue you miss is a pull request with a sentence in the recall test.

How well it reads. tests/test_promises_wider_net.py holds a synthetic fortnight of the Oslo persona (tests/fixtures/promises/wider-net.json): 24 planted commitments and 12 planted requests across mail, iMessage, WhatsApp and one transcript, among 60 distractor lines (others' promises, your own questions, negations, quoted replies, newsletters, chit-chat). The test asserts recall of at least 20 of 24 and 10 of 12 and precision of at least 0.8, and prints the numbers; the rules read 22 of 24, 10 of 12, at precision 0.97. Three misses are the three sentences planted with no cue on purpose; the fourth is the marina's "please confirm your crane booking", from an address the fixture names nobody behind, so no person's request (who wrote it); the one false proposal is the farewell.

docs.title: The JSON
docs.text: Under --json the report is one object: since, open_only, mine_only, theirs_only, sources (the kinds read, in mail, message, transcript, note order), all, threshold (0.6), extractor (name, version, and languages for the rules), judge (what a --judge run just did; null when none ran), unjudged (how many commitments have no verdict yet), proposals and skipped. Each proposal carries id, status (open or done), closed_by (the task line's id), disposition (value, day and line, the signed-day line's, when the standing signature of its day disposed of the line it was read in; null otherwise), day, at, line (the origin, for day sign --confirm), seq, kind (mail, message, transcript or note), source (the adapter), title (a transcript's or a note's title, a mail's subject), speaker (label, spoken, person, owner, or null), role (promise when you made it, request when you were asked, theirs when a resolved person made it, null when nobody is behind the label), counterpart, direction (owed_by_owner for a promise and a request, owed_to_owner for theirs, null otherwise), certainty (always inferred), language, cue, class, quote, due (phrase and date, or null) and judgement (below, or null). The fields are this reader's own; commitment/v1 (RFC 0007), which they once mirrored, was withdrawn by RFC 0031. The MCP tool promises returns the same proposals (mcp).

docs.title: The judge
docs.text:
--judge reads every commitment the rules found that has no verdict yet, oldest first, with a local instruct model, and prints one progress line per candidate on stderr. A request is never judged: the judge's question is whether a sentence is a commitment, and a request is not one. The model sees the candidate sentence marked among the two sentences before and after it in the same line, across turns, each with who said it as the report names them (you, Ola Nordmann, Speaker A); the kind of line, its title or subject and the counterpart; the day; your name as the record resolves it; and the names the record resolves in that line. It answers one JSON object, sampled at temperature 0, so the same candidate gets the same verdict from the same model:

Field What is_commitment whether the sentence is a specific thing a specific person said they will or must do; "we'll see", "I'll have a look", "let me think" and reports of what someone else will do are not by who made it: owner, a name from the list, or unknown to whom it binds them to: owner, a name, or unknown what the commitment in one line, in the speaker's own words shortened due YYYY-MM-DD, resolved against the day it was said, or null when the words name no day confidence 0 to 1

A judged candidate stays in its section when the verdict is a commitment at confidence 0.6 or above (promises.THRESHOLD) and is set aside otherwise; --all lists what was set aside, with the verdict. A judged row carries the verdict after the due hint: the confidence, by <name> when it is not the speaker, to <name> when known, and no 0.95 for a judged non-commitment. The due hint is the verdict's day when it gave one, else the rules' reading with its phrase. The quote stays the sentence as written, since the id is a digest of it.

judged 10 candidates with mlx-lm (mlx-community/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-4bit)
2 promises proposed: 2 you made, 0 asked of you; read by rules, not facts; 10 judged (a commitment at confidence 0.6 or above stays); confirm one with `logbook promises done <id>` or `logbook day sign DAY --confirm <line>`
I promised
  2026-06-08  09:10  to Ola Nordmann  “I'll send the mooring photos by Friday.”  due 2026-06-12?  0.92 to Ola Nordmann  3b9e5d0f2a71c846  line 019e…-…
  2026-06-11  14:00  to Ola Nordmann  “I will book the crane for next week.”  due 2026-06-15? (next week)  0.8 to Ola Nordmann  a1f0…  line 019e…-…
I was asked
  none

The verdicts are kept in the record, outside the chain, in policy/promises-cache.json: {"version": 1, "judgements": {"<candidate id>": {"is_commitment", "by", "to", "what", "due", "confidence", "engine", "model", "judged_at"}}}, the ids sorted. A candidate is judged once, however often the command runs and whatever --model is set later; the model that read it is in its entry. The file is rewritten after every verdict, so an interrupted run keeps what it did and the next carries on; --limit N judges at most N candidates in one run. An answer with no whole verdict in it is counted, not kept, and the next --judge tries that candidate again. Delete an entry, or the file, to have a candidate judged afresh.

The engine is mlx-lm, Apple's MLX runner for language models, with mlx-community/Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-4bit by default (judge.DEFAULT_MODEL); --model names any instruct model the hub serves in MLX format. It needs the extra: uv pip install 'openlogbook[judge]', Apple silicon only; without it --judge stops with the message that says so, and everything else works. It is imported only when --judge runs, and while it runs the hub is told it is offline (HF_HUB_OFFLINE), so no socket is opened for any reason. A model not yet on the machine stops the command naming the one flag that fetches it, --fetch-model, which downloads the model before the first candidate and nothing else, ever. There is no cloud model and there will not be one: a record's words are read on the record's machine.

The judge is a second reading of the rules' candidates, never a third extractor: it changes neither a proposal, nor its id, nor what done writes, and it writes nothing to the chain.

docs.title: Closing one: promises done <id>
docs.text:
done appends one task/v1 line (RFC 0016) and nothing else: source manual, kind task, tier 2, at now. Its payload is the sentence as title, status done, the due hint as due when there was one, completed_at, list promises, your --note as notes, and under extra the proposal's promise id, its origin line, the speaker and the extractor that proposed it, so a reader can trace the close back to the words. raw_id is promise:<id>@<time>, the snapshot form the profile asks for. Nothing is edited: the mail, the message, the transcript and the note stay as they were, and the close is a line beside them. A request closes the same way: you were asked, you did it, one task line says so.

--open hides a proposal whose latest standing task line (by extra.promise) has status done or cancelled, and one whose day's standing signature kept, missed or dropped the line it was read in (a carried one is still open, and done closes it as any other). done on a proposal already closed, by a task line or by the signed day, writes nothing and says so; an id the record does not propose is refused with status 2. A proposal is yours to close only: the command never closes one on its own, and nothing it reads can close another.

Why task/v1? commitment/v1 and commitment-close/v1 (RFC 0007) were the lines a confirmed promise and its keeping would have become. Nothing ever wrote or read them, and RFC 0031 withdrew them. The one act the owner takes is "that was done", and RFC 0016's task is the line that says exactly that with a title and a status.

docs.title: Replacing the rules with a model
docs.text: The command does not know the rules. promises.extract(lb, since, extractor=RULES, sources=...) takes any object with a name, a version and __call__(text) -> list[Match], where a Match is the quoted sentence, the cue, the class (future, obligation, offer, deadline or request), the language, the date phrase and, when the extractor resolved it itself, the due day. The extractor sees text and returns sentences; the command owns the record, who wrote each line, the counterparts, the days and the closes, and never lets an extractor write. A local model that reads a text and returns the same shape slots in with no change to the report, the ids (a digest of line and sentence, so a model quoting the same sentence agrees with the rules) or done, whose task lines record which extractor proposed what.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It does not read the free-text notes files (notes/<YYYY>/<date>.md) or calendar entries. It does not know whether a promise was kept: that is logbook promises tasks --propose-done's question (tasks), asked of the mail, the calendar and the transactions. The counterpart is whom the line was with, not whom a promise binds in a group: a promise in a group chat is to the group, and a request in one may have been to everyone. It does not write commitments, retract anything, or run a model you did not ask for.

docs.title: Receipts as payments
docs.text:
logbook review receipts [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--json] proposes the receipt mails the record already holds as payments, and you confirm each one. It is the money bridge of RFC 0043 §12: until a payment source (your bank's or card's app, Google Wallet, Splitwise) covers your days, a receipt mail is the best evidence of a payment the record has. The ledger stays the truth. A receipt is only a proposal, and nothing is written until you accept it.

logbook review receipts                          # the receipts of the last 90 days, numbered
logbook review receipts --since 2026-09-01       # from a given day
logbook review receipts --since 2026-09-01 --json
logbook review receipts --accept 1,3             # each one becomes a payment (tier 3)
logbook review receipts --reject 2               # not a payment, never proposed again

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
5 receipts proposed · 1 already in the record · 0 accepted · 0 not a payment · since 2026-09-01 · tier 3
  1  2026-09-03  Fjordkaffe  CHF -1 234.50  0.80
       fjordkaffe.example.org · an order or no-reply address · a total · the subject says so
  2  2026-09-05  Bokhylla  EUR -12.90  0.80
       bokhylla.example.org · an order or no-reply address · a total · the subject says so
  3  2026-09-08  Seilloftet AS  NOK -1 840.00  0.95
       seilloftet.example.org · an order or no-reply address · org in the Manifest · a total · the subject says so
  4  2026-09-10  Chartroom  USD -12.90  0.80
       chartroom.example.org · an order or no-reply address · the subject's amount · the subject says so · subject only: the line keeps no body
  5  2026-09-14  Bokhylla  EUR +12.90  refund  0.80
       bokhylla.example.org · an order or no-reply address · a total · the subject says so · a refund
  —  2026-09-16  Fjordkiosk  NOK -45.00  already in the record: google-takeout #10
--accept N,N writes each as a payment; --reject N writes that it is not one; both tier 3

Each proposal has a number, the day and the merchant. It shows the amount from your side, as the ledger signs it (a purchase is negative, a refund positive), and a confidence between 0 and 1. The line below gives the merchant's domain and the reasons. The queue never shows a sender's address: not in its rows, not in its JSON (domain there too), and a display name that is itself an address is no name. Numbers count from 1 in time order and belong to this listing: after an accept or a reject, list again before giving more numbers. review with no kind lists this queue with the others. Everything this queue shows is tier 3.

docs.title: What it reads
docs.text:
It reads only the record's mail/v1 lines (RFC 0015), from --since (default: 90 days ago) to today. Nothing is looked up and no model is asked. A mail line keeps:

  • from, the address and the display name as the message gave them;
  • subject, when the message has one;
  • body, when the road kept one: the text/plain part, else the HTML stripped to text, at most 64 KB. The mbox import, sync mail (IMAP) and sync gmail all keep it.

The subject is always read. The body is read only when the line keeps one, and a proposal read from the subject alone says so. Attachments are never opened.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
A mail is a receipt candidate when all of these hold:

  1. You received it (a mail you sent is never a receipt).
  2. Its sender is a merchant. That means three things:
  3. The sender is not a person the record names: an address a resolution/v1 line resolves to a person is never a merchant, and neither is any of your own addresses.
  4. The address is an order or no-reply address (orders@, orders.eu@, ordre@, no-reply@, no_reply@, auto-confirm@, receipts@, kvittering@, billing@ …), or its domain is bound to an org in the Manifest.
  5. An org in the Manifest on the domain raises the confidence and gives the merchant its name. Otherwise the merchant is the display name without the generic words (Orders, No-Reply), else the first label of the sender's domain.
  6. Its text carries an order or receipt marker: receipt, your order, order confirmation, invoice, kvittering, ordrebekreftelse, Quittung, Rechnung, reçu, facture and the like, each as a word of its own (recurring holds no reçu). A refund word (refund, refusjon, Rückerstattung, remboursement) counts too. A price alone is not a receipt: a newsletter that says from CHF 14.90 is never proposed.
  7. Its text carries an amount with a currency, in the common forms: CHF 1'234.50, € 12,90, 12,90 €, $12.90, US$ 1,250.00, NOK 1 840, 1.234,50 EUR, 99.- CHF. kr on its own names three currencies, so it is not taken as a currency, the same rule the Google Wallet reader follows. A number glued to a word (XY1234), one after another number and a space (07700 900123) and one that a code then a number follow (Ordre 5531 NOK 1 840, 2026-09 EUR 12.90) is not the amount: the code goes with the number after it.

Which amount. A total wins over the line items. An amount is a total when the words before it on its line (or the line above, when it stands alone) say total, sum, å betale, amount paid and not subtotal, VAT, MwSt, shipping, discount or savings. Total incl. VAT and Sum inkl. mva are totals. The largest total wins. In Total EUR 12.90 (approx. NOK 150.00), only the first amount has Total before it. With no total, the amount in the subject is used. Failing that, the one amount the text names. Failing that, the largest amount, with less confidence.

A refund is money coming in. The mail is a refund when its subject says so, or the words before the chosen amount do (Refund total), or a minus sign is on the amount. A footer that mentions refunds (non-refundable, refund policy, refunds within 30 days) does not make a receipt a refund.

docs.title: What is written, and only when you say
docs.text:
• --accept N,N writes one transaction/v1 line per receipt, through the one writer every line goes through (Logbook.append). The line is tier 3, the tier money always has (RFC 0021).
  • source and provider are receipts; at is the time of the mail.
  • amount, currency and merchant are what the queue showed.
  • raw_id and extra.from are the mail line's id; extra.confidence is the confidence; extra.refund is set for a refund.
  • A mail is never written twice. Under the writer lock, each mail is checked once more for a standing receipt's line before anything is written. If one has appeared since the listing, nothing is written and the queue says so. A retracted line holds nothing, so a mail whose receipt line you retracted can be accepted again.
  • One payment, one line, within a batch too. Two mails of one payment (an order and its confirmation on the same day) are both proposed while neither is in the record. Accepted together, the first is written; the second, of the same merchant, day, currency and amount, is refused and counted (1 duplicate refused; in the JSON, verdict: "duplicate", line: null and same_as the number written in its place). Listed again, it is already in the record.
  • --reject N writes one receipt-review/v1 line, kind receipt-review, labelled not-a-payment, with extra.from the mail line's id and the words not a payment: no amount, no currency and no merchant. It is tier 3, like the payments. That mail is never proposed again, unless you retract the line.
  • Why not a note: a note/v1 is tier 2 whoever writes it (RFC 0010). The no is a line of its own, as a scene's no is (scene-review/v1, RFC 0040 §5), and a receipt is none of the five kinds of thing entity-review/v1 answers for.
  • Every number is checked before the first line is written. --name and --all-above are refused: a receipt is accepted by its number.

docs.title: Already in the record
docs.text: Some receipts are already paid in the record: another standing transaction/v1 line has the same currency and amount (the same sign), falls within two days of the mail, and names the same merchant (one name contains the other once case, spaces and punctuation are removed: Fjordkiosk and FJORDKIOSK AS). Such a receipt is shown as already in the record, with the line that holds it. It gets no number and is never written.

docs.title: When the ledger delivers it later
docs.text:
You may accept a receipt before your payment source is imported. When that source later delivers the same payment, both lines stand for one payment. The queue lists the pair as covered:

  —  2026-09-03  Fjordkaffe  CHF -1 234.50  receipt #12 is covered by google-takeout #14, which wins: logbook repair retract 12 "covered by google-takeout #14"

The payment source's line wins, and it is counted once already, before you do anything: every reader that sums the ledger (the Day's spend, rollup ledger, rollup money, a trip's spend, an org's money, the money slot) pairs a receipt's line with the payment source's line that holds the same payment, by the rule above (the currency, the signed amount, within two days, the merchant), and counts the source's line alone, the receipt named as its evidence (1 with its receipt on the Day). One source line holds one receipt: two dinners of one price are two payments until the source has delivered both.

The receipt's line is still the one to take back, and the row prints the command that does it: logbook repair retract SEQ, a retraction appended through the same writer. A retracted line is out of every reader, the ledger included. The queue writes nothing on its own: you run the command.

Why not a superseding line? The record's rule (SPEC §3) puts a line that names another in payload.supersedes in its place. Only the payment source's own line could do that, and an adapter does not know the receipt's id. A new line written here to supersede the receipt would be a second copy of the source's payment. The pairing is a reader's rule of the reference (logbook.core.ledger.receipts_held); writing it into RFC 0021, so that a second implementation pairs the lines the same way, is an open proposal.

docs.title: Who sees it
docs.text: The queue's output is tier 3, and so is every line --accept writes. A reader held to tiers 1 and 2 (an export at the crossing ceiling, a page or a tool that does not carry money) sees no proposal, no amount, no accepted line and no not-a-payment line: everything this writes is tier 3.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: The rules run in time linear in the text: a 64 KB body is read in milliseconds, whatever it holds. One indexed read of the window's mail lines, which are read once and checked by the rules in memory. On a record of five million lines with half a million mails, the default 90 days is a few thousand mails; --since far back reads every mail of the span. The transactions from two days before --since on, and every receipt's own line, are read once for the dedupe. The not-a-payment lines come through the index's kind and source columns. No other line is read.

docs.title: When verify fails
docs.text:
logbook verify reads the files alone and says one of a few things. Each has one answer; none of them is "edit a month file". The chain is the record, so every repair below moves lines, appends lines or brings logbook.json forward, and never rewrites a line in place. The two commands that give every line a new hash, repair migrate and key seal --all, verify the whole record first, every hash under the rule it was written with and every link, and refuse with the first failing line and its id when it does not, so a record in this table is put right before it is migrated or sealed and never by being migrated or sealed.

verify says What happened What to run logbook.json says seq=N …, files say seq=N+k … and nothing else a crash between the files and logbook.json (SPEC §3, write order): the files are ahead, every line past seq is a chained tail. Every writer refuses until it is mended, naming this command logbook repair tail --dry-run, then logbook repair tail (below). Never repair index and append: that wrote a second line of the same seq … line n: the file ends inside this line (cut short) a crash tore the last line of a month file; the lines before it are whole and verify reports their head restore that month file from the last backup, or cut the torn line and bring logbook.json to the head verify printed; repair fork does not mend a torn file seq N expected N+1 and prev does not match previous hash on every second line from one seq two chains fork at one head (#234): a long writer wrote its batch chained from a head another writer had already moved past logbook repair fork, then logbook repair fork --apply created as logbook/0.1 … the record was hashed by the rule before the RFC 8785 fix logbook repair migrate hash does not recompute on one line a byte of a line changed on disk, or was changed restore from backup; the chain says which line line n: at '…' is not an RFC 3339 instant (SPEC §2), or end, recorded_at the line carries a timestamp that names no instant (not-a-dateZ, 2026-02-30T07:30:00Z): a line made by hand or by another tool, or one an earlier release appended, which took any stamp ending in Z. The index cannot place it either the stamp is inside the line's hash and no command edits a line: restore the record from the last backup taken before that line, then sync again (sync skips what the record already has) and add back by hand what came after line n: attachments/<sha256> holds bytes that hash to …, not its name (SPEC §1.1) the file the line names changed on disk: the line is right, the store is not restore that one file from a backup; logbook backup --verify hashes a snapshot's files the same way line n: attachments/<sha256> opens to bytes that do not hash to its name (SPEC §1.1) a sealed file was replaced by one that opens with your identity and holds other bytes, which anyone with your recipients can make; only the identity tells the two apart restore that file from a backup, and find what wrote it line n: attachments/<sha256> does not open with this identity: … a sealed file sealed to other recipients, or damaged restore that file from a backup; logbook key show names the recipients the record seals to

A file the lines name that the store does not hold is not in this table: verify lists it and stays valid (below).

docs.title: The files ahead of logbook.json
docs.text:
The shape: a writer appends a line to its month file, flushes and fsyncs it, and the process is gone before logbook.json is replaced (a kill, a power cut, a crash: the write order of SPEC §3 puts the line on disk first, so this is the shape a crash leaves once the line is whole; the row below it is the shape when it is not). The files end at seq N+1, logbook.json says N, and verify says exactly that and nothing else. A logbook.json behind by one sync batch is the same shape: append_many writes a whole batch, fsyncs each month file, then logbook.json.

Until logbook.json is brought forward, every writer refuses, in one sentence that names this command, and writes nothing:

add: the files are ahead of logbook.json: they end at seq 2 head 4dc18fde900d…, logbook.json says seq 1 head 9c1b3e2a7f04… (a crash between a line and logbook.json, SPEC §3); nothing was written: run `logbook repair tail`

A writer that went ahead would chain its line from the head logbook.json names, which the files are already past, and the record would hold two lines of one seq: a fork, repair fork's case, made from a crash that had left a clean tail. That is what the procedure this page gave before (repair index, then append) did: the rebuilt index held the tail under a logbook.json that did not, the next append wrote a second seq N+1 and the index refused it, after the file had taken it.

logbook repair tail --dry-run    # the tail, listed; writes nothing
logbook repair tail              # the repair

The dry run reads every line past the seq logbook.json names, in seq order, and checks each as verify checks it from that head: the envelope, its seq, its prev against the line before (the head itself for the first), its hash, its timestamps, the sealed envelope rule, and a sealed line opened against its digest when the identity is here. It lists each line by seq, file, line number and hash, never its contents, and says what the repair would set logbook.json to:

logbook.json says seq=1 head=9c1b3e2a7f04…; the files hold 1 line past it, each verified (envelope, seq, prev, hash):
  seq 2  logbook/2026/09.jsonl line 2  hash 4dc18fde900d…
would set logbook.json to seq=2 head=4dc18fde900d…, and extend the index by 1 line
nothing written — run without --dry-run to repair

The repair does the same, and only when every line passes sets logbook.json to the last line's seq and head, then brings the index along: extended by those lines when it is current with the old logbook.json, built again from the files when it is there and stale (or was built while the files were ahead, as repair index on this record builds it, so it holds the tail already), left to the next reader when there is none. The order is SPEC §3's own, the files first, logbook.json second, the index last, so a crash inside the repair leaves the same shape it was mending, never logbook.json or the index ahead of the files. It ends with verify on the chain and prints its verdict. No month file is touched; nothing is rewritten.

It refuses, and changes nothing, when a line past the head does not verify (the first failing line, as verify names it, then nothing was changed: a hash that does not recompute, a prev that is not the line before, a second line of one seq, a month file cut inside its last line); when the files end before logbook.json (no crash leaves that; month files restored from an older backup under a newer logbook.json do, and the answer is the backup, not a rewind); and when the files end at the seq logbook.json names under another head, which is not a lag (verify says what it is). A tail that does not verify is a torn or changed line and the rows for those are above. The writer lock is held throughout, so a sync that is running is waited for, or refused under --no-wait.

docs.title: Two chains forked at one head
docs.text:
The shape: a sync that walked a source for two hours read the head when it started. Meanwhile another command appended a batch, correctly chained from that head. When the long sync wrote its own batch it chained it from the head it had read, into the month files, before the index refused it (UNIQUE constraint failed: lines.seq). The files now hold two chains from one head; the index, which never took the second batch, still describes the first; logbook.json names the second's head.

logbook repair fork            # the diagnosis; writes nothing
logbook repair fork --apply    # the repair

The diagnosis walks every line of every month file, links the lines into chains by prev, and prints what it found, counts and hashes only, never a line's contents:

fork at seq 4803133, head da9813c3cf40…: 2 chains continue from it
  main chain: 4,804,871 lines, seq 1–4804871, head 4dc18fde900da55538fbd134e48652282d044bc2ec8c28ac0573fee15506b599; the index agrees (its head is on it)
  orphan chain: 4,309 lines, seq 4803134–4807442, head e4b3b64c294d1f0a7c3e9b2d8f6a4c1e0b5d7f9a3c2e8d6b4f1a0c9e7d5b3a2f, forked at seq 4803133; sources: immich 4,309; files: logbook/2026/09.jsonl, logbook/2026/10.jsonl
logbook.json says seq=4807442 head=e4b3b64c294d…; the main chain ends at seq=4804871 head=4dc18fde900d…
nothing written — run with --apply to repair

Which chain is the record is decided in this order: the chain the index agrees with (the index records the head it was built at; the chain that head is on); with no index, or one built before the fork, the longer chain; and when two chains are equally long and the index cannot say, no one: the diagnosis says cannot tell which chain is the record and --apply refuses. Every other chain is an orphan. Look at the orphan's sources and seq range before applying: it should be the batch you know went wrong.

When you know which chain is the record, say so: --keep-head <head> takes the full head of the chain to keep, as the dry run prints it for every chain, or a unique prefix of eight characters at least, and overrides both rules; a head no chain ends in is refused. Without an index the longer chain is only a guess, and the dry run says in one sentence that --keep-head is the safer choice: in the incident above the stray batch was the longer chain, and only the index knew better.

logbook repair fork --keep-head 4dc18fde900da55538fbd134e48652282d044bc2ec8c28ac0573fee15506b599
logbook repair fork --keep-head 4dc18fde900d --apply

--apply does, in this order:

  1. copies every orphan line, in seq order, to repair/<UTC stamp>-removed.jsonl inside the record folder, and writes repair/<UTC stamp>-report.json with everything the diagnosis printed. Nothing is deleted; the lines leave the chain and stay in the folder;
  2. writes each touched month file again without the orphan lines: every kept line is the bytes it was, copied through a temporary file and renamed into place, fsynced. No main-chain line is touched, and a file that changed since the diagnosis stops the command before anything is written;
  3. sets logbook.json to the main chain's last seq and head, rebuilds the index, and runs verify. Its result is the command's: valid — …, or INVALID with exit 1, in which case it says so and does not try again.

It refuses, and writes nothing, when the record's chain cannot be told, when a line chains from no line of the record (a break, not a fork), when a month file is cut inside a line, when an orphan line is sealed and the identity that opens it is not here (what leaves the chain is read first), and when the record folder is under a sync client's folder (doctor's folder check: iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Google Drive). The dry run always works.

The orphan lines are observations too; a source that is synced again will bring them back, chained correctly, and append_many skips the ones the record already has by raw_id. To put them back by hand, logbook add repair/<stamp>-removed.jsonl appends them as new lines at the head.

docs.title: The files the lines name
docs.text:
The chain covers lines, not bytes, but a line names its files by digest (SPEC §1.1), so after the lines verify looks for every file of the attachment store a line names: a reference whose path is attachments/<sha256>, or an adapter's pre-attach hash (extra.media with a local_path, the file logbook attach import-backup fills in), in a sealed line when the identity opens it. A digest alone names no file of the store and is not looked for: a mail attachment counted and not kept, a body hashed and never kept, a signed day's page. Each file is looked at once, the first line that names it standing for the rest, and every line counts, a retracted one too:

  • missing: listed under attachments: with that line, and not an error: verify stays valid and exits 0, as SPEC §1.1 requires. logbook attach status counts them by source; a phone source's media is missing until attach import-backup has run.
  • present and plain: hashed against its name; bytes that hash to anything else are an error naming the line (the table above). --no-attachment-digests leaves present plain files unhashed, for a store too large to read on every run, and counts them not hashed; a missing file is still listed.
  • present and sealed: with the identity, opened and its plaintext hashed against its name; a mismatch, or a file that does not open, is an error (the last two rows). A verifier with the key must make this check (SPEC §1.1 and §3), so --no-attachment-digests does not skip it. Without the identity, or with --keyless, a sealed file is counted sealed and not opened.
valid — 1204 lines, head 4dc18fde900da55538fbd134e48652282d044bc2ec8c28ac0573fee15506b599
  attachments: 3 files named by the lines; 2 present, checked against their name; 1 missing, reported and not an error (SPEC §1.1):
    attachments/9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08 (line 29)

Twenty missing files are listed by name, the rest counted. doctor looks for the same files and counts the missing ones in its record line, which still passes; it does not hash them, since it runs four times a day (The doctor). logbook attach verify is the other walk: every file in the store, named by a line or not, against its name (The attachment store).

docs.title: Timestamps
docs.text:
at, end (when it is not null) and recorded_at are RFC 3339 instants (SPEC §2). append refuses a stamp that is not one, whatever it ends in, and keeps one that is exactly as it was given, since the string is hashed as written: 07:30:00Z and 07:30:00.000Z both stand. verify reports a line whose stamp is not one as an error naming the line (the table above); a stamp that is an instant but is written with an offset, +01:00, is a warning this release and an error in the next. A leap second (23:59:60Z) and the year 0000 are refused too: no reader here can place them on a day.

Backup says how to keep a snapshot so that the first row of the table, which repair tail mends from the files alone, is the only one you ever meet.

docs.title: The relationship reader (experimental)
docs.text:
A question asked across time about one person, answered by a model from what passed between you and them, and nothing else, with every claim citing the lines it rests on or listed as unsupported. The boundaries in full are in logbook/contrib/relationship/README.md; this page is how to use it.

logbook people ingest "Ola Nordmann" --window 2026-06-01 2026-06-30
logbook people ask "Ola Nordmann" "What did we plan for the boat?"
logbook dream person "Ola Nordmann" --window 2026-06-01 2026-06-30

docs.title: The entry
docs.text:
Nothing crosses without its own entry in policy/crossing.json, with a last day:

{"relationship": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2026-11-15"}}
  • max_tier: the highest tier of a line that may be read and sent, and of the names that say whom a line is with: 1 or 2. While the model is a cloud one, an entry that says 3 is refused, and nothing above the ceiling is read.
  • until, required: the last day the lend holds. From the next day nothing is read or sent, and the command says so in one sentence; write a new date to lend it again.
  • model, optional: the one model a person may go to. When LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL names another, the command refuses.
  • include_unsigned, optional: true lets the lines of days you have not signed cross too. Without it only the lines of signed days cross (day sign, RFC 0034).

The dream entry never stands in for it: a record with a dream entry and no relationship entry sends no person anywhere.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Until a model runs on your own hardware, the reader uses the model the dream uses, through the same three variables (docs/dream.md): LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT, LOGBOOK_DREAM_MODEL and, for a cloud model, LOGBOOK_DREAM_KEY. The key goes in the request's header and nowhere else: an error from the endpoint is said with it replaced by <key>.

What the model is sent is the person's name, the window, your question and their lines in it: the messages of your direct chat (both ways), your calls, the mail between you, the events you both attended and the calls that were recorded, each with its time, who spoke and its words, and the promises read in those words. Each line goes as a reference (L1, L2, ...), never its id. Nothing else of the record: no note that names them, no group chat, no photo, no draft. The days you spent together in the window go too (RFC 0036 amendment 2): each its date, the name places.json gives the place you shared (a place with no name when it has none, never its coordinates) and the references of the lines it rests on, under the same gate as the lines (the entry's max_tier, your signed days), so a sentence about time together cites them; --json counts them, days_together. The place's name is read from your location lines, so it takes their tier: a day together goes only when the highest tier of the location lines behind the stay, and of the line that says who was there, is at or under max_tier. At max_tier 1 a day spent at a stay your tier-2 locations found is not sent, not even as a place with no name, and is counted as held back. A person dreamed before at the same head is not dreamed again for them (rule 1 keys on the head, not the prompt): their next draft, once the record moves, reads the days together. people ask --show-prompt prints exactly what is sent.

docs.title: people ingest and people ask
docs.text:
people ingest NAME --window FROM TO reads the person's lines into a store under state/relationship/<id>/, beside the record and never in it. people ask NAME QUESTION sends the lines the store holds that the record still allows, and prints the answer: each supported claim with the lines it cites under it, then, under unsupported, every claim that cites no line of theirs, a line outside the set, or a reference it was not given. --json carries the same, and the claims in the draft/v1 segment shape. An answer is never written.

The store serves only under the head and the entry it was read under: a new line, a retraction, a signed day, or the entry changed, and ask asks you to ingest again.

docs.title: dream person
docs.text:
