dream person NAME [--window FROM TO] (default: the 90 days that end today) reads the same lines from the record and writes one draft/v1 line about the person, as dream day writes one about a day: what passed between you, the threads still open, the promises, two questions, every sentence citing their lines or marked unsupported, refused when more than 30 % is unsupported. It is a proposal, never a fact. Dreaming the same person over the same window at the same head writes nothing; another window, or a record that moved, writes a new draft that supersedes the standing one. --dry-run asks and writes nothing. No page shows a person draft yet.

A person draft follows the relationship entry it was written under, never the dream entry: once the entry's until has passed, or its max_tier is below the draft's tier, the door holds it back as a line above its ceiling, a crossing package leaves it home (counted as held_back_by_entry), and logbook doctor names it on its drafts line, while the days' drafts still show under a live dream entry.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text: What each version changed for you, in five bullets. CHANGELOG.md has every change in full; Upgrading has the two migrations a record may need.

docs.title: 0.7.0, 18 October 2026
docs.text:
• You close the day. logbook day reflect takes the day in your words, typed, from an audio file heard on this machine, from the microphone on macOS or from the day's Wispr Flow dictation, and the Day page of logbook serve has Reflect and sign at its foot. star marks a line worth keeping, with says who was there when no device saw, and setup day_start 06:00 ends your day when you do.
  • A model drafts; you decide. dream day, dream journey and dream week have a model you name (LOGBOOK_DREAM_ENDPOINT, any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) draft a day, a journey or a week under the dream entry of policy/crossing.json, every sentence citing its lines or marked unsupported; an event it proposes enters the record only when you accept it at day sign. transcript synthesize does the same for one call.
  • Your goals, your chapters, your verdicts. goal add and goal review keep your goals in your own words with your verdict on each, chapter open names a stretch of your life, review KIND is one sitting for the people, orgs, ideas, assets and places the sources saw, and status says what you decided about each. serve has shelves for them: the Manifest, Ideas, Promises, Goals and Agents (the shelves).
  • More of your life comes in. One Google service-account key reads Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Tasks, Meet and your own sign-ins, read-only; sync github, sync notion, sync beeper, sync mail over IMAP, your Telegram bots, Claude Code sessions and the Claude apps' export join them; and the family's home videos in a Drive folder are cut into scenes on this machine, each scene's place and date proposed and confirmed by you. With the speakers extra, derive transcripts tells the voices of a recording apart and review speakers names them.
  • It looks after itself. The schedule runs four times a day, the 06:00 run closing the day, with doctor after each and, with the Telegram notifier set, one message when something is wrong; backup --restore-test restores the latest snapshot and verifies it, monthly on the schedule; serve --install-service keeps the pages running; doctor --packet is a diagnostic to hand a collaborator; and export world draws your places and your assets' tracks on one page with a time scrubber.

docs.title: 0.6.0, 6 October 2026
docs.text:
• Starting is a conversation, and the record reads back as days. logbook setup asks one question at a time, each with its default and the reason it is asked, and logbook doctor says whether this machine is set up to keep the record. logbook day is one calendar day: the night, the stays, who was there, health, weather, what you wrote. days is a window of them one line each, year composes a year, and digest is the day in 25 lines ending in one question that now comes from your own record and a policy file you can edit.
  • The record comes off the screen. logbook serve shows every page in a browser on this machine only. year --html FILE --print and trip --html FILE --print lay a year or a trip out for A4 or Letter with a cover and page numbers. export vault renders the record as a folder of Markdown with wikilinks for Obsidian or Logseq. logbook mcp serves it to an agent on this machine behind a tier gate that defaults to tier 1.
  • More of your life reads back. search across notes, transcripts, messages, mail and events; ledger for your money by month or trip; people and person for everyone the record knows, with people merge for the duplicates and rollup people --drifting for the ones you are losing touch with; promises for the sentences in your own words that read as commitments, with a local model to judge them; tasks with the evidence one was done; rollup listen and rollup attention for what you listened to and where your screen time went.
  • You hand a day or a trip to a friend. share day writes a signed bundle of one day for one named member of your circle, export trip-bundle does the same for a whole trip at the tier you choose, and receive verifies the signature and keeps their side beside your record, never in its chain, so a shared trip has a merged page with both sides' words and photos. backup copies the record to another disk, verifies it there and restores it.
  • New sources and better old ones. Apple Wallet, Spotify, Apple Music, Apple Podcasts from a phone backup, Screen Time, weather, Apple Photos faces and albums, voice memos transcribed by a local model, ten more Google Takeout products, a 20 GB Takeout mailbox read in chunks, and a ship's deck log as declared passages. logbook demo --years 40 writes a whole synthetic life to try it all on. Three Takeout adapters that silently skipped every row of a current export read them again, and every reader now works in a pipe and on a timezone this machine's zone database does not know.

docs.title: 0.5.0, 1 October 2026
docs.text:
• An iPhone backup is a dozen sources in one go. logbook import-backup <folder> --only <sources> reads WhatsApp, iMessage, calls, Photos, Health, Books, Voice Memos, Wallet, Reminders, Safari, Podcasts, Flighty, Splitwise and more from a Finder or iTunes backup, encrypted ones included with your password, locally. Nothing in the backup is modified, and a source you switch off in policy/import.json stays off.
  • Health is right, and a wrong record is repaired. Resting heart rate and heart rate variability are stored as the Health app keeps them, in beats per minute and milliseconds; earlier imports were 60 and 1,000 times too large. logbook repair health-units writes a corrected line and a retraction for each wrong one, nothing rewritten. Withings and MyFitnessPal join Apple Health as sources, and a night's sleep is summed properly across devices.
  • Your trips, places and company are derived from the record. trips finds runs of nights away and names them by place or airport; derive stays turns a track into stays and moves; the rollups sum countries, flights, nights, places and people over a year; and show person, show place and show asset are pages read from the whole record. Who was with you comes from calendars, transcripts, notes and tagged faces, and you are never counted as your own company.
  • Boats and aircraft are subjects of their own. assets.json registers the vessels and aircraft whose tracks the record keeps, AIS and ADS-B feed their positions live, a flight you declare with add flight is evidence, and infer flights finds the ones your tracker shows. verify streams a record of any size, dedupe runs through the index, and export crossing hands a window of lines to one named destination at a tier ceiling.
  • The format grew without breaking. Thirteen payload profiles were written down as RFCs (calls, flights, health samples, mail, tasks, browsing, watching, listening, trips, transactions, highlights, voice memos, keepers), the conformance sample carries one line of each, and the independent TypeScript implementation agrees with this one on a record either writes, checked on every pull request.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text:
The captain releases (GOVERNANCE.md); this is the checklist, in order. X.Y.Z is the version being released.

  1. Only the captain and bots have ever committed. git log --all --format='%an %ae %cn %ce' | sort -u shows bighydro, GitHub and dependabot, nothing else.
  2. Bump the version in pyproject.toml and __version__ in logbook/__init__.py together, then uv lock so uv.lock carries it too.
  3. Assemble the changelog. uv run python scripts/changelog_assemble.py X.Y.Z folds every fragment in changelog.d/ (and the ## Unreleased block of CHANGELOG.md, while one exists) into ## X.Y.Z — <today> at the top of CHANGELOG.md and deletes the fragments. --dry-run prints the section first. Read the result: headings come in the order the fragments named them, and a release reads better when they are reworded or reordered by hand, as 0.5.0 was.
  4. Commit on a branch and open the release pull request, labelled no-changelog: it is the one pull request that edits CHANGELOG.md. git commit -s -S, then git log -1 --format='%G?' prints G.
  5. Tag the merged commit. git grep __version__ HEAD -- logbook/__init__.py prints X.Y.Z; CHANGELOG.md has X.Y.Z with today's date; then git tag -s vX.Y.Z -m vX.Y.Z && git push origin vX.Y.Z. The release workflow builds the wheel, attests it, publishes to PyPI and makes the GitHub release.
  6. Point the Homebrew formula at the release. Once PyPI lists X.Y.Z, put the sdist's URL and SHA-256 (read from PyPI's JSON, the command is in homebrew/README.md) into homebrew/logbook.rb, build and test it on a Mac as that page says, open a no-changelog pull request for it, and when it is merged copy the file to Formula/logbook.rb in bighydro/homebrew-logbook and push. brew upgrade on every Mac that tapped it then installs X.Y.Z; until this is done they stay on the previous release while pipx and uv users already have the new one.

docs.title: Review: what the sources saw
docs.text:
Your sources see more than you have named. A mail domain recurs, a group chat is about a company, a Notion page grows into a project, the receiver reports a hull the registry no longer names. logbook review is one sitting for all of it (RFC 0037): for each of the five kinds of thing the record names, what the sources observed and the record has not placed, proposed against what you named, with the evidence, numbered. Nothing is written unless you say so, and nothing is looked up: no register of companies, no code host, no Notion, no geocoder. A sixth queue is no kind of thing the record names but the same sitting: review video, the scenes of the family's videos that videos infer proposed a place or a date for (the video queue), listed after the five and before the speakers' below.

logbook review                       # every kind with its queue, one block each; nothing written
logbook review org                   # the queue of one kind: person, org, idea, asset or place
logbook review org --accept 1 --name 3 "Fjordkiosk AS" --reject 4
logbook review idea --json           # the queue, the unplaced and the placed count, as JSON
logbook review asset --all-above 50  # accept every proposal at or above the score
logbook review video --accept 1 --date 2 "summer 1994" --ask 3   # a scene's own answers

review person is people review and review place is setup places review: the same sitting, the same numbers, the same output byte for byte, under one name. review speakers is the voices of your recordings not yet named (RFC 0038 §4), in the same shape with answers of its own (--unnamed, --same-as, --consent, --play, --named): who they are. review goal is your goals, each asked once a week (below). review alone lists every queue, the videos', the goals' and the voices' after the five.

docs.title: The five queues
docs.text:
An observed thing's identity is the strongest identifier its observation carries, never the id a source gives one observation; keyed the other way, one company explodes into a row per mail.

Kind Observed by, strongest first Proposed against person an email address, a phone number, the name's words folded (people) the people the resolutions name org the registered domain of a mail, calendar or transcript address (a public mail provider, your own domains and a service's own hosts, a calendar's rooms among them, name nobody's org); a code-host org of a url, a task's link or an act sync github wrote (your own account is yours, never an org); a group chat's name; a ledger merchant seen on 3 lines or more the orgs: entity/v1 lines, and resolution/v1 lines of type company read as orgs idea a Notion page's root (a page under it is the root's idea; a database row is its own root, never the page above its database, and is proposed only when its Type says Idea, idea_rows in policy/entities.json); a code-host repository of a url, a task's own url or links, or an act sync github wrote; a task's or a transcript's title on 2 lines of 2 sources or more; never a line a bot made or an agent wrote, nor a relations line the ideas the entity/v1 lines name asset a track's subject the registry does not name (its MMSI or icao24 when the instrument said); an aircraft registration on 3 flights or more the assets of assets.json place a cluster of your stays within 75 m (places) the names the sources gave it

The score is a plain sum of what speaks for a pair, as people review's is:

Kind Evidence Points org the same domain · the same code-host org · the same name (the words in any order, AS, ASA, Ltd, Inc, GmbH, AB aside; two words, or one of six letters) · the org's people on its lines · the same days 60 · 50 · 20, +5 a further source up to +10 · 10 a person up to 30 · 2 a day up to 20 idea the same page · the same repository · the same title (the articles aside) · its people · the same weeks 60 · 50 · 20, +5 … · 10 … · 5 a week up to 20 asset the same identifier · the same registration spelled another way (ZZ-ABC, ZZABC) · the same name 60 · 50 · 20

Days, weeks and people alone never propose. A domain, a code-host org, a page, a repository or a title that matches nothing, and an asset the registry does not know, is proposed as a new one, after the matches; a group chat and a merchant are only ever proposed against an org you have. Among equal scores an org's hint decides — company (a domain), community (a code-host org, a group), brand (a merchant), personal (a family's domain: every name on it is a given name and a surname, the given name the address's own, kari@ "Kari Nordmann", and they share the surname the domain spells; or a person's own code-host account, a github: handle a resolution names) — for ranking only; the hint is never written to a line.

$ logbook review org
4 proposals · 5 observed orgs not yet placed, 1 placed · tier 2
  1  [34]  group "nordmann verft" (Nordmann Verft; message 3) → Nordmann Verft AS: same name Nordmann Verft ~ Nordmann Verft AS · 1 person on both · together on 2 days
  2  [25]  git.example.org/nordmann-verft (nordmann-verft; browse 1, task 1) → Nordmann Verft AS: same name nordmann-verft ~ Nordmann Verft AS across chrome, gtasks
  3  [new]  fjordkiosk.example.org (Fjordkiosk; mail 2) → ____
  4  [new]  nordmann.example.org (Kari Nordmann, Per Nordmann; mail 2) → ____
nothing written: `review org --accept N[,N]`, `--name N "…"`, `--reject N[,N]`, or `--all-above SCORE`

$ logbook review asset
2 proposals · 2 observed assets not yet placed, 0 placed · tier 2
  1  [50]  ZZ-ABC (flight 3) → Lerka: same registration ZZ-ABC ~ ZZABC
  2  [new]  970123456 (GAMLE SOLVIND; location 3) → ____

docs.title: Your say
docs.text:
Kind --accept / --name --reject person the resolution/v1 alias lines people merge writes one entity-review/v1 line, type person org one entity/v1 line binding the observed identifiers (a domain, a code-host org, a group, a merchant); a new org's id a UUIDv7, minted after its dedupe key is looked up, so a key that resolves already reuses its id one entity-review/v1 line, type org idea one entity/v1 line binding the page, the repository or the title one entity-review/v1 line, type idea asset a new one registered in assets.json as setup assets add writes it, under the id its lines carry; one entity/v1 line binding its identifiers one entity-review/v1 line, type asset place the places.json entry with its fitted radius, and the naming as one note/v1 line one entity-review/v1 line, type place, the spot's centre and the name video one attribution/v1 line binding the scene to the place and/or the date its draft proposes, or your own (--place, --date), beside the video's line and never inside it one scene-review/v1 line (RFC 0040 §5), never an entity-review/v1 line: no other queue reads it

--name N "…" accepts a new one under your own name; on a proposal that matched an entity you have, it is refused (accept the match; a rename is an entity/v1 line that supersedes the standing one). A rejected pair is never proposed again; retract the line and it returns. An entity/v1 line is tier 2 and never cites a tier-3 line, so a merchant matched from the ledger is bound as a merchant ref and the payments are not its evidence; an entity-review/v1 line that cites them is tier 3. The profiles are on their own page.

Every number is checked before the first line is written: a number the queue does not have, a number both accepted and rejected, a score that is not a whole number, or an option of another kind exits 2 and writes nothing. On a terminal, an org's, an idea's, an asset's and a place's queue asks for each proposal: y, n, a name for a new one, Enter to skip, q to stop; each answer is written at once. The video's asks the same for each scene: y, n, a to keep it to ask the family where and when it was filmed, Enter to skip, q to stop.

docs.title: The video queue
docs.text:
review video is the scenes of the family's videos (Videos, RFC 0040): each scene of a file's latest inference that you have not answered, the surest proposal first, with the sentences, frames and speech it rests on. --accept takes the place or the date its draft proposes and writes one attribution/v1 line beside the video's, never inside it; --reject writes the scene's no, one scene-review/v1 line of RFC 0040's and never an entity-review/v1 line, so no other queue reads it; --json is the queue or what was written. Its own options go with it alone, and every other kind refuses them as it refuses a place's:

Option --place N NAME, --date N WHEN accept scene N with your own place (a places.json name, an asset's id or name) or date (1994, 1994-07, 1994-07-14, summer 1994, 1994-06..1994-08), or none --ask N[,N] keep the scene to ask the family: one open task/v1 line in the list videos --asked, --answered the scenes kept to ask, or those you confirmed, to answer or correct them --top N the first N scenes (a place's option too)

The lock is the sitting's, the same for every queue: the queue is read and you are asked with no lock held, and each answer's lines are appended under the record's writer lock.

docs.title: Ideas from calls
docs.text:
A call's synthesis (logbook transcript synthesize, transcript synthesis) may propose up to three ideas the call put forward: a new one, or a refinement of an idea you named, by its id. They are proposals and nothing more. review idea lists them after the observed ones, marked [call], with the call and the utterances they rest on:

$ logbook review idea
2 proposals · 0 observed ideas not yet placed, 0 placed · tier 3
  1  [call]  “Fjord Kiosk” (call “Yard plans” 2026-06-10; U4) → Fjord Kiosk, refines: The kiosk sells mooring lines too.
  2  [call]  “Shared haul-out calendar” (call “Yard plans” 2026-06-10; U8) → ____: One calendar the yard and the owners share.
nothing written: `review idea --accept N[,N]`, `--name N "…"`, `--reject N[,N]`, or `--all-above SCORE`

--all-above never takes a call's idea: it has no score.

Nothing reaches the Ideas shelf until you say yes here (or on the Ideas page of logbook serve, which reads the same queue). --accept (or --name N "…" for a new one) writes one entity/v1 line: a new idea, minted as any other, or, for a refinement, a line of the idea's own id. That line is tier 2 and never cites a tier-3 line, and a Granola call is tier 3: so of such a call it carries the name you accepted and nothing else, as an observed title of a tier-3 line is accepted; of a call at tier 2 or below it cites the call and keeps the words (extra.pitch for a new idea, extra.refines for a refinement). --reject writes the entity-review/v1 no as for any idea, on the idea's title for a new one and on the call against the idea for a refinement, at the call's tier: it is never proposed again; two calls that put the same new idea forward are one candidate that cites both. A home video's soundtrack is no call and proposes nothing; a synthesis the dream entry withholds today proposes nothing either, and comes back when the entry allows it again.

docs.title: Goals, once a week
docs.text:
review goal asks each of your goals once a week: every standing goal open today (begun, not closed by a verdict, not past its until) that has no review dated this ISO week, of any period. You answer with the verdict, one of the five of goals: advancing, stalled, done, let-go or superseded, and your words when you want them.

$ logbook review goal
2 goals to review this week (2026-W42) · 1 reviewed · tier 2
  1  #2  Sail to Lofoten and back between June and August, at anchor more nights than not.  (year) · last: advancing on 2026-10-08
  2  #3  Rebuild the engine over the winter.  (quarter) · never reviewed
nothing written: `review goal --say N advancing|stalled|done|let-go|superseded`, `--note N "…"`
$ logbook review goal --say 1 stalled --say 2 advancing --note 1 "The boat is on land."
stalled 1 “Sail to Lofoten and back between June and August, at anchor more nights than not.”: review/v1 (seq 7)
advancing 2 “Rebuild the engine over the winter.”: review/v1 (seq 8)

Each verdict is written by the writer goal review uses, for the period week, at now: the line is the one goal review N stalled --period week writes, byte for byte (RFC 0036 amendment 1). A goal answered this week is not asked again until the next; a second verdict on the same day for the same period writes nothing and says so. Every number and every word is checked before the first line: a number the queue does not have, a sixth word, a goal said twice, or a --note on a goal not said exits 2 and writes nothing. A goal has no score, no no and no name of its own, so --accept, --reject, --name and --all-above are refused for it; --say and --note are refused for every other kind, as a place's and the speakers' options are. On a terminal each goal is asked in turn.

docs.title: The table
docs.text: What the sources saw is one derived table in the index, observed_entities in index.sqlite: a row per observed person, org, idea, asset and place, keyed by the kind and its strongest identifier, with the names seen, the identifiers as the lines wrote them, counts per source and per line kind, the days, first and last seen, the tier of the evidence, a few line ids, the canonical people seen on its lines, the org's hint and the canonical entity it resolves to. It is stamped per kind with the head and the settings it was built under, served while they stand and built again when they move; its shape is checked with PRAGMA table_info. observed_people and observed_places, the tables people review and places review read until 0.7, are views over it for one release. Nothing of it is in the record.

docs.title: What happened to a place's no
docs.text: Until 0.7 a place you rejected was kept in state/places-review.json, never as a line, and a backup left it out. It is a line now (RFC 0037, decision 3): setup places review --reject, review place --reject and the Places page of logbook serve each write one entity-review/v1 line of type place, and the file is a cache rebuilt from the lines, never the truth. The pairs the file held from before still count; setup places review --migrate-rejects (or review place --migrate-rejects) writes each once as an entity-review/v1 line, at the moment you said it, and a second run writes nothing. Until you run it, review says how many pairs are not lines yet.

docs.title: The rollups
docs.text:
logbook rollup <kind> [--year YYYY | --since YYYY-MM-DD --until YYYY-MM-DD] [--json] sums the record up over a window of days. Every rollup is a reader (ADR 0013): a function of the record at its head, derived every time and never written, and under --json every number carries the ids of the lines it came from. The window is the whole record unless --year or --since/--until narrow it, and it is clipped to the days the rollup's own lines cover, so a day the record knows nothing about is nothing, not a night in transit and not a zero.

logbook rollup countries --year 2026   # days per country from the overnight stay; in transit apart
logbook rollup flights                 # count, km, long-haul, by evidence, from the flight lines standing
logbook rollup nights                  # home, away, in transit, nights aboard, the longest trip
logbook rollup places                  # nights, stays, hours, people per named place and asset; the top unnamed clusters
logbook rollup places --with           # the place × person table: stays, days and nights at each place per person
logbook rollup people                  # days and nights together, last real contact, places shared, per person
logbook rollup people --drifting       # whose contact frequency fell most, this year against the year before: see below
logbook rollup health --by week         # sleep, steps, resting heart rate, HRV, per month or ISO week
logbook rollup listen --year 2026       # listens, hours, skips, the top artists by hours, podcasts by show, hours by month
logbook rollup attention --year 2026    # hours by app and by category from the app-use lines; --by month|week
logbook rollup money --year 2026        # the transactions by month, by country of the stay, by category: see ledger.md

The window is --year, or --since and --until, clipped to the days the owner's track covers (the first to the last day with a location line; for flights, with any line), so a day outside them is nothing, not a night in transit. Without either, the whole record.

docs.title: Places
docs.text:
rollup places is the year per place. For every named place in places.json: the nights whose overnight stay is there, the stays, the hours, the first and last visit (the first stay's start day, the last stay's end day), and with, the people confirmed present through the with module, most days first. Then aboard, the same per asset in assets.json: a stay aboard is one run of your stays and moves aboard it, whatever the asset did inside it (docs/day.md, Aboard an asset), its hours the run's whole span, its nights the nights whose overnight stay was aboard. Then the unnamed places: your stays at no named place — the berths and anchorages inside a stay aboard among them, each marked aboard <asset> — grouped as places propose groups them (within 300 m of a group's first stay) and ranked by hours, the top five of the year, each under the stay id places name takes, so a hotel you keep returning to is one line and one command away from a name. A night aboard counts at the anchorage the asset lay at.

places 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-30
  2026
        Home (home)                                 18 nights · 19 stays · 273.5 h · 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-30
        Office (other)                              14 stays · 107 h · 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-30 · with Per Hansen, Liv Berg
        Marina (asset-berth)                        1 night · 3 stays · 26.8 h · 2026-06-13 – 2026-06-21 · with Anders Vik, Ola Nordmann, Sigrid Moen
        Cabin (other)                               1 night · 1 stay · 25.9 h · 2026-06-06 – 2026-06-07 · with Ola Nordmann
        aboard, by hours (a stay is one run aboard, whatever the asset did inside it):
        Nordlys (nordlys) (yacht)                   6 nights · 3 stays · 148.4 h · 2026-06-13 – 2026-06-21 · with Anders Vik, Ola Nordmann, Sigrid Moen
        unnamed, by hours (the ids `places name` takes):
        47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich)                     3 nights · 3 stays · 58.5 h · 2026-06-08 – 2026-06-11 · with Marta Keller   stay:owner:20260608T0830Z@47.3769,8.5417
        59.0500,10.0300 aboard nordlys (Sandefjord) 2 nights · 2 stays · 40.7 h · 2026-06-17 – 2026-06-19   stay:owner:20260617T1200Z@59.0500,10.0300
        59.8500,10.6000 aboard nordlys              2 nights · 2 stays · 40 h · 2026-06-15 – 2026-06-20   stay:owner:20260615T1100Z@59.8500,10.6000
        55.6850,12.5500 (Copenhagen)                2 nights · 2 stays · 33.1 h · 2026-06-25 – 2026-06-27 · with Freja Lund   stay:owner:20260625T1630Z@55.6850,12.5500
        59.4300,10.4800 aboard nordlys (Sandefjord) 1 night · 1 stay · 17.9 h · 2026-06-16 – 2026-06-17   stay:owner:20260616T1300Z@59.4300,10.4800

An unnamed place reads as its coordinates; aboard <asset> when the stays were aboard one; near <place>, x km for a named place within 5 km; else the city of the nearest large airport within 30 km in parentheses, the rule trips and day label an unnamed stay by. A place's nights are printed when there are any; an asset's always, since zero nights aboard a car is the point.

Under --json, each year has places, aboard and unnamed; each place, asset and unnamed cluster carries stays, hours, nights, first, last, people and lines; an asset also asset, name and kind; an unnamed cluster also id, lat, lon, label, aboard, nearest ({name, kind, metres}, the closest named place whatever the distance) and city. Each person under people carries their stays, days and nights at that place and the lines that put them there. unnamed_top says how many clusters a year lists.

docs.title: Who, where: --with
docs.text:
rollup places --with turns the same reading into the place × person table: one row per person per place, the places in the order the rollup lists them, the people by days there.

places 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-30 · with
  2026
        place                        people, the most days there first
        Office                       with Per Hansen, Liv Berg
        Marina                       with Anders Vik, Ola Nordmann, Sigrid Moen
        Cabin                        with Ola Nordmann
        Nordlys (nordlys)            with Anders Vik, Ola Nordmann, Sigrid Moen
        47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich)      with Marta Keller
        55.6850,12.5500 (Copenhagen) with Freja Lund
  • stays: the stays at the place the person was confirmed at.
  • days: the distinct local days of the evidence that put them there.
  • nights: the nights at the place on a day they were there. A night counts for a person when the evidence that put them at the stay is dated the night's day: dinner on the 16th is the night of the 16th together, not every night of a four-night stay.

Under --json each year carries the rows under with: place (the place's name, the asset's id or the unnamed cluster's stay id), label, kind (place, asset, unnamed), id and name of the person, stays, days, nights, lines. --with goes with places only.

docs.title: People
docs.text:
rollup people is the year per person, from the confirmed set of the with module only: an attendee of a timed calendar entry held at the stay, a participant of a transcript recorded inside it whom the record resolves to a person, a note written inside it that says with <name>. A tagged face and an all-day entry's attendee are proposals, and a proposal is not a day together: it is not counted, not listed and not among the lines, so a person the record knows only by a face does not appear here (the Day and the pages still show them as proposed). You are never your own company (present.owner_of).

people 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-30
  2026
        Per Hansen               last 2026-06-30 · Office
        Liv Berg                 last 2026-06-29 · Office
        Ola Nordmann             last 2026-06-15 · Cabin, Marina
        Anders Vik               last 2026-06-15 · Marina
        Jonas Weber              last 2026-06-09 · 47.3700,8.5300 (Zurich)
        Marta Keller             last 2026-06-09 · 47.3700,8.5300 (Zurich), 47.3769,8.5417 (Zurich)

Per person: days together (the distinct local days of the confirmed evidence, by the evidence's own day), nights together (the nights whose overnight stay they were confirmed at on that day, the --with rule), the last real contact (the last such day), the places shared (a named place, aboard <asset>, else the unnamed place's label) and the confirmed evidence count. Under --json each carries stays (the stays shared) and lines too. A confirmed name the record resolves to no person — an attendee with a display name and no resolution line (RFC 0006) — is listed apart, under unresolved, so that a resolution can be written for them.

docs.title: Who fell quiet: --drifting
docs.text:
logbook rollup people --drifting [--until YYYY-MM-DD] [--window 365] [--min-contacts 3] [--json] lists the people whose contact frequency fell most. It is a reader like the rest: it says what the record holds and suggests nothing.

The method, plainly. Two windows of the same length: the recent one is --window days (365 by default) ending on --until, which is the record's last day with a line of any kind unless given; the earlier one is the same number of days before it. --year and --since do not apply: the window is a length, not a range. For every person the record's resolution lines name (RFC 0006; never the owner), the contacts in each window are counted: a message/v1 either way in a direct chat with them, a call/v1 whose counterparty they are, answered or not, an event/v1 they attend and did not decline, and a stay of the owner's the with module confirms them at (together, one per day and stay, People above) — the channels of logbook people, read twice through people.md's reader, once per window. A mail is not a contact, because the record cannot tell a letter from a newsletter; a tagged face is not one, because a face is a proposal. A retracted line is out, and so is a calendar entry a later line supersedes.

A person is listed when their earlier window has at least --min-contacts contacts (3 by default; one never heard that often is not drifting, they were never close in the record's terms) and their recent window has fewer than the earlier. The fall is the share of the earlier count lost, and the table is ordered by it, the larger share first, then the larger count, then the name. Per person: the two counts, the fall, the last real contact as days before the recent window's last day (a message, an answered call or a day together, the people reader's rule: a missed call and an all-day entry are not one; never when the two windows hold none), the channels that went quiet (heard in the earlier window and silent in the recent; together is the stays), and the last shared place, the latest day the record confirms them at one of the owner's stays, named as the people reader names it (an em dash when the record never put you in one place).

people · drifting · recent 2026-06-15 – 2026-06-28 · earlier 2026-06-01 – 2026-06-14 · at least 2 contacts earlier
        person                   last real contact  quiet                      last shared place
        Eva Nordmann             last 2026-06-12    messages, calls            —
        Liv Berg                 last 2026-06-03    calls                      —
        Ola Nordmann             last 2026-06-16    calls, calendar, together  Office

Under --json one object: kind (drifting), window (recent and earlier, each since, until, days), min_contacts, a warning when the record began inside one of the windows, and people, one entry per person in the table's order: id, name, earlier and recent (each contacts, then messages, calls, calendar and together as {count, lines}, and lines, every id behind the total once), fall (the count lost), fell_by (the share, to three places), quiet, last_real_contact ({day, via, line} or null), days_since_real_contact (null with it) and last_place ({where, day, lines} or null). As in every rollup, the ids are the lines the numbers came from, so each one can be read back with show.

Blind spots, because the record only holds what was logged:

  • A person you now see in person every day looks "drifting" when nothing is logged about it: no calendar entry at the stay, no transcript, no note that says with <name>, no message. The rollup counts contacts the record holds, not contact.
  • A channel the record stopped importing goes quiet for everyone on it. A source that was not brought up to date reads as silence; sources --gaps says which.
  • A record that began inside the earlier window undercounts it, and one that began inside the recent window has nothing to compare; the rollup prints a warning in both cases. A --window longer than half the record cannot say anything.
  • A group chat names nobody as its counterpart: messages in a group are not a contact with anyone in it, the people reader's rule, so a friendship that moved into a group looks like a fall.
  • A person the record names twice, once per address, is two people here, each with half the contacts; people merge finds them.
  • Frequency is a count. A weekly call and a daily one-line message weigh one and seven; the table does not say which mattered.

docs.title: How it reads
docs.text: Both rollups come from one reading.read of the window: the lines through the index (Index.between, one sweep of the files), one stays.derive, the night of each day. The company of a stay is read from present.Evidence, the window's evidence lines bucketed by every local day their span touches, so each stay looks at the lines of its own days and nothing is read per place. Nothing is written, not even policy/stays.json.

docs.title: Countries, flights, nights
docs.text: countries: days per country per year from the overnight stay, by a place's own country else the nearest large airport's zone; in-transit nights and nights whose country is unknown apart; the method printed with the numbers. flights: count, kilometres between the airports table's coordinates, long-haul (over 3,500 km), unmeasured, by evidence (tracked, inferred, declared), from the flight lines standing (RFC 0013 rule 4). nights: home, away and in-transit nights, nights aboard each asset, the longest run of nights not at home. A home region is a place of kind home; a night whose stay centre is within 400 m of one is home whatever that place's radius. Without a home place every night is away, and the rollup says so.

docs.title: Per month or week: health
docs.text:
logbook rollup health [--year YYYY | --since YYYY-MM-DD --until YYYY-MM-DD] [--by month|week] [--json] sums the health-sample/v1 lines (RFC 0014) up per calendar month, or per ISO week with --by week. It reads the health lines of the window through the index and nothing else: no reading of the track, so a record of health lines alone rolls up, and the window is clipped to the first and last day with a health line.

Per period:

  • sleep — the mean of the nights' hours, and how many nights had a line. A night is the one that ends on the day: its asleep stages (asleep, core, deep, rem; never in_bed, never awake), per device the union of their spans, so a night a source wrote twice counts once (rule 4), and the longest device taken, never a sum across devices (rule 5).
  • steps — the mean of the days' counts, and how many days. A day's count is the larger device per quarter hour, summed (rule 5).
  • resting — the mean, lowest and highest of the days' resting heart rates in bpm, and how many days; a day's rate is the mean of its readings.
  • hrv — when the record has any: the mean of the days' heart-rate variability (SDNN) in ms, and how many days.

The rules the numbers follow:

  • The latest correction wins. A line another health line supersedes (a correction, such as the one logbook repair health-units writes) is out and the correction stands; when a line was corrected more than once, the latest correction stands and the earlier ones are out with it. A retracted line is out.
  • Units as stored. A value is read in the unit its line states. A resting heart rate in count/s is multiplied by 60 to read in bpm; one in bpm or count/min is taken as it is. Sleep is the span's seconds in hours; steps are counts; HRV is milliseconds.
  • Missing is missing. Every month or week the window touches is a row, including one with no line at all. A field no day of the period has a line for prints an em dash (—) and is null under --json; it is never a zero, because a zero would be a measurement.
health 2026-06-01 – 2026-08-20 · by month
  2026-06  sleep 6.5 h (2 nights) · 2,125 steps (2 days) · resting 57 bpm (54–60, 2 days) · hrv 45 ms (1 day)
  2026-07  sleep — · steps — · resting — · hrv —
  2026-08  sleep — · 5,000 steps (1 day) · resting — · hrv —

A week is an ISO week, 2026-W23, Monday to Sunday, and belongs to the ISO year, so the first days of January can fall in the old year's last week. A period at the window's edge is the part of it inside the window, and first and last say which days under --json.

docs.title: The JSON
docs.text:
--json prints one object: kind (health), window (since, until, days), by (month or week) and periods, one entry per period in order — period (2026-06 or 2026-W23), first and last (its days inside the window), then sleep (mean_h, nights, lines), steps (mean, days, lines), resting_hr (mean, min, max, days, lines) and hrv (mean_ms, days, lines), each null when no day of the period has a line for it. Under lines are the ids of the health lines each number came from: the asleep stages of the nights, the winning quarter hours, the readings.

The same day rows feed stats --health and the health line of the Day, so the three agree on every day.

docs.title: Listening
docs.text: rollup listen is the year per listen/v1 line standing (RFC 0019), whichever adapter wrote it: spotify, apple-music, shazam, apple-podcasts. Per year: the listens, the hours played (played_s summed; a line with no playhead is a listen with no hours, counted under untimed), the skipped lines, the lines per service, the podcast episodes with their hours, the top artists by hours played then listens (ten, the performers as the services spell them, never resolved), the podcasts section — the episodes' hours by show and by month, for a year that has one — and by month every month the window touches with its hours, listens and skips — a month with no listen is an em dash, never a zero. The window is clipped to the days the listen lines cover; a correction that supersedes a line wins and a retracted line is out. It lives in logbook/core/listen_rollup.py, beside rollup.py and in its manner. The adapters and the rollup are described in adapters/listen.md.

docs.title: Per year, month or week: attention
docs.text:
logbook rollup attention [--year YYYY | --since YYYY-MM-DD --until YYYY-MM-DD] [--by month|week] [--json] sums the app-use lines (logbook add screentime) up as hours by app and by category — communication, browser, media, work, other — per calendar year, or per month or ISO week with --by. It reads the app-use lines of the window through the index and nothing else, clipped to the first and last day with one; a retracted line is out, and so is one another app-use line supersedes. An app is its bundle id, named by the built-in table or by policy/apps.json, which also re-sorts it; a period with no line is an em dash, and a period with lines carries every category, one with no app at zero.

attention 2026-06-08 – 2026-08-20 · by month
  2026-06  6.2 h · communication 0.7 h · browser 1.5 h · media 0.8 h · work 3.0 h · other 0.2 h
        Xcode                    3.0 h · work · 2 sessions · com.apple.dt.Xcode
        Safari                   1.0 h · browser · 1 session · com.apple.Safari
        …
  2026-07  —
  2026-08  1.0 h · communication 0.0 h · browser 1.0 h · media 0.0 h · work 0.0 h · other 0.0 h
        Safari                   1.0 h · browser · 1 session · com.apple.Safari

Under --json: kind (attention), window, by (year, month or week), categories and periods, each with hours, seconds, by_category ({hours, seconds} per category, or null for a period with no line) and apps (bundle_id, app, category, hours, seconds, sessions, devices — seconds per device —, lines). The whole of it, the stores, the categories and the owner's table, is in docs/adapters/screentime.md.

docs.title: The schedule
docs.text:
logbook sync --install-schedule makes the machine run the record four times a day, at 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 local: logbook sync --scheduled at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00, and logbook sync --scheduled --close at 06:00, the run that closes the day (below). That is two jobs: two launchd agents on macOS (~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.logbook.sync.plist and org.logbook.sync.close.plist), two systemd user timers on Linux (~/.config/systemd/user/logbook-sync.timer and logbook-sync-close.timer, each with its service). The plists or units are printed before they are written, nothing is written outside that directory, and --uninstall-schedule removes them again, all four runs. The agents run the Python that installed them and point at the record found at install time; the keys your sources need they read from ~/.config/logbook/sync.env (KEY=value lines, mode 600), which you write and the command never does.

logbook sync --install-schedule                   # 00:00, 06:00, 12:00 and 18:00 local
logbook sync --install-schedule --system          # a machine nobody logs in to: prints two sudo commands
logbook sync --scheduled                          # what the schedule runs, by hand
logbook sync --scheduled --close                  # what it runs at 06:00
logbook doctor                                    # the last-run and restore-test lines
logbook sync --uninstall-schedule [--system]

A schedule installed before the four runs (one agent or timer at 07:00 and 19:00, under the same name) moves to them when you run logbook sync --install-schedule again: the files are written over, the agents loaded again, and a timer restarted so it takes the new times. --uninstall-schedule removes it whichever it is.

docs.title: The four runs, and the 06:00 close
docs.text:
The day ends at your day_start (midnight unless you set one, the record's settings). The 06:00 run is the one after it for most settings, so it closes the day: sync --scheduled --close is the scheduled run below with one step more, in this order:

  1. the sync: sync --all, as at every run;
  2. the dream's catch-up: dream --catch-up, when this version of logbook has the dream command and policy/crossing.json has a dream entry (sending a day to a model is a crossing like any other): the drafts of the last 14 days that have none or whose lines changed, then the synthesis of each call of the last 7 days that has none (the synthesis of a call). When it has not, one line says why (dream: this version has no dream command; nothing to catch up, or dream: policy/crossing.json has no dream entry; nothing to catch up) and the run goes on: absence is not an error. The close passes nothing after --catch-up, never a --since, so an older call is never sent by the schedule however many the record holds: the catch-up counts them in one line (3 calls before 2026-10-07 not synthesized; run …), doctor on its synthesis line, and they wait for you to send them by hand. A draft is a proposal, so what the dream does never changes the run's exit status;
  3. the rest of the run: the restore test on the first Sunday of the month, doctor, the outcome in state/last-run.json, the message when something is wrong, then, when the notifier is set, the morning message of the daily loop;
  4. one summary line: scheduled run, the close (dream caught up): clean; state/last-run.json, or (no dream command), (no dream entry), (dream --catch-up exit 1).

The runs at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00 never dream. If your day begins later than 06:00, the close still runs at 06:00: the catch-up drafts the days that have ended, and the one that has not waits for the next morning.

docs.title: On a machine nobody logs in to: --system
docs.text:
An agent runs while you are logged in. The record's home (ADR 0022) is often a machine nobody logs in to, where an agent never loads. --system writes the schedule for the system domain instead, as logbook serve --install-service --system does for the pages: two launchd daemons (UserName you, HOME your home directory) or two pairs of system units (User= you, EnvironmentFile= your sync.env by its path), with the same four times, written to your home directory, and the two sudo commands that copy them into /Library/LaunchDaemons (or /etc/systemd/system) and start them printed, never run:

$ logbook sync --install-schedule --system
…
written: 2 files for the system domain, running as ines from boot: …; nothing runs until you install
them, as an administrator:
  sudo cp /Users/ines/org.logbook.sync.plist /Users/ines/org.logbook.sync.close.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons
  sudo launchctl bootstrap system /Library/LaunchDaemons/org.logbook.sync.plist /Library/LaunchDaemons/org.logbook.sync.close.plist

Installing again over copies already there prints the commands that stop and replace them; run as root, it is refused (the jobs would run as root, with root's home). --uninstall-schedule --system removes the copies in your home directory and prints the commands that stop the jobs and remove the system's. Moving from the agents to the daemons, remove the agents (--uninstall-schedule): with both, every run happens twice, and doctor says so.

docs.title: What the scheduled run does
docs.text:
sync --scheduled is sync --all followed by doctor, and nothing you could not run by hand (the 06:00 run adds the dream's catch-up after the sync, above):

  1. sync --all: every configured live source in turn, each from its own watermark, a failure in one never stopping the next, printed exactly as sync --all prints it (the tour), except that a source with no watermark yet reads its last 14 days and not its whole history (below).
  2. The restore test, on the first Sunday of the month, once that day: the latest snapshot of the last backup is restored into a temporary folder, verified there, compared with what the record said when the backup was taken, and deleted again (the monthly restore test). A record that seals tiers 2 and 3 needs its identity to open them: put LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE=<path> in sync.env or the test is skipped, and doctor says how to enable it.
  3. doctor: every check, printed as by hand.

The outcome goes to state/last-run.json, bookkeeping beside the sync watermarks, never in the chain and never in a backup:

{
  "at": "2026-10-08T17:00:12Z",
  "sources": {"immich": {"result": "ok", "lines": 12}, "gcal": {"result": "failed (status 1)", "lines": 0}},
  "doctor": {"pass": 12, "warn": 1, "fail": 0, "warned": ["sync:gcal"], "failed": []},
  "first_failing": "gcal  failed (status 1)",
  "clean": false,
  "week": [{"at": "2026-10-08T17:00:12Z", "clean": false, "lines": {"immich": 12}}],
  "weekly_sent": "2026-10-04"
}

at is when the run began. sources has one entry per source sync --all listed, with the lines it appended. doctor is the counts and the names of the checks that warned or failed. first_failing is the first line that was wrong, as the run printed it: a source's summary line, else the first doctor line that is not a pass. clean is no source failed and the doctor had nothing to say. week is one short entry per run of the last seven days, for the Sunday message. The file is written twice: once after the sync, so the doctor's own last-run line reads this run, and once at the end.

The exit status is 1 when a source failed or a check failed, as sync --all and doctor would exit. The run never prompts: a source that needs a value it does not have is skipped and said so, a sealed record without its identity skips the restore test, and the scheduler's log holds the output (~/Library/Logs/logbook-sync.log on macOS, journalctl --user -u logbook-sync.service on Linux).

docs.title: A source's first scheduled run
docs.text:
A live source you add to the schedule has no watermark yet, and a run that starts from nothing walks the source's whole history: every activity Google keeps for a Drive, twenty years of a mailbox, a photo library. That is a backfill, and a backfill is something you ask for, not something a timer does: one first scheduled walk of 1.25 million Drive activities used up the account's API quota for the day. So the scheduled run reads a new source's last 14 days and no more, and says so in one line:

drive: first scheduled run read from 2026-09-25; for the history run `logbook sync drive --since <date>`
  • Which run. sync --scheduled (and sync --scheduled --close), the command the installed agents or timers run and that nothing else passes; typing it yourself is the same run. logbook sync drive and logbook sync --all by hand start where they always did: from the watermark, or from the beginning for a source that has none. --since always wins.
  • Which source. One with nothing in state/<name>.json: no watermark, no marks of its own (mail and gmail keep theirs under resume), no walk under way. A source you synced by hand before carries on from where it is. A source whose record already holds lines (an export imported, which sync resumes from) starts from its newest line, less the source's lookback, when that line is inside the 14 days, and from the 14 days when it is older. A record restored from a snapshot has no state/, so every source is new to it: each reads its last 14 days, and a --since from before the snapshot's day reads what lies between. ais, adsb and telegram have no history to read (a stream, the present, the day of updates a bot keeps) and are never bounded, and weather asks about yesterday alone on its first run whatever runs it.
  • The 14 days are the record's local days, today included, from your day_start (midnight unless you set one), taken once per run from its own clock and the same for every source in it. They are counted in the source's own clock, as the watermark is: for a calendar, the events changed in those days; for Drive, the activity in them. The watermark after the run is what the run saw, as after any run, and the next scheduled run carries on from it.
  • The mark. Before it pulls, the bounded run writes "first_run": {"from": "2026-09-24T22:00:00Z", "day": "2026-09-25"} in the source's state file, and a run from it that finishes adds "complete": true. A run that fails or is interrupted, or one that found nothing in the window and so left no watermark, is followed by runs from that same instant, never from a window that slid on: nothing after it is skipped, an interrupted walk (immich) resumes, and the record refuses what a failed run already wrote. mail and gmail carry on from their own marks once a run from it has finished.
  • The history is yours to read when you want it: logbook sync drive --since 2020-01-01T00:00:00Z (an instant in UTC, as every --since but weather's, earlier than the day the line names: a day before it is always enough), or --restart for a source that walks a library (immich, mail, gmail). The record refuses the two weeks it already holds, the watermark never moves back, and the mark goes. Until then doctor says so on the source's own line — pass sync:drive configured (LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY, LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER); first run bounded to 14 days; history not read (before 2026-09-25: `logbook sync drive --since <date>`) — a note on a pass: nothing is broken, and a warn would send the message at every run for a history you may never want.

A dry run never waits out a source's quota or rate limit either: the first such answer (a 429, Google's rate-limit and quota 403s, GitHub's hourly limit) ends it on one line, exit 1, nothing written — sync: drive: dry run stopped at the source's limit after 0 lines: HTTP 429: Quota exceeded for quota metric 'Queries' and limit 'Queries per day' …. A run that writes waits the limit out as it always did.

docs.title: What doctor says about it
docs.text:
Two lines, in every logbook doctor, wherever it runs:

pass  last-run      2026-10-08 18:00 (2 h ago): immich 12, gcal 3 lines; doctor 14 pass, 0 warn, 0 fail
pass  restore-test  passed 2026-10-04 (2026-10-04T030000Z, 12,772 lines)
  • last-run is a warn when the last scheduled run is older than 26 hours (the schedule runs four times a day, so a day and a little means the machine was off or the agents are gone), or when it failed (a source failed, or a check failed), with the first failing line. The run is the record's state/last-run.json, read the same whichever install wrote it: your agents or timers, the system's daemons or units (--system), or a schedule on another machine. No scheduled run yet is a pass on a machine with no schedule, saying how to install one, and a warn where one is installed and has not run. Both installed at once — the agents and the daemons, the user timers and the system's — is a warn whatever the run said, since every run then happens twice: keep one (--uninstall-schedule, or --uninstall-schedule --system for the system's).
  • restore-test is a pass when a restore test passed within 35 days (the first Sundays of two months are at most five weeks apart), a warn when there has been none, the last is older, or it was skipped, each saying what to do, and a fail when the last test failed, with the reason.

docs.title: What it tells you, and when
docs.text:
The scheduled run can send one Telegram message. It is off unless both variables are set, in ~/.config/logbook/sync.env beside the sources' keys:

LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_TOKEN=<the bot's token, from BotFather>
LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_CHAT=<your chat id with the bot>

Without them nothing is sent and nothing is said about it. With them, the run sends one message, and only when:

  • something is wrong: a source failed, or doctor warned or failed; or
  • it is Sunday evening (the 18:00 run, or any run on a Sunday at or after 18:00 local in the record's timezone), once a week, with the week's counts.

Nothing is sent when nothing is wrong and it is not Sunday evening. The format is fixed. The first block is the alert, the second the week; both in one message when both apply:

logbook 2026-10-08 18:00: something is wrong
sync: 5 sources: 3 ok, 1 failed (gcal), 1 skipped
doctor: 12 pass, 1 warn, 1 fail; fail: record; warn: sync:gcal

logbook week to 2026-10-11: 14 runs, 13 clean
lines: immich 1,204, gcal 31; 1,235 in all
doctor: 13 pass, 1 warn, 0 fail
restore test: passed 2026-10-04

A message carries counts, source names and check names, and nothing else: never a line's content, never a name from the record, never a check's detail (the detail is in state/last-run.json and in logbook doctor, on the machine). The token is never printed, not in the log either. A standing warn (an extra not installed, a source whose key is missing) is a message every run until it is fixed at its source: disable the source in policy/import.json, install the extra, or set the key. That nagging is the point: the earlier set-up had weekly dumps and monitors that spoke up when something broke, and the record has had the pieces without anything running them or saying so.

Who authorised the call. No logbook command talks to a third party unless you ask it to by name (the project's rule: never a network call on a default path). Installing the schedule is that ask: sync --install-schedule, run by you, is the explicit command that authorises the scheduled run's one request to the Telegram Bot API when the variables are set. sync --all by hand sends nothing, doctor sends nothing, and --uninstall-schedule ends it. A test points the request at a local server through LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_API; you never need to set it.

A message the API refuses, or an endpoint that cannot be reached, is one line on stderr (notify: telegram: …) and never changes the run's exit status or what was written: the outcome is on disk before the message goes.

docs.title: The daily loop: the morning and the evening message
docs.text:
With the same two variables set, the schedule sends two more messages a day, each on its own and each at most once a local day:

Your Day page for 2026-10-16 is ready · 42 lines
https://logbook.example.org/day/2026-10-16

Your question for 2026-10-16: What were you glad of today?
  • the morning: after the 06:00 close, for the day it closed: the date, how many lines the day holds (a retracted line not counted), and the link to its Day page when LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_LINK_HOST names the host logbook serve answers on (logbook.example.org, or https://logbook.example.org:8443; https:// when no scheme is given). Without it there is no link. The Library reads only for this machine and your phone through Tailscale Serve (who may read it), so the host is the tailnet name logbook setup phone names (server.tail1234.ts.net); any other host's link opens a refusal.
  • the evening: at LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_EVENING_HOUR (a local hour, 0 to 23), the day's question, the one logbook digest closes with (the digest). Without the variable there is no evening message. An hour that is not one of the four runs is one more time the runs' job runs, set when you install the schedule (in the shell or in sync.env): change it, and install again.

Nothing else of the day is in either: no place, no person, no line's text, no source. A question the bank fills from the day (Was {proposed} with you?) would carry a name of the record, so it is not sent; the message says the question waits in logbook digest. The day each message last went out is kept in state/notify-daily.json, written before the request and given back when the request fails, so running the close again, or any later run of the day, sends nothing more, and a failed request is one line on stderr that a later run of the day may try again.

docs.title: A sealed record on this disk
docs.text: A record is sealed when logbook.json names its recipients ("recipients": [...], two or more; RFC 0029): every tier 2 and 3 line is written as ciphertext, and only a machine that holds the identity opens it. This page is about what a sealed record leaves on this machine's disk in plain text besides its own folder, and the one setting that changes it.

docs.title: What stays off the disk
docs.text:
On a sealed record, nothing read from its tier 2 and 3 lines is kept on this disk in plain text by default. The readings the Library and the commands keep between one head and the next stay in the process's memory for its life, and go when it stops:

  • The kept readings beside the index (the whole record's people, the promises, each person's last real contact, the orgs, ideas, places, gaps, agents' sessions and the World's years: <cache dir>/logbook/<owner_id>/*.json on a record that seals nothing). Every such file left there from before, whatever reading kept it, and any a crash left half written, is removed by the first reading of the record in each process.
  • The review pages' tables of observed people, orgs, ideas, assets and places, which a record that seals nothing keeps in index.sqlite. Rows left there from before are removed by the next reading.
  • The Library's built pages (built ahead): logbook serve --built renders every page as it is asked for, to its end as live does, and says so when it starts; logbook serve --build refuses in one sentence, and the 06:00 close says the build is off. A build left from before is removed. No page is built, not even one of tier 1: it still names who is who from the resolutions, which are tier 2.

The cost is time, not correctness: a server reads the whole record once after it starts, where a record that seals nothing would bring a kept reading forward, and every page is rendered as it is asked for. Each page is the same either way.

docs.title: plaintext_cache: keeping them on the disk
docs.text:
To keep those readings and pages on this disk anyway, set plaintext_cache in logbook.json:

{
  "...": "the keys already there, unchanged",
  "plaintext_cache": true
}

Off by default; absent, false or anything but true is off. With it on, a sealed record keeps its readings, tables and built pages on this disk as a record that seals nothing does: in the cache folder beside the index, never in the record's folder, each file 0600 and the folders 0700, so only this machine's user reads them, and a copy of the record never carries them. They then hold, in plain text, what the Library shows of the sealed lines. No command writes this setting yet: edit logbook.json by hand, keep it valid JSON, and leave seq and head as they are. Turning it off again removes the readings and pages the next time each would be kept.

This was decided for v1 in RFC 0047 §15 (question 11); the owner may revisit it.

docs.title: What is on the disk regardless
docs.text:
• The index, index.sqlite, in the cache folder. For every line, sealed or not, it holds the envelope (its seq, id, time, local day, kind, source, tier, end) and where the line is in its file. For a sealed line opened with the identity it also holds, in plain text, a few fields of the opened payload that readers look lines up by: the id it supersedes, the entity a resolution mints, the digest of its attachment, the subject of a point, and a point's lat and lon. Its raw_id is blinded (RFC 0029 §8). These columns are the index's own, decided in RFC 0029 §8, and this setting does not change them.
  • Rows removed from index.sqlite can stay in the file's free pages until it is written again whole. To be sure none of them is left after you turn plaintext_cache off, delete index.sqlite (it is a cache: the next command builds it again, ADR 0007).
  • The browser's own cache of the pages you opened, as for any site.
  • What you export or hand on yourself: a vault, a site, a crossing, a relationship store, a dream's input. Each is a command you run, and each says where it writes.

docs.title: Search
docs.text:
logbook search TEXT [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--until YYYY-MM-DD] [--kinds note,transcript,message,mail,event] [--tier 1|2|3] [--limit N] [--standing] [--json] is full-text search over the record: the words of every line that carries any, found through the index and read back from the files, grouped by day with the row show prints and a snippet of the matching words. It is a reader (ADR 0013): it derives from the record at its head and writes nothing.

logbook search kari                          # every line with the word, tiers 1 and 2
logbook search "zürich hotel"                # both words, in any order, anywhere in the line
logbook search '"with kari"'                 # a phrase: the words in that order
logbook search 'kar*'                        # a prefix: Kari, Karin, Karlsen
logbook search kari --since 2026-06-01 --until 2026-06-30
logbook search standup --kinds event,transcript
logbook search invoice --tier 3              # tier 3 — money, health, the transcripts at 3 — only when you say so
logbook search kari --json                   # the query, the hits by day with rank, snippet and summary

docs.title: What it prints
docs.text:
2026-06-13 Saturday
  12:00  note       manual         Kari said the run was good
         [Kari] said the run was good
2026-06-11 Thursday
  11:00  mail       mail           ✉ Zürich hotel booking — Hotel Example → kari.nordmann@example.org
         …reservations@example.org · Hotel Example · Zürich hotel booking · [kari].nordmann@example.org
2026-06-10 Wednesday
  20:00  note       manual         Dinner with Kari at the cafe, running late
         Dinner with [Kari] at the cafe, running late
3 hits in 3 days

One block per local day, the latest day first; inside it one hit per line in time order. The first row of a hit is the line as logbook show prints it on its day — the local time, the kind, the source, the profile's own summary with senders, attendees and participants named as the record's resolution lines name them (RFC 0006). The second row is the snippet: up to sixteen words of the line's text around the match, each matching word in [brackets], … where the snippet cuts the text and · between two fields of the line (a title and its text, a mail's subject and its body). The last row counts. Nothing matches: nothing matches: <text>, and a reminder that tier 3 was not searched when it was not.

--json is one object: query (text, the FTS5 expression it became, since, until, kinds, max_tier, limit), hits, more (the limit was reached) and days, each with its lines — seq, id, at, kind, source, tier, rank, snippet and summary, the text part of the show row.

docs.title: The query
docs.text:
• A word matches the word itself, case and accents aside: zurich finds Zürich, cafe finds Café. It never matches a stem or an inflection: run does not find running, Haus does not find Häuser, in English or in German. The search is literal.
  • A run in double quotes is a phrase: the words in that order, adjacent. "with kari" finds Dinner with Kari, not Kari with. The shell wants the quotes protected: '"with kari"'.
  • A term ending in * matches by prefix: kar* finds Kari and Karlsen; "with kar*" the phrase with its last word a prefix.
  • Several terms must all match, anywhere in the line, in any order. There is no OR, no NOT and no field filter: AND, OR, NOT, NEAR, a colon and a caret are words like any other, so a search for kind:note looks for that text. A term with no letter or digit (-, *) is dropped; a query with none at all is refused.
  • Punctuation inside a word is a word boundary, as the index tokenises it: kari.nordmann@example.org is the phrase kari nordmann example org, so the address finds the mail and so does nordmann.

docs.title: What is searched
docs.text:
The index holds the words of every line of a kind that carries any: note, transcript, message, mail, event, task, highlight, voice-memo, browse, watch, listen, trip and journey (one profile under two spellings, RFC 0031: asking for either kind searches both). A location point, a photo, a health sample, a call, a flight or a crossing has no words and no row — searching Oslo finds the notes and mails that say it, never the ten thousand points whose reverse geocode does. --kinds narrows to some of the twelve; any other kind is refused with the list.

For each line, every string in its payload at any depth is text: a note's words, a message's and the names its chat and sender show, a mail's subject, body and the names and addresses on it, a calendar entry's title, location, notes and attendees, a task's title and notes, a highlight's quote, a page's title and URL. Not the ids, digests, stamps and types (raw_id, sha256, path, media_type, thread, modified_at, status, …): nobody searches for those, and a snippet never shows one. A transcript's text lives in the attachment store, never inline (RFC 0004); the index reads it from there as the promises reader does — WebVTT, SRT, Granola's JSON or Speaker: text prose — and holds every turn as Speaker: text, so a sentence said in a meeting is found and the snippet says who said it. A transcript whose file is not in the store is searched by its title and participants alone.

The window is local days, inclusive, in the record's zone (--since, --until; the whole record without them). A retracted line is never a hit, and neither is a retraction. A line that is not standing because a later line of its own kind supersedes it (SPEC §3) is still a hit, marked: its row ends · superseded by #N, the line that took its place, in the words show uses for the kinds it marks (search marks every kind), and in --json every hit carries standing (true or false) and superseded_by (the id of that line, else null). A superseder that is itself retracted supersedes nothing, and a line of another kind naming it does not count, as every reader has it. --standing leaves the superseded hits out and lets the next by rank take their place, so --limit still counts standing hits; nothing is left out without it. The mark is read from the index's lines_kind_supersedes lookup, not from the search table, so no rebuild is needed for it.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text: Tiers 1 and 2 are searched by default. Tier 3 — money and health, and the transcripts the reference adapters write at 3 — is searched only with --tier 3, as export crossing crosses it only with --tier 1,2,3 and mcp serves it only with --allow-tier-3; --tier 1 searches tier 1 alone. No line is ever printed above the tier asked for, and a search that finds nothing says when tier 3 was left out.

docs.title: Ranking and the limit
docs.text: The hits are ranked by FTS5's bm25 — a line where the words are rarer and denser ranks higher — and the best --limit (50 by default) are kept, in the query, before anything is read from the files. What is shown is those hits grouped by day, latest first: the rank decides which lines you see, the day where you read them. When the limit was reached the last row says so; narrow the window or the kinds, or raise --limit. --json carries every hit's rank (lower is better).

docs.title: The index
docs.text:
The words sit in one FTS5 table, search, inside index.sqlite (schema 6), beside the lines table that locates every line: the rowid is the line's seq, the body its words, and kind, tier and day beside them so the query cuts the kinds, the tier and the window inside the table and the join to lines is one lookup per hit kept. The tokeniser is unicode61 — case and diacritics folded, no stemmer in any language — which is what makes the search literal.

The table is written as the index is: Logbook.append and append_many add each new line's words in the same transaction as its row, so a note added a second ago is found with no rebuild; logbook index rebuilds the table with the rest, reading every transcript's text from the store once; a record whose index was built by an earlier schema is rebuilt once, by the first reader that opens it. Like the rest of the index the table is a cache (ADR 0007): the files are the record, verify never opens it, and deleting index.sqlite loses nothing.

The cost of a query is the lines that contain the words, never the size of the record: a name in a record of two million lines answers in well under a second, the first time, from a cold file (tests/test_search.py, LOGBOOK_SLOW=1). A very common word — one in most lines — costs its matches, every one of them ranked; narrow with a second word or a window.

A Python whose SQLite was built without FTS5 (every official build has it; a distribution's may not) builds an index with no search table and logbook search says so and exits 1; every other reader is unaffected.

docs.title: In the Library
docs.text:
logbook serve has the same search at /search (logbook/contrib/search_page.py), under search in the navigation: a form with one field, the words as you would type them after logbook search, sent as a GET. It calls the two functions the command calls (search.query, search.search), so the words, the phrases, the prefixes, the ranking and the retracted lines are the command's own.

/search?q=kari                          every line with the word
/search?q=kari&kind=note                notes only (trip and journey are one kind, as with --kinds)
/search?q=kari&year=2026                lines of 2026 only, by local day
/search?q=harbour&kind=note&page=2      the next fifty
  • The tier is the page's. The hits are held to the Library's tier gate as every other page holds its lines: logbook serve reads every tier on this machine, as its Day and /line/ID do, so a search there finds tier 3 too; a gated page (export site's, a test's Site(tiers=…)) finds only what its gate lets through, and a hit above it is not on the page and not in a page's count; a gate of some tiers only (1 and 3) searches further until its page is full. The header says the highest tier among the hits shown.
  • A hit is one row under its day, the date a link to the Day: its local time, a link to the Day too, to the hit's own row on it for a note, a mail and a calendar entry (the kinds the Day lists as rows of their own; a message is under its conversation there); its kind; an excerpt of up to sixteen words around the match, each matching word marked (the command's [brackets], drawn; a bracket the record itself holds, [urgent] in a note, stays as written); and its line's id, a link to /line/ID, the line as the record holds it. A hit a later line supersedes says so as the command does, superseded by #N, a link to that line: the last correction the page's gate lets through, as the Day marks one, so a correction above the gate is never named.
  • The filters are links: every kind with words and every year the record runs over (its span, as the front page says it, whatever the gate), the filter in force in bold and every to take it off. They are never counted: a count would cost the matches of the words a second time, and would say how many lines a gate holds back. A filter that finds nothing says so in its sentence (In 2025, nothing in the record matches marina.). Nothing about a filter is kept in the browser: the address is the whole search, so it can be bookmarked, reloaded and sent back to.
  • The pages are links of fifty hits. The rank decides which page a hit is on, the day where it is read on that page, as the command does with --limit. Page 20 is the last (a thousand hits); past that, a kind or a year narrows the search.
  • An empty query is the form and nothing else. A query that finds nothing says so in one sentence.

The page is the Library's: one document with the Day's tokens and type, no script, nothing fetched, no reference but the server's own paths, nothing written, and phone width first, every link and control a 44 px target. No person is a filter and no number stands beside a name. An exported site (logbook export site) has no server to answer a form, and has no search.

A page of hits is kept by its tag like every page of the record (Site.etag): asked again at the same head, it is not searched again (a millisecond). Otherwise the cost is the command's: the matches of the words, never the size of the record. On the five-million-line synthetic record of scripts/bench_library.py (ten years, 4 vCPUs), a fresh query in a running server answers in 0.07 to 0.9 s — a name (kari, 205,000 lines) 0.63 s, a word (fjord) 0.45 s, a phrase ("running late", 346,000 lines) 0.87 s, a name and a word together 0.07 s, page 5 of fjord 0.46 s, each with its superseded hits marked — and kari from a cold disk, the first request after a restart with nothing in the operating system's cache, 1.5 s. A word in most lines costs its matches, every one ranked: the persona's surname, in 2.2 million of the five million, takes 4 s, as logbook search does. Narrow with a second word, a kind or a year.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: Not a question answered: it finds the lines that say the words, and ranks them; it does not read them for you. Not a scan: the MCP search tool still reads the standing lines of a window and keeps those whose payload contains the text, behind the crossing gate (mcp); this command is the ranked search through the table, for the owner at the keyboard, with the tiers as its only gate.

docs.title: The record in a browser
docs.text:
logbook serve reads the record in a browser, on this machine only.

logbook serve                     # http://127.0.0.1:8765/
logbook serve --port 8080
