Earlier and later move by the zoom's own step, never past the bounds.
  • Not yet placed: a chapter line with no first day, and the command that dates one.
  • Volumes: the years of the record as spines, this one being written, each a link to its days.

Through a gate (export site --tier 1, a page read at tier 1), Life shows no chapter, goal, name or reflection, each your own words at tier 2, and says so; the trips, the signed days and the silences are read at the gate's tiers. It reads no track over the whole record: the Year reads its year as /journeys does, and shares that reading with it; the Life zoom reads the marks the index hands out by kind and the days kept beside the index (the reading /gaps keeps).

docs.title: People
docs.text:
/people is the People door (RFC 0047 §4.3): who is in your life, and where you stand. The orbit draws you at the centre and the people the record names on four rings: Home (someone who spent at least 30 nights of the year with you at a place places.json calls home), Family (someone who carries your family name as the record spells you: policy/owner.json's names, your own resolution lines' labels, an address of yours that reads given.family@), Friends (a call, a message or a night together this year) and Everyone else. The record holds no "family" or "friend" of its own, so the ring is a rule's reading, set in pencil with the rule on hover. The order is closeness: the people you live with first, always (they sit on the innermost ring), then days together in the last year (or in the year ?year= names), then calls and messages, then how long the record has known them. It is never shown: no number stands beside a name anywhere on the door. The closest 30 are drawn; the rest are listed A to Z under "Everyone else".

Beside the orbit (below it on a phone) is the thread of the person ?sel=ID names, or of the closest: the ring, the name, the last real contact in words ("A call, three weeks ago."), the five newest moments (today's open item, what is coming up with them, the days together, a stay away as one span, calls, entries, recordings, messages back and forth, each a link to its day), the beginning (the first day the record holds with you both, or how to give one: logbook with DAY "NAME"), the promises open both ways and two links on: your years together (on Life, once that door is built) and the places you have shared. A thread is read from the index's rows of the person's lines, never the lines.

Under them, Heard in the last year (or in the year ?year= names) lists the people heard then, in the same order, as the People page always listed them: each name a link to their whole thread, the last real contact, and the evidence folded, uncounted. No count stands beside a name; the order says it.

Review. Below the list is the review queue of logbook people review (people), in its order: each observed person (what one source saw: an address, a number, a spoken name) proposed against someone the record names, with the score and the evidence open, and two acts. Merge writes what people review --accept N writes: an alias line per identifier the observed person was seen as, through people_review.accept. Not the same person writes what --reject N writes: one people-review/v1 line saying the two are not the same, through people_review.reject, so the pair is never proposed again (RFC 0035 defines that one verdict, so the act is a pair's, not a verdict that someone is no person at all). The observed people that match nobody are folded below. This section is the only place an observed person appears on any page. Both acts post to /people/review, from this machine only; a proposal no longer in the queue is a 409.

/people/ID is one person's whole thread: the person's page's facts, each with its evidence folded (the days together and nights under one roof counted, the last real contact and what it was, the drift); the days together as a strip over the years, one mark per day and each a link to it, then counted by year; every moment newest first; the promises open both ways, the day each was said and is due; the anniversaries of the coming month; what was said, the words of the last few messages and recordings read only when asked (?said=1, as an org's money is); the places shared; what a model drafted about them (draft/v1, unit person) in pencil, with the lines it rests on, under the relationship entry it was written under, a sentence that sets a figure beside a name held; and how the record knows them (the addresses its resolution lines bind to them). ?at=DAY marks that day's moment.

docs.title: The Manifest
docs.text:
/manifest is the shelf of RFC 0037 §11, the orgs you named (review org), each under what you decided about it (logbook status org): holding (hold, add, sell), exited, passed (the anti-portfolio, each with your reason in full), let go, then no status; within a heading the most recent touch first. A touch is a line that reaches the org through one of its refs: a mail or a meeting with an address at its domain, a transcript one of its people spoke in, a page or an act on its code-host org, its group chat, its merchant. Each row is the org (a link to its page), the status and since when, its portfolio, stale when the status is one stale_days names in policy/entities.json and nothing has touched it or restated it for that long (a hold, three years), the last touch and what it was, the people on its lines and the documents, with the evidence folded: the last touch's line and the status line. It is the text of logbook show orgs (orgs read back). Above the shelf, the portfolios your orgs are in (RFC 0037 §10.2): each a link to /manifest?portfolio=…, the shelf of the orgs that portfolio holds and the people across them, as show orgs --portfolio prints it, case and spaces aside.

Review. Below the shelf is the review queue of logbook review org (review), in its order, twenty a page: each observed org proposed against one you named, or as a new one, with its score, its hint and its evidence folded. Accept writes what review org --accept N writes, one entity/v1 line binding what the sources saw to the org; Name, for a new one, what --name N "…" writes, the org minted (its dedupe key looked up first) under the name in the field; No what --reject N writes, one entity-review/v1 line, so the pair is never proposed again. They post to /manifest/review and go through entity_review.accept and reject, the functions the command calls, so the lines are the command's byte for byte.

/org/ID is one org (RFC 0037 §7): its refs, its status, reason and portfolio, the status form, which posts to /manifest/status and writes what logbook status org ORG DISPOSITION [--reason "…"] [--at DAY] [--portfolio "…"] writes through entity_status.write (one status/v1 line, tier 3, your reason and your portfolio on it and never a note), every touch newest first (thirty, the rest folded), the people, who introduced whom where a mail's subject says so (Intro: Ines <> Liv), the documents as references, every status line with the portfolio it carried (a retracted one struck), and the proposals that would place something with it. The ledger is read only when you ask (show the money, ?money=1): its in, out and net per year and its lines on the timeline, derived at read time from the transactions the org's merchant refs match.

The status form's portfolio box shows the portfolio that holds the org. Left as it is, the line carries no portfolio, as the command without --portfolio; typed, it carries what you typed, as --portfolio "…"; emptied, it clears the portfolio, as --portfolio "". The form also sends what the box showed, so a page older than the record never puts back a portfolio that has moved since: a box left alone moves nothing.

/manifest/people is the co-investor graph: everyone who appears with more than one org, the most orgs first, with the orgs and the tier of the lines that put them there; then the anti-portfolio.

Tier 3 stays tier 3. An org's status, its reason, its portfolio and the money are tier 3. The pages read the record through the server's gate; logbook serve reads every tier, on this machine. Through a gate without tier 3 there is no status, no reason, no portfolio and no money on any of them, every org is under no status, and the shelf says how many status lines it may not show; no filter by portfolio is offered, and one asked for lists no org, the same page for every portfolio; a person who is with an org only on a tier-3 line is no edge of the graph. Such a page offers no act either, neither the queue nor the status form, and refuses both (403): a status is tier 3, and so may a no be. logbook export site has no Manifest: its pages are the Day, the days, the trips, the places, and none of them names an org's status.

Writing, never waiting. The acts are POSTs from this machine only (a loopback client, an Origin of 127.0.0.1 when the browser sends one, else 403), one at a time, under the record's writer lock. While another command holds it the act is answered as every act of the Library is (409, the one sentence, the command that holds the lock, the form kept; above), and nothing is written (the owner's word for every act of the Library, 14 October 2026); a proposal no longer in the queue, or an org the record no longer names, is a 409 too; an answer the record refuses (a passed with no reason, a day ahead) a 400. Done, a 303 back to the page the form came from.

docs.title: Ideas
docs.text:
/ideas is the Ideas shelf of RFC 0037 §11, the ideas you named (review idea), each under what you decided about it (logbook status idea): build, exploring, spark, built, killed, then no status; within a heading the most recent touch first. A touch is a line that reaches the idea through one of its refs, as review idea finds them: a Notion page under its root (a database row is its own root), an act on its repository or a link into it, a task or a call of its title. A line a bot made or an agent wrote (extra.machine), and a relations line, is never one. Each row is the idea (a link to its page), the status and since when, your reason (the latest you gave, with its status and day when a later status replaced it), stale when the status is one stale_days names and nothing has touched it or restated it for that long (an exploring, two years), the last touch and what it was, the words written this year, its repositories, how many people it was discussed with and never their names, the days since its spark and its latest titles, with the evidence folded: the last touch's line, the status line and the reason's note. It is the text of logbook show ideas (ideas read back).

Review. Below the shelf is the review queue of logbook review idea (review), in its order, twenty a page: each observed idea proposed against one you named, or as a new one, with its score and its evidence folded. Accept writes what review idea --accept N writes; Name, for a new one, what --name N "…" writes, the idea minted (its dedupe key looked up first) under the name in the field; No what --reject N writes, one entity-review/v1 line. They post to /ideas/review and go through entity_review.accept and reject, the functions the command calls, so the lines are the command's byte for byte. A Notion row is proposed only when its Type is Idea (idea_rows in policy/entities.json).

/idea/ID is one idea (RFC 0037 §7): its refs, its status and reason, the status form, which posts to /ideas/status and writes what logbook status idea IDEA DISPOSITION [--reason "…"] [--at DAY] writes through entity_status.write (with a reason, first one note/v1 line in your words, then the status/v1 line naming it, both tier 2, RFC 0037 §10.5), first said, every touch newest first (thirty, the rest folded), the people it was discussed with by name (the only page that names them), its documents as references, its title thread, the words by month, every status line (a retracted one struck), and the proposals that would place something with it.

Writing, never waiting. As on the Manifest: the acts are POSTs from this machine only, one at a time, under the record's writer lock; while another command holds it an act is answered as every act of the Library is (409, the one sentence, the command that holds the lock, the form kept; above), and nothing is written (the owner's word for every act of the Library, 14 October 2026); a proposal no longer in the queue, or an idea the record no longer names, is a 409; an answer the record refuses (a killed with no reason, a day ahead) a 400. A page read through a gate without tier 2, an idea's status's tier, offers no act and refuses both (403). logbook export site has no Ideas.

docs.title: Phone first
docs.text: Every page is one column that works at 400 px: the navigation wraps, a row is a short head and its facts with the evidence folded under it, a day never breaks inside its hyphens, the canvas scales to the column, and on every page (the Day's Sources, the days, the trips, the places, the assets, the gaps; in the server and in an exported site) a table wider than the column scrolls inside its own box rather than the page sideways. tests/test_library_walk.py walks the pages the server serves, from / through the links on every page it reads, one page of each kind (the Day, every shelf, the Manifest, each detail page, an error, a redirect), and holds each to that column without a browser; the list of pages it must reach is read from the server's own routes, so a page added there and not walked fails it. tests/test_library_pages.py and tests/test_manifest_page.py hold the four years' widest shelves and the Manifest's pages besides, and tests/test_ideas_page.py the Ideas shelf and an idea. tests/phone_width.py parses each page with every disclosure open, applies the page's own stylesheet as a 400 px phone would (its phone breakpoint included), and fails when an element's fixed width, min-width or row of columns, with the margins, borders and padding around it, passes the column, when an image or a pre has no max-width to keep it inside, or when the stylesheet has no phone breakpoint. Its estimates err wide, and a stylesheet it cannot read fails the test rather than passing it. The Day is held to the column like every other page: its Sources table, wider than the column on some days, scrolls inside its own box.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: Not an editor: the pages write nothing but the namings, the reviews, an org's or an idea's status, the reflection, the notes kept at the close, the signature, the stars and the company said above, and the captain's other words — a note, a confirmation of a line — go through the CLI as lines in the record, which the next page reads. Not a web application: no framework, no build step, no state but the record, and two inline scripts, a dozen lines for three keys and a score for one button. Not the circle (ADR 0009): a page here is for the owner's eyes on the owner's machine; a shared page is a signed bundle, and that is another layer.

docs.title: The record's settings
docs.text:
A setting is how you want the record read, not something that happened: it has no at, so it is never a line. The record's own settings live in logbook.json beside the chain's head; the readers' settings live in files beside the log, each yours to edit. logbook setup asks about the ones a first run needs, and logbook setup <setting> changes one later.

setting where set with your timezone logbook.json, timezone logbook setup --step timezone where your day begins logbook.json, day_start logbook setup day_start 06:00 the bounds of your life on the Library's Life door logbook.json, life by hand (below) your own addresses logbook.json, owner_emails logbook setup --step owner whether your phone writes through the Library logbook.json, phone (off by default) logbook setup phone --origin URL --login LOGIN (from your phone) whether a sealed record keeps readings on this disk in plain text logbook.json, plaintext_cache (off by default) by hand (sealing) your other names, addresses, numbers and handles policy/owner.json logbook setup --step owner; handles by hand your own bots, by the sender id Beeper gives them policy/agents.json logbook setup agents add SENDER --name NAME (your own agents) the named places, your home places.json logbook setup places the assets you track assets.json logbook setup assets the digest's questions policy/questions.json logbook setup questions what may leave, and to whom policy/crossing.json by hand (the signed day) how long a stay is, the night policy/stays.json by hand what names nobody's org, the review's thresholds policy/entities.json by hand (the profiles)

policy/owner.json is {"names": [...], "emails": [...], "phones": [...], "handles": [...]}: the ways the record meets you, so you are never your own company and never a person to review. handles are your logins on a service — ines-example, @ines-example, or github:ines-example for GitHub's alone, case aside — by which sync github and add github-export mark your own commits, issues and comments owner (GitHub). Every key is optional: a file written before handles existed lists none.

Changing a setting rewrites nothing: no line, no hash, no month file. The index is a cache of the record's days and is rebuilt when a setting it depends on changes (timezone, day_start).

docs.title: Where your day begins: day_start
docs.text:
Out of the box a day is the calendar day: from midnight to midnight in your timezone. If you live late, the concert that ended at 01:30 is the evening's, not the morning's, and the Day of the 13th should not open with it. day_start moves the line:

logbook setup day_start           # where it begins now: midnight unless you set it
logbook setup day_start 06:00     # a line before 06:00 belongs to the day before
logbook setup day_start 00:00     # back to the calendar day

The value is a clock, HH:MM, from 00:00 to 23:59. logbook init leaves it out, which is 00:00. With "day_start": "06:00" in logbook.json:

  • a line at 01:30 on the 13th is on the 12th; a line at 06:00 or 07:00 on the 13th is on the 13th; a line at 23:30 on the 13th is on the 13th, as it always was;
  • the day runs from 06:00 to 06:00 the next morning, and the Day says so in its header (2026-10-12 Monday · unsigned · 06:00 to 06:00 the next day);
  • the comparison is on your wall clock after localising, so the night the clocks change moves no line: at 06:00 on the last Sunday of October the day begins at 06:00, whatever the offset was at 01:30.

Every reader that puts a line on a day goes by it, from one rule in the code (logbook/core/day_start.py): the index's day_local, show, day and days, the nights before and after a day, trips, gaps (doctor sources --gaps), the digest and its week paper, promises, the rollups, the Year, people, the signed day's page and the crossing of signed days, the vault, the printed pages, the shared page, the MCP tools' days, and the pages logbook serve keeps, /today included (at 05:59 it is still yesterday's page). Nothing that writes goes by it: add, the adapters and the month files keep at as it is, in UTC.

The index. logbook setup day_start rebuilds the index under the new boundary when there is one, with progress, and says so; on a record without one it says the next reader builds it (or logbook repair index now). The index records the boundary it was built with, and a reader rebuilds it when logbook.json says otherwise, as it does when the head has moved. logbook doctor prints a day-start line when the day does not begin at midnight, and warns when the index was built under another boundary.

Signed days. The page of a day is the lines on the day so defined, and a signature covers that page. Moving the boundary moves lines between pages, so a signed day whose page changed reads as the page has changed since, exactly as it does when a line is appended to it; logbook setup day_start counts them (signed days: 3 of 41 no longer match their page). Read each again and sign it, or set the boundary back. Set it once, early.

The night. The night window of policy/stays.json (22:00 to 08:00) is unchanged: it finds the night's stay. day_start says which night is a day's: the night after a day is the one whose window holds the day's end, so with 06:00 the night after the 12th is where you were at 06:00 on the 13th, the night of the 12th, as at midnight. A boundary at or after the night's start (23:00, say) makes a day end inside the next date's night, and the night after the 12th is then the night of the 13th.

A value that is not a clock. "6am", "24:00" or "6:00" is refused by every reader that groups by day, naming the key and the value (logbook.json has day_start '6am', which is not a clock …), exit 2; nothing is guessed. add, verify and the adapters go on as before, since they never group by day, and doctor fails the day-start line until it is fixed. A reader that does not implement the rule (RFC 0036) must refuse in the same way; the conformance samples carry no day_start, so it passes as before.

docs.title: Your life: life
docs.text:
The Library's Life door (/life, serve) draws one line of your life, from its first day to a bounded future. The bounds are yours: two local days in logbook.json,

"life": {"from": "1986-07-01", "to": "2035-12-31"}

from is where the line begins (your birth, say), to where it ends; nothing is drawn past to, and from on or before to. Without it the line runs from the record's first day to the last day of next year, and never to the last line the record holds: a calendar entry in 2055 is not a reason to draw thirty years of nothing. There is no command that writes it yet: edit the file (a later logbook setup life may). A value that is not that shape is said on the page, in one sentence naming the key, and the line runs as without it. Changing it rewrites nothing and rebuilds no index.

docs.title: The shelves: promises, goals, agents
docs.text: Three shelves of the Library in logbook serve, after Ideas in the navigation. Each one only reads: there is no form on them and nothing is written. Each reads through the server's tier gate, as the other shelves do. A line above the gate is not listed, not counted and not reachable by its own address, and the page's header gives the highest tier it read. No page opens a connection or runs a model.

docs.title: Promises — /promises
docs.text:
These are the promises the record's own words suggest, as logbook promises reads them (promises), in three sections:

  • Open comes first, oldest first: your promises and what was asked of you, carried ones included.
  • Kept, newest first: closed by logbook promises done ID (a task line marked done), or kept on a signed day.
  • Dropped, newest first: closed by a task line marked cancelled, or dropped or missed on a signed day.

Each row gives who it is with, the sentence as written, the day it was said, the due hint, and the line it was read in, linked on its Day. In a conversation with one of your agents, the agent is named as the agent, never as a person. Rows are read by rules: they are proposals, not facts.

The local model's verdict shows where logbook promises --judge has already given one. The page uses the reader's own words, its parts apart: the judge's due day, then judged and its confidence, by whom and to whom. Nothing is judged here. A promise the judge set aside is not listed, as in logbook promises.

One person. /promises?person=NAME keeps the promises with one person: the counterpart, or a name the line resolves. The names to choose from head the page. An agent is never one of them.

One promise. /promises/ID shows the sentence, the sentences around it as the reader read them, the verdict, and the evidence. The evidence is the transcript (or note, mail, message) line it was read in, linked on its Day, plus the task line or the signed day that closed it.

The gate covers what closed a promise too. A task line or a signature above the gate does not close the promise on that page.

docs.title: Goals — /goals
docs.text:
Goals, reviews and chapters are your own words.

The page opens with the chapter you are in today, its rules, and any clash with another standing chapter. The other chapters are listed under it.

Then come the goals by horizon: life, this year, this quarter. Open goals come first. Each shows its standing wording, its state (open, done, let go, superseded, past), and the latest verdict you gave it with the day the verdict is for.

If there are no goals yet, the page says how to add the first:

logbook goal import ~/goals.txt      # one goal a line: `Sail the whole coast to Lofoten | life`

One goal. /goals/ID takes the id of any line of the goal's chain, the first wording included. It shows the goal, its earlier wordings, and every review newest first: the disposition, the period, the day, the note, and when it was written if that was later.

Goals, reviews and chapters are tier 2. A page whose gate does not read tier 2 says so, and shows none of them.

docs.title: Agents — /agents
docs.text:
These are your sessions with your own agents (your own agents), by day, latest first. Each page holds fourteen days (?page=N), and ?day=YYYY-MM-DD shows one day. The words of a session are read only for the days on the page. Sessions and bot chats are tier 2, as #279 wrote them (a --tier on import sets another), so a page that does not read tier 2 shows none and says so. A session is one of these:

  • a Claude Code session, or a conversation from the Claude apps' export: one standing transcript line (a session that grew is its latest line);
  • a day of messages with one Telegram bot.

Each session shows:

  • the source, and the agent's name;
  • the length: minutes, your turns and the agent's, the words on each side, and the tool calls, as the source counted them;
  • your words: the first three turns, each cut at 280 characters with the whole turn in a fold, and the rest folded whole;
  • the agent's summary: the provider's own summary when it made one. Otherwise it is the title the source gave the session (Claude Code's own summary, the apps' name for a conversation), when that is not your own first line;
  • the agent's words, folded whole and marked as machine text.

A session at a lower tier than the review that names it (below) is shown at the review's tier.

A forward you sent a bot is someone else's words. It is never shown as yours.

docs.title: Which goal a session served (provisional)
docs.text:
A session served a goal only when a review of that goal says so. The review names the session's line (or one of its messages) under extra.lines:

{"schema": "review/v1", "goal": "<goal line id>", "disposition": "advancing", "period": "day",
 "note": "the planner session", "extra": {"lines": ["<session line id>"]}}

The session then links the goal, and the goal's page lists the session. No goal is ever guessed from a session's words. extra is where RFC 0036 lets a review keep anything else; the key lines is this page's reading and is provisional until an amendment of RFC 0036 names it. No command writes extra.lines yet, so on a record today no session shows a goal.

docs.title: The signed day
docs.text:
Agents draft. The owner signs. Only signed days cross.

A record fills itself: the tracker writes the points, the mail import writes the threads, a calendar sync writes the entries, and an agent with MCP may run the adapters and draft. None of that is you reading the day. The signed day is: you open the page, you read it, and you say these are the day's facts. That sentence is one line in the chain, and it is the gate on what leaves the record.

logbook show 2026-06-09                 # read the page; the header says `unsigned`
logbook day 2026-06-09                  # the Day: the readiness row says whether every usual source is in
logbook day sign 2026-06-09             # sign it: every line on the page is confirmed, pencil aside
logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --confirm all          # signed before: confirm the whole page again
logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --note "Quiet day. The call with Kari was the thing."
logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --confirm 4181,4183   # only these lines, by seq or id as `show` lists them
logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --kept 4181 --carried 4183   # and what became of the commitments on them
logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --confirm none               # nothing on the page is a fact of the day
logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --at 2026-06-09T19:30:00+02:00   # signed when you clicked, not when this ran
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --audio evening.m4a --sign      # or close it by voice (below)
logbook serve                           # or on the Day page: Reflect, tick, Sign (below)
logbook show 2026-06-09                 # the header now says `signed 2026-06-10 08:15`

docs.title: What signing writes
docs.text:
One line, signed-day/v1 (RFC 0034, docs/rfcs/0034-the-signed-day.md), tier 1, source manual, appended through the same append every other line goes through. It carries:

  • the day signed, and you as its subject (the record's owner_id);
  • the ids of the lines you confirmed, in the page's order: every line on the page but pencil (below) unless --confirm names some, or none at all with --confirm none (below); a day you signed before keeps what you confirmed then (below);
  • the digest of the page as shown: the SHA-256 over the hashes of the lines the page listed, in order. Not over the text: the words are a reader's own, the lines are the record's. Anyone with the record recomputes it, and a day that grew after you signed is seen to have;
  • an optional one-line note, in your words, tier 1 because it crosses with the day;
  • when the day was signed before, the id of the signature this one supersedes;
  • optionally, what became of the commitments on the page (below): by line id, kept, missed, dropped or carried.

It rewrites nothing. A day that was wrong is corrected the way the record corrects anything, by new lines, and then signed again; the later signature stands and the earlier stays in the chain. Retracting a signature (repair retract SEQ) leaves the earlier one standing, or the day unsigned.

Signing again keeps your confirmations (RFC 0034 amendment 4). A day you signed before, signed again without --confirm, confirms what the standing signature confirmed and is still on the page, not retracted; a line added to the day since stays unconfirmed until you confirm it, so signing again never confirms a line you have not read (a line the act itself writes, an event you --accept or the reflection you sign with, is confirmed by it). The dispositions and the note come along too, and whatever you type wins: --kept 4183 on a line the earlier signature said was carried makes it kept, --note replaces the note and --note "" clears it. day sign says what it kept (keeps from the signature it supersedes (#812): 14 lines confirmed, kept 1, the note). --confirm all confirms the whole page, --confirm none nothing, and --confirm 4181,4183 just those: each is a fresh reading and keeps nothing. The Day page's Sign again, day reflect --sign and the door's sign_day follow the same rule.

Only you sign: here, on the Day page of logbook serve, or through the door when you allow it (below).

docs.title: Signing on the Day page
docs.text:
logbook serve is the Library, and its Day page is your own Sign path. At its foot, Reflect and sign takes your reflection (typed, the day's Wispr Flow draft offered prefilled, or a recording where this machine can hear one), shows the proposals the rules read in it as boxes, none ticked, and Sign signs the day through the code day reflect --sign runs: the ticked delegations written as notes, then signing.sign with every line on the page confirmed but pencil, your reflection among them, and the ticked dispositions in the signature. The line is byte for byte what logbook day reflect DAY --sign --accept N,N writes for the same reflection and ticks. A day you signed before is signed again, the new line superseding the standing one and keeping what it said, and the page then shows the signature with its page digest. It answers this machine only, and nothing is written until you click (serve).

It needs no policy. The page is not the door: it never reads policy/crossing.json, and the write list there may stay empty. The Purser, the orchestrator that builds your Day page elsewhere, remains an alternative front door, through sign_day below, and only when you name the tool in that list.

docs.title: Signing through the door
docs.text: An orchestrator that builds your Day page somewhere else, on a phone or a VPS, used to print a day sign command for you to run by hand. When you name it in policy/crossing.json, {"mcp": {"max_tier": 1, "write": ["sign_day", "note_day"]}}, it carries your verdict back itself through the MCP tool sign_day (ADR 0022, RFC 0034 amendment 3): the same arguments as the flags, confirm, kept, missed, dropped, carried, note and at, the same checks, the same supersession, through the same code, and the same line day sign would have written, byte for byte. It never waits for another writer and never signs a day more than 60 days back (write_window_days); without the entry it is refused in one sentence. Its companion note_day keeps the proposals and your notes on the day as note/v1 lines, so the page can be rebuilt from the record alone (the MCP server).

docs.title: What the readers say
docs.text: logbook show DAY prints the state in its header, 2026-06-09 unsigned or 2026-06-09 signed 2026-06-10 08:15, and lists a signature on the day it was written as any line. logbook day DAY prints the same after the weekday, with , the page has changed since when a line was added to the day after you signed, and carries it in --json under signed: when, which line, how many lines were confirmed and on the page, the page digest, whether the page still matches, the note.

docs.title: Dispositions: what became of the commitments
docs.text:
A page has commitments on it: a note that says "I'll send the mooring photos by Friday", a transcript in which you said you would book the crane. The evening you sign the day is when you know what became of them, so the signature can say so (RFC 0034, amendment 1):

logbook day sign 2026-06-09 --kept 4181 --missed 4190 --dropped 4192 --carried 4183,4185

Each flag takes lines by seq or id as show lists them, and a line given one is confirmed by that, whatever --confirm says. The four words:

  • kept: it was done. promises closes it.
  • missed: it was not, and you say so. promises closes it and says missed on 2026-06-09.
  • dropped: you let it go on purpose. promises closes it, with nothing to flag.
  • carried: still open, taken to a later day. promises keeps it open; you dispose of it when you sign the day it was kept or missed on.

A line that is not on the page, a retracted line, a line named twice (in one flag or two, by seq or by id) and a flag that names no line are each refused in a sentence, and nothing is written. The field is optional: a signature without it is what it always was.

On a signed day logbook day prints the symbol before each line you disposed of, on the line's own row: ✓ kept, ✗ missed, – dropped, → carried; an unsigned day, and a line given none, print as before. --json carries the map under signed.dispositions. show lists the counts on the signature's row (kept 2, missed 1). logbook promises reads the standing signature of each promise's day: kept and dropped are done, missed is done and flagged, carried is open, and --open hides the first three. The crossing carries the field with the line.

docs.title: Confirming nothing, and the moment you signed
docs.text:
Two things a day signed from a phone needs (RFC 0034, amendment 2).

--confirm none. You read the page, you untick every proposed fact, and the day is still signed: the line carries an empty confirmed, the page digest is still over what you were shown, and the header says signed as for any signature. The day's lines cross with it, as the lines of any signed day do: the gate is the signature, not the list. The word goes alone: --confirm none,4181 and --confirm none --kept 4181 are each refused in one sentence, because a line given a disposition is confirmed by that. --confirm "" is still refused as naming no line, so an empty shell variable never signs a day by accident; you type the word.

--at RFC3339. The signature carries the moment you clicked, not the moment the command ran: --at 2026-06-09T19:30:00+02:00, with an offset or Z, stored in UTC like every at in the record and shown by show and day in the record's local time (signed 2026-06-09 19:30). Three things are refused, each in a sentence with nothing written: a moment that is not RFC 3339 with an offset or Z (the message shows the shape); a moment more than five minutes ahead of this machine's clock (a phone runs a few minutes fast, never hours); and a moment before the day you are signing starts, in the record's zone. Without --at, the signature is at now, as before.

When the day begins at day_start. The day starts where the record says it does (settings), and --at is checked by the same rule the index puts every line on its day by, so the moment you sign and the page you sign agree. With "day_start": "06:00", 01:30 on the 10th is still the 9th: day sign 2026-06-09 --at 2026-06-10T01:30:00+02:00 signs the 9th, whose page is its lines up to 06:00 on the 10th, the lines day 2026-06-09 shows, and the same moment for the 10th is refused, since the 10th has not begun (--at … is before 2026-06-10 starts at 06:00 in Europe/Oslo). The check is made when a signature is written and never again: a signature already in the record stands as it was written, even one whose moment would be too early under a boundary set later. No signature records the boundary it was signed under; one written before day_start was set was signed under midnight. Its page is read under the boundary the record has now, so a page the move changed reads the page has changed since until you sign it again (RFC 0036).

docs.title: Closing the day by voice
docs.text:
At the end of the day you say a few sentences about it: what went out, what did not, what you will do tomorrow, what Ola should do. logbook day reflect makes that the close of the day. The words become part of the record, and what you said about your commitments, and about what others should do, is proposed to you, so that the day can be signed with it in one go.

logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --audio evening.m4a        # a recording, heard on this machine
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --text "The photos went out. Ola should book the ferry."
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --mic 60                   # on macOS: sixty seconds from the microphone
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09                            # the Wispr Flow dictation that begins with "reflect"
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --from-wispr               # take that dictation as it is
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --dry-run                  # what it would write, and nothing written
logbook day reflect 2026-06-09 --sign --accept 3,6        # sign the day with the proposals you accept

The reflection is one note/v1 line on the day (RFC 0010: tier 2, as every note is, whoever writes it), source reflect, with reflection in its labels, the same convention note_day uses through the door, and written through the same code. --text is typed; --audio FILE is heard by the local whisper engine of the openlogbook[transcribe] extra, exactly as derive transcripts hears a voice memo: nothing leaves the machine, the hub is offline while it listens, and a model that is not on the machine stops the command until you run it once with --fetch-model. Without the extra, --audio says which extra to install; --text always works. --mic SECONDS records from the default microphone on macOS with ffmpeg, then hears it the same way, and keeps no recording; elsewhere, without ffmpeg, or with no microphone, it says so in a sentence. The reflection is printed back a sentence a line, numbered. Without --sign, nothing else is written. The same words already on the day are not written twice: run the command again and it reads the reflection that is there.

The Wispr Flow convention. If you dictate with Wispr Flow all day, there is no new habit: a dictation that begins with the word reflect is the reflection. The first word counts, in any case, after any spaces and punctuation: "Reflect: a long day on the water...", "reflect, the photos went out...". The word must be reflect itself; "reflection" or "reflecting" does not count, and neither does the word later in a dictation. logbook day reflect DAY with no input offers the latest such dictation of the day as the draft, without that word: on a terminal you answer y to take it, e to type it again as it should read, or n to leave it; elsewhere it prints the draft and writes nothing until you say --from-wispr. --from-wispr SEQ takes the dictation with that seq instead. The note keeps the dictation's id under extra.dictation and the moment you spoke as its at, and a dictation taken up is not offered again. The dictation itself stays what Wispr Flow made it, tier 3; the reflection is a note and tier 2, because you confirmed it as one.

The proposals are read out of the reflection by rules, no model, with the cue tables promises uses, and printed numbered, each with its evidence; every one is a guess until you accept it:

  • commitment — a sentence that reads as your promise: "I'll fix the bilge pump on Saturday", "ich werde die Rechnung morgen bezahlen", with the day its date phrase names. The reflection is a note in your words, so promises lists it from the reflection itself; accepting it writes nothing more.
  • delegation — what someone else should do: "ask Ola to ...", "tell Ines to ...", "Ola should ...", "Ola must ...", "Ola soll ...", "frag Ines, ob ...", "Ola, can you ...", with the name as you said it. A name is a capitalised word or two that is not a pronoun or a day and does not follow an article ("Die Fähre soll ..." asks no one). Accepted, it is one more note/v1 line on the day, label delegation, extra.to the name and extra.reflection the reflection's id: no profile promises reads requests from fits a request you make of someone else, so it is a note, in your words.
  • kept, missed, dropped, carried — a sentence that says what became of a commitment already on the day's page: "went out", "done", "sent" for kept; "didn't", "not yet" for missed; "drop", "forget it" for dropped; "tomorrow", "next week" for carried; and their German ("erledigt", "noch nicht", "vergiss es", "morgen"). The first such word in a sentence decides. The sentence must also be about the commitment: its words and the commitment's (casefolded, three letters or more, a plural s dropped, function words, days and the disposition's own words left out) overlap by a Dice coefficient of 0.5 or more, reflect.MATCH; the best match wins. "The mooring photos went out to the harbour office" matches "I'll send the mooring photos to the harbour office by Friday" at 0.89; "The harbour office sent a letter about the berth fee" shares two of its five words with it, 0.4, and is no reference. Accepted, the disposition goes into the signature.

--sign signs the day after the proposals are printed, in one go, through the same signing.sign day sign calls. You say which proposals you accept with --accept N,N (or --accept none); on a terminal it asks y or n for each delegation and disposition, and q stops with nothing written. Without a terminal and without --accept, it prints the proposals and refuses, writing nothing. Then, under one hold of the writer lock: the reflection is written (unless it is on the day already), each accepted delegation is written, and the day is signed: the reflection and the delegations among the lines confirmed, the accepted dispositions in the signature, and --at (the moment you spoke, with an offset or Z, on the day) as both the reflection's moment and the signature's. The signature is byte for byte the one day sign DAY --kept ... --at ... writes over the same page. A day you signed before is signed again, superseding the standing signature as RFC 0034 allows, and keeping what it said: the lines it confirmed that are still on the page, its dispositions (an accepted one wins on a line they share) and its note, with the reflection added. Two accepted proposals that give one line two dispositions, a number no proposal has and a moment off the day are each refused before anything is written. Another writer holding the record (with --no-wait) and a head that moved while the page was read are the store's own errors, said in one sentence; nothing is retried. --note, --confirm and the four disposition flags stay with day sign.

Where it shows. logbook day prints the reflection in a section of its own, labelled reflection with the time you spoke: your words in your voice, below the header and above the record, the timeline and everything after it. The Day page of logbook serve shows it the same way, under Reflection, and at its foot lets you write it and sign the day with it (above). day --json carries it under reflection (line, seq, at, at_local, source, text), a key that is there only on a day that has one, so every other Day's object, the conformance sample's among them, is unchanged. The latest reflection standing is the one shown; retract it and the one before it stands. The reflection is still a note of the day like any other: show lists it, and the MCP tool day_lines returns it as it returns every note, under the ceiling.

docs.title: Events the dream proposed
docs.text:
When the morning's dream proposed events for the day (the dream), day sign and day reflect list them, numbered: from 1 under day sign, after the reflection's own proposals under day reflect. Nothing of them is written until you say so:

logbook day sign 2026-06-10 --accept 1                       # write the dinner, then sign
logbook day reflect 2026-06-10 --text "..." --sign --accept 2,4

Each one you accept is one event/v1 line, source owner, written before the signature and under the same hold of the writer lock, and confirmed in it. A number that names no proposal, a proposal confirmed already, one whose lines left the page since the dream, and --confirm none beside an accepted event are refused before anything is written. On a terminal, day reflect --sign asks y or n for each open proposal, the events among them.

The events listed are those of the draft the Day shows. A draft the dream entry of the crossing policy no longer allows is withheld with its proposed events (the dream, When the entry changes): none of them is listed, and --accept naming one is refused with the reason. When an earlier draft the entry still allows stands in on the Day, its own proposals are the ones listed. An event you accepted before the entry changed stays in the record: it is your line, not the model's.

docs.title: Keep and sign
docs.text:
Pencil is what a model or an agent wrote, and no signature confirms it, however it is signed (day sign, --confirm all, day reflect --sign, the Library's Sign, an agent's sign_day): the dream's draft, a note a model derived (a photo's description, a meeting's summary: extra.derived), and any line with source description or mcp. Naming one in --confirm or a disposition, by id or by its seq however written, is refused before anything is written; a disposition a signature made before this rule gave one is not carried into the signature that supersedes it. The page's digest still covers pencil: you signed what you were shown.

The dream's draft is pencil: nothing in it is yours until you keep it (RFC 0043, §5). logbook day DAY numbers what you can keep, after the proposed events: each proposed link keeps its own number (link 2), and each sentence learned, decided, about an idea, and the photo of the day is numbered after the last proposal, at the end of its row (keep 3). The numbers are the draft's, so they read the same under day sign and day reflect. day sign and day reflect --sign keep them, and more, before they sign:

logbook day sign 2026-10-20 --keep 3,5,2 --word calm
logbook day sign 2026-10-20 --keep 4 --revisit 4=2026-11-20 --mend 4="Kari sails on Saturday, not Sunday."
logbook day sign 2026-10-20 --done 1 --tomorrow 2 --let-go 3
logbook day reflect 2026-10-20 --text "..." --sign --accept 1 --keep 3 --word steady
  • --keep N,N: a sentence learned, decided or about an idea becomes one note/v1 line on the day, labelled learned, decision or idea, with extra.from the draft's id, extra.segment its part and place among the draft's sentences, and extra.proposal its part and the draft's words (so a later draft that says the same is shown kept, not proposed again); an idea's note carries the idea's id (extra.entity). A link becomes the entity/v1 line review idea (or review org) writes for it, binding what the line shows to the entity, with extra.from. The photo of the day becomes a star with the sentence as its note, as logbook star writes one (a keeper/v1 of lane memory).
  • --mend N="…": keep a sentence in your own words; the note carries them, and extra.from still names the draft.
  • --revisit N=YYYY-MM-DD: on a decision you keep, the day it comes back: extra.revisit, a day after the day you sign, which Looking back reads.
  • --word WORD: the day in a word, one of your own, as a note/v1 labelled word. One word, not a number, and one a day: a re-sign keeps the first, and to change it you retract it (logbook repair retract SEQ "another word") and sign again with --word.
  • --done T,T, --tomorrow T,T, --let-go T,T: the plan's tasks of the day answered, by the numbers logbook show plan DAY prints. Each answer is one note/v1 labelled task, the task's title its text (the plan).

Everything is checked before the first line is written, and one refusal writes nothing, in one sentence: a number the draft does not give, an event (--accept writes it), a sentence with nothing under it, one kept already, a photo starred already, --mend or --revisit for a sentence you did not keep, a revisit that is not a later day, a word that is two words or a number, a second word on the day, a task given two answers, one show plan does not list, one answered already. Then, under one hold of the writer lock, the lines are written in that order (the sentences, the links, the photo, the word, the answers), after the events you --accept and, under day reflect, after the reflection and before its delegations (RFC 0043 §5); then the signature, which confirms them. Signing again keeps them, as it keeps any line it confirmed, and never writes them twice. A busy record (another command writing) is said in one sentence and nothing is written. Bare logbook day DAY refuses these flags; day reflect takes them only with --sign.

A signature never confirms the draft (RFC 0043 §6 rule 3). A draft line on the page, the evening's dream of the day, is left out of confirmed by day sign, --confirm all, day reflect --sign, the Day page's Sign and the door's sign_day; --confirm or a disposition that names it is refused. The page digest still covers it, so you signed what you were shown. A day signed before this rule that confirmed its draft loses it on its next signature.

The Day page keeps and signs the same from one form, Keep and sign, in its evening shape and when a signed day is signed again: every box, field and choice is one of these flags, and the page writes these lines byte for byte (serve). --mend stays at the command line.

--keep sits one letter from --kept, the disposition: --kept says what became of a commitment on the page, --keep keeps the dream's pencil in ink. The door's sign_day takes neither --keep nor any of these: agents propose, you keep.

docs.title: Readiness: is the day all in?
docs.text:
Before signing you want to know whether everything that usually arrives has arrived. The Day's readiness row says, for six classes of source, whether the day has lines of it and which usual sources have not delivered:

  readiness     mail none · message present · meeting none · location present, missing dawarich · photo present · calendar present

The classes are mail, message, meeting (a transcript), location, photo and calendar. A source is usual for a class when it delivered that class on four in five of the logged days of the last four weeks and policy/import.json has not disabled it. none means nothing is in and nothing usually is; missing <source> names what has not come. It is computed from the record and the policy alone: no connection is opened, nothing is written. It is advice, not a gate: sign a day with the tracker missing when you know the phone was off.

docs.title: The gate on the crossing
docs.text:
logbook export crossing (RFC 0005, the package a member of your circle pulls) crosses, by default, only the lines of days you have signed: a line's day is the local day of its at, and a signature crosses with the day it signs. The console says how many lines were held back on unsigned days, and --unsigned crosses them too. The tier ceiling (ADR 0016) still applies on top: a tier-3 line on a signed day never crosses without the policy and --tier 1,2,3. The manifest records which it was (policy.signed_days, only or any), and so does the crossing/v1 line the export appends (policy.signed_only).

The shared page (export share day), the trip bundle, the vault and the site keep their own selections and are not gated by signatures.

A destination that should see only what you have looked at lately gets signed_within_days on its entry in policy/crossing.json (RFC 0036, draft): {"cloud-model": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2026-12-31", "signed_within_days": 14}} crosses, through that entry, only the lines of days whose standing signature you wrote in the last fourteen days, today included; a day unsigned or signed earlier crosses nothing but its header, the day and its signed state. Signing a day again refreshes it. Absent, there is no restriction, which is the behaviour above. The key is the entry's, not the command's, so it holds for every crossing that reads the entry, the shared page, the bundle, the vault, the site and the MCP read tools included, and --unsigned does not lift it; the tier ceiling and until apply on top, as always.

docs.title: In the conformance sample
docs.text: conformance/sample-logbook signs its first day on its last evening, so a verifier meets the profile and show 2026-03-01 prints signed in its header.

docs.title: The site
docs.text:
logbook export site <folder> [--tier 1|1,2] [--with-drafts] renders the readers as a folder of static HTML: one Year page per year, a Day page for each of its twelve picks, every Trip page, a Days index per year, the places and the people, written as plain files with relative links, one inline stylesheet each, no script, no image, nothing fetched. It is logbook serve written down — the same renderers, the same text — so the folder reads the same from a file manager, under any prefix on any web server, or in twenty years. It is an export, not a reader: it is tier-gated exactly like the vault (tier 1 by default, the shape of the record and no text of any note or message), and every run appends one crossing/v1 line to the chain so the record shows it left. Re-running rewrites only the files whose content changed.

logbook export site ~/Site                 # every year the record has a line in, tier 1
logbook export site ~/Site --tier 1,2      # notes, transcripts and mail cross too; needs the policy below
logbook export site ~/Site --with-drafts   # a model's drafts on the Day pages too, each headed with its model
open ~/Site/index.html                     # or serve the folder with anything that serves files

The demo persona's forty years are published this way, by the docs workflow on every push to main: bighydro.github.io/logbook/ines/ is logbook demo --years 40 --seed 1 exported with --tier 1,2, so a stranger can browse a life that never happened without installing anything (demo.md). The demo site is exported at tier 2, her notes and messages shown, because the person does not exist: the workflow writes the site entry into that throwaway record's policy/crossing.json, and her health and money, tier 3, stay off it as they stay off every site. One of her days is the way in, at the same path on every build since the seed is fixed: the June pick of 2025, a night at the cabin with Ola, days/2025-06-14.html.

docs.title: The folder
docs.text:
<folder>/
  index.html                    the root: the years with their days, trips, nights away and people
  years/2026.html               the Year, as `logbook year 2026 --html` writes it, with the site's navigation
  days/2026.html                the Days index: `serve`'s /days table over the year's days the record covers
  days/2026-06-13.html          a Day the Year picks, as `serve`'s /day/2026-06-13 renders it
  trips.html                    every trip of the record, one row each, linked to its page
  trips/trip-2026-06-15-2026-06-17.html   the Trip, as `logbook trip --html` writes it, the map inside
  places.html                   `serve`'s /places table
  people.html                   everyone confirmed present by a line that crosses, by days together
  people/kari-nordmann.html     one per person: the years together, the trips

A person's file stem is their name as a slug — lower-case ASCII letters and digits, anything else a dash, accents dropped (Zürich café is zurich-cafe, Bjørn is bjorn) — so it is a URL on any server and a file name on any platform with nothing to percent-encode; two names that fold to one slug are two pages, the second -2. A trip's is its id with dashes, trip-<first day>-<last day>; a year's is the year; a Day's is the day.

Every link is relative (../trips/trip-2026-06-15-2026-06-17.html) and every link resolves to a file in the folder; the test suite follows each one. A Day page is written for the Year's twelve picks alone, the days it renders in full — a page for every day would be fifteen thousand over forty years — so a pick's row in the Days index links its page, and any other day's row is an anchor (days/2026.html#2026-06-12), not a link.

docs.title: The pages
docs.text:
The Year is the page logbook year --html writes (year.md): days per country, nights, the trips (each linked to its page), the flights, the places by nights, the people by days together (each linked to their page), health and keepers by month, and twelve picks, one day a month, the Day rendered in full. Above it, the site's navigation: the root, the trips, the places, the people, the year's Days index, and the years either side.

The Day of each pick is serve's Day page (serve.md): the nights before and after, the country, the timeline with what attached to each stay and who was confirmed there — a note's own words when tier 2 crosses — the health line and the sources. Every toggle is open and there is nothing to submit: no Reflect and sign, no expand or collapse. Above it, the site's navigation, its year and its Days index; the days either side link their rows, and the fortnight around links the Days index at the fortnight's first day. Like the root and the tables, it needs no sideways scroll on a phone; a table wider than the column scrolls inside itself.

The Trip is the page logbook trip --html writes (trips-shared.md for what it holds): the route as an inline SVG map, the stays with their nights, the legs, the days from the leaving day to the return day, the flights in and out, the people confirmed (linked) and proposed, the nights aboard, the keepers, health and spend. A trip across New Year is one page, found whole from its first day, though each Year lists its own part of it.

The Days index is serve's /days table: one row per day the record covers in the year, the night after, the kilometres moved, the flights, the stays and what attached to them, the people confirmed, the health line and the usual sources that went quiet. The form and the pager a server offers are not on a static page; the row's date is its anchor, and a pick's date links its Day.

Places is serve's /places table of places.json. People is a table of everyone a crossing line confirms present — days, nights, the years, the last contact, the trips — and each person's page lists the years together with the places shared, and the trips.

docs.title: A model's drafts (pencil)
docs.text: What a model drafted — a day's draft, its week's, a call's synthesis (logbook dream, RFC 0036) — is pencil, never the owner's ink, and a site leaves it out: no Day page and no Year pick carries a draft, its words, the line that points to its week, or the model among the day's sources. --with-drafts puts them in, each headed as the Day page heads it, draft · model:qwen2.5-7b-instruct · read at …, so a reader sees it is a model's text and which model wrote it; the footer of the Day, Days and Places pages says so too. A draft is held to the site's --tier and to the dream entry of policy/crossing.json either way, as on the Day page. The owner's own reflection (day reflect, tier 2) is not a draft: it is on its day whenever tier 2 crosses, flag or not. The crossing line records which, under extra.site.drafts.

docs.title: The gate (ADR 0016)
docs.text:
A line is in the site when its tier is in --tier, and nowhere otherwise: the readers read the record through the gate before anything is derived from it (reading.read(..., tiers)), so a line the gate holds back is not a row of a Day, not a night, not a companion, not a count on any page. The default, tier 1, is the shape of the record: where you were, how you moved, the flights, the calendar entries, the photos counted, who the calendar confirms present. No text of any note, message, transcript or mail is on a tier-1 page, and a person a tier-2 note names is on no page until tier 2 crosses. The root page counts what was held back (held back: 2,547 lines above tier 1), and the crossing line records it by tier and by kind.

The resolution lines — the record's name overlay, a ref to an entity — are read whole whatever their tier, as the vault reads them: the gate is on the line that puts someone somewhere (a calendar entry, a transcript, a note), never on the line that names them. The MCP server's gate is stricter and holds the overlay back too; an agent reading a private record and a page the owner publishes are not the same crossing, and the site follows the export. A voice is the one exception (RFC 0038): its name keeps the highest tier of the lines that give it, so a person whose name only a tier-3 line gives is a named voice on a tier-1,2 site, the voice still theirs, and their name is not in its company either. Health and money are tier 3 and never go to a site; --tier 1,2,3 is refused.

How far the gate opens is a setting in the record, not in the code: policy/crossing.json maps a destination to its ceiling, and the site's destination is site. A file that does not name it allows tier 1, so --tier 1,2 needs one line added:

{"hermes": {"max_tier": 2}, "mcp": {"max_tier": 1}, "site": {"max_tier": 2}}

You write each entry yourself; a new record names only mcp, at 1. A request above the ceiling is refused naming the file, and nothing is written or appended.

docs.title: The record shows it left (RFC 0011)
docs.text: Every run appends one crossing/v1 line with the destination site, the window as instants (the first day's local midnight to the midnight after the last), the tiers, the counts (how many lines the record logged, how many crossed, how many were held back, by tier and by kind), the ceiling in force, the head before the line, and package_sha256: the digest of the folder as written, one line per file — <sha256 of its bytes> <path> in path order — hashed, as the vault's. Under extra.site are the years, whether a model's drafts were included (drafts), the pages per kind and how many files were written and how many were unchanged. Nothing else is written to the record, and that one write goes through Logbook.append.

docs.title: Re-running
docs.text: Every page is a function of the record's lines and its settings alone: no head (the Year's and the Trip's footers name none here, since the crossing line a run appends would move it), no timestamp, no counter. A run compares each page's bytes with what is on disk and writes only the differences; the console says 92 written, 0 unchanged the first time and 0 written, 92 unchanged the next. Nothing is deleted: a page the record no longer produces stays until you remove it, and a file beside the pages — a CNAME, a .nojekyll, your own index — is never touched.

docs.title: Publishing it
docs.text:
The folder is static: copy it anywhere that serves files. The project publishes the demo persona under its own docs site, and the way it does so is the template:

  • .github/workflows/docs.yml runs on every push to main: logbook demo --years 40 --seed 1, the site entry in that record's policy, then logbook export site docs/ines --tier 1,2, then the docs build, which copies the folder as it is to /ines/ on GitHub Pages. No new infrastructure: the same gh-pages branch, the same deploy.
  • Before the build, scripts/check_synthetic.py docs/ines fails the workflow if any page carries an identifier outside CONTRIBUTING.md's synthetic allowlist — an email at a domain other than example.org, a phone number outside 07700 900xxx and +47 9000 000x, a nine-digit number in an assigned MMSI range, a URL of any kind — or, when the owner's ~/.config/logbook/pii-patterns exists, anything it names: the scrub rule CONTRIBUTING describes, applied to the rendering rather than the diff. It prints file:line and a count, never the text.
  • The demo only. A real record's site is tier-gated like any export, but publishing it is a decision the gate does not make for you: a tier-1 site still says where you slept every night.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: It is not serve: nothing listens, nothing is read on request, and the pages are as old as the last run. It is not a reader of the record for other software: the day package (export --day) and the crossing package (export crossing) are that, and they carry lines, not prose. It is not a backup: logbook backup is. It renders what the readers derive — a stay, a trip, a companion — and a derivation is disposable (ADR 0013): rename a place, raise the ceiling, and the next run rewrites the pages that changed.

docs.title: Speakers: who spoke
docs.text:
A recording made in a room has one channel, so until now every word of it read as yours. With the diarizer on this machine, derive transcripts separates the voices of each recording it hears and gives each voice an anonymous label in the transcript/v1 line: S1, S2, … for the voices of a room, mic and system for the two sides of a call. Nothing leaves the machine, and nothing names anyone: a label says a voice, never who.

This page covers builds 1 to 3 of RFC 0038: the labels at ingest (§2); saying whose voice a label is, one resolution/v1 line per voice, written by you alone through review speakers, which the readers then join (Who they are, §3–§4); and the voiceprints that let the review propose a name by how a voice sounds, a sealed cache that never leaves the machine (Voiceprints, §5). The browser's Who spoke? and the text-only road for recordings whose audio is gone are later builds.

uv tool install "openlogbook[transcribe,speakers]"   # the Whisper engine and the diarizer (or pipx install --force)
logbook setup speakers                          # what is here: the engine, each model, what the record holds; no socket
logbook setup speakers --fetch-model            # the one network event: the models, with HF_TOKEN for those requests only
logbook derive transcripts voice-memos          # transcribes, and separates the voices when the models are here
logbook derive transcripts voice-memos --no-speakers   # transcribes only
logbook derive speakers --dry-run               # the transcripts heard before, and what separating them would change
logbook derive speakers [--since DAY] [--speakers N]   # heard again and separated: a new line supersedes each
logbook setup speakers --rebuild                # the voiceprint registry made again from the record; no socket

docs.title: What a transcript gains
docs.text:
Two payload fields, both optional, added to transcript/v1 by a dated amendment of RFC 0004 under RFC 0031 rule 1; the JSON Schema of the payload is schema/transcript-v1.schema.json. A transcript without them is valid, byte for byte what it was, and every reader reads it as before.

  • speakers: the voices, in order of first speech, each { label, seconds?, turns, channel?, from_me?, name? }. seconds is how long the voice speaks (each voice's own speech: two voices that talk over each other for a minute both count the minute); turns is how many segments of the text are the voice's (the lines of a plain-text transcript, the elements of Granola's JSON); channel is mic or system; from_me is true on the microphone's voice when the source says the microphone is yours and the voice is alone on it; name is a name the source displayed, never a resolution.
  • diarization: how the labels were made: engine (pyannote, or the provider whose labels an adapter took, granola), model, audio (the digest of the audio heard), channels (1 for a room, 2 for a call), overlap_s (the seconds in which two voices or more speak at once), and spans, a reference to the spans file.

The dinner of RFC 0038 §11, three voices in one room:

"speakers":[{"label":"S1","seconds":1862.4,"turns":212},{"label":"S2","seconds":861.0,"turns":97},{"label":"S3","seconds":41.5,"turns":4}],
"diarization":{"engine":"pyannote","model":"pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1","audio":"c41d…","channels":1,"overlap_s":38.2,
 "spans":{"sha256":"a9e2…","path":"attachments/a9e2…","bytes":21877,"media_type":"application/json"}}

docs.title: The spans file
docs.text:
One JSON object in the attachment store beside the text, sealed when the record seals (SPEC §1.1), never inline in the line: format speaker-spans/1; content, the digest of the text it labels, so it is never read against other text; segments, one per line of the text in order, {from, to, speaker, overlap?}, seconds from the line's at to two decimals, speaker the voice that speaks most of the line (of its words, when the engine gave word times), null when nobody did, overlap the other voices that speak a second or more of it; and turns, the diarizer's own {from, to, speaker}, overlapping where the voices did. The labels and their counts are in the line, because every reader that asks who was in this recording needs them; the spans grow with the recording and are in a file, because only the readers that split the words need them.

Its bytes are written one way (sorted keys, no spaces), so the same voices in the same text are the same file and the same digest.

docs.title: Labels
docs.text:
A label is the diarizer's, not a person's, and it means something only inside its line: S2 of one recording and S2 of another are unrelated.

  • S1, S2, … for the voices of one channel, numbered by first speech (the pipeline's own SPEAKER_00 says nothing about order);
  • mic and system for a channel in which one voice speaks; mic.1, mic.2, … or system.1, system.2, … when several do;
  • a label never holds # or a line break, and is at most 64 characters, so a later speaker ref (<line id>#<label>) splits at its first #.

docs.title: Two channels
docs.text:
A call recorder keeps your microphone on one channel and the far end on the other. Such a recording is diarized a channel at a time: a channel with one voice is labelled by the channel, and the microphone's voice carries from_me: true; a channel with several voices (a speakerphone in the room, a conference at the far end) is numbered, and none of them carries from_me.

A recording counts as two channels only when its source says so. A voice-memo/v1 line says it under extra.channels, the file's channels in order, mic and system once each: ["mic", "system"], or ["system", "mic"] when the far end is the first channel. No adapter writes that yet; a call recorder's will. Anything else is one room, an iPhone's stereo memo included: two microphones in one room are not a call, and no voice of it is from_me. A file that does not hold the channels its source named, or whose channels the diarizer cannot decode apart, is heard as a room too, and the run says so.

Granola keeps the two sides apart itself and marks each segment as the microphone's (me) or the system audio's (them). sync granola takes those marks as the labels: mic and system (system.1, system.2 where Granola's own diarization tells the far end's voices apart), from_me on mic, the name Granola displayed as name, engine granola and no audio, since Granola kept it. With every segment timed it counts the seconds and writes the spans file, each segment the voice Granola gave it.

docs.title: When the audio is gone
docs.text: A memo imported without --attachments, a copy of the record missing a file, a provider that never handed over audio: nothing is diarized at ingest, derive transcripts skips such a memo as it always did, and nothing breaks. A provider's own marks, when it gives them, are still taken by its adapter.

docs.title: Without the extra, or without the models
docs.text:
When the diarizer (the openlogbook[speakers] extra) or one of its models is not on this machine, derive transcripts transcribes exactly as before, writes no speakers, and says once at the end which is missing. openlogbook[transcribe] alone, the diarizer not installed:

speakers: not separated (install openlogbook[speakers], then logbook setup speakers --fetch-model)

The extra installed and a model not fetched:

speakers: not separated (logbook setup speakers --fetch-model)

Without the extra, setup speakers and derive speakers exit 2 with the first sentence, and setup speakers --fetch-model fetches nothing: the hub client comes with openlogbook[transcribe] too, and models nothing here could run are never downloaded. derive speakers --dry-run hears nothing and needs no extra. --no-speakers turns separation off for a run and says nothing of it.

docs.title: Heard again: derive speakers
docs.text:
A transcript heard before the voices were separated has no times in its text, so the labels cannot be added to it: the recording is heard again. derive speakers takes each standing transcript with no speakers whose recording (the voice memo its provenance.source names, not retracted) has its audio in the store, hears it again with the Whisper model that heard it, separates the voices, and writes a new transcript/v1 line with the new text and the labels. That line supersedes the old one and keeps its source, at, end, tz and title; its raw_id is <the old raw_id>#speakers@<the first 12 hex of the spans file's digest>, so the same voices heard in the same text write nothing twice. The old line stays in the record, superseded, as every correction does. --speakers N tells the diarizer the room held N voices (a call heard a channel at a time does without it, and the command says so). A transcript from a provider or a file has no recording here and is left alone, counted; so is one whose memo was retracted or superseded by a later memo line. One recording has one line of its voices: a recording a standing line has separated already is not heard again.

It is not free, and the command says so before it writes:

  • a new line on a signed day changes the day's page, so the signature reads page_matches false until you sign the day again (logbook day sign DAY);
  • a promise closed on an old line is proposed again from the new line, a promise's id being its line's (SPEC §3.2.10 rule 2): each is listed, by the seq of the task that closed it and its sentence, and promises done ID closes it again;
  • a call's synthesis belongs to the line it was written about: the new line has none until transcript synthesize writes one.

--dry-run lists the transcripts and those costs, writes nothing and needs no engine. A transcript that a line retracted later no longer supersedes stands again, and hearing it again into the same spans writes nothing.

docs.title: The models, and the one download
docs.text:
The diarizer is pyannote.audio's pipeline pyannote/speaker-diarization-3.1, its own extra, openlogbook[speakers], which brings torch to every platform (and CUDA's libraries on Linux). openlogbook[transcribe] does not bring it, so a memo is transcribed without a gigabyte of torch; a machine that separates voices installs both, openlogbook[transcribe,speakers]. It runs on the CPU and on Apple silicon behind either Whisper engine. The pipeline reads two more models, pyannote/segmentation-3.0 and the embedding model pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM; all three are gated on Hugging Face. Accept the conditions on each model's page while signed in, make a read token, and:

HF_TOKEN=hf_… logbook setup speakers --fetch-model

That is the one network event, and the only command that fetches a speaker model. The token is read from HF_TOKEN for those requests and nothing else: never written, never printed. When the hub refuses, the command names the page to accept the conditions on. derive transcripts --fetch-model fetches the Whisper model and only that.

Every run that separates voices does it with the hub offline (HF_HUB_OFFLINE, and the switch the hub client read when it was first imported, set for the run and put back after) and with pyannote.audio's own usage reporting, which its 4.x releases switch on by default, switched off (PYANNOTE_METRICS_ENABLED=0). The audio is decoded on this machine and never leaves it. The same guard now serves every command that runs a local model (transcribe.offline, which promises --judge and describe use, set the variables only, which the hub client ignores once imported). A cache the hub says holds the models but whose files are not whole (an interrupted fetch) stops the run with one sentence naming setup speakers --fetch-model. A test separates voices with every socket refused; no test loads a model: the diarizer is a fake, as the transcription engine is.

docs.title: Reading them back
docs.text:
show, the Day and serve's Day name a transcript's voices after its title, the one who spoke most first and never with their minutes, since no number stands beside a person (RFC 0043; and show drops a writer's 0 turns beside them, and marks a transcript heard again superseded by #N):

  09:15  transcript transcription  Samtale · you · Ola Nordmann

A voice not yet named reads as the name its source displayed, else its label; the owner reads as you from from_me, the source's statement, or from your own answer, never from a guess. day --json gives a transcript's entry speakers, only when the line has voices: {label, person, name, seconds, basis, consent, owner} (what each holds once a voice is named: Who they are). A transcript that another standing transcript of the day supersedes is not listed beside it. A transcript without speakers reads exactly as before.

docs.title: Who they are
docs.text:
A label says a voice. Who that voice is, is yours to say, and nothing says it for you: no adapter, no model, no dream and no tool binds a voice. Each answer is one resolution/v1 line beside the transcript (RFC 0006, amended for RFC 0038 §3), and the transcript itself never changes.

logbook review speakers                          # the queue: voices not yet named, numbered, with the evidence
logbook review speakers --json                   # the same, with each row's stable id and the counts
logbook review speakers --accept 4 --name 1 me   # row 4 is whom it proposes; row 1 is you
