logbook review speakers --name 2 "Kari Nordmann" --consent 2=yes
logbook review speakers --name 3 "Per Hansen"    # a name nobody has: a person is minted under it
logbook review speakers --unnamed 3              # a person, not you, whom you will not name
logbook review speakers --unnamed 5 --same-as 3  # the same unnamed person as voice 3
logbook review speakers --reject 4               # not that person; never proposed again
logbook review speakers --all-above 40           # every row whose one best candidate scores 40 or more
logbook review speakers --play 2                 # the voice's first twenty seconds alone, here; nothing written
logbook review speakers --named --recording ID   # the voices of a recording already named, to correct one
logbook review speakers --named --day 2026-10-03

docs.title: The queue
docs.text:
A row is an observed voice, keyed by the strongest thing the voice carries, never by its label across recordings: the far end of a call (the one voice on the system channel of a recording that overlaps a call/v1 line whose counterparty is an address or a number) is keyed by that address or number, so every call with one number is one row; else the voice itself: voices not yet named that sound alike, each within match of the others' centre in the voiceprints, are one row, so the same guest heard at four dinners is one row of four recordings (never two voices of one recording: two labels the diarizer kept apart are not merged by a guess); else the name the source displayed, its words folded and sorted; else the label alone, one row per voice. A row with several recordings numbers them N.1, N.2, …, and --accept 4.2 answers that recording's voice alone, which is how a row that joined two people is split. Your own microphone's voice (from_me) is yours without a question and never in the queue; a row the voiceprints propose you for comes first, since one answer settles most voices.

4 voices not yet named in 2 recordings, 4 rows · 0 named · tier 2
   1  [20]  Sat 2026-10-03 19:40 · Home · "Middag" · S1 · 31 min · "Har du sett hvor høyt vannet står?"
            → Kari Nordmann: on the entry "Middag med Kari" · seen that day (message 18:02) (as good for S2, S3 of the recording: not taken by --all-above)
            that day: Kari Nordmann (message, calendar)
   2  [20]  same recording · S2 · 14 min · "Beklager, ferja var sen."
            → Kari Nordmann: on the entry "Middag med Kari" · seen that day (message 18:02) (as good for S1, S3 of the recording: not taken by --all-above)
            that day: Kari Nordmann (message, calendar)
   3  [20]  same recording · S3 · 42 s · "Hei, jeg skal bare levere en pakke."
            → Kari Nordmann: on the entry "Middag med Kari" · seen that day (message 18:02) (as good for S1, S2 of the recording: not taken by --all-above)
            that day: Kari Nordmann (message, calendar)
   4  [40]  Tue 2026-10-06 09:15 · Home · "Samtale" · system · 3 min · "I'll call the yard tomorrow."
            → Ola Nordmann: the far end of the call 09:15
            that day: Ola Nordmann (call)
nothing written: `review speakers --accept N[,N]`, `--name N "…"`, `--unnamed N`, `--reject N[,N]`, `--consent N=yes|no|unknown`, or `--all-above SCORE`

Each row says the day, the place (the stay the recording overlaps, as people names it), the recording's title, the voice's label and how long it spoke, its first words, the candidate and what speaks for it, and who else the record saw that day. The rows run in the order the recordings were made, and within a recording by how long each voice spoke. On a terminal the command asks row by row: y accepts, n rejects, u is unnamed, p plays, anything else is a name, Enter skips, q stops; after a name or unnamed for a voice that is not yours it asks recorded with their consent? y / n / Enter for unknown. Each answer is written at once.

docs.title: The score
docs.text:
A plain sum per candidate and voice, a row's the lowest of its voices':

Evidence Points the same voice: the voice's embedding against the person's voiceprint, 70 at a similarity of match or more, falling in a straight line to 0 at floor, nothing below it; against yours as against anyone's up to 70 the far end of a call: the voice is alone on system and the recording overlaps a call whose counterparty is the person 40 on the entry: the person attends a timed calendar entry the recording overlaps, held at the same stay 15 a participant: the transcript's participants name the person by address, number or provider id; by a name alone 15; 5 the source's name: the name the source displayed for the voice is the person's, or a word of it nobody else's has 10 seen that day: another line of the recording's day is the person's (a message, a call, a tagged face, their voice in another recording), one not already counted above 5

Context never stands in for a voice: with neither the same voice nor the far end of a call a candidate scores 40 at most, so --all-above over 40 never names a guest from context alone. The first time a guest is recorded there is no voiceprint of them: context proposes, low, and your answer is what makes the voiceprint. Two candidates within 5 points are both shown and neither is taken; context belongs to the recording, not to one voice of it, so a person who is the best for two voices of one recording at the same score is shown for each and taken by --all-above for neither. A person already named for one voice of a recording, you included, is not proposed for its others. A pair you said no to, and a person under forget in policy/speakers.json, are never proposed. You are proposed by your voice alone (→ you: same voice 0.86); until you have a call on record or have answered once for yourself there is no voiceprint of you, and you answer me. With enrol_unnamed, a voice that sounds like a person you would not name is proposed as the same unnamed person, and accepting it writes --unnamed for that person, not a new one. matched says same voice 0.86, the similarity, never the vectors; a row of several recordings reads as its least similar voice, as it scores.

docs.title: What each answer writes
docs.text:
Every number of one command is checked before the first line is written; a number the queue does not have, a voice answered twice (--accept 2 --reject 2, or 2 and 2.1), a consent for a row the command does not answer, a consent for your own voice, a score that is not a whole number, or a name several people have exits 2 and writes nothing.

Answer Writes, per voice of the row --accept N one resolution/v1: ref {kind: speaker, value: "<transcript id>#<label>"}, entity the candidate, label the person's, method owner, basis, consent when stated, evidence the transcript and the lines the score rested on, logbook_head, and under extra the row's id, the score and what matched --name N "…" the same, to me (your owner_id, no label, no consent), the one person the record labels so (case aside), a person by id or by a ref the record resolves (email:…, phone:…); a name nobody has mints a person with that label, once per name in a command --unnamed N the same, entity a person minted with no label, and unnamed: true; one person for the row; with --same-as M, the person voice M is bound to unnamed (or the one minted for M in the same command) --reject N one entity-review/v1 line of type person (RFC 0035 amendment 1: people-review/v1 is read and no longer written): ref the row's first voice, refs every voice, entity the candidate --consent N=… nothing of its own: the consent of the line N's answer writes (yes, no or unknown; absent reads as unknown)

basis is channel when the person is the far end of the call the recording overlaps, voice when the recording's audio is in the store, and text otherwise, which then carries confidence: the score the record gives that person for that voice, over 100 and at most text_confidence_cap (0.6) of policy/speakers.json, whichever flag named them; a person the record scored nothing for (a name only you knew, --unnamed, me) the cap itself, your word being the most a voice named without its audio may say. So a voice named without its audio never reads as surer than one heard. A line is tier 2, or the transcript's when that is higher. The same person, basis and consent as the voice's standing line (a consent left out reading as unknown), a no the record already holds, and --unnamed on a voice already unnamed write nothing and say so; an answer that names the same person again keeps the consent stated before unless it states another. Two labels may be one person (a voice the diarizer split): naming one person for a second voice of a recording is allowed, and said (Kari Nordmann is also S2 of the recording); the queue does not propose a person for a recording's other voices once one is theirs. A ref given to --name (email:…, phone:…) that no person of the record has is refused, never minted as a name.

The line RFC 0038 §11 writes for the call's far end:

{"schema":"resolution/v1","ref":{"kind":"speaker","value":"019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-0000000004a2#system"},
 "entity":{"type":"person","id":"019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-043f5aabf2a9","registry":"logbook"},"label":"Ola Nordmann",
 "method":"owner","basis":"channel","evidence":["019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-0000000004a2","019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-0000000004e3"],
 "logbook_head":"8f1c…","extra":{"proposal":"3c9a51d0e2f4b7a6","score":40,"matched":["the far end of the call 09:15"]}}

Its JSON Schema is schema/resolution-v1-speaker.schema.json.

docs.title: A wrong answer
docs.text: The record keeps the mistake and the correction. --named --recording ID (its id or seq) or --named --day DAY lists the voices already named, numbered as the queue is, each with its standing line; any answer to one (--name, --unnamed, or --accept N --consent N=… to state the consent again) writes a new line for the same voice that supersedes the standing one, and the wrong line stays in the record. A wrong no is undone by retracting its line, and the pair is proposed again; a wrong yes by logbook repair retract SEQ, which returns the voice to the queue. A transcript heard again (derive speakers) is a new line with new labels: its voices are new refs, back in the queue, and the old line's answers name nothing on it. people merge moves a person's addresses and numbers, never a voice: a voice bound to the person merged away stays bound to them, and so they stay a row of people, until you name it again here; the merge says how many (1 voice stays bound to Kari).

docs.title: How the readers read it
docs.text:
Each voice of a standing transcript is then yours (bound to you, or from_me with no line; a line binding your microphone's voice to someone else wins over from_me: someone else spoke into your phone), a person's, unnamed, or not yet named.

  • The Day names who spoke and says the consent you stated for the guests, when it is not yes: Middag · you · Kari Nordmann and 1 unnamed · recorded with consent: unknown. In day --json each voice is {label, person, name, seconds, basis, consent, owner}: person your id for your voice and the person's for theirs, null for an unnamed voice and one not yet named; name the person's label (for a voice not yet named, the name its source displayed); consent as stated, unknown when a guest's line states none.
  • With (who was there): a voice bound to a person, in a recording that overlaps the stay, is confirmed company, spoke in Middag, ahead of the participants, at the line's confidence (a text attribution's 0.2 reads as 0.2), else 1.0, your own assertion. The far end of a call (the system channel) spoke and was not there: never company, not even through that recording's participants. An unnamed voice is counted, with.unnamed, and never named; a voice not yet named is nobody's company.
  • People count a voice bound to someone on their transcripts channel, the far end of a call included, with spoke_s, the seconds; the person page says spoke 14 min. A person you would not name is never a row: the head says and 1 unnamed, the JSON unnamed, and how many voices are not yet named, review speakers. rollup people counts a year's unnamed the same way.
  • Promises take a sentence's speaker from the voice of its segment, through the spans file: your voice's sentences are yours, a guest's are owed to you, a voice not yet named stays as spoken (S2).
  • The digest says who spoke that day and, once, how many voices wait, with the command.

docs.title: Voiceprints
docs.text: A voiceprint is an embedding of a voice: a short list of numbers the speaker model computes from the audio, close to the numbers of the same voice in any other recording. That makes it biometric: it recognises a person by their body, in a recording anyone could make, and it could recognise a guest who never agreed to be in your record to someone who has never seen it. Everything below follows from that (RFC 0038 §5).

docs.title: The registry
docs.text:
The voiceprints are one file, voiceprints.age, in the record folder beside places.json: one JSON document, voiceprints/1, sealed with age to the record's own recipients (Encryption at rest), written whole each time to a temporary name beside it and renamed over it, so a crash leaves the old file or the new one and never half; the plaintext never touches the disk. It holds the embedding model and the digest of its files, the length of its vectors and the head it was written at; per person (by entity id, never a name) their voiceprint, the centre of their voices' embeddings weighted by clean seconds, the clean seconds it rests on, and the voices it was built from, each with its own embedding, so a voiceprint can be recomputed at any write without the model; and each voice not yet named with its embedding, so the review compares without loading the model. No audio, no words, no names.

A voice is embedded from its clean speech only: its turns in the spans file less every moment another voice speaks, each piece two seconds or more, so an evening of interruptions does not blur two people into one. A voice with less than min_clean_s of it (8 seconds) is neither embedded nor proposed by voice. The model is the diarization pipeline's own, pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM, so the registry and the diarizer agree on what a voice is.

A record that names no recipients keeps no registry on disk. The review then hears the voices it compares for that run, from the audio, when the speakers extra and its models are on this machine, and forgets them when it ends; without them it proposes from context and the channels alone. That costs a decoding of every recording with voices at each review speakers; a record sealed to recipients pays it once, in the file.

docs.title: A cache, never the record
docs.text:
The registry is made from what the record holds, the audio the transcripts' diarization.audio names, their spans files and the attributions that stand, and is thrown away without loss, like index.sqlite:

logbook setup speakers                  # registry   voiceprints.age written 2026-10-11 10:12 with pyannote/wespeaker-voxceleb-resnet34-LM, for 3 people, you among them; 2 voices not yet named
logbook setup speakers --rebuild        # made again from the record, with the model; no socket
  • A derive transcripts or derive speakers that separates a recording adds its voices, and hears any other voice the file should hold and does not; the run says voiceprints: 4 voices heard; 3 people, you among them, 2 voices not yet named. A run with nothing new to hear does not load the model and leaves the file as it is.
  • Every answer in review speakers that writes a line updates it, without the model: the person you named gains the voice; a voice named away, retracted or whose transcript was heard again leaves the voiceprint it was in, because each voiceprint is recomputed from the answers that stand. The queue itself reads the file as the record stands now, so a retracted answer counts for nothing at once.
  • A model change makes it again from the record: two models' vectors cannot be compared.
  • A recording whose audio is not in the store is skipped and counted; the answers already written stand.
  • verify ignores the file; backup leaves it out, one copy of a biometric being the most there should be. A restored record makes it again: setup speakers --rebuild, from the audio the backup carries.
  • logbook key add-recipient and key remove-recipient seal it again to the new recipients with the record's lines and files, in the same hold of the writer lock: before the record when a recipient goes, so a removed identity opens no copy of it even when the change stops half way, and after it when one comes. A file this machine cannot open or seal again is removed, to be made again, and so is one whose sealing again was interrupted; a link under its name is removed, never read through, and what it pointed at is left as it was, said. One that can be neither sealed again nor removed (another program holds it open) stops a removal before the record is touched.

A voice the file let go (one you answered --unnamed, or a person under forget) and that later returns to being kept (the answer retracted, forget emptied) is heard again by the next derive that separates a recording, or by setup speakers --rebuild; until then it is compared as a voice without a voiceprint.

docs.title: Your voice
docs.text: Your voice is enrolled without a question and without a line: every voice with from_me (your own microphone on a call recorder, alone on its channel) whose audio is in the store, and every voice you have bound to yourself (--name N me, or accepting a row that proposed you), is folded into your voiceprint. Every other voiceprint begins with your first answer for that person and grows with each later one.

docs.title: policy/speakers.json
docs.text:
One setting, read each run, never a line, backed up with policy/. Without the file, the defaults:

{"match": 0.75, "floor": 0.5, "min_clean_s": 8, "text_confidence_cap": 0.6, "enrol_unnamed": false, "forget": []}
  • match and floor: the similarities at which a voice scores its full 70 points and none. They are the embedding model's, hypotheses until calibrated, as policy/stays.json's constants are.
  • min_clean_s: the clean speech, in seconds, below which a voice is neither embedded nor proposed by voice.
  • text_confidence_cap: the most a text attribution's confidence may say.
  • enrol_unnamed, false: the voices of a person you would not name are folded into no voiceprint, so a stranger you would not name is not recognised next time either. With true they are, and the queue proposes the same unnamed person.
  • forget: entity ids (as people --json gives them) whose voiceprint is never kept and against whom no voice is ever proposed. Their voices leave the file at its next write. An entry that is no one's id (a typo, a name, an id in capitals) matches no one and forgets no one.

A file that is not this shape is refused in one sentence naming the key, and nothing is written: a number outside 0 to 1, floor not below match, seconds below 0, an enrol_unnamed that is not true or false, a forget that is not a list of non-empty strings, a key that is no setting.

docs.title: It never leaves
docs.text: The registry is part of no crossing, whatever the tier and whatever a policy entry says: not the crossing package, a shared page, a trip bundle, the vault, the site, an MCP tool's answer, a dream's material, a backup or any export. A tier says what a line may give away, and the registry is not a line. Nothing opens it but review speakers, the commands that write it (derive transcripts, derive speakers, setup speakers --rebuild), setup speakers and doctor, which say that it is there, when and with which model it was written and for how many people, never what is in it (the doctor). The index holds no embedding, and no reader prints a vector: the review says same voice 0.86, a similarity. A test builds every crossing and export over a record with a registry and looks in each for the file and for every one of its vectors, as text and as packed numbers.

docs.title: Assumptions that stand
docs.text:
RFC 0038 leaves fifteen questions open for its comment period. Four of them were asked of it from the start, and this build stands on the RFC's present answer to each until the comment period settles it:

  1. Two guests with the same voice score. A label is a voice as the diarizer heard it, not a person: two people it could not tell apart are one label, and two labels may be one person. The review shows two close candidates and takes neither, a row's N.2 answers one recording alone, and a later diarization with --speakers N may split a label; a label two people share is left not yet named, or named --unnamed.
  2. A guest who asks to be forgotten. The transcript and the audio are your record and are never rewritten. What the record can do is retract the attribution lines that name them (their voices return to not yet named) and list them under forget in policy/speakers.json, so the registry drops their voiceprint at its next write and no voice is ever proposed as theirs; keeping their words home is the crossing's keys, a later build.
  3. Group calls with more than two channels. A recording is one room, or two channels, mic and system. A conference that arrives mixed on the far end's channel is diarized inside it (system.1, system.2); a recorder that writes one track per participant is not read as such yet.
  4. Labels in the payload, not the envelope. The labels are payload fields, sealed with the words at tier 2 and 3, invisible to a reader that does not want them: no spec version bump, no regenerated conformance fixture, no new ADR. A stolen disk shows nothing of who spoke.

Build 3 stands on two more:

  • The unnamed (open question 7). enrol_unnamed is false by default: a person you would not name is minted for the voice and kept in no voiceprint, so a stranger heard twice is two strangers unless you say --same-as.
  • Calibration (open question 12). match and floor are fixed settings, 0.75 and 0.5 by default; the registry does not learn your thresholds from your answers.

docs.title: Not in these builds
docs.text:
• the browser's Who spoke? (§4.6), the text-only road (§6), and the crossing's keys (§9);
  • the channels engine of §2.5 (two channels labelled with no model on the machine): §2.1 has the run transcribe exactly as before without the model, and this build follows §2.1;
  • SPEC §3.2.10 rule 2's change that RFC 0038 asks for (a promise's id from the first line of a supersedes chain): the SPEC is unchanged, which is why derive speakers says what it reopens;
  • the SPEC's own words for the readers RFC 0038 §12 changes (§3.2.5 rule 2, voices by attribution and the far end of a call out of company; §3.2.10 rule 3, a sentence's speaker from its voice): the readers do it, as Who they are says, and the SPEC text follows when the RFC is adopted; the demo record has no voices, so every reader compared under §6.1 compares as before;
  • people review --speakers, the RFC's stand-in until review existed: review speakers is it.

docs.title: The synthesis prompt
docs.text: logbook transcript synthesize sends a model two messages: the prompt, which is the file logbook/contrib/synthesis-prompt.md in the package with the call and the language filled in, and the call as JSON. This page explains the prompt; transcript synthesize ID --show-prompt prints both as they go. The prompt's name, transcript-synthesis/2 (the second added ideas), is kept in every synthesis's extra.prompt, so a draft says which wording wrote it, and a call synthesized under an older prompt is synthesized again; a change to the prompt that changes what a synthesis holds bumps the number.

docs.title: What it asks for
docs.text:
One JSON object with six keys, each a list, in this order, which is the order the record keeps and the Day prints whatever order the model answers in:

Key What Each item actions what someone is to do after the call, one item per action text, assignee (as the transcript names them, me for the owner, or null), due (the call's own words for when, or null), evidence topics the themes of the call, each once, however often it came back topic (two to five words), text (one or two sentences), evidence decisions what the call agreed and closed text, evidence open_threads what it left unanswered or said to come back to text, evidence personal anything personal that came up: at most three short neutral sentences text, evidence ideas at most three ideas the call put forward to make or try: a new one, or a refinement of one the material lists under ideas (I1, ...) name (two to five words), idea (the reference it refines, or null), text, evidence (utterances, always)

evidence is a list of the material's references: U12 for an utterance, T for what the header alone says. An item that rests on no utterance carries "unsupported": true in its place.

docs.title: The rules it gives the model
docs.text:
1. Evidence. Every item names the utterances it rests on, or says unsupported. Never an invented reference, never one the material did not give, never an utterance cited for an item it does not support. The record checks every reference afterwards (the synthesis), so the rule is enforced, not only asked.
  2. Work only. The actions, topics, decisions and open threads are the work the call was about. Whatever is personal (health, family, feelings, a private plan, anyone's life outside work) goes to personal, as a pointer and never its details ("A family matter of Ola's came up."), or nowhere. This is the synthesis's only filter, and it is the model's to apply: the code sends the whole call and decides nothing about what is personal, because a word list would both miss and over-reach.
  3. Actions on top, one item per action, with the assignee and the due hint the call gave. An action nobody took on is still an action.
  4. Topics are consolidated across the whole call. A theme that comes up at minute 2, again at minute 20 and at minute 45 is one topic citing all three places, never three topics, and never one topic per stretch of the call. The utterances carry their time into the call when the recording gives it, so the model can see the theme return. The record holds the model to it as far as names go: two topics with the same name, case and spacing aside, are merged into one.
  5. Decisions are settled, not discussed. A proposal nobody agreed to, or a question talked over and left, is an open thread.
  6. Open threads are what was left unanswered or said to come back to.
  7. Only what the transcript says, names as it gives them, plain and brief; no greeting, no headings, no bullet marks.

The prompt names the call (title, weekday, day, zone, how many utterances) and the language to write in: the language most of the call is in, decided as the dream decides it, by counting each language's commonest words over the title and the utterances.

docs.title: What the model is not given
docs.text: Addresses, phone numbers or provider ids of the participants (names only); any other line of the record; the provider's own summary; the draft of the day. Its answer becomes a draft/v1 line whose segments carry the transcript line's id and whose extra.segments carry the utterance numbers; nothing of the prompt or of the call's words is kept.

docs.title: Tasks
docs.text:
logbook tasks [--open] [--propose-done] [--json] reads the record's tasks back: every task/v1 line (RFC 0016) a task app's export or logbook sync gtasks left, as the task it describes, in the state it was last seen. --propose-done asks the record whether an open task was done without anyone ticking it off: a booking confirmation in the mail for "book flights to Zürich", a calendar entry for "call Ola", a card payment at the marina for "pay the berth fee at Marina Solvind". It finds them by rules, in English and German, with no model and no network, and prints each as a proposal with the id of the line that is the evidence, never as a fact. tasks done <id> --evidence <line> is the one thing the command writes: a task/v1 line that marks the task done, carrying the evidence, and nothing else.

logbook tasks                              # every task as it stands, oldest first
logbook tasks --open                       # the open ones
logbook tasks --propose-done               # for each open task, the evidence it was done, with line ids
logbook tasks --json                       # the report as one JSON object
logbook tasks done 0dd9108fb6d5d715 --evidence 01a0fda3-99b0-7af6-a986-0a377117a94b
logbook tasks done ba26f9651977a75b        # done, with no line to show for it

docs.title: What a task is
docs.text:
A task app's export is a set of snapshots, and the log keeps every one (RFC 0016 rule 2): the same to-do exported again after it was ticked off is a new line whose raw_id ends in a newer modification time. The command takes, per source id (the raw_id before its last @), the standing line with the newest suffix (the later line when two share it; a line with no @ is keyed whole, its suffix its modified_at) and calls that the task. A retracted line is out; a line with no raw_id or no title is skipped.

7 tasks, 6 open (the latest snapshot of each task is its state, RFC 0016)
  2026-06-01  11:00  open                  “Renew the boat insurance”  3096daca87cd18f9
  2026-06-08  08:30  open  due 2026-06-20  “Book flights to Zürich”  [Work]  0dd9108fb6d5d715
  2026-06-09  09:00  open                  “Call Ola about the mooring”  [Boat]  ead035a05df19fee
  2026-06-11  14:10  done                  “Buy the long rope”  [Boat]  75c34488134f6542
  • The day and time are the newest snapshot's at, in the record's zone: for Google Tasks the last modification (the export keeps no creation time), so a done task sits on the day it was done.
  • The status is the snapshot's: open, done or cancelled. --open keeps the first.
  • The due day and the list are the snapshot's due and list, when it has them.
  • The id is a digest of the source id, sixteen hex characters: the same for every snapshot of one task, however often it is exported, and the handle tasks done takes.

Under --json the report is one object: open_only, propose_done, window_days (14), matcher (which matcher read the evidence, or null when none did), tasks and proposals. Each task carries id, key (the source id), title, status, due, list, at, day, seq, line (the newest snapshot's line id) and source.

docs.title: The evidence: --propose-done
docs.text:
For every open task the command reads the standing mail/v1, event/v1 and transaction/v1 lines of the fourteen days after the task's at (taskdone.WINDOW; both ends included), through the index, and asks the matcher about each. A line before the task, or after the fortnight, is never evidence; a retracted line, and one a later line of its kind supersedes, is not read.

4 open tasks with evidence of being done, read by rules, not facts; close one with `logbook tasks done <id> --evidence <line>`
  “Book flights to Zürich”  (2026-06-08, 0dd9108fb6d5d715)
    2026-06-12  12:00  mail         “Your booking confirmation: Oslo – Zürich, 20 June”  zürich  01a0fda3-99b0-7af6-a986-0a377117a94b
  “Call Ola about the mooring”  (2026-06-09, ead035a05df19fee)
    2026-06-15  15:00  event        “Call with Ola Nordmann”  ola  ×2 sources  01a0fda3-99b0-7631-aeac-6035128fe018
  “Pay the berth fee at Marina Solvind”  (2026-06-10, 5314e1030197326b)
    2026-06-14  12:00  transaction  “Marina Solvind”  marina solvind  01a0fda3-99b1-7769-906c-19117862caf9
  2 open tasks with no evidence found

Under each task: the evidence's day and time, its kind, its text (a mail's subject, an entry's title, a transaction's merchant, never a body), the task's words it carries, ×N sources when the same calendar entry comes from several calendars (the same instants and the same title are one proposal naming every line; the first line's id is printed), and the evidence line's id. Under --json every proposal carries task (the task's id), line, lines, kind, source, sources, at, day, tier (a transaction's is 3), text and evidence (rule, shared, confidence).

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
The matcher takes the task's title apart into its key nouns and its verbs (taskdone.words_of). A verb is a word on the lists of things a task asks for, in English (book, buy, call, pay, send, order, renew, cancel, meet, visit, …) or German (buchen, kaufen, anrufen, bezahlen, bestellen, schicken, verlängern, kündigen, treffen, …); a noun is every other word of three letters or more that is not an article, a preposition, a pronoun or a filler in either language (the, to, about, my, next; die, nach, wegen, bitte). Book flights to Zürich is the nouns flights, zürich and the verb book; Flüge nach Tromsø buchen the nouns flüge, tromsø and the verb buchen. A task with no noun (Do it) has no evidence.

Two words are one when they match case, accents, an English plural s and German compounds aside (taskdone.same_word): Zürich is zurich, Tromsø is tromso, flights is flight, Flug is the start of Flugtickets. The compound rule needs four letters, so Ola never matches Olav and fee never feel.

A line is evidence when its text carries a key noun of the task and, by kind:

Kind And Rule mail/v1 the subject confirms something — confirmation, confirmed, booking, booked, receipt, ticket, itinerary, reservation, invoice, order; Bestätigung, Buchung, gebucht, Rechnung, Quittung, Reservierung, Bestellung, Beleg, as a word or inside a compound (Buchungsbestätigung) mail-confirmation mail/v1 the owner sent it (direction sent): "send the photos to Ola" and a sent mail "Mooring photos" mail-sent event/v1 the task is an appointment (its verb call, phone, meet, see, visit, talk, anrufen, treffen, besuchen, or a noun appointment, meeting, lunch, Termin, Besprechung, …), or the entry's title repeats the task's verb, or it carries two of the task's nouns event transaction/v1 the merchant carries a noun: the task names where the money went transaction

A received mail that shares a noun but confirms nothing (Zürich newsletter: 10 things to do) is not evidence; nor is a mail that shares only the task's verb (Book club: June reading for Book flights); nor a calendar entry that shares one place name with a task that is no appointment (Zürich standup for Book flights to Zürich); nor a payment at the marina five days before the task was written. The confidence is 0.6, a tenth more per noun shared beyond the first, a tenth more for a confirmation cue, 0.9 at most; it is the rules' own estimate and is printed under --json only.

The rules will miss evidence phrased another way and propose a line that is none — a newsletter with a receipt in its subject, a transaction at a shop whose name is a word of the task — which is why nothing here is a fact until you close the task.

docs.title: Closing one: tasks done <id> [--evidence <line>]
docs.text:
done appends one task/v1 line and nothing else: source manual, kind task, tier 2 (RFC 0016: MUST), at now. Its payload is the newest snapshot of the task: raw_id <source id>@<now> so that it is, by rule 2, the task's state from here on; the title, due and list carried over; status done; completed_at and modified_at now; supersedes the snapshot it replaces; and, when --evidence names a line, extra.evidence with that line's id. The evidence must be a line the record holds; an id it does not is refused with status 2, and so is a task id tasks does not print. A task already done or cancelled is left alone and said so; a second done writes nothing.

--open and --propose-done then leave the task out, since its newest snapshot is done. The app's own export, imported later, may bring a newer snapshot still open; by rule 2 the newest wins, and the task is open again until the app agrees. Nothing is edited: the earlier snapshots, the mail and the transaction stay as they were, and the close is a line beside them.

--evidence is optional: a task done with nothing in the record to show for it closes the same way, and the payload then carries no extra.

docs.title: Replacing the rules with a model
docs.text: The command does not know the rules. taskdone.propose(lb, matcher=RULES) takes any object with a name, a version and __call__(task, candidate) -> Evidence | None, where the Task is the title and its state, the Candidate one line as a matcher sees it (its kind, its one text, whether the owner sent it) and the Evidence a rule of the matcher's own naming, the task's words it found and a confidence from 0 to 1. The command owns the record, the tasks, the window and the candidates, dedupes a calendar entry across sources and never lets a matcher write. The promises judge's engine (judge.Engine, docs/promises.md: a local instruct model that answers one JSON object per candidate, never the network) is the shape of the next matcher: one that reads a task and a line and says whether the line shows the task done. Its proposals land in the same report, with the same task ids, and done is unchanged. The report's matcher field says which one ran.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: It does not read a mail's body, a calendar entry's notes or a transaction's amount; it does not look at messages (message/v1), notes or transcripts for "I booked it", which is promises' ground; it does not close a task on its own, retract anything, or run a model. A task whose evidence is in no line of the record — the plants were watered — is yours to close with done and no evidence.

docs.title: The timeline
docs.text:
The timeline is the record's moments beside the map, at five zooms: a day, a week, a month, a year and all years. The Library serves it at /timeline; logbook show timeline prints the same thing, and with --json the very object the page is drawn from. It is RFC 0043's timeline (§11) and the owner's places (§12), slice F: the map itself comes with slice G.

logbook serve                                   # then http://127.0.0.1:8765/timeline
logbook show timeline                           # today
logbook show timeline --day 2026-06-12          # one day: its moments and the moves between them
logbook show timeline --week 2026-W25 --json    # an ISO week, a line per day
logbook show timeline --month 2026-06           # a calendar of the month's nights
logbook show timeline --year 2026               # twelve months and the journeys
logbook show timeline --life                    # all years, per place and per vessel

docs.title: A moment
docs.text:
A moment is a stay of note: one of your stays, as the Day lists them (a stop that holds a line, a photo or a call is already a stay), or a run aboard an asset (aboard Solvind). It says:

  • the place: the name places.json gives it, else the stay's label (an airport, coordinates with what is near);
  • the time: the part of the stay on the day, 19:30–22:40, and its length;
  • who was there: the confirmed in one list and the proposed in another, in grey with a ? and the reason in words: invited (an attendee of a calendar entry), spoke (a recording), you said (your own note), face on photos (a photo library's face, however many photos), and no other reason. Nothing new proposes anyone here: these are the Day's own proposals, and a proposal is never shown as confirmed;
  • the photos taken during it, your own camera's first and the starred first;
  • what passed during it, placed by time and never by subject: the messages by conversation (who and where, Kari Nordmann · iMessage), the calls (who and which way, Ola Nordmann · call in), the sessions with an agent (your words, and the agent's marked as machine text), the mail threads, the notes, the calendar's entries. Never how many messages or how long a call: no number stands beside a person;
  • paid, at tier 3 only: the transactions whose time falls inside it, with the merchant. A day no payment source covers says No payment source covers this day, with the last day one does: a day is covered when it lies between the first and the last day of a transaction that stands (a retracted one covers nothing).

On the page each moment is folded to one line, Saltbu · 19:30–22:40 · 6 photos · 2 conversations · with Ola Nordmann, Kari Nordmann, Per Hansen?, the people last, so no number stands beside a name, and opens to the rest. The moves between moments are one line each, walk · 07:25–07:41 · 460 m.

docs.title: The zooms
docs.text:
zoom /timeline/... what it shows day day/2026-06-12 the moments and the moves between them; the night after and its class; the day's track week week/2026-W25 a line per day: its night and its moments as chips month month/2026-06 a calendar: each day in its night's colour, its photos, signed or open year year/2026 the twelve months as a strip of their nights by class; the journeys as bands all years life per place, its visits since the first; per vessel, its nights and passages; who was there, by name

Every zoom is a link; the page keeps no state and runs no script. /timeline alone is the day you are in. The month and the year count the nights apart: home 21 · the family's places 4 · aboard 6 · away 3 (and in transit when no stay held a night). All years reads Saltbu · 23 visits since 2014 and aboard Solvind · 41 nights on 9 passages, with the people who were there by name only: no number ever stands beside a person.

A visit is a run of your stays at the place with no other named place (or vessel) between: a bench on the walk home does not end one. A passage is a run aboard one vessel, from going aboard to coming ashore (stays.fold). A journey on the year is a run of nights away from home, the rule of show trips (a night in transit continues it), drawn for the part of it inside the year and linked to its first day.

docs.title: The map
docs.text: On a phone the map's place comes first and the list under it; on a wider screen the list is on the left and the map on the right. Until slice G draws a map from an offline map file, the place is a box that says the map comes with slice G and holds the day's track as the Day page draws it: the stays as numbered dots and the moves between them, from the record's own coordinates. Nothing is fetched.

docs.title: A place's class
docs.text:
Each night is one of four classes, its colour on the month and the year. The class is read from what places.json already has (kind and tags, SPEC §3.2), never from a key of its own, in this order:

class when aboard a night aboard an asset home a place of kind home, or a night within reach of one (the Day's 400 m rule) family a place with the tag family (case aside) away everything else

So a place of kind other or asset-berth without a family tag, and a night at no named place, is away. To make a place one of the family's, give it the tag: --tags family when you add or name it (logbook setup places add or name), or by hand in the file:

{"Saltbu": {"lat": 59.66, "lon": 10.63, "radius_m": 150, "kind": "other", "tags": ["family"]}}

docs.title: Tiers and speed
docs.text:
Every zoom reads through the page's gate, as every page of the Library does, and says the highest tier it read. A reading without tier 3 has no money slot at all: not an empty one.

The day and the week read the lines of their own days, as the Day does. The month, the year and all years read your track from the index alone and count photos and signatures from the index's columns, and the Library reads each once for the record as it stands (the head, the settings beside the chain and the day): a reload, or another tab, is served from that reading until the record moves.

All years is not rebuilt each time the record moves. The first time it is opened after a move, the Library starts one build of it and waits up to ten seconds for it, so a record of a few years shows it at once. On a record of many years the build takes longer (about a minute at five million lines), and meanwhile the page says, in one line, that all years is being built; a reload shows it once it is done, and it is kept until the record moves again. show timeline --life builds it every time it runs.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: Not a summary: every count is a count of lines, and the words are yours or the sources'. Not an editor: the page writes nothing. Not a map: that is slice G.

docs.title: The tour: every command on your own record
docs.text: Try it is five minutes on a demo record and The first hour is logbook setup screen by screen. This page is the long form: what each command does on a record of your own, in the order you are likely to meet them. Every example is synthetic; the person lives in Oslo and does not exist.

docs.title: Sixty seconds with an iPhone backup
docs.text:
Plug the iPhone into a Mac, select it in Finder and press Back Up Now. The backup lands in ~/Library/Application Support/MobileSync/Backup/<udid> (on Windows under %APPDATA%\Apple Computer\MobileSync\Backup\). Then:

export LOGBOOK_DIAL_PREFIX=47                       # your country code, for numbers saved without one
logbook import backup ~/Library/Application\ Support/MobileSync/Backup/<udid> --dry-run   # what is there, how big
logbook import backup ~/Library/Application\ Support/MobileSync/Backup/<udid> --only <sources>   # the stores the dry run found
logbook import backup <the same> --only contacts,whatsapp        # just some of it

One command reads the backup's Manifest.db, finds the stores the adapters know — Contacts, WhatsApp's contacts and chats, Messages, Calendar, Notes and more — copies each one with its -wal/-shm siblings and its media folder into inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/<source>/, checks every copy against the stored blob, and runs the adapters on the copies: contacts first, so the chats that follow already have their people. The backup itself is only ever read. Per source it prints found or not found, the lines added and what was skipped, and it ends with verify. Re-running it appends nothing already logged. inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/copies.json lists every copy. The manifest's Size is what a file measured on the phone and can be stale against the stored blob; a copy that matches the blob but not Size is one warning naming the file and both sizes, recorded in copies.json, never an error.

An encrypted backup (Encrypt local backup ticked in Finder) holds more than an unencrypted one: Health, the call log and Safari's history are only ever backed up encrypted. import backup reads one with the crypto extra and the password in one environment variable, never a flag:

pipx install --force "openlogbook[crypto]"   # or: uv tool install "openlogbook[crypto]"
read -s LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD && export LOGBOOK_BACKUP_PASSWORD   # typed once, never echoed
logbook import backup ~/Library/Application\ Support/MobileSync/Backup/<udid> --only <sources>

The keybag in Manifest.plist is unlocked first, so a wrong password fails on one line before any file is touched; then Manifest.db is decrypted into the inbox folder and every file is decrypted a chunk at a time on its way to the same inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/<source>/ layout, so the adapters run unchanged. The password is never printed, never written anywhere, and never part of an error. copies.json records encrypted: true and each file's protection class. The stores only an encrypted backup carries come along: the call log (ios-calls/CallHistory.storedata) runs through its adapter like the others; Health (health/healthdb_secure.sqlite, healthdb.sqlite) and Safari (safari/History.db) are copied out beside them: Health runs through apple-health (RFC 0014; healthdb.sqlite is copied first so the store finds its source names beside it), Safari runs through safari; --only calls,health names them too. Without the extra installed the command prints the pip install line and exits 2; without the variable it says which one to set.

docs.title: Where to keep the record
docs.text:
Never in a folder that iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Google Drive or OneDrive syncs. Those services evict files to the cloud and fetch them back on demand, so reads stall on files that are not really there, and the record ends up on someone else's server. Keep it in a plain local folder and point LOGBOOK_HOME at it:

logbook init ~/Records/Logbook           # once
export LOGBOOK_HOME=~/Records/Logbook    # in your shell profile, so every command finds it

logbook setup asks for the folder and refuses one a sync client owns, with the reason; then the timezone, your own names, emails and phones (policy/owner.json, so you are never your own company), your home as coordinates pasted from a maps app, and what is on this machine to import — a Takeout in ~/Downloads, an iPhone backup, Messages on a Mac — each with a dry run first. One question at a time, each with its default and why it is asked; q stops and logbook setup again continues where it stopped (state/setup.json); --yes takes every default. It never asks for a secret: a live source is named by its variable and where the key comes from. docs/first-hour.md shows every screen.

Back it up with logbook backup DEST: one verified snapshot of the record under DEST/<owner_id>/<timestamp>/ on another disk — the month files, logbook.json, policy/, places.json, assets.json, attachments/ and notes/; never index.sqlite, inbox/ or state/ — with every file the previous snapshot already holds unchanged hard-linked to it, so a daily snapshot of a record with gigabytes of attachments costs the bytes that changed. The copy is verified where it lands and its head must be the live head, or nothing is kept; --keep N prunes to the newest N; --verify also hashes every attachment against its name. backup list DEST shows each snapshot with its lines, head and size; backup restore SNAPSHOT TARGET copies one back into an empty folder and verifies it. A destination inside the record or under a sync client's folder is refused. Time Machine or an equivalent that copies the folder as it is works too. docs/backup.md has the launchd and systemd examples for a nightly run.

logbook backup /Volumes/Backup/Logbook --keep 14     # a verified snapshot, the newest fourteen kept
logbook backup list /Volumes/Backup/Logbook
logbook backup restore /Volumes/Backup/Logbook/<owner_id>/2026-06-02T071500Z ~/Records/Logbook

logbook doctor checks that this machine is set up to keep the record, one line per check, pass, warn or fail, and exits 1 when anything fails: the record is found and verify is green with logbook.json at the head; index.sqlite is current; policy/owner.json names at least one alias; places.json has a home; assets.json is a registry; each optional extra (ais, crypto, sealed, speakers, transcribe) is installed, with its install line when not; the variables of every live source the record uses are set, by name only, never a value; the volume has room; and the folder is not one iCloud Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive or Google Drive syncs, which is a fail with the reason; the last scheduled run was recent and clean, and a restore test of the backup passed within 35 days (the schedule). It reads and never writes, so it is safe to run any time.

logbook doctor
pass  record             12,772 lines, head 53d39fda0b2c…, verified; /Users/ines/Records/Logbook
pass  index              index.sqlite is current with logbook.json
warn  owner              policy/owner.json is empty: add your other names, emails and phones so you are never your own company
pass  places             4 place(s), home: Home
pass  assets             1 asset(s): nordlys
pass  extra:ais          websockets is installed
pass  extra:crypto       cryptography is installed
pass  extra:sealed       pyrage is installed
warn  extra:speakers     pyannote.audio not installed: pipx install --force "openlogbook[ais,crypto,sealed,speakers]"
warn  extra:transcribe   mlx-whisper or faster-whisper not installed: pipx install --force "openlogbook[ais,crypto,sealed,transcribe]"
warn  sync:dawarich      set LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY
pass  disk               184.2 GiB free on the record's volume
pass  folder             a plain local folder, no sync client
13 checks: 9 pass, 4 warn, 0 fail

docs.title: Sealing tiers 2 and 3
docs.text:
The envelope of every line is plain: when, what kind, which source. What a tier 2 or 3 line says, a note, a message, a transaction, a health sample, can be sealed at rest with age to keys only you hold (SPEC §2 and §4, RFC 0029, ADR 0020). The chain is untouched: verify checks every hash without any key and says how many lines it did not open; with your identity it opens each one and checks it against its digest too. Tier 1 is never sealed.

pipx install --force "openlogbook[sealed]"   # pyrage, age's Rust implementation; nothing else changes
logbook key init --recovery                # this machine's identity, and a recovery identity printed once for paper
logbook key seal --all                     # seal the tier 2–3 lines written before the record had recipients
logbook verify                             # valid — …; sealed: 4,100 lines, every one opened and checked
logbook key show                           # the recipients, and whether this machine's identity opens the record
logbook key add-recipient --recipient age1…   # a new laptop, a hardware key: resealed, no hash changes

Two recipients or none: key init refuses to seal until a recovery identity exists, because a record that can lose its only key is not sealed, it is lost. The identity lives at ~/.config/logbook/identities/<owner_id>.txt (%APPDATA%\logbook\identities\ on Windows), readable by you alone, never inside the record, never in a variable that is on disk; --identity-file PATH or LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE=PATH name another file. A machine without it reads tier 1, lists every day, verifies the chain and refuses to write tiers 2–3 in one sentence. Attachments a sealed line points at are sealed under the same name. The index is a plaintext locator and lives in your cache directory (~/.cache/logbook/<owner_id>/), not in the record, with chat ids blinded; logbook search does not search sealed lines. export writes opened payloads unless --sealed; a crossing package reseals to the destination's recipient from policy/crossing.json, or ships opened under --open. key seal --all replaces the plain files and shreds nothing: a backup from before still holds the plaintext.

docs.title: Docker and Nix
docs.text:
The repository builds both; in a clone of it:

docker build -t logbook .
docker run --rm -v ~/Logbook:/data logbook show today   # the record is /data inside
nix build                                               # then result/bin/logbook

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
0.3.0 changes how lines are hashed (format logbook/0.2, SPEC §3.1). A record written by 0.1.0 or 0.2.0 is refused until it is migrated. Back up first, then migrate once:

cp -a ~/Logbook ~/Logbook.bak    # or wherever LOGBOOK_HOME points
logbook repair migrate           # same lines, new hashes; keeps the old files at logbook-0.1/

Format logbook/0.3 (sealing, SPEC §3.1) hashes by the same rule as 0.2, so a 0.2 record is read as it is and needs no migration; logbook key seal --all is the one optional step, and it leaves a migration/v1 line.

0.5.0 corrects the units apple-health gave resting heart rate and HRV (RFC 0014). A record that imported a Health store with an earlier version carries those lines 60 and 1,000 times too large; put them right once:

logbook repair health-units --dry-run   # how many lines it would retract and re-emit
logbook repair health-units             # per wrong line a corrected line and a retraction; nothing rewritten

docs.title: What is in the folder
docs.text:
~/Logbook/
  logbook/          the record. one file per month. append only. never edit.
    2026/09.jsonl
  inbox/            drop anything here. `logbook import inbox list` says what was read; `import inbox clean` moves or deletes it.
  notes/            what you write. plain Markdown, one file per day.
  logbook.json      who this is, your timezone, the chain head; `day_start` when your day does not begin at
                    midnight ("06:00": a line at 02:00 belongs to the evening before; RFC 0036, draft).
  policy/           crossing.json: the highest tier each circle member may receive, `until` when the access is
                    lent for a while, `signed_within_days` when only days you signed lately may cross (RFC 0036, draft). yours to edit.
                    stays.json: how long a stay is, how far a place reaches. yours to edit.
                    import.json: the sources you switched off, each with a reason. yours to edit.
                    owner.json: your own other names, emails and phones, so you are never your own company. yours to edit.
                    questions.json: the digest's closing questions, each with the facts it asks on. yours to edit.
  assets.json       the boats, aircraft and cars whose tracks the record keeps (ADR 0018). yours to edit.
  places.json       the named places: lat, lon, radius_m, kind (home, asset-berth, other), tags, country. `logbook setup places`.
  state/            where each live source left off, and which question the digest asked. bookkeeping, not the record.
  exports/          crossing.json: where the last crossing to each member ended. bookkeeping.

Nothing here needs the app to make sense. Open the files in any editor twenty years from now.

If you also keep a clone of this repository, set LOGBOOK_HOME to your record's folder and pass that path to logbook init. On a case-insensitive disk (macOS by default) ~/Logbook and a clone named ~/logbook are the same folder; init refuses a folder that contains pyproject.toml, .git or logbook/__init__.py, and the CLI never picks such a folder as your record.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text:
Two ways in. add reads a file you already hold; sync asks a service you run for what is new.

logbook add ~/Downloads/dawarich-export.json      # any export the adapters recognise, or a folder
logbook add ~/Takeout/"Location History (Timeline)"/Records.json   # Google Takeout; Timeline.json works too
logbook add ~/Takeout/"Google Photos"                 # Google Takeout photos: one line per file, the pixels stay put
logbook add takeout-chat ~/Takeout/"Google Chat"      # Takeout by name: pay, chat, meet, contacts, keep, tasks, chrome, youtube, … (docs/adapters/takeout.md)
logbook add takeout-pay ~/Takeout/"Google Pay" --dry-run   # any import: count against the record, write nothing
logbook add ~/backup/31bb7ba8914766d4ba40d6dfb6113c8b614be442   # iOS Contacts from an unencrypted Finder/iTunes backup
logbook add ~/backup/7c7fba66680ef796b916b067077cc246adacf01d   # WhatsApp (iOS) ChatStorage.sqlite from the same backup
logbook add ~/backup/4f98687d8ab0d6d1a371110e6b7300f6e465bef2   # Apple Notes NoteStore.sqlite from the same backup
logbook add ~/backup/2041457d5fe04d39d0ab481178355df6781e6858   # iOS Calendar.sqlitedb from the same backup
logbook add ios-calls ~/inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/ios-calls/CallHistory.storedata   # the call log, by adapter name
logbook add health ~/inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/health/healthdb_secure.sqlite   # Apple Health, by adapter name (or apple-health)
logbook import backup ~/backup --only contacts,whatsapp,notes,calendar,calls,health   # all of the above from the backup folder, in one go
logbook import inbox list                         # every file under inbox/: size, the import that read it, whether every line is in
logbook import inbox clean --to /Volumes/Archive   # move what is imported in full to an external disk (or --delete it); the rest stays
logbook import attachments import-backup ~/backup --only whatsapp,imessage,photos   # then the media the lines name, into attachments/
logbook add transcript ~/Meetings/tromso.md --source manual   # a transcript: JSON (transcript/v1), WebVTT, SRT, Markdown, text
logbook add ~/Zoom/GMT20260301-130000_Recording.transcript.vtt --source zoom   # VTT and SRT are recognised on sight
logbook add mail ~/Takeout/Mail --account you@example.org --skip-labels Spam,Trash   # Gmail via Google Takeout: one mail/v1 line per message
logbook sync granola                              # every Granola recording, and its summary as a derived note
logbook sync mail                                 # the same mailbox live over IMAP, read-only; dedupes against the Takeout import
logbook sync notion                               # what happened in Notion each day: pages created, edited, moved, archived; never their text
logbook sync github                               # commits, issues and pull requests created, closed, merged, reviews and comments (docs/adapters/github.md)
logbook add github-export ~/code/oldboat          # an old project's clone or GitHub's account export: its commits and each version of its docs
logbook add flights ~/Downloads/flighty.csv       # a Flighty export: one flight/v1 line per flight, evidence tracked
logbook add flight "LX 561 NCE ZRH 2026-09-27 pilot"   # your own word: evidence declared
logbook add story ~/Stories/lake.md --teller ola@example.org --listener kari.nordmann@example.org --refers-to 1961   # a told story (RFC 0028): on the day it was told, about the time it names
logbook derive flights                            # calendar entries + your location points leaving one airport for another: evidence inferred
logbook derive transcripts voice-memos            # a transcript/v1 line per voice memo, by a local model (openlogbook[transcribe]); nothing leaves the machine
logbook add screentime --mac                      # this Mac's Screen Time sessions (knowledgeC.db, behind Full Disk Access): app, span, device; never a title or URL
logbook add screentime --backup ~/backup          # the phone's Screen Time store out of an iOS backup: hourly totals per app (docs/adapters/screentime.md)
logbook sync immich                               # everything since the last run; safe to repeat
logbook sync immich --since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z  # or everything Immich received or changed since then
logbook sync immich --dry-run                     # count and summarise, write nothing
logbook sync immich --restart                     # the whole library again, whatever the watermark says

sync remembers where it got to in state/<source>.json and re-runs append nothing that is already in the log. The watermark is the source's own clock, when it received or last changed an item, not the capture time, so a photo taken in 2015 and uploaded tomorrow is picked up by tomorrow's sync and still lands on its 2015 day. Each live source is configured by environment variables; missing ones are named and the command exits 2.

The first sync immich by hand walks the whole library, which takes hours for hundreds of thousands of assets (the first scheduled run reads the last 14 days: the schedule). It says what it is walking before it starts — immich: 426,121 assets on the server, 0 already in the record (the count the server gives; total unknown when it will not say) — and then counts every page as x of N assets, so a long walk is told from a loop. An interrupted walk (Ctrl-C, a lost connection, a server error) is checkpointed in state/immich.json as the lines land, and the next run says resuming where the last run stopped, at x of N assets and asks the server for nothing before that point; --restart walks the library from the beginning instead. Each asset is fetched once: the pages are ordered by capture time, which a burst or a batch of scans shares to the second, and the server serves such a run again at a page boundary; the adapter sees through that and the record's own refusal of a line it already holds stays the safety net.

sync mail is the mailbox over IMAP (LOGBOOK_IMAP_HOST, LOGBOOK_IMAP_USER, LOGBOOK_IMAP_PASSWORD, an app password): read-only, every folder resumed from its own mark, and a message the Takeout import already wrote is refused by Message-ID before its body is fetched (Mail).

logbook sync --all runs every configured live source in turn — configured: at least one of its LOGBOOK_* variables set, and all it needs present — each from its own watermark; a disabled source or one with no variable set is skipped and said so, and a failure in one never stops the next. The quick sources go first and immich last, and the first line says the order, so a photo walk of hours never holds up the messages, the calendar, the positions or the weather. Each source prints its own summary as it runs, then one line per source closes the run (ok, failed (status 1), skipped (LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_KEY not set)), and the exit status is 1 when any failed. A dry run never waits out a source's quota or rate limit: the first such answer ends that source's dry run on one line (sync: drive: dry run stopped at the source's limit after 0 lines: HTTP 429: …), exit 1, nothing written, and --all goes on to the next. logbook sync --install-schedule makes the machine run sync --scheduled at 00:00, 12:00 and 18:00 local and sync --scheduled --close at 06:00, the run that closes the day (the dream's catch-up after the sync, when the dream is there and allowed): two launchd agents on macOS (~/Library/LaunchAgents/org.logbook.sync.plist and org.logbook.sync.close.plist), two systemd user timers on Linux (~/.config/systemd/user/logbook-sync.timer and logbook-sync-close.timer). The plists or units are printed before they are written, nothing is written outside that directory, and --uninstall-schedule removes them again; --system writes daemons for a machine nobody logs in to and prints the two sudo commands that install them. Installing also names this machine the record's home in state/home.json (ADR 0022): the one machine that writes, which logbook doctor checks on every machine and warns about on any other. The agent runs the Python that installed it and points at the record found at install time; the keys your sources need it reads from ~/.config/logbook/sync.env (KEY=value lines, mode 600), which you write and the command never does. The scheduled run is sync --all (a source's first scheduled run reads its last 14 days, never its whole history: the schedule), then doctor, with the outcome in state/last-run.json, the restore test on the first Sunday of the month, and, with LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_TOKEN and LOGBOOK_NOTIFY_TELEGRAM_CHAT in that file, one Telegram message when something is wrong or on Sunday evening (the schedule). sync weather is the one source that asks a third party about your days: it asks nothing, by name or in --all, unless that file (or the environment) says LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1, and then each run asks about the days since the last, yesterday on the first.

logbook sync --all                                # every configured source, one after the other
logbook sync --all --dry-run                      # count per source, write nothing
LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1 logbook sync weather --since 2026-06-01   # the weather of your days' places, one decimal of latitude (docs/adapters/weather.md)
logbook sync --install-schedule                   # 00:00, 06:00 (the close), 12:00 and 18:00 local
logbook sync --scheduled                          # what the schedule runs: sync --all, then doctor
logbook sync --uninstall-schedule

A nightly logbook backup goes on the same scheduler, by hand: docs/backup.md has the launchd agent and the systemd timer for a 03:00 snapshot that keeps two weeks.

Contacts become resolution lines (RFC 0006): each contact mints a person or company id in the record, and every phone number and email address points at it. Set LOGBOOK_DIAL_PREFIX (for example 44) so numbers saved without a country code get one, with the national trunk 0 dropped (07700 900123 becomes +447700900123); a number that already starts with the prefix digits but no +, or any number when the variable is unset, is kept as entered and flagged unnormalised.

WhatsApp messages become message/v1 lines (RFC 0008), one per message, with the sender as the same kind of phone ref, so one resolution of a number covers the address book and the chats. Media files are not copied with the lines: a file found under Message/ beside the database is hashed and its digest kept under extra.media, and logbook import attachments import-backup <backup> --only whatsapp,imessage,photos later streams every file the lines name out of the backup into the content-addressed store, checked against the line (docs/attachments.md); set LOGBOOK_WHATSAPP_HASH_MEDIA=0 to skip the hashing on a large store. A group message sent from a linked device carries a @lid id instead of a phone number, which no contact list knows; add WhatsApp's own ContactsV2.sqlite (it sits beside ChatStorage.sqlite) and each lid becomes an alias of the phone number WhatsApp pairs it with (RFC 0006 alias_of), so the sender takes the name your contacts import gave that number, whichever import came first.

Google Photos from a Takeout become photo/v1 lines (RFC 0002), one per media file in the Google Photos/ folder, timed by the sidecar's taken time, with the place, the album, the caption and the names Google tagged as extra.people refs (never resolved); a live photo's still and motion halves are one camera line, a photo from a shared album is received, an edited copy with no sidecar is still a line, timed by the file. The sidecar naming Google uses (.json, .supplemental-metadata.json, the truncated and (1)-numbered variants) is matched defensively and a sidecar with no file is counted. Media files are hashed into extra.media as for WhatsApp, never copied; set LOGBOOK_TAKEOUT_HASH_MEDIA=0 to skip the hashing.

Apple Notes become note/v1 lines (RFC 0010), one per note, with the plain text pulled out of the note archive, the title, the folder and the modification time. A note edited since the last import is a new line (its raw_id carries the modification time); password-protected notes are skipped because their body is encrypted; notes in Recently Deleted are logged and flagged deleted.

Calendar entries become event/v1 lines (RFC 0009), one per entry as the phone stores it: the span, the calendar, the place, the organizer and attendees as email refs, the status; a recurring entry is one line carrying its rule as RRULE text and a moved occurrence points back at it — occurrences are never expanded. An all-day entry is placed at local midnight in your record's timezone. The store's placeholder rows (a start before 1900, such as 1601) are skipped and counted; a birthday from 1965 is kept.

Calls become call/v1 lines (RFC 0012), one per call the phone's log stores, from the CallHistory.storedata an encrypted backup carries: the start, the end when the call was answered, the direction, whether it connected, the seconds it lasted, the other end as a phone, email or handle ref (the same shape as a message's sender, so one resolution of a number covers the address book, the chats and the calls) and the service as the phone names it — cellular, facetime, facetime-audio, or a third-party app such as whatsapp. A missed call is a line too. Tier 1: a call record is about your own time and carries nobody's words. Any add ios-calls <file> names the adapter for a store copied out under another name; logbook add <file> recognises it by content.

Flights become flight/v1 lines (RFC 0013), one per flight, from up to three places that meet on one key, (date, carrier, number): a Flighty export (add flights <csv>, evidence tracked), your calendar plus your location points leaving one airport and next reaching another, silent in between or not (derive flights, evidence inferred), and your own sentence (add flight "LX 561 NCE ZRH 2026-09-27 pilot", evidence declared). A flight seen twice is not written twice as two flights: the later observation supersedes the standing line with the merge — the tracker's fields win, your declared role always wins — and lists every observation it folded in; a codeshare (two numbers, one aircraft leaving once) is one flight too. An inferred leg is a flight only between airports 150 km or more apart, never one a tracked flight already covers, and carries a number only when it is the flight the calendar entry names. The package ships the world's 1,150 large airports with their zones and OurAirports' type; --airports FILE (or LOGBOOK_AIRPORTS) adds a private field (type optional: medium_airport for a regional field with scheduled traffic). Tier 1; a booking reference is never kept.

Apple Health becomes health-sample/v1 lines (RFC 0014) from the healthdb_secure.sqlite an encrypted backup carries: steps, distance, active and basal energy and flights climbed summed into quarter-hour buckets per device; heart rate at its own resolution, at most one reading a minute per device; resting heart rate, heart-rate variability and weight one line each; every sleep stage as a span with its stage; every workout as a span with its duration, activity, energy and distance. Each line names the device that measured it (Watch7,1) and, when healthdb.sqlite is beside the store, the source's name. Tier 3 (SPEC §4; --tier overrides). logbook add health <file> names the adapter; logbook add <file> recognises the store by content. Re-importing a later backup appends only what is new.

show prints people by name — the sender of a message, the organizer and attendees of an event — and the names come from your own resolution lines, never from the raw lines: import your contacts to get them. The last unretracted resolution of a ref wins (RFC 0006); a ref nobody has resolved shows as the source gave it, after the name the source itself attached, if any. show --raw prints every ref unchanged, and a note's whole text where show prints its first line and … (+N lines). A calendar entry two calendars carry (the same title, or the same flight number, within five minutes) is one row naming both sources. Either way, show only reads.

Transcripts become transcript/v1 lines (RFC 0004), one per recording, tier 3 by default because a transcript carries other people's words in full (--tier overrides). The text is never in the line: the file's own bytes go into the content-addressed store, attachments/<sha256> (SPEC §1.1), and the line points at them; raw_id is <source>:<sha256> unless the file brings one, so the same transcript added twice is one line. logbook add transcript <file|folder> --source <name> reads JSON already in transcript/v1 shape (the interchange format any tool can write: a logbook export line minus the chain fields), WebVTT and SRT (each cue a turn, the speaker from the voice tag or a leading Name:, else unknown), and Markdown or plain text with Speaker: text lines and an optional front-matter block for title, started_at, ended_at and participants. A file with no start of its own takes --at, else a date and time in its name (2026-03-01T13-00-00Z …, Zoom's GMT20260301-130000_…), else it is skipped and counted. Speakers stay as the source labels them; nothing is resolved here. Turn and speaker counts and the duration sit under extra.

Mail becomes mail/v1 lines (RFC 0015), one per message, tier 2 by default (--tier sets another for the whole import, never per message). logbook add mail <file.mbox|folder> reads a Google Takeout Mail/ export — or any mbox — streamed, one message in memory at a time however large the file (the lines read from the last 200 wait while the record is asked about them): the Message-ID as raw_id (prefixed by the mailbox when --account names it, so a re-import appends nothing; a live puller appends nothing either way, since every mail road asks the record by the normalised Message-ID before it writes), the thread root from References, the sender and recipients as {email, name} exactly as the headers spell them (a resolution of the address names them in show, as for a message's sender), the subject, the Date header with its offset kept and at in UTC, Gmail's labels, the body as plain text (an HTML-only message stripped to its text, no library), the size, and every attachment by name, media type and length — never decoded. Attachments are decoded, hashed and put into attachments/ only with --attachments; otherwise the line names them and the record holds no bytes. direction is sent when the sender is one of your addresses — put "owner_emails": ["you@example.org"] in logbook.json, or pass --account — else received. --only-labels/--skip-labels keep or drop by Gmail label, --since cuts by day or instant. A message with no Message-ID is keyed by the digest of its bytes and counted; a message with no readable Date is timed by its mbox separator and counted; a body longer than 64 KB is cut and counted; nothing is dropped silently. Built for a 20 GB Takeout: read in chunks at well over 40 MB/s with one message in memory, a progress line every 10,000 messages with the rate, and resumable — inbox/manifest.json keeps the byte offset of the last message the record holds, so an interrupted add mail picks up there and a finished one reads nothing (--restart reads it all again). show prints ✉ subject — from → to (n attachments), never the body; show --raw prints the body under the row. docs/adapters/mail.md has the whole of it.

show stats is one screen of what the record holds, counted through the index: lines per kind, source and year, retractions, resolutions, attachments. It prints numbers, kinds, sources and dates, never what a line says; --json gives the same as one object. show stats --health is one row per day from the health lines — hours asleep (the night that ends on that day, asleep stages only — never in bed or awake — each device's spans unioned so a night written twice counts once, then the longest device, never a sum across devices), steps (per quarter hour the larger device, summed) and resting heart rate — and prints no device, zone or other field; --json gives the rows as days.

Source Variables What it logs immich LOGBOOK_IMMICH_URL, LOGBOOK_IMMICH_KEY one photo/v1 line per asset: capture time, camera, place, size, faces as person ids, never the pixels dawarich LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_URL, LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY (LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_LOOKBACK_H, default 24) one location/v1 line per point, identical to the line its export gives imessage none required: this Mac's ~/Library/Messages/chat.db (LOGBOOK_IMESSAGE_DB for another store; LOGBOOK_IMESSAGE_LOOKBACK_H, default 24; LOGBOOK_IMESSAGE_HASH_MEDIA=0 to skip hashing) one message/v1 line per message, identical to the line the phone backup's sms.db gives beeper LOGBOOK_BEEPER_TOKEN (LOGBOOK_BEEPER_URL, default http://localhost:23373; LOGBOOK_BEEPER_ALLOW_REMOTE=1 to read a Beeper on another machine, which the design says not to) one message/v1 line per message of every chat Beeper Desktop bridges, source beeper-<network>; attachments referenced by asset id, never fetched; --networks chooses, default every one but imessage granola LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_KEY (LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_URL, default https://public-api.granola.ai/v1; LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_LOOKBACK_H, default 24; LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_SUMMARIES=0 to skip the summaries) one transcript/v1 line per recording, tier 3, the transcript in attachments/; plus Granola's AI summary as a tier-2 note/v1 line with extra.derived_from the transcript line's id notion LOGBOOK_NOTION_TOKEN (LOGBOOK_NOTION_ROOTS: page or database ids or links to limit to; LOGBOOK_NOTION_OWNER_ID: your Notion user id, to mark your own actions) one event/v1 line per page, day and action (created, edited, moved, archived), tier 1: title, path, id, url, who acted, the body's digest and word count, a row's status, select, date and checkbox values, its database and the ids of the rows its relations link to; never the text (Notion) github LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN (a fine-grained token, read-only) and LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS (owner/name, comma-separated, or --all; LOGBOOK_GITHUB_URL for a GitHub Enterprise Server);
