your logins under handles in policy/owner.json one event/v1 line per commit, issue or pull request created, closed or merged, review and comment, tier 1 (tier 2 from a private repository): the message, body or comment in full, who acted (owner or other), agent: true when an agent's session marker is in the text; a watermark per repo (GitHub) gcal LOGBOOK_GCAL_URLS: Google Calendar's private iCal addresses, comma-separated, each optionally name=url (LOGBOOK_GCAL_LOOKBACK_H, default 24) one event/v1 line per event, identical to the line the calendar's .ics export gives (source ics) drive LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY (a Workspace service account's JSON key file) and LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER (the address it reads as); Google Drive one event/v1 line per file, hour and activity — created, edited, renamed, moved, shared, commented on, trashed, deleted, restored — with a count; the file's name, type, id and link, who acted, never its content; tier 1 gtasks the same two; Google Tasks one task/v1 line per task each time it changes, the line a Takeout export gives (source google-takeout), so logbook promises tasks reads it and a later export writes nothing twice; a done one says how long it was open; never the notes; tier 2 meet the same two; Google Meet one event/v1 line per call that has ended, tier 1: when, the meeting code, who joined as Meet names them; and when Meet transcribed it, one transcript/v1 line as Granola's is, tier 3, the words in attachments/ gaudit the same two; Google sign-ins one event/v1 line per sign-in event of yours in the Workspace's login audit log, tier 1: when, what happened, how, and the place Google derived from the address; never the address

Create the Immich key under Account settings → API keys with only the asset.read permission. The logbook only ever reads; a key that cannot write is a key that cannot do harm if it leaks.

docs.title: What never enters the record
docs.text: Demo, sample or placeholder data never enters the record: an adapter existing is not a decision to run it. Your list of switched-off sources lives in policy/import.json, {"disabled": [{"source": "sbb", "reason": "a demo account"}]}; add, sync and import backup skip a disabled source and say so, with or without --only, and logbook doctor sources lists every adapter this build has, file and live, with its state and the reason. init writes the empty list, and a record made earlier gets it on the first run. An alias stands for its adapter (books for apple-books, health for apple-health), and a name no adapter carries is listed as such rather than silently ignored.

docs.title: Keep it flowing
docs.text:
Import your Dawarich export once, then let sync pick up every point your phone sends after it:

export LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_URL=https://dawarich.example.org   # your own server
export LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_KEY=...                            # Settings → Account → API key
logbook add ~/Downloads/dawarich-export.json               # once: the history
logbook sync dawarich                                      # then, as often as you like

Both write the same line for the same point (same raw_id), so nothing you already imported is written twice. The first sync starts from the newest Dawarich point already in the record (the first scheduled run from 14 days back when that point is older: the schedule); after that from the last point it saw. A phone uploads in batches, so a point can reach the server after newer ones: each sync looks back 24 hours before its watermark and skips what the record already has, and says how many that was. Set LOGBOOK_DAWARICH_LOOKBACK_H for a longer or shorter window; --since pulls from an exact time instead.

On a Mac, logbook sync imessage reads the Messages database the Mac itself keeps, read-only, and writes the same line for the same message as the phone backup (same raw_id, the message guid), so a record seeded with import backup carries on from its newest message and nothing is written twice. The first run starts from the newest iMessage line already in the record (the first scheduled run from 14 days back when that line is older, or when there is none), later runs from the newest message seen, each looking back 24 hours (LOGBOOK_IMESSAGE_LOOKBACK_H) for a conversation another device synced late. Attachments stay where Messages keeps them; a file that is there is hashed into the line, one that is not is flagged. The terminal needs Full Disk Access (System Settings → Privacy & Security) to read the database; without it the sync says so on one line and exits 1.

docs.title: Beeper
docs.text:
Beeper Desktop bridges WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, Instagram, Messenger, LinkedIn, X and more into one app, and while it runs it serves a small HTTP API on this machine only. logbook sync beeper reads every chat of every network through it, read-only, and writes one message/v1 line per message under source beeper-<network> (beeper-whatsapp, beeper-signal, …), so readers can tell the networks apart.

export LOGBOOK_BEEPER_TOKEN=...                             # Beeper Desktop → Settings → Developers → Approved connections, +
logbook sync beeper --dry-run                               # count per network, write nothing
logbook sync beeper                                         # every network but imessage, each chat from its own watermark
logbook sync beeper --networks whatsapp,signal              # only these
logbook sync beeper --networks telegram --since 2020-01-01T00:00:00Z   # a network added later: its history, once

Enable the API under Settings → Developers (the switch Beeper Desktop API; it listens on http://localhost:23373 while the app runs), then create a token with the + next to Approved connections. The token is a password: it can read every chat and send as you. Keep it in the variable in your shell profile, never in a file of the record, and revoke it there when you stop using it. Leave Remote Access off: the API is meant to be read from this machine only, and sync beeper refuses a LOGBOOK_BEEPER_URL that is not localhost unless LOGBOOK_BEEPER_ALLOW_REMOTE=1 says you know what you are doing. The sync only ever issues GET requests (listing accounts, chats and messages); nothing here sends, reacts, marks read, archives or changes a thing, and a test holds it to that. logbook doctor says whether sync:beeper is configured and, when it is, whether the app answers — the one other call, GET /v1/info.

Each chat keeps its own watermark (marks in state/beeper.json): a run reads a chat back to its newest message seen, less 24 hours for a message a bridge delivers late, and the record refuses what it already holds. A chat with no watermark yet — every chat on the first run, a new chat later — starts at the source's watermark, or at --since, or, on the source's first scheduled run, 14 days back; to pull the history of a network you add to --networks later, give --since once. Reactions, hidden messages and events with neither text nor attachment (joins, calls, bridge state) are skipped and counted. An attachment is referenced by its Beeper asset id, size, media type and file name under extra.media, never downloaded: the bytes stay in Beeper. When the app is not running the sync says so on one line and exits 1, and sync --all goes on to the next source.

Known overlap. Beeper is a second view of chats other sources already read: an iMessage from this Mac's own database (sync imessage), a WhatsApp message from a chat export or the phone's backup, the Beeper cache in an iPhone backup (the beeper file adapter). Those lines carry other sources and raw ids, so the record does not deduplicate them against the Beeper lines. --networks is how you choose; the default pulls every network but imessage, which the local source has.

docs.title: Notion
docs.text:
logbook sync notion keeps what happened in your Notion workspace — a page created, edited, moved or archived, a task's status changed — as one event/v1 line per page, day and action, so the Day can say worked on Sail plan, +340 words or Book the ferry: Doing → Done. It is a record of events, never a mirror: a line points at the page by its id and link and holds no word of what the page says.

export LOGBOOK_NOTION_TOKEN=ntn_...                         # the integration's secret: a password
export LOGBOOK_NOTION_OWNER_ID=...                          # optional: your Notion user id, to mark your own actions
export LOGBOOK_NOTION_ROOTS='https://www.notion.so/…/Research-…, …'   # optional: only what is under these
logbook sync notion --dry-run                               # count, write nothing
logbook sync notion                                         # then four times a day with the schedule
logbook sync notion --since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z            # every page edited since then, once
logbook sync notion --relations-backfill --dry-run          # rows whose relations the record lacks: count
logbook sync notion --relations-backfill                    # then write them, one line a row

The token. In Notion, Settings → Connections → Develop or manage integrations → New integration, type Internal, for your workspace. Under Capabilities leave Read content on and switch Update content, Insert content and the comment capabilities off; for user information choose Read user information without email addresses, which gives the names of the people who edit (without it a line names them by id). Copy the Internal Integration Secret into LOGBOOK_NOTION_TOKEN in your shell profile, never in a file of the record. Then share the pages: an integration sees nothing until you add it to a page. Open each top-level page you want kept (your ideas, research, notes, tasks and contacts), choose ••• → Connections, and add the integration; it then reads that page and everything under it, and nothing else. LOGBOOK_NOTION_ROOTS narrows that further to the pages and databases you name, by id or by the link Copy link gives. The sync only reads (GET, and POST only to Notion's search, which changes nothing), and a test holds it to that.

Who acted. Each line names the person (or the integration) who made the page, for created, or who edited it last, for the other actions, by Notion user id and name, and marks them owner or other. Notion does not say which user is you: set LOGBOOK_NOTION_OWNER_ID to your user id, or the sync uses the user who owns the integration when Notion names one, which for an internal integration it does not. Without either, the lines say who acted and mark no one, and the run lists the people it saw with their ids, so run logbook sync notion --dry-run first and set yours before anything is written: a line is never rewritten. The owner id marks; it decides nothing else.

On the line What it holds at the page's creation time for created; its last edit otherwise. The day is the record's own local day title the page's title, verbatim; a database row's name raw_id <page id>/<day>/<action>: the dedupe key, so a page edited twice on one day is one line modified_at the page's last edit as the sync saw it, which is also the watermark extra.action created, edited, moved or archived; relations on a line --relations-backfill wrote extra.page the page's id and url (the private link, which opens only for people the page is shared with) extra.path, extra.parent the titles above the page, the top first, as far as the integration can see; the parent's type and id extra.database a database row's database, {id}: every line of a row has it, a page that is not a row never extra.actor id, name, type (person or bot) and role (owner or other) extra.body sha256 and bytes of the page's text, words, and words_delta since the page's previous line: a digest, never the text extra.properties a database row's status, select, multi-select, date and checkbox values, by name extra.changed each of those that changed since the page's previous line, {name, old, new} extra.relations a database row's relation properties, {name: [page id, …]}: the ids of the rows it links to, as Notion gives them and in its order, never their titles extra.relations_changed each relation that gained or lost an id since the row's latest line with relations, {name, added, removed} extra.moved_from on a move, the parent and path the page had

What a line never holds. The page's text, its comments, its files, its cover or icon, its public link, anyone's email or avatar, and every property but the few above: no text, number, person, phone, email, url, file, formula or rollup value, and of a relation only the ids, so a contacts database gives the names of its pages and none of their details. The digest lets you check a copy of the text against the line; a very short body could be guessed from it, as from its word count.

Relations. A database row's links to other rows — an idea's Areas, a task's project — are on the line that holds the row as it is (the one with the body's digest), as extra.relations, one entry per relation property: {"Areas": ["<page id>", …]}, the ids exactly as Notion gives them and in the order the row has them, an empty list for a relation that links nothing. A reader learns which rows belong together from the record alone: the sync never looks a related page up, so the line holds no title, body or rollup of it, and a reader that wants the title reads the related row's own lines. The row's database is on every line of the row as extra.database, so "a row of Notes" needs no question to Notion either. RFC 0009 has no field for links between entries, so the ids go under extra, where the profile keeps whatever else a source reports. A relation is a change like any other: an edit that only links or unlinks a row writes its one line, with extra.relations_changed saying which relation gained and lost which ids (a reorder gains and loses nothing); a re-sync of a row nobody touched writes nothing. As for any change, a relation changed again later on a day whose line is written waits for the row's next line on another day (or the backfill below), which tells it against the row's latest line with relations. Notion serves a relation's first 25 links with a page and the rest on request; the sync asks for the rest, paged, and when it cannot have them all it leaves relations off that line and counts the row, never writing the first 25 as if the others were gone.

Rows synced before the record kept relations get them with their next edit. To have them now, logbook sync notion --relations-backfill writes one line per row whose relations the record does not hold yet — --dry-run counts them first, --since 2026-09-01 takes only the rows edited since that local day. Each line has extra.action relations, is dated at the row's last edit (raw_id <page id>/<day>/relations) and holds the row's reference, path, parent, database and its relations as the backfill reads them; no body, property or actor, and it reads no page's blocks. It also catches links set from the other side of a relation when Notion left this row's edit time alone, saying what changed (two lines then stand at the row's last edit, and the later in the record's order is the newer); to compare, it reads every relation of more than 25 links whole on every run, a request per hundred links. A row the record holds no line of yet is left to the next sync, which writes it with its relations; the backfill never moves the watermark and never stands in for an edit or a move the sync has yet to write. It keeps to the same three requests a second and stops on one line when Notion's rate limit does not lift, the lines already written kept: running it again writes only what is still missing. In the Day a backfilled row shows once more, at its last edit, as a second Notion entry with its title.

Ideas from Notion. logbook review idea proposes a page as an idea by its root, the topmost page above it the record holds; a database row is its own root (RFC 0037 §4.3, amended 2026-10-16), so an Ideas database gives one idea per row and the page that holds the database is never the rows' idea. A row is proposed only when its Type select says Idea, as the row's latest line with extra.properties has it, and a page under a row of another type is not proposed either; a page that is no row is proposed as before. Name another select and option in policy/entities.json ("idea_rows": {"property": "Kind", "value": "Spark"}, case aside). The value is the one the line already holds, the property's name and the option's name and nothing else, at the line's tier. A line an integration made (extra.actor.type bot) is never a touch of an idea, a person on it or words written on it, and a relations line links rows and touches none (review).

The tier. Every line is tier 1: SPEC §4 and RFC 0009 give event/v1 tier 1, and a Notion line is an event with a title, a place in a tree and who acted, as a calendar entry is a title, a place and an organizer. The tier says where a line may travel (tier 1 crosses by default, ADR 0016), never who wrote it: a line Ola's edit made is tier 1 exactly as one of yours is. A note's own words are tier 2 (RFC 0010); a Notion line holds none, which is why it can be tier 1.

Which lines. A run lists the pages edited since the watermark, newest first, by Notion's cursor, and asks the record what it already holds of each. A page made since the watermark gives created on the day it was made; its last edit gives archived when the page is archived or in the trash, moved when its parent is not the one on its previous line, else edited — unless the record already holds the page at that edit. An edit on the day the page was made, seen in the same run, is the created line, which then holds the body and properties. Notion keeps no history the API shows, so a line records the page as the sync saw it: two edits between two syncs are one, an old → new value is against the page's previous line, and an edit later on a day that already has its line is not written again. A page Notion stops listing — deleted for good, or no longer shared — leaves no line. Notion's API withholds some block types from integrations, such as an AI block: a page that holds one is still written, with extra.body {"unavailable": "withheld"} in place of the digest and word count ("not_found" when a block is deleted while the sync reads the page), and the run counts those pages, names the block type once, never the page, and goes on.

The watermark is the newest last-edit time seen (state/notion.json); each run reads back two hours before it, because Notion stamps an edit to the minute and its search lists a fresh edit late, and the record refuses what it already holds. --since reads from an exact time; --dry-run counts and writes nothing. The first run by hand reads every page once, its blocks included, to count its words (a first scheduled run reads the pages edited in the last 14 days, the schedule): at three requests a second a workspace of a few thousand pages takes a quarter of an hour or more, and says how far it is every hundred pages; later runs read only what changed. The sync stays under Notion's rate limit — at most three requests a second; a 429 waits as long as Notion's Retry-After says, a server error is tried again after 1, 2, 4… seconds — and when the limit does not lift it stops on one line, exit 1, the watermark where it was, so the next run carries on. logbook doctor lists sync:notion once the token is set, by name only, and asks Notion nothing; sync --all and the schedule run it with no more configuration.

Granola works the same way (ADR 0017: backfill and live share one mapping). Create the key under Settings → Connectors → API keys (Business and Enterprise plans; scope it to your personal notes), export it as LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_KEY, and run:

logbook add transcript ~/Granola-export/ --source granola   # once, if you have exports; optional
logbook sync granola                                        # then nightly: 0 5 * * * logbook sync granola

Each recording is one transcript/v1 line, raw_id granola:<note id>, with the transcript's segments stored under attachments/ and the attendees as Granola names them; the AI summary follows as a note/v1 line, tier 2, marked extra.derived = true and pointing at the transcript by id (set LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_SUMMARIES=0 to skip it). A note made without a recording (one empty turn, zero seconds) gives no transcript line, only its summary, counted as without a recording. The watermark is the recording's end; each sync looks back 24 hours (LOGBOOK_GRANOLA_LOOKBACK_H) and skips what the record already has. A network failure is retried once, then the sync exits 1 with a clear message and nothing is written: a batch is all or nothing.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
logbook sync github keeps what happened in your repositories — every commit on the default branch, every issue and pull request created, closed or merged, every review and comment — as one event/v1 line each, tier 1 (tier 2 from a private repository, so its text never crosses at tier 1), with the message, the body or the comment in full, as RFC 0009's notes allows, and who acted, marked owner by the handles you list in policy/owner.json. A pull request an agent wrote, by the session marker in its body, is agent: true, so a page can list what your agents did. logbook add github-export DIR reads an old project's clone or GitHub's account export once: its commits, and each version of its README and docs as a digest and a word count, so an old project's ideas have a first-said date; the same commit or issue read both ways is one line. A clone says nothing of whether its repository is public, so its lines are tier 2 unless you add it with --public.

export LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_...                  # fine-grained, read-only: Contents, Issues, Pull requests, Metadata
export LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS='ines-example/sailplan'         # owner/name, comma-separated, or --all
logbook sync github --dry-run                               # count, write nothing
logbook sync github                                         # then four times a day with the schedule
logbook add github-export ~/code/oldboat                    # once per old project

docs/adapters/github.md has the whole of it: the token, who acted, the text and the tier, every field of a line, the watermark per repo and the export.

docs.title: Google, on one key
docs.text:
Six sources read your Google account: sync gmail (your mail), sync gcal (your calendars), sync drive (what happened to your Drive files), sync gtasks (your tasks), sync meet (your Meet calls) and sync gaudit (your sign-ins); and people review --from-google reads your contacts, as names for the review and never as lines (the people page). All of them sign in the same way, with one service account of your own Google Workspace that the Workspace allows to act as you (domain-wide delegation), configured by the same two variables, read-only, one scope each. A service account signs in with a key file and nothing that expires: every run signs a short request with the key and gets an access token good for an hour, which it keeps in memory for that run and never writes anywhere. There is no refresh token to go stale in a scheduled job, which is how a sign-in done once in a browser dies months later. Only you can stop it: by deleting the key or withdrawing the delegation.

Source Scope it asks for, read-only What it covers sync gmail https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly every message, as mail/v1 lines (the mail page) sync gcal https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly the calendars you own, as event/v1 lines sync drive https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.activity.readonly what happened to your files sync drive https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.metadata.readonly the folder path each Drive line names sync drive --videos, videos fetch https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.metadata.readonly, and for the fetch https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.readonly only for the family's videos: the files of one folder, then their bytes into a bounded cache (Videos); not in the list below, add it only if you use them sync gtasks https://www.googleapis.com/auth/tasks.readonly your tasks, each as it stands (task/v1) sync meet https://www.googleapis.com/auth/meetings.space.readonly your Meet calls and their transcripts sync gaudit https://www.googleapis.com/auth/admin.reports.audit.readonly your own sign-ins, from the login audit log people review --from-google https://www.googleapis.com/auth/contacts.readonly your contacts, as names for the review people review --from-google https://www.googleapis.com/auth/contacts.other.readonly your other contacts, the same

Setting it up, once, as the Workspace's administrator:

  1. In the Google Cloud console, in a project of your own (create one if you have none), open APIs & Services → Library and enable the Gmail API, the Google Calendar API, the Google Drive API, the Google Drive Activity API, the Google Tasks API, the Google Meet REST API, the Admin SDK API (the audit log) and the People API (the contacts): the ones for the sources you want.
  2. IAM & Admin → Service accounts → Create service account. Call it logbook-sync; it needs no role in the project. Open it and copy its Unique ID (the client ID, a long number).
  3. On the same page, Keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON. The browser downloads one file: that file is the key. If the console refuses, the organisation policy Disable service account key creation (iam.disableServiceAccountKeyCreation, on by default in organisations made since 2024) is in the way: turn it off for this one project under IAM & Admin → Organization policies.
  4. In the Workspace admin console, Security → Access and data control → API controls → Manage Domain Wide Delegation → Add new. Paste the client ID and, as the OAuth scopes, the scopes of the table above, comma-separated, all read-only: https://www.googleapis.com/auth/gmail.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.activity.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.metadata.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/tasks.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/meetings.space.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/admin.reports.audit.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/contacts.readonly,https://www.googleapis.com/auth/contacts.other.readonly. Authorize. A new delegation can take a few minutes, sometimes longer, before Google honours it. A scope you leave out is a source that cannot run: leave out gmail.readonly and sync gmail says so and exits 1 (switch it off in policy/import.json if you mean it); leave out drive.metadata.readonly and Drive lines carry no folder path, said once per run. A key set up before sync meet and sync gaudit existed has neither scope: sync --all then runs both and both fail, each on one line, until you add the two scopes here or switch the two sources off in policy/import.json.
  5. Move the key out of your downloads to ~/.config/logbook/google-sa.json and make it yours alone: chmod 600 ~/.config/logbook/google-sa.json. Never commit it, and never put it in the record's folder, a cloud folder, a repository or a message: whoever holds it reads your mail, your calendars, your Drive's activity, your tasks, your calls and their transcripts, your sign-ins and your contacts for as long as the delegation stands.
  6. Name it in the environment, in your shell profile and in ~/.config/logbook/sync.env, the file the schedule reads (docs/schedule.md); the schedule then runs all six with nothing more to set:
LOGBOOK_DRIVE_SA_KEY=~/.config/logbook/google-sa.json
LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER=ines@example.org

(The names say Drive because Drive came first; every Google source reads the same two.) 7. logbook doctor now shows one google line — the key present, the user set, which sources are on the key, a source switched off in policy/import.json named as disabled, and what people review --from-google reads on it — and a sync:<name> line for each source. It reads the key and checks that no one else on the machine can, and asks Google nothing:

pass  google       key present, user set; sources on the key: gmail, gcal, drive, gtasks, meet, gaudit; people review --from-google: contacts, other contacts

unauthorized_client means the delegation does not yet grant the scope named in the message (step 4); invalid_grant that the key was deleted, this machine's clock is wrong, or LOGBOOK_DRIVE_USER is not a user of the domain. Signing needs the crypto extra (pipx install --force "openlogbook[crypto]"); without it a sync says so. Every request is retried with a doubling wait on a rate limit or a server error, and stops on one plain line, exit 1, the watermark where it was, when that does not pass. sync --all runs the six in the order mail, gmail, gcal, drive, gtasks, meet, gaudit are registered: mail (IMAP) before gmail, so a mailbox you read both ways is written once by whichever comes first.

docs.title: Gmail
docs.text:
logbook sync gmail reads your mailbox over the Gmail API with the key above, and writes exactly the line logbook sync mail (IMAP) writes for the same message: the same parser, the same fields, the same dedupe key, the account and the Message-ID. A mailbox you synced over IMAP yesterday and over the API today is written once. The mail page has what a line holds, what is left out (drafts, Spam, Trash) and when to use which (Gmail over the API).

logbook sync gmail --dry-run                               # counts, nothing written
logbook sync gmail --since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z            # a first run from a day you choose
logbook sync gmail                                         # then from Gmail's history id

A first run by hand without --since lists every message; the first scheduled run reads the last 14 days and leaves its mark there (the schedule).

docs.title: Google Calendar
docs.text:
logbook sync gcal reads the calendars you own. With the two variables above set it reads them over the Calendar API (calendar.readonly): every calendar whose owner you are, your primary first, never one shared with you or a subscribed one such as a holidays calendar. Without them it reads the private iCal addresses you list (Google Calendar → Settings → the calendar → Integrate calendar → Secret address in iCal format), one whole calendar per URL; with both, the key wins and the URLs are not read. Either way each event goes through the reader logbook add uses for an .ics export, so a calendar you imported from a Takeout or settings-page export, the same calendar pulled by URL and the same calendar read over the API are one line per event (same raw_id, the event's UID and last-modified time; ADR 0017). The API has no field for an event's GEO coordinates or an attendee's delegated answer, so a line read over the API lacks those two where a feed had them; the record keeps the line it has. The watermark is the newest last-modified time seen; each run keeps the events changed in the 24 hours before it (LOGBOOK_GCAL_LOOKBACK_H) and reports, per calendar, how many it saw and how many were new. A calendar that fails (an expired secret address is a 404) is one line on stderr, the others are still written, the watermark stays put and the exit is 1. A first scheduled run keeps the events changed in the last 14 days (the schedule); an event planned long ago and unchanged since comes in with --since.

export LOGBOOK_GCAL_URLS='Sailing=https://calendar.google.com/calendar/ical/…/private-…/basic.ics,https://…'
logbook sync gcal --dry-run                                # counts per calendar, nothing written
logbook sync gcal

Moving from the feeds to the key. Set the two variables and run sync gcal as before; nothing else changes. The watermark in state/gcal.json is the same clock either way (the API's updated time is the feed's LAST-MODIFIED), so the first run on the key carries on from where the feeds stopped, less the lookback, and writes nothing twice: the events it reads again are already in the record by their raw_id. You can then delete LOGBOOK_GCAL_URLS, and reset the secret addresses in Google Calendar, since nothing reads them any more.

docs.title: Google Drive
docs.text:
logbook sync drive writes down what happened to your Drive files each day: created, edited, renamed, moved, shared, commented on, trashed, deleted, restored. It reads the Drive Activity API, read-only, as you, with the key of Google, on one key.

logbook sync drive --dry-run                               # counts per activity, nothing written
logbook sync drive --since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z            # a first run from a day you choose
logbook sync drive                                         # then from where it left off

A first run by hand without --since reads all the activity Google keeps. The first scheduled run reads the last 14 days (the schedule), and a dry run that meets the project's daily quota stops on one line instead of waiting it out.

The family's videos, the digitised tapes in one Drive folder, are a source of their own on the same key: sync drive --videos with LOGBOOK_DRIVE_VIDEOS_FOLDER set to the folder's id, then videos fetch, videos infer and review video, one more queue of the one review sitting, listed with the others by review alone (Videos, Review).

What a line holds. One event/v1 line per file, per hour and per kind of activity, so an afternoon of editing is a handful of lines with a count, Edited Budget 2027 ×14, not hundreds. It holds the file's name, its type, its id and a link that opens it in Drive; the folders it is in, root first (["My Drive", "Boat"]), read with the metadata scope, each folder's name asked once and kept in state/drive-cache.json for a week (never in the record) and asked again when an activity renames or moves it; who acted, you as owner and anyone else as Google names them (people/…, a person's account, not their address); for a share, with whom (a person's people/… name, a group's address, a domain, or anyone with the link) and the role; for a move, the folder it went to and came from; for a rename, the old name and the new. An hour is written once it is over, so a run at 07:00 leaves 06:00–07:00 for the next. Someone else's activity on someone else's file that was shared with you is left out and counted.

What a line never holds. The file's content, a comment's words, the file's size or modified time. The path is where the file is when its line is written; a line already in the record is never rewritten, so lines written before the metadata scope was delegated keep no path. Lines are tier 1, like calendar entries, whoever acted: the tier says where a line may travel, and a file's name and what happened to it are the same fact whoever did it.

docs.title: Google Tasks
docs.text:
logbook sync gtasks reads your Google Tasks, read-only, with the key of Google, on one key (the Tasks scope in step 4). A task is an idea or a promise you made yourself; the record keeps each one as it stands, the way a Takeout export of your tasks would, and logbook tasks reads them back.

logbook sync gtasks --dry-run                              # counts per list, nothing written
logbook sync gtasks

What a line holds. One task/v1 line (RFC 0016) per task as it stands: its title in your own words, open or done, its list, its due day if it has one, its parent for a subtask, and when it was done. Google keeps no creation time, so a line is dated when the task last changed, which for a task captured and left alone is when you wrote it down, and for one ticked off is when you ticked it. A task that changes — ticked off, renamed, reopened, deleted — is a new line beside the old one, which it supersedes; an unchanged task writes nothing, and nothing is ever rewritten. A done task says how long it was open, from the first time the record saw it open (unknown when it never did). It is the line the Takeout Tasks adapter writes for the same task, with the same source (google-takeout) and the same raw_id, so a Takeout export imported later adds nothing sync already wrote, and a sync after an export carries on where it ended.

What a line never holds. The task's notes: only their digest and how many words they have. Lines are tier 2, as RFC 0016 makes every task: sealed at rest when the record seals, and crossing only after review.

docs.title: Google Meet
docs.text:
logbook sync meet writes down the Meet calls you were in, read from the Meet REST API with the key of Google, on one key (meetings.space.readonly, read-only, as you).

logbook sync meet --dry-run                                # counts, nothing written
logbook sync meet --since 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z             # a first run from a day you choose
logbook sync meet                                          # then from where it left off

A first run by hand without --since reads every call Meet keeps; the first scheduled run reads the last 14 days (the schedule).

The call. One event/v1 line per call, once it has ended (a call still going on is counted and written by the next run): when it started and ended, and who joined as Meet names them — a signed-in participant is a Google account, users/…, kept as an attendee (never turned into a name here: people review sees them, and so does a review with your contacts), a guest by the name they typed, a caller by the number Meet shows, partly hidden. Meet keeps no title for a call, so the line is titled by its meeting code, Meet abc-mnop-xyz; the calendar entry you planned it in is a line of its own, from sync gcal. The conference record's name (conferenceRecords/…) is the line's reference back. Lines are tier 1, like the calendar's.

The transcript. When Meet transcribed the call, one transcript/v1 line more, built exactly as a Granola recording's is — the same mapping, the same profile, tier 3: who spoke, how many turns, the language, a link to the transcript's Google Doc, and the words themselves in attachments/, named by their digest, never in the line. A call transcribed in several sittings is one line. Google finishes a transcript a while after the call; until it has, the call is written without it and the transcript comes with a later run.

Granola too? If Granola also recorded the call, its transcript stays a line of its own beside Meet's. They are two transcripts, by two providers, with their own words, speakers and ids; that they are of one call is for a reader to see from the times, not for a source to decide by joining them.

Each call is keyed by its conference record (meet:<id>, and meet:<id>:transcript), so a re-run writes nothing twice, and a call already in the record is not asked about again. The watermark is the newest call's start; each run looks back a day before it, for a call that ended or a transcript Google finished since.

docs.title: Google sign-ins
docs.text:
logbook sync gaudit writes down your own sign-ins to your Google Workspace, from its login audit log (the Admin SDK Reports API, admin.reports.audit.readonly, with the key of Google, on one key). It asks for your sign-ins only, never the other users of the Workspace; Google answers it only for an administrator, which you are of your own Workspace.

logbook sync gaudit --dry-run                              # counts per kind of sign-in, nothing written
logbook sync gaudit

What a line holds. One event/v1 line per sign-in event, tier 1: when, what happened (Signed in, Sign-in failed, Signed out, Sign-in challenge, …), how (login_type, the challenges asked and how they went, why one failed, whether Google thought it suspicious), and where, as Google derived it from the address: a country, a subdivision and, when the log says one, a city (Oslo, NO-03, NO).

What a line never holds: the address. The IP address a sign-in came from is never written — not in the line, not in its key, not as a digest, since a digest of an address hides nothing (there are only four billion of them to try) — and neither is the network it came through. What may travel with a line is the place Google made of the address, coarse, never a coordinate. (A Takeout export's Access Log Activity is another file, every access to every service, read by the google-takeout-access-log adapter, off by default.)

Each event is keyed by the log's own id for it, so a re-run writes nothing twice; each run looks back a day before the newest sign-in seen, since Google can add one to the log hours later.

Your boat, your aircraft and your car are subjects with tracks of their own, not places (ADR 0018). Register each once in assets.json, then let sync ask the receivers that hear them:

logbook setup assets add solvind --kind yacht --name Solvind --mmsi 999000001  # synthetic MMSI; use your own
logbook setup assets add ln-zz1 --kind aircraft --name "the club's Cub" --icao24 000a01 --registration ZZ-ZZ1
logbook setup assets list
logbook setup assets status                                 # where each one last was, and how old that fix is
export LOGBOOK_AISSTREAM_KEY=...                            # free key from aisstream.io
uv sync --extra ais                                         # or: pipx install --force "openlogbook[ais]"
logbook sync ais --dry-run                                  # listen for 60 s, count, write nothing
logbook sync ais                                            # then: */10 * * * * logbook sync ais
logbook sync ais --listen 3600                              # or: one long sitting, written at the end
logbook sync ais --until 18:30                              # … until the record's clock next shows 18:30
logbook sync adsb                                           # OpenSky, no key needed; LOGBOOK_OPENSKY_USER/PASS optional

Each position is a location/v1 line like your own, with subject set to the asset's id and raw_id from the receiver, the identifier and the fix time (aisstream:<mmsi>:<unix seconds>, opensky:<icao24>:<unix seconds>), so a report heard twice is one line, and a stream you saved to a file (logbook add messages.jsonl) and the same reports heard live are one line too. state/ais.json and state/adsb.json keep a watermark per asset. show lists the boat's points as their own run, named by the asset; whether you were aboard is for an engine to decide from the two tracks, never written on a line. sync ais listens for --listen SECONDS, or --until HH:MM (the record's local time, the next time the clock shows it), or else LOGBOOK_AISSTREAM_LISTEN_S (default 60 s; a vessel under way reports every few seconds), and writes at the end; while it listens it prints one line a minute with the messages heard per asset, reconnects with a wait that doubles from 1 s to 60 s when the socket drops, and on Ctrl-C still writes what it heard, then exits 130. The key is read from LOGBOOK_AISSTREAM_KEY only and never printed. OpenSky's states/all is the present, one fix per aircraft per poll, so poll as often as its rate limit allows.

A secret iCal address is the whole calendar to anyone who holds it; Google can reset it. Keep the URLs in the shell environment only, as the Dawarich key below: the logbook never prints one, naming a calendar by its name or by eight characters of the URL's hash.

A Dawarich API key is full access to your account: it can read and delete every point you have. Keep it in the shell environment only (your shell profile, a password manager's CLI, a secrets file outside the record) and never in the record, the repository or a script you share. The logbook sends it only in the Authorization header and never prints it.

Is every source still flowing? logbook doctor sources --gaps reads the index alone, never the files, and prints one row per source with lines: how many, its last line's time, the longest silent stretch (between two lines, or since the last one, still running) and the days with no line from it, folded into runs, so a phone that stopped sending or a sync that died is seen on one screen. The range runs from each source's first line to today in the record's zone, or from --since YYYY-MM-DD; a line dated after today (a calendar's future entries) is outside it, and today counts as a missing day only once the source has been silent a full day. --expect dawarich imessage shows only those sources, marks one that has been silent a day or more at any point of the range, or has no line at all, with !, and exits 1 when any is marked, so a cron job can tell you: 0 7 * * * logbook doctor sources --gaps --since 2026-09-01 --expect dawarich imessage. Every line counts, retracted or not; --json gives the same report as data.

docs.title: Reading the day back
docs.text:
logbook derive stays is the first reader of the record: it turns the day's location/v1 lines into stays, stops and moves and prints them in your local time, or as JSON with --json. Nothing is written to the record; the thresholds live in policy/stays.json (created with defaults on the first run) and an optional places.json at the root names places.

logbook derive stays                          # today
logbook derive stays --day 2026-09-30
logbook derive stays --since 2026-09-01 --until 2026-09-30 --json
logbook derive stays --subject solvind        # one asset's own track (assets.json)

A stay is a span at one place of twenty minutes or more, or of any length when something is attached to it: a calendar event, a transcript, a note, a call, a message or a photo whose time falls inside it. An event counts when it happened somewhere — a calendar entry, Google Home's door, an event with a location or attendees — and a Notion or Drive edit does not. Evidence promotes; duration is the fallback. A shorter span with nothing attached is a stop, kept and flagged. A move is what lies between: its distance along the points, its duration, and a mode from the speed (walk, car, train, flight; flight also when a gap starts and ends near airports). The night of each day is the longest stay between 22:00 and 08:00; a night with none is in transit.

A tracker such as Dawarich sends no points while you are still, so a silence is read as time at the place: a gap whose next point is back inside the stay's radius continues the stay however long it was, and a stay lasts until the tracker's next point when that point comes after a silence and lies within a short walk (1.2 km by default) — even when it is the next morning and already on your way out, so the night at home is seen. In policy/stays.json, merge_gap_s (600 s by default) governs an excursion, not a gap at the same place: step outside the radius and come back within it and the stay is one; come back later and it is two stays with a move between. A gap of merge_gap_s or more is a silence, and walk_max_kmh for merge_gap_s is the hop a silence may end with and still count as time at the place. An asset registered in assets.json (ADR 0018) gets its own stays and moves; when its position lies within the radius of yours for aboard_min_s (20 minutes) or longer you are aboard it, and the run of your stays and moves aboard it is one stay aboard <asset> with the run inside it, so the asset's movement never fragments your stay (docs/day.md, Aboard an asset). A night aboard names the asset and carries its position.

docs.title: The Day
docs.text:
logbook day 2026-06-13 is the day read back whole (docs/day.md): the night before and the night after (home, away or in transit), the country of the day, the timeline of stays, stops, moves and flights with what attached to each (events, transcripts, notes, mail threads, calls, keepers named; messages and photos counted) and who was there — confirmed by a note, a transcript or a timed calendar entry; proposed by a face or an all-day entry — then what the calendar planned where the track has nothing, the night's sleep, the day's steps and resting heart rate, and which sources spoke and when they last did. A run of stays and moves aboard a boat or an aircraft is one stay aboard <asset> with the anchorages inside it; a silence of the tracker is a gap row that places nothing. --json gives the Day as one object, every row with the ids of its lines. Nothing is written.

A story someone told — "in 1961 we moved to the house by the lake" — is a line on the day it was told, never on the day it is about (add story <file> --teller <ref> --listener <ref> --refers-to 1961, RFC 0028, a draft). show prints it on its told day as 📖 refers to 1961 — told by Ola Nordmann to Kari Nordmann; day 1961-05-04 lists it under Stories about this day, apart from the timeline, because a told year is a claim and the timeline is what was observed.

docs.title: In a browser
docs.text:
logbook serve is the record read in a browser, on this machine only (docs/serve.md): the Day as a timeline with each row's attachments under a toggle (/day/2026-06-17), a window one row per day (/days), the trips of a year (/trips), the places, the assets with their last fix, and where each source went quiet — the same readers as the commands, rendered as HTML with one inline stylesheet and no script, nothing fetched from anywhere. The server binds 127.0.0.1 and refuses any other host; no page references a URL outside itself; nothing is written.

logbook serve                                 # http://127.0.0.1:8765/

docs.title: Reading the record
docs.text:
The readers above the day page derive, and never append: every one of them is a function of the record at its head, and the same record reads the same way twice. The only lines they ever add are the captain's own namings.

logbook setup places propose                  # unnamed stays ranked by hours, with the nearest known place and a suggested name
logbook setup places propose --write          # name the ones you accept: places.json, and one note/v1 line each
logbook setup places add Home --lat 59.9139 --lon 10.7522 --kind home
logbook setup places name 59.92,10.74 Cafe    # or a stay id from `propose`; the naming is a note in the record

logbook rollup countries --year 2026          # days per country from the overnight stay; in transit apart
logbook rollup flights                        # count, km, long-haul, by evidence, from the flight lines standing
logbook rollup nights                         # home, away, in transit, nights aboard, the longest trip
logbook rollup places                         # nights, stays, hours, people per named place and asset; the top unnamed clusters
logbook rollup places --with                  # the place × person table: stays, days and nights at each place per person
logbook rollup people                         # days and nights together, last real contact, places shared, per person
logbook rollup health --by week               # sleep, steps, resting heart rate, HRV per month or ISO week; — when missing
logbook rollup listen --year 2026             # listens, hours, skips, the top artists by hours, hours by month, from every listen/v1 line
logbook rollup attention --year 2026          # hours by app and by category (communication, browser, media, work, other) from Screen Time
logbook rollup money --year 2026              # the transactions by month, by country of the stay, by the source's category

logbook show trips --year 2026                # runs of nights away: route, places, people, flights in and out
logbook rollup ledger --month 2026-06         # the transactions at the stay and in the trip, per day; shares per person
logbook show year 2026 --html ~/2026.html     # the year read back: the rollups, the trips, one day a month; a page that prints
logbook show trip trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-20  # one trip: the route as stays with a map, days, flights, people, keepers, health, spend
logbook show year 2026 --html ~/2026.html --print   # a Volume: a cover, contents, a spread a month with the keepers as hero photos; A4 or Letter
logbook show trip trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-20 --html ~/week.html --print   # the same for one trip, a spread a day; docs/print.md says how to make the PDF
logbook export trip-bundle trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-20 --to kari --tier 1,2   # that trip for a member of the circle; `import trip-bundle` takes one in
logbook show person "Kari Nordmann"           # first and last contact, days together, places, the last shared stays
logbook show asset solvind                    # trips aboard, nights, people, the track's summary
logbook show place Office                     # visits, people, photos
logbook people --year 2026                    # everyone the record names: channels, days and nights together, last real contact
logbook people ola@example.org                # one page: the numbers, then the shared days, most recent first
logbook people merge                          # the same person named twice: proposals with the evidence; --apply ID merges
logbook search '"with kari"' --since 2026-06-01   # full-text, literal, ranked, by day: notes, messages, mail, events, transcripts

logbook derive keepers                        # favourites → keeper/v1 (memory); the Art album → keeper/v1 (art)
logbook show keepers --since 2026-06-01 --lane art
logbook show keepers --people                 # who appears on the keepers, per month: the faces the library named, proposed
logbook derive descriptions keepers --photos ~/Pictures/Photos\ Library.photoslibrary   # a local vision model's sentence per keeper photo (openlogbook[describe]); never a name, never a place

logbook promises --judge                      # a local model reads every "I'll…" the rules found; the commitments, as proposals
logbook promises --all --since 2026-06-01     # every candidate the rules found, judged or not
logbook promises done 3b9e5d0f2a71c846        # it was kept: one task/v1 line, so --open hides it

logbook promises tasks --open                 # the task/v1 lines as they stand: the latest snapshot of each
logbook promises tasks --propose-done         # the mail, calendar entry or transaction that says an open task was done
logbook promises tasks done 0dd9108fb6d5d715 --evidence 01a0fda3-99b0-7af6-a986-0a377117a94b   # one task/v1 line, done

logbook digest                                # today in 25 lines at most, with one question you answer in a word
logbook digest 2026-06-10 --markdown          # the same lines as Markdown; --json the sets behind them

Every command takes --json, and under --json every number carries the ids of the lines it came from: a stay by its first and last location line (one unbroken run of points), a flight by the flight line standing, a person by the lines that put them there. The rollups are described in docs/rollups.md. The ledger, the transactions in context, in docs/ledger.md. A home region is a place of kind home in places.json; a night whose stay is within 400 m of one is a night at home whatever that place's radius, so a trip never starts or ends with the guest room across the street. Without a home place no night is home, there are no trips, and the commands say so.

Who was there. A stay's company comes from the record's own evidence: an attendee of a timed calendar entry held at the stay (its location geocodes within a kilometre of the stay — coordinates on the entry, or a location that names a place in places.json — or it has no location and overlaps the stay by more than an hour; an all-day entry places nobody), a participant of a transcript recorded inside it whom the record resolves to a person (Speaker A, me and Unknown are nobody), a note written inside it that says with <name> — all confirmed — and a face the photo library tagged, proposed only. Names resolve through the record's resolution lines (RFC 0006); a bare address nobody has named and a calendar system address (calendar.google.com, noreply, reservations@, invite@) are dropped. You are never your own company: the with module knows you by owner_id and owner_emails in logbook.json, by every resolution line that names those, and by policy/owner.json, {"names": [...], "emails": [...], "phones": [...], "handles": [...]}, where your other spellings and your logins go; init writes it empty. show trips lists at most twelve names, most evidence first.

Countries, coarsely. rollup countries has no map. The country of a night is the one a place in places.json carries (country, your word), else the nearest large airport within 300 km and the country its zone is filed under in the bundled zone.tab. That is wrong near borders and far from airports, and the method is printed with the numbers; name the place and give it a country when it matters.

Trips are derived, never written (ADR 0019). A trip is a run of consecutive days whose overnight stay is outside every home region, recomputed every time; a trip's name, when you give one, is a note (logbook add --trip ID "NAME", or the field on its page in serve). Its route is the night places in order: the named place, else an airport's code and city (ZRH, Zurich) when the stay is at one — within 3.5 km of the reference point of an airport with scheduled traffic (OurAirports type large or medium; a terminal often lies well off the runway midpoint the row marks), within 2 km of any other row — else the coordinates with near <place>, x km for a named place within 5 km, else the coordinates with the city of the nearest large airport within 30 km in parentheses (53.5998,10.0130 (Hamburg); the city, never the airport's code); consecutive points within 200 m of each other are one. logbook day labels an unnamed stay the same way.

Keepers (RFC 0024) are the photos you marked: a favourite in the library is a memory, a photo in an album named Art is art. add photos writes them with the photo lines, and derive keepers reads the marks out of any library's photo lines once; show <day> lists the day's keepers first, as its hero photos. show keepers --people is who appears on them per month, from the names your library gave its faces — proposed, never confirmed; a face's name is a person only when it is exactly a label a resolution line carries (docs/adapters/photos.md). derive descriptions keepers (docs/describe.md) has a local vision model (openlogbook[describe], mlx-vlm on Apple silicon) write one factual sentence and the visible things for each keeper whose file is reachable, as a derived note on the photo's day, once per photo; it is never told who is in the picture or where it was taken and may not guess either.

Promises (docs/promises.md) are proposals, never facts: every sentence of a transcript or a note that reads as a first-person future or obligation, in English or German (I'll send, we'll get back, let me, I need to, ich schicke, ich melde mich, ich muss), with the day, the line, the speaker when the record resolves one and a due hint when a date phrase is in it (by Friday, next week, bis Montag), found by rules. The rules find far too many, so --judge has a local instruct model (openlogbook[judge], mlx-lm on Apple silicon, a 4-bit Qwen2.5 by default) read each candidate in its context and say whether it is a commitment, by whom, to whom, what and by when; the verdicts are kept in the record and never redone, and the command shows the commitments it is sure of (--all for everything). No model runs unless you ask, never a cloud one, and nothing leaves the machine. promises done <id> is the one thing it writes: a task/v1 line marked done.

Tasks (docs/tasks.md) are the task/v1 lines a task app's export left, each as its latest snapshot (RFC 0016); promises tasks --propose-done asks the record whether an open one was done without anyone ticking it off: within the fortnight after the task, a mail subject that names its key nouns and confirms something (a booking confirmation for "book flights to Zürich"), a calendar entry for an appointment ("Call with Ola" for "call Ola"), a transaction at a merchant the task names — by rules, English and German, no model, no network — each a proposal with the evidence line's id. promises tasks done <id> --evidence <line> appends the closing task/v1 line and nothing else. The matcher is a value, so the promises judge's engine can replace the rules later without changing the report.

The digest (docs/digest.md) is the day in 25 lines at most, composed from the readers above and never a list of everything: where, with whom confirmed, what attached; the flights; the open promises due within the week; the usual sources with no line; tomorrow's timed calendar entries; and one closing question you can answer in a word, so the day closes itself (ADR 0005). It writes nothing and sends nothing; delivery is a later decision.

docs.title: Handing a window to someone
docs.text:
A crossing package (RFC 0005) is the bundle you hand a named member of your circle: the lines of a window, verbatim, the attachments they point at, and the resolution lines that let the reader name the people in them, so they need nothing else from your record. Kari, say, gets one every night. A member is a person: a name the policy keeps for a reader or a door of its own (mcp, hermes, vault and the rest) is refused.

logbook export crossing --to kari --since 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z --dry-run     # counts per kind and tier, writes nothing
logbook export crossing --to kari --since 2026-03-01T00:00:00Z               # the first window, tier 1 only
logbook export crossing --to kari --since last --tier 1,2                    # every night: since the last one, tiers 1 and 2
logbook export crossing --to kari --since last --tier 1,2 --kinds message,event --out ~/Handover/kari/tonight

The window is [--since, --until), --until defaulting to now; --since last starts where the last crossing to that destination ended (exports/crossing.json), and the first run must say where to start. The bundle lands under export/crossing/<destination>/<time>/ unless --out says otherwise: manifest.json, entries.jsonl, attachments/<sha256> for every referenced file the store holds (a missing one stays a reference), and resolution.jsonl when any exported line names someone your contacts have resolved, alias hops included. A JSON parser is all a reader needs.

How much may cross is a setting in your record, not in the code (ADR 0016): policy/crossing.json maps each destination to its ceiling, {"kari": {"max_tier": 2}}, and you write each entry yourself: a new record names only mcp, at 1. Tier 1 crosses by default; tier 2 only with --tier 1,2, and the manifest then lists every tier-2 line under review; tier 3 only when the file allows it and you type --tier 1,2,3, and the manifest and the console say loudly that it did. A request above the ceiling is refused with the file's name. Every real export appends one crossing/v1 line (RFC 0011) to the chain — destination, window, counts per tier, the ceiling in force, the package's digest — so the record itself shows every time anything left it. --dry-run writes nothing and appends nothing.

docs.title: Handing a day to a friend
docs.text:
A shared page (RFC 0025, docs/rfcs/rfc-0025-shared-page-bundle.md) is one day of your record for one person in your circle, as one signed zip: the day's lines verbatim, the attachments they point at, the day-package summary, and a manifest signed with your record's sharing key — made the first time you share, kept at ~/.config/logbook/share/<owner_id>.key, its public half in logbook.json as share_key. The other side verifies the signature under the key they hold for you, recomputes every line's hash, and keeps the page beside their record, never in it.

logbook key circle key                               # your public key; give it to Ola
logbook key circle add ola 5df798a3…                 # Ola's, once; policy/circle.json
logbook export share day 2026-06-13 --to ola         # tier 1, under the ceiling policy/crossing.json gives ola
logbook export share day 2026-06-13 --to ola --tier 2 --out ~/Desktop/saturday.zip
logbook import page ~/Downloads/saturday.zip         # Ola's side: verified, then circle/ines/2026-06-13/
logbook day 2026-06-13                               # … and the Day ends with a `from ines` section

The same ceiling as a crossing applies, per destination, a draft is held to the entry it was written under as every crossing holds it, and a page is a crossing: every share appends one crossing/v1 line, so the record shows each day that left it. A page that fails any check — the signature, a line's hash, a file the manifest does not name — is refused with the check named and nothing of it is kept. The two pages under tests/fixtures/share/ are the fixture a second implementation reads. A day that holds sealed lines (a record with recipients, a tier-2 or tier-3 line at a tier the page would send) does not share yet: export share day refuses it before anything is written, until a page can carry sealed lines to the receiver after v1 (RFC 0029); a sealed attachment on an otherwise plain day still shares.

docs.title: Opening it in Obsidian
docs.text: logbook export vault ~/Vault renders the record as a folder of plain Markdown with wikilinks — a page per day, place, person, trip and year — that Obsidian or Logseq opens as a vault, its graph view the record's shape (docs/vault.md). It is tier-gated exactly like a crossing: tier 1 by default, the shape of every day and no text of any note or message; --tier 1,2 when policy/crossing.json names vault with a ceiling of 2. Every run appends one crossing/v1 line, and re-running rewrites only the files that changed.

docs.title: Asking an agent
docs.text:
logbook serve mcp serves the record to an agent on this machine over the Model Context Protocol, on this process's stdin and stdout and nothing else: no port, no socket. The host starts it, and the tools are the readers above — day, days, trips, places, people, person, promises, gaps, and a search over the index — plus write tools that go through Logbook.append and nothing else, each refused until the mcp entry of your policy names it: add_note (one note/v1 line, as logbook add, source mcp) and promise_done (one task/v1 line, as logbook promises done, source mcp), among them.

pipx install --force "openlogbook[mcp]"       # the official Python MCP SDK
logbook serve mcp --inspect                   # the tool table and a sample request; no record needed
logbook serve mcp                             # what a host runs; LOGBOOK_HOME or --root names the record

Every answer passes the crossing gate of ADR 0016: policy/crossing.json names the mcp destination and its ceiling, 1 unless you raise it, and the answer says how many lines sat above it and were left out (gate.withheld). At 1 the agent sees the record's shape and no note, message or name; at 2 your notes and your circle too; tier 3 only when the file allows it and you start the server with --allow-tier-3. docs/mcp.md has the host's config snippet and the tools.

docs.title: The synthesis of a call
docs.text:
A model reads one transcript, a work call, and writes one line about it: what someone is to do after the call, on top; the topics, each theme once however often the call came back to it; what was decided; what was left open; and a short personal part. Every item points at the utterances it rests on. The line is a draft/v1 (RFC 0036, the profile) of unit event whose subject is the transcript line, and the Day shows it under the call's row, collapsed.

logbook transcript synthesize 01a1377b-5609-7db6-955c-a2a2b3db9660   # one call, by its line id
logbook transcript synthesize '#5432'                                 # by its seq
logbook transcript synthesize a2b3db9660                              # by the end of its id, as the Day shortens it
logbook transcript synthesize --day 2026-06-10                        # every call of a day
logbook transcript synthesize --day yesterday --dry-run               # ask the model, check the answer, write nothing

--show-prompt prints the prompt and the material as they are sent; --again asks once more when this model has already synthesized the call. The morning's dream --catch-up synthesizes every call of the last 7 days that has no synthesis yet, or whose synthesis was made under another version of the dream entry, and never an older one unless you ask with --since (The week the close covers).

docs.title: What a synthesis is, and is not
docs.text: A synthesis is a proposal; the transcript is the record. Nothing derives a fact from it: not a task, not a promise, not a person. An action it proposes is not a task until you make it one; a decision it reports is the model's reading of the call. The synthesis never writes a note, a task or a signature. It writes one draft line, source model:<name>, and nothing else; a synthesis again writes a new line whose supersedes names the one before, and the earlier text stays in the record.

docs.title: The policy entry and the endpoint
docs.text:
It runs on the dream's engine, so it is governed by the same dream entry of policy/crossing.json and reaches the same model (the dream, the endpoint): no entry, or an expired one, and it refuses in one sentence and nothing leaves the machine.

The entry's max_tier is the ceiling, and a transcript is one line with one tier: a call above the ceiling stays home whole. The granola, transcript and wispr-flow adapters write transcript/v1 at tier 3, so under the usual "max_tier": 2 a call is held back: transcript synthesize ID says so and exits 2, --day says it in the call's row, and the catch-up counts it. To let calls cross, write "max_tier": 3 on the entry, which also lets the dream read the day's tier-3 lines (health, money), or import the calls at tier 2 (logbook add --tier 2). The draft's tier is the transcript's.

docs.title: When the entry changes
docs.text:
A synthesis is a draft/v1 line derived through the dream entry, so it follows the entry, not the head, as the day's draft does (the dream; ADR 0016, Derived material follows the policy, not the head).

  • Every synthesis names the entry it was made under: extra.policy_version, the same SHA-256 of the entry's max_tier, until and model that the dream records.
  • A reader shows a synthesis only while the entry allows its tier, through the same rule as the day's draft. A synthesis above the entry's max_tier today (lowered, expired, removed) is not on the Day, not on serve's Day page and not through the MCP door. The line stays in the record. day puts one row under the call that says so and nothing of the synthesis:
      transcript   Yard plans
                   superseded by policy: tier 3, above max_tier 2 of the 'dream' entry; the call stays home until the entry allows its tier

day --json carries the same under syntheses_withheld, one row per call (transcript, line, seq, tier, max_tier, why), a key present only then; serve shows the row as one muted line under the call; --no-dream leaves it out. A reader through a gate of its own (the MCP door) hides the synthesis without the row, counts it among the lines it withheld, and its line tool refuses it. - Synthesized again under the entry as it is now. A synthesis made under another version of the entry (an until moved, another model, a ceiling raised) is no longer unchanged: transcript synthesize sends the call again, and dream --catch-up does so for the calls of its week (or from its --since day), the row saying synthesized under another dream entry; an older call keeps its synthesis until you send it again by hand. The new synthesis supersedes the old one. A call above a lowered ceiling is above it as its synthesis is (they share the tier), so it stays home and is counted as held back; its synthesis shows again once the entry allows its tier. - A synthesis written before syntheses named their entry has no version to compare: a new entry alone synthesizes nothing again, and its tier still decides what a reader shows. doctor's drafts line names the days whose draft is withheld, not the calls.

docs.title: What the model sees
docs.text:
The call and nothing else: a header, reference T, with the title, the provider, the day, the start and the end, the participants by name (never an address) and how many utterances there are; then every utterance in order, as the transcript's text in the attachment store reads (U1, U2, ...), each with its speaker as the transcript labels them and, when the recording gives times (Granola's segments, WebVTT and SRT cues), where it is in the call (20:05). A transcript whose text is not in the store, or is sealed on a machine without the identity, is said and not sent.

The prompt (docs/synthesis-prompt.md explains it) fixes the schema and the rules: actions on top, topics consolidated across the whole call, decisions settled and not merely discussed, and work only. That last one is a rule of the prompt and not a filter in the code: the whole call reaches the model, and the model is told that anything personal goes to the personal part, at most three short neutral sentences, and nowhere else. No code decides what is personal.

Ideas. The material also lists the labels of the ideas you have named (I1, I2, ...: the label alone), when the call is tier 2 or above, so an idea's label never raises the draft's tier; the model may propose up to three ideas the call put forward, new or a refinement of one of those, each resting on utterances of the call. They are kept beside the segments under extra.ideas (the name, the words, the idea it refines by its entity id or none, the utterances, the transcript's id), never as a segment, and wait in review idea until you say yes (ideas from calls). An idea that rests on no utterance or names a reference the material did not give is dropped. A synthesis written under the first prompt (transcript-synthesis/1) proposes none; synthesize ID sends it again under the new one.

docs.title: Evidence: the transcript line, and the utterances beside it
docs.text:
A transcript's utterances are not lines of their own: transcript/v1 keeps the text in one attachment (RFC 0004), so the only line a synthesis can point at is the transcript. Every supported segment's evidence is that line's id, and which utterances it rests on is kept beside the segments, under extra.segments, one object per segment:

{"part": "actions", "utterances": [{"n": 10, "offset": "46:30"}, {"n": 11, "offset": "47:00"}],
 "assignee": "Ola Nordmann", "due": {"phrase": "by Friday", "date": "2026-06-12"}}

n is the utterance's place in the transcript's text, from 1, in the order transcripts.turns_of reads it; offset is where it is in the recording, when the recording says. due.date is the phrase read against the day of the call, as promises reads a due hint (SPEC §3.2.10 rule 4), and is shown with a question mark because it is a reading of the words.

Before anything is written, every reference of the answer is checked: T, the transcript's own id, or U<n> for an utterance the material gave. An item that cites anything else, alone or beside good references (an utterance past the end, another line, a day's L1), is unsupported, as RFC 0036 rule 6 asks; an item without text is dropped; topics the model names twice are one topic, their texts joined and their utterances united; and when more than 30 % of the items are unsupported the answer is refused and nothing is written, as the dream refuses. The line holds the segments, the ids and the utterance numbers, never the prompt, the material or the call's words.

docs.title: Once, and again
docs.text:
A call the same model has synthesized under the same prompt (transcript-synthesis/2, kept in extra.prompt) and the same dream entry (extra.policy_version) is unchanged: nothing is sent, nothing is written, and the standing synthesis is printed. Another model, a new prompt, another entry, or --again writes a new line that supersedes the standing one. A transcript that is retracted or superseded is not the call as the record stands and is refused.

The run holds the record's writer lock and reads the head again before it appends: a head that moved under the reading is HeadMoved, one sentence, nothing written.

docs.title: The week the close covers
docs.text:
dream --catch-up, the 06:00 close's second step (the schedule), synthesizes, after the days, each call of the last 7 days that no model has synthesized yet, or whose synthesis was made under another version of the entry, one row each; a call held back by the ceiling or without its text is counted in the closing line. A call's day is its own: the local day of its start (at) on the record's clock, day_start included, so a call at 05:30 under a day that begins at 06:00 is on the day before, and a call held three years ago and imported last night is three years old. Today's calls wait for the next morning, as today's draft does.

An older call is never sent by the close. A record that holds years of transcripts would otherwise send every one of them to the model the first morning after an upgrade: unasked, and the whole backlog's cost in one night. It is the rule a source keeps on its first run, which never reads back further than its window without an explicit --since. The calls before the week that have no synthesis are counted and named in one line, with the two ways to them, from the oldest one's day:

$ logbook dream --catch-up
2026-06-06  empty     nothing logged
…
2026-06-14  dreamed   #5440 · no draft yet · 4 segments
2026-06-18  dreamed   #5441 · no draft yet · 3 segments
2026-06-14  synthesized #5442 · “Hull survey” · 6 segments
2026-06-18  synthesized #5443 · “Mooring lines” · 6 segments
2 dreamed · 12 empty · 2 synthesized
1 call before 2026-06-13 not synthesized; run `logbook transcript synthesize --day 2026-05-11` or `dream --catch-up --since 2026-05-11`
  • logbook dream --catch-up --since DAY synthesizes the calls from DAY on, not only the week's, and only those: it is the explicit ask that reaches back, a day at a time or a year at once. The days it dreams are still the last --days N (14 by default); --since is about the calls. A --days under 7 narrows the calls to those days too; it never widens them.
  • logbook transcript synthesize --day DAY (or ID) is unchanged: it sends the calls you name, whatever their age.
  • Either way, a call already synthesized by the same model, under the same prompt and the same dream entry, is never sent again (Once, and again, above). A call above the ceiling is not among the ones named: it stays home whatever you ask, and only doctor counts it.

The scheduled close runs dream --catch-up with nothing after it, so it never reaches further than the week. logbook doctor counts the calls without a synthesis on one synthesis line (the doctor): those of the week and today, which the close will synthesize; those before it, which the close leaves, with the --since that reaches the oldest; and those above the ceiling.

docs.title: On the Day
docs.text:
Under the call's row, one row, collapsed: what the synthesis holds and which model wrote it. A synthesis is the call's draft, never the day's: the Day's own draft (dream day) is of unit day alone and is what it is without the synthesis, above the note as ever, and each keeps its one standing draft (RFC 0036 amendment 1).

  09:00–12:00  stay   Home · 3 h · 1 transcript
      transcript   Yard plans
                   synthesis · 1 action, 2 topics, 1 decision, 1 open thread, 1 personal · model:qwen2.5-7b-instruct

The items are behind it: in serve, a toggle under the call opens them, actions on top, each with its assignee and due hint and where in the call it rests (the line on hover), an unsupported one muted and marked; day --json carries them under syntheses; transcript synthesize ID prints them:

2026-06-10 10:00 “Yard plans”: synthesized as #5441 draft/v1 · model:qwen2.5-7b-instruct · tier 3 · 11 utterances read at b7e3ddf2 · 6 segments, 1 unsupported
    action    Send the survey report to Ines.  → Ola Nordmann · due by Friday (2026-06-12?)  [46:30, 47:00]
    topic     Hull survey: The yard in Vollen surveys in week 26; the keel is to be checked too.  [02:00, 20:00, 45:00]
    topic     Mooring lines: The new mooring lines arrived.  [08:30]
    decision  The survey goes to the yard in Vollen.  [12:00, 12:20]
