    open      Who pays for the haul-out is still open.  [31:00]
  ~ personal  A family matter of Ines's came up.  unsupported
  a synthesis is a proposal: the transcript is the record

A synthesis the dream entry no longer allows is not among them: its row says superseded by policy and why (When the entry changes). day --no-dream leaves syntheses, and that row, out with the day's draft. show lists the draft line on the day it was written, as every line.

docs.title: Shared trips
docs.text:
Two people on one trip keep two records of it. logbook export trip-bundle hands one of them to the other as a folder; logbook import trip-bundle takes it in as received lines that never mix with your own; logbook trip then shows the trip as both records saw it — who was there according to each, the places they agree on, and what one of them saw alone. The format is RFC 0030, a crossing package (RFC 0005) cut to one trip, under the same ceiling as every crossing (ADR 0016).

# Ola's record: the cabin weekend, for Ines, names included (tier 2)
logbook trips                                              # find the trip's id
logbook export trip-bundle trip:2026-06-12:2026-06-13 --to ines --tier 1,2
logbook export trip-bundle 2026-06-13 --to ines --dry-run  # any day inside the trip; count, write nothing
logbook export trip-bundle trip:2026-06-12:2026-06-13 --to ines --tier 1,2 --attachments --out ~/for-ines

# Ines's record: take it in, then read the trip
logbook import trip-bundle ~/from-ola --dry-run
logbook import trip-bundle ~/from-ola
logbook trip trip:2026-06-12:2026-06-13
logbook trip trip:2026-06-12:2026-06-13 --html ~/cabin.html

docs.title: What crosses
docs.text:
Only the trip's days, and only what a reader of a trip needs:

  • the lines: the photo/v1 lines of those days, with their hashes and never their pixels unless you pass --attachments, and the trip's standing flight/v1 lines — verbatim, so each still hashes as you wrote it;
  • the rows your readers derive (trip.json): the stays away from home with their nights and labels, the moves between them, the flights, and the people confirmed present (the calendar, a recording, your own words; never a face alone) with the addresses and numbers that name them;
  • the resolution lines that give those people their names (RFC 0006).

Nothing of home crosses, and nothing else of the days does: not the location points, not the calendar entries or notes the company was read from, not the health or money lines.

The destination must be named in policy/crossing.json with a max_tier, as for any crossing; a request above it is refused naming the file. --tier defaults to 1. The people, your own refs and the resolution lines are tier 2 — a name is a resolution's work — so with the default the bundle carries the places and the photos and says how many names it held back; pass --tier 1,2 to name people. Every real export appends one crossing/v1 line to your chain naming the trip (show prints it as crossed to ines: 3 lines); a dry run appends nothing.

docs.title: What comes in
docs.text:
The import checks every digest the manifest names and every line's own hash, and refuses a bundle that does not match, a folder that is not one, and a bundle your own record exported. Then it appends:

  • one received line per line of the bundle: kind received, source received, the sender's line verbatim under payload.line, extra.from the sender's owner id. It lands on its day at its own tier, and show lists it as from Ola Nordmann: photo immich · …;
  • the page, one received line of schema trip-share/v1, keyed by the bundle id.

A received line is never one of yours. No derived reader takes the kind, so the sender's photos are not your photos, their flights are not in your rollup, and their resolutions name nobody in your registry. A line whose raw_id your record already holds — the same shared photo under the same asset id, the same invite — is skipped and counted as kept as yours; a line received before is skipped and counted too. Nothing is ever rewritten.

Ola Nordmann: trip:2026-06-12:2026-06-13 2026-06-12 – 2026-06-13 · bundle 01a0ffdb…
  2 lines received, 3 resolutions, page received
  skipped: 1 kept as yours, 0 received before

docs.title: The merged page
docs.text:
logbook trip <id> finds every received page whose trip touches yours and adds a shared with block per sender:

  shared with Ola Nordmann · their trip:2026-06-12:2026-06-13 · 2 nights · received 2026-06-20 · 2 photos
    who            yours                 theirs                             seen only by
    you            owner                 confirmed (calendar)
    Ola Nordmann   confirmed (calendar)  owner
    Kari Nordmann  –                     confirmed (calendar, note, photo)  Ola Nordmann
    where            theirs                             seen only by
    Cabin, 2 nights  Hytta, 2 nights
    –                60.8700,8.5701 near Hytta, 1.5 km  Ola Nordmann
  • who: you and your confirmed people on one side, the sender and their confirmed people on the other. A person of theirs is yours when one of their refs is one of your own identities (then they are you) or resolves in your record to someone confirmed here; else when the names match, case aside. Ola matched Ines's own Ola Nordmann through his address; Kari is in Ola's calendar, note and a tagged photo, and in nothing of Ines's.
  • where: each stay of your route with the sender's stays within 300 m of it beside it — the cabin Ines calls Cabin is the one Ola calls Hytta — and, apart, the stays of theirs that match none of yours: the bakery Ola walked to on the Saturday.
  • seen only by: you, the sender's name, or nothing when both records have it.

Under --json the same is shared, one object per sender with from, bundle_id, received_at, logbook_head, trip, people (name, person, yours, theirs, seen_only_by), places (label, nights, theirs, their_nights, seen_only_by, lat, lon), flights and photos. The HTML page has a Shared section with the same two tables.

The page compares; it confirms nobody. A person seen only by the sender stays theirs until you say otherwise in your own record, and nothing is written when the page is read. What a received page is, in your chain, is the fact that the sender's record said this at that head, with the package digest to show for it.

docs.title: The fixture
docs.text: tests/cabin.py builds the two records the tests and this page use: Ines's and Ola's weekend at a cabin, 12 to 14 June 2026, with Ola's bakery walk, Kari in his calendar and his note, one photo shared between the two libraries under one asset id, and one photo whose bytes are in his store. Every coordinate, address and id is invented; nobody in it exists.

docs.title: Five minutes with a demo record
docs.text:
Nothing to import, nothing of yours. logbook demo writes a month of a person who does not exist and every command reads it back. The record is invented in code (logbook/contrib/demo.py), read from nowhere, and the same arguments give the same record on any machine.

pipx install openlogbook                 # or, in a clone: uv sync && uv run logbook …
logbook demo --out ~/Demo/Logbook        # 30 days, seed 1; --days N --seed S to vary it
export LOGBOOK_HOME=~/Demo/Logbook

demo record: 30 days, 2026-06-01 to 2026-06-30, seed 1; nothing in it is real
wrote 12,772 lines to ~/Demo/Logbook, head 3ee025e7a9fb…
  export LOGBOOK_HOME=~/Demo/Logbook
  logbook show 2026-06-08

docs.title: Open it in a browser
docs.text:
logbook serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8765/day/2026-06-17: one day of a person who does not exist, a week aboard. The page is computed on this machine from the lines you just made. Press Ctrl-C in the terminal to stop it.

docs.title: Who
docs.text:
Ines Nordmann lives in Oslo with Ola. She has a sister, Kari; colleagues, Per and Liv; a crew for the yacht Nordlys, Anders and Sigrid; a cabin neighbour, Nils; clients in Zürich, Marta and Jonas; a friend in Copenhagen, Freja; a mother, Eva; and a running friend, Tore. Twelve people, each resolved from an example.org address and a 07700 900xxx number, some from a face the photo library tagged. None of them exists.

Her June: an office week with a weekend at the cabin; Zürich for a client, Monday to Thursday; a week aboard Nordlys down the fjord; and a long weekend in Copenhagen. After 28 days the story starts again, so --days 90 is a summer.

docs.title: The chain
docs.text:
logbook verify

valid — 12772 lines, head 3ee025e7a9fbdbbbf5b91de0ec3bfac7ca27c22d53255aecd615e75fbca0c609
  attachments: 2 files named by the lines; 2 present, checked against their name

Every line is hash-chained to the one before. Change one character of any line and verify says so. The head is the same every time you run logbook demo with the same days and seed.

docs.title: What is in it
docs.text:
logbook show stats

Counts by kind, source and year, never what a line says: ten thousand location points from the phone and the boat's AIS, two and a half thousand health samples, and a handful of everything else — events, messages, transcripts, notes, photos and the keepers inferred from them, calls, mail, tasks, browsing, videos watched, music and podcasts, paid trips, book highlights, voice memos (metadata and a digest; no audio), transactions, four flights, and the resolution lines that name the circle.

logbook show stats --health

One row per day: hours asleep (the union of the night's stages, never in bed or awake), steps (the larger device per quarter hour, summed), resting heart rate.

One trip read back whole, by the id at the end of its row or by any day inside it (docs/year.md, One trip): the route as the stays slept at — the week aboard is its five anchorages, each with its nights — the legs between them, the days one line each, the flights, the crew confirmed and proposed, the keepers, the health of the span, the spend; --html writes one page with an inline SVG map of the route, no tiles:

The whole year on one page — the rollups, the trips in order, the places by nights, the people by days together, health and keepers by month, and one day a month read back with the day reader, the day with the most evidence (docs/year.md):

docs.title: Keepers and pages
docs.text:
logbook show keepers                # the photos she marked favourites, and the one in the Art album
logbook show person "Ola Nordmann"  # a page: when they were together, by the evidence
logbook show asset nordlys          # the boat's page
logbook show place Cabin

docs.title: Out and back in
docs.text:
logbook export --day 2026-06-17 --out ~/Demo/pages    # one day as a package: 528 entries

A window for someone in the circle is a crossing (RFC 0005): name them in policy/crossing.json with the highest tier they may see, then logbook export crossing --to <name> --since … --until ….

docs.title: Make it yours
docs.text:
The month is a function of two numbers. --seed 2 is the same story with other noise, other step counts, other times for the messages; --days 90 is a summer; --days 365 a year of 150,000 lines, enough to feel what the index is for. --years 40 instead writes a life: forty years from her birth, in phases, thin until the phone and dense in the last month (demo.md). When you are done:

rm -r ~/Demo/Logbook
unset LOGBOOK_HOME
logbook init                         # your own, in ~/Logbook

Nothing of the demo is real: the people, the boat, the airline XY, the aircraft ZZ-ABC, the addresses, the numbers. The persona lives in Oslo and does not exist.

docs.title: The vault
docs.text:
logbook export vault <folder> [--since YYYY-MM-DD] [--until YYYY-MM-DD] [--tier 1|1,2] renders the record as a folder of plain Markdown that Obsidian or Logseq opens as a vault: one page per day, one per named place, one per person, one per trip, one per year, every page linked to the others with wikilinks. It is an export, not a reader: it is tier-gated exactly like a crossing (tier 1 by default, the shape of every day and no text of any note or message), and every run appends one crossing/v1 line to the chain so the record shows it left. Re-running rewrites only the files whose content changed.

logbook export vault ~/Vault                            # every day the record covers, tier 1
logbook export vault ~/Vault --since 2026-06-01 --until 2026-06-30
logbook export vault ~/Vault --tier 1,2                  # notes, transcripts, mail and calls named; needs the policy below

Then open the folder in Obsidian (Open folder as vault) or point Logseq at it. Nothing in it needs a plugin: the links are [[Name]], the front matter is YAML, the files are UTF-8 with \n line endings on every platform.

docs.title: The folder
docs.text:
<folder>/
  Logbook.md                      the root: years, places, people and trips, each a link
  years/2026.md                   the year: days per country, trips, places by nights, people (the most days first, names only), one line per day
  days/2026/2026-06-13.md         the Day, as `logbook day` reads it
  places/Home.md                  one per place in places.json: its days, the people met there, its trips
  people/Kari Nordmann.md         one per person confirmed present by a line that crosses
  trips/Trip 2026-06-15 to 2026-06-17.md   one per trip, as `logbook trips` derives them

A page's file stem is its link text, so the stems are one namespace for the whole vault and every one is a file name on every platform: whitespace is collapsed, the characters a file system or a wikilink refuses (< > : " / \ | ? * [ ] # ^) become dashes, trailing dots are dropped, and two names that differ only by case are two pages, the second with (2). A day is 2026-06-13, a year 2026, a trip Trip <start> to <end>; a place and a person keep their names.

docs.title: A day
docs.text:
The front matter is what the graph and a search can filter by; the body is the Day:

---
date: 2026-06-13
weekday: Saturday
country: "NO"
nights:
  before: "Home"
  after: "aboard Solvind"
places:
  - "Home"
  - "Marina"
people: []
trip: "Trip 2026-06-13 to 2026-06-13"
---
# 2026-06-13

Saturday · night before [[Home]] · night after aboard Solvind · NO · [[2026]] · [[Trip 2026-06-13 to 2026-06-13]]

## Timeline

- 00:00 – 09:00 [[Home]]
- 09:00 – 09:15 walk 1.4 km
- 09:15 – 24:00 aboard Solvind · 1 photo · held back: 1 note
    - 09:15 – 10:00 [[Marina]]
    - 10:00 – 12:00 boat 9.7 km
    - 12:00 – 24:00 59.8500,10.6000

## Sources

dawarich 888, immich 1, manual 1

country is quoted because a bare NO is false in YAML. nights are the night before and the night after as the Day names them: a named place, aboard <asset>, coordinates with the nearest place or city, or in transit. places are the named places stayed at, in order of first stay; people the ones confirmed present — attending a timed calendar entry held at the stay, speaking in a transcript, named in a note — by a line that crosses (below). A proposed face in a photo is not on the page: it is a proposal, not a day together (docs/day.md).

The timeline is the Day's rows, each clipped to the day: a stay at a named place is a link, a stay elsewhere its coordinates with the nearest place or city, a move its mode and kilometres, a stay aboard an asset one row with the berths, passages and anchorages indented inside it, a flight its own row. What attached to a row is counted on the row and named under it (event: Lunch), who was there is linked, and what the gate held back is counted: held back: 1 note. Then the all-day entries, the lines the track could not place, the notes in full (only when their tier crosses), and the sources with their line counts.

docs.title: The gate (ADR 0016)
docs.text:
A line is in the vault when its tier is in --tier, and shows only as a count when it is not — the same rule a crossing applies, line by line. The default, tier 1, is the shape of the record: where you were, how you moved, the flights, the calendar entries, how many photos and messages and notes, who the calendar confirms present. No text of any note, message, transcript or mail is in a tier-1 vault, and a person a tier-2 note names is not on the page until tier 2 crosses: the Saturday above says held back: 1 note and names nobody; with --tier 1,2 the same row reads 1 note, 1 photo · with [[Ola Nordmann]], the note's first line under it and its text under Notes. A message's text is never rendered: a vault is a diary, not a chat archive, and at tier 2 messages stay a count per row. Health and money are tier 3 and never go to a vault; --tier 1,2,3 is refused.

How far the gate opens is a setting in the record, not in the code: policy/crossing.json maps a destination to its ceiling, and the vault's destination is vault. A file that does not name it allows tier 1 — the vault is a folder on your own disk, like the mcp client — so --tier 1,2 needs one line added:

{"hermes": {"max_tier": 2}, "mcp": {"max_tier": 1}, "vault": {"max_tier": 2}}

You write each entry yourself; a new record names only mcp, at 1. A request above the ceiling is refused naming the file, and nothing is written or appended.

docs.title: The record shows it left (RFC 0011)
docs.text: Every run appends one crossing/v1 line with the destination vault, the window as instants (the first day's local midnight to the midnight after the last), the tiers, the counts (how many lines the window logged, how many crossed, how many were held back, by tier and by kind), the ceiling in force, the head before the line, and package_sha256: the digest of the folder as written, one line per file — <sha256 of its bytes> <path> in path order — hashed, which is what a crossing's manifest digest is for a bundle that has a manifest. Under extra.vault are the pages per kind and how many files were written and how many were unchanged. logbook show lists it as crossed to vault: 888 lines (tier 1: 888). Nothing else is written to the record, and that one write goes through Logbook.append.

docs.title: Re-running
docs.text: Every page is a function of the record's lines and its settings alone: no head, no timestamp, no counter is in any file, so a day that did not change is a file that did not change. A run compares each page's bytes with what is on disk and writes only the differences; the console says 23 written, 0 unchanged the first time and 0 written, 23 unchanged the next. Nothing is deleted: a page the record no longer produces (a place renamed in places.json, a window narrowed with --since) stays until you remove it, and Obsidian's own .obsidian/ folder and your own notes beside the pages are never touched. A nightly run is a reasonable thing, and it costs one line in the chain.

docs.title: The graph it produces
docs.text:
Obsidian's graph view draws one node per page and one edge per link; the vault is built so that the picture is the record's shape, without a screenshot:

  • Days are the most numerous nodes, each with few edges: its year, the places it was spent at, the people confirmed present, and its trip when it is in one. A home day links to Home and the office; a day away links to no named place and hangs off its trip.
  • Places are hubs. Home has an edge to almost every day and is the centre of the graph; the office to the weekdays; a marina or a cabin to the weekends. A place with a country in places.json carries it in its front matter, so the graph can be coloured by it.
  • People sit between the days they were met on and the places they were met at; a person met only on trips floats near the trip nodes, a colleague clusters with the office.
  • Trips are short chains: the trip node with an edge to each of its days, its named places and its people, and to its year. A week aboard is one node with seven day spokes.
  • Years gather everything: one edge to every day, place, person and trip of the year; the root page Logbook links the years.

Local graph on a day page shows that day's week of places and people one hop out; on a person it shows the days together, the places shared and the trips. In Logseq the same links are the page references, and the journals view is empty: the day pages are ordinary pages named by date, not Logseq journals, so they sit under All pages and in the graph.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: It is not a reader of the record for other software: the day package (export --day) and the crossing package (export crossing) are that, and they carry lines, not prose. It is not a backup: logbook backup is. It renders what the readers derive — a stay, a trip, a companion — and a derivation is disposable (ADR 0013): rename a place, raise the ceiling, and the next run rewrites the pages that changed. Your own notes beside the pages are yours; the pages are the record's.

docs.title: The week
docs.text:
logbook serve has a page for every ISO week, /week/2026-W25: the Sunday's week draft (dream week) grown into a page, beside the seven days it covers. Every Day links to the week it is in (the pager under its date), and so does the Sunday's week draft. The week's own pager links the week before and after while they hold a day of the record (or today); past its first and last week they are named, not linked. At its foot, Close the week: one form, no script, through the writers that exist (below; RFC 0043 §8, the second part).

The week 2026-W25          15–21 June 2026 · read at tier 3
← 2026-W24 · its Sunday, 2026-06-21 · 2026-W26 →
From the draft as written, by qwen2.5-7b-instruct: its numbers are the code's, its sentences pencil.

▸ The seven days        7 days with lines · 2 entries planned
▸ Where the week went   6 places · 4 threads
▸ Goals                 2 goals · 0 touched this week · 1 verdict proposed
▸ Next week             one proposal, pencil
▸ The question          one question, asked once
▸ People who moved      against the week before, names only
▸ The plan              Sprint 12 · next trip in 12 days
▸ Hold                  1 sender · 1 file

Each part is a fold with a summary line complete in its counts, so a closed fold says what it holds. A part with nothing in it is not drawn: the empty ones are named once, in one muted row, Nothing from. ?open=1 opens every fold, for printing.

docs.title: The parts
docs.text:
1. The seven days. One ribbon a day, Monday to Sunday, the same ribbon as the Day's (the Day): the calendar's timed entries planned above, the stays, moves, time aboard and calls lived below, the hours on one scale, so the days read against each other. Each day's name is a link to its Day. No now line: the page is the week's.
  2. Where the week went. The week draft's numbers, which the code computed from the lines and never the model (extra.numbers): the hours by place and the threads (a chat, a mail subject, a calendar title, a call), each with the lines it rests on, linked to each line as written. Sleep and training only on a page that reads tier 3: health is tier 3, a draft that read it is tier 3, and through a lower gate that draft is not read at all. Who you spent the week with is under People who moved, by name: a chat, or a title that names a person, is shown without its count.
  3. Goals. Each goal open on the Sunday, or touched in the week: the days the week touched it, your latest verdict, the verdict the week's draft proposes (in pencil), and the command that gives one of the five verdicts, logbook goal review GOAL advancing|stalled|done|let-go|superseded --period week --at SUNDAY (or logbook review goal, the week's sitting), which Close the week gives on the page. Under the goals, the two honest moves when a goal stalls: change the days (the week's one proposal) or change the sentence (reword it, goal add … --supersedes GOAL, or let it go). The page never draws a verdict of its own.
  4. Next week. The intention you kept on the Sunday, in ink, when you kept one; and the week draft's one proposal for next week, in pencil, headed with the model that wrote it, with its lines. A proposal only: showing it writes nothing.
  5. The question. The week's one stale question about a holding or an idea, asked once (the dream); answer it with logbook status, or leave it.
  6. People who moved. The people whose contacts in this week's draft differ from the week before's, the largest change first, five at most: names only, never a count, a direction or a score beside a name. Among the people each week's draft counts; a week whose week before has no draft has none.
  7. The plan. The sprint and the next trip (the plan), as the plan stood on the week's last day the clock has reached: titles and dates, each linked to its line, never to Notion.
  8. Hold. Hold's senders and Drive censuses as they stand: the counts of the reports logbook lab hold census senders and drive last wrote under state/hold/, each with its day, and only where the page reads every tier the report read; never a file's name or a sender. The page never runs a census: run one again and the page follows. On the week page only.

A week with no draft says so in one line, with the command that writes one once its Sunday is over, and the parts that rest on the draft (2, 4, 5, 6 and the proposed verdicts) are not drawn: nothing is invented in their place.

docs.title: The rules
docs.text:
• Through the gate. Every reader on the page reads through the page's tiers: the days, the draft (drafts.for_unit, as the Sunday's Day reads it), the goals (tier 2), the plan (tier 1), Hold's reports (by the tier each says it read). A tier-1 page shows the ribbons, the plan and Drive's counts, and no name, goal or sentence of tier 2.
  • Ink and pencil. The numbers are the code's; the proposal and the proposed verdicts are the model's, in pencil, each with its lines. A site built without its drafts (logbook export site without --with-drafts) reads no draft: the page says so in one line and shows no pencil.
  • No number beside a person. A model's sentence, a thread's title, the question or a kept intention that would put a digit beside a person's name is withheld, its row saying so and linking the line as written; the field of Close the week is left empty rather than hold it.
  • Nothing fetched, nothing written until you press. One document, one inline stylesheet, no script; the Library's three rules hold. Reading the page writes nothing; only Close the week does, and only what you chose.

docs.title: Close the week
docs.text:
At the foot of the week, on logbook serve (a static site carries no form), and only where the page reads tier 2: the goals and the intention are your own words. One form and one button. Each control has, beside it, the command that writes the same line, byte for byte:

On the page The command beside it each goal open on the Sunday: one choice of five, advancing, stalled, done, let-go or superseded (or no verdict, where it starts), and your words on it logbook goal review GOAL VERDICT --period week --at SUNDAY --note "…" change the sentence, when a goal stalls: the goal's page, and the command written out with its id and horizon logbook goal add "…" --horizon year --supersedes GOAL change the days, when a goal stalls: next week's intention, the field under the goals, and Keep these words as next week's intention logbook day reflect SUNDAY --intention "…" 
Close the week
  Goals
    Sail to Lofoten and back this summer.
      (•) no verdict  ( ) advancing  ( ) stalled  ( ) done  ( ) let-go  ( ) superseded
      [your words on it, if any]
      logbook goal review 019c… advancing|stalled|done|let-go|superseded --period week --at 2026-06-21 --note "…"
      When it stalls: change the days, keep next week's intention below; or change the sentence,
      reword it: logbook goal add "…" --horizon year --supersedes 019c…
  Next week's intention
    The week's proposal is in the field, pencil until you keep it; change the words first if they need it.
    [Send Kari Nordmann the harbour map.]
    [ ] Keep these words as next week's intention
    logbook day reflect 2026-06-21 --intention "…"
  [Close the week]
  • A verdict is one review/v1 line on the goal, for the period week, at the Sunday: now when you close the week on the Sunday, else the Sunday's last minute (goals). A goal reviewed already on a day of the week (by review goal, goal review, or here) shows its verdict and no choice: the same verdict on the same day again writes nothing, and another is refused.
  • The intention is one note/v1 line labelled intention on the Sunday, source reflect, tier 2, your words as one line. Once kept, the words are shown in ink above an empty field (other words kept there take their place); before, the field holds the week draft's proposal when it is shown and supported (pencil until you keep it), else nothing; it is written only when Keep is ticked. The same words again write nothing; other words are a new line whose supersedes names the first, so one intention stands for a week, never two. Next week's mornings show it under For, in ink, with its Sunday, in place of the pencil (the Day); this page shows it under Next week.
  • One press, every item checked first. Every verdict and the intention are checked before the first line is written, under one writer lock: a sixth word, a goal that is no goal, your words on a goal given no verdict, an empty intention, a second verdict for the week (or the same one in other words), or a sealed record on a machine without its identity each refuse the whole press (a 400, its sentence naming what and why), and nothing is written. Another command writing the record is the 409 of every act, your words kept in its form.
  • The gate is every act's (serve): from this machine, through the server's own pages, or from your phone once logbook setup phone names it; anything else is a 403 and nothing written.
  • The week closes on its Sunday. Before its Sunday the part says when it closes and carries no form; day reflect refuses a day ahead of today, or one that is not a Sunday.

From the command line, the same week closed:

$ logbook goal review 019c… stalled --period week --at 2026-06-21 --note "The boat is on land."
$ logbook day reflect 2026-06-21 --intention "Send Kari Nordmann the harbour map."
kept the intention for the week after 2026-W25 as #412 note/v1 (intention, source reflect, tier 2) on 2026-06-21

day reflect SUNDAY --intention is the command because an intention is a note in your words on a named day, and day reflect is the command that writes those (notes.write, source reflect). It stands alone: a reflection, --sign or --at beside it is refused.

docs.title: Later
docs.text: Time by project (the plan's projects against the lived hours), the sprint's outcomes (done, rolled to next week, let go: they need the signed day's dispositions in the crossing, RFC 0043 slice C), and the tasks untouched for 90 days, let go together in one decision.

docs.title: Who was there
docs.text:
The record sees a lot of who was with you: the people on a calendar entry, the voices of a recording, the faces your photo library names. It sees none of it for certain. A face is a library's guess; an invitee may not have come. Who was there is how you answer once for a whole stretch, instead of once a stay, and how you tell the record the two things only you know: who lives with you, and where your people live. Built from RFC 0043 §11 (Who was there) and §12 (Lives with, on a journey day), as commands and readers; no page yet.

Every answer is one note/v1 line in your words, tier 2, source manual, appended through the one note path like the other acts. Nothing is written unless you say so, and nothing is fetched.

docs.title: With, across a stretch
docs.text:
$ logbook with --from 2026-06-08 --to 2026-06-12 Ola
#5612 with Ola Nordmann  2026-06-08 13:00
#5613 with Ola Nordmann  2026-06-09 13:00
#5614 with Ola Nordmann  2026-06-10 04:00
#5615 with Ola Nordmann  2026-06-11 13:00
#5616 with Ola Nordmann  2026-06-12 13:00

One with note per person per day, the same line logbook with DAY NAME writes (the same function, presence.state), at the clock of that day's longest stay: the middle of the part of it that falls in the day's waking hours, so the note lies inside the stay and the Day, people and the journeys read the person there.

Which hours count: the waking hours of a day run from your day_start (in logbook.json, the clock your day begins at) on its date to local midnight after it. With "day_start": "06:00" the night after a day belongs to the day until 06:00 next morning, but its hours after midnight never count towards the longest stay, so that night never wins and no line lands after midnight. With no day_start (the default, "00:00") the waking hours are the whole calendar day, so a night at home from midnight to 08:00 can still be the longest stay, as on the Wednesday above.

A day with no stay is stated as logbook with DAY states it, at noon (now, for today). A person already stated on a day is not stated again. Every day is written under one hold of the writer lock, and everything is checked before the first line: a stretch longer than 60 days, a day still to come, or a name that is nobody, two people or you is refused in one sentence, and nothing is written.

docs.title: Not with
docs.text:
$ logbook people not-with Kari --from 2026-06-08 --to 2026-06-14
#5617 note  not-with: Kari Nordmann, 2026-06-08 to 2026-06-14

One note labelled not-with, the person's id and the stretch under extra (person, from, to). The review-with queue stops proposing that person on those days.

docs.title: Lives with, lives in
docs.text:
$ logbook people lives-with Kari --from 2026-01-01
#5618 note  lives-with: Kari Nordmann, from 2026-01-01
$ logbook people lives-with Kari --until 2026-09-30      # ends the standing one
$ logbook people lives-in Per Bergen
#5619 note  lives-in: Per Hansen, Bergen

A lives-with note (person, from, until when given) means that at a home stay (a stay at a place of kind home in places.json, or near one) that person is with you without asking, so the queue never asks about them there; away from home their faces propose as anyone's do. --until alone closes the stretch that is open, and is refused when none is. A lives-in note (person, city, from) is where they live; the latest one of a person counts.

Each note is written on the day you say it, and its words are <label>: <name>, …: the with module reads company from a note that says with Ola, and the colon keeps these notes out of it. A reader never parses the words; the label and extra say what a note states. A retracted note stands no more (logbook repair retract).

docs.title: The review-with queue
docs.text:
$ logbook review with --week 2026-W24
who was there, 2026-06-08 – 2026-06-14 (week 2026-W24)
  Kari Nordmann
      faces on 2 photos across 2 days · invited to 'Lunch'
      on Tue 9 Jun, Wed 10 Jun
      --accept 1
  Ola Nordmann
      in the meeting notes of 'Boat plans'
      on Thu 11 Jun
      --accept 2
  answer: --accept N[,N] (every day of it) · --accept N --days D,D · --not NAME

review with --journey ID (trip:FIRST:LAST, or a day of it), --week YYYY-Www, or --from D1 --to D2 (60 days at most); --json for one object. Per person, on a line of its own, the name; under it the evidence in words and the days it lies on. The evidence is the with module's:

  • faces on photos taken by your own camera (below); a photo received in a chat, by AirDrop or through a shared album never proposes anyone;
  • invitees of the calendar entries held at a stay: invited to 'Lunch';
  • the voices and participants of a recording: spoke in 2 calls; of a meeting note-taker's transcript (Granola, Meet): in the meeting notes of 'Boat plans'.

A day you already answered is not asked again (a with note, or a note at the stay that says with them); nor a day you said not-with; nor a home stay of someone who lives with you. The strongest come first (the most days, then the most evidence), ten at most, the rest counted. A name the record does not place is counted for logbook people review, never listed. No number stands beside a name: the order is the only rank, and the counts live in the sentence of the evidence.

Each person's number is their place in the queue, from 1, as the rest of review numbers its proposals; it is printed on a line of its own under them, --accept 1, never beside the name, and in --json it is the person's place in people. The answers are the acts above:

$ logbook review with --week 2026-W24 --accept 1                     # every day of it that has begun
$ logbook review with --week 2026-W24 --accept 1,2                   # two of them
$ logbook review with --week 2026-W24 --accept 1 --days 2026-06-10   # some days
$ logbook review with --week 2026-W24 --not Ola                      # not with me

The numbers are the queue's as it stands when you answer: once someone is answered they leave it, and the people below them move up, so list the queue again before the next --accept. A name given to --accept is refused in one sentence that names the number form; --not still takes a name, and so does logbook with --from D1 --to D2 NAME, for someone the queue does not ask about. Any option review with does not take (another kind's, such as --top or --since) is refused in one sentence, and nothing is written.

docs.title: Your people in a city
docs.text:
$ logbook people city Bergen --trip 2026-07-02
your people in Bergen, on journey trip:2026-07-01:2026-07-03
  Per Hansen  not yet

The people the record places in a city, by their lives-in note, and with --trip (the journey, trip:FIRST:LAST or a day of it) whether each was seen on it: confirmed by the with module at one of its stays (a timed calendar entry they accepted, their voice or name in a recording, a note there that says with them), or stated with you on one of its days (logbook with, or an accepted answer of the queue). Names and seen / not yet, never a count. No contacts import keeps a city today (the iOS and Google contacts and WhatsApp's keep names, numbers and addresses only), so the lives-in note is the only source. --journey is --trip's old name here, kept until the release after 1.0 and said once on stderr; everywhere else --journey is people nearby's, a journey or a flight line.

docs.title: Your own camera
docs.text:
A photo proposes a face for presence only when your own camera took it. What each library keeps of that today:

Library What it keeps What is missing Apple Photos provenance: camera (a live photo, a camera video, an import by the back or front camera, ZIMPORTEDBY 1 or 2, or by the Camera app), received (another app, AirDrop or sharing, shared with you: 3, 8, 13), screenshot, other; and extra.imported_by which device of yours took it, and who added a photo to an iCloud Shared Library Immich provenance from the EXIF (camera: a make and model and an original capture time, or a live pair; received: a messenger's file name and no EXIF), and camera, the make and model which of the server's users and devices uploaded it (Immich's ownerId, deviceId): a partner's phone uploading to the same library reads as camera too Google Photos (Takeout) the origin: mobileUpload is camera, a shared album received the device

So the rule (who_was_there.own_camera) is: provenance is camera, and no import the line keeps says it was received. Telling your phone from a partner's in one Immich library needs the adapter to keep the uploader, which is a change to the adapter, for later.

docs.title: Meeting note-takers
docs.text: The record reads Granola and Google Meet today. Granola's notes become a transcript/v1 line, tier 3, whose participants are the meeting's attendees as Granola names them (name and email), and its summary a separate note/v1 line, tier 2. Meet writes one event/v1 line per conference, tier 1, its signed-in participants as attendees, and its transcripts as transcript/v1 lines, tier 3. The attendees are kept, so the queue reads them as proposals, in the meeting notes of 'Boat plans', as the with module reads them at the stay. A tier-3 line stays home under the crossing as every transcript does.

docs.title: What is not here yet
docs.text: The Day page and the timeline still show faces from any library and do not set aside not-with or lives-with: that is a change to the with module (logbook/core/present.py) the pages share, left to the slice that builds the page. The journey page's seen / not yet list and the morning reconnect read people_in_city, and are built with their pages.

docs.title: The world
docs.text:
logbook export world draws the record as one page: a globe you can scrub. The world's outline, the places you have named as anchors, your boat and your aircraft as dots moving along their own tracks, your stays as dots, your journeys as tracks, and at the bottom a time scrubber that moves all of it. It is not 3D and needs no graphics card: a canvas, one script, one file. The Library serves the same page at /world.

logbook export world                                   # <root>/export/world/world.html, the whole record
logbook export world --out ~/World                     # ~/World/world.html
logbook export world --from 2026-06-01 --to 2026-08-31  # one summer
logbook export world --tier 1                          # where you were and how you moved, nothing you wrote
open ~/World/world.html                                # any browser, from the disk, offline
logbook export world --style chart                     # world-chart.html: the record on a period chart
logbook export world --style chart --journey trip:2026-07-10:2026-07-11   # one page of one journey

The chart, below, draws the same record on paper: Mercator's sea chart drawn on the canvas, or your own scanned chart.

docs.title: What the page shows
docs.text:
• The outline. Natural Earth's 1:110m land polygons, drawn on an orthographic globe. Drag to turn it, scroll (or + and −) to zoom down to a marina, fit frames what the record holds, globe shows the whole hemisphere. At the 1:110m scale a fjord is not water; the anchors and the tracks are as precise as the record, the coast is not.
  • The anchors. Every place in places.json, a ring the size of its radius and its name.
  • The assets. Every asset of assets.json (ADR 0018), and any other subject the record's lines name under its own id: a dot where its track puts it at the scrubber's time, the last hours of the track drawn behind it, the whole track faint. Between two fixes the dot moves along the line between them; after a silence of twelve hours (more on a thinned track) it is drawn hollow at its last fix, "not seen" until the next.
  • Your stays. Every stay of the stays reader, folded as the Day folds them: a run aboard is one stay aboard. A stay already over is a solid dot, one still to come a faint one; a night's stay is larger. Your own dot is the stay you were in at that minute, between two stays it moves from one to the next, and aboard it rides with the boat: the boat's dot is ringed and named "you aboard".
  • Your journeys. Every standing journey/v1 (and trip/v1) line, RFC 0020: a passage of the deck log along its route, a ride or a train from one end to the other, a parking as a square. One still to come is dashed, one under way is drawn as far as it has come, one done is a line.
  • The chapters. When the record holds chapter/v1 lines (RFC 0036), each standing chapter is a band on the scrubber over the days it covers, named, and the line above the globe says which chapter the scrubber is in. A chapter named after its stretch began still shows: chapters are read from the whole record.

Above the globe: the window, the tiers, the zone, how many lines were held back, and the scrubber's time as a sentence: Fri, 10 Jul 2026 19:12 · chapter Sommer på sjøen · aboard Havbris. The scrubber takes the arrow keys (an hour; a day with Shift, or Page Up and Page Down); play runs the window in forty seconds. Times are in the record's zone (logbook.json); a browser that does not know that zone shows UTC and says so, and never another zone.

docs.title: A place's or an asset's summary
docs.text:
Click an anchor or an asset (or its name in the list on the left) and its summary opens, counted from the whole window as logbook show place and show asset count:

a place an asset nights the nights whose stay lay at the place (aboard, the stay the boat lay at) the nights aboard it journeys the journeys that start or end there: by the name the line gives, or by a position inside the place's radius the journeys whose subject it is photos the photos taken during one of your stays at the place the photos taken while you were aboard, a passage included visits / fixes the first and the last day of a stay there the first and the last day of a fix

An asset's summary also gives its identifiers (mmsi, icao24, registration) and where it is at the scrubber's time; a place's its position and radius.

docs.title: Everything is in the page
docs.text:
The page is one HTML file and fetches nothing. Inside it are three blocks: the record's JSON, the land table and the script. No URL is in the page: no font, no image, no tile server, no geocoder, no stylesheet or script from anywhere. The file carries a Content-Security-Policy (default-src 'none', the one script allowed by its SHA-256) so the browser holds it to that even if a payload carried markup (every value is escaped, and the page writes text, never markup). The Library sends the same policy as a header. The test suite reads every attribute that can hold a URL, runs the export with every socket refused, and passes the page through the synthetic check the published site is held to.

The land table is logbook/tables/land.json: Natural Earth's 1:110m land (ne_110m_land), which is in the public domain, every polygon kept and each coordinate rounded to a hundredth of a degree and delta-encoded, 36 KB. Its cap is 48 KiB (world.LAND_BYTES). scripts/make_land.py writes it from the GeoJSON file, read from disk; nothing in the package or its build fetches it.

The record's JSON is at most 1,000,000 bytes (world.CAP_BYTES), so the whole page stays under about 1.1 MB. A track is drawn at one fix per five minutes at most: a fix is kept when the asset has moved 100 m since the last one kept, every six hours when it has not, and at both ends of a silence. When the record does not fit, the tracks are thinned first (a fix per ten minutes, twenty, … one a day), then the stays shorter than one, three, six and twelve hours are left out, a night's never. The counts are never thinned: a summary says the same at any thinning. A window that still does not fit is refused, naming --from and --to, and nothing is written. The console says how many fixes were drawn and what was thinned.

Every id it names is in it. A stay names its place and the asset it was aboard, a journey its asset and its places, the summaries every place and asset; before the page is written, world.validate checks each one, and a page that refers to anything it does not hold is never written.

No coordinate is more precise than the record's own. A place is as places.json spells it, a fix and a journey's route as their line does, to five decimals at most (about a metre). A stay's centre is computed by the stays reader; it is written to the fewest decimals any of your fixes inside the stay carries, and to four at most, the precision of the stay's own id. A tracker that writes three decimals gives stays at three.

docs.title: The gate (ADR 0016)
docs.text:
The record is read through the gate, a year at a time (reading.read(..., tiers)): a line whose tier is not asked for is not a stay, not a track, not a journey, not a band, not a count. The default is tiers 1 and 2, as far as the ceiling goes: where you were and how you moved (tier 1), and the chapters and the notes that make a stay a stay (tier 2). A journey with a price is tier 3 (RFC 0020) and is in no default page; nor is health or money, which the page does not draw at any tier.

The ceiling is the world entry of policy/crossing.json, and 1 when the file does not name it: the page is one you hand to people, so it fails closed, and without the entry it shows where you were and nothing more (logbook doctor says so on its world line). {"world": {"max_tier": 2}} adds the chapters; --tier 1,2,3 needs the entry raised to 3, and prints the tier-3 warning a crossing prints; --tier 1,2 without an entry of 2 is refused, naming the file:

{"hermes": {"max_tier": 2}, "mcp": {"max_tier": 1}, "world": {"max_tier": 3}}

You write each entry yourself; a new record names only mcp, at 1. An entry may carry an until day, as every entry may (ADR 0022); past it, nothing crosses to the page.

docs.title: The record shows it left (RFC 0011)
docs.text:
Every export appends one crossing/v1 line with the destination world: the window as instants, the tiers, the counts (lines logged, crossed and held back, by tier and by kind), the ceiling in force, the head before the line, and package_sha256, the digest of the folder as a vault's is digested (<sha256 of the page> world.html, hashed). Under extra.world: the page's bytes, the JSON's, how many places, assets, stays, journeys and chapters it holds, and the thinning. Nothing else is written to the record, and that one write goes through Logbook.append. The Library's /world appends nothing: nothing leaves the machine.

The page is a function of the record's lines and settings alone: no head, no clock. A re-run over an unchanged record writes the same bytes, and the file is not rewritten ((unchanged) in the console).

docs.title: In the Library
docs.text: logbook serve answers /world with the page export world writes by default — the same request, the same JSON, the same script — under the Library's navigation, with the policy in the header rather than in the page. /world?from=2026-07-01&to=2026-07-31 narrows it. Like every page of the record, it carries an ETag and a reload at the same head is a 304.

docs.title: The chart
docs.text:
A logbook is a ship's instrument, and the record drawn on a chart is what a logbook always looked like. --style chart draws the page on paper instead of the globe, beside it in the same folder (world-chart.html), with the same scrubber, the same summaries, the same gate and the same JSON:

logbook export world --style chart                     # Mercator's chart, drawn: no image in it
logbook export world --chart ~/Charts/oslofjord.png \
  --control-points ~/Charts/oslofjord.json \
  --chart-credit "my scan of a chart in the public domain"   # your own chart as the paper
logbook export world --style chart --journey trip:2026-07-10:2026-07-11  # one page per journey

Two rules hold on it, whatever the paper. The chart is paper, the track is evidence. The record's JSON in a chart page is the globe's, byte for byte (the test suite compares them): every position as the record has it, every minute as the record has it. The script draws a position where the paper puts it and nowhere else. An asset's track is the straight segments between its own fixes (on Mercator's chart that is the rhumb line a navigator lays off between two fixes), never smoothed, broken at a silence, never displaced to look drawn by hand. An asset is at its last fix, never slid between two (the globe slides it; the chart does not), and its summary says that fix and when. Between two of your stays the chart draws no position for you: the record has the stays, not the way between them. A day mark is a bar across a journey at a recorded position — the first fix of each of the record's days on the journey's own asset's track (at or after the journey's start), and the journey's two ends where its line puts them — and its date is the record's day of that fix or that end, as the record's zone and day_start cut it. The export works the dates out from the record's own instants and writes them into the page: never from the page's minutes, which are rounded (a fix half a minute before midnight is on the day it was taken), and never from the browser's clock, so a browser that does not know the zone still writes the record's dates (the clock under the scrubber says UTC then, as the globe's does). A night's stay is written with its first day on the page. Nothing is fetched. The paper is drawn on the canvas or carried in the page (below); the names and dates are in the system's serif, since a bundled font would have had to be fetched to be vendored, and nothing is.

docs.title: The drawn chart
docs.text: Mercator's projection (north up, a rhumb line straight), on sepia paper: the coasts of the same land table as the globe (Natural Earth's 1:110m land, public domain), hachured on the land side, the graticule engraved at a step the zoom has room for, degrees and minutes in a graduated border (the latitude cells widen towards the pole, as Mercator's do), and a compass rose with its thirty-two rhumb lines across the chart. Your stays are pricked positions — the prick and the ring a navigator draws round a fix, a night's larger and written with its day — your journeys dashed tracks in red ink with their day marks, your assets' tracks in ink (what each had sailed by the scrubber's time dark, the rest faint) with the asset's name written along the leg that brought it to its last fix, and your named places ringed and named. The legend, folded to one line at the foot, names the chart's source. Drag to move the chart, scroll (or + and −) to zoom, fit frames the record, chart shows the world. The paper is paper: in a dark room it stays light. At 1:110m a fjord is still land; the coast is as coarse as the globe's, the record as precise as itself.

docs.title: Your own chart
docs.text:
--chart FILE makes your own chart the paper: a PNG or a JPEG on your disk — a scan of a chart in the public domain, or one you own — read once, never fetched, never looked up. Three more things go with it:

  • --control-points FILE, a small JSON of three or more pixels of the image tied to positions, the pixels counted from the top-left corner of the file as you give it (x to the right, y down), best at crossings of the chart's own graticule, spread over it; a point's name (at most 80 characters) is how the corner and the console call it:
{"points": [
  {"name": "59°40′ N 10°33′ E", "x": 212.5, "y": 1648.0, "lat": 59.6667, "lon": 10.55},
  {"name": "59°40′ N 10°45′ E", "x": 1530.0, "y": 1702.5, "lat": 59.6667, "lon": 10.75},
  {"name": "59°55′ N 10°45′ E", "x": 1612.0, "y": 252.0, "lat": 59.9167, "lon": 10.75},
  {"name": "59°55′ N 10°33′ E", "x": 296.0, "y": 198.5, "lat": 59.9167, "lon": 10.55}
]}
  • --chart-credit "…", the chart's source in your words, which the legend writes as you give it. Nothing is read from the file to credit it.

The fit. The positions are taken to Mercator's plane, as a sea chart is drawn (on a chart of a few degrees any projection is that close to it), and the transform from the plane to the image's pixels is the simplest one your points check:

points the transform checked 3 affine, through them exactly no: three points fit an affine transform whatever they say. The corner and the console say unchecked 4 or more affine by least squares: a scan, turned, scaled, sheared yes 6 or more, when the affine one does not hold projective by least squares: a chart photographed at an angle yes

Each point's residual is how far the fit of the other points puts it from the pixel you gave (leave one out). A fit whose worst residual is more than 1 % of the image's diagonal (chart_fit.RESIDUAL_LIMIT; 36 px on a 3000 × 2000 scan) is refused, naming the point the others place worst and listing every residual, and nothing is written or appended. One wrong point raises the others' residuals too — the point named is not always the wrong one — so check them all. A latitude mistyped by a few hundredths of a degree is caught that way, and so is a chart drawn in a projection the track cannot honestly be laid on. Refused too, whatever the residuals: points nearly in a line, points that make a mirror image of the chart (a latitude and a longitude swapped, or y measured up from the bottom edge), and a projective transform whose horizon crosses the image. A projective transform is never fitted through four or five points: it has eight parameters, so the fit of the others would pass through them exactly — a check of nothing — and bend the chart to every error of a click. A thin-plate spline is not offered for the same reason: it passes through every point whatever the point says and bends the track towards it, which the track may never be. One transform takes every position of the record to the image: the track is laid on the chart, the chart is not laid on the track.

Where the check holds. The residuals vouch for the fit inside the control points' spread (the smallest polygon round them). Beyond it a position is placed by extrapolation, which no residual checks: a chart photographed at an angle, its points bunched in the middle, can pass the check and still put a position at its far corner well off. Spread the points over the part of the chart the record crosses; the corner and the console count the positions that lie beyond the spread.

On the page the image is the paper (the globe's coasts are not drawn on it, nor the rose: your chart has its own), the control points are crosses with their names, and the fit sits in a corner: its kind, each point's residual in pixels and as a share of the diagonal, the limit, and how many positions lie beyond the points' spread. The console prints the fit's kind, its worst residual and the limit, how many positions lie beyond the spread, and how many fall off the chart (they are drawn where the fit puts them, on no paper; beyond a projective fit's horizon, not at all).

Only the picture crosses. An image file carries more than its pixels: a phone's photograph of a paper chart says where and when it was taken and with what. None of it reaches the page. A PNG keeps the chunks that draw it (IHDR, PLTE, tRNS, gAMA, cHRM, sRGB, IDAT, IEND), a JPEG the segments that decode it (the frame, the tables, the scans, Adobe's colour marker): EXIF and XMP, text chunks, comments, colour profiles and anything after the image's end (a second picture, a gain map) are left out, and the console names what was. An image stored turned or mirrored (an EXIF orientation other than 1) is refused: you measured the control points on the picture as a viewer turns it, and without its EXIF the page would not. Save it upright and measure on that.

The cap. The image is carried in the page as base64 in a data block, at most 4 MiB (chart_image.IMAGE_BYTES) and 40 megapixels (IMAGE_PIXELS), and the script makes a picture of it with createImageBitmap, so the page's policy stays default-src 'none' with its one script by its hash — no data: URL, no img-src. A PNG over the cap is downscaled by the export: by a whole factor (2, 3, …, the smallest that fits), each block of pixels averaged, written again as a PNG, lossless. Your control points stay in the pixels of the file you gave; the page draws each pixel of the smaller picture as that many of yours, so the fit is unchanged. It takes a while on a large scan: the standard library, no image library, a row at a time (some ten seconds for a six-megapixel scan where it was measured, more for one whose rows are filtered by Paeth). An interlaced PNG over the cap is refused: save it without interlacing. A JPEG is never decoded or re-encoded — the standard library has no JPEG codec — so a JPEG over the cap is refused, saying about how wide to save it; measure the points on the smaller file, or give a PNG. A whole chart page is at most 7 MiB (world_chart.PAGE_BYTES): the record's JSON (1,000,000 bytes at most), the land table, the largest image as base64 and the page around them fit under it with room, and a page that would not is refused.

docs.title: One page per journey
docs.text:
--journey ID makes the page of one journey, in either style, under its own name so that no page overwrites another:

  • a trip, as logbook show trips prints it, trip:FIRST:LAST, or any day inside it (as show trip takes it): the page covers its days to the return day and draws every journey line of them. The trip is found through the same gate as the page. File: world-trip-FIRST-LAST.html (world-trip-FIRST-LAST-chart.html with --style chart).
  • one journey line, by the id of its journey/v1 (or trip/v1) line — a passage of the deck log, a ride: the page covers the local days from its at to its end and draws that line alone. One above the tiers asked for, retracted, superseded or cancelled is refused. File: world-journey-ID.html (…-chart.html).

--journey again for another page; every page is built before any is written. --journey sets the page's days, so it does not go with --from and --to.

What the line says. Each page appends its own crossing/v1 line, as every export does. A chart's or a journey's line carries under extra.world what the globe's does not: style, journey (the id as given), and for your own chart chart — its credit in your words, the digest, bytes and type of the image as the page carries it, how far it was downscaled, the fit's kind, its number of points, its worst residual, and how many positions fell off the chart (outside) or beyond the points' spread (beyond_spread). The globe's line of a window is as it was.

The Library's /world stays the globe.

docs.title: What it is not
docs.text: It is not a map service: there are no tiles, and the outline is coarse on purpose. The chart is not a georeferencing tool: it lays the record on your chart, and refuses a chart it cannot lay it on honestly. It is not 3D: the globe is a projection on a canvas. It is not a reader of the record for other software: the day package and the crossing package are that. And it is not a place to publish a real record without thinking: a tier-1 page still says where you slept every night.

docs.title: The Year
docs.text:
logbook year YYYY [--html PATH] [--json] reads one calendar year back from the record: the days per country, the nights home, away and aboard each asset, the trips in order with their nights and companions, the flights and their kilometres, the places by nights, the people by days together, the health lines by month, the weather of the year when the record has it (adapters/weather.md), the keepers by month, and twelve picks, one day each: for every month, the day with the most evidence, rendered with the day reader. It is a reader (ADR 0013): a function of the record at its head, composed from the readers that already exist — rollup, trips, day — over one reading of the year's days, derived every time and never written.

logbook year 2026                      # the year as text
logbook year 2026 --html ~/2026.html   # one self-contained page: inline CSS, no script, no asset; prints
logbook year 2026 --json               # the same Year as one JSON object, the picks' Days inside

docs.title: What a Year is
docs.text:
The window is the year's days the owner's track covers — the first to the last day with a location line, clipped to the year, as rollup --year clips it — so a day the record knows nothing about is nothing: not a night in transit, not a zero, not a pick. A year the record has no day in says so and the page is empty.

One reading.read of the window serves every section, and each section is the reader it names, for that year:

  1. Countries — days per country from the overnight stay, in transit and unknown apart (rollup countries, and its rule: a place with a country in places.json, else the nearest large airport's zone).
  2. Nights — home, away, in transit, and the nights aboard each asset (rollup nights).
  3. Trips — every run of nights away from home, in order (trips): the dates, the nights (aboard <asset> for an asset trip), the route, the flights in and out, the named places visited and the people confirmed present.
  4. Flights — the count, the kilometres, the long-haul count and the count by evidence, then every flight (rollup flights).
  5. Places, by nights — every named place and asset, then the top unnamed clusters, each with its nights, stays, hours and the people confirmed there (rollup places), ordered by nights and then hours; the page says 0 nights for an office, since that is the point.
  6. People — by days together: days, nights, the last real contact and the places shared (rollup people, the confirmed set only; a tagged face is a proposal and not a day together).
  7. Health, by month — sleep, steps, resting heart rate and HRV (rollup health --by month); a field no day of the month has a line for is an em dash, never a zero.
  8. Keepers, by month — the keeper/v1 lines standing (RFC 0024), by lane, for every month the window touches.
  9. One day each — twelve picks, one per month, each rendered with the day reader exactly as logbook day prints it, the night before included.

docs.title: The pick
docs.text:
The evidence of a day is counted from its Day: the attachments across its rows — events, transcripts, notes, mail threads, calls, messages, photos and keepers, as the Day counts them — plus the people confirmed present (never a proposal), plus one when the day has a flight or a new place. A new place is a named place not stayed at earlier in the year, or an unnamed stay further than 300 m (the distance places propose groups by) from every earlier unnamed stay of the year; home is never new, and a stay counts on the day it began.

score = attachments + people confirmed + (1 if a flight or a new place)

For each month, the pick is the day with the highest score; of equals, the day with more lines logged; of equals still, the earlier day. A month with no line is no pick (no days), and a month whose days have lines but no evidence shows its fullest day. Under --json every day of the window is listed under scored with its evidence, so the choice can be checked.

On the persona's fortnight (tests/persona.py, nobody in it is real), the Wednesday lunch — an event and a photo, Kari confirmed, the cafe a new place — scores four, and so does the Saturday aboard Solvind — a note and a photo, Ola confirmed, the marina and the anchorage new; the Saturday has the boat's own track in the record too, so it has more lines, and it is June's pick. The Monday flight to Zürich scores two: the calendar entry attached to the move, and the flight; the new places that day are not a second one.

docs.title: The page
docs.text:
--html PATH writes the same Year as one HTML file and prints year 2026: wrote PATH. The page is self-contained: its CSS is inline, it has no script, loads no font, image or stylesheet, and links nowhere, so it reads the same in twenty years and offline, and it prints: the sections have tables whose headers repeat on every sheet, the picks start on a fresh sheet and none of them is split across two. Everything the record says is escaped; a note that reads <b> stays text. The picks are the day reader's rows, in a monospace block, so the page shows exactly what the terminal does.

--html PATH --print writes a Volume instead — a cover, a contents page and one spread per month with the facts, a map drawn from the location lines and the keepers as hero photos, for A4 and US Letter — and On paper says how to make the PDF.

The Year also prints: --html PATH --print is a Volume (a cover, contents, a spread a month) and --poster one sheet, A2 or A3, a square a day in the ink of its night — both in On paper.

docs.title: The JSON
docs.text: --json prints one object: year; window (since, until, days; null for a year the record has no day in); head, the chain head the Year was read at; warnings (the trips reader's, when places.json names no home); countries (countries as {country, days}, in_transit, unknown); nights (home, away, in_transit, aboard as {asset, name, nights}); trips, each as trips --json gives it with people as names, without its flights and lines keys, and with one key more, asset_name, the name of the asset the trip was aboard (Nordlys; asset stays its id, nordlys), null for a trip on land; flights (count, km, long_haul, unmeasured, by_evidence, flights); places (places, assets, unnamed, each entry with nights, stays, hours, first, last and people as names; an unnamed cluster with its id, the stay id places name takes, label, lat, lon, aboard and city); people (id, name, days, nights, stays, last_contact, places, confirmed); health, one entry per month with the rollup's sleep, steps, resting_hr and hrv, their line ids inside; keepers, one entry per month with count, memory and art; picks, twelve entries of month, day, evidence (attachments, people, flight, new_place, lines, score) and page, the Day as logbook day --json gives it; and scored, the evidence of every day of the window. Nothing is written.

docs.title: One trip
docs.text:
logbook trip <id-or-date> [--html PATH] [--json] reads one trip back the same way: one of the runs of nights away that trips lists, named by its derived id (trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-20, the last part of every trips row) or by any day inside it, the return day included. It is a reader too (ADR 0013, ADR 0019): composed from trips, days, rollup health, the keepers and the transaction lines over one reading of the days around the trip — a week either side, widened while the run of nights away touches the window's edge, so a week is read from a month and never from a year — derived every time and never written.

logbook trips --year 2026                            # every trip of the year, its id last on the row
logbook trip trip:2026-06-15:2026-06-20              # the yacht week as text
logbook trip 2026-06-17 --html ~/yacht-week.html     # the same trip, named by a day inside it, as one page
logbook trip 2026-06-17 --json                       # the Trip as one JSON object

The sections, in order:

  1. Route — the stays slept at, in night order, each with its nights and dates: a named place, else the coordinates labelled as the Day labels them (the airport, near <place>, x km, the city in parentheses). A week aboard is its anchorages, one stay each, with the asset beside them — where trips folds the week into aboard Nordlys, the page says where the boat lay each night. Consecutive nights at one point (within 200 m) are one stay; a night in transit is a stay with no place. The legs between consecutive located stays carry their great-circle kilometres, and a leg that crosses a night in transit says so.
  2. Flights — in (dated the leaving day) and out (dated the return day), as trips has them.
  3. People — the people confirmed present at the trip's stays (the calendar, a transcript, a note, a resolved face), and apart the ones only proposed (a tagged face the record does not confirm, an all-day entry's attendee); someone confirmed at one stay is never a proposal at another.
  4. Nights aboard — per asset, when any night was spent on one; an asset trip says so in the header (6 nights aboard Nordlys).
  5. Days — from the leaving day to the return day, one line each exactly as logbook days prints it: the night, the kilometres moved, the flights, the stays and what attached, the people, the health triple, the gaps.
  6. Keepers — per day of the span, by lane, with the photos' names (RFC 0024).
  7. Health — sleep, steps, resting heart rate and HRV over the span as one period, the rollup health rule; a field no day has a line for is an em dash, never a zero.
  8. Spend — every transaction/v1 line (RFC 0021) dated inside the span, summed per currency with a minus sign for money that left (−119 NOK (1 transaction)), then each transaction with its merchant and category. The section is there only when the record holds a transaction in the span.

On the demo record's yacht week (logbook demo; nobody in it is real):

docs.title: The trip page
docs.text: --html PATH writes the Trip as one HTML file and prints trip <id>: wrote PATH. Like the Year's it is self-contained — inline CSS, no script, no font, image or stylesheet fetched, nothing linked — and prints with table headers on every sheet. Its route section opens with a map: an inline SVG drawn from the stays' coordinates in an equirectangular projection about the route's mean latitude (longitude scaled by the cosine of it, so a kilometre is the same length either way), one path per leg — dashed when a night in transit lies between — one mark per point with the numbers of the stays at it (a bay slept in on the way out and the way back is one mark, 1, 4), and a scale bar in whole kilometres. No tiles and no external map: the page shows the shape of the trip, and the table under it says where each point is. A single stay is still a map, drawn at a twentieth of a degree across. Everything the record says is escaped.

docs.title: The trip JSON
docs.text: --json prints one object: id, start, end, until (the return day), nights, in_transit, asset (the asset every night was aboard, else null) and nights_aboard ({asset, name, nights}); head, the chain head it was read at; window, the reading's days; warnings; route, one entry per stay with n, first, last, nights, label, place, lat, lon, aboard, asset, stay (the stay id) and in_transit; legs (from, to, km, through_transit); places; days, one object per day as days --json gives it; flights_in, flights_out and flights; people (confirmed and proposed, each id, name, status, confidence, sources, lines); keepers (count, memory, art, and days with each day's counts and photos); health (sleep, steps, resting_hr, hrv, the rollup's shape with line ids); spend (by_currency as {currency, amount, count} and transactions with date, merchant, amount, currency, category, provider, line; null when there is none); and lines, the trip's line ids. Nothing is written.

docs.title: Adapters
docs.text:
One adapter per source. A module with three names: NAME (the source it writes), sniff(path) -> bool ("is this file mine?", cheap, never raises) and run(input_path, since) -> iterator[dict] where each dict has the keys at, end, tz, source, kind, tier, payload (see SPEC §2) — everything except the chain fields, which the logbook adds on append. Give every line a stable payload.raw_id; logbook add skips lines whose (source, raw_id) are already in the log, so re-adding an export appends nothing.

Adapters built by the project ship inside the package under logbook/adapters/ (ADR 0012); the first are dawarich, google-takeout-location (Google Takeout's Records.json and Semantic Location History, and the phones' own Timeline exports, Android's Timeline.json and the iPhone's location-history.json; see docs/adapters/takeout.md), google-takeout-photos (the Takeout Google Photos/ folder → one photo/v1 line per media file from its JSON sidecar, RFC 0002; the pixels are hashed, never copied; the logbook/contrib/adapters/takeout/ package has calendar beside them and will gain activity) and google-takeout-keep (the Takeout Keep/ folder → one note/v1 line per note, RFC 0010: raw_id keep:<created usec>@<modified_at> so an edit is a new line and a re-import nothing, labels, pinned/archived/trashed/colour under extra, list notes as [x] lines, attachments by digest from the file beside the note and stored only with --attachments) and google-takeout-tasks (the Takeout Tasks/Tasks.json → one task/v1 line per task, RFC 0016: raw_id <task id>@<updated> so a ticked task is a new line, status open/done, due as a day, completed_at, list, notes, parent for subtasks) and google-takeout-chrome (the Takeout Chrome/ folder: History.json → one browse/v1 visit per entry, Bookmarks.html → one bookmark per link with its folder path, RFC 0017; raw_id from the instant and the url's digest, never the file) and safari (Safari's History.db from an iPhone backup — import-backup copies it out and runs this — or the Mac's own → one browse/v1 visit per row, the columns discovered by PRAGMA so an older or newer Safari still reads; the same visit from the phone and the Mac dedupes) and google-takeout-youtube (the Takeout YouTube and YouTube Music/history/ JSON → one watch/v1 line per video watched and per search, RFC 0018: title, channel, url, video id, the product as the service; ads and other activities skipped and counted; streamed with ijson). Not an adapter but of the same family: logbook places import-takeout reads Takeout's Maps (your places)/ GeoJSON and Saved/ CSVs and proposes entries for places.json, written only with --write. shazam (the app's shazamlibrary.csv → one listen/v1 track per identified song, RFC 0019, the zoneless tag time read in the record's zone) and apple-podcasts (Apple Podcasts' MTLibrary.sqlite, a copy through add, the phone's out of an iPhone backup through import-backup --only podcasts, or the Mac's own through logbook sync apple-podcasts → one listen/v1 episode per played episode with its show, how much played, completed from the playhead, and the feed's transcript URL under extra, recorded and never fetched; raw_id the episode uuid with its last-played time so a replay is a new line; the columns discovered by PRAGMA, so a store with more or fewer still reads; see docs/adapters/listen.md) and spotify (Spotify's extended streaming history, the folder of Streaming_History_*.json or one file → one listen/v1 line per stream, RFC 0019: at when playback started (the stop time less the milliseconds played), end the stop, the track, album artist and album or the episode and its show as Spotify spells them, played_s, the skip flag, the device, the reasons and the country under extra; raw_id the URI with the stop time as spelled; audiobook chapters and unnamed rows counted; streamed with ijson; the IP address never kept; see docs/adapters/listen.md) and apple-music (the Apple Music CSVs of Apple's data export, one file at a time by its header → listen/v1: the play activity as one line per PLAY_END with start, end, duration, played, skip flag and device; the library as a snapshot per last-played time, as apple-podcasts; the daily play history coarsely, one line per track per day at its first hour in the record's zone; the columns found by name, so a missing one still reads; the Apple ID and the IP address never kept; logbook add music <file>) and pocket (a Pocket CSV export → one browse/v1 save per saved page with its tags and read state, RFC 0017: not a note, since a saved page is not the owner's words) and ios-contacts (an iPhone's AddressBook.sqlitedb → one resolution/v1 line per phone number and email address, minting the record's person and company ids — how a record gets its people, ADR 0013.2) and whatsapp (an iPhone's ChatStorage.sqlite → one message/v1 line per message, RFC 0008; media by digest only until the §1.1 store exists) and imessage (an iPhone's sms.db from a backup, or live, the Mac's own chat.db through logbook sync imessage — one message/v1 line per message either way, with the same raw_id, so the two dedupe each other; media by digest only) and whatsapp-contacts (an iPhone's WhatsApp ContactsV2.sqlite → one resolution/v1 alias line per contact with a linked-device id, RFC 0006 alias_of: the @lid a group message carries paired with the phone number the address book resolves; nothing is minted) and ios-notes (an iPhone's Apple Notes NoteStore.sqlite → one note/v1 line per note, RFC 0010; the body decoded from the gzip+protobuf archive with a stdlib-only walker) and ios-calendar (an iPhone's Calendar.sqlitedb → one event/v1 line per stored entry, RFC 0009;
