rules as RRULE text, occurrences never expanded) and ios-calls (an iPhone's CallHistory.storedata, which only an encrypted backup carries → one call/v1 line per call, RFC 0012: direction, answered, duration, the other end as a source-native phone/email/handle ref, never resolved, the service as the phone names it) and apple-health (an iPhone's healthdb_secure.sqlite, which only an encrypted backup carries → health-sample/v1, RFC 0014: steps, distance, energy and flights in 15-minute buckets per device, heart rate capped at one reading a minute, resting heart rate, HRV and weight as readings, sleep stages and workouts as spans; healthdb.sqlite beside the store names the sources) and ics (any iCalendar file, RFC 5545 — a Google Calendar or Takeout Calendar/ export, an Apple Calendar export, a saved feed — or a folder of them → one event/v1 line per VEVENT with the same shape as ios-calendar; a small tolerant stdlib parser, occurrences never expanded; or live through logbook sync gcal, the calendars you own over the Calendar API on the one Google key or their private iCal feeds, read by the same reader so the API, a feed and an export of one calendar dedupe each other (ADR 0017)) and apple-wallet (an iPhone's Apple Wallet passes — the unpacked .pkpass folders a backup keeps under Library/Passes/Cards/, which import-backup --only wallet copies out, or any .pkpass zip → one flight/v1 line per air boarding pass, RFC 0013, evidence declared: the route, the carrier and number, the date and the seat and class read from pass.json's front fields by their keys and labels, which differ per airline, and from its semantic tags; one event/v1 line per event ticket and per train, boat or bus pass, RFC 0009, the issuer as the calendar; a coupon, store card or generic pass becomes an event only when it carries a relevantDate, else it is counted; pass.json is the one file read — the barcode, the back fields, the images and the Passes database never — and the booking reference and the passenger's name never reach a line; raw_id from the pass type and serial, hashed, so a re-import appends nothing and an updated pass supersedes; logbook add wallet <folder|pass.pkpass>; see docs/adapters/wallet.md) and ios-wallet (an iPhone's Apple Wallet passes — the unpacked .pkpass folders a backup keeps under Library/Passes/Cards/, which import-backup copies out, or any .pkpass zip → one flight/v1 line per leg of an air boarding pass, RFC 0013, evidence tracked, read from the airline's IATA BCBP barcode, the year from the pass's own dates and never guessed; one event/v1 line per event ticket and per bus, boat or train boarding pass, RFC 0009, the issuer as the calendar, the front fields under extra minus names and credentials; store cards, coupons and generic passes skipped and counted; the PNR, the passenger's name and the barcode never kept; logbook add wallet <folder|pass.pkpass>) and easypark (the EasyPark app's recentparkings_<user>.json from an iPhone backup → one trip/v1 line per recently used parking area, RFC 0020 mode parking: the area's description, signage code, operator and coordinates as from, at the app's last-used time, no end and extra.observed last_used, because the phone keeps no sessions; import-backup copies the file out and runs it) and wispr-flow (the Wispr Flow dictation app's database.sqlite from an iPhone backup → one transcript/v1 line per dictation, RFC 0004: the typed text, else the tidied text, else what the recogniser heard, as a text/plain attachment in the §1.1 store and never inline; provider wispr-flow, the language, the app it was typed into under extra; tier 3 by default; logbook add wispr <database.sqlite>) and flighty (a Flighty CSV export → one flight/v1 line per flight, RFC 0013, evidence tracked: carrier spelled as IATA, the airports' wall-clock times converted to UTC through the shipped airports table, the PNR never kept; logbook add flights <export.csv>; a flight the owner already declared or the record already inferred is superseded by the merged line, never duplicated; the same adapter reads the app's own MainFlightyDatabase.db from an iPhone backup, which import-backup copies out, with the same mapping and raw_id, so the store and an export of the same flights dedupe) and transcript (the universal transcript file adapter, RFC 0004 transcript/v1: JSON already in transcript/v1 shape — the interchange format for any tool — WebVTT, SRT, Markdown and plain text with Speaker: text lines → one line per file, the file's own bytes as the SPEC §1.1 attachment, raw_id <source>:<sha256>, tier 3 by default; logbook add transcript <file|folder> --source <name>) with granola as its live sibling (logbook sync granola: one transcript/v1 line per recording through the same mapping, raw_id granola:<note id>, plus the AI summary as a derived note/v1 line); ais and adsb (ADR 0018: the positions of the owner's own vessels and aircraft, registered in assets.json, as location/v1 lines with subject set; ais reads a saved aisstream.io stream and logbook sync ais listens to its websocket for the registered MMSIs — for --listen SECONDS or --until HH:MM (the record's local time) or LOGBOOK_AISSTREAM_LISTEN_S, one progress line a minute per asset, a reconnect with backoff when the socket drops, Ctrl-C writes what was heard — raw_id aisstream:<mmsi>:<unix seconds>; adsb reads a saved OpenSky states/all response and logbook sync adsb polls it for the registered icao24 addresses, raw_id opensky:<icao24>:<time_position>) and mail (an mbox mailbox — Google Takeout's Mail/ export, or any mbox file or folder of them → one mail/v1 line per message, RFC 0015, streamed one message at a time: raw_id the Message-ID (<account>: first when --account names the mailbox, so the live IMAP source dedupes against the export, ADR 0017), the thread root, sender and recipients as {email, name} refs never resolved, subject, date with its offset, Gmail labels, the body as text (HTML stripped without a library, at most 64 KB of it), size, attachments by name and length never decoded — only with --attachments are they decoded, hashed and put in the §1.1 store; direction from owner_emails in logbook.json; --only-labels/--skip-labels/--since; a message without a Message-ID keyed by its digest, never skipped; built for a 20 GB Takeout: chunked, well over 40 MB/s, progress every 10,000 messages, resumable through the cursor in inbox/manifest.json, --restart to read it all again; and live, the same mailbox over IMAP through logbook sync mail — read-only (EXAMINE and BODY.PEEK, never a flag change), configured by LOGBOOK_IMAP_HOST, _USER and _PASSWORD alone, resumed per folder by UIDVALIDITY and UID from the last batch written, the headers fetched first so a message the export already wrote costs no body, Gmail's labels and thread id taken once at ingest; and a Gmail mailbox over the Gmail API through logbook sync gmail, on the one Google service-account key, the same line and dedupe key as IMAP; docs/adapters/mail.md) and apple-reminders (an iPhone's Reminders stores, one Data-<UUID>.sqlite per account → one task/v1 line per reminder, RFC 0016: title, status, due — a day for an all-day reminder, an instant for a timed one — completion time, list and notes; raw_id reminders:<uuid>@<modified>, so a reminder completed later is a new line; subtasks by parent, priority as three words; logbook add reminders <folder> reads every store below the folder) and copilot (Copilot Money's CopilotDB.sqlite → one transaction/v1 line per transaction, RFC 0021, tier 3 always: amount signed from the owner's side, currency, the cleaned merchant or the owner's override, Copilot's own category slug, the account id, pending or posted, the owner's note; the bank's original string, the type, tags and a split's parent under extra) and splitwise (Splitwise's database.sqlite → one transaction/v1 line per expense the owner is part of, tier 3: the owner's share signed from their side, currency, description, category, the group as the account; every member's shares with source-native refs under extra; the owner found by owner_emails, else taken as the person on most expenses and said so) and beeper (Beeper's BeeperStore.sqlite, the phone's cache of a Matrix account bridging WhatsApp, Telegram, Instagram and Facebook → one message/v1 line per message in clear: decrypted cached events and each room's last message, RFC 0008; encrypted events without a decrypted copy are counted, never guessed at; senders as contact hints from the bridge — phone, email or Matrix handle — never resolved; extra.network names the bridge; or live, every chat of every network Beeper Desktop bridges through its local API with logbook sync beeper, read-only, one line per message under beeper-<network>, attachments referenced by asset id and never fetched) and notion (live only: logbook sync notion reads the pages an internal Notion integration is shared with and writes what happened to each on each day, one event/v1 line per page, local day and action — created, edited, moved, archived — at tier 1, with the title, the titles above it, the page's id and url and who acted; never the text, only its SHA-256 and word count, and of a database row only its status, select, date and checkbox values, old and new against the page's previous line, its database and its relations as the ids of the rows they link to, never their titles (--relations-backfill for rows synced before); read-only, under Notion's rate limit) and meet (live only: logbook sync meet, the Meet REST API on the one Google key → one event/v1 line per call that has ended, tier 1, the participants as Meet names them, and when Meet transcribed the call one transcript/v1 line through transcript.draft, the mapping and tier granola uses; a Granola transcript of the same call stays its own line) and gaudit (live only: logbook sync gaudit, the Workspace login audit log on the one key → one event/v1 line per sign-in event of the owner's, tier 1, the place Google derived from the address and never the address) and line (LINE's Line.sqlite → one message/v1 line per message, RFC 0008; a sender's phone from Contacts.sqlite and a group's name from UnifiedGroup.sqlite when they are beside the store, as import-backup puts them; calls are counted, not logged) and twitter (the X app's <account>-dmv2.db direct-message stores, one per signed-in account → one message/v1 line per message, RFC 0008: the conversation as the chat, named after the other account or its custom title; senders by screen name, never resolved; links and photos as media_kind) and apple-books (Apple Books' AEAnnotation*.sqlite, from an iPhone backup or a Mac → one highlight/v1 line per highlight and bookmark, RFC 0022: the quote and the owner's note verbatim, the EPUB CFI as text, the title and author looked up in the BKLibrary*.sqlite beside it and never guessed; reading positions and deleted marks skipped and counted; logbook add books <store-or-folder>; import-backup copies both stores out) and voice-memos (Voice Memos' CloudRecordings.db with the audio beside it → one voice-memo/v1 line per recording, RFC 0023: title, duration, the file hashed a chunk at a time and named by digest, put in the §1.1 store only with --attachments (import-backup --attachments too); a recording whose file is gone is a line without media, counted; no transcription — that is the later, local step logbook transcribe voice-memos: one transcript/v1 line per memo with its audio in the store, heard by mlx-whisper or faster-whisper on this machine with the hub offline, raw_id the memo's own and provenance.source the memo line's id, see docs/adapters/voice-memos.md) and apple-photos (an iPhone's Photos.sqlite → one photo/v1 line per asset not in the trash, RFC 0002: the original file name and the capture time — the merge key a reader folds the Immich line for the same asset on —, coordinates, size, duration, live photo, provenance from the store's own record of how the asset arrived, the number of faces, the ids of the people the owner named under people and their names under extra.faces (a proposal of presence a reader never confirms), favorite, hidden and the owner's own albums; the favourites and the Art album become keeper/v1 lines in the same run, written once (RFC 0024); the pixels stay where they are, named by path and, through import-backup, by digest (content_hash), so logbook attach import-backup --only photos can fetch them; logbook add photos <store>; see docs/adapters/photos.md) and withings (the Withings app's per-profile <profile>_WTHealth.sqlite and <profile>_Measure.sqlite → health-sample/v1, RFC 0014: the scale's weight and body composition — body fat %, fat, fat-free, muscle and bone mass, body water, BMI, VO2 max — one line per quantity at the instant of the standing, and the app's heart-rate readings; readings the app relayed from Apple Health or another app are skipped and counted, so the record gets them once; either store brings its partner, a folder brings every profile; the same adapter reads the account's data export, logbook add withings <folder> — the scale's standings from weight.csv, the cuff's pulse from bp.csv with the pressures under extra, the nights and the tracker's sleep stages, heart rate, steps, distance and calories from sleep.csv and the raw_* files, the activities as workout — and a later export that changes a sample writes a correction that supersedes the line in the record, never a duplicate and never a rewrite, see docs/adapters/health.md) and myfitnesspal (MyFitnessPal's maindb.sqlite → health-sample/v1: logged foods as energy_intake in kcal from the portion and quantity with the meal, food and portion under extra, weights (pounds converted), exercise as workout; an entry the app keeps only the day of is a span over that local day; daily step totals skipped; the same adapter reads the account's Nutrition-Summary CSV export, one energy_intake per meal per day with the macros, water and note under extra, a re-logged meal a correction as above) and sbb (SBB Mobile's SbbMobile.db and the past journeys store beside it → one trip/v1 line per bought ticket group — validity window, the stations on the ticket, the price as {amount, currency}, class and head count, cancelled when refunded — and one per saved journey the owner took, with its legs, the real clocks and the stations' coordinates, mode transit, provider sbb, RFC 0020; the traveller's name, the QR code and the order reference are never read) and screentime (a Mac's knowledgeC.db — the /app/usage stream only, behind Full Disk Access — and an iPhone backup's Screen Time store RMAdminStore-Local.sqlite → one app-use line per session, or per app per hour on the phone, with an event/v1 payload at tier 2: the bundle id, the app's name when known, the span and the device; raw_id <device>:<bundle id>:<start>; never a window title, a URL or a web domain; logbook add screentime [--mac DB | --backup DIR], import-backup --only screentime; read back by rollup attention as hours by app and category, the categories from a built-in table under policy/apps.json; see docs/adapters/screentime.md). and passages (a ship's deck log transcribed as CSV → one declared trip/v1 sea leg per row, RFC 0020 mode passage, the registered vessel as subject, logbook add passages <csv> --asset <id> --routes <dir>; each end positioned from the ECDIS route (RTZ) whose name names both places, else places.json, else a bundled gazetteer of Mediterranean, US East Coast and Bahamas ports, with a location/v1 line of the vessel at each positioned end so the readers see the leg as her own movement; see docs/adapters/passages.md). And the owner's own agents, their words marked as machine text and never a person's (see docs/adapters/agents.md): telegram (Telegram Desktop's JSON export of the owner's bot chats → one message/v1 line per message, the owner's as theirs and the bot's with extra.machine, the bot as the counterpart of kind agent, media referenced by path and digest; logbook add telegram-export <folder>; or live, logbook sync telegram over the Bot API for the owner's own bots, read-only and never confirming an update, the same lines and the same key so the two dedupe each other) and claude-code (Claude Code's session transcripts under ~/.claude/projects/ → one transcript/v1 line per session, the owner's turns as owner and the assistant's as a participant marked machine, tool calls counted and their output never kept; logbook add claude-sessions <folder>) and claude (the Claude apps' data export, its zip or the folder it unpacks to → one transcript/v1 line per conversation in the shape claude-code writes, the owner's turns as owner and the assistant's as a participant marked machine; files and tool calls named and counted, never copied, an attachment's extracted text, a tool's input and output, thinking and users.json never read into a line; the project's name only; a conversation that grew supersedes its line; logbook add claude-export <zip>). Third-party adapters are separate packages registering the logbook.adapters entry point. logbook add <file-or-folder> tries every registered adapter's sniff and runs the first match.

The Takeout package also has google-takeout-pay (the Google Pay/ folder: the transactions CSV → one transaction/v1 line per payment at tier 3, signed from the owner's side, the currency read from the amount text; the passes that are tickets, transit or flights → one event/v1 line each, loyalty cards, offers and gift cards counted), google-takeout-chat (Google Chat/ → one message/v1 line per message, the chat from the conversation folder and group_info.json, from_me from owner_emails or the one user under Users/, the first attached file hashed and stored only with --attachments), google-takeout-meet (Google Meet/Call history/ → one call/v1 line per call, outgoing when the organizer is the owner), google-takeout-contacts (Contacts/ vCards → one resolution/v1 line per email and phone, one entity per card, merged with the people the record already resolves through the resolved option logbook add passes, so a person ios-contacts resolved is never minted twice), google-takeout-access-log (Access Log Activity/ → one event/v1 line per access to a Google service at tier 3, device and location when the row has them; off by default in policy/import.json) and google-takeout-activity (My Activity/ → searches, visited results and apps opened as browse/v1, YouTube entries through the YouTube adapter's own mapping as watch/v1, Chrome entries left to the Chrome adapter; off by default), google-takeout-maps (Maps (your places)/ → the reviews as highlight/v1, the place as title, the words as quote, the stars under extra; the saved places never lines but candidates for places propose --takeout, with their list and the day they were saved) and google-takeout-home (Home App/HomeHistory.json → arrivals, departures and the alarm armed or disarmed as event/v1, the evidence the Day attaches to a night at home; sound events and alarm clips never read) and google-takeout-fit (Fit/ → health-sample/v1 at tier 3 with the types and units apple-health writes, RFC 0014: the All Data/ streams as steps and distance in quarter-hour buckets per device, heart rate capped at one reading a minute, weight, body fat and sleep stages as spans, each line naming the device and the app Fit recorded it from; All Sessions/ as workouts with their aggregates under extra, a sleep session as the night in bed; Daily activity metrics/ as the fallback, a day's quarter hours as buckets and a day-long span for a day no stream touched; calories and the other derived figures never a type; the same quarter hour counted by Apple Health stays a second line, see docs/adapters/takeout-fit.md). The YouTube adapter reads Takeout's default HTML as well as JSON, the clock in the record's zone only when the abbreviation is that zone's. Every Takeout sub-adapter also answers to takeout-<name>; logbook add --dry-run counts any import against the record and writes nothing. The owner's page is docs/adapters/takeout.md.

Rules: pure by default (no network), never write to the source, never invent tier lower than the source deserves, fixture-tested with synthetic data only. Backfill and live share one mapping (ADR 0017): where a source has both an export and an API, one function maps it and both add and sync call it, so a backfilled line and the same line pulled live have one raw_id and dedupe to one line.

One live adapter asks a third party about your days: weather (logbook sync weather, RFC 0026, weather.md) takes the places your own track says each day was spent at, rounds each to a tenth of a degree so no exact place leaves the machine, and fetches that day's weather from Open-Meteo's free archive, cached under inbox/weather/ so nothing is asked twice. It runs only when LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1 is set, by name or in sync --all, and then asks about yesterday and the days since the last run, never your history unless you name the days; no reader opens the network.

One live adapter is deliberately not in the registry, so sync --all never lists its folder: drive-videos (logbook sync drive --videos, RFC 0040, videos.md) writes one video/v1 line per file of the family's videos folder on Drive, from its metadata alone; videos fetch downloads a file at a time into a bounded cache, and videos infer finds its scenes and proposes where and when each was filmed on this machine, for the owner to confirm with review video, one more queue of the review.

Planned first (ADR 0008): google-takeout, apple-health (done), then email — the last now mail, file mode; its live IMAP mode is the next step under ADR 0017.

Wanted — pick one and open an issue with the adapter template: strava, garmin, apple-fitness, eight-sleep, oura, withings, telegram, signal, imap (the live mode of mail), google-calendar, flightradar24, notion, obsidian, spotify, apple-music, letterboxd, goodreads, kindle-highlights, twitter-archive, instagram-export, bank-csv (generic, with per-bank mapping files), revolut, paypal, amazon-orders, uber, airbnb, vivino, steam, boat-passage logs.

docs.title: Delete after import
docs.text:
An export is read once and then only takes up disk: a Takeout is tens of gigabytes, a phone backup's copies under inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/ a few more. The record does not need the input again — every line is in logbook/, every file worth keeping is in attachments/ by digest — and add and import-backup say so with their last line (inbox: Records.json can be cleaned now …). Nothing is deleted for you; two commands do it on request:

logbook inbox list                        # every file under inbox/: size, the import that read it, whether its lines are all in
logbook inbox clean --to /Volumes/Archive # move what is imported in full to the external disk, keeping its path under inbox/
logbook inbox clean --delete --dry-run    # or remove it; --dry-run says what would go and how much, and touches nothing

How list knows: a run of add or import-backup that reaches its end appends one entry to state/imports.jsonl (bookkeeping, like the sync watermarks; never the record) — the input, the adapter, how many lines it produced and how many were new, the seq span appended and the hash of its last line, the record's owner_id, the input's size. A file is ready when its run wrote to this record, the file has not changed since (size, and a lone file's modification time), and the run's last line still stands at its seq with its hash: the record is append-only, so that line standing means every line before it stands, and a line the run skipped was already there. A run that stopped early (an adapter error, Ctrl-C) records nothing, so its input reads not imported and clean keeps it, as it keeps a changed file, a file imported into another record and a file already at the destination — each said so with its reason. A store's -wal/-shm sibling goes with the store; a backup's copies.json and decrypted Manifest.db go when every other file in their folder has. Adapters need do nothing for this: the CLI records the run, and an adapter that is pure (never writes to its source) leaves the input exactly as it found it, which is what the size and time check relies on.

docs.title: Your own agents: Telegram bots, Claude Code and the Claude apps
docs.text:
You talk to agents of your own: bots you run on Telegram, a coding assistant in Claude Code, Claude in its apps. Those conversations are part of the record. Your words in them are yours, at their tier, and read like anything else you wrote. The agent's words sit beside them, marked as machine text, and no reader takes them for a person's: an agent is never in people, never someone's company, never proposed in people review, and its "I'll have it ready by Friday" is never a promise.

logbook add telegram-export ~/Downloads/"Telegram Desktop"/DataExport_2026-03-02   # your bot chats, both sides
logbook sync telegram                                                            # what you sent your bots since
logbook add claude-sessions ~/.claude/projects                                   # every Claude Code session on this machine
logbook add claude-sessions ~/.claude/projects --dry-run                         # what would be added; nothing written
logbook add claude-export ~/Downloads/claude-data.zip                             # your conversations in the Claude apps
logbook add claude-export ~/Downloads/claude-data.zip --dry-run                   # how many new, grown and unchanged

docs.title: The machine mark
docs.text:
No payload profile has a slot for "an agent wrote this", and none is invented for it. The mark rides in the slots the two frozen profiles already leave for a source's own fields (logbook/core/machine.py reads it, and every reader below goes through it):

Where The mark What it means message/v1 (RFC 0008, whose extra keeps anything else a source reports) extra.machine: true the agent wrote this line message/v1 extra.counterpart: {"kind": "agent", "ref": {kind, value}, "name"?, "username"?} the line belongs to a conversation with an agent, whoever wrote it; on every line of it, yours and the agent's transcript/v1 (RFC 0004, whose consumers ignore a participant's fields they do not know) a participant {"name": "assistant", "machine": true} that participant is an agent, and every turn under its name is machine text

The counterpart is an observed entity of kind agent: what a source saw, keyed by its ref (provider_id telegram:<bot id> for a bot, provider_id claude-code for the assistant in Claude Code, provider_id claude for Claude in its apps), never resolved and never a person. RFC 0037 (draft) names the observed entities a review will one day place: person, org, place, asset, idea. agent is not among them yet; it is defined here, by these lines, so that an Agents page, when one exists, reads the same field. Only the literal true marks anything, and a line without the mark is read as it always was.

A tier is where a line may travel, never who wrote it: an agent's message is tier 2 because message/v1 is, exactly as your own; a session or a conversation is tier 2 because transcript/v1 is.

docs.title: Telegram: the export
docs.text:
Telegram Desktop → Settings → Advanced → Export Telegram data, Machine-readable JSON. Tick Bot chats; nothing else is needed, and the file stays small. A chat's own export (⋮ → Export chat history, in a bot's chat) has the same shape and is read the same way. The export is a folder holding result.json and the media it downloaded beside it.

logbook add telegram-export <folder> (or the folder, or its result.json: they are sniffed) reads every chat of type bot_chat and nothing else. A personal chat, a group, a channel and your saved messages are counted (chats that are not with a bot, never read) and never opened, so no person's words come in through here. Your Telegram chats with people are not read by this adapter.

Field From at the message's date_unixtime; an export older than that field has only a local time without an offset, read in the record's zone chat {id: <the bot's user id>, type: direct, name: <the bot's name>} from_me false for a message from the bot (from_id user<bot id>), true for every other: a private chat with a bot has two sides. When the export names its owner (personal_information.user_id), a message from anyone else is counted and skipped sender for the bot's lines: {kind: provider_id, value: telegram:<bot id>, name: <bot name>} text the message's text (or caption) with its formatting dropped media_kind the export's own classification: image, voice, video, gif, audio, sticker, document, location, contact reply_to the key of the message replied to, when the export holds it edited when the export says the message was edited; extra.edited_at is when extra counterpart (the bot, kind agent), machine (the bot's lines), view export, message_id (the export's own id), reply_to_message_id, forwarded and forwarded_from, media and media_missing

Media is referenced, never copied. A file the export holds is named under extra.media by its path in the export (local_path, POSIX, resolved by its parts and never outside the folder), its SHA-256, its size, its media type and file name when the export gives them. A file the export left out ((File not included…)), or a path that would leave the folder, is extra.media_missing, and the line is written all the same. payload.media is never set: the bytes are not in the record.

A forward is not your words. A message you forwarded to a bot keeps extra.forwarded and the name it came from; promises never reads it, since what someone else wrote is not a promise of yours.

docs.title: Telegram: live, sync telegram
docs.text:
export LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKENS="<bot id>:<secret>,<bot id>:<secret>"   # BotFather's tokens, your own bots
export LOGBOOK_TELEGRAM_OWNER_ID="<your numeric Telegram user id>"
logbook sync telegram

A token can read and send as its bot, so it is a password: it lives in the environment (or ~/.config/logbook/sync.env for the schedule), never in the record, never in a line, never printed; an error names the bot by its id or username, never by its token. The owner id is what makes "a bot's updates are only its chat with you" a rule rather than a hope: a message from anyone else is counted (from someone other than the owner, never written as theirs) and never written, so a stranger who finds a bot never speaks in your name. A message outside a private chat is counted too.

sync telegram asks each bot three read-only methods, with GET and nothing else: getMe (who the bot is), getWebhookInfo (whether its updates go to a webhook, and how many are pending) and, only when updates are pending and no webhook is set, getUpdates?timeout=0&limit=100. It never passes offset, so it never confirms an update and your bot's own program still receives every one; it never passes allowed_updates, which would change what the bot is sent; it never calls deleteWebhook, getFile or a method that sends. A test holds it to that.

What that leaves is narrow, and it is worth saying plainly:

  • Only your side. Telegram never sends a bot its own messages, so the bot's replies never come through sync; they come through the export.
  • Only what is still pending. The Bot API keeps an update until the bot confirms it, and for 24 hours at most. A bot that is running confirms its updates as they arrive, so sync finds little or nothing; it is for what arrived while the bot was down, and for the edits and replies around it.
  • At most the first 100 pending, since reading further would need an offset, which confirms.
  • A bot on a webhook is not read: its updates go to the webhook, and getUpdates would be refused. It is one line naming the bot, the other bots are read, and sync exits 1; sync never touches the webhook.
  • A bot that long-polls while sync asks may see one 409 Conflict and retry, as the libraries do; a bot with nothing pending is never asked, so a quiet bot is never interrupted.

The complete conversation, both sides, is the export's. sync telegram writes the same lines by the same mapping (extra.view is bot, extra.message_id the bot's own id for the message, the counterpart with its username from getMe) and the same key, so a message the export already wrote is not written again, and the other way round. There is no watermark: what the API holds is small, every run reads it whole, and the record's dedupe is the mark. --since still leaves out what came before it.

docs.title: Why the key is not the message id
docs.text:
Telegram numbers the messages of a private chat per account: the message you send your bot has one id in your account (the export's) and another in the bot's (the API's). A key on (chat, message id) would dedupe each view against itself and never one against the other. So raw_id is what both sides see alike:

<bot id>/<unix seconds>/<me|bot>/<digest>        e.g. 900000001/1772360100/me/3f1c2a9b0d4e

the digest being the first twelve hex characters of the SHA-256 of the text (or caption, whitespace collapsed, NFC) and of whether the message carries media. The n-th message of one chat with the same four parts gets ~n after them (three photos sent as an album, in one second, with no caption). The view's own id stays under extra.message_id.

Two consequences, by design. An edited message is keyed by the text it has now, which is what both views give once the edit is made; when sync saw the message before the edit too, the version first sent is a line of its own, beside the edited one. And the ~n of a burst is counted within what one view saw: when sync sees only the second photo of an album whose first it never saw, the two views number it differently and the record holds that photo twice. Both are rare, both leave a line too many rather than one too few, and a duplicate can be retracted.

docs.title: Your bots through Beeper
docs.text:
A bot of yours that Beeper bridges (a Telegram bot in Beeper's Telegram account, say) reaches the record through the Beeper adapters too: logbook add beeper (the phone's cache, from an iPhone backup) and logbook sync beeper (Beeper Desktop's local API). Beeper does not say which of its senders are bots, and nothing in the code guesses: you name yours, by the sender id the line carries, and the record's settings keep the list (policy/agents.json).

logbook setup agents list                                                   # the senders named, and the name you gave each
logbook setup agents add @telegram_900000001:beeper.local --name Fyr        # one of your bots
logbook setup agents remove @telegram_900000001:beeper.local                # no longer

The sender id is extra.matrix_user on a line of the phone's cache and extra.sender_id on a line of sync beeper (logbook show and logbook search find the lines it wrote). The file is {"senders": [{"id": "<sender id>", "name": "<optional>"}]}, yours to edit by hand as well.

From the next add beeper or sync beeper on:

On The mark a line a named sender wrote extra.machine: true every line of a one-on-one chat with a named sender, yours and the bot's extra.counterpart: {"kind": "agent", "ref": {"kind": "handle", "value": <sender id>}, "name"?}, the name yours from the setting, else the one Beeper shows a group a named sender is in its own lines extra.machine: true; no counterpart, since the people in the group are people, and their lines stay as they are

The readers below then pass the bot over exactly as they pass a Telegram bot from the export. A line already in the record keeps what it was written with: naming a sender changes no line, and a message imported before is not imported again (the record's dedupe by source and raw_id), so name your bots before the first import of a store. logbook doctor says how many lines are marked machine, per source, and how many senders the file names:

pass  agents  lines marked machine: telegram 412, beeper-telegram 96, claude-code 31; 1 sender named in policy/agents.json

docs.title: Claude Code: the sessions
docs.text:
Claude Code keeps every session on the machine it ran on, under ~/.claude/projects/: one folder per project, named from its working directory (/Users/ines/code/solvind-log is -Users-ines-code-solvind-log), one <session id>.jsonl per session. logbook add claude-sessions <folder> reads the projects folder, one project's folder or one session's file, each sniffed, so a bare logbook add ~/.claude/projects finds them too.

Your turns are the text of the user entries. Never yours, and never kept as anyone's: a tool's result (the tool_result blocks, the entry's toolUseResult), which is the machine's output; an entry marked isMeta (a caveat Claude Code adds) or isCompactSummary (the model's own summary of the conversation, written in the user's role); a slash command and its output; the interrupt marker. The assistant's turns are the text blocks of the assistant entries; its thinking is never kept, and an API error is not a turn. A subagent's conversation (entries marked isSidechain, and a file named agent-*.jsonl), whose "user" is the main agent, is counted and skipped. An image you pasted is counted and never stored.

Field From kind, source, tier transcript, claude-code, 2 (RFC 0004's; --tier sets another for a run) at, end the session's first and last entry participants [{"name": "owner"}, {"name": "assistant", "machine": true}]: owner is a word every reader takes for you, as me content the turns as JSON, {"turns": [{"speaker", "text"}, …]}, stored once in the attachment store (SPEC §1.1); its sha256 is the session's digest title Claude Code's own title for the session (its summary entry), else the first line of your first turn raw_id claude-code:<session id> extra session and project (the working directory's last part) and cwd, git_branch, version (Claude Code's), models, tool_calls and tools (the calls by tool name: a count, never what they did or returned), images, words ({owner, machine}), counterpart ({kind: agent, ref: {provider_id, claude-code}, name: Claude Code}), and the counts every transcript has

A session that grew. A session goes on after an import, or is resumed. Run again, a session whose text differs from the line standing for it is written as a new line, raw_id suffixed :v2 (:v3 …), that supersedes the line before (grown since the last import); an unchanged session is the same line and nothing is written. The proposals promises read in the old line are read again in the new one under new ids, so a promise you closed against the old line shows as open again; close it once more. A session Claude Code copied into a new file when you resumed it is a second session here, as it is there.

docs.title: Claude: the export of the apps
docs.text:
Your conversations with Claude in its apps (the web, the desktop, the phone) live with your account, not on a machine. Ask for them: claude.ai → Settings → Privacy → Export data. A link to a zip arrives by email; the zip holds conversations.json (every conversation, its messages in it), projects.json (your projects, when you have any) and users.json (your account). logbook add claude-export <zip> reads the zip as it came, nothing unpacked to disk; the folder it unpacks to and its conversations.json are read too, and all three are sniffed, so a bare logbook add finds them. Another app's conversations.json (one without chat_messages) is not taken for it.

Your turns are the text blocks of the messages you sent (sender human), the assistant's the text blocks of its own; an export older than the blocks gives only text, read without the placeholder the export writes for a block it cannot show ("This block is not supported on your current device yet."). Never kept, as anyone's words: its thinking; a tool call's input (an artifact's content, a search query), counted by the tool's name; a tool's result; the thinking and the artifacts an export from before artifacts were tool calls writes inline in the text (<antThinking>, <antArtifact>: dropped, each artifact counted as an artifacts call); the text the apps extracted from a file you gave them; the conversation's own summary; a message from neither side, counted. A file you gave or uploaded is named and counted, never copied: its name, its type (the export's, else the name's suffix) and its size, never its text, preview or link; a name is cut at 255 characters. Of projects.json only a project's name is read (never its description, its instructions or its documents), and users.json is never opened.

When the export links each message to the one before it (parent_message_uuid) and names where the conversation stands (current_leaf_message_uuid), only that branch is read: a prompt you edited or an answer you asked for again leaves the other branch behind, counted (messages on a branch the conversation left). Without the links, or when they lead to a message the export does not hold, every message, in the export's order.

Field From kind, source, tier transcript, claude, 2, exactly as a Claude Code session (--tier sets another for a run) at, end the conversation's first and last message (its own created_at and updated_at when the messages have no time) participants [{"name": "owner"}, {"name": "assistant", "machine": true}], as a session's content the turns as JSON, {"turns": [{"speaker", "text"}, …]}, stored once in the attachment store (SPEC §1.1); its sha256 is the conversation's digest title the conversation's name, else the first line of your first turn raw_id claude:<conversation uuid> extra conversation (its uuid), project (the name, when the conversation names a project projects.json lists), created_at and updated_at (the conversation's), tool_calls and tools (the calls by tool name: a count, never what they did or returned), attachments (each file's name, type and size in bytes, as the export gives them), words ({owner, machine}), counterpart ({kind: agent, ref: {provider_id, claude}, name: Claude}), and the counts every transcript has

A conversation that is not an object with a uuid and a list of messages, or that has no time at all, is skipped and counted (conversations in a shape this version cannot read); one with no words in it is counted too. An export that does not parse, or a zip that is damaged, is one sentence, and nothing is written. conversations.json is read whole, so an export takes a few times its size in memory while it is read.

A conversation that grew (or changed: a prompt edited, an answer asked for again) is a new line, raw_id suffixed :v2 (:v3 …), that supersedes the line before, exactly as a session that grew; a conversation unchanged since the last import writes nothing, and nor does one whose text any of its lines already holds. Neither does an export older than one already imported, so a folder of exports can be added again and again: a conversation earlier than the line standing for it (by its updated_at, else by where it ends) is counted (older than the line in the record) and never written back over the newer one, its text never stored. A conversation you moved back to an earlier branch ends earlier but is later, and is a new version. Every run, and --dry-run before it, says how many conversations the export holds and how many are new to the record, grown, unchanged and older. A conversation you deleted in the apps is not in the next export, and its line stays in the record: retract it if you want it gone. A conversation you only renamed is unchanged (the text is what counts), so its line keeps the old title.

docs.title: What the readers do with them
docs.text:
• people, person, rollup people, drift and the company of a stay count no line of a conversation with an agent, whoever wrote it, and no participant marked machine, whatever its name: a bot you named after your sister is still not your sister.
  • people review never observes an agent and so never proposes one, not even by its name; a record that held agent lines before this version rebuilds its observed table once.
  • promises reads only your own words in a conversation with an agent: your messages to a bot and your turns in a session or a conversation in the apps. A message a bot wrote and a message you forwarded are counted under skipped (messages_by_an_agent, forwarded_messages); an agent's turn is dropped before your turns are read, and a line inside your own turn that its text gives the agent, by its label or by its own name (assistant: …, Claude: …, Claude Code: …, pasted back), is dropped too, with the lines after it in that turn up to the next speaker's label.
  • The dream gives the model your messages with an agent marked (agent on the counterpart, machine on what it wrote) and tells it that agents are not people (dream-day/3, rule 5); an agent's words do not decide the language of your day.
  • day, show and search list and find these lines like any other: an agent's message is a message of the day, and a session a transcript of it.

docs.title: GitHub
docs.text:
What happened on GitHub, one line per act: a commit, an issue or a pull request created, closed or merged, a review submitted, a comment left. logbook sync github reads them from GitHub's API, read-only; logbook add github-export reads an old project's clone, or the account export GitHub makes, and adds what the API cannot give back: each version of a README or a doc, so the ideas an old project wrote down have a first-said date. Both write the same line for the same act, so a commit (by its hash) and an issue (by its number) read both ways are one line. Every line is event/v1 (RFC 0009): tier 1 from a public repository, tier 2 from a private one (below).

export LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN=github_pat_...                  # a fine-grained token, read-only: a password
export LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS='ines-example/sailplan, ines-example/harbour-notes'   # or --all
logbook sync github --dry-run                               # count, write nothing
logbook sync github                                         # then four times a day with the schedule
logbook sync github --since 2026-01-01T00:00:00Z            # every repo from then, once
logbook add github-export ~/code/oldboat                    # an old project's clone: its commits and its docs
logbook add github-export ~/code/sailplan --public          # a clone of a public repository: tier 1
logbook add github-export ~/Downloads/github-export         # GitHub's account export, unpacked

docs.title: The token and the repos
docs.text:
On GitHub, Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Fine-grained tokens → Generate new token: the repositories it may read (all of yours, or the ones you choose) and, under Repository permissions, Contents, Issues, Pull requests and Metadata set to Read-only, nothing else. Keep it in LOGBOOK_GITHUB_TOKEN in your shell profile, never in a file of the record. The sync sends GET and nothing else, and a test holds it to that.

LOGBOOK_GITHUB_REPOS names the repos, owner/name, comma- or space-separated, or the links GitHub copies (https://<host>/<owner>/<name>.git, or the SSH form git@<host>:<owner>/<name>.git). --all reads every repo the token sees, less the forks, which are someone else's history (name a fork to read it). LOGBOOK_GITHUB_URL is another address for the API, a GitHub Enterprise Server's https://<host>/api/v3: https, or http to this machine only. A repo the token cannot read is said on one line, the others are read, the run exits 1 and the watermark stays.

docs.title: Who acted
docs.text:
Each line names who acted under extra.actor: login, id, type (User, Bot) and, for a commit, the author's name, and marks them owner or other. You are the handles in policy/owner.json:

{"names": ["Ines Nordmann"], "emails": ["ines.nordmann@example.org"], "phones": [], "handles": ["ines-example"]}

ines-example, @ines-example and github:ines-example are one login, case aside. With no handle listed, the sync takes the token's own user for you and says so; list yours before the first run that writes, since a line is never rewritten. A commit whose author GitHub links to no account is yours when its address is one of yours (owner.json's emails, owner_emails in logbook.json) or its author's name one of your names. The address is read for that, and to find the login in a GitHub noreply address, and is never written.

Everyone else is other, and a person's login is the line's organizer, {"kind": "handle", "value": "github:ola-example"} (a bot's never is): a handle is a name source as a phone number is, so logbook people review lists github:ola-example as an observed person, named by the name his commits give, and proposes him to the person of that name (People). Your own handles are never listed, however late you add them to owner.json.

docs.title: The text, and the tier
docs.text:
event/v1 has notes, "the description body" (RFC 0009), so the text is kept in full, verbatim: a commit's message, an issue's or a pull request's body, a review's and a comment's text. A README's or a doc's text is never kept: a version is its digest, its length and its word count, as a Notion page is.

The tier is where a line may travel (tier 1 crosses by default, ADR 0016), never who wrote it, so it follows where the words were written:

  • A public repository's lines are tier 1, whoever wrote the words: Ola's comment is tier 1 as yours is. SPEC §4 and RFC 0009 give event/v1 tier 1 ("tier SHOULD be 1"), and the profile says it outright, "an entry whose notes carry someone else's words is still tier 1 by default". Anyone can read those words on GitHub already.
  • A private repository's lines are tier 2, every one of them: a commit's message, an issue's text, a review, other people's comments, a doc's version, and a pull request's created, closed and merged lines (and the agent mark they carry). Its text was written for the people the repository is shared with, so it does not go wherever tier 1 crosses; it crosses at tier 2, when you ask for it, and in a record that names recipients it is sealed at rest (RFC 0029). The line says why: extra.tier_reason is private repository. SPEC §4 lets a producer write a higher tier than a SHOULD default "for a reason it states", and event/v1's tier is a SHOULD, not a MUST.

Which repositories are public. sync github takes GitHub's word at each run: the repository as the API answers it (GET /repos/{repo}, or the --all list) carries private and visibility, and a repository is public only when what it carries says so (private false, visibility public) and nothing in it says otherwise. An internal repository (GitHub Enterprise) is private, and so is one whose answer carries no mark (tier_reason repository visibility not known; the run says so). A repository you make public or private is read at its new tier from the next run on; the lines already written stay as they are, since a line is never rewritten. add github-export reads no network: GitHub's account export marks each repository it lists, and that mark decides. A clone says nothing of its visibility, and neither does an export's repository without a mark or an issue of a repository the export does not list, so their lines are tier 2 (repository visibility not known), and the run says so, unless you pass --public for that run. --public never makes a repository the export marks private tier 1, and it decides only the lines not yet in the record: pass it the first time (--dry-run says what the run would do), since adding the same clone again writes nothing.

The same act read twice. A line is never rewritten and never written twice: the record knows an act by its raw_id whatever its tier, so the first road to write a commit or an issue decides its tier. Lines written before private repositories were tier 2 stay at tier 1, and a sync that reads one of them again writes nothing; a clone added before the sync (tier 2) keeps its commits at tier 2 when the API later says the repository is public, and the other way round. A commit in two repositories, a public one and a private one, is one line (commit/<sha>), at the tier of the repository read first.

In a record that seals (RFC 0029, recipients in logbook.json), a tier 2 line is sealed at rest and its raw_id blinded, so only the identity can see that the record holds an act sealed. Since the same act may come at tier 1 or 2, sync github and add github-export need the identity to write anything there, a tier 1 line too: without it they refuse on one sentence, before asking GitHub anything, rather than write a sealed act a second time, plain. --dry-run writes nothing and needs none.

docs.title: What a line holds
docs.text: On the line What it holds at when the act happened: a commit's author date, an issue's creation, its close, a merge, a review's submission, a comment's creation raw_id commit/<sha> (one commit, one line, whichever repo); <repo>/issues/<n>/created, <repo>/pull/<n>/created, <repo>/pull/<n>/merged, <repo>/issues/<n>/closed@<when> (closed, reopened and closed again is a second line), <repo>/pull/<n>/reviews/<id>, <repo>/issues/comments/<id>, <repo>/pulls/comments/<id> (on a line of the diff), <repo>/file/<path>@<blob> (a doc's version); <repo> in lower case title a commit's first line; an issue's or a pull request's title, also on its reviews and comments; a doc's path notes the message, the body, the review or the comment, in full; never a doc's text calendar {"id": "github", "name": "GitHub"} for every repo, so two repos' acts are never folded into one modified_at the source's own clock: a commit's committer date, an item's last update; the watermark organizer the person who acted, as a handle ref; absent for a bot or an unlinked author extra.action committed, created, closed, merged, reviewed, commented, revised (a doc's version) extra.repo owner/name as GitHub spells it extra.commit, extra.issue, extra.pull, extra.review, extra.comment what the act was done to, by reference: {sha, url}, {number, url}, {id, state, url}, {id, url}; never a copy extra.branch, extra.files a commit's branch (the default one) and how many files it changed extra.files, extra.commits, extra.base, extra.head a merge: what it changed, from which branch into which extra.labels, extra.path an issue's labels; the file an inline comment is on extra.file, extra.content a doc's version: {path, blob}, and {sha256, bytes, media_type, words, words_delta} extra.actor who acted: login, id, type, name, role extra.agent true when the line's own text carries an agent session's marker (below) extra.tier_reason on a tier 2 line, why: private repository, or repository visibility not known

docs.title: What an agent did
docs.text: You build with coding agents whose pull requests are the honest log of what each did. A line is agent: true when its own text carries one of these markers: Generated with Claude Code (or Generated by, the link's brackets aside), a session link claude.ai/code/session_…, or a commit trailer Claude-Session: or Co-Authored-By: Claude. A pull request's body flags every line of it (created, merged or closed); a commit's message, a review's or a comment's text flags its own line. The markers are AGENT_MARKERS in logbook/contrib/adapters/github.py, so a page that lists what agents did reads extra.agent and never guesses.

docs.title: Which lines, and the watermark
docs.text:
A run reads, per repo: the commits on its default branch, the issues and pull requests (one list), the comments on them and on their diffs, each pull request's reviews; every list paged by GitHub's Link header, a next page at another address never followed (the token would go with it). It writes a line for each act at or after where the repo starts: an item's created when it was created then, its closed or merged when that happened then, a comment or a review when it was left then. How many files a commit changed, who closed an issue and who merged a pull request are asked once each, and only for a line the record does not hold yet. A comment edited after its line was written is not written again: the record keeps what was said when the sync first read it.

The watermark is per repo (marks in state/github.json): the newest modified_at seen there, read back a week — the commits list filters by the committer's date, and a commit pushed days after it was made would otherwise be missed. A repo with no mark yet is read from its beginning, so a repo you add to the list later is read whole; --since reads every repo from an exact time; --dry-run counts and writes nothing, and stops on one line at a rate limit instead of waiting it out. The source's first scheduled run reads every repo from 14 days back, not from its beginning (the schedule); --since reads the rest. A run with --since, the scheduled first run among them, marks a repo it found nothing in at that time, so the next run reads it on from there and never from its beginning. A commit pushed more than a week after it was made comes in with --since or the export.

Rate limits. At most ten requests a second. GitHub's secondary limit is waited out as its Retry-After says (a minute when it says nothing), its hourly limit until its reset, a 429 or a server error after 1, 2, 4… seconds; a wait over five minutes, or a limit that does not lift, stops the run on one line, exit 1, the watermark where it was, and the next run carries on, the record refusing what it already holds. logbook doctor lists sync:github once the variables are set, by name only, and asks GitHub nothing; sync --all and the schedule run it with no more configuration.

docs.title: An old project: add github-export
docs.text:
logbook add github-export DIR reads, by name only (a folder is never guessed to be a project):

  • a clone — a working copy (DIR/.git) or a bare repository — of GitHub or anywhere else: its history on the branch HEAD names, a line per commit with its message in full and the files it changed, and a line per version of a README or a doc: a file at the top whose name starts with readme or ends in .md, .markdown, .mdx, .rst, .adoc, .asciidoc, .org or .textile, or one under docs/ or doc/ with one of those or .txt. A version is a path's content: its git blob, digest, length, words and the words since the path's previous version. The same bytes back at the same path later are no new version, so the first-said date stays the first. The repo is named by the clone's origin when that is a hosting link, else by its folder.
  • GitHub's account export (Settings → Account → Export account data, the migration archive, unpacked): each repository's bare clone as above, under the name the export gives, and its issues, pull requests (who closed and who merged from its events), reviews and comments as the lines sync github writes for the same acts, read leniently: a row without what a line needs is skipped and counted. Each repository's mark in the export (private, visibility) sets the tier of all its lines, as above.

--since keeps the acts at or after it (a doc's earlier versions are still read, so an old version is never new); --dry-run counts; --public says the clone, and any repository the export does not mark, is public, so its lines are tier 1 (a clone's lines are tier 2 without it). Git runs read-only (rev-parse, symbolic-ref, config, log, cat-file), never a shell and never fetching: no lazy fetch of a partial clone, no prompt, no fsmonitor. Adding the same clone again writes nothing, and add never says a clone can be deleted: it is your working copy. A folder that is none of these is one sentence, exit 2.

docs.title: Health: Apple Health, Withings, MyFitnessPal, Google Fit
docs.text:
Four adapters write health-sample/v1 (RFC 0014): one measurement the body made and a device recorded — a weight, a heart-rate reading, a quarter hour of steps, a stage of one night's sleep, a logged meal — with its number, its unit, the span it covers and the device, never what it means. Every line is tier 3 (logbook add --tier lowers it). Interpretation is a reader's job: logbook stats --health, rollup health and the Day sum the lines up.

logbook import-backup ~/backup --only health,withings,myfitnesspal   # the apps' own stores, from an iPhone backup
logbook add withings ~/Downloads/data_KN_1718000000             # the Withings data export, the folder as unzipped
logbook add withings ~/Downloads/data_KN_1718000000/weight.csv  # or one of its files
logbook add myfitnesspal ~/Downloads/Nutrition-Summary-2026-06-08-to-2026-06-14.csv
logbook add withings ~/Downloads/data_KN_1718000000 --dry-run   # what would be added, what the record has; nothing written
Source What it reads What it writes apple-health healthdb_secure.sqlite from an encrypted iPhone backup steps, distance, energy and flights in quarter-hour buckets per device; heart rate capped at one reading a minute; resting heart rate, HRV, weight; sleep stages and workouts as spans withings the app's per-profile stores from a backup, or the account's data export (below) weight and body composition, one line per quantity; heart rate; from the export also sleep, steps, distance, calories and workouts myfitnesspal the app's maindb.sqlite from a backup, or the account's CSV export (below) logged foods or meals as energy_intake in kcal; from the store also weights and exercise google-takeout-fit the Fit/ folder of a Google Takeout (page) steps and distance in quarter-hour buckets per device, or per day where only the daily sheet has them; heart rate capped at one reading a minute; weight and body fat; sleep stages and workouts as spans; source is google-takeout

The stores are what import-backup copies out of a phone backup; the adapters' module docstrings have the tables. Google Fit comes only as a Takeout folder and has its own page; a phone running Fit and a watch feeding Apple Health count the same quarter hour twice, and the record keeps both lines, each under its source and device (rule 5), for a reader to choose between. This page is about the exports, which hold the whole history where a phone keeps weeks, and about what happens when a later export changes a number.

docs.title: The Withings data export
docs.text:
Settings → Download my data on the Withings site sends a zip; unzip it and add the folder. logbook add <folder> recognises it without the adapter's name. The files read, by name — any other file of the export is left alone — and the columns found by header, so a column the reader does not need may be missing or renamed; a file without one it needs is counted (CSV files without the columns this reader needs), never a traceback:

File Lines weight.csv one standing per row: weight, fat_mass, bone_mass, muscle_mass, body_water (the export's Hydration), each its own line at the same instant (rule 9), and body_fat_pct or bmi when the export carries them; a mass in pounds is converted to kg with the entered value under extra.original; a comment under extra.comment bp.csv the cuff's pulse as heart_rate (raw_id heart_rate:bp:<at>) with the pressures beside it, extra.systolic_mmhg and extra.diastolic_mmhg: blood pressure is no type of the profile (rule 8), and extra is what else the source reports; a row without a pulse is counted sleep.csv one in_bed span per night, from to to, the totals the export computed (light, deep, REM, awake seconds; the night's average, lowest and highest heart rate) under extra; a reader never sums in_bed (rule 4) raw_<device>_sleep-state.csv the stages: one sleep span per run of equal states — 0 awake, 1 (light) core, 2 deep, 3 rem — with the device (tracker, bed); a state this version does not know is counted raw_<device>_hr.csv heart_rate in bpm, the first reading of each minute per device (rule 3); the rest counted raw_<device>_steps.csv, …_distance.csv, …_calories-earned.csv steps, distance (m), active_energy (kcal), summed into quarter hours aligned to the UTC hour, one bucket per device (rule 2), extra.samples how many samples went in activities.csv one workout span per activity, value its duration in seconds, the type under extra.activity, the steps, calories and distance the row's Data carries under extra, tz the row's zone height.csv, raw_*_elevation.csv counted, of a type this version does not know aggregates_*.csv the export's daily totals, derived data: counted, daily totals

The raw files hold one row per run of samples: start with its offset, then duration and value as lists, one sample per pair, each starting where the one before ended; the reader walks them out. A naive clock (weight.csv, bp.csv: 2026-06-08 07:12:33) is the account's local time and is read in the record's zone; a stamp with an offset is taken as it says. tz is the record's zone, since an offset names no zone. device is the export's own word for it (tracker, bed) on the raw files' lines, and absent on the scale's and the cuff's, which the export does not name.

raw_id is the instant: weight:2026-06-08T05:12:33Z, heart_rate:tracker:…, steps:<bucket start>:tracker, sleep:night:<from>. A later export of the same account gives the same keys, so adding it again appends nothing — unless a sample changed (below).

docs.title: The MyFitnessPal export
docs.text:
Settings → Export data on the MyFitnessPal site mails a zip with Nutrition-Summary-<from>-to-<to>.csv (one row per meal per day: date, meal, calories, then the macros and a note). logbook add myfitnesspal <file>, or logbook add <file>, writes one energy_intake line per row (rule 10):

  • value the calories as the export summed them, unit kcal; source_name MyFitnessPal.
  • A span over that local day in the record's zone — at midnight, end the next midnight — with extra.all_day true: the export keeps the day and never the clock, and nothing is invented about when it was eaten.
  • extra.meal the meal; every other numeric cell under extra keyed by its header slugged — fat_g, carbohydrates_g, protein_g, sodium_mg, and saturated_fat, fiber, sugar, cholesterol, potassium, vitamin_a … unitless as the export leaves them; water_ml when the export carries water; the note under extra.note. Nothing about nutrition beyond kilocalories is a type of the profile, so the macros and the water ride on the meal's line.
  • raw_id energy_intake:<date>:<meal> (energy_intake:2026-06-08:breakfast), the same in every later export.

Date, Meal and Calories are the columns it needs; a file without them is counted. A row with no number in Calories is counted (without a value), one whose date will not parse too (with an unusable date). The exercise and measurement summaries the same zip may hold are not read yet.

docs.title: When a later export corrects a sample
docs.text:
An export is a snapshot. A weight re-measured, a meal re-logged, a night the app re-scored comes out of the next export under the same date, so the same raw_id — and appending it would be deduped against the line already there, keeping the old number. Instead logbook add hands the adapter the record's standing line for each key (one batched lookup through the index per round, never one per line), and a draft whose sample differs from what stands — value, end, stage, device, unit or extra — is written as a correction: raw_id suffixed :v2 (:v3 … when corrected before) and supersedes the id of the line it replaces. The old line stays, as every line does; a reader that follows supersedes (health.standing: stats --health, rollup health, the Day) sees the correction only, the latest when there are several. add says 1 corrected beside what it added. A draft equal to what stands appends nothing; adding the first export again after a correction writes it as the next version, since the record's latest number is not the one it carries.

This is the one place an adapter writes supersedes (RFC 0014's payload table); logbook repair health-units is the other writer, with the same suffix rule.

docs.title: --dry-run
docs.text: logbook add <adapter> <path> --dry-run runs the adapter and prints what would be added, how many of its lines the record already has (the dedupe append_many would do, asked of the index in one batch) and what was skipped, and writes nothing — not a line, not a correction. It goes with a file or folder, never a sentence.

docs.title: Listening: Spotify, Apple Music and Apple Podcasts
docs.text:
Three adapters write listen/v1 lines (RFC 0019) from the services' own exports and stores, beside the shazam adapter that already does: one line per listen, media track or episode, the title, the performer, the album or the show as the service spells them and never resolved, how much played, and under extra the skip flag and the device when the export carries them. Tier 2, as the profile says. One reader sums them up: logbook rollup listen.

logbook add spotify ~/Downloads/"Spotify Extended Streaming History"           # the folder: every history file in it
logbook add spotify ~/Downloads/"Spotify Extended Streaming History"/Streaming_History_Audio_2025_3.json
logbook add apple-music ~/Downloads/"Apple Music Activity"/"Apple Music Play Activity.csv"
logbook add apple-music ~/Downloads/"Apple Music Activity"/"Apple Music Library Tracks.csv"
logbook add spotify ~/Downloads/"Spotify Extended Streaming History" --dry-run  # what would be added; nothing written
logbook import-backup ~/Library/Application\ Support/MobileSync/Backup/<udid> --only podcasts  # the phone's Podcasts library
logbook sync apple-podcasts                                                    # this Mac's own Podcasts library, nightly
logbook rollup listen --year 2026                                              # listens, hours, skips, top artists, podcasts, by month

Both are file adapters in the sense of the overview: pure, no network, never a write to the export, every line keyed by a raw_id so that a second add of the same export appends nothing. Both are sniffed, so a bare logbook add <path> finds them; logbook add spotify <path> and logbook add apple-music <path> (or add music) name them outright.

docs.title: Spotify: the extended streaming history
docs.text:
Spotify's account page (Privacy settings → Download your data → Extended streaming history) mails a zip a few days later. Inside is one folder, Spotify Extended Streaming History/, holding Streaming_History_Audio_<years>_<n>.json and Streaming_History_Video_<years>.json: one JSON array each, one object per stream, with ts (when the stream stopped, UTC), ms_played, the track's name, album artist and album, its spotify:track: URI, or an episode's name, show and spotify:episode: URI, or an audiobook chapter, and the flags skipped, shuffle, offline, reason_start, reason_end, the platform and the connecting country and IP address. The adapter reads the folder (every history file in it) or one file, streamed through ijson (the stream extra: pip install "openlogbook[stream]") so a decade of history never sits in memory at once. The shorter Account data export (StreamingHistory0.json, end time to the minute, no URI) is not this format and is not read.

Field From at, end ts less ms_played (when playback started); ts (when it stopped) raw_id spotify:<URI without its spotify: prefix>:<ts as spelled> — spotify:track:1a2b…:2026-03-04T20:19:03Z media track for a track, episode for a podcast episode title, artist, album the track's name, album artist and album, as Spotify spells them title, show an episode's name and its show url the open.spotify.com page of the URI played_s ms_played in seconds extra ms_played, skipped, device (Spotify's platform), reason_start, reason_end, shuffle, offline, country (conn_country)

A stream of 0 ms — a track touched and skipped at once — is a listen with played_s 0 and its skip flag, since the export says the owner put it on; rollup listen counts it as a listen and adds no hours for it. An audiobook chapter is skipped and counted (RFC 0019 has tracks and episodes, not books). A row that names nothing — a local file, an item since removed — is skipped and counted. An older export (no platform, no skipped, a username column) reads with what it has: no device, no skipped under extra. The IP address and the username are never kept.

docs.title: Apple Music: the three CSVs of Apple's data export
docs.text:
privacy.apple.com → Request a copy of your data → Apple Media Services information delivers Apple_Media_Services.zip, and in it Apple Music Activity/. Three of its files describe listening, three ways; the adapter reads whichever one it is given, by its header, and finds the columns by name, so a column it does not need may be missing or new.

Apple Music Play Activity.csv is the record of listening: one row per player event. The adapter writes one line per PLAY_END row (a PLAY_START, a lyric view and the rest are counted, not lines): at the event's start and end its end, title the Song Name (or the older export's Content Name), artist, duration_s from the media duration and played_s from the play duration, and under extra ms_played, skipped (true for TRACK_SKIPPED_FORWARDS and the like, false for NATURAL_END_OF_TRACK, absent for a pause or a scrub), device (the Device Identifier Apple assigns), end_reason as Apple spells it, and offline. The file carries no track id, so raw_id is apple-music:<sha256 of the artist and title, 16 hex>:<start as spelled> — the rule browse/v1 and watch/v1 use for a source with no id of its own. The Apple ID and the client's IP address are never kept.

Apple Music Library Tracks.csv is one row per track in the library with its Last Played Date, Play Count and Skip Count. As with apple-podcasts, the store keeps one row per track and moves its time, so the adapter writes one line per last-played time it sees: raw_id apple-music:<Apple Music Track Identifier, else Track Identifier>@<Last Played Date as spelled>, at that time, end null, title, artist, album, duration_s, extra.play_count and extra.skip_count. A track never played is counted (RFC 0019 rule 5). Added after every export, this turns the library into a sparse listening history; it is not a record of every play.

Apple Music - Play History Daily Tracks.csv is coarse: one row per track per day, with the Hours of the day it played in (20, 21), the milliseconds played that day, play and skip counts, and Track Description as Artist - Title. The adapter writes one line per row at the first hour listed, read in the record's zone (rule 4: the file gives no zone), played_s the day's total, extra.hours, extra.play_count, extra.skip_count and extra.end_reason; raw_id apple-music:<Track Identifier>:<Date Played> <Hours as spelled>. A row with no hour is at the day's local midnight.

The three files describe the same listening with three different keys, so they do not dedupe against one another: adding all three triples the count. Add the play activity, which is the complete record; add the library only from an export that has no play activity; add the daily history only when neither is there. A re-add of the same file appends nothing.

docs.title: Apple Podcasts: the library, from the phone's backup or the Mac
docs.text:
Apple Podcasts keeps its library in one Core Data store, MTLibrary.sqlite: on the Mac under ~/Library/Group Containers/243LU875E5.groups.com.apple.podcasts/Documents/, on the phone under the app group group.com.apple.podcasts at Documents/MTLibrary.sqlite, which an iPhone backup carries. import-backup --only podcasts copies it out of the backup into inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/apple-podcasts/ with its -wal/-shm and runs the adapter on the copy; logbook sync apple-podcasts reads the Mac's own store, nightly (LOGBOOK_PODCASTS_DB names another); logbook add apple-podcasts <copy> reads any copy. One mapping for all three, so the phone and the Mac dedupe each other (ADR 0017).

The store has one row per episode and overwrites its last-played time when the episode is played again, so the adapter writes one line per last-played time it sees (RFC 0019 rule 1): raw_id apple-podcasts:<episode uuid>@<last played>. Added after every backup or sync, that turns one row per episode into a sparse listening history; it is not a record of every play.

Field From at ZLASTDATEPLAYED, the last-played time; end null title, show, publisher the episode's title; the show's title and author from ZMTPODCAST, else the episode's own author url the episode's web page, else its enclosure duration_s, played_s ZDURATION; ZPLAYHEAD when above zero completed the playhead within 30 s of the duration, or rewound to zero with a play counted (the app rewinds an episode played to the end); absent when the store has no playhead column, false when it cannot show either — never a guess published ZPUBDATE extra play_count; transcript_url, the transcript the episode's feed publishes (<podcast:transcript>), when the store keeps its URL and it is an http(s) URL

The columns are discovered with PRAGMA table_info; only the title, the uuid and the last-played time are required, every other column is read when present and left out when not, and a store without the shows' table still reads, without show. An episode never played, or without a title, is skipped and counted (rule 5). The store is opened read-only and immutable, never written.

Transcripts are recorded, never fetched. extra.transcript_url is the URL and nothing more: the adapter, like every reader, never touches the network. Apple's own transcript identifiers, which are not public URLs, are never recorded. Fetching the transcripts the record points at is sync heard (RFC 0046, What you heard): each URL read once, the text kept as it came beside one heard/v1 line that names the listen, never a transcript/v1 line (a podcast is someone else's published words, not a conversation the owner had).

docs.title: The rollup: logbook rollup listen
docs.text:
logbook rollup listen                     # the whole record, per year
logbook rollup listen --year 2026
logbook rollup listen --since 2026-01-01 --until 2026-03-31 --json

Per calendar year of the window: the listens, the hours played (played_s summed; a line with no playhead, a Shazam tag, is a listen with no hours and is counted under untimed), the skipped lines (extra.skipped true), the lines per service, the podcast episodes with their hours, the top artists — the tracks' performers as the services spell them, ranked by hours played, then listens; ten — the podcasts section, the episodes' hours by show (the shows as the services spell them, by hours then episodes) and by month, printed only for a year with an episode — and by month, every month the window touches with its hours, listens and skips, a month with no listen printed as an em dash and never a zero. The window is --year, or --since/--until, clipped to the days the record's listen lines cover. The lines standing are read: a correction that supersedes a line wins, the latest when a line was corrected more than once, and a retracted line is out. Read through the index, nothing written. Under --json every number carries the ids of the lines it came from. Every listen/v1 line counts, whichever adapter wrote it: spotify, apple-music, shazam, apple-podcasts, the demo's.

listen 2026-01-01 – 2026-03-20
  2026  10 listens · 2.3 h · 2 skipped · 1 without a playhead · 3 episodes · spotify 8, apple-podcasts 1, shazam 1
        top artists
          Ola Nordmann                 played 0.3 h · 3 listens
          Kari Nordmann                played 0.2 h · 4 listens
        podcasts  3 episodes · 1.8 h
          by show
            Havnepodden                  1.5 h · 2 episodes
            Knots Weekly                 0.2 h · 1 episode
          by month
            2026-01  0.2 h · 1 episode
            2026-02  —
            2026-03  1.5 h · 2 episodes
        by month
          2026-01  0.3 h · 2 listens
          2026-02  0.3 h · 1 listen
          2026-03  1.6 h · 7 listens · 2 skipped

The rollup lives in logbook/core/listen_rollup.py, in rollup.py's manner but beside it, so the listening rollup grows without touching the others.
