One event/v1 line per row, tier 3: a sign-in from a city on a date says where your devices were, which is a location fact as sensitive as a transaction. The title is Gmail: Sign in, the calendar Google Account access, the location the city, region and country as text, never a coordinate; the product, the activity, the channel, the device and the place go under extra. The IP addresses, the user agent and the account id are never written: the address and the browser are hashed into the line's id only, so two accesses in one second from two addresses stay two lines. The folder's other file, Devices - A list of devices (…) used to access.csv, is not read. Every open of Gmail is a row, so the source is off until you say otherwise.

docs.title: My Activity → browse/v1, watch/v1 (off by default)
docs.text: My Activity/<Product>/MyActivity.json, when you asked Takeout for JSON (the .html is not read). What fits a profile is a line, tier 2: a search and a visited result are browse/v1 visits with the query or page as the title and google-<product> as the browser; an app opened under Android is a visit to its Play Store page, browser android; a YouTube entry goes through the YouTube adapter's own mapping (ADR 0017), so a watch here and the same watch in YouTube and YouTube Music/history/ are one line. A Chrome entry is skipped and counted: Chrome/History.json has the same visit with Chrome's own clock, and takeout-chrome reads that. Ads, entries with no url or no time, and other activities (Viewed area …, Said …) are skipped and counted. Google's guess at where you were when you searched is kept as text under extra.location_hint, never as a location line.

docs.title: What is not read
docs.text: Gmail is its own adapter (mail, logbook add mail ~/Takeout/Mail). Drive, Play, Assistant, News, Shopping, Voice and the rest of the archive are not read yet; drop a folder in inbox/ and it stays there until an adapter exists. Of the Home App, the sound events and the alarm clips are left alone on purpose; of Maps, a saved place is never a line, only a candidate for a name; of Fit, the TCX files under Activities/ (a workout's route) are not read. A whole Takeout/ folder handed to add is walked into every product folder, four levels down; what no adapter reads is counted in the last line (--verbose names each file). The package's own walk, which would dispatch by the Takeout layout without sniffing, and a zip reader are on the roadmap.

docs.title: The family's videos
docs.text:
The family's home videos live in one Google Drive folder: tapes and DVDs digitised years ago, each an MP4 of two to four gigabytes and an hour or more long, holding many separate recordings from different years and places, one after another. Their titles are numbers (Home 01, 14), and Drive's dates say when they were digitised or uploaded, never when anything on them was filmed. Four steps bring them into the record, and only the owner's own answer ever says where or when a recording was made:

logbook sync drive --videos                 # one video/v1 line per file, from Drive's metadata; nothing downloaded
logbook videos fetch --models               # once: the speech and vision models videos infer uses
logbook videos fetch                        # the next files into a bounded cache (8 GB), one at a time, md5 verified
logbook videos infer                        # on this machine, no network: the scenes, a draft per scene
logbook review video                        # the proposals, one scene at a time; nothing written unless told
logbook review video --accept 1,2 --reject 3 --ask 4
logbook review video --place 5 "Vollen Brygge" --date 5 "summer 1994"
logbook doctor                              # the videos line: files, fetched, inferred, proposed, confirmed, the cache

Every line this writes is tier 2: a family's video holds other people's faces and voices, and its title may name them. The line formats are RFC 0040.

docs.title: The folder: a setting, never in the repository
docs.text:
LOGBOOK_DRIVE_VIDEOS_FOLDER is the folder's Drive id. Open the folder in Drive in a browser: its address is https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/<id>, sometimes followed by ?usp=...; the id is the part after /folders/ and before any ?, letters, digits, - and _. Put it in the env file on the record's home machine, ~/.config/logbook/sync.env, beside the one Google key's two variables (the tour's Google, on one key):

printf 'LOGBOOK_DRIVE_VIDEOS_FOLDER=%s\n' '<the folder id>' >> ~/.config/logbook/sync.env
set -a; . ~/.config/logbook/sync.env; set +a   # by hand: the variables into this shell

The id is a setting of that machine and never belongs in the record or in a repository. sync --all and the schedule do not list the folder: sync drive --videos is run by hand, when the folder changed.

The listing uses the metadata scope sync drive's folder paths already need, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.metadata.readonly. videos fetch reads a file's bytes and needs one more, https://www.googleapis.com/auth/drive.readonly: add it to the key's client id in the Workspace admin console, Security → Access and data control → API controls → Domain-wide delegation. Without it, videos fetch says so in one sentence and fetches nothing. Older Drive files carry a resource key; your own account needs none to read your own files, so nothing fails on one: the line records it and videos fetch sends it.

docs.title: sync drive --videos: one line per file, from the metadata
docs.text:
The folder and every subfolder below it are listed, a page at a time, asking only for folders and video files (mimeType contains 'video/'), never what is in the trash: the photos and scanned lists beside the videos are never listed, and a subfolder of photos is walked and gives nothing. One video/v1 line per video file, source drive-videos, tier 2:

Field What it holds raw_id the Drive id: a file is written once however often the folder is listed library google-drive title, description the file's name; Drive's description, when it has one file id, name, path (the folders from the listed one down), mime_type, url (opens it in Drive), resource_key when Drive keeps one bytes, duration_s, width, height Drive's size and its video metadata, when Drive has processed the file digest {md5}: the checksum Drive reports, which videos fetch verifies the bytes against extra.drive_created, extra.drive_modified Drive's own times: the upload, recorded as what they are

The line's at is when the folder was listed: when the record learned of the file. Drive's times are never the line's time and never a filming time; when a scene was filmed is only ever the owner's attribution (below). No byte of a video is downloaded. Every run lists the whole folder (it is small, and only folders and videos are asked for), so a file moved in later is found, and the record's dedupe on the Drive id writes nothing twice. A quota answer from Drive (its daily limit, or a rate limit that outlasts the retries) stops the walk: what was listed before it is written, one line says what happened, the watermark stays where it was, and the run exits 1; run it again later.

docs.title: What is downloaded, and when
docs.text:
Only videos fetch downloads, and only what videos infer is about to read. It takes the video lines nobody has inferred yet and that are not in the cache, in the folder's order, and downloads them one at a time into state/videos/ in the record folder: bookkeeping, never the record, and left out of every backup. Nothing downloads the folder, and no video is ever copied into the record.

  • The cap. The cache holds 8 GB unless you give another with --cache-gb N, which is kept in state/videos.json for the next run and for doctor; 8 GB holds the largest file of a folder of 2–4 GB tapes twice over. A file bigger than the cap is refused and said so, with the --cache-gb that would hold it; the run stops when the next file would take the cache past its cap, and videos infer makes room as it goes.
  • Verified. Each file is hashed as it is written and compared with the md5 Drive reported when the line was written; a file that does not match is deleted, never kept, and said so.
  • Resumable. A download that drops, whether the connection fails or the answer just ends short, is resumed from the byte it reached (Range), three times in a run; past that the part is kept, and the next videos fetch hashes it and carries on. A file Drive no longer has is said and skipped; a full disk stops the run.
  • Once inferred, not again. A file with scene drafts is not fetched again; --again fetches the inferred files too, for videos infer under other models or settings, or after a release reads the picture another way (the key carries how: a file cut by an earlier reading is inferred again).
  • --limit N fetches at most N files; --models instead fetches the speech and vision models videos infer uses, once (the only other network use of the videos).

docs.title: What a scene is, and how it is found
docs.text:
A scene is one continuous recording. A tape holds many, so where and when are proposed per scene, never per file. videos infer asks ffmpeg on this machine (it must be on the PATH; it is told to open nothing but files) for two signals: the picture's scene score of each frame, from 0 (the same picture) to 1 (another picture entirely), and the soundtrack's loudness in windows of a quarter of a second. Every frame is scored against the one before at the file's first frame size and pixel format, so a join between clips stitched without re-encoding, where the size, the pixel format or the colour tags change, is scored like any other (ffmpeg would otherwise start its filters again there and score that frame against nothing). A scene begins at:

  • a cut: a frame scoring 0.30 or more;
  • a weak cut with a break in the soundtrack: a frame scoring 0.10 or more when, within half a second of it, the loudness of the second after differs from the second before by 6 dB or more, or the sound falls silent (-55 dB or less). Two recordings in the same room look alike; their sound seldom does;
  • a gap in the soundtrack: a second or more of silence, the blank between two recordings on a tape, at its middle, whatever the picture does.

A camera that pans, a child running past the lens, someone who stops talking: none of these is a boundary on its own. Breaks within 3 seconds of the first of a run are one (the strongest kept), so a glitch of a few frames between two recordings is one boundary, and no run of weak breaks swallows a strong one beyond it; none is kept within 3 seconds of the file's start or end; every scene is therefore 3 seconds or longer. The rules lean one way on purpose: a sudden change of light inside a recording (a camera's flash, a lamp) can split it in two, which costs one more draft to answer, while a missed join would mix two recordings in one proposal. A fade or a dissolve changes the picture too slowly to score a cut, and is found only when the soundtrack breaks with it. The numbers are hypotheses, as policy/stays.json's are, and they are part of what a file is inferred under: other settings infer it again.

Of each scene, videos infer hears the sound (the transcribe extra, through its own hear, the scene's sound cut out at 16 kHz) and looks at three frames, at a fifth, a half and four fifths of it (one, at its middle, for a scene under six seconds), each shown to the describe extra's vision model with a prompt of its own: what is visible, the setting, the season, every text on signs, boats and banners as written, and the date or time a camcorder burned into the picture; never a person's name, never a guess at the place. Each frame is deleted as soon as it is read: the descriptions are kept in the scene's draft, the pixels nowhere.

docs.title: What videos infer writes
docs.text:
For each cached file not yet inferred under these models, prompt and scene settings, oldest in the folder first, --limit N at most:

  • one transcript/v1 line for the file, source video-transcription, tier 2: the speech of every scene as WebVTT, each cue with its times in the file, so a scene's speech is a time range of it. Its at is the video line's and its end null: when it was said is not known. (Every transcript is presence evidence to the stays reader, SPEC §3.2.3 rule 5, so this one sits at the moment the record learned of the file, as an instant, and promotes at most the stop the owner was at then. It is no call: transcript synthesize --day and the 06:00 close leave it out, and transcript synthesize named by its id or #seq refuses it in one sentence, exit 2, so its words go to no model endpoint; the MCP server's line gives it with text null, whatever the ceiling.)
  • one draft/v1 per scene (RFC 0036), unit event, its subject the scene as a media fragment, <video line id>#t=<start>,<end>, source model:video-rules/1, tier 2. Its sentences say what the scene shows and says that places or dates it, each citing the video line (the frames) or the transcript line (the speech), with the frames and time ranges under extra.segments; the proposal (extra.proposal: a place, a date or date range, a confidence word) beside them; the frame descriptions under extra.frames; the models, the prompt and the settings it was made under. A file inferred again (videos fetch --again, other models or settings) writes a new draft per scene, which supersedes the earlier draft of a scene cut the same way (RFC 0036 rule 2).

The proposals are made by rules, not by a model behind an endpoint, so the draft can say nothing its evidence does not:

  • a place only from your own registries: a name of places.json, or an asset's name or registration of assets.json (a boat's name on her hull), read whole, case and punctuation aside, on a sign in a frame (high), in what was said (medium for a name of two words or more, low for one word; a name shorter than five letters is never matched in speech: "Hjem", "Home"), or in a frame's description (low). The draft names the place; its coordinates are the registry's, never the draft's. A sign that names nothing you have is said, and proposes nothing; two places with the same weight propose neither.
  • a date from the camcorder's burned-in stamp, to the precision it shows: a day, a month, a year; a stamp whose day and month could be either way round (07.08.94) is one or the other and proposes the span from one to the other, and stamps that disagree their range; a stamp that is no real date (31.02.1994, a date after today) dates nothing; 1 January at midnight is a clock never set and dates nothing, and 1 January without a time is proposed low and said so; the time in a stamp is never read as a year. Without a stamp, a year written in a frame or said aloud (low), but never one a shop or a banner has stood since ("SINCE 1952", "etablert 1965"), narrowed to spring, summer or autumn when the frames agree on the season (the north's seasons); a season alone dates nothing.
  • nothing to go on: a scene with neither gets a draft that says so, and proposes nothing.

Nothing opens a socket while it runs: no model is fetched (a model that is not here is one sentence naming videos fetch --models), the Hugging Face hub is told it is offline before any engine is even imported, and ffmpeg opens files only. The file is deleted from the cache once inferred, unless --keep; a run that stops keeps what it wrote and the next carries on. --dry-run says which cached files would be inferred and needs no engine.

docs.title: review video: one scene at a time
docs.text:
review video is one more queue of the one review sitting (Review, RFC 0037): review alone lists it after the person's, the org's, the idea's, the asset's and the place's, --accept, --reject and --json mean what they mean for every kind, and the options below are its own: any other kind refuses them, as it refuses a place's. The queue is every scene of each file's latest inference that you have not answered, the surest proposals first, then the scenes with nothing to go on. Each row shows the file, the scene and its offsets, the proposal, the sentences with the frames and speech they cite, what the frames showed, and, when the proposal is one day the rules trust (its date not low), where the record had you and your assets that day (the Day's stays, the assets' positions), or the nearest day within three that has any. On a terminal it asks for each scene: y confirms, n refuses, a keeps it to ask the family, Enter skips, q stops; you are asked with no lock held, so a scheduled sync never waits on you, and each answer is written at once under the record's writer lock, as every queue's is. With flags, every number is checked before the first line is written:

Answer Writes --accept N[,N] one attribution/v1 line per scene, tier 2, source manual: the scene (ref {kind: scene, value: <video line id>#t=<start>,<end>}, scene {video, start_s, end_s}) bound to the place ({type: place\|asset, id, registry, label}) and/or the date or date range ({from, to, precision}) proposed, method owner, the draft, the video and the transcript as evidence. The video's own line is never touched --place N NAME, --date N WHEN the same, with your own place (a places.json name, an asset's id or name) or date (1994, 1994-07, 1994-07-14, summer 1994, 1994-06..1994-08), or none to leave that part out --reject N[,N] the scene's no: one scene-review/v1 line (RFC 0040 §5), a line of its own that no queue of a place, an asset or any other kind reads: the scene, verdict different, the proposal it answers as the draft carried it, the draft, and supersedes the scene's standing no when a later inference proposed something else; while the no stands, that proposal is not offered for that scene again: retract it, or refuse what a later inference proposes instead (the new no supersedes it), and it may be asked again --ask N[,N] one open task/v1 line in the list videos, so a later shared page can put the scene before the family; the scene leaves the queue, --asked brings it back, and answering it closes the task --answered the scenes you confirmed, to correct one: a new answer supersedes the standing line; the same answer twice writes nothing --top N only the first N scenes of the queue (a place's option too, where it counts places)

Nothing else writes: no place is added to places.json, no line is rewritten, and the review reads the record and the registries alone, with no connection.

docs.title: Tiers
docs.text: The video line, its transcript and the transcript's text, the scene drafts with their frame descriptions, the attributions, the noes and the asks are all tier 2, and nothing derived from them is written lower. They cross only to a destination whose ceiling is 2 or more (the crossing); in a record with recipients they are sealed like every tier-2 line (RFC 0029). The scene drafts are made by models on this machine and nothing crosses to make them, so no crossing entry governs them as one governs the dream's.

docs.title: Voice memos and their transcripts
docs.text:
Two steps, two lines. logbook add voice-memos (or import-backup --only voice-memos) writes one voice-memo/v1 line per recording Apple's Voice Memos app holds (RFC 0023): when it started, how long it ran, what you called it, and the audio by digest. logbook transcribe voice-memos then writes one transcript/v1 line per memo (RFC 0004) with the words, heard by a model running on this machine. The memo line never changes; the transcript sits beside it and points back.

logbook add voice-memos ~/backup/voice-memos/CloudRecordings.db --attachments   # the audio into attachments/
logbook transcribe voice-memos --dry-run        # which memos would be transcribed; nothing written, no engine needed
logbook transcribe voice-memos --fetch-model    # the first time: download the model, then transcribe
logbook transcribe voice-memos                  # every standing memo with its audio in the store and no transcript yet
logbook transcribe voice-memos --since 2026-03-01 --model medium
logbook transcribe voice-memos --no-speakers    # transcribe only, even with the speaker models here
logbook derive speakers --dry-run               # transcripts heard before the voices were separated

logbook transcribe is logbook derive transcripts since 0.6; both spellings run the same command.

docs.title: The recording: voice-memo/v1
docs.text:
The adapter reads CloudRecordings.db with the audio files beside it (under Recordings/ as import-backup copies them out, or next to the store as the phone and the Mac keep them). Every recording is a line, whether or not its file is there; one whose file is gone is a line without media, counted. The audio is hashed a chunk at a time and the line carries {sha256, bytes, media_type}; only with --attachments are the bytes put in the record's attachment store (SPEC §1.1), and then the reference also carries its path. A second add --attachments writes no new line (same raw_id) but does put the files in the store, where the digest the earlier line carries finds them. Tier 2.

Transcription needs the bytes: a memo whose audio is not in the store is skipped and counted ("without their audio in the store (import with --attachments)").

docs.title: The words: transcript/v1
docs.text:
logbook transcribe voice-memos reads the record through its index, finds every voice-memo line that stands (not retracted, not superseded by a later line), whose audio is in the store, and for which no transcript line exists yet, and transcribes them in time order. Each memo becomes one line:

Field What it holds source transcription, whatever engine heard it, so the same memo is one line on any machine kind, tier transcript; 2 (RFC 0004), or the memo's own tier when that is higher at, end, tz the memo's payload.raw_id the memo's own raw_id: the dedupe key, so a re-run writes nothing twice (ADR 0017) payload.provider the engine: mlx-whisper or faster-whisper payload.provenance {"source": <the memo line's id>, "engine": …, "model": "small"} payload.title the memo's title payload.participants empty: a memo is the owner's own voice; nothing is resolved here payload.language what the engine detected on the first chunk, as it names it (en, nb) payload.content the text, one segment per line, a text/plain file in attachments/ by digest; never inline payload.extra recording (the memo's raw_id, as RFC 0023 says), chunks, segments, duration_s, turns 0, speakers 0 payload.speakers only when the voices were separated (below): the voices, S1, S2, … or mic/system, each with its seconds and turns payload.diarization with speakers: {engine, model, audio, channels, overlap_s, spans}, the spans file in attachments/ beside the text

The transcript never carries supersedes. A memo that was retracted is left alone; a memo another memo line supersedes (a re-import after a trim) is left alone and the standing one is transcribed, its transcript pointing at the standing line.

A synthetic example, the Oslo persona's:

{"at":"2026-03-02T20:14:07Z","end":"2026-03-02T20:15:49Z","tz":"Europe/Oslo","source":"transcription","kind":"transcript","tier":2,
 "payload":{"schema":"transcript/v1","provider":"mlx-whisper","raw_id":"7A1B2C3D-0000-4000-8000-000000000001",
 "title":"Idea for the talk","participants":[],"language":"nb",
 "content":{"sha256":"3f1a…","path":"attachments/3f1a…","bytes":412,"media_type":"text/plain"},
 "provenance":{"source":"019a2c3d-0000-7000-8000-000000000042","engine":"mlx-whisper","model":"small"},
 "extra":{"recording":"7A1B2C3D-0000-4000-8000-000000000001","chunks":1,"segments":7,"format":"text","turns":0,"speakers":0,"duration_s":102}}}

docs.title: The voices (RFC 0038)
docs.text:
When the diarizer (the openlogbook[speakers] extra) and its models are on this machine (logbook setup speakers says whether they are; logbook setup speakers --fetch-model fetches them, the one download), the same run separates the voices of each memo on the audio it decoded, and the line gains speakers and diarization: each line of the text is given the voice that speaks most of it (the engine is asked for word times), a spans file goes into attachments/ beside the text, and the progress line says how many voices it heard (Middag: 4,212 words, nb, 3 voices, 41.8s). Without the diarizer the line is exactly as before, and the run ends with one sentence, naming the extra when it is not installed and the fetch when a model is not here:

speakers: not separated (install openlogbook[speakers], then logbook setup speakers --fetch-model)
speakers: not separated (logbook setup speakers --fetch-model)

--no-speakers turns separation off for a run. A memo is one room, its voices S1, S2, … by first speech, unless its source says the file keeps a call's two sides apart, extra.channels naming the file's channels in order (["mic", "system"]); then each channel is heard on its own and the microphone's voice is from_me when it is alone there. Memos transcribed before the voices could be separated are heard again by logbook derive speakers, each into a new line that supersedes the old one. The fields, the labels, the spans file, the cost of hearing a transcript again and what the readers show are on Speakers.

docs.title: Resumable
docs.text:
One line is appended per memo as soon as it is heard, and the command prints a line per memo as it goes (2026-03-02 21:14 Idea for the talk: 212 words, nb, 3.4s). Stop it at any point: what was heard is in the record, and the next run skips every memo that already has a transcript and carries on with the rest. --since YYYY-MM-DD takes memos from that local day on. --dry-run lists what would be transcribed and needs no engine installed.

Long recordings are heard in fixed windows of ten minutes; segment times are offset by the window's start and the language detected on the first window is asked of every later one, so one recording is heard in one language. A recording with no words in it writes no line and is counted.

docs.title: The engine, and nothing leaves the machine
docs.text:
Transcription is an optional extra, installed with openlogbook[transcribe]: on Apple silicon that is mlx-whisper (it decodes audio with ffmpeg, which must be on the PATH), anywhere else faster-whisper. The engine is found at run time; with neither installed the command stops with a message naming the extra. --model names a Whisper size (tiny, base, small, medium, large-v3; small by default) or a Hugging Face repository; a size becomes mlx-community/whisper-<size>-mlx or Systran/faster-whisper-<size>.

Audio never leaves the machine and the command opens no network connection: while it transcribes, the Hugging Face hub is told it is offline (HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1, and the switch the hub client read when it was first imported), so the engines cannot reach out whatever they would do on their own, and pyannote.audio's own usage reporting is switched off (PYANNOTE_METRICS_ENABLED=0). The one exception is explicit: a Whisper model not yet on this machine stops the command, and --fetch-model downloads it before the first chunk is heard; it never fetches a speaker model, which is setup speakers --fetch-model's alone. The diarizer is a second extra, openlogbook[speakers]: pyannote.audio, and with it torch on every platform. openlogbook[transcribe] does not bring it, so [transcribe] alone transcribes and [transcribe,speakers] separates the voices too. A test fakes the engine and the diarizer, feeds them a two-second synthetic WAV and refuses every socket for the length of the run; no model is downloaded in CI.

docs.title: Apple Wallet: boarding passes and tickets
docs.text:
logbook add wallet reads the passes in Apple Wallet and writes one flight/v1 line per air boarding pass (RFC 0013, evidence declared) and one event/v1 line per event ticket and per train, boat or bus pass (RFC 0009). A coupon, a store card or a generic pass becomes an event only when it carries a relevantDate; otherwise it is counted and skipped. One file of each pass is read, pass.json; the barcode, the back of the pass, the images and the Passes app's database are never read, so the booking reference and the passenger's name cannot reach a line.

logbook import-backup <backup> --only wallet     # the passes of an iPhone backup, copied out and read
logbook add wallet ~/copies/apple-wallet/         # a folder of passes: unpacked .pkpass folders, .pkpass zips, or both
logbook add wallet boarding.pkpass                # one pass, zipped as the airline sent it
logbook add ~/copies/apple-wallet/                # the same, sniffed by content

docs.title: Where the passes are
docs.text:
An iPhone keeps every pass in Wallet under Library/Passes/Cards/<id>.pkpass/ in the home domain, each as a folder holding the pass unpacked: pass.json, manifest.json, a signature and the images (icon.png, logo.png, strip.png, …). Beside them the Passes app keeps its own database (nav.db, passes23.sqlite): Wallet's cache of the same passes, the order of the cards, the notifications it showed. import-backup --only wallet copies the pass.json files alone, below inbox/ios-backup-<udid>/apple-wallet/<id>.pkpass/, with the folder names the phone gave them, and runs the adapter on that folder. The database is not copied and not read: it holds nothing a pass does not say.

A .pkpass an airline or a venue emailed is the same files as one zip. The adapter reads a zip, an unpacked folder, a bare pass.json, or a folder of any of them, in name order. pass.json may be UTF-8 (with or without a byte-order mark) or UTF-16 with one; a trailing comma is forgiven; a file that will not parse is counted ("passes that would not parse").

docs.title: What is read, and what is never read
docs.text:
Read, from pass.json and nothing else:

Key Used for passTypeIdentifier, serialNumber raw_id, hashed together (below); also calendar.id on an event organizationName extra.organization; the title of a dated coupon or card; calendar.name on an event description the title of a ticket when nothing else names it relevantDate, or the first of relevantDates the date of a flight when no schedule is known; the start of a ticket or a transit pass; the moment of a dated coupon or card; kept as extra.relevant_date boardingPass, eventTicket, coupon, storeCard, generic the style, and under boardingPass its transitType headerFields, primaryFields, secondaryFields, auxiliaryFields each field's key, label and value, matched by role as the next section says semantics these tags only: airlineCode, flightCode, flightNumber, departureAirportCode, destinationAirportCode, originalDepartureDate, originalArrivalDate, departureStationName, destinationStationName, eventName, venueName, eventStartDate (or eventStartDateInfo.date), eventEndDate

Deliberately never read:

Key Why barcode, barcodes an air pass's barcode is an IATA BCBP message carrying the passenger's name and the booking reference; a ticket's carries the ticket's secret. Nothing in it is needed: the pass's front says the same flight backFields terms, contacts, the booking reference, the frequent-flyer number nfc, authenticationToken, webServiceURL, userInfo, beacons credentials and Wallet's plumbing locations, expirationDate, voided where Wallet surfaces the pass and until when: not the plan every other semantic tag passengerName, confirmationNumber, membershipProgramNumber, seats, … any front field whose key or label names a person or a credential passenger, name, holder, member, guest, booking, order, ticket number, …: never a title, never anything manifest.json, the signature, the images never opened nav.db, passes23.sqlite the Passes app's database: not copied, not read

No field is copied wholesale. A line carries only the values the mapping names; a key the mapping does not know is simply not there. A test holds the adapter to this on passes whose fields, barcode and semantic tags all carry the fictional passenger and booking reference.

docs.title: An air boarding pass is a flight
docs.text:
A boardingPass whose transitType is PKTransitTypeAir (the default when absent) is one flight/v1 line: kind flight, tier 1, source apple-wallet, evidence declared. A boarding pass is the airline's word for a seat it sold, a plan; a tracker's export (flighty) is the record of a flight that flew, and it wins when both are in the record (RFC 0013 rule 3). Before 0.6.0 the adapter was ios-wallet and decoded the barcode as tracked; a record may still hold its lines.

Field keys differ per airline — one writes origin and destination, another from and to, a third f1 and f2 with the labels DEP and ARR — so every value is found by its field's key or label, split into words (departureDate → departure date) and matched case-insensitively:

Field Found by Value from, to the semantic airport codes; else a field saying origin, from, dep, departure, outbound (the origin) and one saying destination, to, arr, arrival, inbound (the destination): of the three-letter upper-case tokens in the value (OSL, Oslo (OSL), NEW YORK JFK), else in the label, the one the airports table knows, else the last; else the first two codes among the other plain fields spelled through the airports table, {iata, icao} carrier, number the semantic airlineCode + flightNumber or flightCode; else a field saying flight: XY 561, YZ0562, XY-561, or a bare 561 with the carrier from a field saying airline, carrier or operator the carrier through the airlines table; leading zeros dropped date the local date at the origin of the scheduled departure when the pass names one; else relevantDate's own date; else a field saying date or day whose value carries a year (2026-03-14, 14.03.2026, 14 Mar 2026, 14MAR26) a pass with none is counted ("without a date"), never placed by a file time scheduled_departure, scheduled_arrival the semantic originalDepartureDate and originalArrivalDate; else a field saying departure or arrival whose value is a timestamp RFC 3339 UTC extra.seat a field saying seat as written extra.class a field saying class, cabin, compartment or fare as written extra.organization organizationName the airline's name extra.relevant_date relevantDate as written, with its offset

relevantDate is the instant Wallet shows the pass: boarding for one airline, departure for another. It is kept as it is, and it is the line's at when the pass names no schedule, but it is never written as a scheduled time. at and end follow RFC 0013: the scheduled departure and arrival when known, else relevantDate, else the date's local midnight at the origin; tz is the origin airport's zone, else the record's. A pass with no readable route or flight number is counted ("boarding passes without a readable flight").

A synthetic example, the Oslo persona's pass for XY 561:

{"at":"2026-03-14T06:05:00Z","end":null,"tz":"Europe/Oslo","source":"apple-wallet","kind":"flight","tier":1,
 "payload":{"schema":"flight/v1","raw_id":"wallet:8c1d0e5a9b2f3a4b@3f9a1c2b7e4d","date":"2026-03-14","carrier":"XY","number":"561",
 "from":{"iata":"OSL","icao":"ENGM"},"to":{"iata":"ZRH","icao":"LSZH"},"role":"passenger","evidence":"declared",
 "observations":[{"evidence":"declared","source":"apple-wallet"}],
 "extra":{"organization":"Nordic Example Air","seat":"12A","class":"Economy","relevant_date":"2026-03-14T07:05:00+01:00"}}}

docs.title: A ticket is an event
docs.text:
An eventTicket is one event/v1 line, tier 1: title from the semantic eventName, else a field saying event, title or show, else the first primary field that names no person; location from venueName or a field saying venue, location, where or place; at from relevantDate, else eventStartDate, else a field saying start, doors, time or date — a day with no clock makes an all-day line in the record's zone; end from eventEndDate or a field saying end. calendar is {id: the pass type, name: the issuer}; extra holds pass_style, organization and relevant_date. A ticket with no date is counted.

A boardingPass for a train (PKTransitTypeTrain), a boat, a bus or a generic transit is an event titled origin → destination, from the semantic station names or the fields saying origin and destination as text, with extra.transit_type (train, boat, bus, generic), at from relevantDate or the departure field, end from the arrival field, and its seat and class under extra as a flight keeps them.

A coupon, a storeCard or a generic pass is counted ("coupons", "store and loyalty cards", "generic passes") unless it carries a relevantDate: then it is one event titled with the issuer's name, extra.pass_style saying which kind it was. A loyalty card without a date says nothing about any day; a coupon for one morning says where the owner meant to be.

docs.title: Re-imports and updates
docs.text: raw_id is wallet:<16 hex of sha256(passTypeIdentifier, serialNumber)>@<digest of the mapped line>. The pass type and serial identify a pass across every device it was on; the serial is often the booking reference, so the pair is hashed and never carried. Importing the same Wallet again appends nothing. A pass the airline updated — a delay pushed as a new relevantDate, a new seat — has the same serial and a different mapped line, so it is a new observation of the same flight: flights.reconcile folds it into the line that stands for the flight's key and supersedes it (RFC 0013 rules 3 and 6), and a Flighty export of the flight later supersedes both, carrying the seat along. A pass rescheduled to another day is, by the key, another flight.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text:
The weather of the places your days were spent at, one weather/v1 line (RFC 0026) per local day and place: the lowest and highest temperature, the precipitation, the strongest wind, a WMO weather code, sunrise and sunset. The places come from your own track, the values from Open-Meteo's free historical archive, and nothing finer than a tenth of a degree ever leaves the machine.

export LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1                             # the one setting: without it nothing is asked
logbook sync weather --dry-run                       # how many cluster-days, how many requests; nothing fetched
logbook sync weather                                 # yesterday on the first run; then the days since the last
logbook sync weather --since 2026-06-01 --until 2026-06-30   # a backfill, by name
logbook day 2026-06-16                               # … night after  Hotel · away · 27° · cloudy
                                                     # … weather      14°–27° · 0.3 mm · wind 19 km/h · partly cloudy · sun 05:30–21:25

Tier 1, evidence external: the line says what a provider says about a 10 km square on a day, and no reader derives presence, company or an act from it.

docs.title: What is asked, and about where
docs.text:
For every local day of the window the command takes the owner's overnight stay (the night of the day, as derive stays and the Day read it) and every stay of three hours or more that touches the day, including the anchorages of a stay aboard a boat. Each place is rounded to one decimal of latitude and longitude — about 11 km north to south and, at Oslo, 6 km east to west — and the day's places are deduped after rounding: home and an office across town are one place, so one line. A day the track does not place (no stay reached three hours, the night was in transit) gets no line.

The window: --since and --until are local days. Without --until the window ends yesterday (today is not over). Without --since the first run asks about yesterday alone — the record's past is asked about only when you name it, with --since, and the first scheduled run is no different — and every later run starts a week before the last day the previous run covered (state/weather.json, since), so points that reach the record late still get their days, but never before the first day any run covered (from): turning the source on never sends your history. Days already in the record are counted as already there and not written again — one line per day and place, the dedupe key <day>@<lat>,<lon> — and the cache (below) means they are not fetched again either, so a backfill with --since costs only the days that are new.

docs.title: Open-Meteo
docs.text:
Open-Meteo serves daily values from a reanalysis for any point on earth from 1940 on, free for non-commercial use, without a key. Days older than a week come from the archive API (archive-api.open-meteo.com, which runs a few days behind the present); the last seven days from the forecast API (api.open-meteo.com), whose past days are the model's analysis, not a forecast. Open-Meteo's data is under CC BY 4.0: a page that shows these lines should say "Weather data by Open-Meteo.com".

One request covers one place and a run of days: the days a place needs are sorted and split only where a gap exceeds a week or a run a year, so a fortnight at one place is one request and a year at home is one too. Between requests the command waits a second. The provider asks for fewer than 600 calls a minute and 10,000 a day; a record's whole history is a few hundred requests, and the daily run is a handful. A request that fails is said on stderr, the others still go out, the run exits 1 and the watermark stays where it was, so the next run asks again.

docs.title: The cache
docs.text: Every day a response carries — the days asked for and the days between them — is kept under <root>/inbox/weather/<lat>_<lon>/<day>.json, under the rounded coordinates, so a re-run never refetches, and a stay that appears later for a day already fetched costs no request. inbox/ is not the record (SPEC §1): the cache can be deleted and the lines stand. A day the provider had no values for (a place in the sea before the model covered it) is not cached and is counted (skipped … days the provider had no values for), so it is asked again another time.

docs.title: The switch: LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1
docs.text: The source's one setting, and nothing else configures it: no key, no account, no place. Set LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1 in the environment — for the schedule, a line in ~/.config/logbook/sync.env — and logbook sync weather runs, and sync --all and the schedule take it too, each run covering the days since the last. Unset, empty or 0, nothing is asked of anyone: logbook sync weather says sync: weather: off; set LOGBOOK_WEATHER=1 … and exits 2 without a request, a dry run included, and sync --all says weather: LOGBOOK_WEATHER not set; skipped. A {"source": "weather"} entry in policy/import.json disables it either way.

docs.title: What the readers show
docs.text:
• day says the weather in short beside the place of the night after, night after Home · home · 4° · rain — the day's high (the low when the high is unknown) and the WMO code in one word (clear, cloudy, overcast, fog, drizzle, rain, snow, thunder) — when the day's weather row is of that place. Then one weather row after the health line when the day has lines: the place of the night when the day has one, else the first, and · 2 places when the day was spent in more than one. The JSON carries the row with every place of the day under places, each with its line id; the short form is the text's own, so the JSON is unchanged. A day with no weather lines has no row and "weather": null. Under a day_start the row is the line's own day's: the line starts at midnight, on the page of the day before, and the Day of its day still shows it.
  • year adds one weather row — the coldest and warmest day, the precipitation summed over the days (the wettest place of a day, so two places never count one rain twice), the wet days (1 mm or more), the strongest wind, and how many of the year's days have a line — and the HTML page a section.
  • trips says the same for each trip's days, first to the return day, after the people.
  • serve shows the Day's row under a Weather heading.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
What leaves the machine is a GET to Open-Meteo with a latitude and a longitude of one decimal, two dates, the list of daily variables, and the record's time zone; no key, no account, no cookie, no referrer; the user agent names this software and its version. The provider learns that someone asked about a 10 km square on some days — a valley, not a street; a town, not a house — and over many requests, the squares a person's life touches. If that is more than you want a third party to know, leave LOGBOOK_WEATHER unset (nothing is asked), turn it on for the days you choose and off again, or disable the source in policy/import.json. The line, the cache and the request all carry the same rounded coordinates: the stays themselves stay in the location lines, and nothing here lets a reader of the weather lines rebuild them. The request never carries the record's owner id or any identifier of yours.

The reference adapter is logbook/contrib/adapters/weather.py; the clustering and the readers' side are in logbook/core/weather.py; the tests run against a fake Open-Meteo in memory and never open a socket, and one of them checks every request URL for a coordinate with more than one decimal.

docs.title: Architecture decision records
docs.text: One file per decision, numbered, never edited after acceptance — superseded by a new ADR. This is the project's own logbook.

docs.title: ADR 0001 — Files are the truth; databases are caches
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Context. The private predecessor stored the log in Postgres/PostGIS and mirrored it to JSONL. A standard cannot require a database server.

Decision. The JSONL files under logbook/<YYYY>/<MM>.jsonl are the record. Any database is a derived index that may be deleted and rebuilt. verify and export read files only.

Consequences. Engines that need spatial queries bring their own index (SQLite + R*Tree by default; PostGIS as a plugin). Chain order is seq, not file order, because backfilled history lands in old month files.

docs.title: ADR 0002 — Canonicalisation and hashing
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Decision. Content is canonicalised per RFC 8785 (JSON Canonicalization Scheme): sorted keys, no whitespace, UTF-8, ES6 number serialisation. The reference implementation uses Python's json.dumps(sort_keys=True, separators=(",",":")), which agrees with JCS for all fixtures; a JCS conformance vector is tested and a full JCS implementation is a v0.2 task. Hash is SHA-256. Line ids are UUIDv7 (time-ordered) and sit outside the hash so they may be assigned at write time. Signatures (Ed25519 over the month's head) and encryption (HPKE, RFC 9180, or age) are v0.2.

docs.title: ADR 0003 — One log
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Context. Earlier designs sketched a separate events.jsonl event stream for other tools alongside the Logbook, and a future reader ("Aion") consuming it.

Decision. There is one log: the Logbook. Any other tool that wants to record an event writes a line here through an adapter or as a manual line. Readers read the Logbook. No parallel event stream exists.

Consequences. Every derived system is a consumer of the Logbook, never a peer of it. Adapters are the only way in; Logbook.append is the only write.

docs.title: ADR 0004 — Human notes live in the Logbook
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Context. External tools (a notes app, a places database) could own the human-written meaning about places, people and days, with the Logbook holding only machine facts.

Decision. Notes, confirmations and visibility choices are written into the Logbook as tier-2 lines. External tools may receive exports; they are never the source of truth for anything a person wrote here.

Consequences. Export to other tools is one-way. A note survives any recompute and any export because it is a line in the chain, not a field in someone else's database.

docs.title: ADR 0005 — One nudge, one channel
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Context. Several automations could each ask the owner questions in the evening (place confirmations, discoveries, the day's question).

Decision. There is one nudge queue and one evening message. Every automation that wants to ask something puts it in that queue; the delivery layer sends at most one message a day and suppresses routine noise. No streaks, no scores.

Consequences. A second bot is a bug. The queue is a layer-5 concern; the Logbook itself never sends anything.

docs.title: ADR 0006 — The hash chain is mandatory
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Context. An optional chain would lower the bar for new implementations; a mandatory one makes every conformant logbook tamper-evident.

Decision. The chain (SPEC §3) is required for conformance. It is invisible to the person: add computes it, verify checks it, nothing else mentions it.

Consequences. A file that does not chain is not a logbook. Implementations must pass the conformance fixture. Simplicity is delivered by hiding the chain, never by removing it.

docs.title: ADR 0007 — SQLite is the default index
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13 · extends ADR 0001

Decision. Engines index the log in SQLite (with R*Tree for spatial queries) by default. PostGIS is a plugin for installations that want it. The index is disposable and rebuilt from the files at any time.

Consequences. pipx install gives a complete, working system with no server. Anyone who deletes the index loses nothing.

docs.title: ADR 0008 — The first three adapters
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Decision. The first adapters shipped by the project are, in order: Google Takeout (location history, photos metadata, calendar, mail headers, YouTube and Chrome history from one archive), Apple Health (sleep, heart, steps, workouts and routes), and WhatsApp chat exports (tier 2). An email adapter is in scope and tracked as a task, not left as a table row.

Rationale. Three drops cover location, photos, calendar, health and messages for most people. Takeout alone is six witnesses in one zip.

Amendment (2026-09-14). The captain's own first adapters are dawarich (location; Dawarich already holds imported Google Timeline history) and immich (photos with faces, camera and live-photo metadata), because both already run on his server. They are published as ordinary adapters. Takeout remains the first onboarding adapter for someone with no server.

Consequences. Every other source is a community adapter from the template. The "wanted" list lives in adapters/README.md.

docs.title: ADR 0009 — Shared pages are core, not an add-on
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Context. The earlier private design had a data model for a moment shared between two people but no interface and no task for it.

Decision. The circle — a page handed to a named person, who hands one back — is one of the three core ideas (VISION.md) and gets a user interface and a bundle format in the roadmap (phase 3), before books and publishing.

Consequences. The shared-page bundle format is specified before any transport is chosen, so two logbooks can exchange a page by file first.

docs.title: ADR 0010 — bighydro is a pen name
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-13

Decision. The project is stewarded under the pen name bighydro. Anonymity of data is strict: nothing personal enters the repository, ever (synthetic fixtures only, scrub before every push). Anonymity of identity is soft: the steward does not lead with a legal name and does not link the project from personal accounts, but treats being identified as an inconvenience, not a catastrophe.

Consequences. Commits are signed by bighydro's key. The project can accept talks, partnerships or funding later without a crisis of identity.

docs.title: ADR 0011 — Log everything that is cheap; judge everything downstream
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-14

Context. Real sources are noisy: most email is bulk, most photos are not worth showing, screenshots are neither photos nor junk. The temptation is to filter at ingest.

Decision. Ingest is not the place for taste. An adapter records every item the source offers, as cheaply as possible (metadata first; bodies and pixels only where the tier and the source allow), and attaches a classification it can compute from the item itself — class for mail, provenance and faces for photos. What is shown, hidden, summarised or queued for review is decided by later passes, which are versioned and can be re-run over all history when the rules improve.

Two exceptions: (1) an adapter never reads what the source itself has already judged as junk — spam folders, trash, deleted items; (2) the body of an item classed as bulk or automated is never logged, only its header line.

Consequences. - Mail is a headers-first adapter: one small line per message with class ∈ {human, bulk, automated}; bodies (tier 2) only for human. - Photos: one line per asset with provenance ∈ {camera, received, screenshot, other} and a face count. Faces surface on the day by default; screenshots and other feed a review pass that drafts what the image says about the day. - A classification rule is data plus a version, never a hard-coded decision in the adapter's control flow, so it can be reconsidered.

docs.title: ADR 0012 — Adapters built by the project ship inside the package
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-14

Context. ARCHITECTURE.md places adapters in layer 2 and lists them as separate repositories (logbook-adapter-<source>). The first one the captain needs, dawarich (ADR 0008, amendment), is small: one file, one fixture, no dependencies. A separate repository, package, release train and version pin for every such adapter is more ceremony than code, and logbook add <export> should work out of the box for the sources the project itself maintains.

Decision. Adapters built by the project live inside the package, one module each under logbook/adapters/. Third-party adapters are separate packages that register the logbook.adapters entry point. The CLI discovers both through one registry (logbook.adapters.all_adapters()), built-ins first.

Every adapter, built-in or not, is a module exposing three names:

  • NAME: str — the source its lines carry, lowercase, dashes only.
  • sniff(path) -> bool — "is this file mine?"; cheap, reads only what it must, never raises.
  • run(path, since=None) -> Iterator[dict] — line drafts with exactly at, end, tz, source, kind, tier, payload (SPEC §2 minus the chain fields, which Logbook.append adds). tz may be None, meaning the logbook's own timezone. since is RFC3339 UTC.

logbook add <path> asks each registered adapter to sniff the file, runs the first that says yes, and appends through Logbook.append_many, which skips any draft whose (source, payload.raw_id) is already in the log so that re-adding an export appends nothing. add also accepts a folder and processes every file in it.

Rationale. The contract is what matters, not the packaging. Keeping the project's own adapters in-tree means one test suite, one uv run pytest, one release, and a working add on day one. The entry point keeps the door open for adapters the project does not want to own: proprietary sources, sources needing heavy dependencies, sources with a different release cadence. Both kinds are found the same way, so moving an adapter in or out of the package is a packaging change, not an API change.

Consequences. - logbook/contrib/adapters/<name>.py + tests/fixtures/<name>/ + tests is the whole cost of a built-in adapter. The rules of adapters/README.md still apply: synthetic fixtures only, no network on the default path, never write to the source. - The template in adapters/template/ gains NAME and sniff so a copy is registrable as-is. - The layer-2 row in ARCHITECTURE.md ("Repo: logbook-adapter-<source>") now describes third-party adapters; built-ins are in this repo. - Dedupe on (source, raw_id) is a property of append_many, not of any adapter; an adapter that wants idempotent re-adds gives every line a stable raw_id.

docs.title: ADR 0013 — Downstream interpreters
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-14

Context. Other systems will read the Logbook and turn it into understanding and action: a personal wiki, a task database, a calendar, an agent. One such system proposed an interoperability contract. Most of it fits; four points would have moved decisions upstream that belong to the record.

Decision. A downstream interpreter relates to the Logbook as follows.

  1. Everything enters; the interpreter receives a curated view. The Logbook ingests every item its adapters can reach, classified but not filtered (ADR 0011). What an interpreter receives is a derived export chosen by later, versioned passes. The interpreter never defines what enters the log.
  2. The Logbook mints identity. People and places get their ids here. An interpreter stores a logbook_ref and never a parallel id space. An interpreter's existing registry of people or places may be imported once, through an adapter, to seed names and aliases.
  3. Open keys for the world. Places reference OSM / Wikidata ids, never a private namespace. Person ids are Logbook UUIDs.
  4. The day package is the hand-off unit. logbook export --day <date> writes a day-package/v1 directory: a manifest with the day's lines (ids, kinds, tiers, tags), derived entities when they exist, attachments by content hash, and logbook_head — the chain head at generation time — so the consumer can prove which state of the record it read. The package is a view; it never replaces the log.
  5. Tags and lifting are downstream and confirmed. A personal taxonomy (life areas) is applied as tags by a classification pass, in the owner's private layer, never by the public spec. Lifting a tier-2/3 line into an interpreter's cloud store is a per-line visibility choice recorded in the log (ADR 0004); a tag may propose it, a human confirms it.
  6. Writes back are proposals. An interpreter may return suggestions (a trip, a person, a task) and, on acceptance, a reference to what it created; the acceptance and the reference are recorded as manual lines. An interpreter may append observations through the agent path with its own source; it never writes notes, confirmations or visibility.
  7. Raw and derived never share a line. A source's own fields (a provider's summary, participants, ids) are the raw line. Anything a model extracted (decisions, action items, entities) is a separate extraction, a draft until accepted.

Consequences. The interpreter can be replaced, or run alongside a second one, without touching the record. Every question of the form "should X enter the Logbook?" is answered "yes, classified"; every question "should X go to the interpreter?" is answered by an export rule the owner can change and re-run.

docs.title: ADR 0014 — Canonicalisation is fixed, not versioned
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-15 · amends ADR 0002

Context. ADR 0002 chose RFC 8785 for canonical_json and let the reference implementation use Python's json.dumps(sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":")), "which agrees with JCS for all fixtures". Running the RFC's own test vectors (tests/test_jcs.py) showed where it does not: floats with an integer value or a small magnitude (0.0, 120.0, 1e-06) and object keys outside the Basic Multilingual Plane. Adapters write such floats (alt_m, speed_mps, heading_deg), so records made before the fix carry hashes that a conformant implementation cannot recompute. Two ways out: keep the old rule in the code behind a per-record version, or fix the rule and move the records.

Decision. One canonicalisation, RFC 8785, for every record. The code carries no other rule and no version switch; logbook.json format names the rule a record's hashes were computed with, and the implementation refuses to verify or write a record whose format is not its own. A record hashed under the old rule is migrated forward, once: every line keeps id, seq, the content fields and recorded_at; prev and hash are recomputed in seq order; the old files are kept beside the record; logbook.json gains a lineage entry with the old format and head; and the migration appends one migration/v1 line naming the old head, so the migration is itself part of the chain. The old serialiser survives only in the test that builds a synthetic 0.1 record.

Consequences. A second implementation implements RFC 8785 and nothing else; that is what "the spec fits in an afternoon" needs. An old head is still meaningful: it is in lineage and in the chain, and anyone holding a 0.1 export can recompute it from the kept files with the 0.1 rule. Migration is the one operation that rewrites prev and hash; it rewrites nothing else, refuses a record whose 0.1 links are already broken, and writes into a temporary folder first, so an interrupted run leaves the record as it was. Any future change to the hash rule takes the same road: a new format name, a refusal, a migration, a lineage entry.

Amendment (2026-10-13). The 0.1 rule now also lives in store.hash_0_1, read by migrate's gate alone: before any line is rehashed, every 0.1 hash is recomputed under the rule it was written with and every link checked, so a 0.1 record that does not verify is refused and nothing is touched. Writing and verifying a record still use one canonicalisation, RFC 8785; the test that builds a synthetic 0.1 record keeps its own copy of the old serialiser.

docs.title: ADR 0015 — Attachments are content-addressed
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-18

Context. Some observations come with a file: the text of a transcript, a photo, a voice message, a note's image. Such a file is too large, binary or private to sit inside a line, and the line is hashed, so whatever goes into it is canonicalised on every verify. Four profiles already point at such files (transcript/v1, crossing-package/v1, message/v1, note/v1), each waiting for the spec to say where the bytes live and what a missing file means for verify. Three ways to hold them: inline in the line as base64; in a store the record carries with it; in a blob service the record refers to.

Decision. A file is stored once, inside the record, at <root>/attachments/<sha256>, named by the lowercase hex SHA-256 of its exact bytes, with no extension and no subdirectories. A line references it by the digest, the path, the length and an IANA media type; a profile chooses the field name and keeps the shape. The store is write-once and never pruned: the same bytes imported twice are one file, and a line that points at a file is the reason the file stays (ADR 0001: attachments are record, not cache). The chain covers lines, not bytes: the digest is in the line, so a changed file is detectable, but the file is not in the hash pre-image. verify reports a missing attachment separately and exits 0 when the chain is intact; a present file whose bytes do not match its name is an error. A record with no attachments/ directory is valid, and conformance does not require the store. SPEC §1.1 states these rules.

Rejected: base64 inline. Putting the bytes in the payload keeps the record in one set of files, but every byte then enters the hash chain: a decade of photos would be canonicalised on every verify, the month files would be gigabytes of base64 nobody reads, and the line, meant to be one observation a person can read, would be a wall of encoded data. It also loses de-duplication: the same file imported from two sources would be two copies in two lines.

Rejected: an external blob service. Naming the file by a URL in an object store keeps the record small, but the record then depends on something outside itself (ADR 0001: files are the truth). A folder copied to a new disk in ten years would have lines that point at a service that no longer answers, and verify could not tell a lost file from a lost network. Content addressing keeps the digest as the reference, so a future exporter MAY copy the bytes anywhere, but the record itself holds them.

Consequences. attachments/ is part of what a backup must copy and what a migration must carry across; a store command, when it is built, writes the file before the line that points at it, so a crash leaves an unreferenced file, never a dangling reference. verify grows a second report, missing attachments, that does not change its exit status. A crossing package (RFC 0005) ships copies of the referenced files under the same names, so a recipient checks them the same way. Encryption of tier 2 and 3 attachments at rest is for the version that defines the encryption envelope (SPEC §4).

docs.title: ADR 0016 — The crossing ceiling is the owner's setting; a crossing is never invisible
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-29

Context. A crossing package (RFC 0005) hands verbatim lines, payloads included, to a named member of the circle. RFC 0005 states the tier policy in prose: tier 1 crosses automatically, tier 2 after a batched review, tier 3 never. Written as a constant in the code, that policy would be wrong twice: too strict for an owner whose circumstances change (a partner who should see the money lines, a doctor who should see the health lines), and too loose the moment anyone edits it, because nothing would then say that the ceiling moved. The first consumer, Hermes, runs nightly and unattended; whatever it can pull must be exactly what the owner meant to let cross, and the record must show every time it crossed.

Decision.

  1. The ceiling is a setting in the record, not a constant. <root>/policy/crossing.json maps a destination to the highest tier that may cross to it: {"hermes": {"max_tier": 2}}. logbook init writes that default; so does the first real export into a record that has none. The code reads the file and never decides a ceiling on its own. A destination the file does not name has no ceiling and cannot receive a crossing until the owner adds it.
  2. Every export names its destination and the tiers it asks for. logbook export crossing --to <destination> --tier 1|1,2|1,2,3. A request above the destination's ceiling exits non-zero with a message that names the file, so the owner raises the ceiling deliberately, in the record, or does not.
  3. Tier 1 crosses by default; tier 2 only when asked; tier 3 only when both the policy allows it and the owner types --tier 1,2,3. A policy edit alone never lets tier 3 cross. When tier 2 crosses, the manifest carries a review section listing every tier-2 line in the package by id, kind, source and time, so the batch can be reviewed as a whole (ADR 0005: one message, never line by line). When tier 3 crosses, the manifest and the console say so in words nobody can miss.
  4. A crossing is never invisible. Every real export appends one crossing/v1 line (RFC 0011) to the chain: the destination, the window, the counts per tier, the policy in force and the digest of the package. The record therefore holds, in order and under the hash chain, every time anything left it and under what ceiling. A dry run writes nothing and appends nothing.
  5. What crosses is bounded by the request, overlay included. The resolution lines a package ships so a reader can name people (RFC 0006) are lines like any other: one above the requested tiers stays home and is counted as held back. Nothing crosses that the request did not ask for, whatever the ceiling.

Consequences. The owner's circumstances can change and the record follows: raising a ceiling is one edit to one file, in the record, and the next crossing line shows it took effect. An unattended consumer can be trusted with a fixed command line, because the command cannot exceed the ceiling and cannot let tier 3 through on its own. The circle stays auditable from the record alone: given the crossing lines and the policy file, every bundle is accounted for. The price is that a crossing line is tier 1 and crosses too, so a destination learns when the record last crossed to it and to others; that is data about the record, not about the owner's day, and it is the point.

Amended by ADR 0022. The mcp entry may also name, under write, the write tools an orchestrator may use through the door: sign_day (the day's signature) and note_day (a note on a day), none by default and none once the entry has expired, within write_window_days (60). The ceiling still governs what is read; write governs what may be written, and neither ever lets tier 3 through (docs/mcp.md, "Write tools").

Amended 2026-10-15: the notion entry. logbook export notion (docs/export-notion.md) hands the record's facts about people, ideas and orgs to the program that keeps the owner's Notion, and is a crossing like any other: nothing leaves without a notion entry, its max_tier and until hold as every entry's do, tier 3 never leaves for it, and every real run appends one crossing/v1 line. The signed-day gate of RFC 0034 holds for it as for every crossing, and one key may lift it: an entry that says "include_unsigned": true lets --include-unsigned hand over the facts of unsigned days too. Neither the key nor the flag alone does, so an unattended consumer with a fixed command line cannot widen what leaves, and an edit to the file alone cannot either. The key is not part of the entry's version, which stays the digest of max_tier, until and model; the folder's manifest and the crossing line say signed_only beside it. The lines that bind a name to a key, resolution/v1 and the entity/v1 lines of RFC 0037, are this export's overlay, held to the ceiling and not to the signature, as a crossing package ships its resolution lines: an idea's Notion page id or an org's domain bound on an unsigned day is a key the folder may carry, while every fact matched by it rests on signed days.

Derived material follows the policy, not the head. What is derived through a crossing (a model's draft of a day, draft/v1 of RFC 0036, is the first) is held to the entry that let its evidence cross as that entry counts today, not as it counted when the line was written. Lowering a ceiling, passing an until or removing an entry appends nothing, so no new line and no moved head says it happened; the readers therefore check, every time: a derived line above the entry's max_tier today is shown by no reader (the Day says superseded by policy and why, and nothing of its text; the MCP door holds it back like a line above its own ceiling, and counts it), doctor lists the days it covers, and the line stays in the record, as every line does. Each derived line records the version of the entry it was made under (extra.policy_version: the SHA-256 of the RFC 8785 JSON of the entry's max_tier, until and model), so the writer that made it can tell when the entry changed and make it again under the entry as it is now: dream --catch-up dreams a day again when its draft is above the ceiling or was dreamed under another version, superseding the old draft, and dreams nothing under an expired entry (the dream, When the entry changes).

Amended 2026-10-21: a new record names no one. The owner's decision of 21 Oct 2026: the program names no destination. logbook init, logbook demo and the first export into a record without the file write {"mcp": {"max_tier": 1}} and nothing else, and a record without the file reads the same; hermes, like every other destination, is an entry the owner writes. A record whose file already names hermes keeps it: the file is never rewritten.

docs.title: ADR 0017 — Backfill and live share one mapping
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-29

Context. Most sources reach the record twice. First as a backfill: an export, a backup, a folder of files the owner already holds, read once by logbook add. Then live: the same service asked for what is new by logbook sync, night after night. dawarich was the first source built both ways (an export and GET /api/v1/points), imessage reads the same store from a backup and from the Mac it lives on, and the transcript sources that follow — Granola now, others later — all have an export and an API. Written as two adapters with two mappings, the same observation arrives twice with two shapes and two ids, and every reader downstream has to know which half of the history came from which path.

Decision. A source is one mapping with two entrances.

  1. Every source adapter has a file mode (NAME, sniff, run) that reads what the owner already holds: an export, a backup, a folder. Where the source offers it, the same adapter has a live mode (configure, pull, watermark) that logbook sync <NAME> runs. A source without an API has the file mode only; a source without an export format still has the file mode, reading the interchange JSON of its profile (a logbook export line minus the chain fields), so a line can always be re-added from a file.
  2. Both modes produce identical lines with the same raw_id. One function is the mapping, and both modes call it; the live mode hands it what the API returns, the file mode what the file says. Dedupe on (source, raw_id) in append_many then makes a backfilled line and the same line pulled live one line: import the history from the export once, let sync carry on from there, and re-run either in any order without a duplicate.
  3. The mapping owns the identity. raw_id comes from the source's own stable id when it has one (<tracker_id>:<timestamp>, granola:<note id>), else from the content (<source>:<sha256 of the file bytes>). It never depends on which entrance the item came through, on a file name, or on the record it lands in.
  4. What the API gives beyond the file is ignored, not mapped twice. Fields the file mode cannot see (a server-side row id, a processing status) stay out of the line, so the two modes cannot drift apart. What only the API can give and the file cannot — a derived summary, a later edit — is a separate line that points at the shared one by id, never a variant of it.

This is the rule for every adapter from now on. dawarich (dawarich.draft, called by the export reader and by dawarich_live) and imessage (one reader for the backup's sms.db and the Mac's chat.db) are the existing examples; transcript + granola is the first written under the rule (transcript.draft is the mapping; the file adapter and logbook sync granola both call it).

Consequences. - An adapter's test suite has one test more: the file fixture and the same items served by a fake of the API must come out as equal drafts. A live adapter without a file counterpart, or a file adapter with a live sibling that maps differently, is a bug. - A first sync can resume from the record's newest line of its source and kind (Index.newest), because the backfilled lines are the same lines it would have pulled. - A live mode's extra lines (Granola's summary as note/v1 with extra.derived_from) need the id of the shared line whether that line is being written now or was backfilled months ago, so append_many keeps an id a draft brings and a live adapter may ask the record for one (lookup) before it mints its own. - The interchange JSON of a profile is a first-class file format for its adapter, not a debugging aid: it is how a line leaves and re-enters the record without an API.

docs.title: ADR 0018 — Assets are subjects, not places
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-09-30 · rule 4 amended 2026-10-14 (RFC 0037)

Context. The owner's boat, aircraft and car move, and they move without the owner. A yacht on a delivery passage, an aircraft flown by a partner, a car lent to a friend: each has a position at every instant, and the owner's phone is somewhere else. The record so far has one track, the owner's (location/v1, RFC 0001), and the tempting shortcut is to treat the boat as a place the owner is sometimes at, the way a house or an office is. That is wrong twice. A place does not move, so a visit to it can be derived from the owner's track alone; a boat's position is a second observation, made by a second instrument (an AIS or ADS-B receiver), that the owner's track cannot supply. And the interesting fact, the owner was aboard, is a relation between two tracks, not a property of either: the same boat position means one thing when the owner's phone is on deck and another when the owner is at home and the boat is out with the yard's skipper.

Decision.

  1. An asset is a subject with its own track. A boat, an aircraft or a car is registered once in the record, in <root>/assets.json, as {id, kind, name, mmsi?, icao24?, registration?} with kind one of yacht, aircraft, car. Its positions are location/v1 lines like the owner's, with subject set to the asset's id (RFC 0001, amended). The owner is never a subject: absent means the owner, and there is no id for them.
  2. A position of an asset is written as observed, by the instrument that observed it. logbook sync ais asks aisstream.io for the position reports of every registered MMSI; logbook sync adsb asks the OpenSky Network for the state of every registered icao24. Each report is one line, source ais or adsb, tracker aisstream or opensky, raw_id from the instrument, the identifier and the fix time (aisstream:<mmsi>:<unix seconds>, opensky:<icao24>:<unix seconds>), so a report seen twice is one line (ADR 0017), and each asset carries its own watermark in state/<source>.json. What the receiver reports beyond the position (speed, course, navigational status, callsign, altitude) is kept as RFC 0001 says.
  3. "Aboard" is derived, never written. Whether the owner was on the boat is a downstream judgement (ADR 0011, ADR 0013): an engine pass that compares the owner's track with the asset's over a window and decides, by distance and duration, that they moved together. No adapter writes it, no location line carries it, and a change of mind about the threshold changes no line in the record. The same holds for who was aboard: a guest's phone is not in the record, and the record does not guess.
  4. The registry is a setting, not the chain. assets.json is read by the sync commands and by readers that want to name an asset; it is edited by logbook assets add and by hand; it is not hashed. A line whose subject the registry no longer names is still valid and still shown, under the id it carries. Renaming an asset is editing the registry; the lines keep the id. Amended 2026-10-14 (RFC 0037): an entry is never deleted to say an asset is gone. A status/v1 line says it — sold or let-go, logbook status asset ID sold — and closes the entry with until, the line's local day, written into the entry beside its other keys. The line is the statement and until its copy: a reader of the lines (status list asset) takes the day from the standing line, never from the file, so a retracted status line closes nothing there. A place of places.json let go (a berth given up) is closed the same way. The sync commands still ask for every identifier an entry names, closed or not, until the identifier is taken out of the entry.

Amendment to rule 4 (2026-10-14, RFC 0037, a draft). The registry is a setting, not the chain, and its entries are never deleted. An asset the owner sold or let go stays in assets.json; one status/v1 line (RFC 0037 §10), sold or let-go, tier 2 and with no money on it, closes the entry with until, the last local day the asset was the owner's, and the owner writes it (logbook status asset NAME sold --until YYYY-MM-DD). From the day after until the entry is closed: readers still name the asset by it, sync ais and sync adsb ask for no position of it, and a position line that reaches the record anyway (an import, another machine's sync) is still valid and still shown, as is every line whose subject the registry names or no longer names, under the id it carries. Retracting the status line (RFC 0003) reopens the entry. Renaming an asset is still editing the registry, and the lines keep the id. Where the consequences below say the owner decides "by registering or removing the asset", read "by registering or closing it". The same holds for a place in places.json, closed by a let-go line (RFC 0037 §10.3).
