Consequences. - One profile, two tracks. show collapses runs of points by source and subject, so a day at sea reads as two rows (the phone's points and the boat's), and an engine that derives days, trips and places reads the owner's track by filtering subject absent, as before; nothing already written changes meaning. - Every asset the owner tracks is one entry and two environment variables at most; a new instrument (a GPS tracker in the car, a satellite messenger) is a new adapter that writes the same lines with subject set, never a new profile. - Identity stays with the mapping (ADR 0017 rule 3): re-running sync ais after a network failure, or running it from two machines, appends nothing twice. - The record can hold an asset's history from before the owner had it or after they sold it (the receiver does not know who owns the hull). Whether such lines belong is the owner's call at sync time, by registering or removing the asset; the record records what was asked for.

docs.title: ADR 0019 — Trips are derived, never written
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-10-01

Context. The readers now turn the record into stays, nights, countries and company (derive stays, rollup, the with module), and the next thing a person wants to read back is the trip: the weekend aboard, the week in Zürich, with its route, its nights, who was there and the flights at each end. A trip is the first derived thing that feels like a fact of its own — people name trips, remember them, and would expect one to be in the logbook. The tempting design is a line for the derived trip, written by an engine when it finds one, so that show and the pages can read it like a flight or an event. That would put a judgement into the chain. A trip exists because of a threshold (what counts as away, what counts as a night), a setting (which places are home), and a derivation that improves with every version of the readers; a line, once written, is what the chain says happened. The record already has a rule for this, ADR 0013 rule 7 and ADR 0018 rule 3: raw and derived never share a line, and aboard is derived, never written.

Decision.

  1. A trip is a reader's output. logbook trips computes trips from the nights of a window every time it runs: a run of consecutive days whose overnight stay is outside every home region (places.json, kind home) or in transit, with its route, nights, places, people and the flights in and out, and asset set when every night was aboard one asset. Nothing is appended. Changing the home places, the night window or the readers' rules changes the trips the next run prints and changes no line.
  2. A trip has a derived id, not a line id. trip:<first day>:<last day>, reproducible from the record (ARCHITECTURE: derived ids are stable so that human notes stay attached). It is what a note or a page refers to; it is never the id of a line.
  3. The captain's naming is the line. When the captain names a trip ("Midsummer aboard", "the Zürich week"), that is a note/v1 line, written through logbook add as any note, in the captain's words, dated inside the trip. The name is a fact — the captain said it — and it is the only part of a trip that enters the chain. A reader that shows a trip may show the notes of its days beside it; it does not parse them into fields.
  4. No profile for the derived trip. This ADR declines one rather than deferring it. RFC 0020's trip/v1 is a different thing and keeps its name: one bought movement or metered stop — a ride, a ticket, a parking session — as the service recorded it, raw evidence like a flight line. A source that supplies journeys of its own (an airline's itinerary, a travel app's export, a rail app's tickets) writes what it has — flights, events, trip/v1 records — as those profiles; the trip of this ADR is derived over them and is never one of them.

Consequences. - trips is cheap to change and safe to be wrong: a bad threshold is a bad printout, not a bad line. - The pages and the rollups that mention trips (rollup nights and its longest trip, the asset page's trips aboard) all derive from the same trips function, so they agree. - A circle page that shares a trip shares derived rows (ARCHITECTURE, the circle), signed by the owner at that head, never a trip line. - The cost: there is no list of trips to grep in the files, and a reader that wants one runs the derivation over the window it needs. That is the same cost derive stays already carries, and the same choice ADR 0007 made for the index: derived is disposable.

docs.title: ADR 0020 — Tiers 2–3 are sealed with age; the chain covers a salted digest, the ciphertext sits beside it
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-10-03 · extends ADR 0015, amends nothing in ADR 0014

Context. SPEC §4 promised since v0.2 that tiers 2 and 3 would be "encrypted with the owner's key (a later version)", and SECURITY.md promised a key that never leaves the owner's machine. The adversary is anyone who obtains the files: a stolen laptop, a sync folder, a backup, a disk sold on. Encrypting a payload asks one question of the format that everything else hangs on: what does the hash chain cover once the payload is ciphertext? RFC 0025 worked out three answers and what each breaks. Over the plaintext (A): every existing hash survives and a crossing package needs nothing new, but verify without the key can check no hash past the first sealed line, so a lost key loses the chain as well as the words, and an unsalted hash of a short payload lets an adversary confirm a guess. Over the ciphertext (B): verify is today's code and the second implementation needs no cryptography, but age sealing is randomised and a header changes with its recipients, so adding a recovery key or a new laptop rewrites the chain with a lineage entry every time, a circle member gets ciphertext it cannot open or an opened copy nothing binds to the hash, and the conformance fixture can never regenerate to the same head. A benchmark (docs/rfcs/bench-encryption-2026-10.md) measured per-line age at 128–214 µs to seal and 145–194 µs to open on a slow core, 2.2 times a plain line, keyed verify of three million lines in eight to ten minutes against under three keyless, memory flat.

Decision. Option C of RFC 0029, as the RFC states it after the captain's answers of 2026-10-02:

  1. A sealed line keeps a plain payload that is a reference, and carries the content sealed in payload_enc, outside the hash as id is. The sealed bytes are canonical_json({payload, salt}), the digest their SHA-256, the reference {"schema": "sealed/v1", "of": <the real schema>, "digest"}; payload_enc is the age file, X25519 recipients, binary, as standard base64. The pre-image of SPEC §3 does not change. A verifier without the key checks the whole chain and the sealed-line rule and reports what it did not open; one with the key opens every sealed line and treats a digest mismatch as the record's error, exactly as ADR 0015 treats a present attachment whose bytes do not match its name.
  2. The salt is inside the sealed bytes and the digest, 16 random bytes, so the digest confirms nothing to anyone without the key.
  3. The envelope stays plain: at, end, tz, source, kind, tier, recorded_at. A day is listed, a line located, a chain verified, all without a key. What that gives away (the shape of a life, not its words) is stated in RFC 0029 §2, and sealing kind and source is declined for 0.3.
  4. One identity per record, two recipients or none. The long-term secret is the owner's X25519 identity; the public recipients are in logbook.json; the identity lives at <config dir>/logbook/identities/<owner_id>.txt or where LOGBOOK_IDENTITY_FILE points, never in the record and never in a variable that is on disk; key init refuses to seal until a recovery recipient exists; no passphrase by default. Adding or rotating a recipient reseals payload_enc and the sealed files, changes no hash, and appends one rekey/v1 line.
  5. A writer without the identity refuses tiers 2–3 (it cannot dedupe through the blinded index) and writes tier 1. export writes opened payloads by default, the interchange form of ADR 0017, and the lines verbatim under --sealed.
  6. Attachments are sealed under their plaintext name, the age header the marker, raised and never lowered, so a verbatim reference resolves and two lines sharing bytes share one file.
  7. The index moves to the cache directory and blinds raw_id under a key it keeps sealed to the recipients; the search table holds no words of a sealed line.
  8. A 0.3 implementation reads 0.2 without migration: the hash rule did not change. Sealing the past is a migration with lineage and a migration/v1 line; the plain files are not kept beside the record.
  9. A crossing package reseals sealed lines and files to the destination's recipient from policy/crossing.json, or ships them opened under --open; the owner's hashed fields cross verbatim either way, so RFC 0005's promise holds.
  10. Per-line age, not a record data key. The benchmark's numbers did not force the variant and its costs were not wanted: a key inside the record and a construction the age CLI cannot open. The 20,000 lines a second floor is tier-1-only; sealed lines get a floor of 4,000 a second at two recipients.

Consequences. Level 1 conformance stays an afternoon: one new field outside the hash and one payload shape. Level 2 adds age, and the second implementation's fixture is a sealed sample with a published example identity. verify grows a report of sealed, opened and plain lines. A lost key loses the words of tiers 2–3 and never the chain. Encryption at rest protects copies made after it is turned on; a backup from before holds the plaintext, and seal --all says so once. The price is a record about 2.2 times larger per sealed line and a keyed verify three times slower than a keyless one, both measured and accepted. Every rule of this ADR is SPEC §1, §1.1, §2, §3, §3.1, §4 and §6 as of v0.3, and RFC 0029 is the record of how it was reached.

docs.title: ADR 0021 — journey/v1 is the written form of RFC 0020
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-10-05

Context. ADR 0019 rule 4 says RFC 0020's trip/v1 "keeps its name". RFC 0031 (the profile freeze) renames it journey/v1 for new lines, so that trip names the derived trip alone, and asks whether a one-sentence ADR is worth its number.

Decision. That one sentence of ADR 0019 rule 4 is superseded, and only it: a bought movement or a metered stop (RFC 0020) is written as kind: "journey", payload.schema: "journey/v1" from this date; readers accept trip/trip/v1 and journey/journey/v1 as one profile; nothing is migrated (SPEC §3). Everything else in ADR 0019 stands: a trip is derived, never written, and has a derived id.

Consequences. easypark, sbb and passages write journey; show and search read both; RFC 0020 carries the amendment; a record holds both spellings for as long as it holds its old lines.

docs.title: ADR 0022 — The record has one home; everything else reads
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-10-09 · extends ADR 0001, ADR 0016 and ADR 0020

Context. ADR 0001 made the folder the truth and ADR 0003 made it one log; ADR 0016 put the ceiling for every crossing in the record itself and made every crossing a line. What none of them says is where the folder lives once more than one machine wants it. The owner's set-up now has four kinds of device: one always-on machine at home, a laptop, phones, and an agent on a private VPS that runs the daily loop. The sync schedule (sync --install-schedule), the MCP server and the local models all assume a machine that has the record's files; the writer lock (#237) assumes one process at a time on one machine; doctor already refuses a record under a sync client's folder because that client rewrites files underneath the writer and puts the record on someone else's server. Two writable copies would need a merge the chain does not have (SPEC §3: one head, append only), and a bridge that carries messages through a cloud machine would carry tier-2 content through it before the record has sealed anything (ADR 0020). The question is not new, but every answer so far was a convention nobody wrote down, and the first collaborator and the first cloud model will each need to be told the same thing.

Decision.

  1. One machine is the record's home. It holds the only writable copy. It runs the sync schedule, the MCP server and the local models, and it serves the Day page over the owner's private network (the tailnet), never from a cloud machine when the page shows tier-2 content. Messaging reaches it through Beeper's on-device connections today and may reach it through a self-hosted Matrix homeserver with mautrix bridges later; the lines are the same either way, so the choice of carrier is the owner's and not the format's.
  2. Every other device is a reader. A phone or a laptop holds a sealed backup (logbook backup) or an export, or reads through the MCP server under the mcp ceiling. There is no second writable copy, and the record folder is never in a file sync (iCloud Drive, Dropbox, Syncthing or any other): doctor fails the first and nothing here softens that.
  3. Orchestrators reach the record only through the crossing. An agent on a VPS, a cron, a phone: each reads with the read tools under policy/crossing.json and writes with the few write tools the owner allows by name, today the day's signature and its note (amended 27 October 2026: and add_note and promise_done, which until then wrote with no entry; every line those three write has source mcp, never manual). They never hold the record's files, never get a copy of the key, and never run a writer of their own.
  4. Sources come to the home. A messaging app connects on the home machine, as a linked device or a local database (iMessage, Telegram, Signal, WhatsApp), and writes through sync under the lock. A bridge on a cloud machine would carry tier-2 content through that machine, so it is not done.
  5. A collaborator's access is a separate OS user on the home machine, after sealing at rest (ADR 0020), with the MCP socket and the tailnet and not the record's files. Never on the owner's working laptop.
  6. The cloud ceiling is the owner's and is written down. Every cloud model or service that may see record content has its own entry in policy/crossing.json with a max_tier and, where the access is temporary, an until date ({"cloud-model": {"max_tier": 2, "until": "2026-12-31"}}). The entry holds through that day; an entry that has expired counts as tier 0, and doctor names it. There is no entry that covers "the cloud"; each service is named.
  7. The home is recorded and checked. sync --install-schedule writes state/home.json with the hostname and the date; doctor passes when it runs on that host or when no home is set, and warns on any other machine that writers belong on the home. The writer lock records the hostname beside the pid and the command, so a lock left by another machine is read as such.

Alternatives considered.

  • The record on the VPS, beside the agent. The agent would then hold the files, the key and the ceiling in one place that is not the owner's, and every tier would be one misconfiguration from the cloud. The crossing exists so that an orchestrator never needs the files; moving the files to it inverts ADR 0016.
  • The record synced between the laptop and the home machine. Two writers on one chain need a merge the format refuses to have, and a sync client is exactly what doctor fails a record for. A conflict would be found at the next verify, after the files were already wrong.
  • The laptop as the home. A laptop is closed, asleep and away; the schedule, the MCP and the local models want a machine that is on, and the collaborator's OS user does not belong on the machine the owner works at. It may be the home for now (consequences), but it is not the design.

Consequences. The owner's laptop may be the home for now: sync --install-schedule there names it, and doctor on the always-on machine says so until the record moves. Home moves by copying the record once (logbook backup, then backup restore, or one cp) and running sync --install-schedule on the new machine, which names it; never by syncing, and the old copy becomes a reader or is deleted. A phone is a reader and a camera, never a writer, until the day a reader on it can write through the crossing. Every cloud model the owner tries is one line in the policy with a date, and an experiment the owner forgets to end ends itself. The collaborator's first day is an OS account and a tailnet invitation, not a copy of the folder. What this ADR does not decide: the transport of the shared page (ARCHITECTURE, "The circle"), and whether the MCP server will one day listen on the tailnet itself rather than over stdio on the home; both are RFCs when they come.

docs.title: ADR 0023 — Digital events do not make a stay
docs.text:
Status: proposed · 2026-10-13 · narrows SPEC §3.2.3 rule 5 (SPEC 0.4); records what #263 changed in the reference

Context. derive stays clusters the owner's location points. A cluster shorter than stay_min_s (20 minutes) is a stop unless evidence falls inside it, and SPEC §3.2.3 rule 5 promoted it to a stay on any line of the kinds event, transcript, note, call, message and photo. The rule was written when every event/v1 line came from a calendar (ios-calendar, then ics) or from Google Home's history of the door, and each of those puts the owner at a place at a time. Since then the record has taken events from sources that are not physical: sync notion writes a page edited (#253), sync drive a file changed (#256), and until #263 sync gtasks wrote a task created or completed. Such an event happens nowhere. Say Ola Nordmann changes the crew list in a Drive folder Ines shares with him at 14:05, while Ines's phone sits for ten minutes at a café in Oslo. The café became a stay with one event attached, and places propose, which reads the same stays, offered it as a place to name. The more sources a record has, the more stops become stays for reasons that say nothing about where the owner was. #263 changed the reference (stays.somewhere, and the same test in reading.owner_track for places propose) and left the spec as it was, so the text and the reference disagreed.

Decision.

  1. An event is evidence only when it happened somewhere. It passes any of four tests: its source is a calendar (ios-calendar, ics); it is Google Home's history (source google-takeout, calendar.id google-home); its payload carries a location with something other than whitespace in it; or its payload carries attendees, a list with at least one member. SPEC 0.4 §3.2.3 rule 5 states the four tests exactly; in the reference they are stays.somewhere, stays.CALENDARS and stays.HOME_HISTORY.
  2. What the line carries decides, and a source is named only when its entries are a place and a time whatever they carry. A Wallet pass with its venue, or a ticket with its address, promotes from any source, and a new source needs no change to the rule. An event that carries neither, from a source that is neither (Notion, Drive, a task list), is a digital event. It promotes nothing and attached does not count it. show still lists it on its day.
  3. Only events are narrowed. #263 changed the event and nothing else, and this ADR records that and no more: transcripts, notes, calls, messages and photos promote as before, and a line of any other kind (mail, task, browse, …) was never evidence and is not now. Whether a message that reached the owner's phone in a pocket on a tram is presence is a separate question. A change to it is a new ADR and a new SPEC version.

Alternatives considered.

  • Drop events from evidence altogether. A calendar entry and the arrival at the door are the best evidence the record has that a short stop was a visit: the ten-minute meeting, the drop-off at home. Without them, real visits would go back to being stops.
  • Name the digital sources instead (notion, drive, …). Every new adapter that writes events would promote until someone remembered to add it to the list. Naming the physical sources and testing the payload fails closed: a new digital source promotes nothing.
  • Count a digital event when the owner made it. For most sources the record cannot tell who changed a file. And even an edit the owner made carries no place: it could have been made from anywhere.
  • Leave the spec as it was and call the reference's test a reader's own. §3.2 exists so that two implementations derive the same stays. §6.1 compares segments, and a segment's kind, promoted and attached all depend on this rule.

Consequences.

  • SPEC goes to 0.4, with rule 5 and the inputs of §3.2.3 rewritten and a version history added. The format does not change: §1–§3.1 stay as they are, a record still names logbook/0.3, no hash changes, and no conformance fixture or head changes. Every event in conformance/ carries attendees or a location, and every event of the seed-1 demo record of §6.1 is an ios-calendar entry, so each passes the tests as it passed the old rule. From 0.4 on, the document's version and the format's name are two numbers.
  • A record with digital events derives some stays as stops that it used to promote. Nothing in the record changes; the next run of derive stays, day, days, trips and places propose prints the new reading (ADR 0013: derived is disposable).
  • The event/v1 lines sync gtasks wrote before #263 stay in the record. They carry no location and no attendees and come from no calendar, so they promote nothing.
  • A new source whose entries are a place and a time whatever they carry joins the list in rule 5 and stays.CALENDARS together, and that is a SPEC version. Any other source writes location or attendees when it has them, and promotes through those.
  • logbook-ts promotes on every event today (promotes in src/day.ts, at 5452b8a). Until it takes the four tests, the two implementations disagree on a record with digital events. Neither the conformance fixtures nor the demo record holds one, so no comparison that runs today shows the difference. logbook-ts is asked to confirm parity.

docs.title: ADR 0024 — The owner's phone writes through the Library
docs.text:
Status: proposed · 2026-10-20 · amends ADR 0022's consequence "a phone is a reader and a camera, never a writer"

Context. ADR 0022 made one machine the record's home and every other device a reader, and said of the phone that it is "a reader and a camera, never a writer, until the day a reader on it can write through the crossing". The Library (logbook serve) binds 127.0.0.1 and answers a form only from this machine's own pages (Site.write). The owner closes his days on the Day page, and travels for two weeks without the Air. On the Air, tailscale serve --bg 8765 already puts the Library behind HTTPS on his tailnet: tailscaled forwards each request to 127.0.0.1:8765 from loopback, the phone reads every page, and every form is refused because the browser's Origin is the tailnet name. #335 asked whether a second, explicit setting should let that one name write; the owner answered yes on 20 October 2026.

Decision.

  1. One setting, off by default. logbook.json MAY carry "phone": {"origin": "https://<machine>.<tailnet>.ts.net", "login": "<tailnet login>"}. It is written by logbook setup phone only, after a yes typed at a terminal, and removed by --off; never by the Library and never by an agent. A reader's setting, as day_start is: no line, hash or month file changes with it, and SPEC §1 already has writers keep keys they do not know.
  2. The gate adds the phone, and takes away only what came through a proxy. A POST to http://127.0.0.1 or http://[::1] from this machine answered today is answered as today (decision 5 says which requests are this machine's). In addition, with the setting, a POST from loopback is answered when it carries exactly one Origin, equal to the setting's after normalisation; exactly one Host, the setting's host; exactly one Tailscale-User-Login, the header Tailscale Serve sets from the device's tailnet identity, equal to the login; and no Sec-Fetch-Dest but document. Anything else is a 403 with nothing written.
  3. The writer is still the home. The phone holds no file, no key and no copy; the Library writes through the CLI's own functions under the writer lock, as for a click on the Air. ADR 0022's one home and one chain are unchanged. What changes is who may click: the owner's own phone, on his tailnet, by his login.
  4. Not the crossing. The policy's write list (ADR 0022, the MCP door) is the agent's door and is never read here. An agent never writes this setting.
  5. A proxied request is the phone's or nothing. A request is proxied when its Host is not a loopback literal (127.0.0.1 or [::1], any port) or when it carries any Tailscale-* or X-Forwarded-* header. A proxied POST is answered only through decision 2's checks and refused (a 403, nothing written) when the setting is off, whatever Origin it sends or leaves out; requests to http://127.0.0.1:8765 or http://[::1]:8765 from this machine (any port, no proxy header) are answered as before; a request naming any other host, localhost included, is treated as coming through a proxy.

Considered. Binding the tailnet address — the server would listen beyond loopback and every device on the tailnet would reach the port directly; refused. The Origin alone — any device on the tailnet, a shared-in user among them, could send it by hand; the login ties it to the owner. A token in the page — a secret the server would keep, and a second thing to get right where the Origin and Tailscale's identity already suffice.

Consequences. A phone is a reader, a camera, and, when the owner names it, the hand that clicks the Library's forms through Tailscale Serve. Tailscale's behaviour is now part of the gate: that serve forwards the Host it was asked for, sets Tailscale-User-Login from the device's identity and drops one the client sent, and sends none for a tagged device or a Funnel request. The setting assumes it and the docs say to verify it with one star from the phone before relying on it; the gate refuses a login header sent twice, in case it is ever appended rather than replaced. tailscale funnel on the port is never to be used: it would put the reading pages on the internet whatever this setting says. A process on the Air can forge every header, as it can already write today. A program on the tailnet that sends no Origin was answered as this machine before this ADR, since behind Tailscale Serve it arrives from loopback; decision 5 closes it (the owner's word of 21 October 2026), and rests on tailscaled sending the tailnet name as Host and adding X-Forwarded-*. A raw TCP forward of the port (tailscale serve --tcp, any port forward) adds no header and keeps the client's Host, so its requests read as this machine's: the Library is served through Tailscale Serve's HTTPS proxy only.

docs.title: ADR 0025 — Derived tables: the whole-record pages in seconds, cold
docs.text:
Status: proposed · 2026-10-21 · builds on ADR 0001, ADR 0007, ADR 0013 and ADR 0019, RFC 0029 §8 and #336; answers #336's first open question; changes no line, no envelope, no SPEC

Context. #336 made every page of the Library answer warm within a millisecond on a record of five million lines (/gaps, which reads its clock again, in 0.06 s). It did that with three things. The server keeps a page by its tag (Site._keep). It reads what several pages read alike once for the record as it stands (Site.shared, keyed by Site._state: logbook.json, the record's today and the files beside the chain). And its readers stream through Index.stream instead of holding a kind whole. Cold is another matter. "Cold" means the first request after the server starts, or after a sync moves the head, and the scheduled runs move it four times a day (docs/schedule.md). At 5 M lines the pages that read the whole record still take minutes cold. These are #336's numbers on main (docs/serve.md, Measured), in seconds:

page cold at 5 M after append peak memory /people 502 354 1.8 GB /people/ID 522 522 1.6 GB /manifest 187 187 700 MB /org/ID 87 188 649 MB /manifest/people 91 91 688 MB /promises 293 277 86 MB /world 280 293 2.8 GB /agents 68 64 96 MB /places 46 47 1.3 GB /trips, /journeys 41, 39 38, 37 1.9, 2.1 GB /ideas 20 20 278 MB

The cause is the same on every row: each reader recomputes from the lines. people.read streams every message, call, mail, event, transcript, photo and note line of its window and derives the owner's stays again. promises.extract runs its rules over every mail, message, transcript and note. orgs.read reads every line of seven kinds whole. world reads the record one year at a time through reading.read, every line of every day. All of that is thrown away at the next head, even when the sync appended a few thousand messages of one day. RFC 0043 §11–12 proposes a timeline with year and all-years zooms (/timeline/life: per place and per vessel, the visits, the years and who was there). Built the same way, those zooms would be the slowest pages of all.

docs.title: 336 asked the owner whether to keep these readings across a restart and grow them with each sync. docs/serve.md calls it a decision for the record's owner, because those readings hold what the pages read of sealed lines. This ADR is that proposal.
docs.text:
The rule stays as ADR 0001, 0007 and 0013 set it. The files are the truth and every database is a cache. Anything derived is disposable and can be reproduced from the files.

Decision.

  1. A derived table is a reader's cache, never a line. Its rows are computed from the standing lines by the reader's own code, the function the page calls on a miss. They are never appended, never in the record's folder and never read by verify. Deleting them loses nothing: a reader that finds them missing, stale or of another version computes from the lines as it does today. The pages' output is unchanged byte for byte (decision 9).

  2. They live in a second cache file beside the index, not in it. The file is summaries.sqlite, in the same cache folder as index.sqlite (<cache dir>/logbook/<owner_id>/, Logbook.index_path; RFC 0029 §8), so a copy of the record folder never carries it. Both places were weighed:

  3. Inside index.sqlite, as observed_entities is (schema 8):
    • for: one file to discard, and one transaction holds the lines and their summaries at one head.
    • against, first: the index is written by every append, inside the writer lock (Logbook.append → Index.add), under SQLite's busy timeout. A build of summaries holds a write transaction for seconds after a sync, and minutes the first time. That is the lock a writer must never wait on, and it is why #336 builds even its two added indexes with a busy timeout of 0 and only from the Library (Index.add_indexes).
    • against, second: Index.rebuild drops and remakes the tables it owns, as it does observed_entities. A rebuilt index would take the summaries with it, even when only the index's own schema had moved.
    • against, third: it moves SCHEMA_VERSION (decision 10).
  4. A second file: its own lock, its own version and its own stamp. A writer never opens it. A build never touches the index's lock, and a reader of the index never waits on a build. It runs in WAL mode, so a page that reads it is not blocked by a build that writes it. Consistency with the index comes from the stamp (decision 3), not from a shared transaction.

Chosen: the second file. The module that owns it is logbook/core/summaries.py, because the core readers (days, trips, people) read from it and core imports nothing above it (ARCHITECTURE.md). The tables of the shelves are built by contrib modules that register with it.

  1. A table is keyed by the head it was computed at, and by everything else it reads. Each table has its own stamp in the file's meta, in the shape observed_entities_meta already has:
  2. the head and seq it was brought to;
  3. a SHA-256 of logbook.json without its head and seq: the timezone, the day_start, the owner_emails that leave the owner's own refs out of their contacts (people.read, present.owner_of), and whatever else a reader comes to read there, as Site._state digests the whole file;
  4. the recipients, and whether the sealed lines were opened (opened, as the index records it);
  5. the table's own version, raised when its reader's rule changes;
  6. a SHA-256 of each settings file its reader reads. Per table these are policy/stays.json, places.json, assets.json, policy/owner.json, policy/entities.json and policy/crossing.json.

A table whose stamp differs in anything but the head is built again whole. Settings change rarely, and a renamed place or a new home moves every night after it. A table whose head is behind is brought forward (decision 4). A process without the identity on a record with recipients never writes a table, since it cannot compute one equal to a keyed reader's. It reads the lines as today.

  1. Brought forward as lines are appended, from the lines appended since its head. The record is append-only, so the lines a table has not seen are those with seq above its stamp. The index finds them by its primary key, and only they are read from the files. Before anything else, the builder reads the line at the stamped seq and checks that its hash is the stamped head. If it is not, the chain was rewritten: a migration that sealed the past (SPEC §3.1), or a fork repaired. Every table is then built again whole, and a migration line forces the same.

Every day a new line touches is computed again whole, from that day's lines, by the reader's own per-day function. Nothing is added to a stored number in place (+=), so a stored day is always what the reader computes for it. That a line can only add to its own day is used only to bound which days are recomputed. Which days a line touches, kind by kind: 1. An observation without supersedes touches its own local day (the index's day_local). A backfill touches the past days it lands on, which is still exact. Three kinds touch more than that: - A line that feeds the owner's stays touches the days whose stays and nights it can change. These lines are a location point of the owner or of an asset assets.json names, and a line of presence evidence (a transcript, note, call, message or photo, or an event that happened somewhere; SPEC §3.2.3 rule 5, ADR 0023). They touch every day from the day of that subject's previous point before the line's at, through the line's own day. A stay runs until the next point (reading._first_points_after), so a point after a silence can lengthen a stay begun days before. They also touch the day before the first of those, whose night runs into the next morning (stays.night_window). - A health-sample line also touches the next day, whose sleep is the night that ends on it (SPEC §3.2.7 rule 8). - A flight line touches every day that holds a flight line with the same payload date. The standing set of flights is decided per key and per pair of numbers for one flight, without supersedes (SPEC §3.2.4, the standing set). 2. A correction, a line whose supersedes names a line of its own kind (SPEC §3; a line so named is not standing, §3.2), touches its own day and the day of the line it names, found by the lines_id index. These can be different days: a calendar event moved to another day, or a session with an agent that grew past midnight. When the named line was itself a correction, the line that one named stands or falls with it. Its day is touched too (#321: a line is superseded while at least one standing line of its kind supersedes it). 3. A retraction (RFC 0003) touches the day of the line it hides, wherever that line is (SPEC §3.2.1), and everything that line touched under rules i and ii: the stays and nights if it was a point or evidence, and the named line's day if it was a correction, since that line stands again. A hidden resolution or entity line is handled by rule iv. A retraction is never retracted (RFC 0003). 4. A resolution (RFC 0006) or an entity line that binds refs to an org or an idea (RFC 0037) is record-wide: one line re-attributes every past and future line with its refs (RFC 0006 rule 2; present's _resolve, orgs' bindings). So no stored row is attributed to a person or an entity. Rows are kept per ref, the handle or address as the line names it. The overlay (resolve.identities_from over the retractions and resolutions, which every reader already reads whole) is applied when the page reads the rows, so a resolution makes no stored row stale. Some rules need the overlay inside a day: present confirming a name written in a note, or the owner's own refs left out of their contacts (policy/owner.json and its closure over the resolutions). For those, the per-ref rows say which days hold a line with any ref the resolution names. Those days, and no others, are computed again. 5. The small kinds the pages read whole today stay read whole and are not summarised: status, task, goal, chapter, draft, story, the signatures, stars and reviews. They are the closing of a promise, the state of an org, the signed day. They are few, and the pages apply them at read time as now.

Bringing a table forward is a reader's act. It writes only the cache file, in one BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction that commits only if the stamp is still the one it started from. Two builders, the scheduled run and the Library, cannot interleave, and the second finds the work done.

  1. Precomputed at the 06:00 close and after each sync. sync --scheduled brings every table forward right after its sync --all, before doctor. That covers the four scheduled runs (commands/sync.py, _sync_scheduled), the 06:00 close (--close) among them. It says so in one line: summaries: 3 days computed again in 2.1 s. A manual logbook sync brings them forward too, but never builds a table whole. The first full build, and any build again whole, is made by logbook repair index, which already shows its progress, and by the scheduled run when the schedule is installed. Installing the schedule is the owner's own opt-in, so no CPU is spent unasked (#336's second open question). The Library brings a table forward on the first request after a head moves, when the delta is all it lacks. It never builds a table whole inside a request: that page is computed from the lines as today, and doctor says why (decision 8).

  2. A warm Library keeps them in memory. What Site.shared builds from the lines today, it builds from the tables: the whole record's people, last contacts and open promises; the year's ranking; the orgs; the promises; the sessions with an agent. It is still keyed by _state and dropped when the state moves, and the page cache is unchanged. A head move costs the bring-forward plus reading the rows: seconds, not minutes. The in-memory form is rows, not the readers' full objects, so the resident size should fall with the cold time. That is an estimate, measured in each slice.

  3. What is summarised, page by page. Every table holds numbers, days, seqs, line ids, place ids, entity ids from places.json and assets.json, tiers and refs. A ref from a sealed line is stored blinded, as HMAC-SHA256 under the file's own key, exactly as the index blinds raw_id (RFC 0029 §8). The key is sealed to the recipients in the file's meta. A ref from a plain line is stored plain, as the index stores it. No word is stored: no quote, subject, title, message text or name. Names come from the overlay and from places.json at read time. The few words a page shows (a promise's quote, the title of a session or of an org's latest mail) are read from the lines that page shows, by seq through the index, as last_real_contact.what already does (person_page.read, one Index.by_id).

table one row per what it holds the readers it serves, and what they compute today days local day, gate the night after (where, home, aboard, in_transit, stay, located), country, moved_m, flights by line id, stays (count, attached, with_attachments), the confirmed people as refs, health (sleep_h, steps, resting_hr, hrv) days.summarise per day for /days and logbook days; the nights trips.trips folds; the night before and after on the Day page; the Year reader's countries, nights and health by month (year.read) day_sources day, source, tier lines, first and newest at the Day's and /days' sources, and the gaps against the usual sources (days.usual_sources) stays stay or stop of the owner's track, gate start, end, kind, place id or rounded position, aboard, promoted, attached counts by kind (messages, photos, calls, …), refs present with confirmed or proposed and the reason the timeline's moments (RFC 0043 §11); people._together's days together and nights; World's nights, photos, first and last per place and asset (world.build); the Places page's nights per named place trips trip, gate trip:<start>:<end>, until, nights, in_transit, route and places as ids, asset, nights_aboard, flights in and out by line id, refs, lines trips.trips for /trips, /journeys and a journey's page; World's journeys. Recomputed whole from days and stays whenever a night changes, which is a fold over a few thousand rows (ADR 0019: a trip is still a reader's output) places place or cluster, year, gate visits, nights, hours, first, last, photos, refs /timeline/life (RFC 0043 §12), World, the Places page's named-place nights. Recomputed whole from stays, like trips contacts ref, day, kind, tier lines, first and last at, the last line's seq, spoke_s for a transcript, and the day's real-contact class (together, call, meeting, message) with its line people.read's channels (lines, first, last, tier, last_line, spoke_s) and days; people_drift.real_contacts; a person's page years, places, nights, drift, anniversaries contact_years ref, year, kind, tier the year's days as a bit string (366 bits), lines, first, last /people's ranking by days and person_page.ranked. A person's days are the union of their refs' bit strings, exact where a sum of counts would count one day twice. Recomputed for the years a touched day is in promise_candidates line holding a proposal seq, day, kind, source, the rule, the match's offsets in the line's body, due, the speaker's and counterpart's refs, tier promises.extract's proposals for /promises, a person's you_owe and they_owe, and the MCP. The section (open, kept, dropped) is applied at read from the task lines and the signatures (promises.closes, signing.disposed_lines), and the quote is read from the shown lines touches ref kind (domain, login, repository, merchant, handle, Notion page), ref, day, kind, source, tier count, the last line's seq, Notion's words_delta orgs.read's touches, people, last, documents and money; ideas.read's touches, words, pages, people. Bound to an org or idea at read through the entity lines (rule iv) sessions session line with an agent seq, day, at, end, source, agent, words, tool calls, the owner's and machine's turns, tier, the line it supersedes shelf_agents' sessions. Titles, summaries and turns are read for the 14 days a page shows, as today

The people review, the orgs' and ideas' review queues and the Places review keep their observed_entities rows (RFC 0037). They are clustered over the whole record (places_review anchors on the longest stays first), so they are not a sum of days, and this ADR does not make them one. What it changes in slice 3 is what their stamp names. Instead of the head, they name the seq of the last line of the kinds they read. A sync that appends only messages then leaves the Places review standing. observed_entities stores the labels it reads from opened lines in plain text (entity_review.py, people_review.py), which decision 7 refuses for these tables. That is noted here and not changed: it is its own issue.

  1. What is never summarised: anything a tier gate decides per request. The Library reads every tier (Site.tiers is None). export site passes its tiers, World takes the world ceiling of policy/crossing.json (1 and 2 by default), and the MCP server reads through GatedIndex. So:
  2. A count row holds the lines of one tier. A gated reader sums the rows whose tier is in its gate, as reading.crossing keeps the lines whose tier is.
  3. A derived row is per gate. Stays, nights, trips, places and presence are not sums: a stay promoted by a tier-2 message is a stop to a reader that cannot see tier 2. Each such row is keyed by the gate it was computed under. The Library's (every tier) is kept always. Another is kept for each ceiling a page or the MCP serves from, built the first time it is asked for. A gate the file does not hold is computed from the lines, as today.
  4. Retractions and resolutions are never gated (logbook/core/reading.py's module docstring), so the overlay is the same under every gate.

  5. The clock is never summarised. Today, this year, a silence and the coming anniversaries are applied at read, as CLOCK_PAGES already digests today into the tag. So are a page's request (?year, ?page, ?portfolio, ?money, ?person, ?from, ?to) and the owner's acts in state/.

  6. A summary is proven equal to the reader's own result. The check recomputes a sample and compares, row by row, as canonical JSON.

  7. What it samples: 20 days at random, seeded by the head so a run can be repeated, plus the last 7 days and every day the last bring-forward touched. For each sampled day it also takes the refs on that day, every trip that day is in, and every promise candidate of that day.
  8. How it compares: each is recomputed from the lines by the reader's own function and compared with the stored rows.
  9. doctor runs it as a check named summaries, reading the file read-only (?mode=ro, as its index check reads the index). A pass names what it compared: summaries 20 days, 41 refs, 3 trips equal at 9f2c…. A warn says the file is missing or behind, and how long a build would take. A fail names the table and the day, never a value, and says logbook repair summaries builds it again. The scheduled run's doctor makes it every run.

  10. The tests hold it three ways:

    • tests/test_library_golden.py's seven records render every page with the tables and without them, byte for byte equal to the fixture taken from main.
    • A property test builds the tables at one head, then appends random lines: backfilled past days, location points after a silence, corrections across days, retractions of points, corrections and resolutions, resolutions merging two refs, flights under two numbers. It brings the tables forward and compares every day, ref and trip with a full build and with the reader.
    • tests/test_library_perf.py counts, never times, that a cold /people, /days or /trips after a bring-forward reads from the files only the lines appended since.

  11. The cost.

    • Disk. Measured here on scripts/bench_library.py's record at 200,000 lines (--build-only, then logbook repair index): index.sqlite is 104 MB, 522 bytes a line. That makes about 2.6 GB at 5 M lines. The same record has 3,653 days, 28,620 distinct (day, kind, source, tier) groups, and 128,905 distinct (ref, day, kind) among 144,366 lines of the contact kinds.
    • At 5 M lines days, day_sources, stays, trips and places are tens of thousands of rows: a few MB.
    • contacts has at most one row per contact line, about 3.6 M at 5 M lines. On the 200,000-line record 89% of (ref, day, kind) are distinct, and only a denser record will show how far they fall below one a line as the handles active in a day saturate. So it is 1–3.6 M rows; at a guessed 60 bytes a row, 60–220 MB.
    • contact_years is a few thousand refs × ten years × kinds: about 100,000 rows.
    • promise_candidates, touches and sessions are smaller than contacts.
    • In all, about 100–300 MB at 5 M lines, a tenth of the index or less. These are estimates, to be measured by each slice.
    • Time to build whole at 5 M. A plain logbook repair index of the 200,000-line record took 9.0 s here (45 µs a line), so about 4 minutes at 5 M. RFC 0029 §9 measured 69 s at 3 M plain, and 382–481 s opening the sealed lines. The tables cost what the readers they replace cost once, sharing one reading of each line, so #336's cold times bound them:
    • days, stays, trips and places: between World's reading of every year, 280 s, and /days' rate: 2.29 s for its default fortnight (WINDOW_DAYS), 164 ms a day, about 600 s for 3,653 days.
    • contacts: about the whole-record people.read inside a person's page, a few minutes of its 522 s.
    • promise_candidates: about /promises' 293 s.
    • touches and sessions: about the Manifest's 187 s and Agents' 68 s.
    • Estimate: 5–10 minutes for slice 1, and 20–35 minutes for all three slices, once, on one core. On a sealed record, add the opening of every sealed line once (145–194 µs each, RFC 0029 §9).
    • Time to bring forward. A scheduled sync appends a few thousand lines over one or two days. That is two to four days computed again, at about a Day's reading each (0.67 s cold at 5 M, /day/DAY), plus the refs of those days: seconds. A backfill of a year touches 365 days, at about 164 ms each (/days' fortnight in 2.29 s): about a minute for days, about as much for contacts.
    • Cold page after. The target, held by slice 1's benchmark, is #336's unmet one: under five seconds cold at 5 M for every whole-record page. Reading the rows, applying the overlay and aggregating replaces reading the lines.
    • SCHEMA_VERSION. index.sqlite does not move: no column, index or table of it changes, and the builder reads it through lines(seq) and lines_day_local, which every index has, and lines_id, one of #336's ADDED indexes. An index built before #336 that the Library has not opened since lacks lines_id; the builder gives it one through Index.add_indexes, as the Library does, or finds a named line by a scan, which is slower but still exact. summaries.sqlite carries its own version, and each table its own. Had the tables gone inside the index, the move would have been 8 → 9, as observed_entities moved 7 → 8. Every existing index would then rebuild once, about 4 minutes at 5 M plain and five to seven times that sealed (RFC 0029 §9: 69 s plain against 382–481 s opening, at 3 M). Any older version that opened the index afterwards would rebuild it again for its own schema.
    • logbook-ts and conformance: no effect. The tables are a reader's cache. They are never in SPEC, never in conformance/, and never compared by §6.1, which compares a reader's JSON, unchanged here. logbook-ts may keep a cache of its own or none. It never opens this file, as it never opens index.sqlite (RFC 0029 §11 item 13 is a recommendation for a cache, not conformance). The envelope, the hash and the format are untouched: no SPEC version, no regenerated fixture.

  12. The plan, in slices, each a pull request.

    1. The days. summaries.sqlite, its meta, stamps and key, and the builder: whole, brought forward, and checked. The tables are days, day_sources, stays, trips and places. Also: the doctor check, logbook repair summaries, logbook repair index building them, and the scheduled run's step after the sync. The readers that move are days.read (/days), trips.trips (/trips, /journeys, a journey's page), the Day page's neighbouring nights and readiness window, and the Year reader. The timeline's zooms (RFC 0043 §11–12, once adopted) are built on these tables from their first commit. The per-day function of each reader is split out so the reader and the builder call the same one. The property test, the golden pages with and without the tables, and scripts/bench_library.py timing cold with the tables all come in this slice.
    2. The people. contacts, contact_years, presence per stay, and promise_candidates, since a person's page shows their open promises. The readers that move are people.read, people_drift.real_contacts, person_page.ranked and everyone (/people, /people/ID), and the people review's second whole-record people.read, with the overlay applied at read. The MCP's people readers go through their gate (decision 8).
    3. The Manifest and the shelves. touches for orgs.read and ideas.read (/manifest, /org/ID, /manifest/people, /ideas, /idea/ID). /promises reads promise_candidates, and /agents reads sessions. World reads stays, trips and places. The observed tables are stamped by the lines they read (decision 7).

    Each slice adds its changelog fragment and its tables to the check. It runs LOGBOOK_SLOW=1 uv run pytest tests/test_fuzz_readers.py before it merges, since it touches readers (CLAUDE.md, the merge rules), even though their output must not change.

Alternatives considered.

  • A long-lived process with everything in memory. This is Site.shared today, and it already makes warm pages a millisecond. What it costs:
  • Every head move reads the whole record again for each whole-record page. Warming them in the background (#336's second question) costs, by the cold column above, up to 36 minutes of one core per sync at 5 M, less what pages share (everyone serves every person's page, orgs.read the Manifest's three). Call it half an hour, four times a day: an estimate.
  • It holds up to 2.8 GB resident (/world) while it does.
  • A restart pays it all again: an upgrade, a reboot, serve --install-service starting the server at login.
  • Nothing outside the Library shares it: logbook people, logbook days, the MCP server.

Applying each delta to the in-memory readings instead is decision 4 without the file: the same rules of invalidation, lost at every restart. This ADR keeps that process, with the tables beneath it (decision 6). - Materialised SQLite views. SQLite has no materialised view, and a plain view is computed again at every query. The readers' rules are a stays clustering with its night window, a promise rule's regular expressions, an alias walk of four hops and a flight's standing set. They cannot be written in SQL, or only as a second implementation of each rule that would drift from the Python one. Triggers on lines that keep counts would make every writer pay inside Index.add, under the writer lock and against the 20,000 lines a second floor (RFC 0029 §9). The counts are the cheap part anyway: Index.source_days is an aggregate over the index already. Rejected. - A columnar file per year (Parquet or Arrow, or a format of our own). The reference stack is the standard library and tzdata (ARCHITECTURE.md). Parquet needs pyarrow, and a format of our own is one more format to keep. A year's file is rewritten whenever a day of that year changes, so a backfill rewrites years. It makes scanning columns fast, but the time is not in the scan: it is in parsing payloads and applying the rules, the stays fold, the regular expressions and present. A columnar copy of the payloads is a plaintext copy of the sealed ones. RFC 0029 §8 would not keep even a plain raw_id column for a sealed line, and rejected decrypting an index to a temporary file (its option 1) as a multi-gigabyte plaintext on disk. Rejected. - Doing nothing. Nothing to build or keep equal, no file, no check. The cost: - The first visit after each of the four daily syncs, and after every start, takes minutes on every whole-record page, and grows with the record: linearly at least, since every reader reads every line. - The owner's "extremely slow, unbearable" of 18 October stays true for that first visit. - The timeline's year and all-years zooms (RFC 0043) would cost what World costs, 280 s at 5 M, or need a design of their own.

Consequences.

  • Equal output. A page computed from the tables is the page computed from the lines, byte for byte, and the golden test holds it. A wrong table is a slow page's bug turned into a fast page's lie. That is why the check runs in doctor at every scheduled run, and why a table that fails it is not read until it is built again.
  • One code path per rule. Every reader whose page reads a table has its per-day part split out. The builder and the reader on a miss call that same function. A rule changed in one place and not the other raises the table's version, or the check finds it.
  • What a copy of the cache folder now shows. Someone with the cache folder learns more of the record's shape than index.sqlite gives them today. They learn that a blinded someone was in contact on these days, so many times by these kinds, and was at these stays. They still learn no name, number, address or word, and cannot confirm a guess without the key (RFC 0029 §2, §8). That is more than the envelope's shape, and it is the owner's decision. The alternative, decided per record, keeps the rows of sealed lines in memory only. A sealed record's people pages are then minutes cold once per start, and seconds after each sync.
  • The cache directory grows by about a tenth of the index (decision 10). doctor's disk check reads the free space of the record's volume, not the cache's, so the summaries check names the file's size.
  • Two processes may build. The stamp's compare-and-commit makes the second a no-op. A writer of the record never opens the file, so append and its floors are unchanged.
  • Out of scope. The Day page's own lines are still read through the index: it shows them, and it is under a second already. observed_entities' plaintext labels (decision 7) are their own issue.

docs.title: ADR 0026 — A day written to a folder is a crossing
docs.text:
Status: accepted · 2026-10-27, amended 2026-10-28 (the ceiling is the policy's) · the owner's decision after the stranger test of 26 October; builds on ADR 0013 §4 (the day package), ADR 0016 (nothing crosses unseen) and RFC 0011 (crossing/v1); changes no line, no envelope, no SPEC

Context. logbook export --day DAY --out DIR wrote one day, every tier, to a folder and appended nothing. The README promises that a page leaves "only on a command you type, to a place you name, and your record keeps a line that says it left". Every other export keeps that promise: export crossing, the vault, the site, the world, the letter, Notion, a trip's bundle and a shared day each append one crossing/v1 line. The day package did not.

Decision.

  1. export --day and export --days read their ceiling from a folder entry of policy/crossing.json, as the vault and the site read theirs (ADR 0016): {"folder": {"max_tier": 2}}. Without the entry the ceiling is tier 1. A folder holds every tier up to the ceiling; --tier (1, 1,2, 1,2,3, or a bare 2 or 3 for every tier up to it) may lower it, never raise it: a tier above the ceiling is refused in one sentence naming the entry to write, and nothing is written.
  2. A run that writes a folder appends one crossing/v1 line, after the folder is written, through Logbook.append. Its destination is folder. Its window is the days asked for. It carries the tiers, the counts (the lines of those days, the ones that crossed, by tier and by kind) and the folder's digest, each file's sha256 and path in path order, as export vault hashes a folder. Under extra it names the folder's last part (never a path of this machine), the days written, the kinds and the line count. policy names the folder entry and its max_tier; without the entry it records "entry": null and the default_tier that applied, 1, never a max_tier no policy set (amended 2026-10-28, the owner's desk's review of #429). A run that writes no folder appends nothing.
  3. The package itself is unchanged, day-package/v1: entries without payloads. The line says which tiers the folder holds.

Consequences. SPEC §3.2 describes export among the readers that write nothing. That was already untrue of export crossing and the other exports above, and now it is untrue of --day too. The sentence is SPEC's to fix at its next version. A consumer of a folder that needs every tier asks the owner for a folder entry at 3. docs/export.md documents the command.

docs.title: Conformance
docs.text:
sample-logbook/ is one week of a fictional person (Oslo, March 2026). Nothing in it is real. Its first sixteen lines are the v0.2 sample; the fifteen after them carry one payload of each profile added since (RFCs 0011–0024, and a location with a subject), fourteen on the Sunday and a keeper on the first photo's day, shaped as their RFCs describe, so a verifier meets every schema the reference implementation writes. Two of them reference an attachment by digest without a path, so there is nothing for verify to report missing. The 32nd line signs the first day on the last evening (RFC 0034, signed-day/v1): the ids of the seven lines on its page and the digest of the page as shown, so show 2026-03-01 prints signed in its header.

Your implementation is conformant with format v0.3, Level 1, when (the sample is a logbook/0.2 record, read as it is):

  1. verify on sample-logbook/ reports valid and prints the seq and head in expected.json;
  2. appending one line to a copy of it yields a logbook that still verifies, with seq + 1;
  3. changing any hashed field of any line (a content field of SPEC §3, seq, prev, recorded_at or hash), or deleting any line, makes verify fail (SPEC §6). id is outside the hash, and the stored form is not hashed: a change to id, or a re-serialisation that leaves the canonical form unchanged, is not detected.

Heads, as expected.json recorded them:

Release Lines Head unreleased (RFC 0034) 32 58bfa9e704e3388d44d74e63f1d84765d24df79e92fce3b522fbef53b765d3df v0.5.0 – v0.6.0 31 035a74e0027faa6872580c3c7b5f7a0efec92f15bb29cee400a6593814fd345c v0.2 – v0.4.1 16 53d39fdad121ce8e448221bbdaa9c86396c16347d050bf630035d6f1d37088e6

The first sixteen lines did not change between the three, so an implementation that reproduced the v0.2 head reproduces every hash of those lines still; only the tail is new, and the 0.6.0 head is the prev of the 32nd line.

docs.title: Level 2: the sealed sample
docs.text:
sample-logbook-sealed/ is the same week with its tiers 2–3 sealed (SPEC §2 and §4, RFC 0029) to two recipients: the identity published in identity.txt (it opens this fixture and nothing else; never use it for a record) and the recipient in recovery-recipient.txt, whose identity is published nowhere. Its logbook.json is logbook/0.3 and names both. The salts come from a seeded generator, so the head in expected-sealed.json is reproducible by anyone who regenerates the fixture; the ciphertext is not, and is outside the hash, so the files churn on regeneration while the head does not.

Your implementation is Level 2 conformant when, in addition to the three rules above:

  1. verify on sample-logbook-sealed/ without the identity reports valid, prints the seq and head in expected-sealed.json, and counts its sealed lines;
  2. verify with identity.txt reports valid, the same head, and every sealed line opened and matching its digest;
  3. changing any byte of a payload_enc leaves the keyless verify valid and makes the keyed one report invalid;
  4. appending one tier-2 line to a copy seals it, and the other implementation opens it.
Release Lines Head (sealed sample) unreleased (RFC 0034) 32 0ab4c3e79bacc9a7c19d074094e81d1674fdf6967ceaf0d1711679e3c11481db v0.6.0 31 c625fd32d553d6f2f64f04dd50858f63a894575f09d6d0d5063d74680e0b43e3

Regenerate with python conformance/make_sample.py (when the spec changes, or a profile is added; it changes the head, and this table gets a row).

docs.title: The profiles: one fixture per frozen payload profile
docs.text:
profiles/<profile>/ holds, for each of the nineteen profiles RFC 0031 freezes (SPEC §5, §6.1), one record of one line (record/: logbook.json and its month file; the line is the one the profile's RFC gives as its example, with a fixed id and recorded_at), expected.json (the profile, its RFC, the line's canonical content form and content hash, its hash, which is the record's head, and its local day), show.txt (what logbook show <day> prints), day.json (logbook day <day> --json) and days.json (logbook show days --from <day> --to <day> --json). Nothing in them is real.

Your implementation passes a profile's fixture when verify on its record/ reports valid with that head; when the canonical form and the content hash of the line recompute to expected.json; and, with show, when it prints show.txt. One that carries a reader of SPEC §6.1's table prints that reader's JSON after dropping the fields §3.2 marks as a reader's own. The fixtures are regenerated by make_profiles.py, and tests/test_conformance_profiles.py holds them byte for byte.

docs.title: The freeze
docs.text:
4 October 2026 · to whoever is building on Logbook

You may be writing an adapter for a service we have never heard of, or a notebook that reads the folder on a Sunday, or the second implementation in a language we do not know. Whichever it is, you have been building on drafts. Every payload profile in rfcs/ says draft at the top, and a draft may change under you. This letter says which ones will not.

What a freeze gives you. A thing that holds still. From the day RFC 0031 merges, nineteen profiles are frozen: location, photo, event, message, note, transcript, call, mail, task, flight, health-sample, listen, transaction, keeper, weather, story, received, resolution and retraction, all at v1. A frozen profile may gain a field. It will not lose one, rename one or change one's type, and the readers that read it will keep every key of their JSON with the meaning it has today. Each one gets a conformance fixture, one synthetic line with its hash and what the readers make of it, that both implementations must pass on every push. The fixture is the promise; a change that breaks it fails a job before it reaches you.

What it costs. Some profiles you may have wanted frozen are parked instead: browse, watch, highlight, voice-memo, crossing, the trip line (about to be called journey), and the one line a migration writes. The rule that sorted them is plain and we applied it to the code, not to our wishes: a profile is frozen when a reader, a rollup or a derive command of the reference reads it. Those seven are written, some of them in great numbers, and read by nothing yet except the row show prints and the words search indexes. A schema nobody reads is a schema nobody has tested against a real day, and we would rather tell you it may change than promise a shape we have not had to live with. Adapters keep writing them. Nothing in your record is touched. They are simply not in the v1.0 promise.

Two profiles are going away: commitment/v1 and its close. Nothing ever wrote them and nothing ever read them. A record that holds one still verifies, since the chain does not care what a payload calls itself, and show still prints it.

What we ask. If you read a parked profile, say so. Open an issue and tell us which one and what you do with it. That is exactly how a parked profile gets frozen: a reader, a fixture in both implementations, one amendment to the RFC. You reading it is the first of the three, and the one we cannot do for you. If you are the one who wrote the reader, send it.

The date. The frozen set does not change before v1.0, and it does not shrink after. v1.0 is the roadmap's last phase; it has no date, and we are not going to invent one for this letter. What we can say is the order: the two deletions, then the rename, then the fixtures on our side, then on the TypeScript side, then the spec's wording. When the five have merged, this letter gets one more paragraph saying so, and nothing else in it changes.

The record holds still by construction. From now on, for these nineteen, so does the shape of what is in it.

— bighydro

docs.title: Letter 0 — why I built it
docs.text:
I learned to sail young, and on a boat someone always keeps the log. Not because anyone will read it that evening, but because years later somebody will ask where we were in that storm, and the log will know, and the people will not. Somewhere in my twenties I noticed my own life had no such book. It had a thousand photos, ten thousand messages, a calendar that remembered every meeting and no meaning, and a feed that remembered only what I had chosen to perform.

I am a people person. The thing I am proudest of is not anything I have built; it is the friends I have kept and the ones I pushed to start something. And yet when I tried to answer the simplest questions — how many days this year with my oldest friend, how many nights at home, who was actually on that trip — I could not. The machines knew. I didn't. The companies that held the pieces would show me an ad before they would show me my own year.

So I started collecting the log. Everything I typed was already recorded somewhere, by something, for someone else. The job was not to write it. It was to gather it once, into a book I hold, and read it back as what it was: days, with people in them. The first weeks of reading my own days back are already changing how I live them. You notice who you didn't call. You notice the week that mattered. You feel, honestly, grateful — a word I used to find soft and now think is the entire point.

I gave it away because a log you cannot take with you is not yours, and because I want it to outlive me and whatever I build next. It belongs to no one; the rules are short; two different programs must agree before anything is called final. I write under a pen name so the format can be bigger than its author.

If it works, people will keep a logbook the way they keep a passport, and hand pages of it to the people who were there. If it doesn't, I will still have the book, and so will the people I love. Either way it was worth the nights.

Record it. Recount it. Hand a page.

— bighydro

docs.title: RFC 0026 — payload profile weather/v1
docs.text:
Status: frozen for v1.0 · 2026-10-05 (RFC 0031; fixture conformance/profiles/) · drafted 2026-10-02 · comment period: two weeks

One statement of the weather of one local day at one place the owner spent it: the lowest and highest temperature, the precipitation, the strongest wind, the WMO weather code, sunrise and sunset. The place is where the owner's own track says they were — the overnight stay, or a stay of three hours or more — rounded to a tenth of a degree, about 10 km, before anyone is asked about it. The values are a weather provider's, not an observation of the owner's: evidence is external, and a reader shows them as the day's weather, never as a presence or an act. A day the owner spent in two such places has two lines.

docs.title: Line
docs.text: kind MUST be weather. tier SHOULD be 1 (SPEC §4: public data about a 10 km square on a day). at is the local day's start — midnight in tz — as RFC3339 UTC; end is the next day's start, so the line spans the day. source is the producer: weather for the reference adapter, which reads Open-Meteo (logbook sync weather, docs/adapters/weather.md); another producer uses its own name.

docs.title: Payload
docs.text: Field Type Req Meaning schema "weather/v1" MUST raw_id string MUST <day>@<lat>,<lon>, the coordinates with one decimal (2026-06-16@47.4,8.5); the dedupe key, so a day and place asked twice is one line day YYYY-MM-DD MUST the local day, in tz lat number MUST the place, to one decimal (rule 1), −90 to 90 lon number MUST the place, to one decimal (rule 1), −180 to 180 t_min_c number or null MUST the day's lowest air temperature, °C t_max_c number or null MUST the day's highest air temperature, °C precipitation_mm number or null MUST the day's precipitation, mm (rain, and snow as water) wind_max_kmh number or null MUST the day's strongest wind, km/h weather_code integer or null MUST the day's weather as a WMO code (table 4677: 0 clear, 3 overcast, 61 rain, 71 snow, 95 thunderstorm, …) sunrise RFC3339 UTC or null MUST sunset RFC3339 UTC or null MUST evidence "external" MUST the values are a provider's (rule 3) provider string MUST who was asked: open-meteo for the reference adapter dataset string MAY the provider's dataset: archive (a reanalysis, days ago and older) or forecast (the recent days the archive does not have yet) supersedes string MAY the id of an earlier weather line for the same day and place this one replaces

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. One decimal leaves the machine. A producer MUST round every coordinate to one decimal place before it asks anyone anything, MUST put only the rounded coordinates in a request, and MUST write only the rounded coordinates in the line. A tenth of a degree is about 11 km of latitude and, at Oslo, 6 km of longitude: a valley, not a street. A payload whose lat or lon carries more precision is not this profile. A coordinate that rounds to zero is written 0.0, never -0.0.
  2. A line is where the owner was. The places of a day are the owner's overnight stay (the night of the day, as the stays reader derives it: the stay with the longest overlap of the night window) and every stay of three hours or more that overlaps the day — a stay aboard an asset by its anchorages as well as by its centre. One line per (day, lat, lon) after rounding: a home and an office 600 m apart are one place. A day with no such stay has no line: nothing is asked about a day the track does not place.
  3. The evidence is external. The values are what a provider says about a 10 km square on a day. A reader shows them as weather and never derives presence, company or an act from them; nothing in a weather line promotes a stay, places the owner or counts as evidence of anything but the weather. A derived row that uses them inherits tier 1 (SPEC §4).
  4. Null is unknown. A value the provider does not have is null, never 0. A day the provider has no values at all for gets no line, and a producer asks about it again another time.
  5. Only an explicit command asks. A producer runs when the owner names it (logbook sync weather) or lists it in the configuration of the run that takes every configured source (sync --all); nothing a reader does — day, days, year, trips, serve, mcp — fetches anything. The request carries no identifier of the owner: no key, no account, no referrer; the user agent names the software.
  6. The cache is inbox, not record. A producer MAY keep the provider's answers under <root>/inbox/weather/, keyed by the rounded place and the day, so a re-run never asks twice; the cache holds the same rounded coordinates and nothing finer, and it is disposable (SPEC §1: inbox/ is not part of conformance).
  7. Corrections are new lines. A better value for a day and place is a new line with supersedes (SPEC §3); the earlier line stands in the chain. A raw_id already in the record is never written again by a producer.

docs.title: Example (synthetic)
docs.text:
{"at":"2026-06-15T22:00:00Z","end":"2026-06-16T22:00:00Z","tz":"Europe/Oslo","source":"weather","kind":"weather","tier":1,
 "payload":{"schema":"weather/v1","raw_id":"2026-06-16@47.4,8.5","day":"2026-06-16","lat":47.4,"lon":8.5,
 "t_min_c":14.1,"t_max_c":26.8,"precipitation_mm":0.3,"wind_max_kmh":18.7,"weather_code":2,
 "sunrise":"2026-06-16T03:30:00Z","sunset":"2026-06-16T19:25:00Z",
 "evidence":"external","provider":"open-meteo","dataset":"archive"}}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Why daily and not hourly. The question a Day answers is "what was it like that day"; the hourly series would be 24 lines a day of a provider's numbers, and the record is the owner's, not the provider's. A later profile may add an hourly form for a stay; it will be a separate kind.
  • Why the place is rounded in the payload too. The line is what a reader joins on. If the line carried the stay's centre, a reader could rebuild the exact track from the weather lines alone, and the rounding before the request would have protected nothing. The stays are in the location lines, where they belong; the weather line names the square.
  • Why the record's zone. A day is a local day of the owner (SPEC §3.2), so a line's day is in tz even for a place in another zone: the day the owner lived, not the day the place had. The provider is asked in that zone, so its daily values cover the same hours.
  • Why one decimal and not a grid. A tenth of a degree is the coarsest rounding that still tells a valley from the next; a provider's own grid is finer than that, so the rounding, not the provider, is the boundary.
  • Why not a field on the stay. The stay is derived and disposable (ADR 0013); the weather is a fetched fact a recompute cannot reproduce without the network. It is a line of its own, joined by day and place.

docs.title: RFC 0027 — Reflection: the digest's closing question comes from the record
docs.text:
Status: draft · 2026-10-03 · comment period: two weeks · amended 2026-10-21 (lenses, ask, below)

The digest (logbook digest, docs/digest.md) ends with one question the owner can answer in a word. Until now the question was chosen in code, by the first of seven rules that applied. This RFC moves the choice into the record: the questions live in policy/questions.json, a setting the owner edits like every other policy file; each carries the facts of the day it asks on and a weight; the digest reads the day's facts, draws one question whose conditions hold, never the same one two days running, and remembers what it asked. Nothing about the record's lines changes: no new kind, no envelope change, no spec version bump. The mechanism is specified here; the content of the bank is not, and is explicitly left to a future author (the last section).

docs.title: Why
docs.text: The seven rules were data-quality nudges — was the tracker switched off, was this person with you, did the meeting happen — and they were right to be there, since the day closes itself on the owner's answer (ADR 0005). But a question is also the one moment the digest speaks to the owner rather than about the day, and what it asks shapes what the owner keeps: gratitude, savouring, people, place, body. Which questions do that well is a research question, with a literature, and not one a coding agent should settle inside a Python module. So the mechanism and the content part ways: the code decides how a question is chosen, the record decides which questions exist, and a person decides what they say.

docs.title: The file
docs.text:
<root>/policy/questions.json is a JSON object with one key, questions, a list of question objects in the order the owner keeps them. logbook init does not write it; the first run of logbook digest or logbook questions writes the defaults, and nothing ever overwrites an edit (the rule every policy file follows). A file that is not this shape stops the digest with the file's path and the key at fault, never a traceback and never a silent default.

Field Type Req Meaning id string MUST the question's own name, unique in the file; what the state remembers and what questions disable takes text string MUST the question, in English; may carry placeholders (below) text_de string MAY the same question in German; the digest prints text today and a reader that knows the owner's language may prefer this kind string MUST one of gratitude, savouring, people, place, body, open when list of strings MUST the conditions: each a fact name of the table below, or one prefixed ! for a fact that must not hold; every condition must hold for the question to be a candidate; an empty list is a question that may always be asked weight number > 0 MUST the question's share of the draw among the candidates of the day source string MUST free text: the research, the book, the person the question comes from; empty in every default enabled boolean MAY false keeps the question in the file and never asks it; absent is true ask string MAY owner (absent is owner): the digest's question, asked of the owner; or day: a lens (amendment of 2026-10-21, below)

Absent kind, when, weight and source are read as open, [], 1 and "", so a hand-written entry needs only an id and a text; a present value that is not what it should be is refused.

docs.title: Placeholders
