docs.title: 12. What changes when adopted, and what does not
docs.text:
Changes, each in the change that implements it, not in this one:

  • RFC 0004 gains a dated amendment, speakers and diarization, additive under RFC 0031 rule 1. Its fixture under conformance/profiles/ is unchanged: its line carries neither field.
  • RFC 0006 gains a dated amendment, the ref kind speaker and the fields basis, consent, unnamed and spans, additive likewise; its fixture is unchanged.
  • RFC 0035's people-review/v1 takes the ref kind speaker; RFC 0036's draft/v1 takes the unit transcript and the segment key attribution. Both are drafts.
  • SPEC §3.2.5 rule 2 (company) reads voices by attribution and keeps the far end of a call out of company; §3.2.10 rules 2 and 3 (promises) take a sentence's speaker from its voice and a proposal's id from the first line of a supersedes chain. §2–3, the conformance samples and the §4 table are untouched; no profile is new. The demo record has no speakers, so the readers compared in §6.1 compare as before.
  • ADR 0016's file gains exclude_people and hold_unattributed; policy/ gains speakers.json; the record folder may hold voiceprints.age, which backup leaves out.
  • derive transcripts diarizes when the model is here; derive speakers diarizes what was heard before; setup speakers fetches and rebuilds; review speakers (or people review --speakers) and the Library's Who spoke? answer; dream speakers proposes from the words.
  • docs/people.md, docs/day.md, docs/serve.md, docs/adapters/voice-memos.md, docs/backup.md, docs/doctor.md and SECURITY.md (the registry, and that it never leaves) say so.

Does not change: the envelope, the canonical form and the hash; any line already written; any transcript line, ever, by any attribution; any adapter, none of which binds a voice; the network on any default path, which stays shut; a reader of a record with no speakers, which reads as before. A page of one person's own words, the guest's page this RFC makes possible, is a derived excerpt of a transcript and a later RFC's: a shared page (RFC 0025) cut to one voice.

docs.title: 13. Open questions
docs.text:
Listed, not solved; each is for the comment period.

  1. Two guests with the same voice score. Siblings, a parent and a grown child, two colleagues on a bad line: two candidates within a few points of each other, or one cluster that is two people. The review shows both and takes neither (§4.3), and sub-numbers let the owner split a row (§4.1). Is that enough, or should a row whose cluster is wide (its voices far from its centre) always be split by recording, at the cost of more questions? And should the registry keep several centres per person (a voice on the phone and in a room are not the same), which helps here and hurts in the next case?
  2. A guest who later asks to be forgotten. What the record can do without breaking rule 2: retract every attribution that names them (readers stop naming them, the voices return to not yet named, and the owner answers --unnamed), add them to forget (the registry drops their voiceprint and never proposes them), and add them to exclude_people on every entry (their words stay home). What it cannot do is remove their words from the transcript or their voice from the audio, which are the owner's record and are never rewritten. Is a forget migration worth a SPEC change: in the shape of RFC 0029 §10.2's (the chain re-hashed, one migration/v1 line saying it happened), replacing one voice's words in the transcripts that hold them, and leaving the old head unreproducible by design? Or is a retraction and an exclusion the honest whole of it?
  3. Group calls with more than two channels. A video call recorder can write one track per participant, often with the participant's address beside it. That is a channel basis far stronger than a voiceprint. Does channel take a track name (track.3), does a speakers entry carry the track's source-native ref (an email, as participants does), and does that ref become the observed voice's strongest identifier ahead of the far end of a call? And when a conference arrives mixed on one system channel, are its voices diarized inside the channel (system.1, system.2), as §2.5 says, or left as one?
  4. Speaker labels in the envelope or the payload. This RFC puts them in the payload, where a transcript's other fields are: additive to a frozen profile, sealed at tier 2–3 with the words, invisible to a reader that does not want them. In the envelope they would be readable without the key (the envelope stays plain, RFC 0029 §2), so a stolen disk would show how many people spoke at every dinner and for how long, and every implementation would need a spec version bump, a regenerated conformance fixture and an ADR for a field most lines never carry. Is there any reader that needs who-spoke without the key, for which the envelope would be worth that?
  5. Inline spans or a file. The labels and counts are inline, the per-segment spans in a file (§2.2). Inline spans make a line self-contained and a crossing simpler; they also make a two-hour transcript line a hundred kilobytes, sealed, in a month file. Which?
  6. A ref kind on a frozen profile, or a profile of its own. speaker widens resolution/v1's ref kinds and adds four fields that mean something only for it. RFC 0037's open question 1 asks whether the ref kinds should be widened at all or moved to a resolution/v2. Is a speaker/v1 profile (one line per voice, the same fields) cleaner than a resolution whose ref is half the payload's meaning?
  7. The unnamed. A person is minted per declined voice, with no label (§4.4). That gives the people reader a count and the crossing a person to hold back, and it fills the id space with strangers. With enrol_unnamed false, a stranger heard twice is two strangers unless the owner says --same-as; with true, the record keeps a voiceprint of someone the owner would not even name. Which default respects them more?
  8. A voice that is no person. A radio, a television, an announcement on the ferry. The owner can only answer --unnamed today, which counts a television as a guest. Is a fourth answer, not a person, worth a line of its own (resolution/v1 cannot say it: every line names a person or an alias), or should the diarizer drop such voices before they get a label, at the risk of dropping a person?
  9. Backfill. §2.8 supersedes an old transcript with a re-heard one, which re-opens signatures and may change promises. A derived line of its own (speakers/v1, at the moment of diarization, pointing at the transcript) would leave the day's page and the old words alone, at the cost of a second road to the labels. Which?
  10. Tier 3 for a guest's voice. Rule 5 says what someone said to you is the highest tier. The file adapter already writes transcripts at 3 for that reason; transcribe writes 2. Once diarization knows a recording holds a guest's voice, should the line be written at 3, so that the guest's words are protected as money and health are?
  11. Whose model reads the words. dream speakers sends a transcript's text, other people's words in full, to the model its entry names, which may be anywhere. Should the entry refuse an endpoint that is not on this machine, as promises --judge and describe never use one?
  12. Calibration. match and floor are the model's, and a similarity of 0.75 means different things for different embedding models, languages and microphones. Should the registry learn the owner's own thresholds from their answers (the similarities they accepted and rejected), and is a threshold that moves with the owner's answers still something a second implementation can agree on?

  13. The extra's weight. pyannote brings torch to every platform, Apple silicon included, where mlx-whisper needed none. Is diarization its own extra (openlogbook[speakers]), so that a memo can be transcribed without a gigabyte of torch?

    Answered 2026-10-15: yes. pyannote.audio is its own extra, openlogbook[speakers], and openlogbook[transcribe] installs exactly what it installed before build 1 (the Whisper engine, nothing of pyannote, torch's diarization stack or CUDA). Voices need openlogbook[transcribe,speakers]. Without the extra derive transcripts transcribes as before and ends with speakers: not separated (install openlogbook[speakers], then logbook setup speakers --fetch-model); setup speakers and derive speakers exit 2 with that sentence. 14. Consent and the crossing. No crossing decides anything from consent here (§7). Should an entry be able to say "consent": "yes", so that only transcripts whose every other voice was stated as consenting cross through it? And is no a statement the record should accept at all, or a reason for the review to ask whether the recording should be kept? 15. The default of hold_unattributed. Absent means false, today's behaviour, so a nightly consumer like Hermes keeps receiving what it received. Rule 5 argues for true: a voice nobody has named is a guest's until the owner says otherwise. Should init write true into new records' default entries, and should absent mean true from some version on?

docs.title: RFC 0040 — Videos: a recording file, its scenes, and the owner's attribution
docs.text:
Status: draft · 2026-10-14 · comment period: two weeks · implemented with sync drive --videos, videos fetch, videos infer and review video (docs/adapters/videos.md)

A family's home videos are digitised tapes: one file of two to four gigabytes holds many recordings from different years and places, and nothing about the file says where or when any of them was made. Its storage's dates are when it was digitised or uploaded. The record needs four things to hold them honestly: a line that names the file without claiming a time it does not know (video/v1, §2); a way to name one stretch of it, a scene, that every other line can point at (§1); a model's proposal per scene that is a proposal and never a fact (draft/v1, RFC 0036, §3); and the owner's statement of where and when a scene was filmed, in a line of its own beside the file's, never inside it (attribution/v1, §4), with the scene's no, a line of its own (scene-review/v1, §5), and "ask the family" (§6) for the answers that are not a yes.

video/v1, attribution/v1 and scene-review/v1 are new profiles, not among RFC 0031's freezes: their schemas may change while this RFC is a draft. The envelope (SPEC §2–3) does not change: no spec version bump, no conformance fixture, no ADR. One draft is amended additively: RFC 0036's draft/v1 (a scene as the subject of unit event). RFC 0037 is not amended: its entity-review/v1 stays the no of the five kinds of thing the record names, and a scene is none of them.

docs.title: 1. Words
docs.text:
• A video file is one recording file the owner holds in a storage the record reads (Google Drive today), named by the storage's id.
  • A scene is one continuous recording inside a video file: from one stop of the camera to the next, or a DVD chapter. It is named by a scene ref, the video line's id (SPEC §2) and the scene's offsets in seconds as a W3C Media Fragments temporal range, two decimals: <line id>#t=<start>,<end> (019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-0000000005a0#t=40.00,90.00). Like RFC 0038's speaker ref, it means something only through the line it names: the same tape listed again is a new line and its scenes new refs.
  • An attribution is the owner's statement that a scene was filmed at a place, or on a date or within a range of dates, or both: one attribution/v1 line (§4). The video line is never touched by it.

docs.title: 2. video/v1: the file, by its metadata
docs.text:
kind MUST be video. source is the reader of the storage (drive-videos). tier MUST be 2: a family's video holds other people's faces and voices, and its name and description may name them. at is when the record learned of the file (the listing that found it); end is null. at is never a filming time and never the storage's own time: when a scene was filmed is only ever an attribution.

Field Type Req Meaning schema "video/v1" MUST raw_id string MUST the storage's id of the file: the dedupe key ((source, raw_id)), so a file is written once however often it is listed library string MUST google-drive title string SHOULD the file's name as the storage shows it description string MAY the storage's description of it, when it has one file object MUST { id, name, path?, mime_type?, url?, resource_key? }: the storage's id and name, the folders above it from the one listed down, its media type, a link that opens it, and Drive's resource key for an older file, kept so a reader of the bytes can send it bytes integer SHOULD the file's size as the storage reports it duration_s, width, height number, integer MAY from the storage's video metadata digest object SHOULD { md5 }: the checksum the storage reports, against which a copy is verified. Not content_hash (RFC 0002 keeps that for a sha256 of the bytes) extra object MAY drive_created, drive_modified: the storage's own times, RFC 3339 UTC, recorded as what they are, the upload's

The bytes are never in the record. A copy made to read a file lives in the bookkeeping under state/ and is deleted once read.

{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","title":"video/v1","type":"object",
 "required":["schema","raw_id","library","file"],
 "properties":{
  "schema":{"const":"video/v1"},
  "raw_id":{"type":"string","minLength":1},
  "library":{"enum":["google-drive"]},
  "title":{"type":"string"},"description":{"type":"string"},
  "file":{"type":"object","required":["id"],"properties":{
   "id":{"type":"string"},"name":{"type":"string"},"path":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}},
   "mime_type":{"type":"string"},"url":{"type":"string"},"resource_key":{"type":"string"}}},
  "bytes":{"type":"integer","minimum":0},"duration_s":{"type":"number","minimum":0},
  "width":{"type":"integer","minimum":1},"height":{"type":"integer","minimum":1},
  "digest":{"type":"object","properties":{"md5":{"type":"string","pattern":"^[0-9a-f]{32}$"}}},
  "extra":{"type":"object"}}}

docs.title: 3. The scene's draft: draft/v1, unit event, a scene as its subject
docs.text:
RFC 0036's draft/v1, amended additively: for unit event the subject MAY be one scene ref ([<video line id>#t=<start>,<end>]) where it was the ids of the lines the unit is. The dedupe key of rule 1, (source, unit, subject, read_head), then tells one scene from another. A reader that looks a subject up as a line id (drafts.by_transcript) finds no line by that string and passes it by.

source is model:<name> as for every draft; the reference writes model:video-rules/1, the rules that wrote the sentences on two local models' readings, which extra.models names. tier is the highest of the lines read (the video line and the file's transcript): 2. Every segment is supported or unsupported as RFC 0036 says; a supported segment's evidence is the video line (what the frames show) or the file's transcript/v1 line (what was said), and which frames and which time range it rests on is kept beside the segments under extra.segments, [{ part, frames?: [offset_s], speech?: [[from_s, to_s]] }], as a call's synthesis keeps its utterances. extra also carries scene ({video, n, of, start_s, end_s, opened_by}), frames (the frame descriptions, never pixels), proposal ({place, when, confidence, when_confidence} or null: confidence the weaker of the place's and the date's, when_confidence the date's own, present when there is a when), inference (the key of models, prompt, scene settings and the picture pass's revision), models, prompt, rules and settings. A proposal's place is {type: place|asset, id, registry: logbook, label}, an entity of RFC 0037 (a place by its places.json name, an asset by its assets.json id), never a coordinate; its when is {from, to, precision} (local days, both inclusive; day, month, season, year or range), never more precise than the evidence. A scene with nothing to go on has one segment that says so and proposal null.

The draft is a proposal (rule 4): no reader derives a place or a date from it. Nothing crossed to make it (the models run on the record's machine), so no policy/crossing.json entry governs it as the dream entry governs a dream's draft; a crossing carries it by its tier like any line.

The file's speech is one transcript/v1 line (RFC 0004), source video-transcription, its content WebVTT whose cues carry their times in the file, provenance.source the video line's id, at the video line's, end null. It is no call: the synthesis of calls (transcript synthesize, the 06:00 close) leaves its source out, and refuses it when it is named by its id, so a home video's words reach no model endpoint.

docs.title: 4. attribution/v1: where and when a scene was filmed, by the owner
docs.text:
kind MUST be attribution. source MUST be manual and method owner: a model proposes, the owner binds; no adapter, model or tool writes one. tier is the highest tier of its evidence (SPEC §4): 2 for a family's video. at is when the owner said it; end is null.

Field Type Req Meaning schema "attribution/v1" MUST raw_id string MUST <scene ref>@<first 12 hex of the SHA-256 of {place, when}>: the same answer for the same scene is one line ref object MUST { kind: "scene", value: <scene ref> } scene object MUST { video, start_s, end_s }: the video line's id and the offsets, so a reader needs no parser place object one of { type, id, registry, label }: type place (id the places.json name) or asset (id the assets.json id), registry logbook (RFC 0037 §3.3) when object one of { from, to, precision }: two local days, both inclusive, and day, month, season, year or range method "owner" MUST draft string MAY the scene draft confirmed, when there was one evidence array of string SHOULD the draft, the video line, the transcript logbook_head hex sha256 SHOULD the head the owner answered against supersedes string MAY the standing attribution of the same scene this one corrects extra object MAY proposal (what was proposed) and changed (whether the owner's answer differs from it)

A line carries place, when, or both, never neither.

Rules. 1. An attribution never modifies the line it names; readers join by ref (RFC 0006 rule 1, RFC 0038 §3.3 rule 1). 2. One standing line per scene: the last one not retracted and not superseded. 3. A correction is a new line with supersedes; the wrong one stays, superseded. 4. A place is an entity of the owner's registries, never a coordinate of the line's own: a map takes the place's coordinates from places.json and an asset's from its positions. 5. A scene ref that a later inference with other settings no longer cuts the same way still names its stretch of the file: the attribution stands.

The review is RFC 0037 §5's review KIND with KIND video: one more queue of the one review sitting, beside the person, the org, the idea, the asset and the place, and listed with them by review alone. --accept N[,N] takes what scene N's draft proposes, --reject N[,N] writes the scene's no (§5) and --json is the queue, or what was written, as for every kind. The scene's own answers are review video's options, refused for every other kind as a place's are refused for the rest: --place N NAME and --date N WHEN confirm with the owner's own place or date, --ask N[,N] keeps the scene to ask the family (§6), --asked and --answered list the scenes kept to ask and those confirmed, and --top N, a place's option too, counts scenes. The lock is the sitting's, one rule for every queue: the queue is read and the owner asked with no lock held, and each answer's lines are appended under the record's writer lock, at once on a terminal; nothing about a scene needs more, and nothing the owner does while looking at one (playing the stretch of the file, say) waits on the lock or holds it.

{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","title":"attribution/v1","type":"object",
 "required":["schema","raw_id","ref","scene","method"],
 "properties":{
  "schema":{"const":"attribution/v1"},
  "raw_id":{"type":"string"},
  "ref":{"type":"object","required":["kind","value"],"properties":{"kind":{"const":"scene"},
   "value":{"type":"string","pattern":"^[^#\\s]+#t=\\d+(\\.\\d+)?,\\d+(\\.\\d+)?$"}}},
  "scene":{"type":"object","required":["video","start_s","end_s"]},
  "place":{"type":"object","required":["type","id","registry"],"properties":{"type":{"enum":["place","asset"]},"registry":{"const":"logbook"}}},
  "when":{"type":"object","required":["from","to","precision"],"properties":{
   "from":{"type":"string","format":"date"},"to":{"type":"string","format":"date"},
   "precision":{"enum":["day","month","season","year","range"]}}},
  "method":{"const":"owner"},"draft":{"type":"string"},"evidence":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}},
  "logbook_head":{"type":"string","pattern":"^[0-9a-f]{64}$"},"supersedes":{"type":"string"},"extra":{"type":"object"}},
 "anyOf":[{"required":["place"]},{"required":["when"]}]}

docs.title: 5. The scene's no: scene-review/v1
docs.text:
The owner's statement that a scene was not filmed where or when its draft proposed, or, for a scene with nothing proposed, that there is nothing to name. It is a line of its own, never RFC 0037's entity-review/v1: a scene is not an observed thing of RFC 0037's five kinds, and a no that named a place or an asset under that profile would be read by every reader of entity-review lines (logbook.contrib.entities.reviews, the person's, the org's, the idea's, the asset's and the place's queues) as a no about that place or asset. No such reader reads this kind.

kind MUST be scene-review. source MUST be manual and method owner: no adapter, model or tool writes one. tier MUST be the highest tier of the lines it answers (the draft, the video line, the transcript), and never under 2 (§7). at is when the owner said it; end is null.

Field Type Req Meaning schema "scene-review/v1" MUST raw_id string SHOULD scene-review:<scene ref>@<first 12 hex of the SHA-256 of {proposal}>: the same no on the same proposal of the same scene is one line ref object MUST the scene's id: { kind: "scene", value: <scene ref> } (§1), as an attribution names it scene object SHOULD { video, start_s, end_s }: the ref's video line id and offsets in seconds, so a reader needs no parser; when present, equal to the ref's, and end_s after start_s (the schema below cannot say either) verdict "different" MUST the scene was not filmed at the place or on the date or in the range proposal names; with proposal null, nothing the review offered names it. No other verdict is defined: a yes is an attribution (§4) proposal object or null MUST the proposal it answers, exactly as the draft carried it under extra.proposal (§3): {place, when, confidence, when_confidence?}, or null for a scene with nothing to go on draft string MUST the id of the scene draft whose proposal it answers supersedes string MAY the scene's standing no this one replaces: a later inference proposed something else for the same scene, and the owner refused that too method "owner" MUST evidence array of string SHOULD the draft, the video line, the transcript logbook_head hex sha256 SHOULD the head the owner answered against extra object MAY

Rules. 1. A scene-review line binds nothing and changes no line: the scene's draft and the video line stand as they were. 2. While a no stands, a review never offers its scene the proposal it answered, from any later draft; a no whose proposal is null holds back a later draft with nothing to propose. 3. One standing no per scene, as SPEC §3 has every derived reader read a kind: the no not retracted and not named in a later no's supersedes. A no on a scene that has a standing no supersedes it: the scene's no is the new one, and the proposal the superseded one answered is held back no longer, so a later inference that proposes it again asks again; show lists the superseded no with a mark. 4. Retraction (RFC 0003) applies: a retracted no counts for nothing, the proposal it answered returns, and a no it superseded stands again. 5. A no on a scene with a standing attribution is refused: an attribution is corrected by a new one that supersedes it (§4 rule 3), or retracted. 6. No reader of entity-review/v1 lines reads a scene-review/v1 line, and no reader of this RFC reads an entity-review/v1 line as a scene's no.

{"$schema":"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema","title":"scene-review/v1","type":"object",
 "required":["schema","ref","verdict","proposal","draft","method"],
 "properties":{
  "schema":{"const":"scene-review/v1"},
  "raw_id":{"type":"string"},
  "ref":{"type":"object","required":["kind","value"],"properties":{"kind":{"const":"scene"},
   "value":{"type":"string","pattern":"^[^#\\s]+#t=\\d+(\\.\\d+)?,\\d+(\\.\\d+)?$"}}},
  "scene":{"type":"object","required":["video","start_s","end_s"],"properties":{
   "video":{"type":"string"},"start_s":{"type":"number","minimum":0},"end_s":{"type":"number","minimum":0}}},
  "verdict":{"const":"different"},
  "proposal":{"type":["object","null"]},
  "draft":{"type":"string","minLength":1},
  "supersedes":{"type":"string"},
  "method":{"const":"owner"},
  "evidence":{"type":"array","items":{"type":"string"}},
  "logbook_head":{"type":"string","pattern":"^[0-9a-f]{64}$"},
  "extra":{"type":"object"}}}

docs.title: 6. Ask the family: an open task/v1
docs.text: "Ask the family" is the owner's to-do, so it is RFC 0016's line, not a new one: source manual, tier 2, list videos, status open, title saying which file and which stretch, raw_id videos-ask:<scene ref>@<time> (rule 2), extra.scene the scene ref. A later page shared with the family reads the open ones. When the scene is answered, the task is written again, done, superseding it.

docs.title: 7. Tiers
docs.text:
Line Tier Why video/v1 2, MUST other people's faces and voices; a title or description may name them transcript/v1 of a video, and its WebVTT 2 (RFC 0004) spoken personal content draft/v1 of a scene, and its frame descriptions 2: the highest of what it read derived data inherits its evidence's tier attribution/v1 2 its evidence is the draft, the video, the transcript scene-review/v1 2: the highest of the lines it answers, never under 2 its evidence is the draft, the video, the transcript task/v1, list videos 2 (RFC 0016) the owner's words

Nothing derived from a family's video is written below 2, so none of it crosses a destination whose ceiling is 1.

docs.title: 8. Example (synthetic)
docs.text:
Ines Nordmann of Oslo, who does not exist, lists her family's folder; one tape, Home 01, digitised in 2019:

docs.title: 9. Open questions
docs.text:
1. A model's proposals. The reference proposes by rules over two local models' readings, so no sentence can claim more than its evidence. A local instruct model could read a scene's speech and frames together (a birthday song and a cake are a birthday), under the same evidence rule; whether that is worth its unpredictability is open.
  2. People in a scene. Faces and voices are the people's, not the scene's place or time; binding a voice is RFC 0038's, and a face's is not yet anyone's. This RFC binds nothing to a person.
  3. The map and the family's page. export world will read the standing attributions (a scene at a place, on a date) when a later change wires them in; the family's shared page will read the open asks. Neither is part of this RFC.
  4. A file replaced in the storage under the same id keeps the md5 its line recorded, and no copy of the new bytes can be verified against it. Should a changed checksum be a new line superseding the old (and its scenes' attributions follow by offset), or a line of its own?
  5. The transcript's at. Every transcript is presence evidence to the stays reader (SPEC §3.2.3 rule 5); a video's transcript has no known time, so it sits, as an instant, at the moment the record learned of the file. Should the stays reader leave out a transcript whose extra.time_unknown is true? (The readers of what was said already do: the synthesis never sends one to a model, and promises never reads one, both by its source.)

docs.title: Benchmark — per-line sealing on a 3,000,000-line record
docs.text: Status: measured, 2026-10-02 · answers open question 1 of RFC 0029, encryption at rest (0029-encryption-at-rest.md) · script: scripts/bench_seal.py · no code or spec change.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: On a 3,000,000-line record with 2,000,000 tier 2–3 lines, per-line age through pyrage costs 128 µs a line to seal to one recipient and 214 µs to two (the age call alone is 88 and 170 µs; the rest is the Option C wrapper, canonical JSON, salt, SHA-256 and base64, in Python), and 145 and 194 µs to open. A plain line costs about 106 µs end to end on the same machine, so a sealed tier 2–3 line is 2.2 times a plain one at one recipient and 3 times at two. The 20,000 lines a second floor is 50 µs a line; per-line age spends 2.5 to 4 times that on the seal alone, so the floor cannot hold for tier 2–3 under age and becomes tier-1-only, with a floor of its own for sealed lines. Keyed verify of the record takes 7.7 minutes (one recipient) or 9.7 (two) against 2.6–2.9 keyless, index rebuild with opening 6.4 or 8 minutes against 1.2 plain, all in flat memory (27–35 MB). The record grows from 1.98 GB to 3.37 GB (one recipient) or 3.63 GB (two). The record data key of §9.1 seals in 40 µs and opens in 10 µs a line, verifies keyed in 3 minutes and adds 0.68 GB; it is the recommendation's comparison point, not its recommendation (see the end).

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
The record. scripts/bench_seal.py generates 3,000,000 synthetic lines in chain order, the shape of the stress tests in tests/test_stress.py: 1,000,000 tier-1 location/v1 points (source sim), 1,000,000 tier-3 health-sample/v1 lines of about a hundred bytes of payload (type, value, unit, device, a raw_id) and 1,000,000 tier-2 message/v1 lines with about 550 characters of text (a chat in the reserved UK range, from_me, a raw_id). The three kinds are interleaved and at is spread evenly over the ten years from 2016-10 to 2026-09, so the record is 120 month files of 25,000 lines each. Everything is synthetic; the Oslo persona does not exist. Generation alone is timed (16.8 s) so the write phases can be read net of it.

Option C as implemented. For every tier 2–3 line, exactly as the draft's §4.3 and §5 say:

plain       = canonical_json({"payload": <the real payload>, "salt": <16 bytes from os.urandom, 32 lowercase hex>})
digest      = sha256(plain)                                   lowercase hex
payload     = {"schema": "sealed/v1", "digest": digest}      hashed, as any payload
payload_enc = base64(seal(plain))                            standard base64 with padding, outside the hash

canonical_json is logbook.core.chain.canonical_json, the product's RFC 8785 serialiser; nothing is reimplemented. seal is one of three:

  • age, 1 recipient and age, 2 recipients: pyrage.encrypt(plain, recipients), X25519 recipients, the identities generated fresh for the run. pyrage 1.4.0 (rage underneath). rage adds a random -> …-grease stanza to every header, so a ciphertext is about 100 bytes longer than the header arithmetic in the draft's §3 gives: a 171-byte plaintext seals to 466 bytes for one recipient and 564 for two, where §3 predicts 371 and 469. The second recipient costs 98 bytes, as §3 says.
  • data key (the draft's §9.1 variant): one 32-byte key for the record, each line ChaCha20-Poly1305 under it with a fresh 12-byte nonce (cryptography 50 has no XChaCha, so the nonce is 12 bytes, not the 24 the draft names; the cost is the same), payload_enc = base64(nonce + ciphertext).

Writing. The plain baseline is Logbook.append_many, the product's own path, index included. The sealed records cannot go through append_many: it hands each draft to Logbook._line as keyword arguments and _line knows no payload_enc. So the script carries a writer of its own that does what append_many does — drafts 10,000 at a time, the chain computed in memory through Logbook._line, the sealed line given its payload_enc after hashing (it is outside the hash), every batch written in the stored form store._dumps writes and fsynced, then logbook.json, then the index extended through Index.add with index.row (so a sealed line's raw_id column is NULL, as the draft's §8 says of an index built without the key). The plain record is written through this writer too, as a control: 317 s against append_many's 339 s, 7% apart (the writer skips the dedupe SELECT), so the sealed columns below are comparable with the plain one. The seal step is timed per line inside the writer (two perf_counter calls a line, well under a microsecond), so "seal step alone" is canonical JSON + salt + SHA-256 + seal + base64, which is what Option C adds to a line; the primitives table isolates seal by itself.

The phases, each in a subprocess of its own so the peak memory is that phase's:

  • Open every sealed line: stream the month files (Logbook.lines_unsorted), and for each sealed/v1 line base64-decode, decrypt, compare sha256(plain) with payload.digest before parsing (§5 rule 6), parse. The decrypt-to-payload step is timed per line; the whole pass is timed too.
  • Keyless verify: the chain, chain.verify_lines over Logbook.lines() (the two lines Logbook.verify is made of), plus, for every sealed line, that payload_enc is base64 of bytes beginning age-encryption.org/v1\n (for the data key: at least a nonce and a tag). The record's logbook.json must name the head reached. On the plain record it is the product's Logbook.verify itself.
  • Keyed verify: the same chain pass, and every sealed line opened and its digest compared. Nothing is held: one line per month file, as verify today.
  • Index rebuild (plain): the product's Logbook.index_rebuild. Index rebuild with opening: the same pass (located_lines, index.row, one INSERT per 10,000 rows, one transaction) into a second SQLite file, every sealed line opened first so raw_id, supersedes, entity and media are filled.
  • Bytes on disk: the sum of the month files; per line, the average stored length per kind, accumulated by the writer.
  • Memory: resource.getrusage(RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss at the end of each subprocess (kilobytes on Linux, bytes on macOS); psutil's peak_wset on Windows when installed.
  • Primitives: 100,000 health-sized and 100,000 message-sized plaintexts held in memory, sealed and opened each way with nothing else in the loop.

The exact command, on this machine:

uv run --with pyrage python scripts/bench_seal.py --out bench-linux.json --markdown

--quick is the same with 300,000 lines. pyrage is pulled in for the run only; it is not a dependency of the project. The whole run took 6,306 s (1 h 45 min) here.

docs.title: Machines
docs.text:
Machine Ran Notes This machine: a cloud container, Linux 6.18 x86_64 (glibc 2.39), 4 vCPU Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 16.9 GB, Python 3.12.3, pyrage 1.4.0, cryptography 50.0.1 yes, the full 3,000,000 lines every number below. A slow core: the stress suite's own 200,000-point append_many test runs at 7,300 lines a second here (LOGBOOK_SLOW=1, measured the same day), against the 20,000 floor, so absolute rates are low and the ratios between columns are what carries over. GitHub ubuntu-latest (4 vCPU, 16 GB) not run workflow in place, not dispatched; see below GitHub macos-latest (arm64, 3–4 vCPU) not run same GitHub windows-latest (4 vCPU, 16 GB) not run same; memory peaks there need psutil, which the workflow adds

.github/workflows/bench.yml runs the same command on the three runners under workflow_dispatch only (never on push), with the line count as an input, and uploads each runner's JSON as an artifact. It could not be dispatched from the session that wrote this page: the GitHub connector and gh both answered 403 Resource not accessible by integration on the dispatch endpoint (the session's token has no Actions write permission), so the three runner rows are empty and every number on this page is from the one machine above. The maintainer dispatches it from the repository's Actions tab (bench, branch bench/encryption; the default is the full 3,000,000 lines, 300000 is a short run of about ten minutes) and reads each runner's JSON from the run's artifacts; scripts/bench_seal.py --markdown prints the same tables from any of them.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
This machine (the only one that ran), 3,000,000 lines, 2,000,000 of them sealed (1,000,000 health-sized, 1,000,000 message-sized). Rates are lines a second of the whole record; "per line" is per sealed line.

Phase plain age, 1 recipient age, 2 recipients data key Write the record, end to end (3,000,000 lines) 339 s · 8,850 lines/s · peak 81 MB 589 s · 5,093 lines/s · peak 110 MB 785 s · 3,820 lines/s · peak 115 MB 420 s · 7,147 lines/s · peak 103 MB Seal step alone, per tier 2–3 line — 128 µs · 7,792 lines/s 214 µs · 4,683 lines/s 40 µs · 24,916 lines/s Open, per sealed line (decode, decrypt, digest, parse) — 145 µs · 6,917 lines/s 194 µs · 5,143 lines/s 10 µs · 99,051 lines/s Open every sealed line, whole pass — 324 s · peak 27 MB 427 s · peak 27 MB 49 s · peak 31 MB Keyless verify 175 s · 17,175 lines/s · peak 27 MB 154 s · 19,527 lines/s · peak 27 MB 160 s · 18,768 lines/s · peak 27 MB 155 s · 19,391 lines/s · peak 27 MB Keyed verify — 460 s · 6,526 lines/s · peak 27 MB 583 s · 5,144 lines/s · peak 27 MB 182 s · 16,487 lines/s · peak 31 MB Index rebuild, plain 69 s · 43,312 lines/s · peak 33 MB — — — Index rebuild with opening — 382 s · 7,850 lines/s · peak 35 MB 481 s · 6,234 lines/s · peak 35 MB 99 s · 30,351 lines/s · peak 41 MB Month files on disk 1.98 GB 3.37 GB (+1.39 GB) 3.63 GB (+1.65 GB) 2.66 GB (+0.68 GB)

The plain column's write is append_many; the script's writer wrote the same plain record in 317 s (9,478 lines/s, peak 81 MB). Net of the seal step the three sealed writes took 332, 358 and 340 s: writing a sealed line is otherwise as cheap as a plain one, a little more for the longer line. The writes' peak memory is the 10,000-line batch and its index rows; every reading phase stays at one line per month file, 27–41 MB whatever is being opened. Keyless verify is a little faster on a sealed record than on the plain one because a sealed/v1 reference canonicalises in fewer bytes than a 600-character message.

docs.title: Per line, stored form
docs.text:
Bytes of the stored line (envelope included, which is about 400 bytes of it), and the ratio to the plain line:

Line plain age, 1 recipient age, 2 recipients data key health-sized (payload ≈ 110 B) 513 1,127 (2.20×) 1,258 (2.45×) 772 (1.50×) message-sized (payload ≈ 600 B) 1,010 1,786 (1.77×) 1,917 (1.90×) 1,431 (1.42×) location (tier 1, never sealed) 460 460 460 460

payload_enc itself is 622 characters for a health-sized line and 1,284 for a message-sized one at one recipient; the second recipient adds 131 characters a line, 261 MB over the 2,000,000 sealed lines; the data key's is 268 and 928.

docs.title: The primitives alone
docs.text:
100,000 plaintexts of each size in memory, the salted canonical text Option C seals, nothing else in the loop (microseconds per operation; ciphertext bytes before base64):

Plaintext age, 1 recipient: seal / open age, 2 recipients: seal / open data key: seal / open ciphertext bytes, 1 / 2 / key health-sized, 171 B 88 / 133 µs 167 / 179 µs 2.6 / 1.9 µs 466 / 564 / 199 message-sized, 667 B 89 / 134 µs 172 / 181 µs 3.1 / 2.3 µs 962 / 1,060 / 695

The size of the plaintext does not matter at these lengths; the cost is the key agreement. Opening is slower than sealing in pyrage. The difference between a primitive and the in-record "seal step alone" (40 µs for the data key, against a 3 µs cipher) is the Option C wrapper in Python — canonical_json of the payload with its salt, token_hex, SHA-256, base64 — about 37 µs a line, paid under every variant.

docs.title: Against the draft's §9 estimates
docs.text: §9 said Measured here Seal, Python via pyrage: 100–200 µs 88 µs (age alone) and 128 µs (with the wrapper) to one recipient; 167 and 214 µs to two. Inside the range for one recipient, at its top for two. Open: 60–120 µs 133 and 145 µs to one recipient, 179 and 194 µs to two. Above the estimate: in pyrage opening costs more than sealing, not less. Five to ten thousand sealed lines a second per core 7,800 sealed, 6,900 opened a second to one recipient; 4,700 and 5,100 to two. One recipient is in the range; two is below it. Keyed verify on two million sealed lines: three to seven minutes 5.1 minutes more than keyless to one recipient, 7.1 to two (7.7 and 9.7 minutes in all). In the range; two recipients at its edge. Keyless verify: unchanged 154–160 s against 175 s on the plain record. Unchanged or better. Index rebuild: the same opening pass as keyed verify, once 382 and 481 s against 69 s plain; the difference is the opening, 313 and 412 s, the same as verify's. Health-sized line about 2.5× its plain size, a 600-byte message about 1.7× 2.20× and 1.77× at one recipient; 2.45× and 1.90× at two. The ciphertext is about 100 bytes longer than §3's arithmetic (rage's grease stanza) but the plain line is longer than §9 assumed too, so the ratios come out close. Two million sealed health-sized lines add roughly 1 GB 1,000,000 health-sized and 1,000,000 message-sized added 1.39 GB at one recipient. 131 base64 characters a line per further recipient, 260 MB per two million lines 131 characters, 261 MB. Memory unchanged Unchanged: 27–41 MB in every reading phase, as the plain record's 27–33. §9.1 data key: opening a line one or two microseconds 1.9–2.3 µs for the cipher, 10 µs with decode, digest and parse.

docs.title: Recommendation
docs.text: Keep per-line age as the format's construction, make the 20,000 lines a second floor tier-1-only, and give sealed lines a floor of their own; do not adopt the record data key for the hot path now. The numbers say the floor cannot hold for tier 2–3 under age on any machine: 20,000 lines a second is 50 µs a line and the age call alone is 88 µs to one recipient and 167 to two, before the line is hashed or written, so even a core twice as fast as this one spends the whole budget on the seal. A sealed-line floor of 4,000 lines a second at two recipients (this slow core does 4,683; a laptop core should do two to three times that — an estimate, not measured) states what the owner actually gets: a backfill of 1,000,000 health samples takes 4 to 7 minutes to seal over the 2 minutes it takes to write, once, and the nightly keyed verify of a 3,000,000-line record takes 8 to 10 minutes in 27 MB where the draft allowed three to seven. The data key would cut the seal step to 40 µs (three quarters of which is the Option C wrapper, which it shares with age) and keyed verify to 3 minutes, a real gain but a one-time one for backfills and a nightly one for verify, and it is bought with everything §9.1 lists: a long-term key in the record where the draft drew the line at "never"; a line the age CLI alone cannot open, so the format gains a construction of its own where it had a file format anyone can check; a writer that needs the identity to seal, losing sync from a machine that holds only the recipient (§6.3); and rotation as a reseal of every line instead of every header. None of those is worth four minutes on a backfill. Two things to carry into the spec text: the second recipient costs 85 µs to seal, 50 to open and 131 characters a line, so two recipients is the right default and five is a decision, as §9 said; and show of a day opens its sealed lines at 145–194 µs each, so a day of a few thousand sealed lines is a few tenths of a second and the under-a-second floor holds, but a day of 5,000 or more (heart rate by the minute plus steps by the quarter hour) is at the edge — if real health records show such days, the middle road §9.1 declines, the data key for health-sample/v1 alone, is the thing to measure next, not a reason to adopt the key for everything.

docs.title: RFC 0025 — bundle format shared-page/v1
docs.text: Status: draft · 2026-10-02 · comment period: two weeks

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The page one logbook hands another (ADR 0009: the circle is core): one local day of the owner's record, chosen for one named person, as a single file they can verify without trusting the transport. It carries the day's lines verbatim, so the receiver recomputes every hash; the attachments those lines point at, under their own digests; the day-package/v1 summary of the same lines; and a manifest the owner signed with an Ed25519 key that belongs to the record. The receiver verifies the signature under the key it already holds for the sender, checks every file against the manifest, and keeps the page beside its own record, never in it. Transport is not defined (ARCHITECTURE.md, The circle): a page travels by mail, by a shared folder, by a USB stick.

logbook share day, logbook receive and logbook circle are the reference implementation (logbook/core/share.py). The two bundles under tests/fixtures/share/, with the two public keys in keys.json beside them, are the fixture a second implementation reads and reproduces.

docs.title: Relation to crossing-package/v1 and day-package/v1
docs.text: A crossing package (RFC 0005) is a window of the record for an unattended consumer, pulled from a folder and not signed. A day package (ADR 0013 §4) is the safe index of a day: identity and shape, never a payload. A shared page is for a person: one day, with the payloads, signed, in one file. It carries the day package of the lines it ships, so a reader that only wants the index has it, and it uses the crossing package's layout for lines and attachments, so a reader of one reads the other.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
A page is a zip file holding exactly these members, and nothing else:

manifest.json          this schema; signed
lines.jsonl            the shared lines, verbatim (the standard envelope, SPEC §2)
package.json           the day-package/v1 of those lines (canonical JSON, one line)
attachments/<sha256>   every file the shared lines reference that the sender's store holds

Member names are exactly as written: no directory other than attachments/, no path with .. or a drive, no file the manifest does not name. The receiver refuses a zip that carries anything else, so nothing a page says can land outside the folder it is kept in.

docs.title: manifest.json
docs.text:
Field Type Req Meaning schema "shared-page/v1" MUST bundle_id uuid MUST one id per page written; the sender's crossing/v1 line carries the same from uuid MUST the sender's owner_id (logbook.json) to string MUST the receiver, by the name the sender's policy/crossing.json gives them date YYYY-MM-DD MUST the local day the page is of tz IANA name MUST the zone that local day is in: the sender's timezone created RFC3339 UTC MUST when the page was written max_tier 1, 2 or 3 MUST the highest tier the page may carry; every line is at or under it lines integer MUST how many lines lines.jsonl holds held_back integer MUST the day's lines that stayed home: above max_tier (a retracted line and a retraction are not counted either way) held_back_unsigned integer MAY of held_back, the lines whose day is not signed (RFC 0034, as the crossing counts them); every page since the rule writes it, 0 when none mail_held_back integer MAY of held_back, the mails no person is on (RFC 0045, as the crossing counts them); written only when the day held a mail lines_sha256 hex sha256 MUST the digest of lines.jsonl's bytes package_sha256 hex sha256 MUST the digest of package.json's bytes attachments array MUST one {sha256, bytes, media_type} per file under attachments/, sorted by digest; empty when none logbook_head hex sha256 MUST the sender's chain head when the page was written, before the crossing line that records it key hex, 64 chars MUST the public half of the key that signed: what the receiver compares with the key it holds signature hex, 128 chars MUST Ed25519 over the pre-image below

A writer MAY add fields; they are signed with the rest, and a reader ignores what it does not know. Every digest is lowercase hex, as everywhere in the format.

docs.title: The signature
docs.text: The pre-image is the manifest without its signature field, serialised as RFC 8785 canonical JSON (the chain's own rule, SPEC §3, chain.canonical_json) and encoded as UTF-8. The signature is Ed25519 (RFC 8032) over those bytes, written as 128 lowercase hex characters. Any added field is in the pre-image too, so a manifest cannot be edited after signing, whichever field is touched.

docs.title: The sharing key
docs.text: Each record has one sharing key, made the first time its owner shares a page. The private half is a 32-byte seed kept outside the record at ~/.config/logbook/share/<owner_id>.key, as 64 hex characters and a newline, readable by the owner alone (mode 0600). The public half goes into logbook.json as share_key, so the record itself says which key signs its pages; writers of logbook.json preserve the field like any other they do not know (SPEC §1). A record whose logbook.json names a key the machine does not hold refuses to share, naming the file: a page is never signed by a key the record does not name, and a key is never replaced behind the owner's back. logbook circle key prints the public half for handing to a friend.

docs.title: lines.jsonl
docs.text:
The day's lines, one per line, each the complete envelope of SPEC §2 exactly as the sender's chain holds it: id, seq, prev, hash, recorded_at included. The stored form may be re-serialised (SPEC §2 hashes only the canonical form), and the reference writes sorted keys. The lines are in the order a reader lists a day (SPEC §3.2): by the instant of at, then by seq.

Which lines: every line whose local date in tz is date, at or under max_tier, that is not retracted; a retraction line is not an event of its day (RFC 0003) and is not shipped. The held_back count is the rest of the day's lines above the tier. A line the policy keeps home takes its attachments with it.

docs.title: package.json
docs.text: A day-package/v1 (ADR 0013 §4, logbook export --day) built from the shipped lines alone: date, tz, owner_id, generated_at equal to created, logbook_head, one entries row per shipped line in the same order (id, seq, at, end, kind, tier, source, raw_id, tags; never a payload), derived empty, and attachments equal to the manifest's list. Written as canonical JSON and a newline, so its digest is reproducible from its content.

docs.title: attachments/
docs.text: Every SPEC §1.1 reference the shipped lines carry whose file the sender's store holds, once per digest, under attachments/<sha256>: the record-relative path a line already names, so a line's path resolves inside the page without rewriting. A file the sender's store does not hold stays a reference and is not listed. The sender hashes each file as it copies it and refuses to ship one whose bytes are not its name.

docs.title: What the sender does
docs.text:
1. Checks the policy first (ADR 0016): policy/crossing.json must name the destination, and the requested tier may not exceed its ceiling; otherwise the request is refused naming the file and nothing is written. Tier 1 is the default; tier 3 crosses only when the file allows it and the owner typed --tier 3, and the console then says so in words nobody can miss. The destination is a person: a name the policy keeps for its own reader or door (mcp, hermes, vault and the rest of policy.RESERVED) is refused in any case. The day must be signed (RFC 0034): an unsigned day is refused in one sentence naming logbook day sign, before anything is written. The lines are then held to the crossing's own rules (review R4): the signed-day gate line by line, and RFC 0045's people's mail, each counted in the manifest.
  2. Makes or reads the sharing key; selects the lines; writes the page to a temporary file and renames it into place, so a crash leaves no half-written page.
  3. Appends one crossing/v1 line (RFC 0011) to its own chain: destination, the local day's window in UTC, the tiers, the counts, the ceiling in force, logbook_head and package_sha256, the digest of manifest.json's bytes; extra carries {"schema": "shared-page/v1", "date"}. A crossing is never invisible: the record shows every page that left it, under which ceiling.

docs.title: What the receiver checks
docs.text:
In this order, and all of it before anything is kept:

  1. The file is a zip whose members are exactly the ones above, by name: manifest.json, lines.jsonl and package.json present, every other member attachments/<64 hex>.
  2. The manifest parses, is of this schema, and every field has the type and shape the table gives.
  3. The sender. With --from NAME, the key policy/circle.json holds for NAME; without, the circle member whose key equals the manifest's key. A key nobody in the circle holds is refused with the logbook circle add line that would add it; the receiver decides whose key that is, never the page. The signature MUST verify under the circle's key over the pre-image above. A key the page carries is compared, never trusted.
  4. lines.jsonl hashes to lines_sha256; it holds lines lines; each parses with no key given twice (SPEC §2), has every envelope field, a tier of 1, 2 or 3 at or under max_tier, a payload.schema, an at whose local date in tz is date, and a hash that recomputes from its own prev, seq, content and recorded_at (SPEC §3); no two share an id.
  5. package.json hashes to package_sha256, is a day-package/v1 of this date and owner_id, and its entries' ids are the shipped lines' ids in order.
  6. Every attachment the manifest lists is in the zip and every attachments/ member is listed; each is hashed as it is extracted and MUST hash to its name at its stated size.

A page that fails any check is refused with the check named, and nothing of it is kept.

A page is not chain-verifiable: the lines are a subset of the sender's chain with gaps, so logbook_head cannot be replayed (RFC 0005, Verification). What the receiver proves is that the sender signed this manifest, that every file is what the manifest says, and that every line is a line that hashes as the chain hashes lines, under the sender's prev and seq. The sender's record can later be audited against it line by line.

docs.title: Where a page is kept
docs.text:
<root>/circle/<from>/<date>/, from being the circle name the signature was verified under: the four kinds of file as they were in the zip, plus received.json, the receiver's own note (the sender's name and owner_id, the key verified under, when, the zip's name and digest). A page is read by logbook day DATE, which prints a from <name> section for each one held: how many lines by kind, the tier and the day it was shared, and the titles of its events, transcripts, notes, mail and calls (received under --json, with line ids).

Receiving the same page again, byte for byte, does nothing. A page newer than the one held (created) replaces it whole, never merged; an older one is refused. The sender's newer view of a day is the view.

docs.title: What the receiver never does
docs.text:
• Never appends to its own chain, and never writes under logbook/, attachments/ or to logbook.json. A received line is the sender's, with the sender's seq and prev; it is not, and cannot become, a line of the receiver's record. Nothing the receiver does changes its head.
  • Never trusts a key the page brought. The key is the circle's, added once by the owner with logbook circle add NAME KEY; a name already there under another key is refused, so a key is never swapped by a typo. The page's key field only says which circle member to check.
  • Never follows a path from the page. Member names are matched against the fixed set; an attachment is named by its digest and placed by the receiver.
  • Never raises a ceiling, never reads the sender's policy as its own, never lowers a line's tier. A received page's tier is the sender's statement about what they shared, nothing more.
  • Never opens, renders or executes an attachment; it hashes bytes.
  • Never touches the network. A page is a file.

docs.title: Example (synthetic)
docs.text:
tests/fixtures/share/ines-to-ola/ is Ines Nordmann's Saturday, 2026-06-13, shared with her brother Ola at tier 2 — two location fixes, a photo with its file, a note; the morning's steps (tier 3) held back, a message she took back not shipped — and ola-to-ines/ is Ola's page of the same day at tier 1, his note and transcript held back. Neither person exists; the keys in keys.json sign nothing but these two pages.

{"schema": "shared-page/v1", "bundle_id": "019cadd3-6bc0-7dcd-9133-00000000a001",
 "from": "c70add25-fcbe-510a-9253-92b542a897e7", "to": "ola", "date": "2026-06-13", "tz": "Europe/Oslo",
 "created": "2026-06-14T18:00:00Z", "max_tier": 2, "lines": 4, "held_back": 1,
 "lines_sha256": "8ccd94815cd6eae339b74c59352de14aefe89699c38c5558e8d7b5d8284888dc",
 "package_sha256": "0f854a6a562eb7b795b5b51cfdd6b52d43db4545d737f402e480152c290bb1a5",
 "attachments": [{"sha256": "b829d2ec5641c7e84d91873c3ae9af0eb49ff5e32620b9da5a8f70433e509d4a", "bytes": 64, "media_type": "image/jpeg"}],
 "logbook_head": "bb97e90d3f946f6cc637e5e223b080ada65e2beb12b07293727e28d2a279b3d8",
 "key": "8965232af604be3294fb964cf0bb9932af098f5f29fe58377578540b4478e9c7",
 "signature": "70f78519c336856f915cdbd0352f932e4dedccda555dda81b84abb534ced8f7967e19cec2460aaba17babfbdc8030cf51135b204143c45a50825239aa96fc40c"}

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Why one day. A page is the unit a person reads, and the unit of the Day (docs/day.md): what someone hands you about a Saturday sits beside your own Saturday. A window is the crossing package's job.
  • Why the lines, not the Day. A derived Day is disposable (ADR 0013) and would say what the sender's engine concluded; the lines say what the sender's sources saw, and the receiver's own readers can read them. The day package rides along for a reader that wants only the shape.
  • Why Ed25519 and a key per record. One signature primitive, small keys, no parameters to get wrong, in every language a second implementation would be written in. The key is the record's, not the machine's: a record copied to another machine shares under the same key once its key file is copied too, and share_key in logbook.json says which.
  • Encryption is not here. A page is as private as the channel it travels; tiers 2 and 3 at rest are a later version of the format (SPEC §4), and a page of them will follow it.
